title: "🔌 MCP Servers Are Spreading. Treat Them Like APIs"
description:
MCP crossed from “interesting RFC” into “paste this server into your agent.”

GitHub READMEs, Discord drops, and one-click installs now ship tools that can read files, hit HTTP, and sometimes run shell. That is power. It is also the same surface that ate API keys in every other plugin ecosystem.

What is actually shipping

A Model Context Protocol server exposes tools and resources to a host (Claude Code, IDE agents, custom runtimes). The host decides which servers attach. The model decides which tools to call. Your job is everything between those two sentences: allowlists, auth, and blast radius.

Community servers move fast. Pin a commit or a release tag. “Latest” is how supply-chain surprises arrive.

Minimum hardening before attach

  1. Run the server as a separate process with the least filesystem and network it needs.
  2. Allowlist tools — if the server offers run_shell, leave it off until you have a reason.
  3. Inject secrets at the edge — the model should not see raw keys; the host or a proxy injects them into approved calls.
  4. Log every tool call with args redacted. You will need the trail. 
// sketch: only expose a subset of tools from an MCP server
const allow = new Set(["search_docs", "get_issue"]);

for (const tool of server.listTools()) {
  if (!allow.has(tool.name)) continue;
  host.registerTool(wrapWithAudit(tool));
}

MCP vs a custom tool adapter

MCP server In-repo tool adapter
Speed to try Fast Slower
Versioning External Yours
Review Often thin PR-reviewed
Fit when Shared protocol across hosts Critical side effects

Use MCP to explore and to standardize. Keep money movement, production deploys, and secret rotation in first-party adapters until the server has the same review bar as your services.

Honest trade-off

Blocking community servers slows experimentation. Opening them without a sandbox is how you buy someone else’s bug. The middle path is a staging host with fake credentials and a recorded allowlist, then promote servers the same way you promote libraries.

Practical checklist

  • [ ] Pinned version / commit
  • [ ] Network egress limited
  • [ ] Tool allowlist reviewed in a PR
  • [ ] Secrets never in model context
  • [ ] Audit log on every invocation

Which MCP servers in your stack could delete data today if the model asked nicely?

title: Sonner Alternative for React: 4 Toast Libraries Compared
description:
TL;DR

The right Sonner alternative depends on what Sonner does not do for you, and if nothing is wrong, keep it: it is by far the most downloaded of the four toast libraries compared here and has a stack, swipe and promise toasts built in. Pick react-hot-toast for the smallest bundle (4.8 kB gzip) and a headless hook, or React-Toastify for progress bars, a queue limit and a notification history. Pick a source-owned toast, such as the free Wingo UI Toast, when you need to change how the stack behaves on phones, for screen readers or in your design system.

You go looking for a Sonner alternative when something about the toast stops fitting: the bundle, a design system that fights its stylesheet, an accessibility review, or action buttons that are hard to hit on a phone. Sonner is still the default React toast for good reasons, so leaving it should fix a specific problem. This comparison puts Sonner next to react-hot-toast, React-Toastify and a source-owned toast on the API, the stack, swipe, screen readers, phones and bundle size, checked in October 2026 against each package's published code and docs.

We build Wingo UI, whose free Toast is the source-owned option here, so read this as a vendor's comparison with sources; it says where each of the others is the better pick. More head to head comparisons live under Comparisons and alternatives, and the guide to shadcn alternatives compares whole component libraries.

What is the best Sonner alternative for React?

The best Sonner alternative depends on what you are leaving for:

  • A smaller bundle and your own markup: react-hot-toast. It measured 4.8 kB gzip in our build, half of Sonner, and its useToaster hook lets you render every toast yourself.
  • More features built in: React-Toastify. Progress bars, a queue limit, toast.update, a stacked mode, RTL and a notification history add-on, with no extra packages.
  • Behavior you can change: a toast whose source lives in your repository, such as the free Wingo UI Toast. It keeps a Sonner-style toast() API, and the stack, the timers and the phone layout are code you can edit.
  • No problem to fix: stay on Sonner. It is the most downloaded React toast notification library of the four by a wide margin, and shadcn/ui installs it for Radix and React Aria projects.

How do Sonner, react-hot-toast and React-Toastify compare?

The table reads the latest version of each package on npm as of October 9, 2026. Sizes are our own measurement: each library's toaster component and toast function bundled with esbuild 0.28, minified, React left external, then gzipped. Sonner and React-Toastify inject their CSS from JavaScript, so their numbers include the styles. Downloads are npm's count for October 1 to 7, 2026.

Sonner react-hot-toast React-Toastify Wingo UI Toast
Version 2.0.8, Aug 9, 2026 2.6.1, Sep 16, 2026 11.1.0, Apr 19, 2026 Toast 1.0.0 in registry 1.7.0, Oct 8, 2026
License MIT MIT MIT Free item, Wingo UI license
Weekly npm downloads 50.8 million 3.7 million 2.9 million Not on npm, copied by the CLI
Size, min + gzip 9.6 kB 4.8 kB 9.8 kB 12.2 kB, plus motion if you lack it
Default position and time bottom-right, 4 s top-center, 2 s for success, 4 s for others top-right, 5 s bottom-right, 4 s
Stack Collapsed, fans out on hover, 3 visible A list A list, or collapsed with stacked Collapsed, fans out on hover or tap, 3 visible
Swipe to dismiss 45px or a flick None Touch only, 80% of the width Touch and mouse, a quarter of the toast or a flick
Keyboard Alt+T focuses the list, Esc collapses it None Alt+T focuses a toast and pauses, Esc resumes Alt+T focuses the newest toast, Esc dismisses it
Screen reader One polite region for all toasts Each toast polite status Each toast role="alert" Each toast polite status, errors alert
Phone layout Full width below 600px None built in Full width below 480px, safe areas Full width below 768px, safe areas
Reduced motion Transitions off Fades instead of sliding No rule in the package Fades instead of sliding
Your own markup unstyled, toast.custom react-hot-toast/headless react-toastify/unstyled Edit components/ui/toast.tsx

The Wingo UI size needs a footnote: in most apps it is the heaviest of the four, because it animates with motion. In a shadcn-style project that already ships tailwind-merge, lucide-react and Radix, it adds 57.6 kB, motion included. If that app already uses motion too, it adds only its own 12.2 kB, and with nothing shared it is 69 kB, seven times Sonner. Its styles are Tailwind classes that compile into your app's stylesheet, so they are not in these numbers.

Sonner vs react hot toast: which one should you use?

Use Sonner if you want a stack, swipe and action buttons without writing them. Use react-hot-toast if you want the smallest package and plan to render toasts your own way. The two look alike at the call site until you need a button:

// sonner: action and cancel are options
import { toast } from "sonner";

export function onDelete(restore: () => void) {
  toast("Listing deleted", {
    description: "City bike, Trek FX 2",
    action: { label: "Undo", onClick: restore },
  });
}

// react-hot-toast: no action option, so the button is your markup
import toast from "react-hot-toast";

export function onDelete(restore: () => void) {
  toast((t) => (
    <span>
      Listing deleted
      <button
        onClick={() => {
          restore();
          toast.dismiss(t.id);
        }}
      >
        Undo
      </button>
    </span>
  ));
}

Beyond buttons, react-hot-toast lists toasts instead of stacking them, has no swipe and no keyboard handling, and pauses its timers only on mouse enter and leave, not for keyboard focus or a background tab. Success toasts default to 2 seconds, which is short for an Undo. Its strength is the headless entry: useToaster from react-hot-toast/headless hands you the toasts plus startPause, endPause and calculateOffset, the right shape if you want full control of the markup and will write the gestures yourself.

Sonner gives you polished defaults: a 356px stack, swipe in the directions its position allows, toast.promise, richColors and a close button, with timers that pause while you hover, while you swipe and while the tab is in the background. Its look comes from its own stylesheet, so matching a design system means CSS variables and classNames, or unstyled and your own markup.

When is React-Toastify the better pick?

Pick React-Toastify when you need features the others leave out: a progress bar on every toast, on by default, and a controlled progress value for uploads. limit holds extra toasts in a waiting queue, toast.update(id, options) changes a toast in place, stacked collapses the list, and the useNotificationCenter add-on keeps a history of toasts for an inbox. It handles RTL and positions its container with env(safe-area-inset-*) on phones.

Its defaults are the loudest of the four: a close button and a progress bar on every toast, 5 seconds on screen, and role="alert" on each toast, so screen readers interrupt the user for a "Saved" message unless you pass role="status". We found no prefers-reduced-motion rule in the 11.1.0 package, so the default Bounce transition plays for everyone; pass transition={Slide} or your own cssTransition if that matters to you.

If those defaults or the styling are why you want a React Toastify alternative, Sonner is the closest swap for the call sites (toast.success, toast.error, toast.promise). The main rename is the promise's loading message: React-Toastify calls it pending and Sonner calls it loading. A history with read state is an inbox, a different job: Wingo UI keeps it in a separate Notification Center with a bell and an unread count.

What does "shadcn toast" mean in 2026?

It depends on the project's base. Since July 2026 new shadcn/ui projects start on Base UI, and for those npx shadcn@latest add toast installs a Toast built on Base UI primitives, called with toast.add({ title, description }) and toast.promise. In Radix and React Aria projects, the old Toast is marked deprecated and the docs point to Sonner: npx shadcn@latest add sonner writes a components/ui/sonner.tsx that wraps the package, maps its colors to your --popover and --border tokens and reads the theme from next-themes.

So the shadcn toast in a Radix project is Sonner with your colors: you own a short wrapper, and the stack, timers and swipe stay in node_modules/sonner. The Base UI version hands you more of the markup, with behavior from Base UI's Toast parts. Per the Base UI docs, that means a 5 second default timeout, a limit of 3, swipe down or right, a priority: "high" option for urgent announcements, and F6 to move focus into the toast region.

What changes on a phone?

The phone is where these libraries differ most, on four points:

  • Width. Sonner spans the screen below 600px with 16px gutters (mobileOffset). React-Toastify spans it below 480px with square corners. react-hot-toast has no phone layout: its toasts cap at 350px and sit 16px from the edges.
  • Buttons. Sonner's default action and cancel buttons are 24px tall, exactly WCAG 2.2's minimum target size, and its close button is 20px, under it. All of them are far from the 44pt Apple recommends for iOS controls; our guide to minimum touch target size has the numbers.
  • Safe areas. React-Toastify positions its container with the safe area insets. Sonner and react-hot-toast do not, so with viewport-fit=cover a bottom stack can sit on the iPhone home indicator until you add the inset to the offset yourself. Tailwind safe area insets shows the pattern.
  • Swipe. Sonner dismisses after 45px of travel or a quick flick. React-Toastify swipes on touch only by default and wants 80% of the toast's width. react-hot-toast has no swipe.

We built the Wingo UI Toast around that list. Below 768px toasts span the width with 16px gutters, each edge uses max(env(safe-area-inset-*), 16px), and mobilePosition="top" moves them clear of a bottom tab bar. Action and close buttons look 32px tall and keep a 44px hit area on touch screens. With no hover on a phone, a tap fans out the stack.

Live demo: Toast. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Hover the stack to fan it out (tap it on a phone), then swipe the front toast toward the edge. Press Failed payment, then Retry: the same toast turns into a loading state and then a success). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Toast docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add toast

How do the toasts sound to a screen reader?

All four announce through ARIA live regions; the difference is what gets interrupted. A polite announcement waits until the screen reader finishes speaking. An assertive one, which role="alert" implies, cuts in.

  • Sonner wraps every toast in one <section aria-live="polite"> labeled "Notifications alt+T". A failed payment is announced as politely as "Copied".
  • react-hot-toast gives each toast role="status" and aria-live="polite", and you can switch a single toast to alert through its ariaProps option.
  • React-Toastify gives each toast role="alert", so every toast interrupts unless you change the role.
  • Wingo UI makes each toast its own polite status and switches errors, and any toast sent with important: true, to role="alert".

For the keyboard, Sonner's Alt+T focuses the list and Escape collapses it, React-Toastify's focuses a toast and pauses every timer until Escape, and react-hot-toast has none. In the Wingo UI Toast, Alt+T (Option+T on a Mac) focuses the newest toast, Tab walks through its buttons, Escape dismisses the focused toast, and timers pause while keyboard focus is inside, so there is time to reach Undo.

When should you skip the toast and use an inline alert?

Skip it when the message has to be read or acted on. A declined card, a form that failed to save, or a session about to expire need a message that stays next to the problem. Toasts time out, sit far from the field that caused them, and on a phone they can cover the submit button. Use an inline alert for those and keep toasts for confirmations, progress and quick undos. The free Alert follows the same split for screen readers: danger and warning tones use role="alert", the others role="status".

Live demo: Alert. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (A declined card belongs next to the Pay button: press Try again and the alert collapses, then press Pay to see it expand back in). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Alert docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add alert

What does a source-owned toast give you?

A source-owned toast puts the whole component in your repository: the store, the stack, the gesture and the markup. You review it like the rest of your code, and nothing changes under you on npm update. The cost is that upstream fixes reach you only when you pull them. The Wingo UI Toast is free; install it with the CLI:

npx wingo-ui@latest add toast

That writes components/ui/toast.tsx plus the button, the spinner and the hooks and helpers it uses. Mount the Toaster once, next to the app:

// app/providers.tsx
"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { Toaster } from "@/components/ui/toast";

export function Providers({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <>
      {children}
      <Toaster richColors mobilePosition="top" />
    </>
  );
}

Then call toast from anywhere, even outside React or before the Toaster mounts:

import { toast } from "@/components/ui/toast";

export function onDelete(restore: () => void) {
  toast("Listing deleted", {
    description: "City bike, Trek FX 2",
    action: { label: "Undo", onClick: restore },
  });
}

export async function publishListing(publish: () => Promise<{ price: string }>) {
  // returns the original promise: await gives you the data or throws the error
  return toast.promise(publish, {
    loading: "Publishing the listing…",
    success: (data) => `Published for ${data.price}`,
    error: "Could not publish the listing",
  });
}

Beyond those call sites, the file gives you:

  • Updates by id. Calling toast.loading("Uploading 3 photos… 2/3", { id: "upload" }) again updates the toast in place. A new type with the same id, such as toast.success, starts it over, so the loading toast's Infinity duration never sticks to the success.
  • Your tokens. The surface uses bg-popover and your theme's status tones, so dark mode needs no theme prop. Visual props such as radius, width and richColors can also be set app-wide through UIProvider defaults.
  • Updates that keep your edits. npx wingo-ui@latest update merges a new release into the file you changed, as the updates docs describe.

The trade-offs, stated plainly. It is younger than the three packages, and Sonner has years of bug reports behind it. It costs more bytes than any of them, even in an app that already uses motion. In a shadcn project created with a Base UI style, install it with the Wingo UI CLI instead of shadcn add, because that style rewrites asChild, which the button relies on. The Notification Center is part of Wingo UI Pro; the Toast and the Alert are free.

How do you move from Sonner to the Wingo UI Toast?

Most call sites only change the import. The API follows Sonner's: toast, toast.success, error, warning, info and loading, toast.promise, toast.custom, toast.dismiss, the action, cancel and toasterId options, and the position, expand, visibleToasts, duration, richColors and closeButton props keep their names and defaults. The differences:

Sonner Wingo UI Toast
import { toast } from "sonner" import { toast } from "@/components/ui/toast"
hotkey={["altKey", "KeyT"]} hotkey="alt+t"
<Toaster id="editor" /> for a second toaster <Toaster toasterId="editor" />
toast.promise(...).unwrap() for the result toast.promise(...) returns the original promise
theme prop, or next-themes in the shadcn wrapper None; the surface uses your tokens
event.preventDefault() in an action keeps the toast open The same, or keepOpen: true on the action
mobileOffset below 600px mobileOffset below 768px, plus mobilePosition
toast.message, toast.getHistory Not available; useToasts() returns the toasts on screen

If you used the shadcn wrapper, delete components/ui/sonner.tsx, point the Toaster import at @/components/ui/toast, and replace from "sonner" in the files that call toast. Then drop any theme prop from the Toaster and the .unwrap() after promise toasts, which TypeScript flags.

Where should you start?

If Sonner works and nobody has complained, keep it. If the complaint is about phones, screen readers or a design system that will not bend, try a source-owned toast: run npx wingo-ui@latest add toast, which is free and needs no account, swap the import on a few call sites, and open the app on your own phone.

Components in this post

  • Toast (Free): Toast notifications: a Toaster mounted once and a toast() you call from anywhere, stacked, swipeable and paused while you read. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add toast
  • Alert (Free): An inline message about a page or a section, from a failed payment to a maintenance banner, in three variants and six tones. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add alert

FAQ

What is the best Sonner alternative for React?

It depends on why you are leaving. react-hot-toast is the smallest and has a headless hook, React-Toastify has the most built-in features, and a source-owned toast like the free Wingo UI Toast keeps a Sonner-style API while every behavior lives in a file you can edit.

Is Sonner better than react-hot-toast?

Sonner does more out of the box: a collapsed stack, swipe to dismiss, action and cancel buttons, a promise toast and an Alt+T shortcut. react-hot-toast is about half the size at 4.8 kB gzip in our build and ships a headless useToaster hook, but it has no swipe, no keyboard shortcut and no built-in action buttons.

Does shadcn/ui still use Sonner for toasts?

It depends on the project's base. In Radix and React Aria projects the old Toast is deprecated and npx shadcn@latest add sonner installs a short wrapper around the sonner package. In Base UI projects, the default for new projects since July 2026, npx shadcn@latest add toast installs a Toast built on Base UI with a toast.add() API.

Which React toast library is the smallest?

react-hot-toast, at 4.8 kB minified and gzipped in our esbuild measurement in October 2026. Sonner came to 9.6 kB and React-Toastify to 9.8 kB, both including the CSS they inject from JavaScript.

Are toast notifications accessible to screen readers?

They are announced through ARIA live regions, but the libraries differ in urgency: Sonner announces everything politely, React-Toastify marks every toast role="alert" by default, and react-hot-toast and the Wingo UI Toast let single toasts interrupt. Anything the user must act on belongs in an inline alert, because toasts time out.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: Sonner Alternative for React: 4 Toast Libraries Compared. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Ghost in the Machine: Giving Digital Ghosts a Place to Live
description:
What happens when the technologies we leave behind refuse to disappear?

Some ghosts haunt houses. Others haunt old terminals, forgotten programming languages, and the memories of the people who built the digital world we live in today.

For Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 4: Ghost in the Machine, I built an interactive experience that brings those digital ghosts back to life.

What I Built

Ghost in the Machine is an offline-capable, open-source AI experience built around three interconnected chambers:

⌨️ 1. NecroShell — The Haunted Terminal

Step into a retro CRT-inspired terminal where ordinary commands become digital incantations. Explore a virtual graveyard of forgotten software, uncover strange system messages, trigger visual glitches, and let the ghost take control of your keyboard.

Commands like whoami, ls /graveyard, cat /souls/lovelace.log, and possession turn terminal exploration into an eerie experience.

🕯️ 2. Spirit Séance Chamber

What if you could have a conversation with the pioneers and forgotten technologies that shaped computing?

Summon digital personas inspired by Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing, Grace Hopper, ALGOL 60, Adobe Flash, and COBOL. You can also create custom spirits from digital history.

The goal isn't simply to generate spooky responses. It's to make computing history feel alive, interactive, and worth remembering.

🏵️ 3. Digital Ofrenda — An Altar for Lost Technologies

Inspired by Día de los Muertos, this interactive digital altar celebrates the people, tools, and technologies we don't want to forget.

Light virtual candles, place offerings such as floppy disks and punch cards, watch marigold petals drift across the screen, and inscribe remembrances for departed mentors, machines, and software.

Because sometimes, preserving a memory is just as important as building something new.

Demo

🔗 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ankitkumar810/ghost-in-the-machine

Clone the repository and open index.html in a modern browser to get started. You can also run it using a local HTTP server.

Code

The project is built with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, keeping the experience lightweight and easy to explore.

The repository includes the interface, terminal interactions, digital altar, procedural audio effects, and configurable AI inference backends.

💻 Explore the code: https://github.com/ankitkumar810/ghost-in-the-machine

How I Built It

I wanted the experience to feel like stepping into an abandoned computer that somehow still remembers everything.

The interface combines a retro CRT aesthetic, interactive terminal commands, atmospheric sound generated through the Web Audio API, visual glitches, candle animations, and falling marigold petals.

For the AI layer, I designed three inference options:

  • Built-in Spirit Neural Core: A lightweight, browser-based response engine that works without downloading a model.
  • Ollama: A local inference backend for compatible open-weight models, including Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Phi, and Qwen variants.
  • Custom local endpoints: Support for compatible local inference servers such as LM Studio, LocalAI, vLLM, and Jan.

The project is designed to work without mandatory cloud services. The built-in experience works offline, while local model inference requires the corresponding model and runtime to be installed and running.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For me, open innovation isn't just about making source code publicly available. It's about ownership, privacy, and the freedom to keep building without asking a platform for permission.

🔒 Memories deserve privacy.

A personal remembrance can contain deeply private thoughts. Local inference offers a way to process these stories without automatically sending them to a third-party AI service.

🌐 Software should survive the internet going away.

A project that depends entirely on a remote API can stop working when that service becomes unavailable. An offline-capable experience gives users a way to explore and create even without a connection.

🧬 Digital history shouldn't depend on corporate memory.

Technologies disappear. Services shut down. APIs are retired. Open code and locally available model weights give future builders more freedom to preserve, inspect, adapt, and extend what came before.

🛠️ Builders should be able to experiment.

Supporting interchangeable inference backends means developers can explore different models and local runtimes instead of being permanently tied to one provider.

That is what open innovation made possible here: an experience designed around creative freedom, local control, and digital remembrance.

My Agent Session

The project repository contains the implementation and supporting code.

Agent session: Add your DevRelay session link here if you save and share one.

The Spirit of It

We spend our careers creating things that we hope will outlast us: programs, tools, languages, communities, and ideas.

Yet the digital world is remarkably good at forgetting.

A website disappears. A programming language falls out of fashion. A tool that once changed everything becomes an obscure entry in a history book.

Ghost in the Machine is my small tribute to the things technology leaves behind.

The floppy disk on the altar represents more than an obsolete storage device. The forgotten terminal represents more than an old interface. Each one is evidence that someone imagined a future, built something, and left a trace.

This Halloween, I wanted to give those traces a voice.

And for Día de los Muertos, I wanted to build a place where they could be remembered.

The machine may be silent. The memory doesn't have to be.

Prize Categories

This submission is intended for the overall Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4.

I'll list partner categories only if the project meets their actual requirements. The current implementation includes support for local open-weight models; I won't claim partner-specific integrations that haven't been verified.

Built with curiosity, a little spooky atmosphere, and a belief that open technology should outlive the platforms that host it.

title: Rent vs Buy a GPU for Side-Project AI: Hours/Week Math + Billing Pitfalls
description:
Side-project AI (ComfyUI, LoRA, small fine-tunes) often starts with “should I just buy a 4090?” The better question is: how many effective GPU-hours per week will you actually burn?

A simple break-even sketch

  1. Estimate capital for a used consumer flagship + PSU headroom.
  2. Spread over 12 months → weekly ownership tax (ignore power/noise for a moment).
  3. Divide by your cloud $/GPU-hour → hours/week where owning starts to win.

If your real work is bursty — a weekend LoRA, a deadline sprint — hourly rental usually wastes less money on idle silicon. Effective hours = GPU busy time, not an open SSH session.

Three billing pitfalls

  1. Stopped compute ≠ stopped bill. Disks often keep charging after the GPU stops. Export weights, verify, delete unused volumes.
  2. Data transfer eats wall-clock. Pushing large checkpoints can take longer than the job. Test with a tiny file first.
  3. Bare images cost setup time. Starting from a ComfyUI / PyTorch template can save a billable hour of dependency hell.

Example public hourly ranges (CNY)

Snapshot only — always trust the live console. Low→high = cheaper community-style tier → higher secure-style tier:

  • RTX 4090 ≈ ¥1.19–3.12/hr
  • RTX 5090 ≈ ¥2.42–4.17/hr
  • H100 SXM ≈ ¥9.41–13.96/hr
  • H200 SXM ≈ ¥12.56–18.52/hr

I maintain TapGPU, an hourly GPU rental console with a public pricing card wall. Disclosure: I’m involved with the product. Use the framework above on any provider.

Checklist for a clean first session

Top up → pick stock → launch a template → run one familiar mini-job end-to-end → log upload + ready + first-result wall-clock → then scale → stop GPU and clean disks.

What break-even hours/week are you using for consumer vs data-center cards?

title: IPNS, um nome que muda
description:
Na série IPFS com o Nabu, o CID (Content Identifier) é permanente: os mesmos bytes, o mesmo nome. Este post é o nome que pode passar a apontar para outro CID.

A proposta

Um site, um perfil ou a cabeça de um feed mudam. Publicar de novo gera outro CID. Quem já guardou o CID antigo continua no conteúdo antigo, que é o combinado do endereçamento por conteúdo. Falta um nome estável, controlado por alguém, que diga "a versão atual é este CID".

A proposta do IPNS (InterPlanetary Name System, o sistema de nomes interplanetário) é esse ponteiro. O nome não muda. O valor muda, e a mudança é assinada por quem tem a chave.

A Demonstração

A chave do registro é o PeerId de quem publica, prefixada pelos bytes de /ipns/. O valor é um registro assinado pela chave privada correspondente. Quem quiser verifica a assinatura sem perguntar a um servidor. O registro traz o valor (em geral o caminho ou o CID atual, em bytes), um sequence, um prazo de validade e um TTL (Time To Live, por quanto tempo uma cópia pode ser reutilizada sem perguntar de novo).

O sequence é um contador. IpnsRecord.compareTo coloca o sequence maior depois do menor. No empate, o registro cuja validade acaba antes vem primeiro. Se a validade deste não acaba antes da do outro, a comparação devolve zero. resolveValue ordena a lista e fica com o último, portanto com o sequence mais alto. Um registro vencido deixa de ser a resposta na validação do prazo. Como o CID do conteúdo continua imutável, a história antiga segue endereçável para quem guardou o CID. O IPNS só move o ponteiro.

A publicação usa a mesma DHT (Distributed Hash Table) do post anterior. O registro é gravado nos pares mais próximos da chave /ipns/ mais o PeerId. Resolver é perguntar a esses pares e ficar com o registro de maior sequence que ainda valida.

No Nabu

IPNS.getKey monta a chave: escreve os bytes de /ipns/ e em seguida os bytes do multihash do publicador. createSignedRecord, em src/main/java/org/peergos/protocol/ipns/IPNS.java, monta o protobuf IpnsEntry. O corpo assinado é um mapa CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) com as chaves TTL, Value, Sequence, Validity e ValidityType. A validade é uma data no formato RFC 3339 com nanossegundos, em UTC, produzida por formatExpiry. A assinatura cobre o prefixo ASCII ipns-signature: mais esses bytes CBOR, e vai no campo SignatureV2. Para Ed25519 a chave pública já está no PeerId, e o registro não repete pubKey. Para outros tipos, o registro inclui a pública em protobuf. Dado extra da aplicação entra no mapa com o prefixo _ mais o sufixo que o chamador passou. O tamanho máximo aceito na validação é MAX_RECORD_SIZE, 10 KiB. Entrada maior, ou sem SignatureV2 e sem Data, é descartada por parseAndValidateIpnsEntry.

EmbeddedIpfs.publishValue é o atalho da aplicação. O publicador é o multihash do PeerId derivado da chave privada. O prazo é LocalDateTime.now() mais hoursTtl. O TTL em nanossegundos é hoursTtl vezes 3.600.000.000.000. O método assina e chama a DHT:

byte[] signedRecord = IPNS.createSignedRecord(value, expiry, sequence, ttlNanos, extraDataKeySuffix, extraData, priv);
return dht.publishValue(pub, signedRecord, node);

O inteiro devolvido é quantos pares guardaram o registro. Há também publishPresignedRecord, para quem já traz os bytes assinados. resolveValue pede resolveRecords e devolve o value do último item depois de sorted(). IpnsRecord.compareTo ordena pelo sequence. O último é o mais novo. Lista vazia vira o erro Couldn't resolve IPNS value.

Kademlia.publishValue valida antes de espalhar. parseAndValidateIpnsEntry precisa devolver um registro, e o publicador desse registro precisa ser a chave pedida. Se já existe um registro local e o novo não é maior na comparação, o antigo permanece. A busca mira pelo menos 30 pares próximos da chave (minPublishes), com 3 consultas em paralelo (queryParallelism). A chave de roteamento é o SHA-256 dos bytes /ipns/ mais o publicador, não o PeerId cru.

No processo standalone o store é DatabaseRecordStore, H2, no caminho datastore/h2-v2.datastore dentro do diretório IPFS. A tabela se chama records. O valor cabe em 10 KiB (SIZE_OF_VAL), o mesmo teto do registro, e o PeerId em 100 bytes na coluna. RamRecordStore existe para testes e para os exemplos, que não precisam do registro depois que o processo morre. A interface é RecordStore: ler, gravar e fechar. EmbeddedIpfs.stop fecha o store.

O que fica de fora: o Nabu não cria uma chave IPNS separada do PeerId por conta própria. A chave de publicação é a chave que a aplicação passa, e no fluxo de publishValue ela é a identidade cujo PeerId entra na chave /ipns/. Não há resolução IPNS por DNS. Um nome ipns:// no navegador fica com o cliente. A API HTTP expõe ipns/get, descrito no post da API, e não expõe publicação.

Nesta série

O anterior é A DHT Kademlia. O próximo é Onde o bloco mora.

If you've been running a separate object storage provider alongside Upsun to handle large asset libraries, you no longer have to.

GLM 5.3 has improvements vs. GLM 5.2 at complex software engineering and at agent tasks that run across many steps, and it reaches those results while producing fewer output tokens than GLM 5.2 did at the same effort level.

Z.ai also reports stronger vulnerability discovery, including reasoning across the successive stages of an exploitation chain. DeepsecBench measures that work directly, scoring how reliably a model finds security vulnerabilities in application code and what a run costs, and it covers GLM-5.3 at both high and max effort.

GLM 5.3 takes text input, with a 1M token context window and a maximum output of 128K tokens, both unchanged from GLM 5.2. It supports function calling, structured output, streaming, and context caching.

To use the model, the slug is zai/glm-5.3:

To use it in a coding agent, run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Pi, and more, then select zai/glm-5.3 inside the agent.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

title: GMO Puts a $1 Million Bounty on Its Hackers After Refusing to Pay Ransom
description:
GMO Puts a $1 Million Bounty on Its Hackers After Refusing to Pay Ransom

When criminals breach a company and demand a ransom, most victims face a grim choice: pay up and hope the data disappears, or refuse and brace for leaks. Japan's GMO Internet Group has chosen a third option this week: turn the tables and pay people who help catch the attackers instead.

On October 28, the Japanese internet and fintech giant officially opened a bounty program offering up to US$1 million (roughly 160 million yen) in total rewards for lawfully obtained information that leads to the arrest of — or an international wanted notice for — the perpetrator of the breach of its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service. The company is seeking tips that connect people, servers, domains, IP addresses, accounts, or cryptocurrency wallets to the attack, the extortion attempt, or the movement of stolen funds.

From cloud desktops to live trading accounts

The incident at the heart of the bounty is unusual in how far the damage reached. Onamae.com Desktop Cloud rents out Windows cloud desktops that traders commonly use to run automated foreign exchange (FX) trading software around the clock. That means the servers didn't just hold customer records — in many cases they held live credentials to brokerage accounts.

GMO first disclosed unauthorized access to the service on October 21, shut the service down the same day, and reported the matter to Japanese police on October 22. Attackers allegedly used trading credentials stored on the rented servers to place unauthorized orders at brokerages, turning a routine-sounding data breach into real-time financial fraud. GMO estimates that around 27,000 servers across all plans could have been at risk, though the company stresses this is the number of potentially affected machines, not a confirmed count of compromised ones.

A ransom demand, and a hard no

According to reporting by TechCrunch and others, the attackers initially emailed GMO on October 21 demanding roughly $50 million (about 8 billion yen). Later statements attributed to the attacker demanded US$1 million with a deadline of noon JST on October 27, threatening to manipulate trading accounts at more than 70 securities and FX firms in Japan and abroad, publish customer information daily at noon, launch ransomware attacks against users' machines, and expose details of GMO's own internal systems.

GMO's response has been unequivocal. The company says it handed all communications with the extortionists over to police cybercrime units and publicly declared it will never give in to the demands. "We are seeking credible information that leads to the identification and arrest of those involved," the company stated on its dedicated bounty portal, which accepts submissions in Japanese, English, and Chinese.

After the deadline passed, material purporting to contain customer personal information began appearing online, and a suspected attacker published what appears to be at least one customer's name and phone number. GMO confirmed on October 27 that information connected to the company and its customers had been published, and on October 28 announced that the domain used for the extortion site had been taken down — while warning that replacement sites could still emerge.

Making customers whole

Alongside the bounty, GMO has moved to compensate affected users. In an October 28 stock exchange filing, the company said it will pay every current user of the service 5,000 yen and cover actual trading losses and fees for any trades it confirms were unauthorized and caused by the breach. It cautioned that it has not yet confirmed how many customers the compensation program will cover, how much information was published, or which trades qualify.

The company has also been collecting customers' devices since October 25 to check for malware, and has urged users to reset passwords for any trading or financial accounts used from the service. Its group CEO wrote in a blog post that internal security researchers had flagged problems with the service before the attack, and that fixes were underway but not deep or fast enough.

Why this case matters

The GMO incident lands in the middle of what some security experts have taken to calling AI's "Black October" — a stretch marked by a sharp rise in AI-accelerated vulnerabilities and attacks. Whatever tools the attackers used, the case highlights a structural risk that is only growing: cloud services that hold live financial credentials turn a single intrusion into direct monetary theft. A breached marketing database is a liability; a breached trading desktop is a loaded weapon.

It also illustrates a shifting stance on extortion. Companies like Kraken have publicly refused ransom demands before, but putting a formal bounty on the attackers' heads — funded at $1 million, coordinated with police, and open to tips worldwide — is a more aggressive posture. Cyber insurance premiums and regulation increasingly discourage paying ransoms, since payment funds future attacks and offers no guarantee data is deleted. Bounty programs flip the incentive: instead of paying criminals, pay the ecosystem that can unmask them.

There are risks to this approach too. Attackers may escalate leaks to punish defiance, and bounties rarely produce arrests when attackers operate from safe jurisdictions. But as a signal of where enterprise incident response may be heading, GMO's move is one of the clearest yet: don't fund the attack — fund the manhunt.

For now, GMO says it will continue working with law enforcement, compensating customers, and pursuing takedowns of any replacement leak sites. The bounty program remains open, and the investigation is ongoing.

title: Prompting for Design-System Compliance Without Dumping the Whole Library
description:
I used to paste half the design system into the agent prompt “just so it knows our Button.” The reply was longer, slower, and somehow still invented a new PrimaryButton with a hardcoded hex.

More context is not the same as better compliance. Agents drown in component catalogs. What they need is a small, sharp contract: which primitives exist, which props are legal, and what “done” looks like when the diff lands.

Here’s the prompting pattern that finally stopped the reinvent-the-wheel PRs.

The failure mode: catalog dump

A prompt that looks like this fails quietly:

Here is our entire components/ui tree (paste 40 files). Build a settings form that matches the design system.

What I got back:

  • A new SettingsCard that duplicated Card
  • Inline styles next to token imports
  • A custom toggle instead of our Switch
  • “Close enough” spacing that wasn’t on the spacing scale

The model saw the library. It didn’t treat the library as the only legal surface. Catalog dumps read like inspiration boards, not constraints.

What “compliance” means in a prompt

I define compliance as four checks the agent can fail against:

  1. Import allowlist — only from @/components/ui/* (or whatever your package is), no parallel primitives
  2. Prop allowlist — use documented variants (size, tone, intent), don’t invent big / fancy
  3. Token rule — colors/spacing/radius come from tokens; no raw hex/rgb/px magic numbers in JSX
  4. Composition rule — assemble screens from existing primitives; new components need an explicit “new primitive approved” flag

If the prompt doesn’t name those four, the agent will optimize for “looks like a settings form,” not “uses our system.”

The slim context pack I actually paste

Instead of the whole library, I keep a design-system cheat sheet under ~80–120 lines and refresh it when the public API changes:

## Legal UI imports
- @/components/ui/Button — variants: primary | secondary | ghost | danger; sizes: sm | md | lg
- @/components/ui/Input — always pair with Label; error via `error` prop, not helper text hacks
- @/components/ui/Select, Switch, Checkbox, Textarea, Card, Stack, Inline, Dialog, Toast
- Forbidden: inventing Button2, PrimaryButton, CustomInput, or wrapping divs that reimplement focus rings

## Tokens
- color: bg.default, bg.subtle, fg.default, fg.muted, border.default, accent.primary
- space: 1–8 (use Stack/Inline gap; no raw margin: 13px)
- radius: sm | md | lg | full

## Composition defaults
- Forms: Stack gap={4}; actions in Inline justify="end" gap={2}
- Destructive actions: Button variant="danger" + confirm Dialog
- Empty states: Card + Stack + muted fg text — no one-off EmptyBox

## Acceptance (must pass before PR)
- [ ] Zero new files under components/ui unless ticket says “new primitive”
- [ ] Zero hex/rgb in changed files
- [ ] All interactive elements use ui/* primitives
- [ ] Story or Playwright covers the primary path

That’s the whole “library” the agent gets for most feature work. Storybook links and full prop tables live in the repo; the prompt carries the decision surface.

Prompt shape that works

My default ask looks like this:

Build X using only the Legal UI imports below.

Do not create new primitives.

If something is missing, stop and name the gap — don’t invent a component.

Match tokens and composition defaults.

When done, paste the Acceptance checklist with pass/fail.

Then I attach the cheat sheet. Short. Boring. Explicit stop rule.

The “stop and name the gap” line matters. Without it, agents fill holes with lookalikes. With it, I get a one-line question: “We don’t have a DatePicker in the allowlist — use native input type=date or open a primitive ticket?” That’s a better outcome than a 200-line custom calendar.

Give examples of illegal diffs, not just legal ones

Positive examples help. Negative ones teach the fence:

- // illegal: new parallel primitive
- export function FancyButton(...) { ... }

- // illegal: token bypass
- <div style={{ color: '#3366ff', marginTop: 13 }}>

+ // legal: compose
+ <Button variant="primary" size="md">Save</Button>
+ <Stack gap={4}>...</Stack>

I keep 3–5 illegal snippets in the cheat sheet. Agents pattern-match hard on “don’t do this” when it’s concrete.

Scope the blast radius in the prompt

Design-system compliance dies when the task is too big:

“Rebuild the billing settings page and modernize the UI.”

Too much room to invent. I split:

  1. Wire data + existing layout shells
  2. Replace one control cluster at a time (plan → payment method → invoices)
  3. Only then ask for empty/error states

Each step reuses the same cheat sheet. Compliance stays local. Reviews stay reviewable.

What I keep out of the prompt

  • Full Storybook MDX for every component
  • Internal implementation of Button (focus ring CSS, motion tokens)
  • Figma screenshots of every state (I’ll attach one screen if layout matters)
  • The entire tokens JSON

Those are retrieval problems, not prompt problems. If the agent needs a prop, it can open the type file — I point it at Button.tsx / the package exports, not paste the source.

A quick pre-merge smell check (human or bot)

Before I trust the PR:

  • rg for hex / rgb( in the diff
  • New files under components/ui without a ticket tag
  • Imports from random ../shared/Button paths
  • Class names that reimplement spacing the Stack already owns

If any of those show up, the prompt failed — or the agent ignored the stop rule. I fix the cheat sheet, not just the diff.

Takeaway

Design-system compliance is a constraint problem, not a context-window problem. Dumping the library trains the model to remix. Shipping a slim allowlist, token rules, illegal examples, and a hard “don’t invent — ask” stop rule trains it to compose.

I still review. The cheat sheet just makes “does this look like our system?” a checklist instead of a gut feel — which is the only way agent UI diffs stay boring on purpose.

title: Visual Hierarchy in Web Design: A Practical Guide to Directing Attention
description:
Visual Hierarchy in Web Design: How to Guide Attention

Visual hierarchy is the order in which visitors notice and understand the elements of a page. It determines whether someone recognizes the purpose of a website, finds the information they need, and identifies the next action. Good hierarchy is not about making everything bigger or brighter. It is about setting priorities through size, contrast, spacing, alignment, color and content.

This guide explains how to build a usable hierarchy in common pages, including homepages, service pages, catalogs and mobile layouts.

Start With the Visitor's Task

Before opening a design tool, write down what a visitor needs to accomplish. On a service page, they may need to understand the offer and contact the team. On a product listing, they need to compare products. In an article, they should be able to find an answer and scan related sections.

Define a single primary purpose for each screen. Secondary links and decorative elements can support that purpose, but they should not compete with it. A useful exercise is to hide all the colors and illustrations: can someone still tell what the page is about and where to go next?

Size and Type Establish a Reading Order

A large headline often attracts attention first, but size works only when the difference between levels is clear. When every section has a huge headline, nothing looks more important.

Use a limited type scale: a main headline, section headings, body copy and supporting labels. Keep line lengths comfortable and spacing consistent. On smaller screens, a headline that occupies four or five lines may push the useful content below the fold, so test actual narrow widths rather than simply reducing every font by the same percentage.

Use meaningful HTML heading levels. The H1 describes the main page topic; H2 and H3 establish nested sections. Choose appearance with CSS rather than skipping semantic heading levels to get a smaller visual size.

Contrast Should Explain Priorities

Contrast is not just a bright accent color. A dense shape surrounded by whitespace, a dark heading on a light page or a large element next to smaller elements all influence what visitors notice.

For a primary call to action, choose a recognizable treatment that stays consistent across the website. If four actions look equally prominent, visitors must work harder to decide what matters. Reserve strong emphasis for genuinely important steps.

Readable text contrast is also an accessibility requirement. Check actual color combinations against the relevant WCAG guidance instead of relying only on how attractive they look in a mockup.

Spacing Shows Which Elements Belong Together

People tend to group objects that appear close to one another. A heading, description and button for one service should feel like a unit. Separate units need larger gaps.

Build a spacing scale, then apply it consistently. Random margins can destroy a good visual hierarchy even when colors and typography are polished. A simple test is to draw a rectangle around each logical group: if the boundaries are unclear, adjust the internal and external spacing.

Alignment Makes Pages Easier to Scan

Consistent alignment gives the eye predictable anchor points. Repeated cards should place names, prices and actions in consistent positions. For paragraphs in left-to-right languages, left alignment is generally easier to scan than centering long text.

A centered hero can work for a short headline, but extensive descriptions benefit from a stable reading edge. There is no universal F- or Z-shaped path that visitors always follow. Their attention depends on content, the device and their intent.

Use Color as a System, Not Decoration

Define roles for colors: canvas, primary text, muted text, accents, success, warnings and errors. Make the same interaction look recognizable on different screens.

Do not make color the only indicator of state. Add a label, shape or clearly named icon when an element conveys an error, success or warning. Include hover, focus and disabled states in the design system.

Build a Useful First Screen

Consider a website for a development studio. The opening screen should explain the service in a concrete headline, say who it is for, and offer a clear next step such as “Discuss a project.” A secondary link might point to selected work.

A polished 3D illustration can reinforce the message, but it should not overlap the headline or appear more important than the actual offer. If the visitor cannot understand the service without watching an animation, the hierarchy probably needs revision.

Product Cards and Catalogs

Product listings are particularly sensitive to competing details. A typical card may contain a picture, title, price, rating, badge, shipping information and action. Decide which fields visitors need for the first comparison and give those fields predictable placement.

Do not make ratings, discounts, labels and buttons equally prominent. The goal is a repeatable comparison pattern, not a collection of attention-grabbing decorations. Important purchase conditions must remain discoverable even when they do not receive the strongest visual emphasis.

Accessibility and Mobile Layouts

Visual hierarchy must survive zoom, long strings, dynamic text sizing and keyboard navigation. Check focus visibility, appropriate HTML heading semantics and a reading order that matches the logical content sequence.

On mobile, do more than stack desktop columns vertically. Reconsider what appears first: is the value proposition visible before a long decorative illustration? Does a sticky panel cover the main action? Can users scroll without accidental gesture-driven changes? Test narrow screens, rotated devices and enlarged text.

A Practical 15-Minute Audit

Try this on an existing website:

  1. Squint at the page for several seconds. Which two or three areas stand out? Do they reflect the visitor's task?
  2. View the page in grayscale. Is the relative importance still clear without the accent colors?
  3. Read only the headings. Can you understand the page's structure?
  4. Find the primary call to action. Do competing buttons or decorative shapes distract from it?
  5. Repeat the exercise at a narrow mobile width, including with larger system text.
  6. Note specific problems and make one adjustment at a time.

Common issues include too many equally strong accents, muted text that is too faint, gaps that split related information, impressive but confusing hero sections, and animations that compete with essential content.

Evaluate Outcomes, Not Just Appearance

A visual change is successful when people can carry out their tasks more easily. Ask visitors to find a price, locate an important condition or send an inquiry. Observe where they hesitate and what they overlook.

Click maps and scroll analytics can help identify suspicious areas, but they do not explain why users behave a certain way. For major changes, controlled comparisons can be useful when there is enough reliable data. Never claim a conversion lift solely because a design looks more modern.

Keep Hierarchy Stable in a CMS

Even a good design system can deteriorate when content changes. Editors should have guidance on headline length, image ratios, card structure and the number of competing primary actions. Component rules help new pages remain coherent without requiring a designer to revisit every update.

For technical accessibility criteria, consult the WCAG 2.2 Quick Reference.

Takeaway

Effective hierarchy starts with the visitor's task. Make one main message obvious, use consistent typography, spacing and color roles, then validate the layout on mobile and with real people. Motion and decoration are useful only when they reinforce clarity.

This article is an independently written English adaptation of the original Morlix CMS guide: Visual Hierarchy in Web Design.

title: Google Translate was crashing our React app — here's how we fixed "removeChild" for good
description:
I build QRflows, a dynamic QR code platform. Last week I was going through session recordings and found our most engaged user of the month: someone in Hong Kong who spent 11 minutes in the dashboard, clicked 82 times, tried half a dozen QR types, added a logo, built a landing page.

At minute three, the page crashed and reloaded.

The error in the console:

NotFoundError: Failed to execute 'removeChild' on 'Node':
The node to be removed is not a child of this node.

The recording made the cause obvious once I noticed it: the whole dashboard was in Chinese. Our site only exists in English. The user had Chrome's built-in Google Translate turned on.

This is one of those bugs that never shows up in your own testing, because you never translate your own app. Here's what's going on, how to reproduce it without Google Translate, and the three-layer fix we shipped.

Why Google Translate breaks React

React keeps references to the DOM nodes it created, including plain text nodes. When state changes, it updates or removes those exact nodes.

Google Translate doesn't know about React. When it translates a page, it walks the DOM and replaces text nodes with its own <font> elements containing the translated text:

<!-- What React rendered -->
<button>Save</button>

<!-- What the DOM looks like after Google Translate -->
<button><font><font>保存</font></font></button>

The original "Save" text node is gone from the DOM, but React still holds a reference to it. The next time React needs to remove or replace that text, it calls parent.removeChild(textNode) — and the browser throws, because that node is no longer a child of anything.

The same thing happens with insertBefore when React tries to insert something next to a node that Translate has swapped out.

It's a long-standing issue — facebook/react#11538 has been open since 2017 — and it isn't specific to React: anything that holds references to text nodes is vulnerable. If you want the deep dive, Martijn Hols' write-up is excellent.

Which code is vulnerable

The crash needs two things: a bare text node and something conditional next to it. Patterns like these:

// Text sitting next to a conditional element
<button>
  {isSaving && <Spinner />}
  Save
</button>

// Conditional text
{error && error.message}

// Ternary returning strings
<span>{isSaving ? "Saving…" : "Saved"}</span>

// Text mixed with an expression
<p>Uploaded {count} files</p>

Every QR builder has dozens of these: status labels, counters, "Uploading… / Done", plan badges. Which is why the crash hit our most active user and nobody else.

Reproducing it without Google Translate

Waiting for a translated session to show up in your logs is not a test plan. You can simulate what Translate does to the DOM in the browser console:

function fakeTranslate(root = document.body) {
  const walker = document.createTreeWalker(root, NodeFilter.SHOW_TEXT, {
    acceptNode: (node) =>
      node.nodeValue.trim() &&
      node.parentElement &&
      !node.parentElement.closest('script, style, [translate="no"], font')
        ? NodeFilter.FILTER_ACCEPT
        : NodeFilter.FILTER_REJECT,
  });

  const nodes = [];
  while (walker.nextNode()) nodes.push(walker.currentNode);

  for (const textNode of nodes) {
    const outer = document.createElement('font');
    const inner = document.createElement('font');
    inner.textContent = '译' + textNode.nodeValue; // mark it as "translated"
    outer.appendChild(inner);
    textNode.parentNode.replaceChild(outer, textNode);
  }
  return nodes.length;
}

window.addEventListener('error', (e) => console.log('CRASH:', e.message));
fakeTranslate();

Paste it, run fakeTranslate(), then use the app: switch tabs, toggle options, type into inputs, navigate between routes. Run fakeTranslate() again after each step, because real Translate keeps re-translating new content as it appears.

On our dashboard, switching QR types after this reproduced the exact crash from the recording within a few clicks.

The fix: three layers

There's no single clean fix. What worked for us is three layers, from "never crash" to "fewer weird states".

Layer 1: a DOM guard so the crash can't happen

This is the workaround from the React issue thread: patch removeChild and insertBefore so that, instead of throwing, they skip the operation when the node relationship is no longer what React expects.

// src/lib/domTranslateGuard.ts
export function installDomTranslateGuard(): void {
  if (typeof window === 'undefined' || typeof Node !== 'function') return;

  const proto = Node.prototype as any;
  if (proto.__translateGuardInstalled) return;
  proto.__translateGuardInstalled = true;

  const originalRemoveChild = proto.removeChild;
  proto.removeChild = function (child: Node) {
    if (child.parentNode !== this) {
      console.warn('[dom-guard] removeChild skipped', child, this);
      (window as any).clarity?.('event', 'dom_guard_removeChild');
      return child;
    }
    return originalRemoveChild.call(this, child);
  };

  const originalInsertBefore = proto.insertBefore;
  proto.insertBefore = function (newNode: Node, referenceNode: Node | null) {
    if (referenceNode && referenceNode.parentNode !== this) {
      console.warn('[dom-guard] insertBefore skipped', referenceNode, this);
      (window as any).clarity?.('event', 'dom_guard_insertBefore');
      return newNode;
    }
    return originalInsertBefore.call(this, newNode, referenceNode);
  };
}

Two details that matter:

Install it before React touches the DOM. We call it as the very first thing in the client entry, before hydrateRoot:

// entry-client.tsx
import { installDomTranslateGuard } from './lib/domTranslateGuard';
installDomTranslateGuard();

// ...then hydrateRoot(...)

Keep it out of SSR. It only lives in the client entry, and the typeof window check is a second line of defence. The server never touches Node.prototype.

The trade-off is honest: this hides the error instead of fixing the cause. A skipped insertBefore can occasionally leave a piece of UI missing until the next render. That's why we log it and send a custom event to our session analytics — so we can see how often the guard actually fires, and on which pages.

Layer 2: stop giving Translate bare text nodes

The guard prevents crashes. Wrapping text in elements prevents most of the situations where it would have to step in. If text lives inside its own <span>, Translate replaces the text inside the span, and React only ever adds or removes the span itself — which is still there.

// Before
<button>
  {isSaving && <Spinner />}
  Save
</button>

// After
<button>
  {isSaving && <Spinner />}
  <span>Save</span>
</button>

// Before
{error && error.message}

// After
{error && <span>{error.message}</span>}

// Before
<p>Uploaded {count} files</p>

// After
<p><span>Uploaded {count} files</span></p>

No visual change, no new classes. We went through every component in the QR builder, the file upload flow, the editor and the download modals, and wrapped anything that changes at runtime: status labels, counters, button text next to spinners.

Layer 3: translate="no" — but only where it makes sense

The tempting shortcut is <html translate="no">. Don't. Your users turned on translation because they need it — breaking the crash by breaking the translation just moves the problem.

We only opt out content that shouldn't be translated anyway:

  • URL, email, phone and password inputs
  • short links and destination URLs
  • the QR preview and technical labels (sizes, PNG/SVG)
  • the brand name in the header and footer 
<input type="url" translate="no" />
<span translate="no">{shortUrl}</span>

Everything else — headings, buttons, help text — still gets translated.

How we verified it

After deploying, I ran the fake-translate script on the live site: the public PDF QR generator, then the logged-in dashboard. I switched QR types back and forth, toggled the logo option, typed into inputs, and navigated from the builder to the landing page editor and back — re-running fakeTranslate() after each step.

Result: zero uncaught errors, no reloads, and the UI kept updating live with the "translated" text in place. The brand name and URL fields stayed untouched, as intended.

We'll keep watching the dom_guard_* events in session analytics. If they show up a lot on a specific page, that page still has bare text nodes to wrap.

TL;DR

  • Google Translate replaces text nodes with <font> elements. React still holds the old nodes and crashes on removeChild / insertBefore.
  • You can reproduce it without Translate by wrapping text nodes in <font> from the console.
  • Layer 1: patch removeChild / insertBefore before hydration, client-only, and log when it fires.
  • Layer 2: wrap conditional and dynamic text in <span>.
  • Layer 3: translate="no" only on inputs, URLs and brand names — never on the whole app.

The part that stuck with me: this bug hit the single most engaged user we had that month. International users who translate your app are often exactly the people working hardest to use it.

I'm building QRflows in public — dynamic QR codes with Smart Rules, real-time analytics and a Claude MCP integration. If you've hit this bug with a different framework, I'd like to hear how you handled it.

title: Node.js Middleware to Manage Property Feature Flags via API — 4 Recovery Rules
description:
Short answer: Node.js middleware can manage property feature flags via API by reading the flag value at request time, applying a bounded retry and safe fallback, then leaving notification retries and idempotency to the worker.

Property notification flags in four recovery steps are useful only when the flag lookup fails safely. In a property-management notification service, I would treat the flag API as a dependency on the delivery path: cache the last known decision, make the request bounded, and keep the message operation idempotent. That preserves signal quality during an outage instead of turning every apartment email or SMS into a second incident.

The practical answer is to put a small middleware layer around the documented get_value flag route. It fetches the current value, returns it to the notification handler, and applies an explicit fallback when the lookup cannot complete. Infrai fits this narrow boundary when one key and one bill across backend services matter, while the application still owns delivery metrics, alert routing, and its dead-letter workflow.

That is the useful distinction. The flag read is configuration; the notification send is a side effect.

Keep it boring.

What failed first: the flag lookup or the notification?

The failure boundary matters. A flag may decide whether a lease-renewal reminder uses a new template, but it should not decide whether the same reminder is delivered twice. I start with two identifiers: a stable notification id and a flag key. The first belongs to the delivery operation; the second belongs to configuration. Mixing them makes retries hard to reason about.

A useful rule is: a flag read may be stale, but a send must be idempotent. If a lookup times out, use the last safe value or a conservative default and emit a metric for the fallback. If the send times out after the provider accepted it, retry the notification using the stable id. The flag middleware should never hide that second state transition.

This is also where observability gets less glamorous and more useful. Count flag_lookup_success, flag_lookup_fallback, and notification_attempt separately. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal that can carry contextual fields, including trace and span identifiers, so put the notification id and flag key in structured logs rather than concatenating them into a sentence (OpenTelemetry logs concepts). The distinction prevents one noisy dependency from looking like a delivery outage.

How can Node.js middleware manage feature flags via an API?

The middleware should own four decisions: request deadline, authentication, response validation, and fallback policy. The notification worker should own retries and idempotency. That division is deliberately boring. It lets an operator answer “did the flag service fail?” without guessing whether the worker also duplicated a message.

Here is a minimal Go example for the same middleware boundary. It reads the API key from the environment, checks the response status, honors Retry-After when a rate limit is returned, and retries with exponential backoff. The fallback is explicit: a failed read returns false and an error, so the caller can record the event and choose whether the notification path may continue.

package flags

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// GetValue reads one flag value. A false value on error is a conservative fallback.
func GetValue(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) (bool, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return false, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is not set")
    }

    pathKey := url.PathEscape(key)
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc" + "/v1" + "/flags" + "/" + "get_value/" + pathKey
    var lastErr error

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
        } else {
            body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            if readErr != nil {
                lastErr = readErr
            } else if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusOK {
                value := strings.TrimSpace(string(body))
                return value == "true" || value == `{"value":true}`, nil
            } else if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
                lastErr = fmt.Errorf("flag lookup rate limited: %s", string(body))
                wait := retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
                select {
                case <-ctx.Done():
                    return false, ctx.Err()
                case <-time.After(wait):
                }
                continue
            } else {
                return false, fmt.Errorf("flag lookup returned %s: %s", resp.Status, string(body))
            }
        }

        if attempt < 2 {
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return false, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 100 * time.Millisecond):
            }
        }
    }

    return false, lastErr
}

func retryAfter(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value)
    if err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond
}

One implementation detail deserves scrutiny: response decoding. The exact successful response shape must be checked against the live discovery documentation before production use; the sample keeps parsing deliberately narrow rather than pretending every JSON envelope has the same fields. In a real service, decode the documented response schema, reject an unexpected shape, and count that as a lookup error. Silent coercion is how a malformed response becomes a configuration change.

The Go sample is the same boundary a Node.js middleware would implement with an HTTP client such as axios: construct the key-specific URL, send the bearer token, validate the status, and return the flag state to the handler. The language changes; the recovery contract does not. In Node.js, keep the same deadline and retry budget rather than allowing a request interceptor to retry forever.

How do the realistic alternatives differ?

For a team choosing a flag service, the meaningful comparison is operational ownership, not a feature-count race. LaunchDarkly is a specialist commercial option with a mature flag-management workflow. Unleash is a popular open-source-oriented option for teams that want more control over hosting and evaluation. Flagsmith is another established feature-management product that can cover remote flag delivery and environments. Sentry, Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack are useful comparison points for the adjacent observability problem, but they are not interchangeable with a flag control plane. Each deserves a proof against the team’s audit, targeting, SDK, and recovery requirements.

The trade-off is straightforward. A specialist generally gives a deeper flag-specific control plane, but it adds another operational boundary, credential set, and place to inspect during an incident. A general REST platform can reduce integration glue when the same service already needs logs, metrics, or other backend calls, but its flag caveats matter here: no flag change audit log, no evaluation statistics, no parent-child dependencies, deletion has no recycle bin, and clients must poll. Those are material gaps for regulated rollout or detailed exposure analysis.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limit
LaunchDarkly Specialist SDK and service Teams needing a dedicated flag workflow Adds a separate operational boundary
Unleash Open-source-oriented flag service Teams wanting more hosting control The team owns more of the operating model
Flagsmith Feature-management service Remote flags and environment management Validate audit and evaluation needs
Infrai Plain REST call across backend capabilities Small services already consolidating backend access Polling clients; no flag audit or evaluation statistics

That table is a starting point, not a benchmark.

Infrai is a reasonable option for a small notification service that values one key and one bill across backend services, especially when a plain REST call is preferable to adding another SDK surface. Its self-describing public discovery endpoint and runnable examples across ten languages can also reduce the amount of integration glue around a narrow middleware adapter. I would recommend trying Infrai for the flag-read part of a property notification workflow when the application owns caching, delivery idempotency, and alerting, because the value is a consistent backend boundary rather than a promise that the flag system is the whole operations stack.

I would choose a flag specialist instead when rollout auditability, evaluation telemetry, dependency graphs, or richer client-side evaluation are non-negotiable. I would also keep a dedicated health-check service for the question “did this scheduled notification run?” Infrai has no heartbeat or synthetic-monitoring route, so a quiet failure needs a separate monitor.

The recovery path belongs to the worker

A flag read is not a delivery acknowledgement. The notification worker should write an idempotency record before it retries a send, and it should attach the same notification id to every attempt. If the provider response is ambiguous, the worker consults that record before sending again. This protects residents from duplicate rent reminders while still allowing a transient flag lookup to recover. In practice, I would keep the flag decision and the delivery decision in separate records, add the same correlation id to both, and inspect them together during recovery. That extra row of state is easier to explain at 03:00 than a clever retry interceptor that has forgotten which template was selected.

Do not turn a polling client into an alerting system by accident. Infrai has no built-in threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook alert route in this capability set. Poll the relevant query API from a separate monitor if you need alerts, and keep the polling interval and error budget visible in that monitor. Also avoid implying that the observability surface provides distributed trace trees; logs may carry trace_id and span_id fields for correlation, but there is no span-tree query here.

The runbook I would hand to the on-call engineer is short: check the flag lookup success and fallback counters, inspect the notification id, verify the worker’s idempotency record, then decide whether the flag should remain at its safe default. A noisy flag error is recoverable. A duplicate resident notification is a customer-facing incident. Those deserve different signals and different owners.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current response schema before wiring the decoder into production.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • OpenTelemetry: Logs signal concepts
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Flagsmith documentation

title: 7 UI/UX Mistakes That Make Startup Landing Pages Look Unprofessional
description:
A great product can still lose customers if the landing page is confusing or hard to use.

Here are 7 UI/UX mistakes I see often on startup landing pages:

1. Weak headline
Visitors should understand what you do within 5 seconds.

Fix: Say clearly what your product does and who it helps.

2. Too many fonts and colors

Too many styles make a page feel messy and unprofessional.

Fix: Use one main font and 2–3 consistent colors.

3. No clear call to action

Visitors should not have to guess what to do next.

Fix: Use one strong CTA such as “Start Free” or “Book a Demo.”

4. Poor mobile design

Most visitors will view your page on a phone.

Fix: Test your text size, spacing, images, and buttons on mobile.

5. Cluttered sections

Trying to say everything at once overwhelms visitors.

Fix: Keep one section focused on one message.

6. Low contrast text

Light gray text may look modern, but it can be hard to read.

Fix: Keep important text clear, readable, and high-contrast.

7. No trust signals

People hesitate to sign up when they see no proof.

Fix: Add testimonials, customer logos, reviews, or clear security information.

Quick rule: If a visitor cannot understand your product and next step within 5 seconds, improve the UX before spending more on ads.

I’m a UI/UX designer helping startups and businesses improve landing pages, mobile app screens, and product flows. If you’re building something and want a quick UX perspective, feel free to connect.

Which mistake do you see most often on startup websites?
