title: Redesigning my TYPO3 portfolio – what actually moved the Lighthouse scores
description:
I recently rebuilt my personal site, www.stefan-andres.at, from scratch. It runs on TYPO3 13.4 with the Bootstrap Package, and the goal was simple: a light, calm design – and a site that scores well where it matters for users, not just in screenshots.

This isn't a "look at my new website" post. It's a list of the things that actually changed the numbers, with code you can copy.

Where I ended up (mobile, PageSpeed Insights):

  • Accessibility: 100
  • Best Practices: 100
  • SEO: 100
  • Performance: 96 (88 at launch, 95 after the font and contrast fixes, 77 after adding Analytics – more on that below)

1. Self-host your fonts – and get the file names right

The biggest single render-blocking item was Google Fonts: one CSS request to fonts.googleapis.com, then a chain to fonts.gstatic.com for every weight. Roughly 750 ms on a throttled mobile connection.

I downloaded the .woff2 files, put them in fileadmin, and wrote one @font-face per weight:

@font-face{font-family:"Plus Jakarta Sans";font-weight:400;font-display:swap;src:url(/fileadmin/Daten/fonts/PlusJakartaSans-Regular.woff2) format("woff2")}
@font-face{font-family:"Plus Jakarta Sans";font-weight:700;font-display:swap;src:url(/fileadmin/Daten/fonts/PlusJakartaSans-Bold.woff2) format("woff2")}
@font-face{font-family:"Plus Jakarta Sans";font-weight:800;font-display:swap;src:url(/fileadmin/Daten/fonts/PlusJakartaSans-ExtraBold.woff2) format("woff2")}
/* … 500, 600 and the italic display face */

Two lessons:

  • Check the file names. My first version pointed to a single plus-jakarta-sans-latin.woff2 that didn't exist – the site silently fell back to system fonts.
  • Remove the old @import. It was still sitting at the top of the main stylesheet and kept loading Google Fonts in parallel.

Then preload only the fonts visible above the fold:

page.headerData.5 = TEXT
page.headerData.5.value (
<link rel="preload" href="/fileadmin/Daten/fonts/PlusJakartaSans-ExtraBold.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/fileadmin/Daten/fonts/PlayfairDisplay-Italic.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
)

Bonus: no third-party font requests means one less entry in the privacy policy and a simpler Content-Security-Policy.

2. Load page-specific CSS and JS only where it's needed

My site has ten free browser tools (contrast checker, favicon generator, minifiers, …). Their CSS and JavaScript were loaded on every page – including the home page, where none of them run.

TypoScript conditions make this a one-liner. All tools live below one page (uid 174):

[174 in tree.rootLineIds]
  page.includeCSS.tools = fileadmin/Template/css/cust03-tools.css
  page.includeJSFooter.customtools = fileadmin/Template/js/tools.js
  page.includeJSFooter.customtools.defer = 1
[END]

tree.rootLineIds matches the page itself and everything below it, so new tools are covered automatically.

3. Load Google Analytics only after consent

Adding GA4 the "standard" way dropped my performance score from 95 to 77. gtag.js is ~177 KB and Lighthouse flags most of it as unused.

But my cookie banner is opt-in anyway – until someone clicks "Allow", GA doesn't collect anything. So why load it?

<script>
window.dataLayer=window.dataLayer||[];
function gtag(){dataLayer.push(arguments);}
gtag('consent','default',{'ad_storage':'denied','ad_user_data':'denied','ad_personalization':'denied','analytics_storage':'denied'});

function loadGA(){
  if(window.gaLoaded)return; window.gaLoaded=1;
  gtag('consent','update',{'analytics_storage':'granted'});
  var s=document.createElement('script');
  s.async=1; s.src='https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=G-XXXXXXX';
  document.head.appendChild(s);
  gtag('js',new Date()); gtag('config','G-XXXXXXX');
}

// returning visitors who already agreed
if(document.cookie.indexOf('cookieconsent_status=allow')>-1){loadGA();}
// first-time visitors clicking "Allow"
document.addEventListener('click',function(e){if(e.target.closest('.cc-allow')){loadGA();}});
</script>

cookieconsent_status and .cc-allow are the defaults of the cookie banner shipped with the Bootstrap Package – check your own cookie name in DevTools → Application → Cookies.

Result: Lighthouse (which never clicks "Allow") doesn't see GA at all, real visitors who consent are tracked normally, and it's cleaner from a GDPR point of view. Score back to 96.

4. Accessibility: contrast was the whole story

The audit flagged two things: contrast and heading order.

Contrast

My brand orange #df532e with white text sits at about 3.6:1 – below the WCAG AA minimum of 4.5:1 for normal text. Instead of changing the brand colour, I added a second token just for text and button backgrounds:

:root{
  --sa-orange:#df532e;       /* decoration: dots, lines, borders */
  --sa-orange-a11y:#c74523;  /* text and filled buttons: ~4.9:1 on white */
}

The less obvious trap: grey on dark. My footer used the same muted grey as the light sections. Darkening that grey (to fix light backgrounds) made the footer worse. Dark backgrounds need their own, lighter muted tone.

Heading order

Two culprits:

  • A card in the hero used an <h3> right after the <h1> – visually fine, semantically a skipped level. It's now a <p> with a class.
  • The Bootstrap Package constant defaultHeaderType = 5 turned every content element without an explicit header type into an <h5> – including my footer. Setting it to 2 fixed that globally.

5. Small things that added up

  • Images as WebP with explicit width/height → CLS dropped to 0.
  • fetchpriority="high" on the first visible image, loading="lazy" on the rest.
  • One CSS custom-property system (--sa-ink, --sa-gray, --sa-shadow-card, …) instead of hard-coded values. That made the contrast fixes a two-line change.
  • Mobile menu on iOS: a position:fixed menu inside a header with backdrop-filter rendered invisible in Safari. Anchoring it with position:absolute; top:100% relative to the header fixed it.

What's on the site now

Besides services and a portfolio, the site doubles as a small toolbox:

  • 10 free browser tools – palette & contrast checker, favicon generator, image optimizer, SEO check, CSS/JS/SVG minifiers, a clamp() calculator, JSON formatter, a TYPO3 Fluid ViewHelper generator and a client-briefing generator
  • 3 apps for iPhone & Mac – no account, no ads, data stays on the device
  • A glossary of print, web and video terms

If you work with TYPO3 or just want a quick contrast check, have a look: 👉 stefan-andres.at/tools

I'd love to hear what you'd improve – or what moved your Lighthouse scores the most.

title: TokenVault – 512KB local-first LLM cost shield & reversible PII vault (Python/Node/Go/Wasm)
description:
Hey HN, I'm Somesh, a 17-year-old builder from India.

While building multi-turn AI apps, I kept running into two problems with existing LLM gateways:

  1. Cloud proxy gateways force you to route every prompt through a third-party server (adding 80–200ms of network latency and creating a PII compliance nightmare).
  2. Most teams silently lose 30–50% of their OpenAI/Anthropic bill to broken 1,024-token prompt cache prefixes (putting dynamic timestamps/UUIDs at token 0), stuck Period-1/Period-2 agent retry loops, and re-sending massive tool/vision payloads across turns.

So I built TokenVault (https://www.tockenvault.com) using a 5-language specialized stack:

  • Rust -> WebAssembly (Wasm) binary kernel in the browser for zero-GC 64-bit FNV-1a 256-token Radix block fingerprinting, Luhn mod-10 card checks, and Shannon entropy secret scanning.
  • Native single-file Python SDK (token_vault.py hooking httpx) and Node/Edge SDK (token-vault.js hooking globalThis.fetch) bounded strictly to a 512 KB in-memory ring buffer.
  • Go streaming gateway (token_vault_gateway.go) with a 12s TTFT zombie-stream watchdog and bidirectional protocol failover (OpenAI <-> Anthropic <-> Gemini).
  • Reversible Ephemeral PII Vault: masks credit cards, emails, DB URIs, and JWTs outbound (<TV_CARD_1>) and re-hydrates them inbound (including across split-token SSE streams).

You can test the client-side forensic log auditor in the browser without signing up (just drop any OpenAI/Anthropic/LangSmith JSONL or CSV trace to get a ghost-leak-optimized.config.json), or run node token-vault.js --self-test locally.

Would love brutal technical feedback from the HN community on the architecture!

title: Node.js Feature Flags Implementation with a REST API for Agent Observability
description:
Short answer: A Node.js feature flags implementation can use a REST API to choose an agent path, while step events reconstruct latency and cost; keep the flag decision separate from the observability pipeline.

The least complex way to reconstruct a marketplace agent incident is to emit one structured event per agent step. Keep a stable run ID, measure elapsed time around every model call, and record usage and cost from the model adapter. A separate telemetry pipeline becomes the better shape when retention, alerting, or trace exploration becomes a product requirement.

The key decision is the event boundary. Agent code owns timing and identity; the service behind that boundary can change. A REST-backed platform such as Infrai is a deliberate option for a small team when one plain HTTP contract and per-call cost, latency, vendor, cache, and request metadata matter. Its public discovery surface also makes the capability contract inspectable before integration.

How should a Node.js feature flags implementation use a REST API?

There are two viable architectures. In the embedded shape, the Node.js process records a start time, finishes a model call, and emits an event beside the marketplace result. Its invariant is that every step has a run ID, step ID, outcome, and duration, including failures. It ships quickly and keeps the request path legible.

In the independent-pipeline shape, the agent emits events to an OpenTelemetry-compatible collector or telemetry service, which owns batching, retention, querying, and alerting. Its invariant is durable delivery: a restart must not silently erase evidence needed for an incident review. This adds moving parts, but separates customer traffic from telemetry work.

For a solo team, choose the embedded shape until a second consumer, a retention policy, or deploy-independent alerts become necessary. Reconstruction comes first. Automation follows.

A small TypeScript event boundary

The provider stays out of decision code. The adapter supplies token usage and cost; the agent supplies identity and timing. Here is a small flag read with the required explicit method, environment-based credential, response check, and bounded 429 backoff. The same decision can be recorded in the step event.

type AgentStep = {
  runId: string; stepId: string; name: string; startedAt: string;
  durationMs: number; inputTokens: number; outputTokens: number;
  costUsd: number; outcome: "ok" | "error";
};

interface TelemetrySink { write(event: AgentStep): Promise<void>; }

async function readFlag(key: string): Promise<boolean> {
  const url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/flags/get_value/marketplace-agent";
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY ?? ""}` },
    });
    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.min(retryAfter * 1000, 8000)));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`flag read failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    const payload = await response.json() as { value: boolean };
    return payload.value;
  }
  throw new Error("flag read rate limit persisted after retries");
}

async function runStep<T>(sink: TelemetrySink, ids: { runId: string; stepId: string }, name: string, work: () => Promise<{ value: T; inputTokens: number; outputTokens: number; costUsd: number }>): Promise<T> {
  const startedAt = new Date();
  const started = performance.now();
  try {
    const result = await work();
    await sink.write({ ...ids, name, startedAt: startedAt.toISOString(), durationMs: Math.round(performance.now() - started), inputTokens: result.inputTokens, outputTokens: result.outputTokens, costUsd: result.costUsd, outcome: "ok" });
    return result.value;
  } catch (error) {
    await sink.write({ ...ids, name, startedAt: startedAt.toISOString(), durationMs: Math.round(performance.now() - started), inputTokens: 0, outputTokens: 0, costUsd: 0, outcome: "error" });
    throw error;
  }
}

The error event is emitted before the original error is rethrown. Make the sink retryable and non-blocking to customer traffic; if telemetry failure can block a purchase, the boundary is in the wrong place.

What should the event prove later?

A reconstruction joins events by runId, orders them by startedAt, and compares each step's duration and cost with the marketplace outcome. It should answer whether retrieval ran, which model step consumed tokens, whether a feature flag altered the path, and whether the final action succeeded. Record the flag key and selected branch in the surrounding event. A flag service handles evaluation; it is not the incident timeline.

Infrai fits the ingestion and correlation side when one REST boundary is more important than a large SDK surface. The contract can stay in application code while the service behind a capability changes. A second practical benefit is one key and one bill across a broad surface: the 2026 discovery snapshot lists 295 routes across 20 modules. That reduces credential and billing reconciliation work when the same agent needs flags, logs, and model calls. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples also make capability checks easier before integration.

This is a trade-off, not a universal win.

The limits matter. The documented flag surface has no change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or push delivery; clients poll. The observability surface has no alert or notification route, no distributed span-tree query, no source-map or crash-symbolication workflow, and no heartbeat monitor. It also has no user-deletion log API or bulk export/subscription interface. A marketplace needing those controls must add them or choose a specialist.

How do the alternatives change the boundary?

LaunchDarkly is the mature choice when flag targeting, auditability, and evaluation analytics are central. Its strength is flag operations, not a complete model-cost timeline. Unleash is attractive when self-hosting and an open-source control plane matter; the team owns deployment and policy. Flagsmith provides remote configuration and self-hosting options, but it does not turn model usage into an incident reconstruction system. Sentry is stronger for error grouping and stack context, Datadog is stronger for a broad hosted metrics and traces workflow, and Grafana is a good fit when a team wants composable dashboards around its own storage. Each specialist adds a boundary; each also covers a deeper part of its chosen problem.

OpenTelemetry is the neutral instrumentation layer. It reduces vendor lock-in, but a collector, storage backend, retention policy, and alerting system still need an owner. That makes the architecture choice concrete: a specialist flag platform plus OpenTelemetry suits a mature platform team, while one REST boundary suits a small team whose immediate question is what happened in one agent run.

Option Boundary Best fit Main limitation
Infrai REST, one key Small teams reconstructing mixed backend runs No built-in alerting or flag audit trail
LaunchDarkly Flag service Targeting and rollout governance Separate telemetry is still needed
Unleash Self-hosted flag service Teams owning their control plane Deployment and policy are yours
OpenTelemetry Instrumentation standard Vendor-neutral telemetry Storage and alerting remain separate

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the ingestion and correlation portion of a marketplace agent loop when one REST contract and per-call metadata matter more than built-in flag governance or alerting. Choose LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or Flagsmith for the flag-control portion when rollout audit and evaluation behavior are the primary requirement. Choose Sentry, Datadog, or Grafana when their deeper error, metrics, or trace workflows are the requirement. Keep the TypeScript event interface either way.

The operational checklist is prose, not ceremony: generate one run ID at the request boundary, give every agent step a stable ID, capture success and failure, take token counts and cost from the model adapter, and make the sink retryable. Test a failed model call and a process restart. Those paths decide whether reconstruction is real.

For a concrete next step, the Node.js REST flag guide shows the adjacent flag workflow.

Further reading

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://launchdarkly.com/docs/home/getting-started
  • https://docs.getunleash.io/
  • https://docs.flagsmith.com/
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/flags/answers/nodejs-feature-flags-api-simple-rollout-percentage-user/

title: Worktrees do not remove the collision. They move it to merge time.
description:
Git worktrees give each coding agent its own checkout, so the agents stop overwriting each other's files. They do not remove the collision between what the agents are trying to do. That collision is still there, and with worktrees you find it later, when you merge the branches.

Sometimes Git stops you at that point. Sometimes it merges cleanly and the damage is only visible if you go looking. Below is a small repository you can build in two minutes that shows both outcomes, then what you can check with Git alone and what you need to move earlier.

A merge-time collision is a conflict between two agents' plans that nothing detects until their branches are combined. The plans were incompatible from the moment both were made. Worktrees keep the files apart while the work happens, so the incompatibility sits unseen until integration.

What do worktrees isolate, and what do they leave alone?

A worktree is a second checkout of the same repository, on its own branch, in its own directory. Two agents in two worktrees cannot overwrite each other's half-written files, break each other's builds with a stray install, or read stale code because the other agent changed it underneath.

That is the whole of it, and it is worth having. But look at what is not on the list:

  • What each agent has decided to build. That lives in a prompt, not in a file.
  • What each agent assumes will still exist. Agent B adds a method to a class because the class is there. It has no way to know Agent A is retiring it.
  • The order in which the work should land. Worktrees do not know that one task has to be merged before the other is started.

Isolation helps while the agents work. It decides nothing about whether their work belongs in the same codebase.

What does Git report when you merge?

Git merges by comparing changed lines against a common ancestor. I ran the same two-agent task through a throwaway repository three different ways, with Git 2.51.0, and Git gave three different answers.

What Agent A did What Agent B did What Git said at merge
Deleted payments.py after moving callers off it Added a method to payments.py CONFLICT (modify/delete). Stopped.
Rewrote the call in checkout.py Added a new function next to that call in checkout.py CONFLICT (content). Stopped.
Moved callers to a new class and left payments.py in place Added a method to payments.py and a new file that uses it Clean merge. No output.

The first two are the cases people mean when they say worktrees "work": the plans touch the same file, Git notices, and a person decides. The third is the one that matters here.

So Git's answer depends on how the agents happened to arrange their edits, not on whether the plans were compatible. The same disagreement is loud in one run and silent in the next.

What does the clean merge look like?

Here is the third case from the table, end to end. The task: Agent A is asked to replace PaymentService with StripePaymentService. Agent B is asked to add PayPal support to PaymentService. Each gets its own worktree and branch.

git worktree add ../agent-a -b agent/stripe
git worktree add ../agent-b -b agent/paypal

Agent A creates shop/stripe_payments.py, moves every caller in shop/checkout.py to the new class, and leaves a note at the top of shop/payments.py: # Deprecated: callers moved to StripePaymentService. Delete next release. It commits.

Agent B adds a charge_paypal method to the end of shop/payments.py and a new file, shop/paypal_checkout.py, that calls it. It commits.

Then the integration, in the main checkout:

$ git merge agent/stripe
 shop/checkout.py        | 4 ++--
 shop/stripe_payments.py | 3 +++
 2 files changed, 5 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
 create mode 100644 shop/stripe_payments.py

$ git merge agent/paypal
 shop/payments.py        | 3 +++
 shop/paypal_checkout.py | 4 ++++
 2 files changed, 7 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 shop/paypal_checkout.py

$ git status --short
(clean)

Now look at what the merged repository says:

$ head -2 shop/payments.py
# Deprecated: callers moved to StripePaymentService. Delete next release.
class PaymentService:

$ grep -rn "PaymentService" shop/ | grep -v Stripe
shop/payments.py:2:class PaymentService:
shop/paypal_checkout.py:1:from shop.payments import PaymentService
shop/paypal_checkout.py:4:    return PaymentService().charge_paypal(cents)

$ python3 -c "from shop.checkout import checkout; from shop.paypal_checkout import checkout_paypal; print(checkout(500)); print(checkout_paypal(500))"
charged 500 via stripe
charged 500 via paypal

Both paths run. Nothing fails. And the codebase now has one class marked for deletion, with PayPal, a new feature, built on top of it. The next person to follow the deprecation note deletes the class and takes PayPal with it. Or they leave it, and the repository permanently has two payment classes, one per gateway.

No test fails, because each branch's tests passed on its own and the merged tests exercise two working paths. Each agent also reported success, and it was right. The only thing wrong is a contradiction between two plans, and no tool in the standard pipeline reads plans.

Why is merge time the expensive moment?

The incompatibility existed the second the second agent started. What changes with time is the cost of resolving it. This is reasoning, not a measurement: I have no timing data to give you.

  • At planning time, you change a sentence in a prompt. Nothing has been written.
  • While the agents work, you stop one and redirect it. You lose part of a session.
  • At merge time, both agents have finished and both branches are green. Now you are choosing between two completed pieces of work, or rewriting one to sit on the other. If the conflict is the loud kind, you also have to understand both diffs to resolve it.
  • After merge, the conflict is in the codebase, and the only evidence of it is a deprecation note and a class that should not have grown.

Worktrees move the discovery from the first row of that list to the third or fourth. They make the work itself smoother and the surprise later. That trade is usually fine with two agents and a small task. It stops being fine as the number of agents grows, because the number of pairs of plans grows faster than the number of agents.

What can you do with Git alone?

Quite a lot, and you should do all of it before you add a tool.

  1. Decide the order of destructive work. If a task replaces, removes, renames or migrates something, nobody else should be editing that thing. Run the destructive task first, merge it, then start the others from the merged commit.
  2. Define the boundary before you split. If two tasks meet at an interface, make one small change that defines it, merge it, and start both agents from that commit. In the example, that is a PaymentProvider interface first, then Stripe and PayPal behind it.
  3. Assign by what a task changes, not by its name. "Modernize payments" and "add PayPal" sound like two features. They change one class.
  4. Test the merged result, not each branch. Merge into a throwaway integration branch and run your real checks there. In the example this would have passed, so it catches the loud failures and not the quiet one, but it catches a lot.
  5. Ask Git whether a merge is clean before you do it. git merge-tree --write-tree agent/stripe agent/paypal performs the merge in memory and reports conflicts without touching your working tree. It is quick, and it gives you the same answer the merge would, which in the third case is "clean". Treat that answer as a statement about text only.
  6. Write the plans down where every agent reads them. A shared file that lists each task, what it changes and what operation it performs catches duplicate work. It catches replace-versus-extend only if someone reads two entries side by side and notices.

All of these are the same move: get the plans into a form you can compare before the code exists. Past two or three agents, the weak point is that a person has to do the comparing.

What changes if the plans are compared before the code?

That is the step we built Foremerge for. It is an open-source coordination protocol that sits above Git. Each agent declares what it is about to change, and what it will do to it, before it edits anything.

foremerge intent publish \
  --agent "$AGENT" \
  --task "modernize-payments" \
  --summary "Replace PaymentService with StripePaymentService" \
  --scope symbol:PaymentService=replace

When another agent declares symbol:PaymentService=extend, the comparison raises a destructive_vs_additive finding at HIGH severity, while both worktrees are still clean:

{
  "kind": "destructive_vs_additive",
  "severity": "HIGH",
  "scope": { "kind": "symbol", "key": "PaymentService" },
  "explanation": "One intent will replace `PaymentService` while the other will extend it; both declare the same semantic scope.",
  "suggestion": "Coordinate on a stable `PaymentProvider` contract first, then implement StripePaymentProvider and PayPalPaymentProvider behind it and migrate callers deliberately. This is a heuristic suggestion, not an automatic design decision."
}

The finding does not block anyone. Claims are advisory, so two agents can still work the same area when that is fine. It is information for the agent or the person, delivered at the cheapest point on the list above. The store is a SQLite file in the repository's Git directory, which every linked worktree shares, so the agents keep isolated files and see the same declarations.

The limits are real. It trusts the declaration: an agent that says extend and then rewrites the class is not caught, though the declaration and the diff are both on record. A scope on a whole class does not match a scope on one of its methods in this release. Two names for the same concept can slip past it. It does not replace review, CI or someone owning the architecture, and a missing finding never shows that two changes are compatible. There are no published results on time saved.

Do you need any of this?

If you run one agent at a time, no. If your agents work on clearly separate parts of the code and you merge in sequence, worktrees and the list above are enough. The collision gets expensive when several agents run at once on one codebase, when they come from different tools, or when you cannot read all their plans before they finish.

Frequently asked questions

Do git worktrees prevent merge conflicts between AI agents?

No. Worktrees stop agents from overwriting each other's files while they work. Conflicts still appear when the branches are merged, and plans that contradict each other without touching the same lines merge cleanly and are not reported at all.

Why did Git merge two agents' branches with no conflict and the code still not make sense?

Git compares changed lines against a common ancestor, not intentions. If one agent retires a class and another builds on it in a different file, no lines overlap. The merge is clean and the codebase now contradicts itself.

Does git merge-tree tell me whether two agent branches are compatible?

It tells you whether Git can combine them without a textual conflict, without changing your working tree. That is useful and fast. A clean answer says nothing about whether the two plans are compatible, and in the example above it is clean.

Should one agent finish before the next starts?

When a task replaces, removes or renames something other work depends on, yes: run it first, merge it, and start the others from the result. Tasks that only add or extend different things can run in parallel.

Should I merge each agent's branch separately or together?

Merge into a throwaway integration branch and run your real checks on the combined result before anything reaches your main branch. Each branch passing its own tests tells you about that branch only.

Does Foremerge replace worktrees?

No. Worktrees isolate files and Foremerge shares plans, so you use both. Foremerge reads the same store from every worktree and from Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, and its claims never lock anything.

If you only ever run one agent, skip this

If you run two or more agents on one repository, worktrees handle the files and a comparison of declared plans handles the part Git cannot see. Foremerge is one Rust binary, local-first and Apache-2.0. Install it with curl -fsSL https://foremerge.com/install.sh | sh, then run foremerge init. One limit to start with: it can only compare what agents declare.

title: Inso CLI vs an OpenAPI CLI
description:
Short answer: The inso CLI runs the client's collections and assertions in CI; an OpenAPI CLI works from the contract and can validate, generate, and verify. The first executes the authored set; the second treats the spec as the source and derives the checks.

What a collection CLI is built for

Running the saved requests and their assertions in a pipeline. It is a reliable runner for a fixed set and is only as current as the collection.

What a spec CLI is built for

Task Collection CLI OpenAPI CLI
Run authored requests Yes Generated
Validate the contract Not its job Yes
Generate surfaces No Docs, mocks, tools
Verify conformance Assertions Schema check

Why the source matters

A spec CLI starts from the artifact that changes with the API, so the checks cannot run against a stale collection. A collection CLI is a runner for a snapshot.

How they fit

Keep the collection CLI for fixed behavioral calls and use the spec CLI for validation and generation. The runner and the source are different concerns.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Finish with collections vs generated.

title: Search Results That Jump Back to an Old Query in React: Finding and Fixing the Race
description:
The problem

A developer built a search bar in React. Each time the user types a letter, the component sends a request to the server and shows the results. Most of the time it works. But sometimes the list shows results for an older, shorter search. The box says "react", and the list shows results for "r". Typing slowly hides the bug. Typing fast makes it show up again.

This is a common bug, and it is easy to miss in local testing, because a local server answers almost every request at the same speed.

The root cause

Every keystroke starts a new request. The network does not promise that answers come back in the same order the requests went out. A short query like "r" can match many rows and take longer on the server. A longer query like "react" can come back fast.

So the timeline can look like this:

0 ms     start request for "r"      (slow, 300 ms)
40 ms    start request for "re"     (fast, 20 ms)
60 ms    "re" answers  -> list shows "re" results   (correct)
300 ms   "r" answers   -> list shows "r" results    (wrong, but it was the last setState)

The buggy code calls setState for every answer, so the last answer to arrive wins, not the last question asked:

// Buggy: every response updates state, in arrival order
useEffect(() => {
  if (!query) return;
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`)
    .then((res) => res.json())
    .then((data) => setResults({ query, items: data.items }));
}, [query]);

The React docs describe this exact case in "You Might Not Need an Effect": the responses for "hell" and "hello" can arrive in either order, and whichever calls setResults() last is what the user sees. They call it a race condition.

The fix

The fix has three parts. Each part solves a different piece, and all three live in the effect's cleanup function, which React runs before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts.

  1. An ignore flag. Each effect run gets its own flag. Cleanup sets it to true, so a late answer from an old run can no longer change state. This is the part that makes the result correct.
  2. An AbortController. Cleanup calls controller.abort(). Per MDN, this can abort a fetch request and the reading of its response body. The aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError, which we treat as normal, not as a failure. This part saves network and server work.
  3. A short debounce. A timer waits until the user pauses before it sends a request. Cleanup clears the timer, so fast typing sends one request instead of five. This part cuts load. It does not fix ordering by itself.

Here is the full hook:

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useSearch(query, { fetchImpl = fetch, delayMs = 250 } = {}) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle', query: '', items: [], error: null });

  useEffect(() => {
    const q = query.trim();
    if (!q) {
      setState({ status: 'idle', query: '', items: [], error: null });
      return;
    }

    const controller = new AbortController();
    let ignore = false;

    const timer = setTimeout(async () => {
      setState((s) => ({ ...s, status: 'loading', error: null }));
      try {
        const res = await fetchImpl(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, {
          signal: controller.signal,
        });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        const data = await res.json();
        if (!ignore) setState({ status: 'done', query: q, items: data.items, error: null });
      } catch (err) {
        if (ignore || err.name === 'AbortError') return; // expected, not a real failure
        setState((s) => ({ ...s, status: 'error', error: err }));
      }
    }, delayMs);

    return () => {
      ignore = true;        // late answers from this run can no longer touch state
      clearTimeout(timer);  // a request that has not started yet never starts
      controller.abort();   // a request in flight is cancelled
    };
  }, [query, fetchImpl, delayMs]);

  return state;
}

Use it like this:

function SearchBox() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const { status, query: shownFor, items, error } = useSearch(query);

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      {status === 'loading' && <p>Loading…</p>}
      {status === 'error' && <p>Something went wrong: {error.message}</p>}
      <p>Showing results for: {shownFor}</p>
      <ul>{items.map((item) => <li key={item}>{item}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}

Two small details matter:

  • Keep the query that produced the results in state next to the items. Then the UI can show which search the list belongs to, and a test can check it.
  • Do not pass a new fetchImpl function on every render, or the effect will re-run each time. Either leave the default, or create the function once outside the component.

Why keep the ignore flag if we already abort?

Abort is best effort. If the response is already done by the time cleanup runs, or if the fetch function you call does not pass the signal along (some wrappers drop it), the old promise can still resolve. The ignore check is a plain, in-memory test, so it works in every one of those cases. The React docs show the ignore flag as the basic fix and say cleanup should "either abort the fetch or ignore its result." We do both.

How we tested it

We ran this on Node 20 with React 19, @testing-library/react, and jsdom. A fake fetch makes one-letter queries slow (300 ms) and longer queries fast (20 ms), and it honors AbortSignal like the real one. Four tests:

test('buggy hook shows results for an old query', async () => {
  const log = []; const f = makeFakeFetch(log);
  const { rerender } = render(h(BuggyBox, { query: 'r', fetchImpl: f }));
  rerender(h(BuggyBox, { query: 're', fetchImpl: f }));
  await act(() => sleep(400));
  assert.equal(screen.getByTestId('out').textContent, 're -> r'); // box says "re", list is for "r"
});

test('fixed hook keeps the newest query and aborts the old one', async () => {
  const log = []; const f = makeFakeFetch(log);
  const { rerender } = render(h(FixedBox, { query: 'r', fetchImpl: f, delayMs: 0 }));
  await act(() => sleep(5));
  rerender(h(FixedBox, { query: 're', fetchImpl: f, delayMs: 0 }));
  await act(() => sleep(400));
  assert.equal(screen.getByTestId('out').textContent, 're -> re');
  assert.ok(log.includes('abort r'));
});

test('debounce: fast typing sends one request', async () => {
  // types r, re, rea, reac, react 30 ms apart with a 100 ms debounce
  assert.deepEqual(log, ['start react', 'finish react']);
});

test('ignore flag still protects when the old request cannot be aborted', async () => {
  // fetch wrapper drops the signal on purpose
  assert.ok(log.includes('finish r'));                               // old answer did arrive
  assert.equal(screen.getByTestId('out').textContent, 're -> re');   // but it was ignored
});

Result: 4 of 4 tests pass. The request logs from the run:

fixed log:    start r, abort r, start re, finish re
debounce log: start react, finish react

The first test proves the bug is real. The other three prove each part of the fix does its own job.

Trade-offs

  • Debounce adds delay. Every search waits for the pause before it starts. A longer delay sends fewer requests but feels slower. A shorter delay feels faster but sends more. Pick a value and measure it with real users.
  • Abort does not undo work. The server may have already run the query. Abort saves bandwidth and frees the browser connection. It does not roll back anything on the server, so never rely on abort for requests that change data.
  • Two requests in development are normal. With Strict Mode, React runs the effect, cleans it up, and runs it again in development. The docs say you will see two fetches in the Network tab, and the cleanup makes the first one harmless. In a production build there is one.
  • A data library may fit better. The React docs point out that caching, server-side fetching, and request waterfalls are still open problems with hand-written effects, and that frameworks and data libraries handle them. If your app already uses one, use its query hooks instead of this hook. If it does not, this hook is a small, clear step, and it is easy to replace later.
  • The ignore flag alone is enough for correctness. If you cannot abort (for example, an SDK that does not accept a signal), the flag still keeps the screen right. You lose only the network savings.

Make sure the stale results are gone

  1. Run the tests. The buggy test should pass (it proves the bug), and the three fixed tests should pass.
  2. Slow the network in the browser. Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, and pick a slow throttling preset. Type a word quickly. You should see older requests marked as cancelled, and only the last one should complete.
  3. Show the source query. Render "Showing results for: …" next to the list, as in the example. Type fast, then compare it with the input. They should always match once loading ends.
  4. Check the console. There should be no errors for aborted requests. If you see AbortError in your error UI, the catch block is not filtering it.

Official sources

  • React docs, You Might Not Need an Effect (section "Fetching data", race conditions and the ignore flag): https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect
  • React docs, Synchronizing with Effects (section "Fetching data", abort or ignore in cleanup, two fetches in development): https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects
  • React docs, useEffect reference (section "Fetching data with Effects"): https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect
  • MDN, AbortController: abort() method: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController/abort
  • MDN, AbortSignal: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal

title: API REST in PHP: integrare sistemi senza complicazioni
description:
Perché le API sono diventate indispensabili

Quasi nessuna applicazione vive isolata nel 2026. Un gestionale deve parlare con il sistema di fatturazione. Un e-commerce deve inviare ordini al magazzino. Un CRM deve ricevere lead dal sito web. Un'app mobile deve accedere agli stessi dati del pannello admin. Le API REST sono il modo standard per far comunicare sistemi diversi senza creare accoppiamenti fragili che si rompono al primo aggiornamento.

Progettare una buona API non significa solo esporre endpoint: significa pensare a chi li userà, come gestire gli errori in modo che il client possa reagire sensatamente, come evitare che un cambiamento rompa le integrazioni esistenti e come proteggere i dati in transito. Un'API ben progettata è un contratto tra sistemi — e come ogni contratto, deve essere chiaro, completo e rispettato.

Il valore di business delle API

Le API non sono solo un dettaglio tecnico — sono un asset strategico. Un'applicazione con API ben documentate può essere integrata con nuovi sistemi senza toccare il codice esistente. Questo significa che quando il business evolve — un nuovo canale di vendita, un nuovo partner, un nuovo strumento interno — l'integrazione è questione di settimane, non di mesi di sviluppo.

Principi che fanno la differenza in produzione

In teoria le API REST sono semplici: risorse, verbi HTTP, JSON. In pratica la differenza tra un'API che funziona e una che crea problemi sta nei dettagli implementativi che emergono solo in produzione, sotto carico reale, con dati reali e integrazioni reali.

Design degli endpoint

Gli endpoint devono essere coerenti e prevedibili. Se l'endpoint per gli ordini è /api/v1/orders, quello per i clienti sarà /api/v1/customers — non /api/getClients o /clienti/lista. La coerenza riduce la curva di apprendimento per chi integra e diminuisce gli errori. Usa i verbi HTTP come previsto: GET per leggere, POST per creare, PUT/PATCH per aggiornare, DELETE per eliminare.

Gestione degli errori

I codici di stato HTTP esistono per un motivo: usali correttamente. Un 404 quando la risorsa non esiste, un 422 quando i dati non sono validi, un 401 quando l'autenticazione fallisce, un 429 quando il rate limit è stato superato. Ogni risposta di errore deve includere un messaggio leggibile per l'umano e un codice strutturato per la macchina:

  • Codici di stato HTTP corretti: non restituire sempre 200 con un campo "success: false" — è un anti-pattern che complica ogni integrazione
  • Messaggi di errore utili: "Il campo email è obbligatorio" è meglio di "Errore di validazione"
  • Codici di errore macchina: un codice come "VALIDATION_ERROR" o "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND" permette al client di gestire l'errore programmaticamente
  • Dettagli per il debugging: in sviluppo, includi stack trace e contesto; in produzione, solo il necessario

Autenticazione e sicurezza

L'autenticazione API è un'area dove i compromessi costano caro. Token JWT con scadenza breve e refresh token sono lo standard per la maggior parte dei casi. Le chiavi API statiche vanno bene per integrazioni server-to-server a basso rischio, ma non per accessi da client. Mai trasmettere credenziali nel query string — finiscono nei log del server, nella cronologia del browser e in ogni proxy intermedio.

Oltre all'autenticazione, considera l'autorizzazione: non basta verificare chi sei, serve verificare cosa puoi fare. Un'API ben progettata implementa controlli granulari: questo token può leggere gli ordini ma non cancellarli, quest'altro può creare clienti ma solo nel proprio account.

Versionamento: proteggere le integrazioni esistenti

Quando l'API cambia, le integrazioni vecchie non devono rompersi. Il versionamento è il meccanismo che lo garantisce. L'approccio più comune è includere la versione nell'URL (/api/v1/, /api/v2/), ma ci sono alternative valide come il versionamento via header.

La regola pratica: mantieni la versione precedente funzionante per almeno 6-12 mesi dopo il rilascio della nuova. Comunica le deprecation in anticipo, fornisci guide di migrazione e dai tempo ai consumer di adeguarsi. Rompere un'integrazione senza preavviso è il modo più veloce per perdere la fiducia dei partner.

Performance e rate limiting

Un'API in produzione deve gestire il carico in modo prevedibile. Il rate limiting protegge il server da uso improprio — intenzionale o accidentale — senza penalizzare l'uso normale. Implementalo con header standard (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset) così i client possono regolarsi autonomamente.

Per le performance, considera:

  • Paginazione: non restituire mai dataset interi — usa cursor-based pagination per dataset grandi
  • Caching: usa ETag e Last-Modified per evitare trasferimenti inutili
  • Compressione: abilita gzip per risposte JSON grandi
  • Selezione campi: permetti al client di richiedere solo i campi necessari (?fields=id,name,email)
  • Eager loading: offri la possibilità di includere relazioni nella stessa richiesta per evitare il problema N+1

Documentazione: il ponte tra chi sviluppa e chi integra

Un'API senza documentazione è un'API inutilizzabile. La documentazione API deve includere: endpoint disponibili, parametri accettati, formato delle risposte, codici di errore, esempi concreti. Strumenti come OpenAPI/Swagger generano documentazione interattiva che permette di testare le chiamate direttamente dal browser.

Un'API ben progettata in PHP diventa un asset a lungo termine. Permette integrazioni future senza riscrivere il backend e apre possibilità che al momento del lancio non erano nemmeno previste. E il costo di farla bene dall'inizio è una frazione del costo di aggiustarla dopo, quando decine di client dipendono da un design sbagliato.
