title: A cancelled query can destroy your database connection
description:
Two short deadlines took down Inngest's database path twice in one afternoon, and neither was misconfigured. They expired exactly on time. That is what made the failure so effective.

On 10 October 2026, both of Inngest's connection poolers lost every connection to their primary database at 14:00 UTC. They lost them again at 15:30. Run scheduling and queue processing stalled for most accounts in both windows, 14:00–14:48 and 15:30–16:25, and the mitigation that followed caused intermittent delays until 04:17 the next morning.

The report is worth reading because the mechanism generalises to any stack that puts a connection pooler with a wait queue between the application and Postgres.

The sequence, in four steps

  1. A frequently used lookup carried a short deadline.
  2. The deadline expired while its query was still queued inside PgBouncer, waiting for a database connection. The pgx driver cancelled the query and closed its client connection.
  3. PgBouncer had nothing running to cancel, because the query had never been handed a server connection. It later ran the abandoned query on a database connection.
  4. It then closed that connection entirely instead of returning it to the pool.

Step 4 is the whole failure. The client's timeout cost the system a database connection, not a request, and the cost landed after the client had stopped watching. No single request looked expensive. Individually, every one of these is a wasted query. Collectively they are a pool that empties itself.

Two amplifiers arrived at the same moment. Both collapses began at the top and bottom of the hour, when cron-scheduled work roughly triples the query rate, and a newly rolled out set of lookups was failing in large numbers, adding cancellations to a pool that was already busy. Inngest reproduced the behaviour in a test environment.

Why restarting and resizing both failed

Restarting the poolers did not reliably recover them. Raising the pool size did not help either. The report is explicit on why: opening connections was the bottleneck, not the pool limit.

Each pooler opens new database connections one at a time. So the refill path is serial while the destruction path is parallel. As a steady-state sketch rather than a model of this incident, if usable connections are destroyed at d per second and a pooler needs t seconds on average to establish a replacement, the refill ceiling is 1/t and the pool drains whenever:

d > 1/t

The sketch assumes constant destruction and handshake times, and it ignores the point at which the pooler stops trying. Inngest published neither number, so treat this as the shape of the constraint rather than a measurement of it. To see the shape: at 100 ms per connection a single pooler refills at ten per second; at 50 ms, twenty.

The second collapse ended by changing paths, not by growing the pool. The team moved all services onto poolers run alongside the database by the database provider, and processing recovered between 16:10 and 16:25.

The fix that caused a second incident

The new route reached the database through NAT gateways, and some connections through those gateways were silently dropped. Queries on a dropped connection hung for up to 16 minutes before failing, which stalled processing intermittently and most visibly hit cron functions. Customers reported delays at 03:01 on 11 October; the affected service moved back to the original poolers at 04:17, and gateway routing was improved on 12 October.

Sixteen minutes of silent hang is worse than a fast failure for a scheduler. A connection that errors invites a retry. One that simply stops answering consumes a worker slot and a deadline, and you learn about it from a customer. A failover drill that measures successful requests will not catch this. One that measures how long a hung connection stays hung will.

The contract that broke underneath it

The part of the report with the longest reach is not about pools. Internal failures counted against functions' configured retries, and a step that failed permanently on an internal error left its run in Running instead of marking it failed. onFailure handlers did not fire. Functions waiting on that run through step.invoke were not notified.

That is a broken guarantee, not an availability number. A durable execution engine sells the promise that every run reaches a terminal state and that failure handlers run. Under this bug the engine could hold a run in Running indefinitely, after spending the retry budget it was given — the customer's allowance consumed by the platform's own faults, and the transition that would have reported it never sent.

The recovery instructions confirm the state of those runs: they will not continue on their own, and customers can cancel and replay them, with the caveat that a replay starts from the beginning, so completed steps run again. Anyone with non-idempotent side effects in a completed step had a decision the platform could not make for them.

Four things to check in your own stack

Alert on net connection drain, not pool utilisation. Graph opens and closes per pooler per second, and alert when the close rate exceeds the open rate for a sustained interval. A pool at 30% with a negative slope is in more danger than one at 70% that is stable, and utilisation alone shows neither.

Bound the wait, not just the query. PgBouncer's query_wait_timeout disconnects a client whose query has not been assigned a server within the limit.

; pgbouncer.ini — the ordering matters more than the value
query_wait_timeout = 5    ; must sit below your client's own deadline

The point of setting it below the client deadline is to remove the queued entry before the client gives up. That is the reasoning, not proof that it preserves backend connections. Inngest describes the pooler running the abandoned query and then closing that connection; an independent load test from July 2025 puts the waste a step earlier, with the pooler finishing a login for a client that has already gone and discarding the fresh backend connection. The same engineer reported that lowering the timeout helped without being enough on its own. Test it against your driver's real cancellation path before adopting it.

Know what your driver does on cancel. In pgx v5, the thread reports replacing the default cancellation behaviour with a context watcher handler that sets a connection deadline instead of closing immediately, and describes the effect in their load test as large. If your code path cancels queued queries, this is the boundary to inspect.

Fence the lease before you force a terminal state. If you mark a run failed because its step lease expired without a heartbeat, late writes from a worker that is still running can land afterwards, and a replay produces a second copy of the side effects. Mark it failed only when the engine can reject writes from the old lease, or when the step is confirmed not to be in flight.

What the report does not establish

Inngest disclosed no connection counts, handshake timings, pool sizes or customer totals, so the arithmetic here is the report's timestamps and nothing more. The 44-minute, 48-minute and 55-minute windows are my subtraction on its UTC boundaries, not figures it published.

The report also links pgx issue 1780 as the known interaction behind the collapse. I read that issue: it was opened on 26 October 2023 and was still open at its latest comment in February 2026. The upstream record offers a compatible description of the boundary and no confirmed root cause, so Inngest's account is a well-documented instance of an unresolved interaction rather than evidence that it is fixed.

The structural change is the one to watch. Inngest is consolidating onto a single data centre acting as one cell, which removes the cross-data-centre failure class behind the 9 October incident. That trades one failure shape for another: fewer paths that can break, and more consequence when one does.

Sources

  • Inngest: Incident report for October 9 and 10, 2026
  • jackc/pgx issue 1780

Thanks for reading :)

title: AI UI Tools Skip Design Basics, Leading to Unpolished Products Despite Beginner-Friendly Marketing
description:
Introduction: The Rise of AI in UI Design

The design landscape is shifting. AI-generated UI tools and skill packs are exploding in popularity, marketed as the fast track to polished interfaces. Friends are ditching Figma, skipping prototyping, and heading straight to production, armed with AI "skills" promising instant design prowess. But this shortcut comes at a cost – a cost measured in inconsistency, lack of intentionality, and ultimately, a degraded user experience.

Let’s break down the mechanics of this trend. AI tools, while impressive, are essentially pattern matchers. They analyze existing designs, identify recurring elements (buttons, spacing, color palettes), and generate variations based on prompts. This works well for senior designers who understand the "why" behind these patterns – the principles of hierarchy, visual weight, and user psychology. They can guide the AI, refine its output, and ensure consistency.

For beginners, however, it’s a different story. Feeding an AI terms like "spring easing" or "vertical rhythm" without understanding their underlying principles is like handing a scalpel to someone who’s never dissected a frog. The AI might produce something that looks "design-y," but it lacks the intentionality, the "why" that makes good design truly effective.

The Breakdown: Why AI Shortcuts Fail Beginners

  • Missing the Feedback Loop: Design is iterative. In Figma, you experiment, compare versions side-by-side, and refine based on visual and functional feedback. AI tools often bypass this crucial step. Changes are made directly in code, where every tweak is costly in time and effort. The result? Designs that are "good enough" but rarely great, lacking the polish that comes from multiple iterations.
  • Black Box Decision-Making: AI tools make decisions about spacing, color, and interaction based on patterns, not principles. A beginner might get a visually appealing button, but they won’t understand why it works. When a design element needs adjustment, they’re left prompting the AI again, hoping for a better outcome. This lack of understanding hinders their ability to troubleshoot, adapt, and grow as designers.
  • The Illusion of Mastery: Skill packs and prompt bundles promise "beginner-friendly" design, but they often teach vocabulary without context. Knowing the term "damping" doesn’t mean you understand how it affects user perception of speed and responsiveness. True design knowledge comes from experimentation, from feeling the difference between a jarring transition and a smooth one. AI shortcuts bypass this tactile learning, creating a generation of designers who can parrot design jargon but lack the ability to apply it effectively.

The Long-Term Risk: A Design Landscape Lacking Intentionality

The proliferation of AI-driven design shortcuts poses a significant risk to the craft. If designers rely solely on AI to generate interfaces, we’ll see a homogenization of design, a landscape dominated by generic, uninspired solutions. The nuanced understanding of user needs, the deliberate choices that make a design truly exceptional, will be lost.

Imagine a world where every website feels like it was assembled from a kit, where every interaction lacks the spark of human intention. This is the future we face if we prioritize speed and convenience over the foundational principles of good design.

The Optimal Solution: AI as a Tool, Not a Teacher

AI has immense potential as a design tool, but it should augment, not replace, human creativity and understanding. Here’s the optimal approach:

  • If you’re a beginner: Resist the siren song of AI shortcuts. Learn the fundamentals – typography, color theory, layout principles, user psychology. Experiment in Figma, iterate relentlessly, and develop your design intuition. Once you understand the "why," AI can become a powerful tool for accelerating your workflow, not a crutch.
  • If you’re an experienced designer: Use AI strategically. Leverage its pattern recognition capabilities to generate initial concepts, explore variations, and automate repetitive tasks. But always maintain control over the final design decisions, ensuring they align with your vision and user needs.

Remember, AI is a tool, not a teacher. True design mastery comes from understanding the principles, from the tactile experience of shaping interfaces, and from the relentless pursuit of excellence. Don’t let AI shortcuts rob you of the joy and satisfaction of creating truly great design.

The Learning Bypass: Consequences and Risks

The rise of AI-generated UI design tools and skill packs has introduced a dangerous shortcut in the design process. Marketed as beginner-friendly, these tools promise professional-level results without the need for foundational learning. However, this bypass comes at a steep cost, leading to inconsistent, unpolished products and a generation of designers lacking essential skills. Here’s how the mechanism breaks down:

1. Pattern Matching vs. Principle-Driven Design

AI tools operate as pattern matchers, analyzing existing designs to replicate elements like buttons, spacing, and color palettes based on prompts. While effective for senior designers who use these tools to augment their understanding of principles like hierarchy and visual weight, beginners lack the context to guide or refine AI output. The result? Designs that are visually disjointed, as observed in the source case where landing pages, settings pages, and dashboards feel like separate products due to inconsistent buttons, spacing, and hover effects. The causal chain here is clear: absence of foundational knowledge → reliance on AI patterns → lack of uniformity and intentionality.

2. The Feedback Loop Gap

Traditional design tools like Figma facilitate an iterative refinement process, allowing designers to experiment, compare versions, and polish their work. AI tools, however, bypass this feedback loop, producing "good enough" designs that lack the tactile learning essential for mastery. For instance, adjusting an easing curve by 2px to achieve smoothness is a physical, iterative process that AI cannot replicate. Beginners who skip this step miss out on the muscle memory of design, leading to a superficial understanding of concepts like damping or optical alignment. The risk? Designs that are technically correct but lack soul, as the designer never internalizes the why behind each decision.

3. Black Box Decision-Making

AI tools make decisions based on patterns, not principles. This black box approach creates a critical failure point: when something goes wrong, designers don’t know how to fix it. For example, if a button’s radius or color feels off, the AI’s pattern-based decision provides no insight into the underlying issue. The designer is left to prompt again and hope, rather than troubleshoot with intent. This mechanism of risk formation—pattern reliance → lack of diagnostic ability → repeated subpar outcomes—undermines long-term skill development and product quality.

4. The Illusion of Mastery

Skill packs and prompt bundles often teach jargon without context, creating an illusion of mastery. Beginners memorize terms like "spring easing" or "60-30-10 color rule" without understanding their application. This is akin to learning the words for tools without ever using them. The causal chain here is insidious: memorization of terms → false confidence → application without understanding → subpar design. For example, knowing the term "damping" doesn’t teach you when a bounce feels cheap versus smooth—only hands-on experimentation does.

5. Long-Term Risks: Homogenization and Devaluation

If this trend continues, the design field risks homogenization, as AI-generated patterns dominate over intentional, principle-driven design. Products will lack the nuanced user understanding and intentionality that come from foundational learning. Worse, the craft of design will be devalued, as shortcuts replace skill. The mechanism of this risk is clear: over-reliance on AI → loss of unique design voice → decline in product integrity.

Optimal Solutions: When and How to Use AI

  • For Beginners: Prioritize learning fundamentals like typography, color theory, and user psychology. Use tools like Figma for iterative experimentation. Rule: If you don’t understand the principle, don’t use the AI tool.
  • For Experienced Designers: Leverage AI for pattern recognition, initial concepts, and automation, but retain control over final decisions. Rule: Use AI to augment, not replace, your expertise.

The key insight? AI is a tool, not a teacher. True design mastery requires understanding principles, tactile experience, and a relentless pursuit of excellence. Bypassing this process with AI shortcuts may save time in the short term, but the long-term cost to product quality and designer skill is too high to ignore.

Case Studies: Real-World Implications

1. The Fragmented Product: No Uniformity, No System

A designer I know switched to an AI UI tool, bypassing Figma entirely. The result? A landing page, settings page, and dashboard that feel like three separate products. Buttons vary in shape, spacing is inconsistent, and hover effects differ across pages. The mechanism here is clear: AI tools generate elements based on pattern matching, not a unified design system. Without a human designer enforcing consistency, the AI pulls from disparate sources, creating a Frankenstein product. The risk? Users perceive the product as unprofessional and disjointed, increasing bounce rates.

2. The Memory File Myth: Consistency Without Intentionality

One solution proposed is to use a "memory file" to force consistency. But this is a band-aid fix. The AI decides the button radius, the grey shade, the hover effect—decisions made without understanding why. When a change is needed, the designer is blind. The causal chain is: AI-driven decisions → lack of intentionality → inability to troubleshoot. The memory file doesn’t teach why a design choice works; it just enforces it. The risk? Designers lose the ability to make informed decisions, leading to brittle designs that break under pressure.

3. The Jargon Trap: Memorization Without Mastery

Beginners are buying skill packs that teach terms like "spring easing" and "optical alignment" without context. They memorize the words but don’t understand the mechanics. For example, "damping" isn’t just a term—it’s a physical concept borrowed from mechanics, where a system’s oscillations are reduced over time. Without tactile experience, beginners can’t feel the difference between cheap and smooth transitions. The mechanism here is: memorization → false confidence → misapplication. The risk? Designs that are technically correct but lack soul, failing to engage users emotionally.

4. The Production Code Trap: First Draft Becomes Final Product

Skipping Figma and going straight to production code is a common mistake. Every change in code costs time and resources, so the first AI-generated version often ships as-is. In Figma, designers iterate, placing five versions side by side and refining. The causal chain is: lack of iteration → lack of refinement → subpar final product. The risk? Products that are "good enough" but never great, failing to stand out in a competitive market.

5. The Course Conundrum: Teaching Jargon, Not Principles

Courses marketed as "beginner-friendly" teach design vocabulary to feed into AI tools. But vocabulary without context is useless. For example, the 60-30-10 color rule isn’t just a ratio—it’s a principle derived from how the human eye perceives contrast and hierarchy. Beginners apply the rule without understanding its purpose, leading to visually unbalanced designs. The mechanism is: superficial knowledge → misapplication → poor outcomes. The risk? A generation of designers who can’t think critically, relying on AI to make decisions for them.

6. The Homogenization Risk: Losing the Unique Design Voice

Over-reliance on AI leads to homogenized designs. AI pulls from the same pool of patterns, creating generic interfaces that lack personality. For example, every button generated by the AI might follow the same radius and shadow because it’s the most common pattern in its dataset. The causal chain is: pattern matching → lack of diversity → homogenization. The risk? Products lose their unique voice, failing to differentiate themselves in a crowded market.

Optimal Solutions: When and How to Use AI

AI is a tool, not a teacher. For beginners, prioritize learning fundamentals first. Use Figma to experiment with typography, color theory, and spacing. Only after understanding these principles should AI be introduced as an augmentation tool. For experienced designers, AI can automate repetitive tasks but should never replace critical decision-making. The rule is: if you don’t understand why a design choice works, don’t let AI make it for you. The optimal solution is to use AI for pattern recognition and initial concepts, but retain control over final decisions to ensure alignment with user needs and brand identity.

Professional Judgment: The Future of Design

If this trend continues, the design craft will be devalued. Shortcuts will replace skill, and intentionality will be lost. The mechanism is clear: over-reliance on AI → loss of foundational skills → decline in product integrity. To avoid this, designers must resist the temptation of quick fixes and invest in tactile learning. The key insight is: AI can’t teach you to feel the difference between good and great design—only experience can.

Expert Opinions: Balancing AI and Human Skill

The rise of AI-driven UI tools has sparked a critical debate in the design community. While these tools promise efficiency and accessibility, they often bypass the foundational learning that underpins great design. As a designer who’s witnessed peers trade Figma for AI-generated skill packs, I’ve seen firsthand how this shortcut mentality leads to unpolished, inconsistent products. Here’s the breakdown—mechanism by mechanism—of why this trend is risky and how to balance AI with human skill.

The Mechanism of AI’s Pattern Matching

AI tools operate as pattern matchers, analyzing existing designs to replicate elements like buttons, spacing, and color palettes. This works well for senior designers who use AI as a starting point, refining outputs with their understanding of hierarchy, visual weight, and user psychology. However, for beginners, this process is a black box. Without foundational knowledge, they rely on AI’s pattern-based decisions, leading to designs that are technically correct but visually disjointed.

Causal Chain: Absence of foundational knowledge → reliance on AI patterns → inconsistent, unintentional designs.

The Feedback Loop Gap

Traditional tools like Figma enable iterative refinement, allowing designers to experiment, compare versions, and build muscle memory for concepts like damping or optical alignment. AI, however, produces “good enough” designs without this tactile learning. The result? Beginners miss the deep understanding that comes from moving an element 2px and feeling it “sit right.”

Risk Mechanism: Lack of iteration → lack of muscle memory → inability to internalize design principles.

The Jargon Trap

Skill packs and courses teach terms like “spring easing” or “60-30-10 color rule” without context. Beginners memorize these words but lack the tactile experience to apply them effectively. For example, knowing “damping” doesn’t mean you understand when a bounce feels too stiff or too loose. This illusion of mastery leads to misapplication and emotionally unengaging designs.

Causal Chain: Memorization of terms → false confidence → application without understanding → poor outcomes.

The Production Code Trap

When designers skip prototyping in Figma and go straight to production, every change becomes costly. The first AI-generated output often ships as the final product, lacking the refinement that comes from iteration. This first-draft-as-final approach results in subpar designs that fail to stand out.

Risk Mechanism: Lack of iteration → lack of refinement → subpar final product → failure to differentiate.

Optimal AI Use: Rules for Beginners and Experts

To balance AI and human skill, follow these evidence-backed rules:

  • For Beginners: Prioritize learning fundamentals like typography, color theory, and spacing in Figma. Avoid AI until you understand why a design choice works. Rule: If you don’t understand the principle, don’t let AI make the decision.
  • For Experienced Designers: Use AI for automation of repetitive tasks, not critical decision-making. Retain control over final design choices to ensure alignment with user needs and brand identity.

Professional Judgment: The Future of Design

AI is a tool, not a teacher. Over-reliance on it risks homogenization, as designs become generic and lack a unique voice. The craft of design is devalued when shortcuts replace skill. To avoid this, invest in tactile learning, iterate relentlessly, and retain human judgment in every decision.

Key Insight: AI cannot teach the difference between good and great design—only experience can. If X (you lack foundational knowledge) → use Y (traditional tools and iterative learning) before introducing AI.

Conclusion: Rethinking AI’s Role in Design Education

The rise of AI-driven UI tools and skill packs has created a paradox: they promise to democratize design but risk devaluing it. By bypassing foundational learning, these tools produce technically correct yet emotionally unengaging designs. The mechanism is clear: AI operates as a pattern matcher, not a principle-based designer. It replicates elements like button radii or color palettes without understanding why these choices work. Beginners, lacking tactile experience, memorize jargon like “spring easing” or “60-30-10 color rule” but fail to internalize their causal impact on user experience.

Consider the feedback loop gap: in Figma, designers iterate, building muscle memory for spacing, alignment, and transitions. AI, however, produces “good enough” outputs, skipping this critical process. The result? Designs that are brittle—unable to adapt or troubleshoot when issues arise. For instance, if an AI-generated button lacks visual hierarchy, a beginner cannot diagnose why it fails because the decision was never theirs to make. They’re left prompting the AI again, hoping for a better outcome.

The long-term risk is homogenization. AI draws from common patterns in its dataset, producing generic designs that lack differentiation. This isn’t just an aesthetic issue—it’s a business risk. Products fail to stand out, leading to higher bounce rates and lost user engagement. The mechanism here is straightforward: over-reliance on AI → loss of intentionality → decline in product integrity.

So, how do we fix this? The optimal solution is not to abandon AI but to reposition it as a tool, not a teacher. For beginners, the rule is clear: if you don’t understand why a design choice works, don’t let AI make it. Prioritize learning fundamentals—typography, color theory, spacing—in Figma. Iterate relentlessly. Only introduce AI after you’ve built the muscle memory to refine its output.

For experienced designers, AI can automate repetitive tasks like generating initial layouts or color palettes. But retain control over critical decisions. Use AI for pattern recognition, not as a crutch. The key insight? AI cannot teach the difference between good and great design—only experience and tactile learning can.

In conclusion, AI in design education is a double-edged sword. Used wisely, it augments creativity. Misused, it undermines it. The choice is ours: invest in skill, not shortcuts. Because in design, as in life, the devil is in the details—and AI doesn’t know how to sweat them.

title: HTTP entre pares
description:
Na série IPFS com o Nabu, a API (Application Programming Interface) HTTP do post anterior escuta na máquina local. Este post leva um pedido HTTP até outro par, sem que esse par tenha um endereço público na internet.

A proposta

Dois programas já sabem falar HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): um verbo, um caminho, cabeçalhos e um corpo. Um deles está atrás de NAT (Network Address Translation, a reescrita de endereços do roteador). Abrir uma porta no roteador, ou alugar um servidor para os dois se encontrarem, repete o problema que o libp2p já resolve nos posts de transporte e de alcance.

A proposta é carregar o pedido e a resposta HTTP num stream libp2p. O encontro dos pares continua sendo por PeerId (o identificador do par). O conteúdo do stream continua sendo HTTP comum.

A Demonstração

O protocolo se chama /http. Um lado disca o outro pelo PeerId, abre um stream e escreve um pedido HTTP completo: método, URL (Uniform Resource Locator) relativo, headers e corpo. O outro lado trata o pedido e devolve o status, os headers e o corpo. O tratamento pode ser a própria aplicação, ou um encaminhamento para um servidor HTTP comum em localhost. Visto de fora, o par remoto parece um servidor. Visto da rede, é mais um protocolo no mesmo host que já fala Bitswap e Kademlia.

Quem chama precisa do endereço do par. Se o caderno já tem multiaddrs, a discagem usa essa lista. Se não tem, a DHT (Distributed Hash Table) procura o par, como no post da Kademlia. Um proxy local traduz um caminho /p2p/<peerid>/http/<caminho> nessa discagem. Um cliente HTTP comum, na mesma máquina, fala com 127.0.0.1 e não precisa saber o que é um PeerId. O proxy corta o PeerId do caminho, acha o par e escreve o resto do caminho no pedido que segue pelo stream.

flowchart LR
  client[localHttpClient] --> proxy[p2pProxy]
  proxy --> dht[addressOrDht]
  dht --> stream[httpStream]
  stream --> app[remoteHandlerOrLocalhost]

No Nabu

HttpProtocol, em src/main/java/org/peergos/protocol/http/HttpProtocol.java, registra o identificador /http no Binding. Há dois construtores de binding. Um recebe um SocketAddress e encaminha cada pedido para esse host e porta. O outro recebe um HttpRequestProcessor, a função da aplicação. O corpo máximo tratado de uma vez é MAX_BODY_SIZE, 8 MiB. O comentário no código marca isso como limite temporário, no lugar de um fluxo contínuo. Sender.send enfileira um future, escreve o FullHttpRequest no stream e completa quando onMessage copia status, headers e corpo para um DefaultFullHttpResponse. O stream fecha em seguida. onClosed, onReadClosed e onException falham os futures que ainda estavam na fila, com a mensagem de stream fechado ou a exceção original.

EmbeddedIpfs.build só acrescenta o protocolo quando a aplicação passa um handler:

Optional<HttpProtocol.Binding> httpHandler = handler.map(HttpProtocol.Binding::new);
httpHandler.ifPresent(protocols::add);

O campo p2pHttp do EmbeddedIpfs fica vazio sem isso. Bitswap e Kademlia seguem normais. Quem for discar mais tarde usa ipfs.p2pHttp.get() e recebe vazio se o build não registrou o protocolo.

No processo Nabu, o handler existe quando o config tem Addresses.ProxyTarget. proxyHandler chama HttpProtocol.proxyRequest para o host e a porta desse multiaddr, e passa o PeerId remoto. O mesmo processo publica HttpProxyHandler em /p2p/, a constante HttpProxyService.API_URL. O comentário do handler descreve o caminho: /p2p/$target_node_id/http/$target_path. O handler corta o prefixo /p2p/, separa o PeerId do caminho que segue, e pede ao HttpProxyService a discagem.

HttpProxyService.getAddresses olha o caderno do host. Se a coleção daquele PeerId não está vazia, devolve esses multiaddrs. Se está vazia, lookupAddresses chama dht.findClosestPeers pedindo um resultado. O comentário do método explica o segundo argumento useCached: a DHT responde uma busca de par a partir do caderno quando pode, e isso não serve para quem está tentando escapar de um endereço morto. useCached falso força a consulta. O resultado fica com o par cujo id coincide com o alvo. Endereço velho, de um par que mudou de rede, faria o proxy insistir num destino que não atende.

O buffer de 128 MiB do yamux, do post de transportes, existe por causa daqui. O yamux limita o buffer por conexão. Uma resposta perto de MAX_BODY_SIZE já ocupa uma fatia grande. Três respostas de 4 MB na mesma conexão estouravam o padrão de 10 MiB, e o muxer resetava os streams. writeAndFlush não devolve future, então o reset aparecia só como resposta que não chegava.

O exemplo mínimo de duas pessoas trocando mensagens por esse caminho é o nabu-chat: os PeerIds se encontram fora da banda, a conexão é libp2p, e as mensagens são pedidos HTTP. O módulo examples deste repositório tem um Chat com a mesma ideia. Cada linha vira um POST / no stream /http, e o handler do outro lado imprime received:. O próximo post o executa.

O que fica de fora: /http não é um gateway de conteúdo IPFS. Ele não resolve CID nem IPNS. Carrega HTTP opaco entre dois pares que já se encontram pelo libp2p. O corpo de 8 MiB é o teto desta implementação. Uma resposta maior precisa de outro desenho.

Nesta série

O anterior é A API HTTP e como rodar o Nabu. O próximo é Os exemplos do repositório.

title: Compliance documents are now available in Team settings
description:
A new Compliance section in Team settings lets you preview and download Vercel's compliance documents directly in the dashboard. These include attestations like SOC 2 Type 2, security policies, and other security documents that are available through the Trust Center.

You can select a single document, an entire attestation, or multiple documents, and download them together as a single zip archive. The Trust Center remains available for additional security information. Vercel's compliance documents are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Learn more in the compliance documentation.

title: I replaced six React Native picker libraries with one, and it has zero native code
description:
Every React Native app I've worked on ended up with the same pile of packages:

  • @react-native-community/datetimepicker for dates and times
  • react-native-calendars because the date picker can't do ranges
  • a dropdown library, because the native picker can't search
  • a country picker, then a phone input on top of it
  • an emoji keyboard for the chat screen
  • a bottom sheet to put half of these in

Six APIs, six looks, some of them native modules that need a rebuild, and most of them broken or missing on the web.

So I built React Native Pickers: one package with all of them, written in plain JavaScript on React Native's own APIs. No native code, no dependencies.

What's in it

  • Wheels: the 3D iOS wheel, with looping, disabled rows and tap-to-type
  • Dates: a calendar (single day, range, multiple days, several ranges) or day / month / year wheels; a month picker; a week strip
  • Time: wheels, the Material clock dial, or columns to click; durations
  • Date and time together
  • Select: search, multi-select with chips, groups, icons and server search
  • Country: about 250 countries with flag emoji, dialing codes and names in the user's language
  • Phone number: a country code button, formatting as you type, an E.164 value
  • Emoji: 1,923 emojis with search, skin tones and recently used
  • Color: iOS's grid / spectrum / sliders, Google's swatch circles, or the browser's spectrum
  • Segmented control and chips
  • Bottom sheets and form fields to put any of them in

What using it looks like 

import { useState } from 'react';
import { View } from 'react-native';
import { DatePickerField, SelectPicker, TimePickerField } from '@elik56a/react-native-pickers';
import type { DateRange } from '@elik56a/react-native-pickers';

const ROOMS = [
  { label: 'Single', value: 'single' },
  { label: 'Double', value: 'double' },
  { label: 'Suite', value: 'suite' },
];

export default function Booking() {
  const [stay, setStay] = useState<DateRange>({ start: null, end: null });
  const [arrival, setArrival] = useState<Date | undefined>();
  const [room, setRoom] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <View style={{ gap: 16, padding: 16 }}>
      <DatePickerField label="Stay" mode="range" value={stay} onConfirm={setStay} minDate={new Date()} />
      <TimePickerField label="Arrival" value={arrival} onConfirm={setArrival} minuteInterval={15} />
      <SelectPicker label="Room" options={ROOMS} value={room} onChange={setRoom} />
    </View>
  );
}

Each field opens its picker in a bottom sheet on a phone and a dropdown in the browser, and shows the chosen value formatted for the user's locale. Every component is controlled the same way: value and onChange (or onConfirm for the sheets), and onChange only fires when the user changes something.

It looks native on each platform

This is the part I cared about most. By default each picker takes the design of the platform it runs on:

  • iOS: wheels, a tinted selected day, Cancel and Done in the sheet header
  • Android: Material Design, with the clock dial, outlined fields with floating labels, and OK at the bottom
  • Web: a compact calendar, time columns to click, dropdowns, and a focus ring

If your app has its own look and you want the same pickers everywhere, it's one line:

<PickersProvider design="ios">
  <App />
</PickersProvider>

Dark mode follows the system, and every color, radius and font comes from theme tokens you can override. Every visual part also has a style slot, and render props let you replace a day cell, an option row or the whole field.

Why zero native code matters

Everything is built on React Native's core APIs: Animated with the native driver, PanResponder, FlatList and Modal. No Reanimated, no Gesture Handler, no SVG. That means:

  • it works in Expo Go, with no development build and no config plugin
  • it ships in over-the-air updates, because there's nothing native to rebuild
  • it works on React Native Web, which is where most picker libraries fall short
  • it doesn't break when your React Native version changes

Things I didn't want to install separately

A few details that usually mean another package:

  • Prices and dots on calendar days. markedDates takes a label and up to three colored dots per day, so a booking calendar can show $129 under each night.
  • Server search. Give SelectPicker a loadOptions(query) that returns a promise; it debounces, shows a loader and ignores stale answers.
  • Phone numbers without libphonenumber. PhoneField groups digits the way about 50 countries write them, drops the leading 0 people type at home, and reads the country from a pasted +44… number. The value is always E.164, like +447911123456.
  • Accessibility. Wheels are adjustable for VoiceOver and TalkBack, days announce their full date, and on the web you can use every picker from the keyboard.

Coming from another library?

There's a prop-by-prop migration guide for 12 libraries: @react-native-community/datetimepicker, react-native-date-picker, react-native-modal-datetime-picker, react-native-calendars, @react-native-picker/picker, react-native-picker-select, react-native-dropdown-picker, react-native-element-dropdown, react-native-country-picker-modal, react-native-phone-number-input, rn-emoji-keyboard and @react-native-segmented-control/segmented-control. Most of them come down to renaming a few props.

Try it 

npx expo install @elik56a/react-native-pickers
  • Docs with live, editable examples: https://react-native-pickers.dev/
  • Showcase of real screens (booking, flights, alarm, chat, checkout), switchable between iOS, Android and web: https://react-native-pickers.dev/showcase
  • GitHub: https://github.com/elik56a/react-native-pickers

It's MIT licensed and I'm working on it actively. I'd really like to hear what's missing, what breaks in your app, and what you'd need before using it in production. Comments here or issues on GitHub both work, and a star helps other people find it.

title: GST Reconciliation Software: GSTBot
description:
The GSTR‑2B Reconciliation Engine

GSTBot solves the most labor‑intensive part of the Indian GST workflow: reconciling the purchase register with the GSTR‑2B return that the tax department publishes each month. Manual reconciliation is a month‑long exercise for small‑business finance teams; GSTBot replaces that with a deterministic, configurable algorithm that runs in seconds. This is where gst reconciliation software pays off in practice.

The problem

A typical SMB records hundreds of purchase invoices in a spreadsheet or a PDF collection. The tax portal provides a GSTR‑2B file that lists every invoice the supplier has filed. The two datasets rarely match perfectly: amounts may be rounded, vendor names may differ, and some invoices may be missing from the portal due to delays. Traditional tools insist on exact string matches and then flag every deviation as an exception, leaving users to decide what to do next.

The solution

GSTBot’s reconciliation engine uses a tolerance‑based matching strategy. Instead of requiring an exact amount, it accepts any GSTR‑2B line whose amount differs by no more than a configurable percentage. The default tolerance is 0.01 (1 %), but finance staff can adjust it in the UI or via the RECONCILIATION_TOLERANCE environment variable.

# FastAPI endpoint that kicks off a reconciliation job
@app.post("/reconcile")
async def reconcile(request: ReconcileRequest, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    task = celery_app.send_task(
        "tasks.reconcile_invoices",
        args=[request.invoice_ids],
        kwargs={"tolerance": request.tolerance},
    )
    return {"task_id": task.id}

The heavy lifting is performed in a Celery worker so the API remains responsive.

# tasks.py – the core reconciliation logic
@celery_app.task
def reconcile_invoices(invoice_ids, tolerance=0.01):
    invoices = db.query(Invoice).filter(Invoice.id.in_(invoice_ids)).all()
    gstr2b_entries = db.query(GSTR2BEntry).all()
    matches = []
    for inv in invoices:
        best = None
        for entry in gstr2b_entries:
            diff = abs(inv.amount - entry.amount) / entry.amount
            if diff <= tolerance:
                best = entry
                break
        if best:
            matches.append((inv.id, best.id))
        else:
            db.add(
                ExceptionRecord(
                    invoice_id=inv.id,
                    reason="No match within tolerance"
                )
            )
    db.commit()

The algorithm is intentionally simple so that it can be audited and tuned. It iterates over each invoice and looks for the first GSTR‑2B line that satisfies the tolerance condition. If none is found, the invoice is logged as an exception and surfaced to the user for manual review.

How it looks to the user

The React front‑end, built with Vite, presents the results in a table that can be filtered by vendor, amount, or exception type. A small component illustrates the typical layout: Getting gst reconciliation software right early saves rework later.

function MatchTable({matches}) {
  return (
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr><th>Invoice</th><th>GSTR‑2B Entry</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        {matches.map(m => (
          <tr key={m.invoiceId}>
            <td>{m.invoiceId}</td>
            <td>{m.gstrId}</td>
          </tr>
        ))}
      </tbody>
    </table>
  );
}

When the reconciliation completes, the table is populated with matched pairs. Unmatched invoices are listed in a separate pane with a recommended action: “Check vendor name spelling” or “Request supplier to file missing invoice.” The UI also shows a score that reflects the proportion of invoices matched, giving the finance team a quick health indicator.

Under the hood

  • FastAPI handles the HTTP layer, exposing a lightweight JSON API.
  • Python implements the matching logic; the code uses SQLAlchemy to query PostgreSQL.
  • PostgreSQL stores the invoice data, GSTR‑2B entries, and exception records. Indexes on amount and vendor fields keep lookups fast.
  • Redis acts as a cache for the most recent GSTR‑2B file, reducing database load when the same file is reconciled against multiple invoice batches.
  • Celery queues reconciliation jobs so the user can continue working while the background worker processes the data.
  • React and Vite provide a responsive, accessible interface that follows WCAG 2.1 AA guidelines.

The entire stack is open‑source, and the project lives on GitHub under the MIT license. The code base is structured so that contributors can add new matching heuristics—such as fuzzy vendor name matching—without touching the core logic.

Why it matters

For Indian SMBs, the cost of a manual reconciliation process can reach several thousand rupees per month. GSTBot reduces that cost by automating 90 % of the work and providing clear, actionable exceptions. Because the tolerance can be tuned, the tool adapts to the quality of the supplier data without compromising compliance. The result is a gst reconciliation software that feels like a natural extension of the existing accounting workflow, not a separate enterprise system.

GSTBot is available at https://gstbot.aiknol.com and the source code can be found on GitHub: https://github.com/r2st/GSTBot. The project is actively maintained and welcomes contributors who want to improve the reconciliation algorithms or add new compliance features.

Related reading

  • Deep Dive: GST Reconciliation Software in GSTBot

title: Planning Frontend Design: A Guide to High-Level Architecture After Requirements Gathering and Backend Completion
description:
Introduction

Planning the frontend after backend architecture is complete is a critical juncture in software development—one that often determines whether a project succeeds or fails. The backend, with its APIs, data models, and business logic, provides the foundation, but the frontend is where users interact with the system. Without a well-thought-out frontend plan, even the most robust backend can result in a clunky, unintuitive user experience. This section explores the key challenges and mechanisms behind frontend planning, focusing on why it’s often overlooked and how to address it systematically.

The Problem: Frontend Planning as an Afterthought

The question of how to plan the frontend after backend completion is rooted in a common development workflow flaw: backend-first thinking. Developers and project managers often prioritize backend architecture because it’s tangible, measurable, and directly tied to functional requirements. However, this approach ignores the causal chain between backend capabilities and frontend usability. For example, an API endpoint designed for efficiency (e.g., returning raw JSON data) may force the frontend to handle complex data transformations, leading to slower load times or increased client-side complexity. The impact is a frontend that "breaks" under the weight of unoptimized backend decisions, resulting in observable effects like poor performance or inconsistent UI behavior.

Key Failure Mechanisms

  • Communication Breakdown: Backend and frontend teams operate in silos, leading to mismatched expectations. For instance, a backend team might assume the frontend will handle pagination, while the frontend team expects the backend to provide paginated data. This misalignment causes delays and rework.
  • Incomplete Requirements: Frontend design relies on understanding user workflows, but requirements often focus on backend functionality. Without clear user stories, the frontend risks becoming a patchwork of assumptions, leading to deformation in the user experience.
  • Overemphasis on Backend Scalability: While backend scalability is critical, over-optimizing for it can heat up frontend complexity. For example, a highly normalized database schema might require excessive frontend API calls, causing latency and increased error handling.

Edge Cases and Risks

Consider a scenario where the backend exposes a single, monolithic API endpoint to fetch all user data. The frontend, designed for real-time updates, now faces a risk formation: every request fetches unnecessary data, expanding network payload and breaking performance under high concurrency. Alternatively, if the frontend assumes the backend will handle state management (e.g., user authentication), a backend change could fail the frontend entirely, requiring a complete rewrite of client-side logic.

Optimal Solution: Align Frontend with Backend Capabilities

The most effective approach is to treat frontend planning as a bridge between user needs and backend capabilities. Start by mapping backend APIs to frontend workflows, identifying potential bottlenecks. For example, if the backend provides a search API with a 1-second response time, the frontend should design search interactions that account for this latency. Use tools like sequence diagrams to visualize data flow between frontend and backend, ensuring both teams agree on responsibilities.

Decision Rule: If Backend Architecture is Complete → Use API Contract Analysis

When backend architecture is finalized, analyze the API contract (endpoints, request/response formats, error handling) to derive frontend requirements. For instance, if the backend returns error codes in a specific format, the frontend must handle these codes consistently. This mechanism ensures the frontend doesn’t fail due to unhandled edge cases, such as network timeouts or invalid responses.

Typical Choice Errors

  • Over-Reliance on Frameworks: Assuming a frontend framework (e.g., React, Angular) will solve all problems leads to expansion of technical debt. Frameworks don’t address architectural mismatches between frontend and backend.
  • Ignoring Performance Budgets: Failing to account for backend response times or data payload sizes causes the frontend to heat up under load, resulting in slow page loads or crashes.

In conclusion, frontend planning after backend completion requires a causal understanding of how backend decisions impact frontend usability. By systematically analyzing API contracts, aligning workflows, and anticipating edge cases, developers can avoid common pitfalls and create scalable, user-centric solutions.

Understanding Frontend Planning

High-level frontend design is the strategic blueprint that bridges user needs with backend capabilities, ensuring the interface is both functional and intuitive. It’s not about pixel-perfect mockups or component libraries—it’s about architectural alignment. Without it, even the most robust backend becomes a liability, forcing the frontend to compensate for inefficiencies like raw JSON APIs that bloat payloads or over-normalized schemas that multiply API calls. The result? A frontend that’s slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain.

Consider the causal chain: Backend decisions → Frontend complexity → User experience degradation. For example, a monolithic API endpoint designed for backend scalability might return a 5MB JSON payload. This payload, when fetched on a mobile device with 3G, triggers a cascade: the frontend’s rendering thread blocks, the UI freezes, and the user abandons the app. The root cause? A backend architect who prioritized database normalization over network efficiency, assuming the frontend could “handle it.”

The risks are mechanical, not theoretical. Communication breakdowns between teams lead to mismatched assumptions—like a backend team assuming the frontend will handle pagination, only to discover the frontend team expected server-side pagination. This misalignment isn’t just a delay; it’s a rewriting of core logic, doubling development costs. Similarly, incomplete requirements (e.g., missing user stories for offline mode) force last-minute frontend hacks, creating technical debt that compounds with every feature release.

The optimal solution? API contract analysis as the linchpin. Treat backend contracts (endpoints, formats, error handling) as the frontend’s constitution. Map these contracts to user workflows using sequence diagrams, identifying bottlenecks like synchronous API calls blocking the main thread. For instance, if a backend contract specifies a 2-second response time for a user profile fetch, the frontend must implement skeletons or optimistic UI to mask latency. Failure to do so results in a 2-second blank screen—a usability failure.

Frameworks like React or Vue are irrelevant here. They don’t resolve architectural mismatches; they amplify them. A React app built without understanding backend payload sizes will still crash under load, regardless of state management libraries. The rule is categorical: If backend architecture is complete, analyze API contracts before writing a single line of frontend code. Derive frontend requirements from these contracts, ensuring edge cases (e.g., 429 rate limits, malformed JSON) are handled proactively. Skip this step, and the frontend becomes a bottleneck—not a bridge.

Key Failure Mechanisms

  • Communication Breakdown: Siloed teams → mismatched expectations → rework loops.
  • Incomplete Requirements: Missing user stories → fragmented UX → technical debt.
  • Overemphasis on Backend Scalability: Normalized schemas → excessive API calls → frontend latency.

Optimal Solution: API Contract-Driven Planning

Step Mechanism Outcome
1. Analyze Backend Contracts Map endpoints to user workflows; identify payload sizes, response times. Prevent frontend performance degradation.
2. Visualize Data Flow Use sequence diagrams to expose synchronous bottlenecks or redundant calls. Optimize API call sequences; reduce latency.
3. Derive Frontend Requirements Translate backend error handling, formats, and edge cases into frontend logic. Eliminate unhandled edge cases; improve resilience.

This approach isn’t theoretical—it’s mechanical. By treating backend contracts as the frontend’s foundation, you eliminate the friction that turns development into a zero-sum game. The rule is simple: If backend architecture is finalized, frontend planning begins with API contracts—not wireframes. Ignore this, and you’re building a house on quicksand.

Key Considerations in Frontend Planning

Transitioning from backend to frontend development requires a shift in focus from functional requirements to user-centric design and performance optimization. Without proper planning, frontend inefficiencies emerge, causing slow load times, inconsistent UI behavior, and costly rewrites. Below are the critical factors to address, grounded in causal mechanisms and practical insights.

1. API Contract-Driven Planning: Bridging Backend and Frontend

The core mechanism for effective frontend planning is API contract analysis. Backend decisions directly impact frontend performance. For example, a monolithic API endpoint returning a 5MB JSON payload forces the frontend to parse and render this data, blocking the main thread and causing UI freezes on slow networks. The causal chain is:

  • Backend decision (e.g., raw JSON APIs) → Frontend complexity (e.g., parsing large payloads) → User experience degradation (e.g., UI freezes, abandonment).

Optimal Solution: Analyze backend contracts (endpoints, formats, error handling) before writing frontend code. Map these contracts to user workflows using sequence diagrams to identify bottlenecks. For instance, synchronous API calls blocking the main thread can be replaced with asynchronous requests or caching mechanisms. This prevents performance degradation and eliminates unhandled edge cases like network timeouts or malformed JSON.

Decision Rule: If backend architecture is complete, always analyze API contracts first. Skipping this step turns the frontend into a bottleneck, not a bridge.

2. User Experience (UX) and Workflow Alignment

Frontend design must align with user workflows, not just backend capabilities. Key failure mechanism: Incomplete user stories lead to fragmented UX, forcing developers to rework components later. For example, a missing user story for offline mode results in a frontend that crashes without internet connectivity.

Practical Insight: Derive frontend requirements from both backend contracts and user workflows. Use sequence diagrams to visualize how data flows from backend to frontend and identify mismatches. For instance, a backend API returning paginated data requires frontend logic to handle pagination, which must be explicitly defined in user stories.

Edge Case Analysis: Anticipate scenarios like rate limits, invalid responses, or network failures. Proactive handling (e.g., skeletons, optimistic UI) masks latency and improves usability. For example, a skeleton screen during API calls prevents UI jank and reassures users that the app is responsive.

3. Performance and Accessibility: Avoiding Technical Debt

Performance budgets are critical but often ignored. Causal mechanism: Backend response times and payload sizes directly impact frontend load times. A 2-second backend delay translates to a 2-second UI freeze if not handled properly.

Technical Insight: Frontend frameworks (e.g., React, Vue) do not resolve architectural mismatches; they amplify them. For example, over-normalized schemas force excessive API calls, increasing frontend latency. Use performance budgets to limit payload sizes and response times, ensuring the frontend remains responsive under load.

Accessibility: Ensure compliance with WCAG standards by designing for keyboard navigation, screen readers, and color contrast. For instance, a missing aria-label on a button breaks screen reader functionality, excluding users with visual impairments.

4. Technology Stack Selection: Frameworks vs. Architectural Mismatches

Choosing a frontend framework (e.g., React, Angular) is insufficient without addressing architectural mismatches. Key error: Assuming frameworks automatically handle backend complexities. For example, React’s virtual DOM does not mitigate the impact of large JSON payloads or synchronous API calls.

Optimal Solution: Select a framework based on its ability to handle specific backend constraints. For instance, if backend APIs return large payloads, use a framework with built-in state management (e.g., Redux) or adopt server-side rendering (SSR) to offload processing from the client.

Decision Rule: If backend APIs are monolithic or return large payloads, use SSR or caching mechanisms to reduce frontend load. Without this, the frontend becomes a performance bottleneck.

5. Communication and Alignment: Breaking Silos

Siloed teams lead to mismatched expectations, causing rework loops. Example: Backend assumes frontend handles pagination, while frontend assumes backend provides paginated data. This results in delayed launches and increased costs.

Practical Insight: Establish a shared language between teams using sequence diagrams and API contract documentation. Regularly review backend changes (e.g., state management updates) to ensure frontend logic remains compatible. For instance, a backend change from REST to GraphQL requires frontend updates to handle new data structures.

Categorical Rule: If backend architecture changes post-frontend planning, re-analyze API contracts immediately. Failure to do so introduces bugs and forces rewrites.

Conclusion: Frontend Planning as a Bridge, Not an Afterthought

Effective frontend planning is not about wireframes or frameworks—it’s about bridging user needs and backend capabilities. By systematically analyzing API contracts, aligning workflows, and anticipating edge cases, you prevent usability failures, reduce technical debt, and ensure scalability. Skip this step, and the frontend becomes a bottleneck, undermining the entire project.

Step-by-Step Frontend Planning Process

Frontend planning after backend completion is not just about aesthetics—it’s about bridging user needs with backend capabilities. Without this alignment, projects risk slow load times, inconsistent UI behavior, and costly rewrites. Here’s a structured, evidence-driven process to avoid these pitfalls:

1. Analyze Backend API Contracts

Start by dissecting the finalized backend contracts. This isn’t optional—it’s the foundation of frontend efficiency. Here’s why:

  • Mechanism: Backend decisions like monolithic endpoints or over-normalized schemas force the frontend to handle large JSON payloads (e.g., 5MB+). This blocks the rendering thread, causing UI freezes on slow networks.
  • Risk Formation: Ignoring payload sizes or synchronous API calls leads to performance degradation under load. For example, a single synchronous call to a 3-second endpoint halts the entire UI until completion.
  • Rule: If backend architecture is complete, analyze API contracts before writing frontend code. Map endpoints to user workflows, identify payload sizes, and flag synchronous bottlenecks.

2. Visualize Data Flow with Sequence Diagrams

Sequence diagrams aren’t just documentation—they’re diagnostic tools. Here’s how they prevent failures:

  • Mechanism: Visualizing API calls exposes redundant requests or synchronous chains that choke the main thread. For instance, a sequence of 5 synchronous calls to fetch user data, roles, and permissions creates a waterfall effect, delaying UI rendering by the sum of all response times.
  • Edge Case: Backend changes (e.g., adding state management) can break frontend logic if not visualized. A sequence diagram acts as a change detector, highlighting incompatibilities before implementation.
  • Optimal Solution: Use sequence diagrams to identify asynchronous opportunities (e.g., parallelizing profile and role fetches) and caching candidates (e.g., infrequently changing data like user roles).

3. Derive Frontend Requirements from Contracts

Wireframes are not enough. Frontend requirements must derive from backend contracts to handle edge cases:

  • Mechanism: Backend error handling (e.g., 429 rate limits, 500 server errors) must be translated into frontend logic. Without this, errors like malformed JSON crash the UI, forcing rewrites.
  • Practical Insight: Implement skeletons (placeholder UI) and optimistic updates to mask latency. For example, show a loading skeleton while fetching data, then update the UI optimistically before confirmation.
  • Rule: If backend contracts specify error handling, replicate it in the frontend. Use fallback mechanisms (e.g., local storage for offline mode) to prevent critical failures.

4. Define Component Architecture

Components aren’t just UI blocks—they’re performance units. Here’s how to structure them:

  • Mechanism: Over-normalized schemas increase API calls. For example, fetching a product requires separate calls for details, reviews, and inventory. This amplifies latency in frameworks like React, where each call triggers re-renders.
  • Technical Insight: Use state management libraries (e.g., Redux) to centralize data fetching. For monolithic APIs, employ Server-Side Rendering (SSR) to pre-fetch data, reducing client-side load.
  • Choice Error: Relying solely on frameworks (e.g., React’s virtual DOM) without addressing backend constraints leads to performance bottlenecks. SSR or caching is optimal for large payloads, not just client-side hydration.

5. Prototype and Validate

Prototyping isn’t about polish—it’s about stress-testing assumptions:

  • Mechanism: Simulate edge cases like network timeouts or invalid responses to expose frontend weaknesses. For example, a 5-second delay in API response should trigger a skeleton, not a blank screen.
  • Practical Insight: Use tools like Charles Proxy to throttle network speeds and test performance budgets. If a page exceeds a 2-second load time, revisit API call sequences or payload sizes.
  • Rule: If a prototype fails under simulated stress, re-analyze API contracts and component architecture. Skipping this step results in brittle frontends that collapse under real-world usage.

Conclusion: The Core Mechanism of Frontend Planning

Frontend planning is not a siloed task—it’s a bridge between user needs and backend capabilities. By analyzing API contracts, visualizing data flow, and deriving requirements systematically, you prevent:

  • UI freezes caused by large payloads blocking the main thread.
  • Rework loops from mismatched backend-frontend expectations.
  • Performance degradation under load due to unoptimized API calls.

Categorical Rule: If backend architecture is complete, frontend planning must start with API contract analysis. Skip this, and the frontend becomes a bottleneck, not a bridge.

Best Practices and Common Pitfalls in Frontend Planning

Planning the frontend after backend completion is less about aesthetics and more about bridging user needs with backend capabilities. Skip this step, and your frontend becomes a bottleneck—slow, brittle, and costly to maintain. Here’s how to avoid the pitfalls and execute frontend planning effectively.

1. Analyze Backend API Contracts: The Foundation of Frontend Planning

Mechanism: Backend decisions like monolithic endpoints or over-normalized schemas force the frontend to handle large JSON payloads (≥5MB). These payloads block the rendering thread, causing UI freezes on slow networks.

Risk Formation: Ignoring payload sizes or synchronous API calls leads to performance degradation under load. For example, a 3-second synchronous call halts the UI, pushing users to abandon the app.

Optimal Solution: Map endpoints to user workflows, identify payload sizes, and flag synchronous bottlenecks before writing frontend code. Rule: If backend architecture is complete, start frontend planning with API contract analysis.

2. Visualize Data Flow with Sequence Diagrams: Exposing Hidden Bottlenecks

Mechanism: Sequence diagrams reveal redundant requests or synchronous chains that choke the main thread. For instance, 5 synchronous calls create a waterfall effect, delaying UI rendering by up to 15 seconds.

Edge Case: Backend changes can break frontend logic if not visualized. Sequence diagrams act as change detectors, ensuring compatibility.

Practical Insight: Use tools like Charles Proxy to throttle network speeds and test performance budgets. Identify asynchronous opportunities (e.g., parallelizing fetches) and caching candidates (e.g., infrequently changing data).

3. Derive Frontend Requirements from Contracts: Translating Backend Logic to Frontend

Mechanism: Backend error handling (e.g., 429 rate limits, 500 server errors) must be replicated in the frontend to prevent UI crashes. Without this, users see blank screens or cryptic errors.

Technical Insight: Use skeletons and optimistic updates to mask latency. For example, show a loading skeleton while fetching data to maintain perceived responsiveness.

Rule: Replicate backend error handling in the frontend and use fallback mechanisms (e.g., local storage for offline mode). Choice Error: Relying on frameworks without addressing backend constraints leads to performance bottlenecks.

4. Define Component Architecture: Balancing Frameworks and Backend Constraints

Mechanism: Over-normalized schemas increase API calls, amplifying latency in frameworks like React. Each call triggers re-renders, slowing down the UI.

Optimal Solution: Use state management libraries (e.g., Redux) for centralized data fetching and Server-Side Rendering (SSR) for monolithic APIs. Rule: Employ SSR or caching for monolithic APIs to avoid frontend performance bottlenecks.

Conditional Failure: SSR stops working effectively if the backend API response time exceeds 500ms, as it delays the initial page load. In such cases, switch to client-side rendering with aggressive caching.

5. Prototype and Validate: Stress-Testing Your Frontend

Mechanism: Simulate edge cases (e.g., network timeouts, invalid responses) to expose frontend weaknesses. For example, a 5-second delay should trigger a skeleton, not a blank screen.

Practical Insight: Use tools like Charles Proxy to throttle network speeds and test performance budgets. If a prototype fails under stress, re-analyze API contracts and component architecture.

Rule: If a prototype fails under stress, re-analyze API contracts and component architecture to avoid brittle frontends.

Common Pitfalls to Avoid

  • Communication Breakdown: Siloed teams lead to mismatched expectations (e.g., pagination handling), causing rework loops. Solution: Establish a shared language using sequence diagrams and API contract documentation.
  • Incomplete Requirements: Missing user stories lead to fragmented UX and technical debt. Solution: Derive frontend requirements from both backend contracts and user workflows.
  • Overemphasis on Backend Scalability: Normalized schemas lead to excessive API calls, increasing frontend latency. Solution: Use performance budgets to limit payload sizes and response times.

Conclusion: Frontend planning is not an afterthought—it’s the bridge between user needs and backend capabilities. By analyzing API contracts, visualizing data flow, and deriving requirements systematically, you prevent bottlenecks, reduce technical debt, and ensure scalability. Categorical Rule: If backend architecture is complete, frontend planning must start with API contract analysis.

Conclusion and Next Steps

Effective frontend planning is the linchpin that connects user expectations with backend capabilities. Skipping this step isn’t just an oversight—it’s a recipe for slow, brittle interfaces that hemorrhage development hours during maintenance. Here’s what you need to walk away with:

  • API Contract Analysis is Non-Negotiable: Backend decisions like monolithic endpoints or over-normalized schemas force the frontend to ingest payloads ≥5MB, blocking the rendering thread and freezing UIs on slow networks. Mechanism: Large JSON payloads serialize in the main thread, halting DOM updates. Rule: Map endpoints to workflows, flag synchronous bottlenecks, and quantify payload sizes before writing a single line of frontend code.
  • Sequence Diagrams Are Change Detectors: Without visualizing data flow, backend updates silently break frontend logic. Example: A new synchronous API call added post-planning creates a waterfall effect, adding 15 seconds of UI lag. Solution: Use tools like Charles Proxy to throttle networks, identify parallelizable fetches, and cache static data.
  • Error Handling Must Mirror Backend Contracts: A 429 rate limit unhandled in the frontend crashes the UI. Mechanism: Backend retries don’t propagate to the client, leaving users staring at blank screens. Optimal Fix: Implement skeletons during fetches and optimistic UI updates for transient errors.
  • SSR Isn’t a Silver Bullet: Server-Side Rendering fails when backend API response times exceed 500ms. Conditional Rule: If API latency >500ms, switch to client-side rendering with caching. Choice Error: Teams often default to SSR for monolithic APIs without checking backend response times, causing TTFB to balloon.

Next, apply these principles with tools like Charles Proxy for network simulation, Lighthouse for performance budgets, and Storybook for component prototyping. If your prototype fails under stress (e.g., 5-second network delay triggers a crash, not a skeleton), re-analyze API contracts immediately. Categorical Rule: Frontend planning without API contract analysis guarantees a bottleneck. Don’t build on quicksand.

title: Insomnia vs Powerduck: Pricing and Lock-In
description:
Short answer: Insomnia offers a free local tier and paid plans; Powerduck keeps the desktop and Hub hosting free within plan limits and exports portable static artifacts. The deeper difference is lock-in: a client vault and a platform are harder to leave than a set of generated files.

What the pricing shapes reward

A classic client prices seats and features around the client and its cloud. A local-first studio keeps the work in files and hosts within plan limits, so a larger surface does not push you across a per-seat gate.

The side-by-side

Property Insomnia Powerduck
Local work Free Free
Hosting Paid tiers Hub within plan
Artifacts Client vault Static, portable
Exit cost Export and migrate Plain files

Why lock-in is the real cost

Pricing changes and feature gates are visible. The cost that compounds is the work trapped in a vault or a platform. Portable artifacts keep the decision reversible.

The honest takeaway

Compare the current prices, but weight the exit cost. A tool that exports the work lets you choose again later; a vault does not.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read the mocking comparison.

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.
