title: Three Errors You Actually Hit Connecting Actions to GCP
description:
Conclusion

Workload Identity Federation failures come from the configuration living in three layers. The error text does not tell you which one.

  • GitHub Actions side — does the job have id-token: write?
  • Pool side — does attribute_condition permit the calling repository?
  • Service account side — is the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser binding still there?

Any of the three missing produces similar text. Without deciding the order of investigation up front you end up poking at permissions at random. Below are the three errors we actually hit, in the order you hit them.

Symptom

1. Unable to acquire impersonation credentials

The first one you meet. The authentication step itself does not pass. There are three candidate causes, and the higher the layer, the cheaper it is to check.

  • The job has no permissions with id-token: write. Entirely on GitHub's side, so look here first
  • You are running from a different repository. The pool's attribute_condition limits the caller via assertion.repository, so forks and other repositories are rejected
  • The roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser binding on the service account was lost to drift. Restore with terraform apply

The third is the awkward one. The code is correct and it still does not work, and it happens unrelated to any recent change. Someone touching IAM by hand puts Terraform's state and the cloud out of sync, and it surfaces in this shape.

2. Permission 'iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken' denied

Here impersonation got as far as the entrance and the target service account refused. It looks like a missing grant; in practice it is usually the wrong target.

  • The service account email is wrong. Where plan and deploy accounts are separate, their permission scopes are separate too. Calling the deploy target with plan credentials is refused, correctly
  • The environment name does not match. If Terraform's env_name and the GitHub Environment the workflow references diverge, you end up pointed at the wrong service account

The error only says "no permission". It does not say "wrong target", so start by confirming the email is the one you meant.

3. Provider or pool not found

The pool or provider simply does not exist. Check:

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe <provider-id> \
  --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=<pool-id> \
  --project=<project-id>

If it is absent, terraform apply has not been run. Apply in that environment's directory.

Cause

All three share a root: the chain of trust is stored in three separate places.

GitHub issues an OIDC token per job. The pool receives it and decides, through attribute_condition, which repositories it accepts. What passes becomes a principal, and if that principal appears in the service account's IAM policy, impersonation succeeds.

Those three are managed in different places: the workflow YAML, the Terraform pool definition, and the service account IAM policy. Break any one and the chain breaks, but the break is only ever observable as an authentication error.

The fix

Reading the service account IAM policy directly is the fastest way to see the real state.

gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy \
  <sa-name>@<project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --project=<project-id>

The expected state has a principalSet of this shape in members:

principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<num>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool-id>/attribute.repository/<owner>/<repo>

If the calling repository is not there, no amount of fixing the workflow will help. If it is there, the lower two layers are alive and you go and look at permissions on the GitHub side.

You can cut it off immediately

Because there is no JSON key in the setup, there is nothing to rotate. Instead you can stop impersonation from a repository directly.

gcloud iam service-accounts remove-iam-policy-binding \
  <sa-name>@<project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member='principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<num>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool-id>/attribute.repository/<owner>/<repo>'

The moment the binding is removed, authentication from that repository stops. There is no key expiry to wait for.

But always update Terraform and open a PR afterwards. Leaving a hand-edited IAM policy drifts the configuration, and the binding you removed reappears the next time someone applies. Pair the stopgap with the code change.

And that drift, surfacing much later, is the first error in this article. A neglected emergency cut-off and an unexplained authentication failure are the same thing from two sides.

Making it less likely to recur

The three layers are not going away. What you can change is fixing the order in which you check them.

Cheapest first: permissions on the GitHub side, then get-iam-policy on the service account, then confirming the pool and provider exist. Following that order, the first is just opening a YAML file and the second is one command — enough to narrow down which of the three layers is broken.

For another case where the error text does not lead to the cause, see terraform's enabled = false cannot tear down an environment, where the error appears in a module other than the one at fault.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

title: How to Export or Back Up Your Railway Database (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis) Before You Migrate
description:
Disclosure: this article was drafted with the help of an AI writing assistant. Facts, times and commands were checked against Railway's official status page, blog and docs, and the dump and restore commands were tested on 23 Oct 2026. Originally published on Medium.

Tested pg_dump, mysqldump and mongodump commands, how to restore them, and the mistakes that break aÂ backup.

Last updated: 23 Oct 2026, 8:43 AMÂ IST.

Quick answer: To export a Railway database, turn on Public Access for the database service (Settings, then Networking), copy its public connection URL from the Variables tab, and run the standard dump tool from your own machine: pg_dump for PostgreSQL, mysqldump for MySQL, and mongodump for MongoDB. Railway's built-in volume backups are useful, but they can only be restored into the same Railway project and environment, so they don't replace a dump file you keep yourself.

TL;DR

  • Railway databases are private by default. Public Access creates a TCP proxy and a public URL variable, such as DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL.
  • PostgreSQL: pg_dump in custom format (-F c), restore with pg_restore. Your pg_dump must be the same major version as the server, orÂ newer.
  • MySQL: mysqldump with --single-transaction --routines --triggers.
  • MongoDB: mongodump --archive --gzip, restore with mongorestore.
  • Redis: redis-cli --rdb saves a snapshot file. Restoring it needs a different method (seeÂ below).
  • Rotate the database password after the export if you opened public access only for theÂ backup.

How these commands were checked: On 23 Oct 2026, every dump and restore command below was run on a test machine against local test databases: PostgreSQL 17 (pg_dump 17.11), MariaDB 11.8 (its mysqldump), MongoDB 8.0 with Database Tools 100.19.1, and Redis 8.0. They were not run against a live Railway database, so the Railway-specific parts (variable names, menus, CLI flags) come from Railway's officialÂ docs.

Why back up your Railway databaseÂ now?

After the October 2026 security incident, many developers want a copy of their data outside Railway. Some are planning a move, and some just want a safety net. That is a sensible habit whatever host youÂ use.

Railway's own position is the same. Its PostgreSQL docs say regular backups and monitoring are "essential" for production databases. If you also need to rotate your database password, Railway's guide on rotating PostgreSQL credentials covers that. You can take the backup first and rotate afterwards.

Step 1: Get a connection URL you canÂ reach

Railway databases are private by default. To reach one from your laptop, you have twoÂ options.

Option A: Public Access (TCP proxy). Open the database service, go to Settings, then Networking, and add Public Access. Railway creates a TCP proxy with a host and port that look like shuttle.proxy.rlwy.net:15140, plus a public URL variable:

  • PostgreSQL: DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL
  • MySQL: MYSQL_PUBLIC_URL
  • MongoDB: MONGO_PUBLIC_URL
  • Redis: REDIS_PUBLIC_URL

Railway notes that traffic through the TCP proxy is billed as network egress. Its pricing page lists egress at $0.05 per GB. Keep that in mind for large databases.

Option B: An SSH tunnel with the CLI, no public access needed. The Railway CLI's connect command has a --tunnel-only flag. It opens a local tunnel, prints connection details for external tools, and holds the tunnel open until you press Ctrl+C. The CLI help says it implies --ssh and works without a public domain. Run railway connect Postgres --tunnel-only (use your database service's name), then point the dump tool at the local host and port itÂ prints.

Keep the URL out of your shell history. The connection URL contains the password. In bash you can paste it into a hidden variable instead of typing it into theÂ command:

read -rs DB_URL   # paste the URL, press Enter (nothing is shown)
echo "${#DB_URL} characters stored"

Step 2: Export a Railway PostgreSQL database withÂ pg_dump

First check versions. The PostgreSQL docs say pg_dump can't dump from a server newer than its own major version. It refuses to try. Check your local version with pg_dump --version, and the server version by running SELECT version(); in psql or the Railway Data tab. Install a matching or newer client ifÂ needed.

Then dump in customÂ format:

pg_dump "$DB_URL" -F c -f railway_backup.dump
pg_restore --list railway_backup.dump | head

The second line lists the dump's contents, which is a quick way to confirm the file isn't empty or corrupt. Custom format is compressed and lets pg_restore pick objects later. Render's migrate-from-Railway guide uses the same pg_dumpÂ command.

If you'd rather have a readable SQL file, run this singleÂ line:

pg_dump "$DB_URL" --no-owner --no-acl -f railway_backup.sql

Big database? Use the directory format for parallel jobs. Parallel dumps only work with the directory format. When I tried -j with custom format, pg_dump stopped with "parallel backup only supported by the directory format". ThisÂ works:

pg_dump "$DB_URL" -F d -j 4 -f railway_backup_dir

Restore it (anywhere) 

# custom format
pg_restore --verbose --no-acl --no-owner -d "$TARGET_DB_URL" railway_backup.dump

# directory format, 4 parallel jobs
pg_restore -j 4 --no-owner -d "$TARGET_DB_URL" railway_backup_dir

# plain SQL file
psql "$TARGET_DB_URL" -f railway_backup.sql

The --no-owner and --no-acl flags skip Railway-specific role ownership, which usually doesn't exist on the new server. In my test, a 1,000-row table came back with all 1,000 rows from each of the threeÂ formats.

Step 3: Export a Railway MySQL database with mysqldump

Railway's MySQL service exposes MYSQLHOST, MYSQLPORT, MYSQLUSER, MYSQLPASSWORD and MYSQLDATABASE, plus MYSQL_PUBLIC_URL through the TCP proxy (MySQL docs). mysqldump doesn't accept a URL, so take the host, port, user and database name from MYSQL_PUBLIC_URL (its format is mysql://user:password@host:port/database). Leaving the password off makes mysqldump prompt for it, which keeps it out of yourÂ history.

mysqldump -h PUBLIC_HOST -P PUBLIC_PORT -u USER -p \
  --single-transaction --routines --triggers \
  DATABASE_NAME > railway_mysql.sql

--single-transaction takes a consistent snapshot of InnoDB tables without locking them. --routines and --triggers include stored procedures and triggers. All three are documented in the MySQL 8.4 mysqldump reference.

Restore it with oneÂ line:

mysql -h TARGET_HOST -P TARGET_PORT -u TARGET_USER -p TARGET_DB < railway_mysql.sql

I tested this pair with MariaDB's mysqldump and mysql client, which accept the same flags. If your target is a managed MySQL service, check its import docs for GTID or privilege notes before youÂ restore.

Step 4: Export a Railway MongoDB database with mongodump

Railway's MongoDB service exposes MONGO_URL, plus MONGO_PUBLIC_URL through the TCP proxy (MongoDB docs). You need the free MongoDB Database Tools, which include mongodump and mongorestore.

mongodump --uri "$MONGO_PUBLIC_URL" --archive=railway-mongo.archive --gzip
mongorestore --uri "$TARGET_MONGO_URL" --archive=railway-mongo.archive --gzip

A single gzipped archive file is easier to move around than a folder of BSON files. Add --drop to mongorestore if you want it to replace collections that already exist on theÂ target.

Step 5: Redis on Railway: what you can and can'tÂ export

Railway's Redis service exposes REDIS_URL, plus REDIS_PUBLIC_URL through the TCP proxy (Redis docs). You can save a point-in-time snapshotÂ with:

redis-cli -u "$REDIS_PUBLIC_URL" --rdb railway_redis.rdb

Restoring is the tricky part. Some guides pipe theÂ .rdb file into redis-cli --pipe. When I tested that on 23 Oct 2026, the target Redis rejected it with an "unknown command" error. That's expected, because --pipe expects Redis commands, not a binary RDB snapshot. Realistic options:

  • If Redis only holds cache or queue data, don't migrate it. Let the new Redis startÂ empty.
  • For a small dataset, copy keys with the DUMP and RESTORE commands.
  • For a self-managed Redis, place theÂ .rdb file in its data directory before it starts. Check your host's docs, because managed Redis services handle imports differently.

What about Railway's built-inÂ backups?

Railway has native volume backups for services with a volume, databases included:

  • Schedules: daily (kept 6 days), weekly (kept 27 days) and monthly (kept 89Â days).
  • Manual backups are limited to 50% of the volume's totalÂ size.
  • Backups are billed like volume storage, for their incremental sizeÂ only.
  • Railway lists two caveats: wiping a volume deletes all its backups, and backups can only be restored into the same project and environment.

For Postgres, the CLI can also start an on-demand backup with railway postgres pitr backup create --service postgres --name pre-migration. See Railway's postgres CLI docs for requirements, such as using the official Railway PostgresÂ image.

These are good for quick rollbacks inside Railway. For a migration or an off-platform safety copy, you still want a dump file youÂ control.

Export files and environment variables too

A database dump isn't your whole app. Before anyÂ move:

  • Volume files (uploads, SQLite files): the volume CLI can download them, for example railway volume files download /backup.tarÂ ./backup.tar. A directory works as the remote pathÂ too.
  • Environment variables: railway variable list --kv prints them in KEY=value format. The CLI help says this prints raw values, so save the output only somewhere safe, never in Git. After the incident, rotate secrets rather than copying old values into a newÂ host.
  • Laravel tip: if you use Laravel's storage/app folder on a Railway volume, back that up along with the database, or you'll lose userÂ uploads.

Checklist before you call it backedÂ up

  1. The dump file exists and isn't tiny. Check it with lsÂ -lh.
  2. You restored it once into a scratch database and counted rows in your keyÂ tables.
  3. The file is stored in two places, for example your laptop plus encrypted cloudÂ storage.
  4. If you opened Public Access only for the backup, remove it, and rotate the password with Railway's Regenerate button (see Railway's rotationÂ guide).

FAQ

How do I export my database fromÂ Railway?

Enable Public Access on the database (or use railway connect with --tunnel-only), copy the public connection URL, and run pg_dump, mysqldump or mongodump from yourÂ machine.

Can I download a Railway database backup from the dashboard?

Railway's native backups are restored inside Railway, into the same project and environment. To get a file you can take elsewhere, run a dump tool yourself.

What does "pg_dump: error: aborting because of server version mismatch" mean?

Your local pg_dump is older than the Railway server's major version. Install a matching or newer PostgreSQL client and run itÂ again.

Does exporting through the TCP proxy costÂ money?

Railway bills TCP proxy traffic as network egress, listed at $0.05 per GB on its pricing page. Small databases cost very little; large ones are worth estimating first.

Can I export a whole RailwayÂ project?

There's no single "export everything" file. Export each database, download volume files, save your variable names (then rotate the values), and keep config files like railway.json or railway.toml inÂ Git.

Is it safe to keep my Railway databaseÂ public?

Only while you need it. Railway's own rotation guide says a credential is usable from anywhere through the TCP proxy while Public Access is on. Remove it when you'reÂ done.

Related reading

  • Is Railway down? What the 21â€“22 October 2026 Railway outage means for developers
  • Railway API token not working? Fix "Not Authorized" and "Project Token notÂ found"
  • Railway alternatives in 2026: Render, Fly.io, AWS or Coolify? A fair migration guide
  • Is Railway safe now? What the October 2026 breach means, plus a hosting security checklist

Sources (checked 23 Oct 2026): Railway PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, TCP proxy, volume backups, CLI, pricing, PostgreSQL pg_dump docs, MySQL mysqldump docs, Render's Railway migration guide.

title: SaaS Application Logging via JSON API: Choosing a Simple Service for Import Freshness
description:
Short answer: Choose a simple JSON logging service only if it can preserve structured run events, support safe retries, and expose enough retention and queryability to detect missing import results; the alert rule still belongs to your application.

A scheduled import should page someone when it stops producing results, but a log line saying job finished is not enough. The least complex design is a structured event for each run, a durable count of accepted results, and an alert based on the absence of a successful result within the expected window. JSON over an HTTP API can carry the event; it cannot decide what success means.

The useful alert is the one that tells the on-call engineer which schedule went quiet, when it was expected, and what evidence is missing. That distinction matters in B2B SaaS, where a scheduler can keep firing while an upstream cursor, tenant filter, or validation step quietly yields zero records.

Can a simple logging service with a JSON API serve SaaS applications?

Imagine the page arrives at 09:20. It says: import produced no successful result for tenant acme-prod; expected every 15 minutes; last success 08:45; run 6f3b. That is enough to start an investigation. A page saying HTTP 200 from logging endpoint is not.

I keep these facts separate because they answer different questions:

  • Did the scheduler start a run?
  • Did the run reach the source and finish its protocol?
  • Did it accept at least one result, or was an empty result valid?
  • Can the run be joined to the tenant, schedule, and deployment?

The first three are domain events. The HTTP response from a log collector is transport evidence. Treating transport success as job success is how a healthy logging path hides a failed import.

A hosted endpoint is a poor fit when policy requires data to remain inside a private network, when retention must be customized beyond its contract, or when the import must continue during a prolonged telemetry outage without a local buffer. In those cases, a self-managed collector or queue can be the better boundary, even though it adds patching and capacity work.

A simple service is still useful for teams that value a small integration surface and can accept those limits. The limitation is operational ownership: a hosted boundary reduces collector maintenance, while a self-managed queue gives more control over residency, buffering, and retention.

Keep it boring.

A compact event can make that distinction explicit:

type ImportRun struct {
    RunID       string `json:"run_id"`
    Tenant      string `json:"tenant"`
    Schedule    string `json:"schedule"`
    StartedAt   string `json:"started_at"`
    FinishedAt  string `json:"finished_at"`
    Status      string `json:"status"`
    ResultCount int    `json:"result_count"`
    ErrorCode   string `json:"error_code,omitempty"`
}

Use a stable run ID. It gives retries and duplicate deliveries one identity, which is more useful than trying to infer a run from a timestamp and a message string. Keep tenant and schedule fields bounded and intentional; high-cardinality labels copied into every metric can create a second operational problem.

Where should the earlier signal come from?

The earlier signal is the completed-run event, not the page. Emit one event when the import reaches a terminal state, with status set to a value such as succeeded, empty, or failed. Then define the alert from the business rule: a schedule that normally produces data must have a recent successful result.

That rule needs an explicit exception for legitimate emptiness. A tenant with no new records can be healthy. If empty and failed are collapsed into one status, the alert will page on normal quiet periods and the team will eventually tune it out. Signal quality is a policy decision before it is a threshold decision.

A JSON API is a reasonable ingestion boundary when the client can set timeouts, retry safely, and preserve the event body for diagnosis. The event should be append-oriented. A retry may deliver it twice, so the consumer needs a uniqueness key such as (tenant, schedule, run_id) or an equivalent idempotency key. Do not use a random request ID as the only deduplication key; it changes on every retry.

For the log record, I would include the same correlation fields in every terminal event and keep the message for a human. The machine-readable fields carry the decision. This follows the broader observability model in which logs are a signal that can be correlated with traces and metrics, rather than a replacement for either one.

How do you instrument the path without creating noise?

Start at the scheduler boundary and trace the state transitions. A minimal sequence is scheduled, started, source_read, and one terminal event. Do not emit a full payload for every imported row. Log counts, bounded error categories, source offsets when safe, and a reference to the run. The raw records belong in the application data path, not in an alerting stream.

Here is a small Go helper that sends a terminal event. It leaves retries to the caller so the caller can apply the same run ID and idempotency key on every attempt.

func postRun(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, endpoint string, run ImportRun) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(run)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("marshal import run: %w", err)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create import event request: %w", err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", run.RunID)

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send import event: %w", err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("import event endpoint returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    return nil
}

The important details are boring: context cancellation, a bounded client timeout configured outside this function, and a response check. A successful network write does not prove that a downstream consumer has indexed the event. The service should expose a health and delivery signal that can be monitored separately from import success.

One trap is logging the retry itself as a new business run. That creates duplicate alerts and inflates counts. Keep transport attempts in a separate diagnostic field or metric, while the terminal business event retains the original run ID.

Which threshold separates a quiet tenant from a broken import?

Use the schedule contract, not a universal five-minute threshold. For a 15-minute schedule, the rule might allow one missed interval and page after the next expected completion plus a bounded grace period. For a daily schedule, the same fixed threshold is meaningless. Record the expected interval with the schedule configuration and evaluate the freshness of the last valid result per tenant and schedule.

The decision table should be explicit:

Observed state Operational meaning Page?
Recent succeeded result Import is producing data No
Recent empty result and emptiness is allowed Healthy quiet period No
Recent failed result Run completed with an error Usually, based on impact
No terminal result past the grace window Missing output or missing instrumentation Yes

The last row deserves special attention. No event can mean the scheduler did not run, the worker stalled, the source call hung, or the logging path failed. The alert should say “no terminal result,” then link the operator to scheduler and worker evidence. It should not pretend to know which failure occurred.

A short test matrix catches most alert mistakes: successful run, valid empty run, failed run, timeout before terminal emission, duplicate delivery, late delivery, and two tenants with different schedules. Run it in CI with fixed clocks. Then exercise one production-like canary schedule during deployment so a schema change cannot silently remove the fields the alert reads.

What does a practical selection checklist look like?

For a simple logging service with a JSON API, I would evaluate the boundary against the workflow rather than a feature count. Can it accept structured records without forcing message parsing? Can the client set a timeout and retry with a stable idempotency key? Can operators retain and query tenant, schedule, run ID, status, and timestamps? Can access controls separate tenants? Can the retention policy match the investigation window?

Also check the failure behavior. If the logging endpoint is unavailable, the import worker should not blindly block a business-critical run forever. Decide whether terminal events go to a local durable buffer, a queue, or a bounded retry loop. Make that choice visible in the runbook. Losing an observability event is bad; turning an observability outage into data loss is worse.

I initially treated the JSON endpoint as the main design decision. The harder part was defining a result that could be trusted by an alert. Once empty, failed, and “no terminal event” had separate meanings, the transport became replaceable and the false-positive discussion became concrete.

A good page is therefore a small contract between the scheduler, the importer, and the on-call engineer. It names the missing evidence, preserves a stable identity across retries, and respects each schedule’s expected cadence. That is enough to make a simple JSON logging boundary useful without asking it to become the source of truth for application state.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • OpenTelemetry Specification, “Logs Data Model”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/
  • RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • RFC 9457, “Problem Details for HTTP APIs”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457

title: Why I built a whiteboard for practising system design
description:
System-design interviews ask you to draw boxes and defend them. Most of us practise on tools that were never built for that, and feedback depends on finding a human who'll read your diagram closely.

So I built Whiteboard.ai: a real-time collaborative system-design whiteboard where an AI reviews your architecture diagram like a senior engineer. This post covers what's in it and, more usefully, the decisions underneath. I'll also be upfront about its limits, which are real.

The problem

A generic whiteboard has no idea that a box labelled "Postgres" is a single point of failure. And interviewers running a live round juggle a canvas, a timer, a question and private notes in four different places.

Building it properly turns out to be mostly not about the canvas. It's about:

  • real-time sync that survives a crashed server,
  • permissions that hold on the WebSocket as well as the REST API,
  • an AI reviewer whose bill and prompt-injection exposure are bounded,
  • and a private mode where the server genuinely can't read the board.

How a board works

Each board is a Yjs document. Shapes (rectangles, ellipses, text, stickies, freehand, arrows that bind to shapes, plus twelve typed system-design components) live in a shared map, and every read and write is validated with zod.

For sync, I wrote my own server rather than using a hosted service: Fastify and ws on one port. I chose that because rooms, backpressure, persistence and revocation are the product. If those are someone else's black box, I can't make promises about them.

"Saved" is a promise

This is the decision I'm proudest of. Live updates broadcast immediately, so collaboration feels instant. But the "Saved" indicator only appears after the update is committed to Postgres, and it carries the exact state that's now durable.

client edit → server room → broadcast to others immediately
                         → write-ahead log in Postgres (within ~50 ms)
                         → only now: tell the client "Saved"

The consequence: an edit that shows Saved survives a hard kill -9 of the server. An edit that doesn't show Saved is still in the browser and re-sends when the connection returns. The label means what it says.

The review pipeline: rules first, AI second

The AI never looks at a picture. The canvas is converted into a typed graph, and then:

  1. Nine deterministic rules run in the browser, in about 17 ms for a 2,000-shape board. They catch things like a database as a single point of failure, a client talking straight to a database, synchronous cycles, and a queue without a dead-letter queue.
  2. Only then does Claude write a structured review: scores on five dimensions, with findings pinned to specific shape IDs.
  3. The response is validated and repaired server-side. If the model invents a reference to a shape that doesn't exist, it's dropped.

Why this order? Cheap, deterministic checks catch the obvious problems reliably, so the model can spend its effort on the judgement calls. And because the model sees data with no tools to call, there's nothing for a malicious board label to hijack.

Private data and permissions

A few details that taught me how much "permissions" hides:

  • Interview notes and hidden hints are never in the shared document. The candidate is an editor and could rewrite anything inside it. Secrets live only behind role-checked REST routes, and a test records every frame a candidate's socket receives and asserts that no secret appears.
  • Private rooms are end-to-end encrypted. A 256-bit AES-GCM key is generated in the browser and kept in the URL fragment; the server stores and relays ciphertext only.
  • Spend is bounded in code. Quota is checked and reserved in one transaction under a per-user advisory lock, so two parallel requests at quota minus one produce one success and one rejection.

Bugs that taught me things

Real ones from the project's log:

  • Viewers sat on "Saving…" forever. The store stamped a schema version into the document on creation, an update the server rightly rejects from viewers. Fix: stamp it at the first local edit.
  • A removed member could still open the board offline from IndexedDB. Fix: revocation now wipes the local copy, not just the live socket.
  • Analytics would have leaked an encryption key. Page-analytics recorded full URLs including the fragment, which is where a private board's key lives. Fix: a hook strips fragments from every event, with a test.
  • A candidate who joined via share link saw nothing. Found by a browser test, since candidates normally join by link.

Honest limits

I'll repeat what the case study says, because it matters:

  • It is not deployed. It runs locally against a dev Supabase project, so there's no live demo. Load numbers come from one Mac and haven't been re-measured on a staging host.
  • The AI review eval has never been run against a real API key. It's written (15 fixture boards, 16 planted flaws, a 12/15 pass bar), but the prompt's catch rate is unmeasured.
  • Payments are tested with a scripted provider, not yet in real test mode.
  • Private boards can't rotate keys. A removed member stops syncing but may keep the key and old content.
  • The design check only understands palette shapes. Boards drawn with plain rectangles get few findings.

What I'd tell someone building something similar

  1. Decide what you'll promise, then write a test that tries to break each promise.
  2. Put cheap deterministic checks in front of expensive AI ones.
  3. Treat the AI as an untrusted component with a budget.
  4. Write down the limits while you still remember them.

Twelve questions to ask of any system-design diagram

Use these on your own diagrams, or on a friend's. They're the sort of thing the deterministic rules in Whiteboard.ai check automatically, and every one can also be asked by a person.

  1. Where's the single point of failure? What happens if each box goes down?
  2. Where does data live, and who owns it? One writer, or many?
  3. What's synchronous and what's asynchronous? Are there synchronous call cycles?
  4. What happens at 10x the load? Which box saturates first?
  5. What happens when a downstream service is slow, not down? (Slow is often worse than down.)
  6. Is a client talking directly to a database? If so, where are the access rules enforced?
  7. Do queues have a dead-letter path for messages that keep failing?
  8. Where are the retries, and are they idempotent? What happens if a message is delivered twice?
  9. How do you know it's healthy? What metrics and alerts exist?
  10. What's cached, and how does stale data get invalidated?
  11. How does it deploy and roll back?
  12. What's the data model's biggest assumption that might not hold?

Print this list. Asking them out loud, even to yourself, is most of the skill.

How to practise with a partner

A simple 45-minute format:

Minutes Activity
0–5 Partner reads the prompt ("design a URL shortener"). You ask clarifying questions.
5–10 State requirements and rough numbers (users, reads vs writes).
10–25 Draw the design. Narrate every box.
25–40 Partner pokes at failure modes using the twelve questions.
40–45 Both note what to study.

Swap roles next time. Being the interviewer teaches as much as being the candidate.

A worked example

Prompt: a URL shortener.

  • Core: a write path (create short code) and a read path (redirect).
  • Data: a table mapping code → URL.
  • Scale thought: reads vastly outnumber writes, so cache hot codes.
  • Failure thought: if the cache is down, reads fall back to the database. Can the database cope? If not, add a rate limit.
  • A question to ask yourself: how do you generate codes without collisions? (Counter-based, random with retry, or pre-generated pool, each with trade-offs.)

Even this tiny walkthrough uses five of the twelve questions.

Why drawing failure arrows matters

Diagrams of the happy path are easy and nearly useless. The valuable part is what happens when something breaks. A good habit: use a second colour (red) for failure paths, and don't consider the diagram finished until every important box has a red arrow out of it.

What an AI reviewer can and can't do

A tool can reliably catch pattern problems: a database with no replica, a queue with no dead-letter path. It can't know your product's real requirements, your team's skills or your budget. Treat automated feedback as a second pair of eyes that needs your judgement, not as a verdict.

What's your go-to first question when you start a system design? And if you've built real-time sync before, what did you wish you'd known?

title: Generate a training set with DeepSeek, then fine-tune a small model on a rented GPU
description:
Short answer: write a few documentation pages yourself, have DeepSeek turn them into question-and-answer pairs through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, filter the pairs with a short script, then train a LoRA adapter on a small base model with LLaMA-Factory on a rented GPU. Generate and filter on your own machine; rent the GPU only for training; download the adapter, then destroy the instance.

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU. The endpoint (https://cloudgpu.app/v1) and the GPU rentals below are ours. Each step links the official documentation it follows and ends with a "What to check" line, because the details (versions, template names, model access) change.

Why this pattern? AI labs describe using models to write or judge training data from written rules. This is the small, single-developer version of that idea. It is our own analogy, not a claim from those papers.

Read these three things first

  1. DeepSeek's terms. This tutorial generates data with DeepSeek only. DeepSeek's Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026) say in section 4.2(3) that you may apply the Outputs of the Services to "a wide range of use cases, including personal use, academic research, derivative product development, training other models (such as model distillation), etc., as long as such usage is legal and adhere to these Terms." Section 3.1 adds that if you publish or disseminate outputs, you must "clearly indicate that the output content is generated by artificial intelligence". So if you publish the dataset, a model card or examples from it, label them as AI-generated. Read the terms yourself, and read CloudGPU's terms and acceptable use policy, which apply to the gateway.
  2. Rights to your source text. The acceptable use policy lists "Training models on datasets you do not have rights to use" under large-scale copyright infringement (section 1.8). In this tutorial the generator only sees documentation you wrote yourself.
  3. The base model's license. Each base model below has its own license. Open the link, read it, and confirm for yourself that your use is allowed.

What you need

  • Python 3 and the openai package on your own machine: pip install openai.
  • A CloudGPU account with balance, and an API key (the API page has a "Get your API key" link). Keep it in an environment variable, never in code: 
export CLOUDGPU_API_KEY="paste-your-key-here"
  • Three to ten Markdown files of your own documentation, with ## section headings, in a docs/ folder. A README of your own project works.
  • A Hugging Face account and a read token if you choose Llama or Gemma (both are gated, see the table below).

What to check: python3 -c "import os; print(bool(os.environ.get('CLOUDGPU_API_KEY')))" prints True in the shell where you will run the scripts, and python3 -c "import openai" raises no error.

API calls are billed per token from the same balance as GPU rentals; the current rate for every model is in the table on the API page. This post does not repeat rates.

Step 1: generate question-and-answer pairs with DeepSeek

The script splits each Markdown file at ## headings, asks deepseek-v4.1-flash for a handful of pairs per section, and writes one JSON object per line. The model ID comes from the live model table on the API page (checked 2026-10-27); the same table lists deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-pro. The OpenAI SDK only needs base_url and the key changed.

# gen_data.py
import json, os, re, sys, time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://cloudgpu.app/v1", api_key=os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"])
MODEL = "deepseek-v4.1-flash"
PAIRS_PER_SECTION = 6

PROMPT = """You write training examples for a support assistant.
Use ONLY the documentation below. Do not invent features or settings.
Write {n} varied question-and-answer pairs that a user might ask about it.
Return ONLY a JSON array. Each item has the keys "instruction" (the question),
"input" (extra context, or an empty string) and "output" (the answer, 1-4 sentences).

Documentation:
{chunk}
"""

def sections(folder):
    for path in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        for part in re.split(r"\n(?=## )", path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")):
            if len(part.strip()) > 200:
                yield path.name, part.strip()

def parse(text):
    fence = "`" * 3  # the model may wrap its JSON in a code fence
    text = text.strip().removeprefix(fence + "json").removeprefix(fence).removesuffix(fence).strip()
    rows = json.loads(text)
    keys = ("instruction", "input", "output")
    return [r for r in rows if isinstance(r, dict) and all(isinstance(r.get(k), str) for k in keys)]

def ask(item):
    name, chunk = item
    for attempt in range(3):
        try:
            resp = client.chat.completions.create(
                model=MODEL,
                temperature=0.8,
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT.format(n=PAIRS_PER_SECTION, chunk=chunk)}],
            )
            return parse(resp.choices[0].message.content)
        except Exception as err:  # network error, rate limit, bad JSON
            print(f"{name}: attempt {attempt + 1} failed: {err}", file=sys.stderr)
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
    return []

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(ask, sections("docs")))
    with open("raw.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for rows in results:
            for row in rows:
                f.write(json.dumps(row, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print("sections:", len(results), "pairs:", sum(len(r) for r in results))

Run python3 gen_data.py. The four-worker pool and the retry loop keep you inside the default rate limits listed on the API page; check those limits there and lower max_workers if you see rate-limit errors.

What to check: raw.jsonl exists and has lines; the script prints how many sections and pairs it got. If a section failed three times it is skipped and the error is on stderr. A 401 means the key variable is not set in this shell.

Step 2: filter and de-duplicate

Model-written data needs a filter before training. This script drops empty rows, answers that are very short or very long, boilerplate such as "as an AI", and near-duplicate questions (token overlap of 0.8 or more). Tune the numbers for your data.

# filter_data.py
import json, re
from pathlib import Path

def tokens(s):
    return set(re.sub(r"\W+", " ", s.lower()).split())

def jaccard(a, b):
    union = a | b
    return len(a & b) / len(union) if union else 0.0

kept, seen = [], []
dropped = {"empty": 0, "length": 0, "boilerplate": 0, "duplicate": 0}

for line in Path("raw.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    row = json.loads(line)
    ins, inp, out = (row[k].strip() for k in ("instruction", "input", "output"))
    if not ins or not out:
        dropped["empty"] += 1
    elif not 20 <= len(out) <= 1200:
        dropped["length"] += 1
    elif re.search(r"\bas an ai\b|\blanguage model\b", out, re.I):
        dropped["boilerplate"] += 1
    elif any(jaccard(tokens(ins), t) >= 0.8 for t in seen):
        dropped["duplicate"] += 1
    else:
        seen.append(tokens(ins))
        kept.append({"instruction": ins, "input": inp, "output": out})

Path("synth_docs_qa.json").write_text(json.dumps(kept, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
Path("DATASET_NOTE.md").write_text(
    "AI-generated data: the examples in synth_docs_qa.json were generated with deepseek-v4.1-flash "
    "from documentation written by the dataset author. Review before use.\n", encoding="utf-8")
print("kept", len(kept), "dropped", dropped)

The output is in LLaMA-Factory's Alpaca format: instruction, optional input, and output, per the data preparation docs. A row looks like this (illustrative, written by hand, not model output):

{
  "instruction": "How do I change the output folder?",
  "input": "",
  "output": "Pass --out followed by a path, for example --out ./build."
}

Then read a sample yourself. Filters catch format problems, not wrong answers:

python3 -c "import json,random; [print(r['instruction'],'->',r['output'],'\n') for r in random.sample(json.load(open('synth_docs_qa.json')), 10)]"

What to check: DATASET_NOTE.md is the label DeepSeek's terms ask for if you publish the data: keep it next to the file. Compare ten sampled answers with your documentation; delete rows that are wrong, or tighten the prompt and regenerate. If the filter drops most rows, the model is probably not returning clean JSON: print one raw response and adjust parse.

If your data is multi-turn, LLaMA-Factory also reads a conversation format; the same docs page shows the dataset_info.json entry for it.

Step 3: rent a GPU

On Deploy, choose a card. The CloudGPU docs say two things that matter here: every template is an image with root SSH, and for anything a template does not cover you can rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. For this tutorial, pick a template that includes PyTorch, or choose Raw GPU and install it yourself. Pick a card with enough memory for your base model: the LLaMA-Factory README has a rough memory table (marked as estimates), and nvidia-smi shows real use during the first training steps.

GPU instances are billed per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum, and billing stops when you destroy the instance (terms). Rates are on the pricing page.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. Then upload the dataset from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -P <ssh-port> synth_docs_qa.json <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/

What to check: connect with ssh -p <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>, then run nvidia-smi (a GPU is listed) and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" (prints True). If torch is missing, install PyTorch with CUDA from the PyTorch install page first.

Step 4: install LLaMA-Factory and register the dataset

These are the install commands from the LLaMA-Factory README (read 2026-10-27; the repository name is spelled LlamaFactory there). The docs FAQ lists a LLaMA-Factory template, but don't count on it being installed or current: check, and install if needed.

cd /workspace
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hiyouga/LlamaFactory.git
cd LlamaFactory
pip install -e .
pip install -r requirements/metrics.txt

Copy the dataset into data/ and add an entry to data/dataset_info.json, which is how LLaMA-Factory finds custom datasets:

cp /workspace/synth_docs_qa.json data/
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
p = "data/dataset_info.json"
info = json.load(open(p, encoding="utf-8"))
info["synth_docs_qa"] = {
    "file_name": "synth_docs_qa.json",
    "columns": {"prompt": "instruction", "query": "input", "response": "output"},
}
json.dump(info, open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
EOF

What to check: llamafactory-cli help prints the command list, and grep synth_docs_qa data/dataset_info.json finds your entry.

Step 5: choose a base model and train a LoRA adapter

Small models are enough to see the pipeline work. Pick one row; the template name must match the model.

Base model LLaMA-Factory template License (read it yourself) Access
Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) llama3 Llama 3.2 Community License Gated on Hugging Face: accept the license, use a token
Gemma 3 4B IT (google/gemma-3-4b-it) gemma3 Gemma Terms of Use Gated on Hugging Face: accept the terms, use a token
Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 (mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) mistral License shown on the model card The model card listed no gate when we looked (2026-10-27)

Template names are from the LLaMA-Factory README's model table; license and access information was read on 2026-10-27 and can change. The Llama license has conditions that apply if you distribute or make available a model built on it. Confirm the license for your use yourself before you train or share anything.

For a gated model, request access on its Hugging Face page, then give the instance a fine-grained read token for just this run (you will revoke it at the end):

export HF_TOKEN="paste-a-read-token-here"

Save this as synth_lora.yaml in the LlamaFactory folder. The keys follow the official LoRA example in the repo's examples/train_lora/ folder; the model, template and dataset lines are the parts you change:

### model
model_name_or_path: meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct

### method
stage: sft
do_train: true
finetuning_type: lora
lora_rank: 8
lora_target: all

### dataset
dataset: synth_docs_qa
template: llama3
cutoff_len: 2048
preprocessing_num_workers: 4

### output
output_dir: saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth
logging_steps: 10
save_steps: 100
plot_loss: true
overwrite_output_dir: true

### train
per_device_train_batch_size: 1
gradient_accumulation_steps: 8
learning_rate: 1.0e-4
num_train_epochs: 3.0
lr_scheduler_type: cosine
warmup_ratio: 0.1
bf16: true

### eval
val_size: 0.1
per_device_eval_batch_size: 1
eval_strategy: steps
eval_steps: 50

Train:

llamafactory-cli train synth_lora.yaml

Open the LLaMA-Factory examples folder and compare your YAML with the current LoRA example: key names change between releases.

What to check: the log prints a training loss every 10 steps and, with val_size set, an evaluation loss every 50; saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth contains adapter_model.safetensors and adapter_config.json. If the base model download fails with a 401 or 403, the Hugging Face access request or token is the problem. An out-of-memory error means a smaller cutoff_len, a smaller model or a card with more memory; nvidia-smi shows the real use.

Unsloth (optional). The LLaMA-Factory README lists Unsloth among its supported add-ons and describes a use_unsloth: true argument for LoRA. Unsloth has its own documentation and install steps, and supports a specific list of models, so check that your base model is on its list before you add it.

Step 6: try the adapter, copy it off, destroy the instance

A quick test in the terminal (no server is started). Save as infer.yaml:

model_name_or_path: meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
adapter_name_or_path: saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth
template: llama3
infer_backend: huggingface

llamafactory-cli chat infer.yaml

Ask ten questions that are not in your training data and that you wrote yourself, and compare the answers with your documentation. That is your real test; the evaluation loss is not.

Now copy the adapter to your own machine before you destroy anything: destroying the instance permanently deletes its local storage. From your own machine:

rsync -avP -e "ssh -p <ssh-port>" \
  <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/LlamaFactory/saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth/ ./adapter-synth/

Check that adapter_model.safetensors is in ./adapter-synth/, revoke the Hugging Face token you pasted on the instance, then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). The minutes you spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your dashboard, and ./adapter-synth/ still opens on your machine.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • Generation (step 1) sends the documentation sections you give it to a model API. Don't send text you would not want processed by a model service, and read the privacy policy for what the service handles.
  • You keep ownership of what you put on the GPU instance. CloudGPU's terms (section 5) say it does not access the contents of your instance except where needed to investigate a credible report of a policy violation, where compelled by valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties. Local instance storage is deleted when you destroy the instance.
  • This tutorial does not start a server. If you later serve your model from an instance, use your own endpoint with your own API key: the terms (section 6) say instance service URLs are not authenticated by default, so add authentication yourself before you share the URL.

Sources

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • DeepSeek, Terms of Use, Last Update March 27, 2026: cdn.deepseek.com, sections 3.1 and 4.2.
  • LLaMA-Factory: README and data preparation docs.
  • CloudGPU: API page, terms (sections 4 to 6), acceptable use policy (section 1.8, last updated April 22, 2026), privacy policy.
  • Licenses: Llama 3.2, Gemma, Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 model card.

title: Zero Downtime Database Migration Explained: Patterns, Risks, and Cutover Planning
description:
Database migrations are a critical part of application modernization, cloud adoption, infrastructure upgrades, and database platform changes. However, moving a production database can introduce service interruptions, data inconsistencies, and unexpected application failures.

For businesses that depend on continuous access to transactions, customer records, inventory, or financial data, even a short outage can affect revenue and customer trust. This is why organizations increasingly plan for zero downtime database migration.

A zero downtime migration aims to move a database to a new environment without interrupting the application's availability. Achieving this requires more than copying tables. Teams must synchronize ongoing changes, maintain data consistency, validate application behavior, and carefully control the final cutover.

This guide explains common migration patterns, key risks, and practical cutover planning techniques.

What Is Zero Downtime Database Migration?

Zero downtime database migration is the process of moving a database from one server, platform, or environment to another while keeping the application available to users.

Typical migration scenarios include:

  • Moving from an on-premises database to the cloud.
  • Migrating from Oracle or SQL Server to PostgreSQL.
  • Upgrading database infrastructure.
  • Moving to a managed database service.
  • Replacing legacy database architecture.
  • Separating a database from an existing application environment.

True zero downtime is difficult to guarantee in every situation. Some migrations may require a brief period of restricted writes or a controlled application transition. The practical objective is to prevent a user-visible outage while preserving data integrity and transaction correctness.

Why Zero Downtime Migration Matters

A poorly planned migration can cause failed transactions, missing records, inconsistent application behavior, or prolonged recovery.

A well-designed migration strategy helps organizations:

  • Maintain business continuity.
  • Reduce customer disruption.
  • Minimize migration-related revenue loss.
  • Preserve transaction accuracy.
  • Support infrastructure modernization.
  • Reduce the risk of emergency rollback.

The required approach depends on database size, transaction volume, application architecture, replication capabilities, and acceptable risk.

Common Zero Downtime Database Migration Patterns

1. Online Migration With Change Data Capture (CDC)

Change Data Capture identifies changes made to the source database and applies them to the target.

The process generally involves:

  1. Provisioning and configuring the target database.
  2. Performing an initial copy of the existing data.
  3. Capturing new inserts, updates, and deletes on the source.
  4. Applying captured changes to the target.
  5. Monitoring replication lag and validating consistency.
  6. Switching application traffic when the target is ready.

CDC is useful when the source database must remain operational during most of the migration.

However, replication lag, unsupported data types, schema changes, and transaction ordering can affect correctness. CDC also does not automatically convert incompatible stored procedures or application queries.

2. Blue-Green Database Migration

In a blue-green approach, the existing production environment is the blue environment, and the new environment is green.

The target is prepared and tested while the current system continues serving users. Data is synchronized between environments, and traffic is switched when the target is ready.

A simplified sequence is:

  • Blue: Existing production database.
  • Green: New database receiving synchronized data.
  • Validation: Confirm data correctness and application compatibility.
  • Cutover: Direct application traffic to green.
  • Monitoring: Verify performance, errors, and transaction behavior.

This pattern can reduce transition risk, but database synchronization is the difficult part. Unlike stateless application deployments, databases contain mutable state. A safe design must prevent conflicting writes and ensure the target has received all required changes before accepting production traffic.

3. Shadow Reads and Application-Level Validation

Shadow reads send selected read-only requests to the new database while users continue receiving responses from the existing system.

The results can be compared to identify differences in query behavior, data representation, or performance.

This technique is particularly useful when moving between database engines because SQL behavior, sorting, null handling, and data type conversions may differ.

Shadow reads should avoid duplicate side effects. Do not replay writes against the target unless the test design explicitly controls them.

4. Expand-and-Contract Schema Migration

Expand-and-contract is a pattern for changing database schemas while maintaining compatibility with running application versions.

It generally involves:

  1. Expand: Add new columns, tables, or structures without immediately removing existing ones.
  2. Transition: Deploy application code that supports the old and new structures.
  3. Backfill: Populate the new structures and validate the results.
  4. Switch: Move reads and writes to the new representation.
  5. Contract: Remove obsolete structures after confirming that no active code depends on them.

This pattern is especially useful when database and application deployments cannot happen simultaneously.

Step-by-Step Zero Downtime Migration Plan

Step 1: Assess the Source Database

Before selecting a tool or migration pattern, document:

  • Database engine and version.
  • Database size and growth rate.
  • Transaction volume and peak activity.
  • Tables, indexes, constraints, and stored procedures.
  • Application queries and integrations.
  • Replication and backup capabilities.
  • Current performance and availability requirements.

For cross-engine migrations, assess incompatible SQL, data types, functions, triggers, and database-specific features.

Step 2: Define Migration Objectives

Agree on measurable requirements before starting.

Key objectives include:

  • Maximum acceptable service interruption.
  • Recovery Time Objective (RTO).
  • Recovery Point Objective (RPO).
  • Acceptable replication lag.
  • Data validation criteria.
  • Performance targets.
  • Rollback conditions.

Zero downtime does not automatically mean zero data loss. These objectives must be defined separately.

Step 3: Prepare the Target Environment

Configure the target database to meet production requirements. This includes access controls, encryption, network connectivity, monitoring, backup policies, indexing, connection limits, and performance settings.

Run compatibility tests and resolve schema conversion issues before transferring the full dataset.

Step 4: Copy Existing Data

Choose an initial-load method suitable for the database size and platform. Large datasets may require parallel loading, bulk export and import, or database-native migration capabilities.

Monitor resource consumption on both environments. An aggressive data copy can overload the source database or affect live application performance.

Step 5: Synchronize Ongoing Changes

Use supported replication or CDC mechanisms to keep the target aligned with the source while production traffic continues.

Monitor:

  • Replication lag.
  • Failed or delayed transactions.
  • Schema changes.
  • Replication errors.
  • Data type conversion problems.
  • Target database resource usage.

Define thresholds that must be met before cutover.

Step 6: Validate Data and Application Behavior

Data validation should go beyond checking whether tables exist.

Compare row counts, primary keys, important aggregates, and checksums where appropriate. Reconcile business-critical records such as account balances, orders, and inventory quantities.

Test the application against the target database, including authentication, writes, reporting, integrations, scheduled jobs, and error handling.

Performance testing is essential because a migration can preserve data while introducing slower queries or connection bottlenecks.

Step 7: Execute the Cutover

A controlled cutover typically includes:

  1. Confirming approval and readiness criteria.
  2. Freezing schema changes and other risky deployment activity.
  3. Preparing the application to stop or queue writes if required.
  4. Waiting for replication to catch up.
  5. Confirming final data consistency.
  6. Switching application connections or traffic.
  7. Running smoke tests and monitoring production behavior.

Depending on the architecture, some of these steps may be automated. The cutover plan should assign clear responsibilities and specify how each step is verified.

Step 8: Monitor and Close the Migration

After cutover, monitor application errors, database latency, query performance, connection pools, replication status, and business transactions.

Keep the old environment available according to the agreed rollback plan, but do not allow uncontrolled writes to both databases. Once the new environment is stable and rollback is no longer required, complete the retirement process and update operational documentation.

Major Risks and How to Reduce Them

Data Inconsistency

Risk: The target may be missing recent transactions or contain incorrectly transformed values.

Mitigation: Use reliable synchronization, reconciliation checks, and explicit consistency criteria before switching traffic.

Replication Lag

Risk: Changes arrive too slowly to meet the cutover window.

Mitigation: Benchmark replication under realistic write loads, optimize the migration path, and establish acceptable lag thresholds.

Application Incompatibility

Risk: Queries, stored procedures, drivers, or transaction behavior differ on the target platform.

Mitigation: Run compatibility assessments and end-to-end tests against the target database.

Performance Degradation

Risk: Queries become slower because of differences in indexing, query plans, configuration, or data distribution.

Mitigation: Benchmark representative workloads, inspect execution plans, and tune before production cutover.

Failed Cutover or Rollback

Risk: The target fails after traffic switches, while the old database no longer contains the latest writes.

Mitigation: Define rollback triggers, preserve a consistent recovery path, and explicitly plan how writes will be handled if traffic must return to the source.

Security Exposure

Risk: Migration credentials, data exports, or temporary infrastructure expose sensitive information.

Mitigation: Use least-privilege access, encrypted connections, secure secret handling, restricted network access, and appropriate cleanup of temporary files.

Cutover Planning Checklist

Before the migration, verify that:

  • [ ] Source and target compatibility has been assessed.
  • [ ] Initial data loading and ongoing synchronization have been tested.
  • [ ] Replication lag is within the agreed threshold.
  • [ ] Data reconciliation has passed.
  • [ ] Application and integration tests have passed.
  • [ ] Performance meets production requirements.
  • [ ] Cutover responsibilities and communication channels are defined.
  • [ ] Rollback triggers and recovery steps are documented.
  • [ ] Backups and recovery procedures have been verified.
  • [ ] Post-cutover monitoring is ready.

Conduct at least one realistic rehearsal where feasible. A timed rehearsal can reveal missing permissions, slow validation steps, unclear ownership, and assumptions that could otherwise delay the production switch.

Conclusion

Zero downtime database migration is a coordinated engineering process involving data transfer, synchronization, application compatibility, validation, and cutover control. CDC, blue-green migration, shadow reads, and expand-and-contract schema changes can help reduce disruption when selected for the right architecture.

The key is to validate the entire migration path before production cutover. Define availability and recovery objectives, test under realistic conditions, reconcile critical data, and document a credible rollback strategy.

With careful planning, businesses can modernize their database infrastructure while keeping services available and protecting the integrity of their data.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Is zero downtime database migration always possible?

Not in every environment. It depends on database capabilities, application design, replication support, and consistency requirements. Some migrations can avoid user-visible outages, while others require a brief write pause or controlled transition.

2. What is the best strategy for zero downtime database migration?

There is no universal best strategy. CDC-based migration is useful for keeping data synchronized, blue-green approaches support controlled environment switching, and expand-and-contract helps maintain application compatibility during schema changes.

3. What is Change Data Capture (CDC)?

CDC captures database changes such as inserts, updates, and deletes so they can be applied to another database. It is commonly used to keep a target synchronized while the source continues serving production traffic.

4. What is the difference between zero downtime and zero data loss?

Zero downtime focuses on service availability. Zero data loss means no committed data is lost during the migration or failure scenario. Achieving both requires appropriate synchronization, consistency checks, and recovery design.

5. How long does a zero downtime database migration take?

The timeline depends on database size, change rate, schema complexity, target compatibility, testing, and cutover requirements. A proof of concept and migration rehearsal help produce a realistic estimate.

6. How do you validate data after migration?

Validation may include row counts, key comparisons, checksums, aggregate reconciliation, constraint checks, and application-level testing. Critical business records should receive additional verification.

7. Can I migrate between different database engines without downtime?

It may be possible, but cross-engine migration is more complex because SQL syntax, data types, stored procedures, and transaction behavior can differ. Schema conversion and application testing are essential.

8. What is the biggest risk during database cutover?

A major risk is switching traffic before the target is fully synchronized or validated. This can cause missing data, inconsistent reads, or failed transactions. Explicit readiness criteria and a rehearsed cutover procedure reduce the risk.

9. Should the old database remain available after cutover?

Usually, it should remain available for a defined period if the recovery plan requires it. However, returning to the old database is not automatically safe once the new database has accepted writes. The team must define how post-cutover changes will be reconciled.

10. What tools are used for zero downtime database migration?

Options include database-native replication, CDC platforms, cloud migration services, and specialized migration tools. The right choice depends on source and target engines, supported versions, workload characteristics, and consistency requirements.

title: asyncio.gather() Still Takes 2.5 Seconds? Find the Blocking Call with Debug Mode
description:
You wrapped five calls in asyncio.gather(), expecting them to finish in about the time of the slowest one. Instead the total is the sum of all five, exactly as if you had written a plain for loop.

gather() is almost never the problem. Something inside one of your coroutines is blocking the event loop: a call that does real waiting without ever handing control back with await. While it runs, no other task can make progress, so your "concurrent" code quietly turns sequential.

Here is how to prove it in a minute, find the exact culprit, and fix it.

The 10-line reproduction 

import asyncio, time

async def fetch_blocking(i):
    time.sleep(0.5)          # looks harmless, freezes the whole loop
    return i

async def fetch_ok(i):
    await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.5)   # waits in a worker thread
    return i

async def main():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_blocking(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(f"blocking: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")

    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_ok(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(f"to_thread: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")

asyncio.run(main())

On Python 3.13 this prints:

blocking: 2.50s
to_thread: 0.51s

Same gather(), same five tasks. The only difference is whether the waiting happens on the event loop thread or off it. In real code time.sleep is rarely the offender. It is usually requests.get(), a sync database driver, open().read() on a big file, subprocess.run(), or a CPU-heavy loop such as parsing a large JSON payload.

Step 1: Turn on asyncio debug mode

You don't need a profiler to find the blocker. asyncio has a built-in detector: in debug mode it logs every step of a task that holds the loop longer than loop.slow_callback_duration (100 ms by default).

Enable it any one of these ways:

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)

PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 python app.py
# or
python -X dev app.py

Make sure warnings from the asyncio logger are visible (for a quick script, logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) is enough). Running the example above with debug=True prints one line per offending step:

WARNING:asyncio:Executing <Task finished name='Task-2' coro=<fetch_blocking() done, defined at demo.py:4> result=0 created at .../asyncio/tasks.py:748> took 0.500 seconds

That line tells you the coroutine name (fetch_blocking), the file and line where it is defined, and how long it froze the loop. Five of those lines, each about 0.5 s, add up to your mysterious 2.5 s.

If your real blockers are shorter, lower the threshold so they show up:

async def main():
    asyncio.get_running_loop().slow_callback_duration = 0.02  # 20 ms
    ...

Debug mode adds overhead, so use it locally or in staging, not as a permanent production setting.

Step 2: Narrow it down inside the coroutine

The warning points at a coroutine, not a line. If that coroutine is long, time the suspect calls directly:

t = time.perf_counter()
resp = client.get(url)          # suspect
print("get took", time.perf_counter() - t)

The rule of thumb: any call that waits on the network, disk, or a subprocess and is not preceded by await is a blocker. So is any pure-Python loop that runs for more than a few milliseconds.

Step 3: Pick the right fix

What blocks Fix
time.sleep(n) await asyncio.sleep(n)
requests an async client such as httpx.AsyncClient or aiohttp
sync DB driver (psycopg2, pymysql) an async driver (asyncpg, aiomysql, SQLAlchemy's async engine), or wrap calls in asyncio.to_thread
a sync library with no async version await asyncio.to_thread(func, *args) (Python 3.9+)
CPU-heavy work (big parsing, hashing, image work) a process pool via loop.run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), func, arg)

asyncio.to_thread is the quickest unblock for I/O-bound sync code, but remember it runs in a thread pool. Because of the GIL, threads will not speed up pure-Python CPU work, which is why that row goes to a process pool instead.

The FastAPI version of this bug

This shows up constantly in FastAPI, and it is sneaky because the "fix" people try first makes it worse.

@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    data = requests.get(UPSTREAM).json()   # blocks the event loop
    return data

With async def, FastAPI runs the endpoint on the event loop. The blocking requests.get() freezes every other request the worker is handling, so under load one slow upstream makes the whole service look dead.

You have two honest options:

  1. Keep it sync. Declare it as plain def report():. FastAPI then runs it in a thread pool, and the blocking call only ties up one worker thread.
  2. Go fully async. Keep async def and use an async client with await: 
@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        r = await client.get(UPSTREAM)
    return r.json()

What you should not do is mix them: async def plus a sync client is the worst of both. If you are still deciding between frameworks for this kind of service, I compared the trade-offs in FastAPI vs Flask: which is better in 2026.

Once it's unblocked: limit concurrency

When the loop is free, gather() fires everything at once, and 500 simultaneous requests can trip rate limits or exhaust a connection pool. Cap it with a semaphore:

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

async def fetch(client, url):
    async with sem:
        r = await client.get(url)
        return r.status_code

async def main(urls):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(client, u) for u in urls))

On Python 3.11+ you can use asyncio.TaskGroup instead of gather() when you want one failing task to cancel the rest.

Quick checklist

  • Total time equals the sum of the tasks? Something is blocking the loop.
  • Run with asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 and read the Executing <Task ...> took X seconds warnings.
  • Lower slow_callback_duration if the blockers are short.
  • Swap sync clients for async ones, or wrap them in asyncio.to_thread.
  • Send CPU-heavy work to a process pool.
  • In FastAPI, never put a blocking call inside async def.

If you're newer to async/await and want the fundamentals first (coroutines, create_task, timeouts and cancellation), there's a beginner walkthrough in this Python asyncio tutorial with examples. And when you're debugging the API payloads themselves, the free browser tools on Blogs World, like the JSON formatter, help you inspect responses without pasting them into random sites.
