title: Memory-Mapped Caching in Go: mmap Mechanics, Page Fault Latency, and the Eviction Boundary Problem
description:
Memory-Mapped Caching in Go: mmap Mechanics, Page Fault Latency, and the Eviction Boundary Problem

Application-layer caches built on map[string][]byte or Redis are the default answer for hot-path read amplification. They work until they don't: GC pressure from large heap allocations, network RTT jitter on Redis reads, or eviction policies that don't align with access patterns. A narrower alternative—memory-mapped files—trades explicit cache management for OS-level page management with zero-copy reads and off-heap storage. The tradeoff surface is poorly understood in Go services. This article works through the mechanics, the failure modes, and where the design boundary sits.

What mmap Actually Gives You

When you call mmap(2) on a file, the kernel maps file-backed pages into the process virtual address space. No data is read from disk at mapping time. Accesses to unmapped pages trigger a minor fault (page already in the OS page cache) or a major fault (page must be read from storage). The kernel manages this transparently. In Go you call into this via syscall.Mmap or the golang.org/x/sys/unix package.

package filecache

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "syscall"
)

type MmapRegion struct {
    data []byte
}

func OpenRegion(path string) (*MmapRegion, error) {
    f, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("open: %w", err)
    }
    defer f.Close()

    fi, err := f.Stat()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("stat: %w", err)
    }
    size := int(fi.Size())
    if size == 0 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("empty file")
    }

    data, err := syscall.Mmap(
        int(f.Fd()),
        0,
        size,
        syscall.PROT_READ,
        syscall.MAP_SHARED,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("mmap: %w", err)
    }
    return &MmapRegion{data: data}, nil
}

func (r *MmapRegion) Slice(offset, length int) []byte {
    return r.data[offset : offset+length]
}

func (r *MmapRegion) Close() error {
    return syscall.Munmap(r.data)
}

The slice returned by Slice points into the OS page cache, not the Go heap. The GC does not scan it. Allocation pressure from large in-process caches disappears. The data is accessible to any goroutine without a copy, and reads that hit warm pages are essentially a memcpy from L3 or RAM, not a syscall.

Where Go's Runtime Intersects

The slice header—pointer, length, cap—lives on the Go heap. The backing array does not. This creates a subtle escape problem: if you return a subslice from Slice and the caller stores it in an interface or passes it to json.Unmarshal, Go's escape analysis sees the header escape but not the data region. The GC won't move it (the runtime only moves heap objects in specific contexts, and mmap pages are not heap-managed), but the GC will not help you if a goroutine holds a stale slice into a region you've already Munmap'd. That's a use-after-free.

The correct contract is: the region owns the lifetime; callers borrow slices within a request-scoped duration and never store them beyond that scope. Enforce this structurally, not by convention.

A second interaction: syscall.Mmap causes the Go runtime's cgo signal handling path to activate for SIGBUS. If a file is truncated after mapping, any access to the now-invalid pages generates SIGBUS, which the Go runtime surfaces as a panic with a specific signal message rather than a clean error. Your service crashes. Validate file size before mapping and use atomic file replacement (write to temp, rename(2)) rather than in-place truncation.

Page Fault Latency Budget

The latency model for mmap reads is bimodal:

  • Warm path (page in page cache): ~50–200ns depending on whether the page is in L1/L2/L3 or main memory. This is on par with a Redis pipelined read within the same host and orders of magnitude faster than a cross-AZ Redis call.
  • Cold path (major fault): Kernel must issue an I/O to the underlying block device. On NVMe this is 100–300µs. On EBS gp3 in AWS it is 200µs–2ms depending on burst credit state. On io1/io2 it is more predictable but not fast enough for a 1ms latency budget on the hot path.

If your service has a 5ms P99 latency budget and you are serving a 2GB index file with a working set larger than available memory, major faults will blow that budget unpredictably. The OS will make eviction decisions based on global page reclaim pressure across all processes on the host, not your per-request deadline. This is the eviction boundary problem: you do not control when pages leave the page cache.

You can influence—but not guarantee—residency with madvise(2). MADV_WILLNEED hints the kernel to prefetch pages asynchronously. MADV_SEQUENTIAL adjusts readahead. Neither is a hard reservation.

func Prefetch(data []byte) error {
    _, _, errno := syscall.Syscall(
        syscall.SYS_MADVISE,
        uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&data[0])),
        uintptr(len(data)),
        syscall.MADV_WILLNEED,
    )
    if errno != 0 {
        return errno
    }
    return nil
}

mlock(2) pins pages in RAM and prevents eviction entirely, but it requires elevated privileges (CAP_IPC_LOCK), consumes locked memory quota (ulimit -l), and prevents the OS from using that memory for anything else. In containers on ECS or EKS, mlock limits are often restrictive or unavailable. Do not rely on it in containerized services without explicit platform configuration.

Operational Failure Modes in Production

Memory overcommit on shared hosts. Kubernetes nodes and ECS hosts run multiple containers. The page cache is shared. When a co-resident service allocates heavily, the kernel's kswapd begins reclaiming pages. Your mmap region, being file-backed, is eligible for eviction without any signal to your process. The next access triggers a major fault, and your latency spikes. This is the same failure mode as noisy neighbor problems on Redis, just lower-level.

File rotation without remap. A common pattern for serving updated index files is to replace the file on disk and expect the mmap to pick up changes. With MAP_SHARED, the mapping reflects the underlying inode. If you replace the file via rename(2) (creating a new inode), the existing mapping continues to point at the old inode's pages. The process keeps serving stale data silently. You must Munmap, open the new file, and remap. During the remap window, you need a fallback read path or the region must be read-locked against concurrent access.

NUMA topology. On multi-socket servers (less common in cloud but present on bare metal or large instance types), page allocation is NUMA-aware. Pages for the mmap region may reside on a remote NUMA node from the goroutine accessing them, adding 50–100ns per access due to cross-socket memory latency. You can observe this via numastat and influence placement with mbind(2), but the window for that optimization is narrow in typical AWS deployments.

Where mmap-Backed Caching Fits

The pattern works well for:

  • Static or slowly rotating read indexes: ML feature stores, precomputed lookup tables, IP geolocation databases, compiled rule sets. Large, mostly read, rotated infrequently. The working set fits in memory on the target instance type.
  • Zero-copy serving of binary blobs: Serving protobuf-encoded records or columnar data segments directly off a file without deserializing into heap structures. Combine with a fixed-offset index structure (array of [offset uint32, length uint32]) for O(1) lookup without malloc.
  • Shared memory between processes on the same host: MAP_SHARED with a named file or POSIX shared memory allows multiple processes to read the same pages without redundant copies. Relevant if you run a sidecar or co-located agent.

It is the wrong tool when:

  • Your cache working set is significantly larger than available RAM and access patterns are not strongly localized.
  • You need fine-grained TTL-based invalidation on individual keys—there is no key abstraction, only byte ranges.
  • You are running on EBS-backed storage with variable I/O latency and cannot tolerate the P99 impact of major faults.
  • You need write visibility—concurrent writers to a MAP_SHARED region require your own synchronization; the OS does not provide it.

Decision Framework

Before adopting mmap as a caching layer, answer these questions:

  1. Does the working set fit in instance memory with headroom? If the ratio of working set to available RAM exceeds ~0.6, major fault rate will be unpredictable under memory pressure. Measure with perf stat -e major-faults or /proc/vmstat under realistic load.
  2. What is the file update frequency? If rotation happens more than once per minute, remap coordination adds complexity that likely exceeds the benefit. A Redis hash or an in-process sync.Map with a TTL wheel is simpler.
  3. Is your latency budget fault-tolerant to P99 spikes? If your SLO is P99 < 2ms and you cannot bound major fault latency via instance type selection and mlock, the design is fragile.
  4. What is the operational context? EKS or ECS with shared node pools increases noisy neighbor risk. A dedicated instance or a memory-optimized instance type (r7g, x2idn) with a reserved memory allocation changes the math.
  5. Can you tolerate the Go lifetime contract? If slice lifetimes are difficult to bound in your codebase—heavy use of goroutines that outlive request context, interfaces that capture byte slices—the use-after-unmap risk may not be worth it.

When all five conditions are favorable, mmap-backed caches eliminate GC pressure, reduce allocator contention, and provide sub-microsecond read latency on warm pages with no network hop. When they are not, the opacity of OS page reclaim will produce latency anomalies that are difficult to attribute without kernel-level profiling tools.

title: How to Add Controller Support
description:
Controller support means letting players use a gamepad instead of touch. It changes how your game's timing and difficulty work. A touch-only platformer built around split-second taps becomes a different game when a D-pad removes the targeting constraint. Most teams add it without realizing it breaks the core mechanic they designed around.

What controller support actually means

Controller support is a second input layer that runs alongside touch. The game reads from both at the same time. Whichever one the player uses, the game responds.

You are not replacing touch controls. You are adding a parallel path: buttons map to actions, analog sticks map to movement, and the game treats controller input the same way it treats a swipe or a tap.

The work splits into three parts:

  • Input mapping - which buttons do what, and how analog stick movement translates to on-screen motion
  • Dual-input architecture - making sure touch and gamepad can coexist without breaking each other
  • UI adaptation - button prompts, pause menus, and navigation that work with a controller

Mapping buttons is the easy part. The real work is handling two input methods that have different timing, precision, and player expectations. A platformer balanced for swipe gestures feels sluggish with a gamepad unless you adjust movement speed and jump height separately.

This is similar to adding AI to a mobile game - the feature itself is straightforward, but it changes how the core mechanic needs to be tuned.

How dual-input changes your game model

Adding controller support means splitting your input layer into two parallel paths that must arrive at the same outcome. You are not adding a second way to tap the screen.

Touch input is direct. The player taps where they want to go, swipes to attack, or drags to aim. Controller input is indirect. A thumbstick sends continuous position data. A button fires a discrete event. Your game model must normalize both into unified actions.

This architecture affects three parts of your game.

Movement becomes continuous instead of discrete. A touch target is a single coordinate. A thumbstick is a vector that updates every frame. Your character controller must handle both without changing how the game feels.

Difficulty curves need recalibration. A platformer tuned for touch might have tight jump windows or precise landing zones. Controller players clear those obstacles faster because analog input is more precise than a tap. Same level. Easier or harder depending on the input method.

UI flow diverges. Touch players navigate menus by tapping. Controller players expect D-pad navigation and button confirmation. One menu system must serve both, or you maintain two. That decision ripples through every screen in your game.

We saw this clearly in Jungle Jump. The original touch build had pixel-perfect platform edges because tapping is exact. When we added gamepad integration, testers cleared levels in half the expected time. We widened platforms and adjusted enemy timing to rebalance difficulty across both input methods. Same game model. Different tuning.

A harder question appears when touch and controller players compete in the same leaderboard systems. An action game with both input types must either segment leaderboards by input method or accept that controller scores will dominate. Neither choice is wrong, but one has to be made before you ship.

What controller support looks like in a real build

We added controller support to Jungle Jump, a 2D platformer that already worked with touch. Players could tap to jump and swipe to move. Both inputs stayed in the shipped version.

The controller path reads button state every frame and maps it to the same movement functions the touch handler calls. One input model, two entry points. Game logic never checks how the player jumped, only that they did.

Jump height was the hardest part. Touch players commit to a jump on press. Controller players modulate it by holding the button. We capped jump velocity so a held button couldn't reach platforms the level designer placed out of range. That preserved difficulty for controller users without breaking the touch path.

Gamepad integration does not mean reworking the model. Route a second input stream into the same state machine. Test both paths against the same progression curve.

Where teams break the core mechanic

Most teams add controller support after the game is already tuned for touch. You discover that a button-press is faster and more precise than a swipe. Your platformer suddenly becomes trivially easy.

The problem is not the mobile app development itself. Touch controls and gamepad integration operate at different speeds. A jump that required careful timing with a finger now executes instantly with the A button. Enemy patterns balanced around imprecise taps become effortless with analog stick movement.

You cannot bolt controller support onto a touch-tuned game and expect it to feel right. Input mapping changes the difficulty curve.

Teams that ship both inputs well tune twice. They test both paths separately and adjust enemy speed, jump arc, and level pacing so each input feels fair. Balance once and enable both, one version will be broken.

How to tell whether your game needs it

Three signals tell you controller support belongs in your build.

Your game demands precise timing or directional input. Platformers like Jungle Jump need exact jump arcs and fast direction changes. Touch controls work, but a joystick and physical buttons let players execute moves they can already picture. If your core mechanic rewards precision, controller support stops the interface from being the bottleneck.

Your target players already own controllers. Mobile gaming controllers sold well in 2025 and 2026, and a portion of your audience expects to use them. If you are building an action game, a racing title, or anything with real-time combat, a segment of your players will try to connect a controller on day one.

You want to expand beyond mobile. Controller support is the input layer for console and desktop ports. Adding it now means one codebase works across platforms later without rewriting your control scheme from scratch.

The decision comes down to whether the mechanical advantage matters for your game. Touch is already comfortable for many core loops. Controller support adds complexity without clear upside in those cases. Precision unlocks better play in others. Then it belongs in the feature list from the start.

title: "⛔ Stop Merging Agents Without a Required Check"
description:
Optional checks are how bad agents reach main.

Teams add agent-evals to Actions, celebrate, then leave the check non-required. The red X becomes a suggestion. The merge button stays green if someone is in a hurry.

Required means required

In GitHub: branch protection → require status checks → select the eval job name exactly. If the name drifts after a workflow rename, protection silently stops enforcing. Pin the check name in the same PR that renames the workflow.

Also fail closed on infra errors. A missing API key in CI secrets is not “skip evals.” It is a red build.

- name: agent evals
  env:
    OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
  run: |
    if [ -z "$OPENAI_API_KEY" ]; then
      echo "OPENAI_API_KEY missing"
      exit 1
    fi
    python -m evals.ci_gate --suite merge

Split suites so merges stay fast

One fat suite that needs twenty minutes will get bypassed. Split:

Suite When Goal
merge every PR 5–15 cases, under 3 minutes
nightly cron broader set, live models, richer traces
release tag full regression before a version bump

The merge suite must be boring and mostly offline. Nightly can spend money. Release can be slow.

Flake is a product bug

If the same case fails one in five runs, do not mute it. Fix the case:

  • pin model + temperature 0 when the vendor allows it
  • assert on tool names and structured fields, not full free text
  • isolate network with recorded HTTP fixtures

A flaky required check trains the team to ignore CI. That is worse than no check.

Trace every failure

Store the run artifact: prompt, tool calls, tokens, final output. Without traces, “evals failed” becomes a Slack shrug.

python -m evals.ci_gate --suite merge --out artifacts/eval-run.json

Upload artifacts/ on failure. The next engineer should replay the case without guessing.

Honest trade-off

Required checks slow the first weeks. People will ask to “just merge this one.” Say no once, then the habit sticks. The cost is friction. The alternative is production loops that look like “the model was weird today.”

Checklist

  • [ ] Eval job name matches branch protection
  • [ ] Secrets missing → fail, not skip
  • [ ] Merge suite under a few minutes
  • [ ] Flaky cases owned, not silenced
  • [ ] Traces uploaded on failure

Is your agent check required on main, or is it still a polite warning?

title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports September 2026 Monthly Recommended Patch
description:
Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports the September 2026 Monthly Recommended Patch (MRP) for Oracle Database version 19c and 26ai. An MRP is a minor engine version that builds on a quarterly Release Update (RU), bundling Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) with additional Oracle-recommended fixes. The September 2026 MRP is applied on top of the July 2026 RU and includes the Oracle September CSPU. We recommend upgrading to the September 2026 MRP as it includes the latest security updates for Oracle Database.

This release also includes the updated Oracle time zone file (DST version 46), which reflects the latest daylight saving time rule changes in several regions, including British Columbia and Alberta in Canada (effective November 1, 2026) and Morocco and Western Sahara (effective September 20, 2026), which are moving to permanent UTC offsets. If you store timestamps that include time zone information for these areas, the updated time zone file keeps that data aligned with the new rules.

You can apply the September 2026 MRP for new database instances, or upgrade existing instances to engine version 19.0.0.0.ru-2026-07.mrp-2026-09.r2 or 26.0.0.0.ru-2026-07.mrp-2026-09.r2 from the Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. To learn more about Oracle MRPs supported on Amazon RDS for each engine version, see the Amazon RDS for Oracle Release notes.

title: PostgreSQL 19 Release Candidate: What Shipped, What Was Cut, How to Upgrade
description:
Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.

PostgreSQL 19 is not out yet. The first release candidate shipped on October 15, 2026, and the project now plans general availability for November 19, 2026, later than many teams expected. Several headline features announced in the June beta were pulled before the RC, so if you planned an upgrade around them, this guide covers what actually made the cut, what changes under your feet, and how to get ready.

Where the release stands right now

The PostgreSQL 19 timeline this year has been longer than usual. Here are the dates that matter, all from the project's own announcements:

Milestone Date
Beta 1 June 4, 2026
Beta 4 (features removed) September 24, 2026
Release Candidate 1 October 15, 2026
RC 2 and minor updates for supported versions November 12, 2026 (planned)
PostgreSQL 14 end of life November 12, 2026
PostgreSQL 19 general availability November 19, 2026 (planned)

The RC 1 announcement explains that the release team chose to fold a large batch of fixes into version 19 before calling it final, which is why a second release candidate is on the calendar. The GA date can still move if a serious issue turns up.

Why so many late fixes? According to a DEV Community write-up that collects the public discussion, long-time committer Peter Eisentraut wrote on October 9 that LLM-assisted code review was at least partly responsible for the wave of reverts, because it surfaced defects in already-committed features much faster than before. The same write-up notes that some community members pushed back, saying a large share of AI-reported bugs turned out not to be real. Either way, the practical result for you is the same: a smaller, more conservative release.

What was cut from PostgreSQL 19

If you read the Beta 1 announcement and got excited, check this list before you plan anything. The official Beta 4 announcement says these were removed so they can be reconsidered for a later major version:

  • SQL/PGQ property graph queries (graph-style queries in standard SQL)
  • Turning data checksums on or off while the cluster is online
  • Temporal UPDATE and DELETE using FOR PORTION OF
  • ALTER TABLE ... MERGE PARTITIONS and SPLIT PARTITIONS
  • pg_get_role_ddl(), pg_get_tablespace_ddl() and pg_get_database_ddl()

GROUP BY ALL, which appeared in the Beta 1 highlights, is also missing from the current release notes. So if a blog post or tutorial shows any of these as "new in Postgres 19", treat it as outdated.

What did make it in

The good news is that a lot of useful work survived. Based on the RC-era release notes, these are the changes most app developers will notice:

Photo: Domaintechnik on Unsplash

For application code

  • INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT ... RETURNING. An upsert can now hand back the row that already existed instead of silently skipping it. That removes a common "insert, and if nothing came back, run a second SELECT" round trip.
  • Faster foreign key checks. The notes list a general performance improvement for foreign key constraint checks.
  • A WAIT command for replicas. A session on a standby can wait until a given WAL position has been written, flushed or replayed. That gives you read-your-writes behaviour when you send writes to the primary and reads to a replica.
  • More jsonpath string methods, including lower(), upper(), replace(), split_part() and the trim family.
  • COPY TO can output JSON, with a FORCE_ARRAY option to produce a single JSON array.
  • Smarter NOTIFY, which now wakes only the backends listening on the relevant channel. Apps that use LISTEN/NOTIFY for real-time features should see less overhead.

Here is the kind of upsert that gets simpler. This is an illustration, not code from the docs:

-- Create a tag if it doesn't exist, and always get its row back
INSERT INTO tags (name)
VALUES ('billing')
ON CONFLICT (name) DO SELECT
RETURNING id, name;

For operations

  • REPACK, a built-in way to rebuild bloated tables, with a CONCURRENTLY option that avoids blocking reads and writes. It shipped with a narrower scope than first planned, and it received many crash and correctness fixes during the betas, so test it on a copy first.
  • Parallel autovacuum via autovacuum_max_parallel_workers, plus a new scoring system for deciding which tables to vacuum first.
  • Automatic I/O worker scaling between the new io_min_workers and io_max_workers settings.
  • pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, new modules for steering and pinning planner decisions.
  • Logical replication of sequences, which makes replication-based online upgrades less fiddly.
  • TLS SNI support through a new pg_hosts.conf file, so one server can present different certificates per hostname.

Breaking changes to check before upgrading

This is the section to read twice. These items come from the migration section and other behaviour changes in the release notes:

  1. JIT is off by default. If you have analytical queries that benefited from JIT compilation, benchmark them and turn it back on explicitly if needed.
  2. RADIUS authentication is gone. The notes describe the UDP-only implementation as unfixably insecure. Move to another method before upgrading.
  3. MD5 password logins now trigger a warning after successful authentication (controlled by md5_password_warnings). It's a nudge to switch to SCRAM.
  4. standard_conforming_strings is always on. Dumps taken from older versions with this setting off will not load correctly into 19.
  5. max_locks_per_transaction defaults to 128 instead of 64, and lock sizing changed. If you tuned this value, the notes say you effectively need to double it to keep the same capacity.
  6. json_array() returns an empty array instead of NULL when there are no rows. Check any code that tests for NULL here.
  7. Default TOAST compression is now lz4 rather than pglz.
  8. vacuumdb --analyze-only now includes partitioned tables when no targets are given.

A quick way to spot settings that matter on your current server:

SELECT name, setting
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN (
  'jit',
  'standard_conforming_strings',
  'max_locks_per_transaction',
  'password_encryption',
  'default_toast_compression'
);

And to find roles still using MD5 password hashes (run as a superuser):

SELECT rolname
FROM pg_authid
WHERE rolpassword LIKE 'md5%';

A practical upgrade checklist

Don't run an RC in production: A release candidate is for testing. Wait for the final 19.0 release, and for most teams, for the first minor release after it, before moving production data.

  1. Know your current version. Run SELECT version();. If you're on PostgreSQL 14, that matters more than 19: version 14 stops getting fixes on November 12, 2026. Plan to move to 17 or 18 now, or straight to 19 once it's stable.
  2. Check your provider. Managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase, Neon and others) adopt new majors on their own schedules. Look up when they will offer 19 rather than assuming it will be there on day one.
  3. Spin up the RC in a container and restore a recent copy of your database into it. Run your test suite and your slowest real queries.
  4. Work through the breaking-change list above, especially MD5, RADIUS and standard_conforming_strings.
  5. Pick an upgrade method. The project recommends a major-version approach such as pg_upgrade (fast, in place) or pg_dump / pg_restore (slower, cleaner). Logical replication is another option if you need minimal downtime.
  6. Run pg_upgrade --check first against a copy. It reports incompatibilities without changing anything.
  7. Update drivers and ORMs (node-postgres, Prisma, Drizzle, psycopg and so on) in staging, then confirm migrations still run.
  8. Have a rollback plan: a verified backup and a tested restore, not just a backup.

What this means for business and app owners

If you run a SaaS product, an e-commerce store or an internal tool on Postgres, PostgreSQL 19 is not urgent. Nothing in it is a security fix you must rush to apply, and the most eye-catching features were deferred. The more pressing date is November 12: if your database is on version 14, it will stop receiving security patches that day.

A sensible plan for most teams looks like this: get off 14 this quarter, test 19 in staging once it hits GA, and schedule the production upgrade for early 2027 after the first point release. The features that did ship, like ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, replica WAIT and faster foreign key checks, are real quality-of-life wins worth adopting once you're there.

If your app was built quickly, perhaps with an AI builder, and nobody is sure which Postgres version it runs, which auth method it uses, or whether backups restore, that's worth finding out before any upgrade. A production audit covers exactly those questions, and if you need help planning a database move as part of backend work, get in touch.

Sources

  • PostgreSQL 19 RC 1 Released (postgresql.org)
  • PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released (postgresql.org)
  • PostgreSQL 19 Beta 1 Released (postgresql.org)
  • PostgreSQL 19 release notes (RC documentation)
  • PostgreSQL versioning policy
  • PostgreSQL 19 Release Date Moved to Nov 19 After AI Review Found Too Many Bugs (DEV Community)
  • Cover photo: Taylor Vick on Unsplash

I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

title: Node.js Compliance Email Delivery with Auditable Event Boundaries
description:
TL;DR: For a B2B SaaS welcome or compliance notice, the best Node.js email API is the one that fits an explicit delivery boundary: your database owns the business event and audit record, while the email provider owns message transport and feedback. Pick the integration that lets the team persist an idempotency key, queue a retryable handoff, verify sender authentication, and ingest delivery evidence without pretending that SMTP delivery is exactly once. Integration effort is the deciding axis because a cheap-looking HTTP call becomes expensive when a duplicate welcome message or an unverifiable notice reaches a customer.

This is an architecture decision record, not a leaderboard. A welcome email is often treated as a small notification, but a compliance notice attached to onboarding can become evidence in a customer dispute. The system therefore has two separate obligations: record what the application decided to send, and record what the transport system later reported. Those are related events, not one status field.

What must be true before the API choice matters

The invariants come first. For each notice, the application should be able to answer which customer-visible event caused the message, which template revision was selected, which recipient was addressed, when the send request was accepted, and which later provider signals were received. The audit trail should remain useful even if the provider is unavailable for several minutes.

I use a narrow state model: pending, submitted, delivered, bounced, and suppressed. submitted means the transport boundary accepted the request; it does not mean the recipient read the message, and it does not prove mailbox placement. A bounce or suppression signal may arrive after a successful submission, so the record is an append-only history plus a current projection, rather than a single mutable boolean.

The exactly-once mindset belongs to the business event. A database transaction should create one welcome-notice intent for one account activation, protected by a unique key such as welcome:{account_id}:{template_revision}. Delivery work is at-least-once by nature: a timeout can occur after the remote system accepted a request, leaving the caller unable to know whether retrying will duplicate the message. The integration must make that uncertainty visible and contain it.

Sender authentication is part of the boundary, too. SPF is a policy mechanism for publishing which hosts are authorized to send mail for a domain; it is not a complete proof of message authenticity or delivery. Domain alignment, signing, bounce handling, and mailbox-provider feedback still need separate treatment.

Keep it boring.

What is the best API for sending welcome emails in Node.js?

There are three defensible shapes. The right one depends on how much operational surface the team is prepared to own, not on the number of lines in the first Node.js prototype.

Boundary Application owns Transport layer owns Main integration cost Appropriate when
Direct SMTP connection policy, retries, response parsing, queueing, feedback ingestion network handoff to an SMTP server highest operational surface mail infrastructure is already a core capability
Generic HTTP email API event ledger, request mapping, authentication, webhook verification SMTP submission, provider retries, delivery events moderate adapter and event work the team wants a small transport adapter with explicit evidence
Internal mail gateway stable internal contract, routing metadata, audit correlation vendor selection, transport policy, provider-specific feedback gateway design and ownership several services need one governed boundary

A generic HTTP API usually has the smallest initial adapter, but only if its response and asynchronous events are treated as transport facts rather than business truth. A gateway can reduce duplicated work across services, yet it introduces an owner, a deployment path, and another place where correlation data can be lost. Direct SMTP can be appropriate for a mail-focused organization; it is a poor default when a product team merely needs a compliance notice.

That convenience has a limitation: a smaller adapter does not remove sender-domain setup, callback verification, retention review, or reconciliation. Those costs move into configuration and operations. A gateway has the opposite trade-off; it standardizes policy, but a small team may not have enough services to justify maintaining another service boundary.

This comparison also explains why naming a “best API” without stating the boundary is misleading. An API that is convenient for a single welcome message may be the wrong choice once an audit reviewer needs the original event, template revision, provider request identifier, and final feedback in one query.

How should a Node.js service make the handoff auditable?

The critical path is short. Commit the intent with the account change, enqueue work through an outbox or equivalent durable mechanism, submit a message containing a stable correlation key, and persist the transport response. The worker must be safe to run again. It cannot assume that a network timeout means rejection.

The following Go example shows the boundary as an interface because the same separation can be implemented in a Node.js worker with a typed adapter. The important part is the ordering and the correlation data, not the transport client.

package mail

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Notice struct {
    ID             string
    AccountID      string
    Recipient      string
    TemplateRev    string
    CorrelationKey string
}

type Transport interface {
    Submit(context.Context, Notice) (providerID string, err error)
}

type Ledger interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, noticeID string) (bool, error)
    RecordSubmitted(ctx context.Context, noticeID, providerID string, at time.Time) error
    RecordFailure(ctx context.Context, noticeID, reason string, at time.Time) error
}

func Deliver(ctx context.Context, n Notice, t Transport, l Ledger, now time.Time) error {
    claimed, err := l.Claim(ctx, n.ID)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("claim notice: %w", err)
    }
    if !claimed {
        return nil // Another worker owns this attempt or it is already recorded.
    }

    providerID, err := t.Submit(ctx, n)
    if err != nil {
        _ = l.RecordFailure(ctx, n.ID, err.Error(), now)
        return fmt.Errorf("submit notice: %w", err)
    }
    return l.RecordSubmitted(ctx, n.ID, providerID, now)
}

Claim is not a magic exactly-once guarantee. It prevents two workers from processing the same local row concurrently, while a crash between remote acceptance and RecordSubmitted still leaves an ambiguity. A retry policy should therefore include an idempotency facility when the transport supports one; where it does not, the product should decide whether a possible duplicate is safer than a possible missing notice. For a welcome message, duplication is irritating. For a regulatory notification, omission can be materially worse. That decision belongs in the record.

The Node.js implementation also needs a durable outbox, bounded retries with backoff, a dead-letter path that an operator can inspect, and a reconciliation job. Do not bury these concerns inside a route handler. The route should commit the customer event; a worker should perform the external handoff.

The failure window is one line wide and still matters.

Suppose the worker receives a notice, the transport accepts it, and the process exits before the local ledger records the provider identifier. A later retry sees an apparently pending row. If the transport has a stable idempotency key, the retry can ask the boundary to collapse the duplicate and the ledger can reconcile the resulting identifier. If it has no such facility, the system cannot derive certainty from its own database: it must choose a policy, expose the ambiguity to operations, and preserve both attempts or the retry decision in the audit history. That is a small amount of additional code, but it is the difference between an explanation supported by evidence and a status label that merely looks complete.

What does the audit trail prove, and what does it not prove?

An audit record proves your system's observations. It can prove that account acct_4821 generated a notice with template revision welcome-7, that the worker submitted it at a recorded time, and that a transport callback later reported a bounce. It cannot prove that the recipient opened the message, saw the intended rendering, or received it in a primary inbox.

That distinction changes the schema. Store immutable event rows with timestamps, event type, correlation key, template revision, recipient hash or governed recipient reference, transport request identifier, and the raw provider event after validation. Keep a current status projection for queries, but never overwrite the event history to make a later state look like the original decision. Protect callback processing with its own deduplication key; webhook retries are normal, and an event counter that increments twice will corrupt operational reporting.

Compliance limits matter here. Retain only the recipient data required for the stated purpose, restrict who can inspect message content, and define retention with counsel and the applicable policy rather than treating an email log as harmless application output. Hashing an address can reduce accidental exposure, but it does not make every privacy obligation disappear.

I would also test the unpleasant timing cases before comparing API ergonomics: the process dies after submission, a callback arrives before the submission transaction finishes, the same callback is delivered twice, DNS authentication is misconfigured, and the template revision disappears during a retry. These cases tell you more about integration effort than a successful local request.

The rejected option and its valid use case

The rejected default is a direct provider call from the account-activation request. It is attractive because the code is visible and the first response can be shown immediately, but it couples customer latency to a remote dependency and makes the database transaction carry an external side effect it cannot roll back. A timeout then forces an unsafe choice: retry and risk duplication, or stop and risk omission.

This shape still has a valid use case for a low-consequence, explicitly best-effort message where the product accepts loss and duplication. It is not the boundary I would choose for a compliance notice with an auditable delivery record. An outbox and worker add integration work up front, but they make failure states inspectable, replayable, and testable.

The final selection rule is therefore concrete: choose the email API or gateway whose authentication, request correlation, asynchronous feedback, retry semantics, and data-retention controls can be represented in your existing event ledger without provider-specific facts leaking into product code. Compare those seams in a small failure-injection exercise. The “best” transport is the one that leaves the fewest unresolved facts at the point where your team must explain what happened.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321
  • RFC 3461, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Service Extension for Delivery Status Notifications: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3461
  • RFC 8617, The Authenticated Received Chain (ARC) Protocol: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8617

title: Architecting AI and OTA Pipelines for Software-Defined Vehicles
description:
Problem

Software-defined vehicles transform cars into distributed edge nodes running complex AI perception stacks. Traditional automotive development relied on static firmware flashed once at the factory. Modern ADAS and autonomous driving features demand continuous software iteration, over-the-air (OTA) updates, and continuous MLOps feedback loops.

This shift introduces severe architectural challenges. Vehicles operate in disconnected, intermittent, and low-bandwidth network environments. Cellular data costs scale punishingly fast across fleets of hundreds of thousands of vehicles. Furthermore, software delivery is bound by rigorous safety standards including ISO 26262 for functional safety and ISO/SAE 21434 for cybersecurity. A failed OTA flash cannot simply result in a reboot loop; it requires deterministic fallback to a known-good gold image without human intervention.

Architecture overview

Building an enterprise-grade automotive AI and OTA platform requires clear separation between vehicle edge compute and cloud-native backend services. The architecture must ingest high-volume telemetry securely, process petabytes of perception data for MLOps retraining, and orchestrate verifiable firmware deployments.

The edge tier runs on automotive-grade hardware with AUTOSAR Adaptive and containerized runtimes. The ingestion tier uses lightweight messaging protocols to handle intermittent connectivity. The cloud platform uses event-driven streaming to decouple ingestion from heavy analytics pipelines, while CI/CD and OTA orchestration services manage the safe lifecycle of binary artifacts.

Step-by-step flow

  1. Vehicle perception logs telemetry locally onto edge storage.
  2. Telemetry agent batches and compresses logs for upload.
  3. MQTT gateway ingests compressed edge telemetry payloads.
  4. Kafka buffer decouples vehicle ingestion from storage.
  5. S3 data lake stores raw logs for MLOps retraining pipelines.
  6. CI/CD pipeline triggers automated regression tests on models.
  7. OTA service packages verified firmware and model binaries.
  8. Fleet manager orchestrates safe delta updates to vehicles.

Design decisions and trade-offs

Decoupling the vehicle ingestion path using a distributed message broker prevents cloud outages from impacting vehicle operations. However, persistent edge buffering requires careful management of local solid-state storage wear leveling and capacity limits.

Network bandwidth optimization forces a hybrid approach to data collection. Instead of streaming raw camera feeds continuously, the edge system runs anomaly detection locally and uploads only interesting edge cases or driver-triggered snapshots. This drastically reduces cellular data expenses but risks missing rare training scenarios that the anomaly detector failed to flag.

Containerizing applications on the vehicle edge provides excellent developer ergonomics, but introduces hypervisor overhead and complex deterministic scheduling challenges required by hard real-time domains.

Failure modes

Cellular network partitions are inevitable in underground garages and remote rural areas. If edge buffering lacks disk quota limits, local logs can consume all available storage, starving critical operating system functions.

Another severe failure mode occurs during OTA updates. If a delta package applies successfully to one ECU but fails validation on an interdependent controller, the vehicle can enter a bus-off state. Systems must implement redundant boot banks with watchdog timers that automatically revert to the previous verified software image upon boot failure.

When not to use this

Do not build a custom cloud ingestion and OTA orchestration platform if your fleet size is under ten thousand vehicles or if your software is strictly non-safety-critical infotainment. Managed IoT platforms and commercial fleet management solutions provide out-of-the-box telemetry and device management that eliminate the heavy undifferentiated lifting of building custom MQTT gateways and delta-patching OTA pipelines.

Key takeaways

Automotive software delivery requires treating vehicle ECUs as remote data center nodes with severe resource constraints and uncompromising safety requirements. CI/CD pipelines must enforce ISO 26262 compliance gates before any binary is signed and packaged for fleet deployment.

ota_manifest:
  target_ecu: "adas_domain_controller"
  version: "2.4.1"
  checksum_sha256: "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855"
  rollback_strategy: "automatic_bank_switch"
  cryptographic_signature: "sig_asn1_secp256r1"

Integrating security, safety, and cloud-native velocity ensures your software-defined vehicle platform can scale safely from prototype to millions of cars on the road.

title: Object Storage for App Data Backups: A US/EU S3-Compatible Restore Test
description:
Short answer: object storage is a sensible low-cost home for app data backups when you keep buckets private, use signed download links for restores, and accept retention measured in whole days. It is the wrong tool when immutable recovery, public URLs, or a provider-managed compliance program is the actual requirement.

I make the decision with a restore-window SLO, not a storage-rate leaderboard. A nightly database dump or ZIP export is only useful if an operator can find it, download it from the right region, and restore it under pressure. Storage, egress, and request charges all belong in the estimate; the smallest monthly byte price alone tells me very little. I've watched estimates miss the transfer leg because someone counted stored gigabytes and ignored the restore path, so I write down the worker region, expected restore frequency, and the person who can authorize a download before I approve a bucket.

What should US/EU app backups require from private S3-compatible storage?

Start with a private bucket and a naming convention that carries the metadata your operator needs: prod/postgres/2026-07-31/tenant-42.sql.gz is easier to list by prefix than an opaque UUID. Scheduled dumps, archive exports, and restore downloads fit this pattern. A restore service authenticates the operator, then mints a short-lived signed URL; the bucket never needs a public-read policy.

US and EU placement still needs an explicit decision. Put each workload and its restore worker in the region you operate and document the residency assumption in the runbook. “US/EU” is a deployment constraint, not proof of compliance, and I'm not sure a vendor label can answer the legal question without your contracts.

Lifecycle rules can expire a prefix, but the smallest interval is one day. There is no hour-level expiry, automatic cleanup for multipart fragments, or server-side metadata search beyond prefix listing. If the application needs those controls, a catalog, queue, or cleanup worker has to own them.

That naming choice becomes a capacity signal as well as a lookup aid. I would separate prod/ from staging/, keep the database engine and date in the key, and record the compressed byte count in the backup manifest. During a restore drill, an operator can list one prefix, select a date, and compare the manifest before pulling a large archive across regions. The same convention makes a lifecycle rule narrow enough to review: expire prod/postgres/ after the agreed number of days while leaving a separate audit prefix alone. It also avoids pretending that object metadata is a query index. If the retention decision depends on a customer, legal hold, or checksum that is not in the key, keep that fact in a database and make the cleanup worker consult it before deletion. This is slower to design than “list everything and inspect names,” but it gives the on-call person a bounded operation and a measurable restore path.

Private means private.

The production-shaped restore path

The implementation should make retries boring and observable. The storage API uses a bearer key, an explicit HTTP method, and a client idempotency key for writes. A 429 is a scheduling signal: honor Retry-After when it is present, back off, and surface the error when attempts are exhausted. Don't turn a retry loop into an unbounded worker; a backup that cannot report failure is worse than a backup that fails loudly.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, method, path string, body io.Reader, idem string) (*http.Response, error) {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" { panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required") }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, baseURL+path, body)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests { return resp, nil }
        resp.Body.Close()
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond
        if retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retry != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retry); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
        }
        select { case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err(); case <-time.After(delay): }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("storage request remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    resp, err := call(ctx, http.MethodPut, "/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", nil, "backup-prod-2026-07-31")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Errorf("upload failed: %s", resp.Status)) }

    link, err := call(ctx, http.MethodPost, "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}", nil, "presign-prod-2026-07-31")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer link.Body.Close()
    if link.StatusCode < 200 || link.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Errorf("presign failed: %s", link.Status)) }
    // Read the returned URL and use it without the Infrai Authorization header.
}

The sample keeps the data plane narrow: upload the archive, then request a presigned response for the restore. In production, send the archive bytes as the PUT body and parse the response before issuing the download. Do not attach the API bearer token to that returned URL.

Which storage option fits the backup SLO?

I compare the real alternatives by operational promise. Amazon S3 has the broadest S3 tooling; Cloudflare R2 can be convenient when the application already depends on Cloudflare; Backblaze B2 is a straightforward archive target; Veeam and Rubrik are dedicated backup products with a different control plane.

Option Good fit Trade-off to price and test
Amazon S3 Mature S3 tooling and broad ecosystem Model requests, egress, region, and lifecycle together
Cloudflare R2 Workloads already centered on Cloudflare Validate residency, restore path, and migration needs
Backblaze B2 Simple object backup archives Test the chosen S3-compatible restore tooling
Infrai storage A platform team that wants one key and one bill across backend services It is not a public-link, version-recovery, or WORM system
Veeam or Rubrik Compliance-heavy recovery and ransomware-resilience programs Higher product and process overhead than dump-to-object storage

Infrai's relevant advantage is administrative: one REST API, one key, and one bill can cover storage alongside other backend capabilities. That can reduce credential and invoice sprawl for a small platform team. It does not change the durability or retention guarantees, so the acceptance test remains a real restore drill.

Where this design is not suitable

The catch is material. There is no object versioning or object lock (WORM), so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable as a prior object version; regulated retention should stick with a dedicated backup platform or an external immutable copy. Conditional If-Match writes are unavailable, which means strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database coordinator.

Public or public-read ACLs are unavailable, so static website hosting, permanent public links, and image-hosting are poor fits. Browser direct-upload workflows also need caution because there is no independently exposed CORS configuration route. There is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and the storage vendor coverage does not include GCS or B2. Finally, trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes; plan for a funded account before the first backup run.

My exit criterion is simple: upload a representative dump, list it by its prefix, mint a signed link, download it from the intended US or EU worker, and restore it into an isolated target. Record elapsed steps against the restore SLO. If the drill needs object lock, version recovery, or public delivery, choose a different option before production.

Test it before you trust it.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage

title: Use ACP-compatible harnesses with the AI SDK harness layer
description:
The AI SDK harness layer now supports any Agent Client Protocol (ACP)-compatible harness with HarnessAgent through the new @ai-sdk/harness-acp package.

Previously, every harness adapter wrapped one specific runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Deep Agents, OpenCode). @ai-sdk/harness-acp wraps the protocol instead. It is a meta adapter: rather than adapting a single harness, it lets you build an adapter for any harness that ships an ACP-compatible package.

Implement a harness by passing that package to createACP and configure basic harness mapping.

Then pass it to HarnessAgent like any other harness:

ACP is an abstraction over coding harnesses, but the AI SDK harness layer stays deliberately decoupled from it. Not every harness supports ACP, and for some, ACP limits or changes how well they expose their internal behaviors, so a direct adapter can produce a tighter integration.

For Claude Code and Codex, prefer the direct @ai-sdk/harness-claude-code and @ai-sdk/harness-codex adapters over an ACP-based implementation; reach for @ai-sdk/harness-acp when a harness has no direct adapter but ships an ACP-compatible package.

Read the ACP harness documentation to get started.

title: I Connected an LLM to Our ERP, and the Permission Model Broke Everything
description:
Connecting a large language model (LLM) to an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system sounds straightforward at first.

You connect the model to your ERP APIs, provide the relevant business context, define a few tools, and let employees ask questions in natural language.

For example:

“Show me the status of my pending purchase orders.”

“Which invoices are overdue?”

“Summarize inventory levels across our warehouses.”

“Find the customers with outstanding payments.”

The first prototype might work perfectly. The problem starts when you connect it to real users, real business data, and the permission rules that have been protecting that data for years.

I learned an important lesson from this architecture: an LLM should never become a shortcut around the ERP's existing authorization model.

The First Problem Was Not the LLM

Most ERP systems already have a complex permission structure. Access may depend on a user's role, department, assigned business unit, legal entity, location, or record ownership.

A finance employee might view invoices but not employee salaries. A warehouse manager might access inventory for one location but not another. A sales representative might see their own customers but not another team's accounts.

Now introduce an LLM that can call ERP tools.

The model receives a question, determines which tool to call, and generates arguments for that tool. If the backend does not enforce permissions correctly, the model may retrieve records that the user could never access through the normal ERP interface.

For example, consider this simplified tool:

def get_invoice(invoice_id):
return erp_client.get_invoice(invoice_id)

The function works technically. It retrieves an invoice when given a valid ID.

But it has a serious security problem: it does not establish whether the requesting user is allowed to access that invoice.

The model might generate a valid invoice ID based on conversation context, a previous tool result, or an incorrectly exposed identifier. The API call could succeed even when the user has no permission to see the record.

This is not necessarily an LLM failure. It is an authorization failure in the integration layer.

Why Traditional ERP Permissions Become Difficult With AI

In a conventional application, the user interface and backend usually follow a predictable authorization flow. The application knows who is signed in, what operation they requested, and which records they can access.

With an LLM, the request passes through an additional reasoning layer.

The model interprets natural language and selects tools, but it should not decide what the user is authorized to access.

Three common problems appear during implementation.

  1. The model gets more access than the user

A quick prototype often uses one service account with broad ERP permissions.

That makes development easier because the integration can query multiple modules without repeatedly handling access restrictions.

However, if every employee's request uses the same privileged account, the ERP may see all requests as coming from that account rather than from the actual employee.

The result is a confused-deputy problem: a privileged service performs an action on behalf of a less-privileged user without properly enforcing that user's restrictions.

  1. Filtering happens after data retrieval

Another mistake is retrieving a large dataset and asking the model to return only the records relevant to the current user.

For example:

records = erp_client.get_all_invoices()

visible_records = [
record for record in records
if record["department"] == user.department
]

answer = llm.generate(
question=user_question,
context=visible_records
)

Even if the filtering is correct in this simplified example, the application has already retrieved data beyond the user's authorized scope.

If the unfiltered records reach the model, logs, caches, traces, or intermediate processing steps, the exposure has already occurred.

Authorization should constrain the data query itself, not merely the final answer.

  1. Tool calls ignore the user's original identity

An LLM may call multiple tools in one conversation. The first call could retrieve an order, and the next might retrieve its customer details or payment history.

If each tool independently trusts the model's arguments, a user may gain access to related records through an indirect path.

Passing a user_id generated by the model is not sufficient. The identity must come from a trusted authentication context maintained by the application.

The Fix: Put Authorization Between the LLM and the ERP

The architecture that worked better was to treat the LLM as an untrusted request planner.

The model can interpret questions and suggest tool calls. A trusted application layer validates those calls, applies authorization policies, and only then accesses the ERP.

The request flow should look like this:

Authenticated employee
|
v
Application authorization layer
|
v
LLM interprets the request
|
v
Tool argument validation
|
v
ERP permission and record checks
|
v
Authorized data returned
|
v
LLM generates the response

The critical boundary is between tool selection and tool execution.

The model can suggest which invoice to retrieve, but the application must independently verify whether that invoice is accessible to the authenticated employee.

A Safer Python Tool Pattern

Here is a simplified example of enforcing record-level access before returning an invoice.

def get_invoice_for_user(
invoice_id: str,
auth_context
):
# Identity comes from trusted application authentication.
user_id = auth_context.user_id

# Validate the requested identifier.
if not invoice_id or not invoice_id.isalnum():
    raise ValueError("Invalid invoice identifier")

# Query only records accessible to this user.
invoice = erp_client.find_authorized_invoice(
    invoice_id=invoice_id,
    user_id=user_id
)

if invoice is None:
    raise PermissionError(
        "Invoice is unavailable or access is denied"
    )

# Return only fields needed for the current task.
return {
    "invoice_id": invoice.id,
    "status": invoice.status,
    "due_date": invoice.due_date,
    "total": invoice.total
}

This example assumes that find_authorized_invoice() enforces the ERP's actual authorization rules. It is not safe merely because a function has that name; its implementation must apply trusted server-side policy checks.

In production, the authorization context should be created and validated by the application, not supplied or modified by the LLM.

You should also validate tool schemas, use parameterized queries, enforce tenant boundaries, and return only the fields required to answer the question.

What About Role-Based Access Control?

Role-based access control (RBAC) is a useful starting point, but it may not cover every ERP requirement.

A user can have the role finance_manager and still be restricted to a specific legal entity. Another user might access an invoice only if they own the relevant customer account.

A safer design combines:

RBAC: Determines which operations a role can perform.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC): Evaluates attributes such as department, region, legal entity, and ownership.

Record-level authorization: Checks whether a particular invoice, order, customer, or employee record is accessible.

Least privilege: Gives the integration only the permissions needed for its task.

These checks should apply to every sensitive tool call, including indirect calls triggered by earlier results.

The same approach matters when connecting an LLM to CRM software, inventory management, accounting systems, or other enterprise applications.

Don't Forget Prompt Injection and Indirect Access

Even with correct user authentication, an ERP-connected AI assistant can encounter malicious instructions inside documents, purchase orders, customer notes, or imported records.

For example, a record might contain text instructing the model to retrieve confidential payroll information.

That text must be treated as untrusted data, not as an authorization instruction.

Prompt-injection defenses can reduce risk, but they cannot replace backend permissions. Even if the model follows a malicious instruction, the tool execution layer must refuse unauthorized access.

For write operations, such as approving purchase orders or updating customer records, add stricter controls. Depending on the impact, require explicit user confirmation, approval workflows, or separation of duties before executing the action.

How I Would Test the Integration Before Release

I would not rely exclusively on successful demo conversations. I would test the authorization boundaries directly.

My test cases would include:

A user requesting an invoice belonging to another department.

A warehouse manager requesting inventory from an unauthorized location.

A user asking the model to reveal records from another tenant.

A tool call with a fabricated or modified record identifier.

A conversation that attempts to reuse data retrieved under a different user's session.

A prompt injection hidden inside an ERP document.

An employee whose role or permissions change while a session remains active.

An unauthorized write request, such as approving an invoice.

For each test, verify that the backend denies access where appropriate and that sensitive information does not leak through model context, tool outputs, application logs, or error messages.

Also log the authenticated principal, tool name, resource identifier, authorization decision, and request correlation ID. Avoid logging sensitive record contents unnecessarily.

Final Thoughts

Connecting an LLM to an ERP is not just an API integration exercise. It changes how users interact with sensitive business operations, and that makes authorization one of the most important parts of the architecture.

The LLM should help employees express what they need in natural language. It should not determine whether they are allowed to receive it.

Keep identity in the trusted application layer, enforce permissions at the data-access boundary, minimize the information returned to the model, and test unauthorized access as carefully as successful requests.

The best ERP-connected AI assistant is not the one with the most access. It is the one that can answer useful questions without exceeding the user's existing permissions.

title: How we join DynamoDB and OpenSearch in one SQL query
description:
DynoTable's SQL Workbench runs one SQL JOIN across a DynamoDB table and an
OpenSearch index. When the AI agent, the MCP server or the editor integration
ran that join, it was correct and took 617 seconds to show five rows. The
statement joined an OpenSearch index of 226,783 documents to a DynamoDB table
of 712,699 items on that table's own partition key. To
return five rows it read 939,482 records, every document in the index and
every item in the table.

Teams that feed OpenSearch from DynamoDB, through a stream or the zero-ETL
pipeline, end up with the same records in two engines and questions that span
both. Which customers in this search result have unpaid orders? How many
documents per country match this table's status? DynamoDB has no JOIN, and
the JOIN in OpenSearch's SQL plugin gave us wrong numbers once a GROUP BY
was added.

The SQL Workbench answers those questions in one
statement:

SELECT c.country, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM dynamodb.orders o
JOIN opensearch.customers c ON o.customerId = c.customerId
GROUP BY c.country

OpenSearch's SQL plugin returned wrong numbers without an error

OpenSearch can run SQL, joins included, through its SQL plugin. The plugin
cannot reach a DynamoDB table, so the probe asked only whether a join of two
indices could go to OpenSearch. We ran it on OpenSearch 2.19.1, against an
orders index of 150 documents and a customers index:

SELECT c.country, COUNT(*)
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customerId = c.customerId
GROUP BY c.country

The answer came back HTTP 200 with no error. It had 150 rows, one per order,
where there should have been six, one per country, and every count was null.
The schema listed three columns for a two-column query: o.COUNT(*),
c.country and c.COUNT(*).

That alone ruled it out, and the same version had two more problems. With a
join, the plugin ignores fetch_size and returns the whole result in one
response, so there is no cursor to page through a large join. A join on an
analyzed text field returns zero rows, again without an error. OpenSearch's
own limitations page
calls joins "best-effort" and says they do "not support aggregations on the
joined result".

So every join that names an index runs in the app.

Reading both sides in full was correct and far too slow

The route the agent, the MCP server and the editor integration share started
with the simple thing. It copied every table and index the statement names, in
full, into a SQL engine inside the app, then ran the statement there. That
works for any statement, and it costs the size of every table and index in it,
whatever the WHERE or the LIMIT says.

The numbers come from an OpenSearch 3.7 domain in eu-west-1 whose index takes
writes all day, so its document count drifts between runs. A five-row peek
with no WHERE took 2.0 seconds over the index alone. Joined to a 599-item
DynamoDB table it took 58.2 seconds, because the join forced a read of the
whole index. Joined to the 712,699-item, 981 MB table it took 617.4 seconds.

The joined table or index is read by key, one batch at a time

Call the first table or index in FROM the base, and every other table or
index a join side. The Workbench grid already read each join side by key. The
fix moved the route the agent, the MCP server and the editor integration share
onto the same key reads. The base is read from its
engine, 5,000 documents per OpenSearch request, and handed on in batches of
100 rows. For each batch, the app collects the join values and fetches only
the matching records:

Diagram: view on dynotable.com

On local test data the key reads return the same answers as the full read,
and an index-to-index join read 302 records instead of 6,002.

A key read needs a key to read by. On a DynamoDB table the join must use the
partition key of a table with no sort key, or the partition key of a
GSI that has no sort key and projects all attributes. A sort-keyed GSI
leaves out every item that lacks its sort attribute, so a key read on it would
lose rows. Every read here is eventually consistent, and a GSI can lag further,
so an item written seconds ago may not join yet. A table whose own key has a
sort key can be the base instead, with the other table or index joined onto it;
for a LEFT JOIN that changes which side's rows are kept. On an OpenSearch
index the join uses _id or any keyword, numeric, date, boolean or ip
field, or a text field with a keyword sub-field, because a terms query
matches whole values there.

The Workbench grid accepts only those joins. On the shared route, any other
join still runs on the full read, as before.

Only the base's filter goes to its engine

The base's own filter now goes to its engine, widened to a superset of the
rows the WHERE keeps. The join side is read by key with no filter. The full
WHERE runs again on the joined rows, so a filter that matches too much costs
extra reads and the answer stays the same. On local test data,
WHERE o.sku > 18.5 read 604 documents instead of more than 6,000. The widened
filter also brought back sku 18, which the full WHERE then dropped.

Three ways a key read would have answered wrong, and one value we drop

A key read is safe only if it finds every record the full read would. We
found three cases where it does not. In each one the shared route falls back
to the full read for the whole statement and returns what the full read
returns, at that cost. The key reads already made are not reused. On the MCP
server and the editor integration the full read also counts against the scan
budget, a cap on how much one client query may read.

A value longer than ignore_above. OpenSearch indexes the document but
skips a keyword value longer than the field's ignore_above, so a terms
query never matches it, while the full read still sees it in _source. We
test each join value against the limit as it arrives. We first sent any field
that carries an ignore_above to the full read. In the indices we measured
nearly every keyword field has one, 200 of 225 on one of them, so almost every
string join would have fallen back. To stay on the key read, join on a field
whose values fit the limit. Raising ignore_above works only after every
existing document is reindexed, for example with _update_by_query. The app
reads the new limit from the mapping at once, but documents indexed under the
old limit still lack the term.

One name backed by several indices. An alias can point at indices that
hold documents with the same _id. The local copy keys documents by _id
alone, so the second document would overwrite the first. The shared route falls
back before any read, and the Workbench grid and the editor flag such a join
side as an error. When one index holds all the documents you mean, name that
index instead of the alias.

A key read that fails on one batch. If one batch's key read fails, an
INNER JOIN would silently lose rows and a LEFT JOIN would silently blank
columns, so the route falls back on either kind. A repeated fallback here
usually means the join side's permissions or throttling. Check those first,
because the full read scans every table and index in the statement, which
needs Scan permission and spends far more read capacity than the key reads it
replaces.

A join value the index cannot parse. This one we fixed by dropping instead
of falling back. OpenSearch rejects a terms query whole when a single value
does not fit the field's type, such as a word sent to a long field. One bad
value used to fail the batch's entire key read and send the statement to the
full read. The join compares typed values, so a value of the wrong type for
the field matches no document whose source agrees with its mapping. The route
now drops it from the key read and keeps the rest.

The early stop was quadratic until we spaced it out

The read can stop early, but only for a plain row read, one that selects
plain columns or * without DISTINCT and has at most a WHERE and a
LIMIT with no OFFSET. It then stops at the LIMIT, or, when there is
none, one row past the output cap, the row that shows the result was cut. The GROUP BY example above aggregates, so
it reads the whole base and saves only on the join side. The stop saves whole
5,000-document requests, so an index smaller than that saves nothing on the
base.

Checking "do we have enough rows yet?" means counting over everything read so
far. The first version checked after every 100-row batch, and the check
blocked the app's main process while it ran. In a worst-case join that never
reaches its LIMIT, 100,000 base rows took 1,000 checks and 1,202
milliseconds, and 226,000 rows took 2,260 checks and 6,115 milliseconds. Two
and a quarter times the rows cost five times the time.

Now each check that comes up short delays the next one by a quarter of the rows
already read. The same two runs make 27 checks in 11 milliseconds and 31 checks
in 27 milliseconds. The spacing makes the stop late. A join that matches one
base row in a thousand stops at row 4,800 instead of 4,100. On an OpenSearch
base that is still inside the first 5,000-document request, so it costs no
extra base reads, only the join-side key reads for those 700 rows.

The MCP scan budget charged 101 items for 5,000 OpenSearch documents

The first version charged the budget for the rows the route handed on, not the
documents OpenSearch sent. On an OpenSearch base those differ by up to one
5,000-document request. One run reported 101 items against 5,000 documents
transferred. The budget now counts what OpenSearch returned for each base
request plus every record the key reads returned.

What transfers if you're building one

  • Probe a database's SQL layer with an aggregate over a join before you build on it. Ours returned HTTP 200 and wrong numbers.
  • Push the base's filter down as a superset and re-check the full WHERE locally. Then a pushdown bug can cost reads but cannot change the answer.
  • Read the joined side by key, batch by batch. A join that reads both sides in full costs the size of both, and no filter speeds up a peek.
  • List every way the key read can miss a record, and fall back for the whole statement when one applies. Falling back for part of a statement would mean testing a third read mode.
  • Space out any "are we done?" check that rescans what you have read.

OpenSearch SQL has the join rules and query examples,
and the JOIN guide covers keyed joins on the DynamoDB
side. The free DynamoDB Expression Builder
builds the key condition a GSI Query on the join side uses.

To try it, download DynoTable, turn on OpenSearch for your
profile, and join an index to a table in a Workbench tab. With an AI provider
set up, you can also ask the agent to answer the question with a SQL join.
