title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
description:
Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic (https://simantic.com). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware.

Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes.

We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago.

To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds.

What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit.

Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ

Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars.

We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time.

Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode (https://github.com/renode/renode) and QEMU (https://www.qemu.org/), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this.

1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast.

2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself.

3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their firmware.

Because of these issues, we made our own simulation engine from scratch, fully written in Rust.

- Our simulation is focused on accuracy. Open source frameworks often focus on expandability and developer experience, which means there were a lot of tradeoffs made to prioritize a breadth of models rather than going deep into a set of select models.

- We have our own hardware validation rigs running 24/7 to ensure our simulation models are as close to real world hardware as possible, and any gaps are detected and fixed as soon as we can. It currently looks like devboards connected to a Saleae Logic MSO and a SWD bus, controlled by a Linux PC, running Claude 24/7 just finding these gaps.

Our cloud-hosted simulator is available to use right now! We also provide a native binary with our developer plan licenses that let you run your firmware on your machines locally without any limitations.

Check it out at https://simantic.com/cloud-sim, and you can start using our AI firmware reviewer bot in your own Github repos here: https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot.

We currently have support for some models of the STM32F0, F4, H7 series MCUs, ESP32-S3/C3, and RP2040, but we’re constantly working to release new models every week, and improve our existing ones.

Thank you, and if you have any questions, feel free to send us an email at founders@simantic.dev

title: Node.js API Queue: Multiple Audio Files, Batch Transcribe (and Why Claims Matter)
description:
The least complicated design that survives a real batch is a durable job record plus a worker that claims one recording at a time. The upload request should create work, return a job identifier, and stop there. A worker can then fetch the audio, call the transcription API, persist the text, and emit usage for the tenant. The Node.js part is the HTTP boundary and worker runtime; the important boundary is the claim, not the queue brand.

Short answer: give every audio object a stable content key, put one transcription job behind it, and make the worker's completion operation idempotent. A retry must be allowed to repeat an HTTP request without creating a second transcript or charging the wrong tenant in your own accounting. RFC 9110 describes idempotent methods as requests whose repeated effect is intended to be the same, which is the right mental model for the state transitions here.

This is the shape I use for a B2B SaaS knowledge base that receives recorded customer calls. Each tenant may upload several files, and the resulting text stays private to that tenant before it is indexed for question answering. Cost visibility is a first-class output. A transcript without tenant_id, job_id, and an auditable usage event is incomplete, even if the text looks perfect.

How should an API batch transcribe multiple audio files?

The API accepts metadata and an object reference, rather than holding an HTTP connection open while audio is processed. A row in the application database owns the lifecycle: queued, running, succeeded, or failed. The queue contains a reference to that row. It is a delivery mechanism, not the source of truth.

That distinction matters after a worker disappears between transcription and acknowledgement. A durable record lets another worker decide whether the lease expired, inspect the attempt count, and continue. The storage key is also where tenant isolation becomes concrete: it should be derived from an authenticated tenant identifier, never accepted as an arbitrary path supplied by a client.

For a batch, the client submits many independent jobs. It does not submit one giant task whose partial progress is hidden. One file per job gives the system a useful retry boundary and makes a tenant's usage ledger explainable. If a 42-file upload has three bad recordings, the other 39 should not wait for a human to split the batch again.

Keep the claim small.

The queue is optional.

The failure boundary is not.

The most revealing test is a deliberately boring one: submit the same audio object twice, let one worker finish the remote call, pause it before the database commit, let another worker claim the lease, and then release the paused worker. That sequence contains the ordinary uncertainty of distributed work in miniature. A design that records only the final transcript cannot explain whether the two submissions were duplicates, a requested reprocess, or two tenants holding identical bytes; a design that records the tenant, content digest, profile revision, attempt, lease token, and usage-event key can answer each question without reading worker logs from last Tuesday. I keep those fields beside the job because operational archaeology is slow, and the customer asking about a bill should not need a reconstruction exercise.

There is a trade-off here. A queue-backed worker adds state, leases, and operational work that a synchronous endpoint avoids. It is a poor fit for a tiny internal tool processing one short file at a time; a direct request is easier to debug there. The queue earns its place when uploads can outlive an HTTP request, failures need replay, or tenants need separate visibility.

Here is the core state transition in Python. The same data contract can sit behind a Node.js endpoint and a queue consumer; keeping the example in one small module makes the failure behavior easier to inspect than a framework-specific sample.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional


class Status(str, Enum):
    QUEUED = "queued"
    RUNNING = "running"
    SUCCEEDED = "succeeded"
    FAILED = "failed"


@dataclass
class Job:
    job_id: str
    tenant_id: str
    object_key: str
    content_sha256: str
    status: Status = Status.QUEUED
    attempt: int = 0
    transcript: Optional[str] = None
    usage_event_id: Optional[str] = None


def claim(job: Job) -> bool:
    """Return True only when one worker owns the next attempt."""
    if job.status is Status.SUCCEEDED:
        return False
    if job.status is Status.RUNNING:
        return False
    job.status = Status.RUNNING
    job.attempt += 1
    return True


def complete(job: Job, transcript: str, usage_event_id: str) -> None:
    """A repeated completion writes the same result, never a new job."""
    if job.status is Status.SUCCEEDED:
        return
    job.transcript = transcript
    job.usage_event_id = usage_event_id
    job.status = Status.SUCCEEDED

In production, claim and complete are database transactions, not in-memory mutations. The example exposes the invariants: a successful job is terminal, an attempt has an owner, and the usage event has a stable identifier. I prefer making those invariants boring before adding concurrency.

Why can a retry duplicate the result?

A worker usually has at least two external effects: the transcription request and the local write. It may receive the transcript, persist it, then crash before acknowledging the queue message. The queue redelivers the job. If completion means “insert another transcript,” the duplicate is real. If billing means “increment a counter whenever the worker runs,” the tenant's report is wrong even when the database has one visible transcript.

Use a deterministic idempotency key for the application operation. tenant_id + content_sha256 + transcription_profile is a useful starting point, provided a deliberate reprocess can include a new profile version. Enforce uniqueness in storage. A process-local set, a worker flag, or a timestamp check does not protect two workers racing on separate machines.

The transcription provider may have its own retry rules, and those rules are a separate contract. Keep the application job key in your request metadata when the API supports it, then still make your own completion write idempotent. Network timeouts do not tell you whether the remote operation finished. Treat an uncertain response as an uncertain response, not as proof of failure.

There is a small but important ordering choice. Write the transcript and an outbox usage event in one database transaction. A separate publisher can deliver that event to the cost ledger, where usage_event_id is unique. This avoids the split result in which search can see text but the tenant report cannot explain its processing. It also means a ledger consumer can retry safely.

How do tenant costs stay visible in a queue?

Cost visibility starts at enqueue time, not at the monthly report. Put tenant_id, job_id, byte size, duration when known, and the selected transcription profile on the job. Record actual provider usage when returned. If the response does not include a value you can verify, store the missing field explicitly rather than inventing a precise number.

The queue should enforce fairness as a scheduling concern. A tenant that submits 10,000 short clips can otherwise occupy every worker while a smaller tenant waits. A simple per-tenant concurrency limit and a global limit are enough to start. The limit is not a cost model; it is a way to prevent one tenant's burst from hiding everyone else's work.

I keep three quantities separate:

  • accepted work, which answers what entered the system;
  • completed work, which answers what produced usable text;
  • billable usage, which answers what the external transcription operation reported.

They diverge during retries, validation failures, and cancellations. That divergence is operational information. Collapsing them into one processed_files number makes an inexpensive dashboard and an expensive investigation.

For private knowledge bases, attach tenant authorization to every read path as well as every write path. A transcript job that is correctly tagged can still leak data if a later retrieval query filters only by document ID. The index record should carry the tenant boundary, and the retrieval service should require it rather than treating it as optional UI metadata.

What happens when the worker vanishes?

Use a lease with an expiry and an attempt count. Claiming a job records a worker token and a deadline. A worker may renew the lease while handling a long recording, but only the current token may complete it. After expiry, another worker can claim the job. The completion transaction checks that token, or checks that the job is already succeeded with the same idempotency key.

That last check handles the awkward race: worker A finishes after its lease expires, worker B has already claimed the job, and both receive a transcript. Only one completion wins. The loser rereads the job and treats an equivalent successful result as done. A database uniqueness constraint is a better guard than timing luck.

Not every error deserves a retry. An unreadable object, unsupported codec, or authorization failure should become a visible terminal failure with a reason safe for operators. A timeout, temporary upstream response, or worker process exit is a candidate for retry with bounded backoff. Keep the original error class and the latest attempt timestamp; “failed” alone does not tell anyone whether replay is sensible.

I also validate before enqueueing. Check the object exists, belongs to the authenticated tenant, has an allowed media type, and has a bounded size. This is cheaper than discovering the same fact inside a worker, and it keeps poison jobs from consuming concurrency. Validation is not a substitute for checking again in the worker because the object or authorization state may change between requests.

A practical rollout checklist

Start with a fixture set that includes one short recording, one long recording, an empty file, a deliberately unsupported format, and two identical files submitted under different job IDs. Run the same fixture through a notebook first, then through the worker. The notebook is useful for inspecting transcripts; it is not evidence that leases, redelivery, or tenant filtering work.

Test the transitions, not just the happy-path text. Kill a worker after the remote call and before acknowledgement. Deliver the same queue message twice. Let a lease expire while the first worker is still alive. Submit two files from two tenants with the same content hash. The expected result is one transcript per idempotency key, isolated retrieval, and two separately attributed usage events where the accounting contract calls for them.

Watch queue age, attempt count, lease expiry, terminal failure reason, transcript latency, and usage-event lag. Add tenant dimensions carefully: high-cardinality labels can make observability expensive. A log field or queryable event is often more useful than putting every tenant into a metrics label.

Finally, document the replay rule for operators. Replaying a failed validation job should not silently bypass validation. Reprocessing a succeeded job should require an explicit new profile or revision. That single distinction prevents a “retry all” button from turning an incident into duplicate work.

The least complex system remains the right one here: an API creates durable, tenant-owned jobs; a queue wakes workers; a lease controls ownership; a transaction records the transcript and usage event; and an idempotency key makes uncertain delivery survivable. Node.js can implement the HTTP and worker edges cleanly, but no queue library can decide which effects are safe to repeat. That decision belongs in the job contract.

Further reading

title: The Most Popular Open-Source Voice Cloning Model Can't Be Used Commercially
description:
If you're building a product on open-source text-to-speech, the licence file deserves more of your attention than the demo audio. I learned this the slow way while picking models for a desktop app, and the specifics are worth writing down because the most popular option in the category is also the one you probably can't ship.

The three models worth knowing about.

Kokoro-82M — 82 million parameters, Apache 2.0, eight languages and fifty-four preset voices. It does not clone voices; you pick from its voice list. What it gives you instead is the ability to run on an ordinary CPU without a GPU anywhere in sight, which no other model here manages comfortably. For narration, app prompts, accessibility features, it's the obvious answer and the licence is the most permissive in the group.

XTTS-v2 — Coqui's model, seventeen languages, clones from a roughly six-second reference clip per its own model card. It is, by a distance, the one people search for and the one most tutorials cover. It's also the problem.

Chatterbox — Resemble AI, 500 million parameters, MIT licence, zero-shot cloning from a few seconds of audio. The base model is English only; a separate Multilingual v3 build covers twenty-three languages. Worth knowing before you ship: every output carries Resemble's PerTh watermark, which they describe as surviving MP3 compression and ordinary editing with near-perfect detection. It's inaudible and generated locally — nothing phones home — but it is detectable, and that's a product decision, not a footnote.

The licensing part.

Kokoro is Apache 2.0. Chatterbox is MIT. Both mean what you'd hope: use it, ship it, sell it, tell nobody.

XTTS-v2 is released under the Coqui Public Model License, which restricts use to non-commercial purposes. Not "attribution required", not "under a revenue threshold" — non-commercial. If you're charging for the thing you build, you're outside the licence.

Historically there was a way out: Coqui sold a commercial licence. Coqui Inc. shut down in January 2024. There is no sales team, no licensing portal, no entity to contract with. The commercial option doesn't exist at any price. So the most-downloaded, best-documented, most-searched open-source voice cloning model has no legal path into a paid product, and the reason isn't cost — it's that there's nobody left to ask.

Why this catches people.

Three things stack up. The weights are freely downloadable, which feels like permission. The ecosystem around it — community packages, wrappers, tutorials — is large and none of it leads with the licence. And "open source" does a lot of unearned work in people's heads; plenty of models described that way carry terms that aren't open source in any OSI sense.

What I'd actually do:

  1. Read the LICENSE file in the exact repository you download from, not a summary and not a blog post. Variants, community re-uploads and quantised conversions don't reliably carry the original terms.

  2. Check whether the licensor still exists. A permissive-sounding licence from a dissolved company with no successor is a different risk from the same licence backed by a live entity.

  3. Do this at model-selection time. Swapping an inference engine after you've shipped is a couple of days of work; discovering the problem after you've built a year of marketing around a model's name is a different cost entirely.

  4. Prefer Apache 2.0 or MIT when quality is close — and in this category it genuinely is close now, which wasn't true two years ago.

If you're running local TTS in anything commercial, the five minutes this takes is the cheapest five minutes in your stack.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: The Physics of AI: Why Your Next Server Needs Liquid Cooling and Heavy Copper
description:
If you follow the tech news, you know that the AI arms race is currently a race for power.

NVIDIA’s latest Blackwell architecture GPUs are pushing power consumption to unprecedented levels—approaching 1,000W per chip, with entire server racks now drawing over 100kW.

As software developers, we usually think of scaling in terms of cloud instances and Kubernetes clusters. But at the physical layer, scaling AI means dealing with extreme thermodynamics. The hardware running your models is hitting the absolute limits of physics.

Here is why AI is forcing a massive shift in server PCB design, and why traditional air cooling and standard copper are no longer enough.

1. The End of Air Cooling: Liquid is the New Normal

For decades, servers were cooled by massive fans pushing air through the chassis. But air has a very low specific heat capacity. It simply cannot carry away the massive heat generated by a 100kW+ AI rack.

This is why tech giants and data centers are rapidly transitioning to Direct-to-Chip (D2C) liquid cooling.

Instead of blowing air, cold plates are mounted directly on top of the hottest components (GPUs and CPUs), and a dielectric or water-based coolant is pumped through them.

The Hardware Challenge: Liquid cooling introduces immense mechanical and chemical stress. The PCB must be highly resistant to moisture and chemical degradation. More importantly, the CTE (Coefficient of Thermal Expansion) of the PCB materials must perfectly match the heavy metal cold plates. If they expand and contract at different rates, the board will warp, and the BGA solder joints under the GPU will crack.

2. Power Delivery: The Heavy Copper Revolution

A GPU drawing 1,000W at sub-1V voltages requires immense current—often exceeding 1,000 Amps.

On standard PCBs, delivering this much current would instantly vaporize the traces. To handle this, AI server boards are shifting to Heavy Copper PCBs (up to 10oz or even 20oz). These aren't just traces; they are physical copper busbars embedded in the board.

The Manufacturing Challenge: Etching 20oz copper is a nightmare. The undercut effect (where etching chemicals eat sideways into the trace) is severe. If a designer routes a 10 mil trace on a heavy copper board without accounting for etching tolerances, it could short out or break during production. This requires highly specialized DFM (Design for Manufacturing) reviews and advanced etching techniques.

3. The Signal Integrity Nightmare: 224G PAM4

To feed data to these monstrous GPUs, networking speeds are jumping from 112G to 224G per lane.

At 224G, signal attenuation through standard FR-4 materials is catastrophic. The data literally dissolves into noise before it reaches the chip.

The Hardware Challenge: This forces the industry to use ultra-low-loss materials (such as M8 or M9 grade laminates) and ultra-smooth copper foils. It also demands extreme precision in impedance control. Even a 5% deviation in trace width or dielectric thickness can destroy signal integrity.

4. The Shift to High-Layer Count HDI

Because the physical distance between the GPU and memory (HBM) must be minimal to reduce latency and power loss, AI server boards are incredibly dense.

Standard boards won't cut it. AI accelerators now use 20 to 30-layer HDI boards (High-Density Interconnect). The BGA pitch is becoming so small that conventional mechanical drills cannot be used. Laser-drilled microvias are mandatory.

The Bottom Line

The AI revolution is not just a software revolution. It is a brutal test of materials science, thermodynamics, and precision manufacturing.

At AnyPCBA, we are seeing this transition firsthand. We support the manufacturing of high-layer HDI, heavy copper (up to 20oz), and high-frequency PCBs for demanding applications. We know that when you are dealing with 100kW racks and 224G signals, a "working" design on a breadboard means nothing without rigorous DFM reviews and precise impedance control.

If you are building hardware for the AI era, or if you need a manufacturing partner that understands the physics behind heavy copper and HDI, let's talk.

At AnyPCBA, we specialize in small-to-medium volume manufacturing of advanced PCBs and PCBA. We hold ISO 13485 and IATF 16949 certifications and are equipped to handle heavy copper, HDI, and rigid-flex boards. Contact us through our website to discuss your high-reliability projects.

What's the biggest physical constraint you've faced when designing hardware for high-performance computing? Share your experience in the comments!

title: ProvenPin this week: stricter checks and more honest version answers
description:
ProvenPin is a library of tested code recipes for AI coding models. Each recipe pins exact package versions, runs its own tests in a clean environment, and carries a receipt showing when it last passed. The goal is to help free and cheap models write code that actually runs. It is served over a free MCP server, no API key, no signup.

This was a quality week rather than a growth week. The live health endpoint shows 556 recipes, up from 555 last Thursday. Most of the work went into making the checks and answers more trustworthy. Here is what shipped (Oct 23 to 29).

Strict type-checks for TypeScript recipes

A recipe can run and pass its tests and still have type errors your editor will flag. CI now runs a strict tsc type-check on every TypeScript recipe a pull request adds or changes. New recipes must pass. Older recipes with type errors sit on a known list that is being cleaned up in small batches (PR #18).

The version check got more honest

When you ask whether a recipe fits your project, ProvenPin compares your versions to the ones the recipe was tested on. Two fixes this week:

  • A range like ^5.3.0 in package.json is a range, not what you installed. It used to count as an exact match for a recipe tested on 5.3.0. Now it reads as "compatible", with a tip to pass your lockfile for an exact answer.
  • A lone upper bound was being judged backwards. For a recipe tested on 5.3.0, <6 used to read as a mismatch and <5.0.0 as compatible. Now an upper bound is judged by whether it allows the tested version (PR #38).

Python receipts list every installed package

A recipe might pin 3 packages while the test run installs 8 once sub-dependencies come in. Python receipts now record every package that was actually installed, with exact versions, not just the pinned ones. That makes sub-dependency drift visible. All Python recipes have it (PR #40).

Try it

Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http provenpin https://mcp.provenpin.com/mcp

Cursor users can use the one click "Add to Cursor" button on the homepage. Other clients: endpoint https://mcp.provenpin.com/mcp, setup steps in the README.

Site: provenpin.com. Source and receipts: github.com/provenpin/provenpin.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.16

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.16.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Performance tile on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard executed redundant database queries during auto-refreshes.

  • Updated advanced reporting filter prompts so they behave consistently across all dashboards and display the complete list of configured values:

    • List-backed filters now open directly into a searchable list on the first click.

    • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

    • Consumer phone number filters now accept a single value instead of multiple values. Saved filters or links that pass multiple numbers apply only one.

    • On the Missed Interactions dashboards, the Activity Status column and filter are renamed to Projection Result.

    • Actor values describing who answered, ended, or disconnected an interaction are now standardized as Human Agent, Virtual Agent, End User, and System. Saved filters, Looks, and schedules that used the previous wording must be reselected.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

For GKE Standard CPU node pools, GKE can now upgrade nodes by updating the existing Compute Engine VM in place, instead of deleting the VM and creating a new one. Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

The stable model for answer generation is updated to gemini-3.5-flash/answer_gen/v1 from gemini-2.5-flash/answer_gen/v1.

For more information, see Answer generation model versions and lifecycle.

title: How to Choose Affordable Logging API for Small Media Projects (and Keep It Replaceable)
description:
Short answer: for a small media product comparing an experiment across tenant cohorts, choose the logging API that gives you ingestion, search, filtering, and a retention period you can explain in an SLO review. Keep the caller behind a tiny Go interface, and treat the provider as replaceable. Infrai is a reasonable fit when a plain REST contract and one existing API key reduce migration work; it is not the right answer if your decision depends on alert delivery, trace exploration, or compliance-grade deletion.

The important signal is not the number of log lines. It is whether a cohort comparison can distinguish a real change in playback or publishing behavior from tenant mix, retries, and duplicate events. Every event needs stable tenant and experiment context in the application payload, while the logging system needs enough search and retention to answer the question later. Do not turn a low bill into the decision rule. A quiet, cheap log store that cannot support the investigation is noise with an invoice attached.

The question is narrower than it sounds.

What should the small-project SLO protect?

Start with the investigation, not the vendor dashboard. For a media experiment, define an SLO for evidence: an engineer should be able to retrieve the relevant cohort window and compare the same event shape for control and treatment. The exact target belongs to the service, but the boundary is concrete: ingestion must work, search must be available, filtering must be supported by the documented contract, and retention must cover the experiment review window. Small projects often do not need years of storage; they do need a retention policy that is explicit enough to prevent an experiment from outliving its evidence.

OpenTelemetry treats logs as one signal alongside traces and metrics, rather than pretending logs alone explain every failure. A trace_id can correlate a record with another signal, but a logging API is not automatically a distributed-tracing query engine. That distinction matters when the cohort result looks suspicious.

Noise wins.

Which logging boundary keeps the choice reversible?

Put one adapter between the application and the provider. Its contract should contain the fields the experiment needs: timestamp, tenant identifier, experiment key, cohort, event name, severity, and a correlation identifier. Define what happens when a provider is unavailable, because silently dropping treatment events can create a convincing but false result. Keep the application-facing interface small enough that changing the transport does not become a quarter-long migration.

The following Go example deliberately calls only the documented search route and does not invent query parameters. The discovery shape does not declare filtering parameters for logs.search, so a production adapter should inspect the published schema and encode only fields that contract supports. The request uses an environment variable, an explicit method, status checking, and bounded exponential backoff for rate limiting.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search", nil)
        if err != nil { fatal(err.Error()) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { fatal(err.Error()) }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if readErr != nil { fatal(readErr.Error()) }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fatal(fmt.Sprintf("log search failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, string(body)))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    fatal("log search rate limit did not clear after retries")
}

func fatal(message string) {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, message)
    os.Exit(1)
}

That snippet is intentionally not a pretend cohort query. A provider can only be compared fairly on filters it documents. Add cohort predicates inside the adapter after schema verification, and test them against known control and treatment fixtures. An undocumented parameter can be accepted by a client while returning an unfiltered result, which is worse than an obvious failure.

How do the real alternatives change the trade-off?

The shortlist should include hosted simplicity, a composable open-source path, and a broad commercial platform. These are different operating models, not interchangeable price cards.

Option Strength for this workflow Boundary to test
Better Stack Hosted logs and a focused operational workflow can shorten the path from ingestion to investigation for a small team. Confirm retention, cohort filtering semantics, and alert behavior against the SLO.
Grafana Loki A label-oriented log store paired with Grafana fits teams already operating that ecosystem and willing to own more of the stack. Capacity planning is yours: ingestion limits, indexing, object storage, and on-call ownership.
Datadog Logs A mature commercial suite is useful when logs must sit beside metrics, traces, and broader service context. Validate retention and export requirements early; breadth can create stronger platform coupling.
Infrai Its plain REST API needs no SDK installation, and one key spans capabilities, keeping a small adapter stable while the application evolves. It has no alert or notification route, span-tree query, Session Replay, per-user log deletion, or bulk export/subscription route in the stated surface.

The fair recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the ingestion-and-search boundary of a small media experiment when your team values a plain REST call without an SDK lifecycle and can poll the search API for any alerting it builds itself. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples make the contract easier to inspect before migration work begins. Pick Grafana Loki when self-hosting and Grafana ownership are deliberate choices; pick Datadog when the experiment cannot be separated from a larger integrated observability program; pick Better Stack when hosted operational focus matters more than a broad platform surface.

There is a hard limit. Infrai does not supply threshold rules, phone, SMS, or webhook notification routes, and it does not provide distributed trace or span-tree exploration. It also does not provide source-map or crash-symbolization workflow, heartbeat monitoring, change audit logs, or a user-deletion interface for logs. A polling job plus a Healthchecks-style monitor may fill part of the gap, but that is additional system ownership.

What should verification and rollback look like?

Before routing production events, create a fixed fixture: the same control and treatment events, two tenants, one duplicate, and one deliberately malformed record. Verify that the adapter surfaces non-success responses, that a rate limit does not cause a tight retry loop, and that results reconcile with application-side counts. Track ingestion volume and retention against the experiment's planned review date. Those are capacity questions, even at small scale.

Run the new provider in shadow mode if the event volume permits it, but keep the old path authoritative until the comparison is stable. The rollback is then a configuration change at the adapter boundary, not a rewrite of every logging call. Preserve the provider-neutral event envelope and keep a small sample of fixtures after migration; otherwise a later vendor change becomes a memory exercise.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the logging API documentation and verify the current discovery schema before adding filters.

References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • Better Stack, “Logs”: https://betterstack.com/logs
  • Grafana Loki documentation: https://grafana.com/docs/loki/latest/
  • Datadog Logs documentation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/logs/
  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc

title: A API HTTP e como rodar o Nabu
description:
Na série IPFS com o Nabu, o nó já guarda blocos e fala com a rede. Este post é a porta de fora: o processo que sobe sozinho e a biblioteca que outra aplicação embute.

A proposta

Quem opera um nó quer o mesmo tipo de chamada que já usa com o Kubo, a implementação de referência do IPFS em Go: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) local, um caminho /api/v0/..., o CID (Content Identifier) na query. Quem escreve uma aplicação quer o contrário: nenhuma porta HTTP, o nó como objeto Java dentro do processo.

A proposta do Nabu é oferecer os dois. A superfície HTTP é de propósito menor que a do Kubo. O objeto embutido expõe o mesmo nó que essa superfície usa por baixo.

A Demonstração

O modo standalone lê um diretório de repositório, no estilo do Kubo. A variável de ambiente ou o argumento IPFS_PATH aponta para ele. Na ausência, o diretório é ~/.ipfs, debaixo do home do usuário. Lá estão o arquivo config e os dados. O config é JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) com a identidade, os endereços e o datastore. O processo abre a API (Application Programming Interface) HTTP no host e na porta que o config chama de Addresses.API.

Uma chamada típica é POST /api/v0/block/get?arg=<cid>. O corpo da resposta são os bytes do bloco. block/put manda os bytes num corpo multipart, o formato em que cada parte traz um arquivo, e recebe de volta um JSON com o campo Hash.

O modo embutido não abre essa porta. A aplicação chama EmbeddedIpfs.build com as peças que escolhe: store de registros, blockstore, se deve anunciar blocos, endereços de swarm, bootstrap, identidade, authoriser e, se quiser, um handler HTTP entre pares. start entra na rede. A partir daí getBlocks, publishValue e o blockstore são chamadas locais, no mesmo processo.

A API compatível com o Kubo cobre bloco, identidade, refs, um pedaço da DHT (Distributed Hash Table) e a leitura IPNS (InterPlanetary Name System). Caminhos de arquivo, add de diretório e pin não estão nessa lista.

No Nabu

A classe do processo é Nabu, em src/main/java/org/peergos/Nabu.java. getIPFSPath lê o argumento IPFS_PATH ou, sem ele, HOME mais .ipfs. readConfig abre config nesse diretório. Se o arquivo não existe, grava um config padrão. O argumento s3.datastore, quando vem na linha de comando, preenche o mount S3 antes dessa gravação. O authoriser é (c, p, a) -> CompletableFuture.completedFuture(true): toda leitura de bloco é autorizada. O store de IPNS é um DatabaseRecordStore em datastore/h2-v2.datastore. O blockstore sai de buildBlockStore. EmbeddedIpfs.build recebe provideBlocks verdadeiro, os endereços de swarm, o bootstrap e a identidade do config.

Se config.addresses.enableUPnP está ligado, enablePortForwarding roda antes de start. start(false) faz o bootstrap de forma síncrona. O endereço da API é o argumento Addresses.API, se foi passado, ou config.addresses.apiAddress. O servidor é com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer, com fila de 500 conexões e um pool de 50 threads. O contexto /api/v0/ recebe um APIHandler. Se o config tem Addresses.ProxyTarget, o HTTP entre pares encaminha para esse host e porta, e o servidor ganha o contexto /p2p/. Um shutdown hook para o servidor HTTP com espera de 3 segundos. Métricas, se config.metrics.enabled, sobem noutro endereço, o do MetricsSection.

APIHandler exige que o caminho comece com /api/v0/. O resto entra num switch. Os casos, em src/main/java/org/peergos/net/APIHandler.java:

  • id devolve JSON com o PeerId em base58, no campo ID.
  • version devolve o campo Version. A constante do handler é 0.9.0.
  • block/get exige um arg. Monta um Want com o CID e o auth opcional. peers vira um conjunto de PeerIds. persist vem da query e, se falta, vale verdadeiro. A resposta são os bytes, ou status 400 se a lista volta vazia.
  • block/put exige format. Lê um único arquivo do multipart, cujo boundary vem do header Content-Type. Recusa tamanho acima de maxBlockSize, o teto da mensagem Bitswap, 2 MiB. O codec sai de Cid.Codec.lookupIPLDName. A resposta JSON traz Hash.
  • block/rm apaga um CID. Sucesso devolve Hash e Error vazio. Falha responde 400.
  • block/rm/bulk lê uma lista cids no corpo JSON.
  • block/stat busca o bloco com persist falso e devolve só Size. A lista de pares vai vazia. Falha responde 400.
  • block/stat/bulk lê {"wants":[...]}, busca com persist verdadeiro e, para cada bloco, devolve size, os links que não são multihash do tipo identity, e os BATs (Block Access Token, o segredo de leitura) encontrados no bloco. Responde 400 se o número de blocos não fecha com o de wants.
  • block/has responde os bytes true ou false.
  • refs/local lista os CIDs de blockstore.refs. O parâmetro use-block-store vale falso se não vier. Cada CID sai num JSON com o campo Ref.
  • bloom/add chama blockstore.bloomAdd e responde o booleano.
  • dht/findprovs exige o CID. num-providers positivo substitui o padrão 20. Cada provedor vira ID e Addrs dentro de Responses.
  • ipns/get exige o argumento signer, um PeerId em base58. Chama resolveRecords pedindo pelo menos um resultado, ordena, e devolve sig e data em hexadecimal do registro de maior sequence. Lista vazia vira Couldn't resolve.

block/get com peers vazio deixa o BitswapBlockService tentar os conectados e depois a DHT. persist falso busca sem gravar no store local.

O cliente Java dessa API é NabuClient, em src/main/java/org/peergos/client/NabuClient.java. O construtor de host e porta assume /api/v0/. O construtor de multiaddr, por exemplo /ip4/127.0.0.1/tcp/5001, lê host e porta dali. Timeout de conexão: 10 segundos. Timeout de leitura: 60 segundos. Os exemplos do último post usam esse cliente contra um daemon.

Embutir segue o trecho do README. A identidade pode ser gerada na hora:

HostBuilder builder = new HostBuilder().generateIdentity();
PrivKey privKey = builder.getPrivateKey();
PeerId peerId = builder.getPeerId();
IdentitySection identity = new IdentitySection(privKey.bytes(), peerId);

EmbeddedIpfs.build recebe o RamRecordStore ou um store durável, o FileBlockstore, a lista de swarm e de bootstrap, e o authoriser. ipfs.start() bloqueia até o host escutar, o identify estar registrado e o bootstrap da tabela ter corrido. getBlocks devolve List<HashedBlock>. Cada item traz o CID e o byte[].

O que fica de fora: a API não replica o Kubo inteiro. Não há files, dag, name/publish HTTP, nem gateway de conteúdo no estilo ipfs.io. O campo Addresses.Gateway existe no config e é lido por AddressesSection. O handler que sobe é o da API, mais o proxy /p2p/ quando há alvo. O pacote Maven publicado pelo JitPack é com.github.peergos:nabu.

Nesta série

O anterior é Onde o bloco mora. O próximo é HTTP entre pares.

title: How we migrated the database behind every Vercel build
description:
Every build on Vercel starts in the build warm pool, which is a set of standby containers that let builds begin without waiting for new compute. The pool runs on state that tracks which containers are ready, the tokens each one uses to authenticate, and the mapping that ties every running build back to the deployment that gets billed for it. When we built the pool, we put all of that in Redis, which was fast and made sense at the time.

Over the years, though, that state turned into a liability. Tokens and container statuses can be rebuilt if they get lost, but the billing mappings can't, and all of it was sitting in a store that we ran as an ephemeral cache. That state needed to live somewhere durable, which is why we decided to migrate it to DynamoDB.

The problem is that the pool never stops. Containers are coming up, polling, picking up work, and expiring around the clock, which meant we couldn't pause the world, copy the data, and restart. The migration had to happen live, under production traffic, in phases, each one behind a flag with a rollback ready if we needed it.

Durable state in an ephemeral store

Redis was a good home for it at first. It was fast, familiar, and efficient for the access patterns the pool started with. But over time the state became more important than the store holding it. If Redis became unavailable or lost data, the pool could no longer reliably authenticate containers, track which of them were ready, or resolve the work in flight.

Lose a token and the pool rebuilds it within about ten minutes. Lose a mapping and the build is never billed, because nothing else records which deployment it belonged to.

We wanted it in durable storage and landed on DynamoDB. On-demand scaling fits bursty deployment traffic, TTL is native, and there are no connections to manage at high concurrency. But what it did not promise was Redis's latency.

What Redis made cheap

Inside Redis, the pool's state looked like this:

  • Tokens lived in a set so we could check membership, and in a sorted set so we could expire them

  • Each lifecycle status (pending, polling, building) had its own sorted set, which meant a status change was a removal from one set and an add to the next

  • A string tied each working container to its deployment

All of these operations were cheap, about a millisecond each, and the code grew to lean on that speed. A single run of the supply loop, which is the loop that refills each warm pool in turn, would make hundreds of count calls just to tally up the pending and polling containers.

That's how the warm pool grew, one easy write at a time, until data we needed to keep was sitting in structures built for speed. Untangling that layout was where the migration started.

Designing the schema from the access patterns

Most migration plans treat the database as the thing being replaced. You map the access patterns, copy the data, and verify that the two stores agree. We planned ours that way too, so before designing any schema, we listed everything the code actually asked of that state:

  • Verify a token when a container polls for work

  • Add a token when a new container comes up

  • Expire tokens past their deadline

  • Count tokens to size the pool

  • Move a container between lifecycle statuses

  • Count containers by status

  • Look up the deployment behind a container's callback

  • Remove expired containers

Almost every operation already knows which container it's touching, and only polling ever starts from a token. So we put the container at the center of the model. The container ID became the sort key, and the token became just a field on the record, stored as a hash so that reading the table never hands you a usable credential. Verifying a token now just means looking up its container and comparing the hashes.

Two of the access patterns couldn't be served by a key lookup alone. Status counts had to skip containers that were already past expiry, which takes a time-aware index. And the deployment lookups feed billing, so they needed consistent reads, and the mapping got a small table of its own.

Reading a container's state, moving its status, and clearing its token all became direct key lookups. Counting a status became a single read against the time-aware index, one query per status with expired containers already filtered out.

Where Redis had let the data structures imply what we needed, DynamoDB made us spell out keys, indexes, conditional writes, and TTL behavior. So instead of carrying the Redis structures forward, we modeled the container and added the indexes that its access patterns needed.

Shadow mode validated every write

The rollout ran as feature-flagged phases: Redis-only, then dual writes, shadow reads, DynamoDB-primary, and finally DynamoDB-only. Every phase kept a rollback open for as long as possible. The last step, which removed the Redis writes, was the only one without an easy rollback, but any lingering token expires within ten minutes anyway.

We started by baselining the existing Redis operations, their counts and their latencies, so that the dashboards had a normal to compare against. The new DynamoDB methods merged days before anything actually called them. Dual writes went out next, with Redis still the source of truth and DynamoDB failures logged instead of fatal. Then came shadow reads, which queried both stores and compared the results. And then primary reads flipped, with the Redis writes kept on until the new path had proven itself.

What the comparisons told us was whether the two stores agreed on the stored values, which is something tests alone couldn't. They said nothing about timing. We checked that every write landed in both stores, that expiration kept moving forward as containers changed status so stale state never piled up, that clearing a token left the rest of the container's record intact, and that the counts stayed close enough to steer the pool.

On top of the comparisons we built dashboards that watched match rates, write errors, per-query latency, and expiration counts while Redis was still serving production. That way any divergence surfaced while it was still cheap to investigate, instead of showing up as a cutover failure. Every mismatch got chased down to a real bug, a dual-write race, or an expected difference before we moved on. Those dashboards decided when each phase advanced, and every time the numbers held steady under production traffic, the next step felt safer.

Two failures along the way

In March, one region's builds went down, and the investigation pointed at our own comparison machinery, which was the added load of checking two stores against each other. The scenario had actually come up in review, and we had throttled the comparisons for exactly that reason, but the throttling wasn't enough. Four days later, a pull request citing the incident added the index that the status counts needed. Without it, every count was O(n) work, and the comparisons were counting constantly. With the index in place, the rollout continued.

Later that month, the Redis infrastructure that we were migrating off actually went down. The warm pool and its token handling stayed up, because both of them were already reading from DynamoDB as the source of truth. Builds still felt the outage, but through services further up the pipeline that hadn't moved yet. The failure we'd been migrating away from arrived before the migration was even finished, and the state that had already moved survived it.

The supply loop stalled on slower reads

In April, the supply loop began to stall. The shadow data had looked healthy when we advanced primary reads, and the per-query latency had looked acceptable on the dashboards. What failed was a behavior that neither one measured.

We drew the loop to see where the time was going.

At P95 on getWarmPoolTokenCount, that check measured 1.29ms on Redis and 5.13ms on DynamoDB. At the time we shorthanded it as two to three times slower per query, which turned out to be an underestimate.

A few extra milliseconds cost nothing when you only pay them once. But the loop was paying them before every container, hundreds of times per run, and that stretched runs out to minutes at their worst, which meant the pool couldn't stay ahead of demand. The loop was an N+1 query, and Redis had just simply been fast enough to hide it.

No one wrote "this loop requires millisecond reads" anywhere. But the assumption lived in the design, and at a millisecond per check, nothing had ever made us stop and look.

We rebuilt the loop around the new latency

DynamoDB was never going to match Redis's millisecond, so instead of chasing it, we designed the requirement out.

The first attempt was batching, which is the shape drawn at the bottom of the sketch. The size of the gap depends on which percentile you look at, and at P90, where it was widest, the gap was about 17x. So the batch design checked state once per 17 containers, with one read amortized across the whole batch, and that constant was lifted straight from the measurement. But the constant was also the reason we walked away from it. It hard-coded a latency ratio that would drift with load, which meant one more unwritten dependency on the store's speed. Concurrency didn't need a constant at all.

What shipped instead let the loop's supply calls run concurrently, so each warm pool was no longer waiting behind the one before it, and each call worked from the last state it saw. Overlapping the reads bought us the same thing that batching would have, which is that no run serialized on any single read. The worst case is a few extra containers created from a stale picture of the pool, and that went into the pull request as an accepted cost. The redesign meant we could keep the more durable store without compromising the thing users actually care about, which is builds starting quickly and reliably. The fixes landed the same way the rollout did, one measured step at a time. As one of us put it, "we have less risk on each iteration because we've corrected for a previous misestimation."

It turned out the loop had stalled under Redis too, sometimes for a minute or more, and we only learned that while we were diagnosing DynamoDB. The evidence had been in our telemetry the whole time, but because the pool sits ahead of demand rather than in any request path, nothing had ever forced us to go look until the migration did. And the redesign ended up removing a flaw that was older than the project itself.

Migrating the assumptions

The migration completed in April, with the Redis calls gone from the warm pool paths. Copying the data turned out to be the easy part. The real work was finding the assumptions that had been built on top of the store, and then redesigning the loop that had held them. The state that every build depends on now lives in a store that was built to keep it, and the loop that manages it no longer serializes on any single read.

The April retrospective put the lesson in one sentence. "Even a 1ms-to-15ms query time degradation on P90 could bring down our warm pool management logic." Nobody had written that sentence in February, when the migration started.
