title: PhotoCraft: the open-source Photoshop rival you can drive from the terminal
description:
Originally published at aifrontierpost.com

Photoshop rebuilt from scratch in Rust, with 74,000 stars in four weeks — and a command-line tool that edits real photos without ever opening a window. This guide downloads the real release, verifies its checksum, and runs every headless command that matters: inspect, edit, batch, convert, and MCP. No account, no API key, no GPU, and every number below is one the installed tool printed.

TL;DR: PhotoCraft (storytold/photocraft) is an open-source, pure-Rust Photoshop rebuild: version 0.17.0 ships a headless CLI that inspects, edits, batch-grades, converts (including PSD), and serves the engine over MCP — all verified here with no account, no API key, and no GPU. The desktop app is early alpha and was not tested; the CLI path is the proven one.

  • Who: PhotoCraft (storytold/photocraft on GitHub), from the ArtCraft team — 74,359 stars, 7,040 commits, 13,130 forks, dual MIT/Apache-2.0, first committed September 30, 2026.
  • What: a clean-room Photoshop rebuild in pure Rust, plus a headless CLI: info, run, batch, convert, commands, and an MCP server — verified here end to end.
  • When: version verified in this guide is photocraft-cli 0.17.0, released and run October 28, 2026; star and commit counts are dated the same day.
  • Requirement: a Linux, macOS, or Windows machine and ~200 MB of free disk for the prebuilt release. No account, no API key, no GPU, no Rust toolchain.

Why this is blowing up now

PhotoCraft is a clean-room reimplementation of Photoshop, written from scratch in pure Rust. Layers, masks, adjustment layers, layer styles, type, vectors, brushes, and real PSD files — in a native app with no Electron and no web view. The repository (storytold/photocraft on GitHub) had 74,359 stars, 7,040 commits, and 13,130 forks when this guide read it on October 28, 2026, under a dual MIT/Apache-2.0 license. It was created on September 30, 2026, which makes that star count a four-week sprint, not a slow accumulation. Version 0.17.0 landed the same day this guide ran, October 28, 2026.

The part that makes it tutorial-worthy instead of just impressive is not the GUI. It is the headless command-line tool that ships in the same release. Every menu item, tool, and dialog in PhotoCraft runs a command from one registry of 500+ commands, and the UI, the CLI, the JSON control channel, and the MCP server all call the same commands. That means anything you can click, a script can do too — and this guide proves it, because every command below was run on a headless Linux server with no display, no account, no API key, and no GPU.

One boundary first, because it decides whether this tutorial is for you. PhotoCraft is in early alpha, and its own README says so plainly: much of Photoshop's feature surface exists in some form, but it is not yet a Photoshop replacement for daily professional work. The gaps it names are AI/generative features, 15 missing tools, depth in typography and pro workflows, and plug-in compatibility. What this guide verifies is the headless editing path — install, inspect, edit, batch, convert, and hand the engine to an agent over MCP. If you need a finished desktop replacement today, this is not that article. If you want a scriptable, offline, open-source photo engine, keep reading.

What you'll need

  • A Linux, macOS, or Windows machine. This guide ran on Linux (x86_64), using the prebuilt release tarball — no Rust toolchain, no source build, no compile wait.
  • About 200 MB of free disk. The Linux tarball is 123 MB; extracted, it is roughly twice that.
  • A terminal and a scratch directory with a photo or two to practise on. Do not practise on originals: the CLI overwrites nothing by default, but work on copies anyway.
  • No account, no API key, no GPU, no sign-in of any kind for anything in this guide. The desktop app's smart-selection features run on your machine with no cloud and no account, per the README; the CLI path here touches no network at all after the download.
  • Optional but useful: Python with Pillow, only if you want to diff pixels before and after like this guide did. It is not required for any step.

One photo in, one graded photo out: the CLI runs the same engine commands the desktop app runs. Image: AI Frontier Post.

Step 1: Get the real binary and check it

Download the release for your platform from the project's releases page. On Linux x86_64, the file is photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz. The release also ships a SHA256SUMS.txt — check your download against it before you run anything from it:

curl -LO https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/releases/download/v0.17.0/photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
curl -LO https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/releases/download/v0.17.0/SHA256SUMS.txt
grep "linux-x86_64.tar.gz" SHA256SUMS.txt
sha256sum photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz

Expected result, verified October 28, 2026: the hash printed by sha256sum is 5259f9c428c8ee3478c35500ece98713561cafc050e4c9eb354a5050f36eb2b8, matching the release checksum. If yours differs, stop — re-download, and do not run the binary.

Extract it and confirm the tool answers:

tar -xzf photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
./photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64/bin/photocraft-cli --version
./photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64/bin/photocraft-cli --help

Expected output:

photocraft-cli 0.17.0 (b8c3f3aa8, 2026-10-28)

The help listing shows eight subcommands: convert, info, run, batch, droplet, commands, mcp, and serve. This guide runs the first four plus commands and mcp. The tarball also contains the desktop app binary (photocraft), which needs a display and is not used here. Put the CLI on your PATH if you plan to use it regularly; the rest of this guide calls it as photocraft-cli for brevity.

Step 2: Inspect a photo before you touch it

Copy a photo into a scratch directory and ask the CLI what it sees. This guide used a 640×400 test image; substitute your own file:

mkdir photocraft-demo
cp your-photo.jpg photocraft-demo/
cd photocraft-demo
photocraft-cli info your-photo.jpg

Expected output (abridged): a JSON document describing the image — its channels (Red, Green, Blue), composite mode (RGB), and layer tree, starting with "activeLayer": 2 for a flat import. The info command changes nothing; it is the read-only way to confirm the CLI can parse your file before you build an edit chain on top of it. If info fails on your file, the edit steps will too, and you have found that out cheaply. Run it on every new format you plan to feed the tool: PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF, and PSD are all on the convert list, but your specific file is the only test that matters.

Step 3: Make your first headless edit

The core command is run: open a file, apply engine commands in order, save the result. This is the exact shape from the project's README, run here verbatim — a Smart Sharpen filter followed by a Curves adjustment layer:

photocraft-cli run your-photo.jpg \
  --cmd filter.sharpen.smartSharpen --params '{"amount":80}' \
  --cmd layer.newAdjustmentLayer.curves --params '{"points":[[0,0],[64,48],[192,212],[255,255]]}' \
  --out graded-photo.png

Expected output, as printed by the run in this guide:

{"command":"filter.sharpen.smartSharpen","result":{"filter":{"amount":80.0,"filter":"smartSharpen","radius":1.0,"reduceNoise":10.0},"layer":2}}
{"command":"layer.newAdjustmentLayer.curves","result":{"layer":3}}
warning: 2 layer(s) flattened; layers, masks and blend modes are not kept

Read that output carefully, because it teaches you three things. First, every command echoes its result as JSON, so a script can check success per step instead of trusting an exit code alone. Second, the defaults are visible: Smart Sharpen at amount 80 also applied radius 1.0 and noise reduction 10.0, which the command line never mentioned — when you tune a look, query the result JSON to see what actually ran. Third, the warning is real and worth understanding: PNG output is flat, so the adjustment layer and the sharpened layer were flattened into one image. The layers survive only in layered formats (the native .pcraft format, PSD, or TIFF with the --tiff-layers flag in batch mode). If your workflow needs the layers back later, export to a layered format; if you need a finished file for the web, PNG is the right, honest end of the chain.

Verify the edit did something, rather than assuming it. Open both files and compare: the output keeps the input's dimensions (640×400 in this guide's test) and the pixels change — a sample pixel moved from RGB (240, 230, 180) to (247, 241, 199) after the sharpen-plus-curves chain. Your numbers will differ with your photo and your curve points; what matters is that you check, because a command that silently no-ops is worse than one that errors.

To find more commands, ask the registry itself instead of guessing names:

photocraft-cli commands | grep -i -E "vibrance|curves|levels|hue"

This lists real, callable command IDs with their menu paths — for example layer.newAdjustmentLayer.vibrance, image.adjustments.levels, and layer.newAdjustmentLayer.hueSaturation. Every command in this guide came from that list or from the README; none was invented, and you should hold any other tutorial to the same rule.

Step 4: Grade a whole folder with one recipe file

Single-image edits are a demo. The real use case is a folder: a shoot, a product catalog, a set of blog images that all need the same grade. That is what batch is for. Write the recipe as a JSON list of steps, one file per look:

cat > grade.json << 'EOF'
[{"command":"filter.sharpen.smartSharpen","params":{"amount":80}}]
EOF
mkdir raw graded
cp photo-a.jpg photo-b.jpg raw/
photocraft-cli batch --actions grade.json --in ./raw --out ./graded

Expected output, verified with two test images:

ok    ./raw/a.png -> ./graded/a.png
ok    ./raw/b.png -> ./graded/b.png
2 succeeded, 0 failed

Two details in that recipe are load-bearing, and both were learned the hard way in this guide's sandbox. First, each step needs the key "command". The batch help also describes [id, params] pairs and bare ids, but a step written with "cmd" instead of "command" fails outright with error: invalid parameters for batch --actions: step needs "command" — that exact error is what this guide got on its first attempt, and the fix is the one-word key change above. Second, batch refuses to write into the input folder unless you pass --in-place; keep input and output separate, as above, so a bad recipe never eats your originals. Useful extras on the same command: --format webp to change the output format regardless of input extension, and --quality 85 for lossy JPEG/WebP output (without a quality value, WebP output is lossless).

Batch mode: one recipe file, every image in the folder, one graded set out. Image: AI Frontier Post.

Step 5: Convert formats, including real PSD files

PhotoCraft's headline format claim is PSD without compromise: its PSD support is a standalone crate written from Adobe's public specification, and the project reports re-saving renders identically for 307 of the 309 files in the psd-tools test set. You do not need Photoshop to test the round trip at the CLI level:

photocraft-cli convert your-photo.png your-photo.psd
photocraft-cli info your-photo.psd
photocraft-cli convert your-photo.png your-photo.webp

All three commands ran cleanly in this guide's sandbox: the PNG became an 84,898-byte PSD that info reads back as a valid RGB document, and the same PNG became a 1,248-byte WebP. The convert list covers .pcraft, .psd, .png, .jpg, .tif, .webp, .exr, and more, with the output extension picking the format unless --format overrides it. Two honest limits, both from the README: HEIC photos from iPhone and Mac are read-only, and AVIF is write-only in official builds. And the PSD fidelity figures above are the project's corpus numbers, not something this guide re-measured — treat them as the project's claim, verified here only to the extent that a real PSD file was produced and re-read.

Step 6: Let an agent drive the same engine over MCP

The same engine is also an MCP server, which is the step that matters if you want a coding agent to edit images instead of you typing commands. Start it on stdio with explicit read and write roots — an omitted root denies that direction of file access, so grant only the scratch directory:

photocraft-cli mcp --automation-read-root "$PWD" --automation-write-root "$PWD"

Send it a standard MCP handshake (JSON-RPC initialize, then notifications/initialized, then tools/list), and it answers with server info photocraft 0.17.0 and a tool list that includes command_list (discover command ids and parameter docs), command_run and command_batch (edit, one history step per command), doc_open, doc_save, and doc_inspect. Its own instructions say to start with doc_new/doc_open, discover ids with command_list, and save as native .pcraft or export by extension. The ui_* tools (inspect, screenshot) require bridge mode against a running desktop app via --bridge 127.0.0.1:PORT and do not work headless — do not build an agent workflow on them unless the app is open.

What this guide verified for MCP is the handshake and the tool list, not a full agent-driven edit session. Wiring it into your MCP client is the documented next step: point the client at the stdio command above with the two root flags, and the agent gets the same 500+ commands the CLI has, scoped to one folder. That scoping is the point — an agent with an image editor should get a scratch folder, not your photo library.

When to use this vs alternatives

PhotoCraft's CLI is the right shape when your edits are a repeatable recipe: grade every photo from a shoot the same way, convert a folder between formats, or hand a bounded set of commands to an agent. It is the wrong shape when you need one-off creative work with a mouse — that is what the desktop app (or GIMP, or Photoshop) is for — and when your pipeline is already Python, where a Pillow script will beat a subprocess call on simplicity. Against ImageMagick, the difference is the model: ImageMagick is a pixel pipeline, while PhotoCraft is a layered document engine with adjustment layers, masks, and PSD round trips, so a recipe can stay editable instead of baked. Against GIMP's Script-Fu, the difference is friction: no Scheme, no display server, one JSON recipe file, and an MCP surface an agent can call. Against Photoshop Actions, the difference is cost and openness: no subscription, no account, and the whole engine is MIT/Apache-2.0 source you can read. And against writing your own editor: do not. This one already has 1,700+ tests behind it, including compositor oracles that check the CPU and GPU renderers against each other.

What this guide did not verify

  • The desktop GUI: it needs a display, and this guide's sandbox has none. Every GUI claim here (68 tools, brush engine, live adjustment layers) is the project's, not a measured result.
  • A full agent-driven edit over MCP: the handshake and tool list were verified, but no agent session edited an image end to end in this guide.
  • PSD fidelity beyond produce-and-re-read: the 307-of-309 corpus figure is the project's measurement, quoted as such.
  • Smart selection and Select Subject: documented as on-device with no cloud or account, but not exercised headless here.
  • Star, commit, and fork counts move with every release. The figures here (74,359 stars, 7,040 commits, 13,130 forks, version 0.17.0) are dated October 28, 2026; re-run --version and check the repository page before quoting them elsewhere.

The takeaway

PhotoCraft earns its stars the way open-source tools used to: it is a real, working engine with a real, working command line, and it does not ask for your account, your money, or your GPU before it does anything useful. Download one 123 MB tarball, check its hash, and you can inspect, sharpen, curve, batch-grade, convert, and hand the whole thing to an agent — all from a terminal, all offline after the download. The alpha label is honest and the GUI is unproven here, but the headless path is not a promise. It ran. Start with Step 3 on a copy of one photo tonight; if the recipe-file workflow in Step 4 feels like the missing piece in your image pipeline, the rest of the engine is already installed.

Sources

  • PhotoCraft repository page (github.com/storytold/photocraft) — star, commit, fork, license, and creation-date figures; the early-alpha status note.
  • PhotoCraft README — the headless CLI examples, the 500+ command registry, the MCP and control-channel description, the format list, and the HEIC/AVIF limits.
  • PhotoCraft release v0.17.0 (October 28, 2026) — the Linux tarball, the SHA256SUMS.txt checksum, and the per-platform download table.
  • The installed CLI itself, run in this guide: photocraft-cli 0.17.0 — every version string, command result, batch count, conversion, and MCP handshake quoted here came from running it, not from documentation alone.

title: Onde o bloco mora
description:
Na série IPFS com o Nabu, o CID (Content Identifier, o identificador do conteúdo) já nomeia o bloco e o Bitswap já o transporta. Este post é o lugar onde os bytes ficam quando o processo guarda uma cópia.

A proposta

Um bloco chega e precisa sobreviver ao reinício. A pergunta "eu tenho este CID?" acontece o tempo todo: a cada want do Bitswap, o motor olha o store. Ir ao disco, ou a um serviço de objetos, para cada pergunta fica caro quando a resposta quase sempre é não. O store também precisa listar os CIDs que tem, para o anúncio periódico da DHT (Distributed Hash Table), e lembrar tamanho e links, para a API (Application Programming Interface) HTTP não abrir o bloco inteiro só para medir.

A proposta é uma interface pequena, dois fundos intercambiáveis e camadas opcionais por cima: um filtro aproximado na frente e uma tabela de metadados ao lado.

A Demonstração

A interface é has, get, put, rm, refs, bloomAdd. A chave de arquivo deriva do multihash em base32, o alfabeto de 32 símbolos, sem o padding =. O diretório reparte os arquivos para uma única pasta não guardar milhões de entradas.

Dois fundos implementam o contrato. O de arquivo escreve cada bloco num .data sob blocks/. O de S3 (Simple Storage Service, o armazenamento de objetos no estilo da AWS) usa o mesmo contrato contra um bucket: uma região, um endpoint, um prefixo dentro do bucket. As credenciais podem vir do JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) de config, das variáveis AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, ou de ~/.aws/credentials.

Por cima do fundo entra um filtro. Ele responde "não tenho" sem tocar o fundo quando o CID está fora de um conjunto aproximado. Um bloom filter é uma tabela de bits. Cada CID liga alguns bits. Se algum bit que o CID exigiria está apagado, o CID com certeza não foi inserido. Se todos estão acesos, o CID talvez esteja: outro CID pode ter acendido os mesmos bits. Essa coincidência é o falso positivo, e a taxa é configurável. O InfiniFilter é um quotient filter que cresce. Em vez de ser recriado do zero quando enche, aumenta a estrutura e alonga a impressão digital (fingerprint) de cada chave. Os dois podem dizer que um CID talvez esteja presente. Só o fundo confirma. Um segundo filtro pequeno guarda ausências recentes, para não repetir a ida ao disco logo depois de um has negativo.

Os metadados ficam à parte, numa tabela H2 aberta por JDBC (Java Database Connectivity, a API Java de bancos relacionais): tamanho, links, o que block/stat precisa. O bloco em si continua no fundo.

No Nabu

EmbeddedIpfs.buildBlockStore escolhe o fundo pelo prefixo do config, em src/main/java/org/peergos/EmbeddedIpfs.java. flatfs.datastore monta um FileBlockstore no diretório IPFS e o embrulha num CachingBlockMetadataStore junto com o metadata JDBC. Se updateMetadb é verdadeiro, updateMetadataStoreIfEmpty percorre os blocos quando a tabela ainda está vazia. s3.datastore faz o análogo com S3Blockstore, lendo região, bucket, rootDirectory e regionEndpoint dos parâmetros do mount. Outro prefixo lança Unrecognized datastore prefix.

O caminho de arquivo está em FileBlockstore.getFilePath. hashToKey codifica o multihash em base32 e corta no primeiro =. A pasta são os dois caracteres imediatamente anteriores ao último. O arquivo é a chave mais .data, e a raiz é o diretório blocks/ criado no construtor se ainda não existe:

String key = hashToKey(cid);
String folder = key.substring(key.length() -3, key.length()-1);
String filename = key + BLOCK_FILE_SUFFIX;

put grava com TRUNCATE_EXISTING e CREATE, e devolve o CID versão 1 com SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm de 256 bits), como no primeiro post. has é file.exists(). hasAny procura o mesmo multihash sob os codecs DagCbor, Raw e DagProtobuf, montando um CID versão 1 para cada um. get lê o arquivo inteiro para um byte[], ou devolve vazio se o arquivo não está.

filteredBlockStore embrulha o fundo se config.datastore.filter.type for BLOOM ou INFINI, com a taxa de falso positivo do config. NONE devolve o fundo direto. Outro tipo é erro. FilteredBlockstore.has só chama o fundo quando o filtro de presentes responde sim e o de ausências responde não. Se o fundo diz não, o CID entra no filtro de ausências. Esse filtro recomeça depois de 10.000 ausências, com um CidInfiniFilter de 1.000 entradas e taxa 0,001. get segue a mesma porta: fora do filtro de presentes, devolve vazio sem ler o fundo. put grava no fundo e só então chama present.add. rm apaga no fundo e não mexe no filtro de presentes. Um CID removido pode continuar "talvez presente" até o filtro ser refeito. O has seguinte vai ao fundo, recebe não, e registra a ausência.

bloomAdd insere o CID no filtro de presentes, sem gravar bytes. É o que a API bloom/add faz. Sem isso, um CID que já está no fundo e ficou de fora do filtro seria invisível: has e get nem consultariam o disco. Se o fundo não tem o bloco, has responde falso e o CID entra no filtro de ausências. O filtro sozinho não afirma a posse.

O metadata nasce em buildBlockMetadata. A URL JDBC é jdbc:h2: mais o caminho de nabu-blockmetadata.sql, com MODE=PostgreSQL. A conexão fica embrulhada em UncloseableConnection para um close acidental não derrubar o banco, e o auto-commit fica ligado. TypeLimitedBlockstore entra por último, quando allowedCodecs não está vazio. put e rm de um codec fora da lista lançam Unsupported codec. get de um codec fora da lista devolve vazio, sem chamar o fundo.

Os exemplos usam RamBlockstore: um mapa na memória do processo, sem arquivo, sem S3 e sem filtro. O processo Nabu usa arquivo ou S3.

O que fica de fora: não há Badger, LevelDB nem outro sharding além da pasta de dois caracteres. O filtro pode afirmar presença à toa, dentro da taxa configurada. A ausência confirmada pelo fundo é a resposta que vale. O InfiniFilter do código segue o artigo de Pagh, cresce por gerações de fingerprint, e a série não reproduz a matemática. O ponto prático é que has barato continua correto o bastante para não ir ao S3 em todo want.

Nesta série

O anterior é IPNS, um nome que muda. O próximo é A API HTTP e como rodar o Nabu.

title: Avoiding Duplicate AI Work: SQLAlchemy Persistence and Fingerprint-Based Caching in FastAPI
description:
When building an AI-powered application, sending every request to an AI provider can create unnecessary work. Users may submit the same information more than once, refresh a page, or update a record without changing the data that affects the result.

During the development of my personal Lead Qualification & Scoring Engine, I worked on this problem by combining SQLAlchemy persistence with a fingerprint-based caching strategy.

The goal was simple:

  • Avoid creating duplicate records for the same lead.
  • Reuse an existing qualification when the relevant input has not changed.
  • Re-run qualification when meaningful lead information changes.
  • Keep the same Lead ID when updating an existing lead.

In this article, I’ll explain the design and the implementation behind it.

  1. The Problem: Repeated Requests

Imagine a sales representative submits the following lead:

  • Name: John Smith
  • Company: Example SaaS
  • Industry: Software
  • Pain point: Manual lead qualification

The application qualifies the lead and saves the result.

If the representative submits the same lead again, creating another database record and repeating the AI analysis is unnecessary.

However, there is an important distinction: if the lead’s buying signal or pain point changes, the application may need to run the qualification process again.

I needed a way to distinguish between these two situations.

  1. The Approach: Identity and Fingerprint

I used two separate hashes because they answer two different questions.

Identity key: Is this the same lead?

The identity key is calculated from the lead’s name and company.

It helps the application find an existing record for the same person at the same company.

Fingerprint: Has the qualification input changed?

The fingerprint is calculated from fields that meaningfully affect qualification, such as the industry, company size, pain point, buying signal, and recent activity.

The application compares this fingerprint with the one stored in the database.

This distinction is important: lead identity determines which record to look up, while the fingerprint determines whether the stored qualification can be reused.

  1. Creating a Stable Fingerprint with Python

I implemented the fingerprint logic using Python’s hashlib and json modules.

Here is a simplified version of the approach:

import hashlib
import json
def normalize(value):
if isinstance(value, str):
value = value.strip().lower()
return value or None
return value
def create_fingerprint(lead_data, fields):
payload = {
field: normalize(lead_data.get(field))
for field in fields
}
stable_json = json.dumps(
payload,
sort_keys=True,
ensure_ascii=False
)
return hashlib.sha256(
stable_json.encode("utf-8")
).hexdigest()

This example illustrates the core technique. In my project, the implementation reads the selected fields from the lead object.

There are three important details here:

Normalization: Trimming whitespace and normalizing string casing means values such as " Software " and "software" produce the same normalized input.

Stable serialization: Using sort_keys=True ensures that dictionary key order does not affect the serialized representation.

SHA-256 hashing: The normalized JSON is converted into a SHA-256 hash. Identical normalized input produces the same fingerprint.

A hash is useful here as a compact comparison value. It does not replace the original lead data, which is stored separately in the database.

  1. Choosing the Fields Carefully

Not every field should necessarily invalidate a cached qualification.

For example, my implementation includes fields such as:

  • Name and company
  • Job title and country
  • Industry and company size
  • Website and LinkedIn URL
  • Pain point and buying signal
  • Recent activity

The implementation deliberately excludes custom_offer, which is treated as a display override rather than a qualification input.

This choice depends on the application’s business rules. If a field starts influencing the qualification result, it should be included in the fingerprint.

Otherwise, the application could incorrectly reuse a result calculated from older information.

  1. Persisting Lead Data with SQLAlchemy

I used SQLAlchemy to store lead information and qualification results in a database.

The lead model includes fields for:

  • The identity key and fingerprint
  • Original lead information
  • Qualification score and classification
  • Scoring breakdown and AI assessment
  • Recommended offer and next action
  • Sales action plan
  • Creation and update timestamps

The model stores structured information in database columns. Some result fields, such as scoring breakdowns and sales action plans, use JSON-compatible columns.

I also created repository functions to keep database operations separate from the API route logic.

For example, the update operation modifies an existing SQLAlchemy model instance:

def update_lead_record(db, record, data):
for key, value in data.items():
setattr(record, key, value)
db.commit()
db.refresh(record)
return record

The important behavior is that this updates the existing record rather than inserting a new one. The existing database ID is therefore preserved.

In the actual project, the repository functions also handle creating records, retrieving a lead by ID, looking up a lead by identity, and listing recent leads.

  1. Applying the Cache in the FastAPI Endpoint

The main qualification endpoint follows a straightforward decision process.

  1. Calculate the lead’s identity key.
  2. Calculate the fingerprint of the qualification-relevant fields.
  3. Find an existing record using the identity key.
  4. Compare the stored fingerprint with the newly calculated fingerprint.
  5. Reuse the stored qualification or run the qualification process, depending on the comparison.

The core decision looks like this:

existing = get_lead_by_identity(
db,
identity_key
)
if existing is not None:
if existing.fingerprint == fingerprint:
# Reuse the stored qualification.
return {
"cached": True,
"lead": _lead_dict(existing),
"qualification": _qualification_dict(existing),
}
# The lead exists, but relevant input changed.
result = analyze_lead(lead)
# Update the existing record with the new result.
else:
# New lead: qualify and create a record.
result = analyze_lead(lead)

This is a simplified illustration of the decision flow; the complete endpoint also builds the response and persists the new qualification results.

The actual implementation returns a cached flag and a qualification_source value. This makes it easier to distinguish between a result reused from the database and one generated through a new qualification run.

  1. What Happens in Each Scenario?

Scenario Application behavior
New person and company Run qualification and create a record
Same identity and same fingerprint Reuse the stored qualification
Same identity but changed fingerprint Re-run qualification and update the existing record
Display-only offer override changes Do not invalidate the fingerprint solely for that change

This approach keeps the behavior predictable while avoiding unnecessary repeat work.

  1. Engineering Considerations

Implementing a fingerprint-based cache requires more than generating a hash.

Keep the fingerprint definition aligned with business logic

If qualification starts depending on a new field, update the fingerprint field list as well. Otherwise, stale results may be reused.

Handle normalization deliberately

Normalization should reflect the meaning of the data. Lowercasing text is reasonable for many names and descriptive fields, but it should not be applied indiscriminately to every type of value.

Consider changes to the scoring rules

The fingerprint in this implementation represents the lead input. If scoring rules or model behavior change, the same input may produce a different result.

For a production system, consider including a scoring-rule version or qualification version in the cache key, or invalidating cached results when those dependencies change.

Think about concurrent requests

Two requests for the same new lead can arrive at nearly the same time. A production implementation should consider database uniqueness constraints, transaction handling, and concurrency so that simultaneous requests do not create duplicate records.

Measure the benefit

Caching can reduce repeated AI calls, but its actual impact depends on how frequently duplicate requests occur. Logging cache hits, cache misses, and qualification duration can help evaluate whether the approach is effective.

  1. What I Learned

This implementation helped me understand that caching is not simply storing a response and returning it later.

The difficult part is deciding when a stored result is still valid.

Separating lead identity from qualification fingerprints made the behavior easier to reason about. SQLAlchemy persistence gave the application a consistent place to store both the input data and its qualification results, while FastAPI provided the endpoint through which the workflow runs.

The same ideas can be useful in other applications that process repeated inputs, including document analysis, product recommendations, reporting tools, and AI-assisted workflows.

Conclusion

Building the Lead Qualification & Scoring Engine gave me an opportunity to apply hashing, database persistence, and caching to a practical backend problem.

The main lesson is that a useful cache needs a clear definition of identity and a reliable way to determine whether the underlying input has changed.

By combining a stable fingerprint with SQLAlchemy persistence, the application can reuse unchanged qualification results and update existing lead records when relevant information changes.

I’m continuing to improve the project and explore ways to make AI-powered applications more reliable, explainable, and efficient.

This article describes the implementation in my personal Lead Qualification & Scoring Engine

title: How Zero Downtime Database Migration Works: A Practical Guide
description:
For modern businesses, databases support essential operations such as online transactions, customer accounts, inventory management, and reporting. Migrating to a new database or infrastructure can improve performance, scalability, and flexibility, but even a short outage may disrupt customers and business operations.

Zero downtime database migration aims to move data and applications to a new environment without interrupting service. Although achieving literally zero interruption is difficult in every environment, a carefully planned migration can minimise downtime and make the transition nearly seamless.

This guide explains how zero downtime database migration works, which techniques businesses can use, and how to reduce risks during the process.

What Is Zero Downtime Database Migration?

Zero downtime database migration is the process of moving a database to a new platform, server, or infrastructure while keeping the application available to users.

Instead of shutting down the existing system for the entire migration, organisations transfer data in stages while the original database continues serving requests. Changes made during the transfer are also synchronised with the target database.

Once the target is verified and ready, application traffic is switched to the new environment.

Common migration scenarios include moving databases to the cloud, upgrading database infrastructure, changing database platforms, and consolidating multiple systems.

Why Is Zero Downtime Migration Important?

For businesses operating online services, downtime can lead to lost sales, failed transactions, frustrated customers, and additional support costs.

A low-downtime migration can help organisations:

  • Maintain access to critical applications.
  • Reduce disruption to customers and employees.
  • Modernise database infrastructure with less operational risk.
  • Improve scalability and resource utilisation.
  • Schedule changes with greater flexibility.

However, keeping an application online is not enough. The migration must also preserve data consistency, transaction integrity, security, and acceptable performance.

How Zero Downtime Database Migration Works

1. Assess the Existing Database

Begin by examining the source database, including its size, schema, indexes, stored procedures, application dependencies, and transaction volume.

Identify compatibility issues between the source and target platforms. For example, moving from SQL Server to PostgreSQL may require changes to SQL syntax, data types, and stored procedures.

Define measurable success criteria, including acceptable replication lag, data validation requirements, performance targets, and rollback conditions.

2. Prepare the Target Database

Create the target database and configure its schema, access permissions, indexes, monitoring, and backup procedures.

Where the source and target use different database engines, convert incompatible objects and update application queries as required.

Test the target environment before transferring production data. This helps identify configuration and compatibility problems early.

3. Perform the Initial Data Load

Copy the existing database data to the target while the source continues operating.

Depending on the database and migration tools, the initial load may involve bulk exports, snapshots, native replication, or managed migration services.

Because users continue changing data during this stage, the initial copy alone cannot provide a complete and current target database.

4. Synchronise Ongoing Changes

To capture changes made after the initial copy, organisations commonly use change data capture (CDC), transaction-log replication, or database-native replication mechanisms.

These techniques continuously transfer new, updated, and deleted records to the target.

Administrators monitor replication lag to confirm that changes are reaching the target within the required timeframe. They must also account for transaction ordering, schema changes, and replication errors.

For cross-platform migrations, verify that the selected tool supports the required source and target features.

5. Validate Data Consistency

Before switching application traffic, confirm that the target contains the expected data and behaves correctly.

Validation may include comparing row counts, checking key records, verifying business-critical totals, and testing application workflows.

For financial or transactional systems, additional checks may be necessary to verify that transactions are neither lost nor applied twice.

Validation should continue during replication and immediately before cutover. A successful replication status alone does not prove that the application is ready.

6. Switch Application Traffic

Once the target is synchronised and has passed validation, move application connections to the new database.

Depending on the architecture, this may involve changing connection strings, updating service discovery, switching a database endpoint, or modifying routing configuration.

A safe cutover typically requires a controlled write transition. The migration team must ensure that writes are not accepted independently by both databases unless the architecture explicitly supports conflict resolution.

The final steps should be rehearsed and monitored closely to minimise interruption.

7. Monitor and Complete the Migration

After cutover, monitor application errors, database performance, replication status, transaction outcomes, and resource utilisation.

Keep the source environment available for the agreed rollback period where feasible. However, returning to the old database may require reverse replication or another data reconciliation process if new writes have already occurred on the target.

Do not decommission the source until the new environment is stable, acceptance criteria are met, and recovery arrangements are confirmed.

Common Challenges to Consider

Zero downtime database migration requires careful engineering. Common challenges include:

  • Data inconsistency: Changes may be missed or incorrectly applied without reliable synchronisation.
  • Replication lag: High transaction volumes can delay updates reaching the target.
  • Schema incompatibility: Different database engines may interpret types, queries, and constraints differently.
  • Application dependencies: Hard-coded connections and database-specific queries can complicate cutover.
  • Rollback complexity: New transactions written to the target must be accounted for before switching back.

Testing, monitoring, and a clearly defined migration strategy help reduce these risks.

Best Practices for a Successful Migration

Before beginning, organisations should:

  • Back up the source database and test recovery procedures.
  • Rehearse the complete migration using representative data.
  • Establish replication monitoring and alerting.
  • Define cutover, validation, and rollback criteria.
  • Test application compatibility and performance.
  • Assign clear responsibilities to database, application, and operations teams.
  • Communicate the migration plan to relevant stakeholders.

A migration rehearsal is particularly valuable because it reveals timing issues and hidden dependencies before production is affected.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Is zero downtime database migration always possible?

Not in every environment. Some migrations require a brief write pause or connection reset. The achievable downtime depends on the database technology, application architecture, and consistency requirements.

2. What is the role of change data capture?

CDC captures changes made to the source database and helps apply them to the target after the initial data load, keeping the two environments synchronised.

3. How long does a zero downtime migration take?

It depends on database size, transaction volume, network capacity, compatibility work, and testing requirements. Preparation and validation may take longer than the actual cutover.

4. Can a business roll back after migration?

Yes, if rollback is planned and tested. The process must account for transactions written to the new database after cutover to avoid losing or duplicating data.

Conclusion

Zero downtime database migration helps businesses modernise their infrastructure while keeping critical applications available. The process relies on careful assessment, an initial data transfer, continuous change synchronisation, rigorous validation, and a controlled cutover.

The key to success is not simply moving data quickly. It is maintaining consistency, protecting transactions, and preparing a tested recovery plan for unexpected issues.

The approach is simple: Use technology to simplify operations—not complicate them.

title: El límite de Shorts en 0 no basta: cómo quitar los Shorts de YouTube en el iPhone y seguir viendo videos normales (2026)
description:
minulo es una app para iPhone que oculta los Shorts de YouTube mientras los videos normales, las suscripciones y la búsqueda siguen funcionando, y ocultarlos es gratis. La otra forma viene en la propia app de YouTube: el Límite del feed de Shorts puesto en 0. También es gratis, pero un adulto puede descartar el aviso y seguir viendo. (Soy el desarrollador de minulo, Ayumu Kitabayashi, así que tenlo en cuenta al leer.)

Abajo explico cada opción con sus límites, incluidos los de minulo.

1. El Límite del feed de Shorts en 0 (gratis, dentro de YouTube)

Los pasos, según la ayuda de YouTube:

  1. Inicia sesión en la app de YouTube.
  2. Toca la pestaña Tú y luego Configuración.
  3. Toca Gestión del tiempo.
  4. Toca Límite del feed de Shorts y elige 0 en la lista.

El 0 está disponible para todos desde abril de 2026. Al llegar al límite, YouTube muestra un recordatorio. Su ayuda lo explica así: «Se te pedirá que rechaces o ignores el límite que has definido». Es decir, con un toque sigues en el feed.

Lo que conviene saber:

  • Con una cuenta de adulto el límite se puede descartar.
  • Los Shorts siguen apareciendo en Suscripciones y en los enlaces que te mandan.
  • Es solo para la app. La ayuda no describe este ajuste en youtube.com.
  • La ayuda no aclara si el límite afecta a los Shorts de Inicio, de la búsqueda o de las páginas de los canales.

2. Otras opciones de YouTube y del iPhone

Mostrar menos Shorts (⋮ arriba de una fila de Shorts en Inicio). Le dice a YouTube que te muestre menos. Son menos, no ninguno, y YouTube no dice cuánto dura. Se puede deshacer en Mi Actividad.

Desactivar el historial de reproducciones. YouTube quita las recomendaciones de la página de inicio cuando no tienes historial reciente relevante. Su ayuda no dice que esto quite la pestaña Shorts.

Cuenta supervisada para adolescentes. Los padres pueden fijar cuánto tiempo pasa un adolescente deslizando Shorts. Sirve solo para cuentas supervisadas.

Tiempo de uso del iPhone. Puede limitar o bloquear toda la app de YouTube, pero no puede apuntar solo a los Shorts. Si bloqueas YouTube, también te quedas sin videos largos y suscripciones. Apple no documenta una forma de bloquear solo la dirección /shorts en Safari.

Apps y extensiones que ocultan los Shorts. Además de minulo, hay otras como UNDOOMED, Nope y LoomWeb. Nope es una extensión de Safari, así que solo funciona en youtube.com desde Safari, no en la app de YouTube.

3. Ocultar los Shorts con minulo

minulo abre el sitio web de YouTube dentro de la app y oculta lo que tú eliges. No hay ningún aviso que puedas saltarte.

  1. Instala minulo desde el App Store.
  2. En el inicio, toca Agregar un servicio y elige YouTube.
  3. Toca el engranaje junto a YouTube y activa Ocultar la sección de Shorts, Ocultar la pestaña Shorts y Abrir los enlaces de Shorts en el reproductor normal.
  4. Si quieres, oculta también las recomendaciones de Inicio. Las suscripciones, Ver más tarde y la búsqueda se quedan.

Si el problema es que abres la app oficial de YouTube por costumbre, abre la pestaña Bloquear, permite Tiempo de uso y elige YouTube en Apps que bloquear. Cuando intentes abrir YouTube aparece una pantalla de Bloqueado, y el botón Abrir en minulo te lleva a la versión sin Shorts.

Ocultar los Shorts y bloquear la app oficial es gratis. Los horarios por día y hora, los bloqueos de más de 2 horas y el Modo estricto son de minulo Pro (9,99 $ al mes o 39,99 $ al año en EE. UU.).

Lo que minulo no puede hacer

Prefiero dejarlo claro antes de que lo instales:

  • No cambia la app oficial de YouTube. En el iPhone ninguna app puede cambiar lo que muestra otra. Los Shorts solo se ocultan dentro de minulo.
  • El bloqueo gratis dura hasta 2 horas. Cuando termina puedes empezar otro. Ocultar los Shorts no tiene límite de tiempo.
  • Solo iPhone (también hay una versión para Mac que funciona en Safari y Chrome). No hay versión para Android (está en pruebas).
  • Sin notificaciones mientras bloquea. Mientras minulo bloquea la app oficial, sus notificaciones no llegan, y minulo no envía notificaciones propias. Si necesitas los avisos de YouTube, no bloquees la app oficial.
  • Cuando YouTube cambia sus pantallas, algo oculto puede volver a aparecer un tiempo. Las reglas se revisan automáticamente cada semana.
  • Es una app nueva (septiembre de 2026) y todavía tiene pocas valoraciones.

Nota técnica para quien desarrolla

minulo no toca la app de YouTube. Carga la web oficial de cada servicio dentro de la app y oculta las partes elegidas en esa vista. El bloqueo de la app oficial usa Tiempo de uso de Apple: al tocar el icono sale la pantalla de bloqueo del sistema con el botón para abrir minulo. Por eso las limitaciones de arriba son las de iOS y las de la web: lo que la versión web no tiene, minulo tampoco lo tiene.

Resumen

  • Si te basta con un recordatorio: Límite del feed de Shorts en 0, gratis, pero se descarta con un toque.
  • Si quieres dejar de ver YouTube del todo un rato: Tiempo de uso, que bloquea la app entera.
  • Si quieres seguir viendo videos normales sin Shorts: minulo, gratis para ocultarlos.

Todos los métodos, con fuentes: Cómo bloquear los Shorts de YouTube en iPhone

Los nombres de los menús pueden cambiar con las actualizaciones de YouTube y de iOS.

title: MySQL or PostgreSQL, Does It Matter to Choose Which?
description:
When we develop a program, or an app, it is important to keep our data on some place. If you learn basic web app programming from Youtube or from other learning platform, you will be guided to choose MySQL as a starter database. MySQL is beginner friendly, easy to use, and versatile when it comes to intermediate level query. But there is other SQL version, which is PostgreSQL. So what is the difference between those two?

What is SQL?

SQL is Structured Query Language. It is a programming language of which we can use to manage MySQL and PostgreSQL. MySQL and PostgreSQL is a database management system. Those two are the places we can store the database, and SQL is the language we can use to access them.

The learning curve of SQL is quite lean. The core concept of the query is simple. But when it comes to complexes database which have tons of tables, it is quite challenging to optimize the syntax of the query. SQL language is quite a lot to explore, but we can grasp the core of SQL quite easy.

For example, the JOIN syntax. There are many kind of JOIN syntax like INNER JOIN or OUTER JOIN which have different purposes, but the concept is the same, to join the columns of the tables. Same as INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, quite explanatory each of those syntax for the SQL.

About MySQL and PostgreSQL

MySQL is commonly used with web application, mostly with PHP and Javascript. Web applications store their user data, config data, and application data within MySQL. In PHP, they have mysqli extension which for some PHP installation is enabled by default. It is the interface for the web application to execute SQL Query to MySQL databases. The query which executed then returns output to the web application or changes data in the database.

But when you familiar with enterprise application like ERP or HRIS, you will heard PostgreSQL much more often. PostgreSQL is a database, just like MySQL. They have quite similar query syntax on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, but on some cases like incremental key, upsert, or concatenate, they have different syntax. PostgreSQL much optimized for bigger application for which they have optimized for larger databases and more complex queries.

So That's It? More optimized?

Well, yes basically. PostgreSQL is more optimized to larger and complex databases.

The truth of deciding of which database to choose is based on what exactly the specifications do you need?

If you only need database for simple web application for about 100 users which not concurrently using, it is better to use MySQL. The installation is simple and will fulfill your app's need. MySQL interface on some programming language mostly pre-installed so it won't be too much of a hassle to install your database.

But if you need a more heavy load transaction and computation, most likely because your app used by a lot of concurrent users and maybe you will be using pgvector to use LLMs, you will need PostgreSQL. It is more optimized for larger JOINs for much more relational tables and even can be setup as Vector Database for your LLMs.

The more we know the capacity of those two database system, the better our app will perform.

title: Where Were the Logs? Building a Log Ingestion Engine That Never Silently Drops a Log
description:
Three hours were lost in this example scenario. Two hours were spent on root cause analysis (where an engineer would log onto each server, open up various log files, and search manually). There was no error reported from any of the applications on the monitoring dashboard, meaning that no panels highlighted the service that was failing. There was also no clear indication of which service was failing the most. The compliance team wanted to see audit trails, but there were none to provide.

The brief is the running example I built this project from, and I later published the project as a repository.

TL;DR: Go service which receives batched JSON on /logs, validates at field level, enriches and routes to three SQLite destinations via RabbitMQ with a bounded in-memory fallback. Admission is durable via a write-ahead spool fsynced before 202; unacked spool entries are replayed on startup. Batch writer with bounded retries and rotating dead-letter file, idempotent writes per log_id. Load test sustained 1,000 logs/s acceptance with 12 pipeline workers, batch 100, on a laptop; default 4 workers do not sustain the target.

1. The problem

There are twelve services, each producing bespoke log files onto individual disks. There is no central search, no live dashboard, and no audit trail. It can take an hour to determine which service (or machine), or which file had the issue. By using grep on a laptop, it can be found in seconds. However, using grep on all twelve different formats takes an entire afternoon.

This resulted in three requirements:

  • A central search of all log files.

  • Signals in minutes about which service has an issue and how big the issue is.

  • An audit trail that is persistent and no data is lost when restarting the service.

The log ingestion engine has been built to provide some of the searchable requirements (see section 7).

2. The goal and the ground rules

Overview

A centralised logging platform to receive logs using an API, validate and enrich log data, route by service, store it reliably, and provide signals so we can see issues occur before our customers do.

Constraints

The brief says we must limit our libraries. I made a few changes here:

  • Used the rate-limiting library golang.org/x/time/rate rather than implementing my own token bucket. The interesting engineering was implementing per-IP keys, request shaping, and Retry-After.

  • The frontend uses React with Vite, Tailwind CSS as a utility CSS framework, Space Grotesk from the Google Fonts CDN, and Chart.js for charts, instead of hand-written HTML/CSS.

Storage is kept within the brief:

  • Three databases using SQLite.

  • One file per destination.

The configuration is simple with only .env files, integer values for duration, and ROUTING_RULES. The cost of using SQLite on real logs is discussed in section 7.

3. Architecture at a glance

This diagram represents the architecture shipped with the project:

flowchart TB
    client(["Clients"])

    subgraph ingress["HTTP ingress"]
        direction TB
        rateLimit["Rate limiter<br/>per IP, in-memory"]
        logsEndpoint["POST /logs"]
        validate["Validate batch<br/>body size + per-entry errors"]
    end

    spool[("Write-ahead spool<br/>fsync before ack")]
    rawQueue[("raw_logs<br/>bounded channel")]

    subgraph processing["Pipeline worker pool"]
        direction TB
        enrich["Enrich<br/>received_at · source_ip · environment"]
        route["Route<br/>service → destination rules"]
    end

    subgraph publishing["Publisher"]
        direction TB
        rabbitPublisher["RabbitMQ publisher<br/>persistent + confirms<br/>5s publish timeout<br/>auto-reconnect with backoff"]
        fallback[("Bounded in-memory fallback<br/>used while disconnected")]
    end

    broker[("RabbitMQ<br/>exchange_service1..3<br/>queue_service1..3<br/>routing key: log.write")]

    subgraph delivery["Consumers and storage"]
        direction TB
        supervisor["Supervisor<br/>one connection<br/>declares topology, reconnects"]
        amqpConsumer["AMQP consumers<br/>one connection per queue<br/>ack after stored"]
        fallbackConsumer["Fallback consumer"]
        batchWriter["Batch writer<br/>per-destination buffers<br/>retry with backoff"]
        sqlite[("SQLite<br/>logs_service1.db<br/>logs_service2.db<br/>logs_service3.db")]
        deadLetters[("Dead-letter NDJSON<br/>one shared file<br/>rotated by size")]
        replay["cmd/replay"]
    end

    client --> rateLimit --> logsEndpoint --> validate --> spool --> rawQueue
    rawQueue --> enrich --> route --> rabbitPublisher
    rabbitPublisher -->|"connected"| broker
    rabbitPublisher -->|"publish fails"| fallback
    fallback -.->|"fallback full: dead letter"| deadLetters
    broker -->|"deliver"| supervisor
    supervisor --> amqpConsumer
    fallback -->|"stored directly, never re-published"| fallbackConsumer
    amqpConsumer --> batchWriter
    fallbackConsumer --> batchWriter
    batchWriter -->|"stored"| sqlite
    batchWriter -->|"retries exhausted"| deadLetters
    deadLetters -.-> replay
    replay -.->|"replay"| sqlite

There are 6 stages within the pipeline:

  • Post

  • Validate

  • Buffer

  • Enrich/Route

  • Publish/Fallback

  • Consume/Store

flowchart LR
    post["1 Post<br/>rate limit,<br/>accept the batch"]
    validate["2 Validate and spool<br/>per-entry errors,<br/>fsync admission"]
    buffer["3 Buffer<br/>bounded raw_logs<br/>channel (10,000)<br/>202 or 503"]
    enrichRoute["4 Enrich and route<br/>stamp fields,<br/>pick destination"]
    publish["5 Publish<br/>RabbitMQ, or the<br/>in-memory fallback"]
    store["6 Consume and store<br/>batched SQLite writes,<br/>dead letters on failure"]

    post --> validate --> buffer --> enrichRoute --> publish --> store

Each stage handles one specific type of failure/slowdown.

  • The rate limiter handles abusive clients.

  • raw_logs handles separating quick HTTP traffic from slow enrichment.

  • The publisher fallback handles outages of the broker. The logs are each written to storage once, as persistence is idempotent on a per log_id basis. They are never ping-ponged between the broker and memory.

  • The batch writer spreads the cost of inserting into SQLite.

  • The dead letter file handles unrecoverable failure.

The fallback is consumed by a dedicated consumer and written directly to storage. No re-publishing occurs. As consumers only acknowledge once data has been stored, it provides at-least-once delivery. Persistence within the database is idempotent on a per log_id basis, so duplicate data can be handled.

4. The stages

4.1 Ingestion and validation

This will validate the Content-Type header, ensure the body is a certain size using http.MaxBytesReader, parse the JSON, and ensure that there are four fields for each log entry. These are:

  • Timestamp (RFC3339)

  • Service (at most 100 characters)

  • Level (INFO/WARN/ERROR/DEBUG)

  • Message (at most 10,000 characters)

Validation runs first. Valid entries are appended to the write-ahead spool and fsynced to disk. The handler then attempts to enqueue the batch onto the bounded raw_logs channel. If the enqueue succeeds within CHANNEL_SEND_TIMEOUT, the handler returns 202 with the batch ID and per-entry rejection details; if the channel is full or the send times out, the handler returns 503. The 202 therefore means the batch is durably admitted for replay and now being processed, not yet in SQLite. The spool guarantees the batch can be replayed on restart. In the 503 case, the spool entry is retained so it can be replayed later; the client may retry and create duplicates, which receive new log_ids and are therefore stored as separate rows (idempotency does not collapse them).

Design decision: I decided to accept partial batches. This will mean that if a log has an invalid time, it will only lose one log instead of one hundred. Each valid log entry will have a UUID added as the log_id field. This means they can be safely resent and played back.

Design decision: The spool fsync is performed inline on the request path to make a 202 durable. This breaks the “no blocking” ideal and adds latency on the critical path, but it guarantees admission durability. The fsync is small per batch, and the cost is accepted for durability; compaction of the spool log and .acked file occurs only when every spooled ID has been acknowledged.

func ValidateLogEntries(logEntries []model.LogEntry) (validEntries []model.LogEntry, rejectedEntries []model.RejectedEntry) {
 for entryIndex, logEntry := range logEntries {
  fieldErrors := validateLogEntry(logEntry)
  if len(fieldErrors) > 0 {
   rejectedEntries = append(rejectedEntries, model.RejectedEntry{
    Index:  entryIndex,
    Errors: fieldErrors,
   })
  } else {
   validEntries = append(validEntries, logEntry)
  }
 }
 return validEntries, rejectedEntries
}

Valid and invalid log entries will be separated by ValidateLogEntries whilst retaining their original index.

Every log entry needs to have a time, service, level, and message. POST /logs can return 202, 400, 413, 415, 503, or a 429 from the limiter.

4.2 Protecting the boundary

Rate limiting middleware using a lazy in-memory token bucket, keyed on the source IP address. Token buckets are purged explicitly when idle.
Rejected requests will not consume a token.

Design decision: The AllowWithoutConsumingCapacity method is used. This method checks how much delay is required. If the delay is positive, the reservation is cancelled, and the request is rejected before any work is done, returning 429 with a Retry-After header in whole seconds. The rejected request keeps its token.

reservation := entry.limiter.Reserve()
delay := reservation.Delay()
if delay > 0 {
 reservation.Cancel()
 return delay, false
}

  • Rate limiting middleware uses a token bucket for each IP address. 429 status code is returned with a delay in whole seconds.

  • No token is consumed on rejection. X-Forwarded-For is trusted only when a trusted proxy is configured; with no proxy list, the socket address is used for identity.

4.3 The raw_logs buffer

I have a bounded channel that defaults to 10,000 entries for RAW_LOGS_BUFFER. Validations happen quickly, but enrichments happen at their own pace.

Design decision: Producers wait for a bounded 100 ms rather than fail instantly. PushBatch rejects oversized batches immediately, then takes the producer lock and waits up to CHANNEL_SEND_TIMEOUT 100 ms for room for the entire batch. This is blocking with a bounded timeout, providing backpressure.

for len(rawLogs) > cap(rawLogsQueue.channel)-len(rawLogsQueue.channel) {
 select {
 case <-capacityCheck.C:
 case <-sendContext.Done():
  return ErrQueueOverloaded
 }
}

Writing straight to SQL would be on the slow path. Using the bounded channel means they are separated. I use back pressure by returning a 503.

4.4 Enrichment

Adds received_at, source_ip, and environment (defaulting to production) from config. Also adds log_id, batch_id, and retry_count (starting at 0) to every log. No I/O operation, so no failure case.

Design decision: All data is captured at the edge as it is based on request context. This means I only have access to the socket address, forwarded chain, and received time. These are stamped and then passed through. If any of these fields are missing, a sensible default is used.

return model.EnrichedLog{
 LogEntry:    rawLog.LogEntry,
 LogID:       logEnricher.logIDOrDefault(rawLog.LogID),
 BatchID:     rawLog.BatchID,
 ReceivedAt:  receivedAt,
 SourceIP:    sourceIP,
 Environment: logEnricher.applicationEnvironment,
 RetryCount:  0,
}

received_at uses the handler clock; source_ip uses the socket address or the first valid X-Forwarded-For header from behind a trusted proxy. All of these are captured at the edge.

4.5 Routing

The destination is stamped based on a validated mapping from the .env file using the ROUTING_RULES=claims=service2,billing=service3 format. If an unknown service is provided, it will default to service1. The config is loaded using only godotenv with no merging.

Design decision: This was a design decision to keep the routing rules in the .env file. I accept unknown services, as I can have new services logging and then add a new rule. All destination names are checked on startup and will fail if an unknown value is found. This means any typo will cause a crash on startup rather than the service being incorrectly routed.

destination, exists := serviceRouter.rules[enrichedLog.Service]
if !exists {
 slog.Warn("service has no routing rule, using default destination", "service", enrichedLog.Service, "default_destination", string(serviceRouter.defaultDestination))
 enrichedLog.Destination = serviceRouter.defaultDestination
}

A validated map of ROUTING_RULES has been created to route to either of the 3 destinations based on the service. The default destination has been set in the config and will show a warning if there is no rule to match.

4.6 Queuing with RabbitMQ

3 direct exchanges (exchange_service1..3) are bound to durable queues with a routing key log.write. Messages are published using amqp.Persistent, with a 5-second timeout (PUBLISH_TIMEOUT) and confirm mode. The publish will only return nil once the broker has acknowledged. The publisher will retry with backoff.

Design decision: Each destination uses an individual exchange and queue so that messages do not queue up in one queue, starving the others. We always get confirms and cannot allow fire-and-forget.

if publishError := publisher.publishOperation(enrichedLog); publishError != nil {
 publisher.markDisconnected()
 slog.Warn("publishing to rabbitmq failed, using in-memory fallback", "error", publishError, "destination", enrichedLog.Destination, "batch_id", enrichedLog.BatchID)
 return publisher.publishToFallbackAndRecord(enrichedLog)
}

publisher.recordPublishedMessage()
return nil

The broker is a persistent buffer, so it can handle bursts of activity and restarts. If it goes offline, messages will be sent to an in-memory store with a maximum size. These messages will be written to the store and will never be republished. The publisher will retry with backoff.

Timeouts on confirms do not necessarily mean the broker has failed. In ambiguous situations, the publisher will fall back to using the in-memory store. This means that a message that has been accepted by the broker may be stored twice. However, storage is idempotent based on the log_id, so duplicate entries will be merged into a single row.

4.7 Storage, retries and dead letters

A single batch writer for SQLite. Consumes:

  • AMQP consumers

  • Fallback consumer

  • cmd/replay

Flush per destination at 100 logs WRITE_BATCH_SIZE or every 1 second WRITE_FLUSH_INTERVAL, one transaction per destination. Failed flush retries: retry one after 1s, retry two after 5s, retry three after 10s. Four attempts over ~16s. If all fail, the whole batch is handed to a dead letter file as NDJSON, rotated by size.

The dead letter file is appended to in NDJSON format. It will be rotated by closing and renaming the file. Each entry is written with a new line and flushed. If a crash occurs while writing, the last line may be truncated. cmd/replay reads line by line and stops with an error on the first unparsable line, so a truncated tail causes replay to fail.

As the same destination databases are opened by cmd/replay, it is safe to run during the service. SQLite will serialise writes to the database per transaction. Both processes will use WAL and a busy timeout. This means the replay process will wait for/obtain a write lock, and the file will never be corrupted.

Design decision: Two triggers have been used to flush the data. This provides a good balance between latency and efficiency. Persistence is idempotent, as each log_id will be persisted using ON CONFLICT (log_id) DO NOTHING on the unique index. Duplicate rows will not occur, as messages will not be duplicated when redelivered, and dead letters will not be duplicated when replayed. The dead letter file can safely be replayed twice.

deadLetterError := batchWriter.deadLetterBatch(enrichedLogs, storeError)

The writer will flush each destination once every 100 logs or 1s. If an error occurs, it will retry with a backoff. The retry_count will be stamped, and the message will be dead-lettered. Recovery can be done using cmd/replay, which will use the same idempotent StoreBatch.

The dead letter store contains NDJSON format for each batch. It contains the full enriched log, storage exception, and time of failure.

4.8 Observation

The in-memory registry contains the following metrics:

  • Receipts

  • Request counts per level/service

  • Rate-limited requests

  • Dead letters

  • Write errors

  • 1-minute moving average of throughput

Design decision: Metrics are collected by the pipeline. The limiter collects the number of times it rejected a request. The writer collects dead letters and write errors. The queue backlog can come from either the RabbitMQ management API or estimated from publish minus store if the API isn't available.

A single registry containing metrics from each stage. Backlog will be collected from local estimate if the management API isn't available. The metrics can be viewed as a JSON snapshot or via server-sent events.

5. Designing for failure

The table maps scenarios to outcomes.

Scenario The client sees Where the log ends up Section and path
RabbitMQ unreachable 202 still, if memory capacity lasts Stored directly by the fallback consumer, never re-published 4.6
RabbitMQ down and fallback full 202 still Dead-letter NDJSON entry with the reason 4.6, publish error path to the sink
SQLite write failure Nothing, by design Retried at 1, 5, then 10 seconds, then the whole batch dead-lettered 4.7
Queue overloaded past the send timeout 503 Durably spooled, not yet enqueued; will be replayed on restart, client may retry and create duplicates handled by idempotency 4.3
Body or batch oversized 413 Not ingested, visibly rejected 4.1
Wrong content type 415 Not ingested, visibly rejected 4.1
Per-IP limit exceeded 429 + Retry-After in whole seconds Not ingested, visibly rejected, token kept 4.2
Ungraceful crash Transport error In-memory buffer and writer batches lost; spooled batches survive on disk and are replayed on restart. What that costs is section 7 7

Two failure mechanisms.

  • Closed/shutting down writer: Consumer nack's messages immediately, and the broker will redeliver shortly. This only happens if the writer is shutting down.

  • SQLite flush failure: Message will be scheduled up to 16s before dead-lettering. This is spread out to reduce retries.

6. Proof

I have 172 individual tests across 15 packages that are CI'd with the race detector. Timings are simulated using clock injection as I am testing out how the retry system deals with exhaustion in milliseconds.

Integration tests under cmd/server/integration_test.go use real components. This includes end-to-end functionality, zero dead letters during an outage, flush functionality triggered both ways, and retry to dead letter when the store fails.

I also have a load that simulates a constant request rate with cmd/loadtest. It uses fifty IPs in the documentation range as sources, and will output statistics on how many requests have gone through per status and latency percentiles.

I ran this with 12 pipeline workers, batch size 100, and 8 senders. This gave me 300 requests, each with 100 entries. This gave me 30,000 logs accepted in total. I ran this on my laptop with RabbitMQ and SQLite, with spool fsync enabled.

Sustained target run Result
Sustained ingestion 1000.0 logs/s, zero rejections
Response latency mean 2.9 ms, p50 2.2 ms, p95 7.1 ms, p99 14.1 ms
End-to-end accounting 300 requests accepted, all 30,000 accepted logs stored when the queue drained 47 seconds later, no dead letters
Server footprint ~26 MB RSS, ~9 percent CPU

This proves:

  • Sustained acceptance rate of 1,000 logs/s on one laptop with local broker and SQLite, confirmed by row-count reconciliation.

  • End-to-end with 30 seconds of sending time and 47 seconds of draining. Ingestion accepted at 1,000 logs/s while storage lagged; the backlog sat in the RabbitMQ queues. 30,000 logs in 77 seconds, about 390 logs/s including tail. This end-to-end rate reflects the publisher confirm loop, not consumers or SQLite. The test was mapped to a single service, so a single SQLite writer did the work; spreading across destinations does not change the per‑log confirm latency.

Does not prove:

  • Rate limiter saturation.

  • Multiple instances.

NOTE: When using 12 workers, you can get a throughput of 1,000 logs per second, but if you use the default of 4, you won't. You should aim for around 100 logs per second per worker. The confirmation loop is the limiting factor.

7. Trade-offs and what I would change

  • Log scale makes columnar storage ideal. Failure logic is contained within the code in SQLite. Batch writer means I can batch inserts. I would use ClickHouse in production. Two triggers mean the contract remains intact.

  • I guarantee at-least-once delivery by having an idempotent storage per log_id. If a crash occurs between inserting a record and sending the ack message, then the records will be delivered again. The command and replay functionality means the dead letters are applied again. The log_id is set during ingestion, and using ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING ensures only one row will exist for both.

  • Dead letters are applied at the batch level. After 16s of failed flushes, up to 99 logs that have done nothing wrong will be moved to a dead letter file. These are stored and can be restored. They are also grouped into batches.

  • In-memory state will be lost if there is an ungraceful crash. The writer has a buffer of less than 1s per destination, and the fallback will be lost. The broker will have the confirmed but unacknowledged messages. Spooled batches survive on disk and are replayed on restart, so admission is durable even if the process crashes; the cost is potential duplicates on retry.

  • The spool adds fsync latency on the request path and requires compaction of the spool log and .acked files on restart. This is a deliberate trade-off for durable admission.

  • Having a single point of state makes scaling out difficult. I have a limiter, counters, and backlog estimation, which are held in memory. The second replica will have its own buckets; these will be reset when the service is restarted. Having a shared rate limiting store such as Redis and storing/persisting metrics allows scaling out.

  • No search endpoint. Initially, this wasn't searchable. Everything is stored centrally and monitored. Logs can be viewed through SQLite and dead letter tools. Next step is to implement full-text search on the logs table in SQLite.

  • No alerts. Counters are in place to trigger, but paging on a threshold with cooldown and dedupe is a monitoring-stack integration.

What I would improve:

  • Search endpoint

  • State for scaling out

  • Alerts

Performance tip: The max we can publish per log is the publish-confirmed rate. If I were to publish the entire batch per confirmation, then this would increase the max per worker.

8. Lessons

  • Defence of the ingest boundary. Inexpensive inline decisions, and things to bound and make visible. All components have capacity and timeout so we can never block or drop.

  • Batching in async pipelines. We can be honest about our options. Either take the whole batch, or fail the whole request. The producer lock ensures we can do this under concurrency. When shutting down, we drain the channel, flush the writer, close the store, and lastly stop the dead letter writer.

  • Designing for queue/store failures. Each failure point has a different decision to make. If the broker fails, we use a one-time fallback store. If SQLite fails, we will retry with a limit, using stamps and dead-lettering out. If we fully fallback, we get dead letters. We can chain these decisions. It makes it easier to have a stage that can't fail.

  • Registry for event-to-action. The least appealing but most useful decision. We can pull from our registry. During integration testing, the broker failed, but the metrics endpoint still responded, as the fallback estimate was in the same registry. We can instrument what we are already doing. The signals will fail at the same time as the pipeline, meaning they are exactly when we need them.

Review Questions

# Question One-line answer
1 Which fields are required, and which status codes can POST /logs return? timestamp (RFC 3339), service (100 characters), level (four values), message (10,000 characters); 202, 400, 413, 415, 503, plus 429 from the limiter.
2 How does the rate limiter work, and what happens when the limit is exceeded? A per-IP token bucket in middleware before the handler; 429 with Retry-After in whole seconds, and the rejected request keeps its token.
3 Why an in-memory channel instead of writing straight to SQLite? The channel keeps the slow path out of the request and turns queue pressure into 503 backpressure with a timed, all-or-nothing send.
4 Which enrichment fields are added, and where does each value come from? received_at from the handler's clock, source_ip from the socket address or a trusted proxy's X-Forwarded-For, environment from configuration, all captured at the edge.
5 How are routing rules structured, and how is a database chosen? ROUTING_RULES from .env maps service to one of three destinations, stamped on the log, with the configured default and a warning when no rule matches.
6 Why RabbitMQ, and what changes when it is unavailable? The broker is the disk-backed buffer absorbing bursts; down means the bounded in-memory fallback stores directly, never re-publishes, and the publisher reconnects with backoff.
7 How does batch writing work, and what is the retry strategy? One writer flushes per destination at 100 logs or one second inside a transaction, retries once per backoff delay stamping retry_count, then dead-letters the batch.
8 What reaches the dead-letter file, and how is it recovered? Batch-level entries as NDJSON with the log, the error and the timestamp, rotated by size, restored by cmd/replay through the same idempotent StoreBatch.
9 Which metrics are tracked, and what does GET /metrics.json return? Receipt, level and service counts, error rate, throughput, queue backlog, rate-limited requests, dead letters and write failures, as one atomic JSON snapshot.
10 Which alert conditions exist, and how is alert spam prevented? None are built: the counters are ready to trigger against, and alerting with its cooldown design is a monitoring-stack integration named in section 7.
