title: Inside the Vercel intern experience
description:
The best way to learn is by shipping product to users in production, and that's why we don’t treat our interns as temporary guests. Every intern at Vercel is expected to operate like a core part of our engineering team from day one.

This past winter, we welcomed a small cohort of those interns to our headquarters in San Francisco. Over an intense four months, they contributed to some of our most important products: the CDN, v0, financial infrastructure, AI Gateway, and more. They shipped features used by millions, helped close the gap for enterprise deals, and in more than a few cases, left a mark that will outlast their time here.

Meet the Winter '26 intern cohort

Yash Kothari, CDN Team

University of Waterloo

What Yash shipped:

Yash's internship spanned the full CDN stack, from infrastructure to CLI to UI in the dashboard.

His first major project was Project-level routing, which is part of the new CDN tab in the Vercel dashboard. This feature lets customers update routing rules, including redirects, rewrites, and header transforms, from the dashboard, API, CLI, or SDK, without needing to redeploy their project or touch a single line of code. Yash built the underlying API endpoints (including a staging/publish workflow), the vercel routes CLI commands, and contributed AI-powered route generation. Right after launch, hundreds of teams immediately adopted it and created thousands of rules.

"One of my favorite things about my internship was that at Vercel you get a lot of autonomy and ownership," Yash said. "I hopped on calls with enterprise customers, saw my work featured on Vercel's changelog, and demoed my work in a live YouTube community session."

In the second half of his internship, Yash worked on Vercel's Firewall and Security products. He shipped the vercel firewall CLI command, enabling users and AI agents to configure custom rules, IP blocks, and firewall controls directly from the terminal. He also built an AI-powered Firewall Rule Builder that lets users describe a desired rule in natural language and generates a WAF custom rule automatically.

Kavin Valli, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kavin shipped:

Kavin worked across the full v0 platform over four months, taking on projects that ranged from user-facing features to cost efficiency for the system’s backend infrastructure.

He started by building Folders and v0 Projects end-to-end: core CRUD operations, a library page redesign, favoriting, visibility controls (private/team/public), and folder sharing. He also closed a critical gap in v0's version history by shipping the manual commit button, which ensured that manual edits in the VM editor properly created commits and blocks, which closed the loop between manual edits and v0's iteration model.

His highest-leverage work came later in the term, when he focused on VM and sandbox infrastructure. By splitting VMs into tiered pools and routing smaller projects to a cost-efficient default pool, Kavin significantly reduced memory usage and infrastructure cost for roughly 80% of sandboxes.

"I worked on v0 and got thrown into the deep end pretty quickly, especially around the v1 launch," remembered Kavin. "It was a bit chaotic at times, but that's something I actually enjoyed."

His final and most involved project was taking ownership of the v0 Slack agent. He shipped Slack preview deployments for safe testing, rebuilt the router agent with improved thread history and SAML re-auth resume, redesigned project context tracking, and built out the full PR flow including v0 labels, Slack thread links, and merged/closed state tracking. The result was an agent that went from rough around the edges to something teams can genuinely rely on.

Mingchung Xia, Financial Infrastructure Team

University of Waterloo

What Mingchung shipped:

Mingchung pushed over 250 PRs in four months and became one of the top contributors on Vercel's central control systems monorepo.

His most externally visible project was the v1/billing/charges API endpoint and the vercel usage CLI command, which let users view their usage and costs in the standardized FOCUS v1.3 FinOps format. Originally scoped as a full-internship project, Mingchung completed it early and expanded its scope into a joint launch with Vantage. The work was subsequently adopted by Meta, Notion, Porsche, and other prominent companies to analyze their Vercel spend in a modern, compliant format.

His most technically complex project was designing and building Vercel's core entitlements system, which is the infrastructure that enables granting, revoking, and provisioning entitlements across project-based monetization, add-ons, enterprise, and marketplace work streams. The system architecture incorporated strong and eventual consistency guarantees, async and synchronous derivations, transactional outboxing, write-ahead logs, plan change manifests, stale-validation sentinels, and materializations. It was rolled out to production and backfilled across all active subscriptions.

"Most companies don't give interns or even existing engineers the opportunity to touch payment systems or billing infrastructure, let alone own it end to end," explained Mingchung. "Correctness is imperative when you're working with money, and I got to experience that firsthand at Vercel."

He finished his internship by shipping Vercel Buy, a new billing service supporting frictionless purchasing for agent credits, gateway credits, v0 credits, and pro subscriptions, complete with a CLI surface.

Mingchung will be joining Vercel full-time on the Financial Infrastructure team after completing his degree.

Kevin Thomas, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kevin shipped:

Kevin's work spanned ML infrastructure, enterprise features, reliability engineering, and incident response, often simultaneously.

His most ambitious self-directed project was v0's auto model routing system: a full pipeline that automatically routes user prompts to the right model tier based on complexity. Kevin proposed the system, built the labeling pipeline, experimented with multiple classifier architectures (embedding-based MLP classifiers, TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned TinyBERT), and integrated everything into TypeScript-only functions for production deployment. By launch, the system had processed over 1.4 million v0 messages and became the default for all non-enterprise users, reducing decision fatigue and latency for a very large share of v0's user base.

"From working on on-call incidents and vulnerabilities in month one to working directly with enterprise customers in April, I've gotten to work on an unusually wide range of meaningful problems," Kevin said at the end of his internship.

In the latter half of his internship, Kevin focused on enterprise work, most notably the v0 × Snowflake integration. He built enterprise admin controls for model access, RBAC for team skill management, resolved issues in SAML and isolated tenant environments, and shipped the integration itself. This work directly unblocked enterprise customers, supported renewals, and addressed live customer issues.

Kevin also served as a primary investigator for several incidents around signup, billing, auth, and account access, staying at the center of v0's reliability work throughout his term.

Sylvie Zhang, AI Gateway Team

University of Pennsylvania

What Sylvie shipped:

Sylvie worked across the AI Gateway service, contributing to everything from database and backend logic to observability, the frontend, and documentation.

Her first project was Price Strikethrough, surfacing provider MSRP as a strikethrough price alongside Gateway pricing, making provider discounts visible to end users. It touched the full stack and gave her a complete view of the AI Gateway product from the start.

"All that sounded daunting to a student like me with little experience," Sylvie said, "but it was the best learning experience I could have asked for."

Her most impactful and technically demanding project was the AI SDK v5 → v6 endpoint migration for AI Gateway's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. As the AI provider landscape had grown significantly more complex since v5 was designed, maintaining the legacy version had become a bottleneck, especially for handling token usage granularity differences across providers. Sylvie led the migration with a disciplined approach: deep cross-provider knowledge to catch incorrect AI-generated assumptions, systematic multi-turn and cross-provider testing scripts, concurrency testing to surface race conditions, proactive customer communication, and a deliberate fallback strategy that left legacy code in place until the migration proved stable.

The result was a cleaner, more maintainable Gateway service better equipped to handle the continued evolution of AI providers and models.

Advice for future interns

We asked these interns to share their top advice for future cohorts.

Take ownership from day one

Vercel gives interns real autonomy, but that means it's on you to use it well. Don't wait to be assigned work. Take initiative, identify what needs to be done, and start shipping.

Ask questions

Every intern said the same thing: no one at Vercel makes you feel like a burden for asking. The team genuinely wants you to succeed, so use that to your advantage and ask.

Work in public

Share your PRs in team channels. Post updates. Present at Demo Days. The feedback loop is fast, and the visibility helps you iterate and build trust faster.

Talk to people outside your team

Some of the best conversations happen across team lines with engineers, designers, finance, and people in roles you've never considered. Go to the office. Grab lunch with someone new.

Give yourself time to ramp up

The codebase, the culture, and the pace can be a lot at once. Don't rush. The first few weeks are for absorbing, not sprinting. Take time to ramp well, and you will be able to run fast.

Apply to become a Vercel intern

There are additional internship opportunities coming soon. If you want to join our next cohort, check our career site in September to apply.

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

title: Full-Stack Go: Domain-Driven Applications with sqlc and templ
description:
Full-Stack Go: DDD + sqlc + templ

A full-stack Go web application for animal sightings: occurrence data from GBIF, persisted in SQLite via sqlc, rendered server-side with templ, and enriched with weather from Open-Meteo.

1. The Modern Go Stack Breakdown

There is a quiet paradigm shift happening in the Go web ecosystem, and this workshop application is its poster child. For years, the "modern" Go stack meant something like: a SPA (React, Vue, or Svelte) in the browser, talking to a Go REST API backed by JSON. It worked, but it came with a familiar tax: a separate TypeScript codebase, duplicated types between client and server, runtime JSON parsing, and an entire discipline of OpenAPI/Swagger contract management just to keep the two worlds in sync.

This project asks a simple question: What if we never left Go?

The stack

Layer Tool What it does
Database SQLite (via modernc.org/sqlite) Pure-Go, zero-dependency SQL database
Query layer sqlc Compile-time, type-safe SQL → Go
View layer templ Server-side rendering with type-safe Go components
Routing chi/v5 HTTP routing
Migrations goose/v3 Database schema migrations
CLI urfave/cli/v3 + huh Interactive command-line interface

The paradigm shift: type-safety from DB to HTML

The traditional stack's type system looks like this:

SQL → JSON → TypeScript types → runtime fetch → React props

Every arrow is a place where types lie, and the compiler can't help you. Change a column name in SQL and nothing breaks at compile time. You find out at runtime, in production, from a user complaint.

This stack collapses the chain to:

SQL → sqlc (compile-time Go structs) → domain types → templ (compile-time HTML)

There is no JSON in the middle. There is no TypeScript. The sqlc tool reads your .sql query files and your schema, and generates Go code with the exact types you need. The templ tool reads your .templ files, which are Go functions returning HTML, and generates Go code that the compiler type-checks against your domain types. If your Sighting struct has a field HappenedAt time.Time, then @components.SightingCard(s) in a template must be passed a sighting.Sighting with that field, or the program won't compile.

This is the key insight: the boundary that used to be a runtime concern (JSON serialization, API contracts) has been pushed back to compile time, where it belongs.

Why this beats the SPA + REST API pattern

  • No API contract drift. There is no API. The handler calls a Go service, which returns a Go struct, which is passed to a Go template function. The compiler is the contract.
  • No build step for the frontend. templ generate produces Go files. go build produces a single binary. There is no webpack, no npm install, no node_modules. The "frontend" is compiled into the same binary as the backend.
  • The database is the only source of truth. Your .sql query files, your migrations/*.sql, and your sqlc.yaml config are the spec. Run make sqlc and the generated code reflects them exactly. Run make templ and your templates reflect your .templ files.
  • Hot reload without a frontend build pipeline. make web-hot runs templier, which watches your source files, recompiles the Go app on any change, and proxies to the browser with a live-reload script injected. Edit sighting_card.templ, save, and the browser refreshes. No npm, no HMR server, no bundler.

2. Architectural Tour: Domain-Driven Layout

The project's layout is a deliberate, opinionated implementation of Domain-Driven Design (DDD) in Go. The README for each internal/ subpackage states its role explicitly. Here is the full tree:

workshop/
├── main.go                    # 9 lines: hands off to internal/cmd
├── migrations/                # goose migrations (0001_init.sql, 0002_weather.sql)
├── queries/                   # sqlc query files, one per table
├── sqlc.yaml                  # sqlc configuration
├── templier.yml               # templier (hot reload) configuration
├── Makefile                   # dev workflows: web, web-hot, templ, sqlc, test, load, etc.
├── internal/
│   ├── cmd/                   # CLI commands and interactive menu (urfave/cli + huh)
│   │   ├── cmd.go             # Root command, bootstrap, interactive menu loop
│   │   ├── app.go             # Wiring: services, stores, clients
│   │   ├── web.go             # `workshop web` command
│   │   ├── sightings.go       # `workshop sightings` (find, list, ingest)
│   │   ├── species.go         # `workshop species`
│   │   ├── animals.go         # `workshop animals`
│   │   ├── stats.go           # `workshop stats`
│   │   ├── db.go              # `workshop db` (migrate, seed, reset, ping)
│   │   ├── migrate.go         # migration status/version/up/down + checkMigrations
│   │   ├── flags.go           # shared CLI flags
│   │   └── internal/
│   │       ├── prompt/        # interactive forms (huh wrappers)
│   │       ├── lookup/        # UUID prefix lookup
│   │       └── view/          # CLI rendering (tables, cards, hints)
│   ├── domain/                # THE RULES: what's true if you delete the DB and API
│   │   ├── sighting/          # Sighting entity, Store interface, Service, ingest, validate
│   │   │   ├── sighting.go    # Store interface, Service, observers() formatting
│   │   │   ├── model.go       # Sighting, Location, Coordinates, CreateParams, Media
│   │   │   ├── ingest.go      # GBIF → sighting pipeline (Ingest, speciesPerSighting, etc.)
│   │   │   ├── filter.go      # ListFilter, TaxonKeys()
│   │   │   ├── validate.go    # CreateParams.Validate(): invariants
│   │   │   ├── summary.go     # sighting summaries
│   │   │   ├── country/       # country.Code type with parsing
│   │   │   └── stores/
│   │   │       └── sightingsqlite/  # sqlc-backed implementation of sighting.Store
│   │   │           ├── store.go     # Find, FindByGbifKey, List, Create
│   │   │           └── transform.go # db.SightingListRow → sighting.Sighting
│   │   ├── species/           # Species entity, Store, Service, Animal catalog
│   │   │   ├── species.go     # Store interface, Service
│   │   │   ├── model.go       # Species struct
│   │   │   ├── animal.go      # 80+ Animal constants + GBIF taxon keys
│   │   │   └── stores/
│   │   │       └── speciessqlite/
│   │   ├── weather/           # Weather entity, Store, Service
│   │   │   ├── weather.go     # Store interface, Service, errors
│   │   │   ├── model.go       # Weather, Temperature, Precipitation, Wind, Condition
│   │   │   ├── validate.go
│   │   │   └── stores/
│   │   │       └── weathersqlite/
│   │   └── README.md          # "The rules. Everything that would still be true if we deleted the database and the API."
│   ├── clients/               # OUTBOUND ADAPTERS: gbif, openmeteo
│   │   ├── gbif/
│   │   │   ├── client.go      # Client struct, BaseURL, New()
│   │   │   ├── occurrences.go # Occurrence type (300+ fields!), Occurrences() search
│   │   │   ├── species.go     # GBIF Species lookup
│   │   │   ├── media.go
│   │   │   ├── pagination.go
│   │   │   ├── common.go
│   │   │   └── testdata/      # JSON fixtures for offline tests
│   │   ├── openmeteo/
│   │   │   ├── client.go      # Client struct, BaseURL
│   │   │   ├── reading.go     # Reading, Request, query builder
│   │   │   ├── codes.go       # WeatherCode enum
│   │   │   └── testdata/
│   │   └── README.md          # "Anything that talks to somebody else."
│   ├── infra/                 # PLUMBING: config, sqlite, sqlc output
│   │   ├── config/config.go   # Config from env (caarlos0/env)
│   │   ├── db/sqlite/         # SQLite connection, error mapping
│   │   ├── db/sqlc/           # AUTOGENERATED sqlc output (db package)
│   │   │   ├── models.go      # Sighting, Species, Weather (sqlc-generated structs)
│   │   │   ├── sightings.sql.go
│   │   │   ├── species.sql.go
│   │   │   ├── weather.sql.go
│   │   │   ├── querier.go     # Querier interface
│   │   │   └── db.go          # New() constructor
│   │   └── README.md          # "The plumbing of the app... decisions don't."
│   └── common/                # GENERIC HELPERS (httputil, logs, server, printer)
│       ├── httputil/          # JSON HTTP client (works in any project)
│       ├── logs/              # request logger, slog setup
│       ├── server/            # HTTP server with graceful shutdown
│       ├── printer/           # CLI console output (tables, trees, styles)
│       └── README.md          # "Generic helpers that happen to be ours."
└── web/                       # VIEW LAYER: routing, handlers, templates, assets
    ├── web.go                 # New(): ServeMux, static assets, route registration
    ├── handlers/
    │   ├── home.go            # Home() handler: calls service, renders template
    │   └── error.go           # renderError(): error page rendering
    └── views/
        ├── layout/layout.templ # Base layout (HTML shell, slots)
        ├── pages/
        │   ├── home.templ      # Homepage: iterates sightings, calls SightingCard
        │   └── error.templ     # Error page
        └── components/
            ├── sighting_card.templ  # Individual sighting card
            └── gallery.templ        # Media gallery (StillImage vs link)

The DDD principles in action

1. Domain owns the rules. internal/domain/sighting/validate.go contains the invariants that every sighting must follow: species ID required, happened-at required, happened-at not in the future, coordinates in range, individual count non-negative. These rules exist regardless of the database or the API. If you deleted SQLite and GBIF, the rules would still be true. That is the DDD definition of a domain rule, and it lives in domain/, not in infra/ or clients/.

2. Ports and adapters (Hexagonal architecture). The domain declares interfaces (ports), and the infrastructure provides implementations (adapters):

// internal/domain/sighting/sighting.go:19
type Store interface {
    Find(ctx context.Context, id uuid.UUID) (Sighting, error)
    FindByGbifKey(ctx context.Context, gbifKey int) (Sighting, error)
    List(ctx context.Context, filter ListFilter) ([]Sighting, error)
    Create(ctx context.Context, id uuid.UUID, in CreateParams) (Sighting, error)
}

// internal/domain/sighting/stores/sightingsqlite/store.go:21
var _ sighting.Store = (*Store)(nil) // Compile-time interface check

The var _ sighting.Store = (*Store)(nil) line is the hexagon. The compiler verifies that sightingsqlite.Store satisfies sighting.Store. If you change the interface, the adapter breaks at compile time. If you swap SQLite for Postgres, you write a new adapter and the domain never changes.

3. Dependencies point inward. sightingsqlite imports sighting. sighting has never heard of sightingsqlite. Only internal/cmd/app.go (the wiring) names both. This is enforced by Go's package system: you literally cannot create a circular import.

4. External adapters are isolated. internal/clients/gbif/occurrences.go contains a 350-field Occurrence struct that mirrors GBIF's JSON wire format. The domain's Sighting struct is a different, smaller, Go-idiomatic shape. They meet in exactly one place: sighting.go:saveSighting(). If GBIF renames decimalLatitude, the blast radius is one file in clients/gbif/. The domain, the templates, the CLI: none of them know or care.

5. The handler is dependency-injected. web/handlers/home.go:15 doesn't take a *sighting.Service. It takes a SightingsLister:

type SightingsLister interface {
    List(ctx context.Context, filter sighting.ListFilter) ([]sighting.Sighting, error)
}

This is the single method the handler needs. main.go is the only file that knows *sighting.Service satisfies it. This means the handler can be unit-tested with a fake that implements one method, without a database, without GBIF, without weather.

3. Deep Dive: The Core Mechanics

3.1 sqlc: type-safe queries from .sql files

The queries live in queries/sightings.sql, queries/species.sql, and queries/weather.sql: plain SQL files annotated with sqlc directives. Here is the full sightings.sql:

-- name: SightingFind :one
SELECT sqlc.embed(sightings), sqlc.embed(species), sqlc.embed(weather)
FROM sightings
    JOIN species ON species.id = sightings.species_id
    JOIN weather ON weather.id = sightings.weather_id
WHERE sightings.id = ?;

-- name: SightingFindByGbifKey :one
SELECT sqlc.embed(sightings), sqlc.embed(species), sqlc.embed(weather)
FROM sightings
    JOIN species ON species.id = sightings.species_id
    JOIN weather ON weather.id = sightings.weather_id
WHERE sightings.gbif_key = ?;

-- name: SightingList :many
SELECT sqlc.embed(sightings), sqlc.embed(species), sqlc.embed(weather)
FROM sightings
    JOIN species ON species.id = sightings.species_id
    JOIN weather ON weather.id = sightings.weather_id
WHERE (sqlc.narg('from_date') IS NULL OR happened_at >= sqlc.narg('from_date'))
    AND (sqlc.narg('to_date') IS NULL OR happened_at <= sqlc.narg('to_date'))
    AND (sqlc.arg('country_code') = '' OR sightings.country_code = sqlc.arg('country_code'))
    AND (CAST(sqlc.arg('any_species') AS BOOLEAN) OR species.gbif_key IN (SELECT value FROM json_each(sqlc.arg('species_keys'))))
ORDER BY sightings.happened_at DESC, sightings.id DESC
LIMIT sqlc.arg('limit');

-- name: SightingCreate :one
INSERT INTO sightings (...) VALUES (?, ?, ..., ?) RETURNING *;

The sqlc.embed(sightings) directive tells sqlc to flatten the sightings table columns into the generated struct. The sqlc.narg('from_date') and sqlc.arg('country_code') directives let you build optional filters: the generated Go function takes an interface{} for nullable params, and the SQL handles the NULL checks.

The generated output (internal/infra/db/sqlc/sightings.sql.go) contains:

  • SightingFind(ctx, id) (SightingFindRow, error) returns a struct with Sighting, Species, and Weather fields, all populated from the JOIN.
  • SightingList(ctx, SightingListParams) ([]SightingListRow, error) is the list query with filter params.
  • SightingCreate(ctx, SightingCreateParams) (Sighting, error) is the INSERT...RETURNING.

The generated SightingListParams struct:

type SightingListParams struct {
    FromDate    interface{} `db:"from_date"`
    ToDate      interface{} `db:"to_date"`
    CountryCode interface{} `db:"country_code"`
    AnySpecies  bool        `db:"any_species"`
    SpeciesKeys interface{} `db:"species_keys"`
    Limit       int64       `db:"limit"`
}

Notice SpeciesKeys interface{}. The store marshals the taxon keys to a JSON array string and passes it as a single argument, which the SQL then parses with json_each(). This is a deliberate choice: sqlc's slice expansion would use numbered placeholders, which SQLite rejects when followed by the LIMIT clause.

3.2 The transform: sqlc rows → domain types

The generated db.SightingListRow is a flat struct with Sighting, Species, and Weather sub-structs. The domain's sighting.Sighting is a richer type with nested value objects (sighting.Location, sighting.Coordinates, species.Species, weather.Weather). The transform.go file bridges them:

// internal/domain/sighting/stores/sightingsqlite/transform.go:14
func transform(row db.SightingListRow) (sighting.Sighting, error) {
    r, sp, w := row.Sighting, row.Species, row.Weather

    var media []sighting.Media
    if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(r.Media), &media); err != nil {
        return sighting.Sighting{}, fmt.Errorf("decode media: %w", err)
    }
    if media == nil {
        media = []sighting.Media{}
    }

    return sighting.Sighting{
        ID:      r.ID,
        GBIFKey: r.GbifKey,
        // ... all 30+ fields mapped ...
        Location: sighting.Location{
            CountryCode: country.Code(r.CountryCode),
            Coordinates: sighting.Coordinates{
                Latitude:  r.Latitude,
                Longitude: r.Longitude,
            },
        },
        Species: species.Species{
            GBIFKey: int(sp.GbifKey),
            // ...
        },
        Weather: weather.Weather{
            Temperature: weather.Temperature{
                Actual:   w.Temperature,
                Apparent: w.ApparentTemperature,
            },
            Condition: weather.Condition{
                Code:        int(w.ConditionCode),
                Description: w.Condition,
            },
        },
        Media: media,
    }, nil
}

This is the only place the sqlc types and the domain types meet. The country.Code(r.CountryCode) conversion is a value-object parse: it ensures the domain's CountryCode field holds a validated country code, not a raw string.

3.3 The ingest pipeline: GBIF → weather → species → sighting

The sighting.Service.Ingest() method (internal/domain/sighting/ingest.go:84) is the heart of the application. It orchestrates a multi-step pipeline:

GBIF Occurrence Search
    ↓
For each occurrence:
    ├─ 1. Check skippers (status must be PRESENT, must have media)
    ├─ 2. Resolve species (find or fetch from GBIF and create)
    ├─ 3. Resolve weather (fetch from Open-Meteo and create)
    ├─ 4. Save sighting (validate, parse coordinates/country, insert)
    └─ 5. Count: created / skipped / duplicates / failed

Step 2: species resolution (speciesPerSighting, line 172). The service first tries s.species.FindByGbifKey(). If the species exists, it returns the ID. If not (ErrNotFound), it fetches the species from GBIF's species endpoint and creates it. This is a classic "find or create" pattern that keeps the database self-populating.

Step 3: weather resolution (weatherPerSighting, line 209). For each sighting, the service calls Open-Meteo's archive API with the occurrence's coordinates and event date. It requests a single hour of data (start_hour = end_hour = the truncated hour), and maps the response into a weather.CreateParams with Temperature, Precipitation, Wind, and Condition value objects.

Step 4: sighting creation (saveSighting, line 253). The service parses coordinates with ParseCoordinates() (which enforces the -90/90 and -180/180 bounds at parse time, the "parse, don't validate" pattern), parses the country code with country.Parse(), maps the GBIF media, and calls s.Create(). The Service.Create() method validates the params and assigns a UUID before handing to the store.

The result is an IngestResult with counts of created, fetched, skipped, duplicates, and failed occurrences, surfaced in the CLI with color-coded output.

3.4 templ: type-safe server-side rendering

The templ files are Go functions that return HTML. They are not strings. They are typed Go code that the templ tool compiles into Go source files that the go build toolchain type-checks.

The layout (web/views/layout/layout.templ):

package layout

type BaseProps struct {
    Title string
}

templ Base(props BaseProps) {
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html lang="en-GB">
        <head>
            <meta charset="utf-8"/>
            <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"/>
            <title>{ props.Title }</title>
            <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/css/app.css"/>
        </head>
        <body>
            <main class="container">
                { children... }
            </main>
            <script src="/assets/js/app.js"></script>
        </body>
    </html>
}

The { children... } expression is a slot: templ's mechanism for parent components to render child content. The Base layout defines the HTML shell, and pages fill the slot.

The homepage (web/views/pages/home.templ):

package pages

import (
    "workshop/internal/domain/sighting"
    "workshop/web/views/components"
    "workshop/web/views/layout"
)

templ Home(sightings []sighting.Sighting) {
    @layout.Base(layout.BaseProps{
        Title: "Sightings",
    }) {
        <h1>Sightings</h1>
        if len(sightings) == 0 {
            <p>No sightings have been ingested yet.</p>
        } else {
            <p>Total: { len(sightings) }</p>
            <ul class="sightings">
                for _, s := range sightings {
                    <li>
                        @components.SightingCard(s)
                    </li>
                }
            </ul>
        }
    }
}

This is the key integration point. The Home function takes []sighting.Sighting, a domain type. It passes each sighting to @components.SightingCard(s). The templ compiler verifies that SightingCard expects a sighting.Sighting and that s is a sighting.Sighting. If you rename a field in the domain struct, every template that references it fails to compile.

The sighting card (web/views/components/sighting_card.templ):

templ SightingCard(s sighting.Sighting) {
    <article class="card">
        <header class="card__header">
            <h2>{ displayName(s.Species) }</h2>
            if s.Species.ScientificName != "" {
                <p class="card__scientific">{ s.Species.ScientificName }</p>
            }
        </header>
        <dl class="card__meta">
            <dt>Seen</dt>
            <dd>{ s.HappenedAt.Format("2 January 2006") }</dd>
            <dt>Where</dt>
            <dd>{ place(s.Location) }</dd>
            if s.IndividualCount != nil {
                <dt>Count</dt>
                <dd>{ individuals(*s.IndividualCount) }</dd>
            }
            if s.RecordedBy != "" {
                <dt>Recorded by</dt>
                <dd>{ s.RecordedBy }</dd>
            }
        </dl>
        <div class="card__gallery">
            @Gallery(s.Media)
        </div>
    </article>
}

func displayName(sp species.Species) string {
    return cmp.Or(sp.VernacularName, sp.CanonicalName, sp.ScientificName, "Unknown species")
}

The card uses Go's cmp.Or for the display-name fallback chain, slices.DeleteFunc for the location join, and fmt.Sprintf for the individual count. These are standard Go functions, not template-specific DSLs. The templ compiler inlines them into the generated HTML output.

The gallery (web/views/components/gallery.templ):

templ Gallery(items []sighting.Media) {
    if len(items) == 0 {
        <p class="gallery__empty">No media recorded.</p>
    } else {
        <ul class="gallery">
            for _, m := range items {
                <li class="gallery__item">
                    if m.Type == "StillImage" {
                        <img src={ m.URL } alt={ altText(m) } loading="lazy"/>
                    } else {
                        <a href={ templ.URL(m.URL) } rel="noopener">{ altText(m) }</a>
                    }
                    if m.Creator != "" {
                        <figcaption class="gallery__credit">{ m.Creator }</figcaption>
                    }
                </li>
            }
        </ul>
    }
}

Note the conditional rendering based on m.Type == "StillImage": images get <img> with lazy loading, other media types get links. The templ.URL(m.URL) call is a URL sanitizer: it marks the value as a safe URL so templ doesn't strip it, while still blocking unsafe schemes such as javascript:.

3.5 The handler: glue between service and template

web/handlers/home.go is the thinnest layer in the application:

func Home(logger *slog.Logger, sightings SightingsLister) http.HandlerFunc {
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        ctx := r.Context()

        items, err := sightings.List(ctx, sighting.ListFilter{
            Limit: 50,
        })
        if err != nil {
            logger.ErrorContext(ctx, "handlers: listing sightings: "+err.Error())
            renderError(ctx, w, logger, http.StatusInternalServerError, "Unable to load sightings.")
            return
        }

        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8")
        if err = pages.Home(items).Render(ctx, w); err != nil {
            logger.ErrorContext(ctx, "handlers: rendering sightings: "+err.Error())
            renderError(ctx, w, logger, http.StatusInternalServerError, "Unable to render page.")
        }
    }
}

The handler:

  1. Calls the service (through the SightingsLister interface).
  2. On error, renders an error page with the appropriate status code.
  3. On success, sets the content type and calls pages.Home(items).Render(ctx, w).

The .Render(ctx, w) call is templ's runtime: it writes the generated HTML to the http.ResponseWriter. The pages.Home(items) call returns a templ.Component, which is an interface. The compiler knows the concrete type and its props.

3.6 The wiring: app.go

internal/cmd/app.go:bootstrap() is where everything comes together:

func bootstrap(ctx context.Context, cfg config.Config, level slog.Level, live bool) (*app, func(), error) {
    conn, err := sqlite.New(ctx, cfg.DatabaseURL)
    // ...

    migrate, err := migrations.New(conn)
    // ...

    queries := db.New(conn)
    speciesStore := speciessqlite.New(queries)
    gbifURL, openMeteoURL := localGBIFBaseURL, localOpenMeteoBaseURL
    if live {
        gbifURL, openMeteoURL = gbif.BaseURL, openmeteo.BaseURL
    }
    openm := openmeteo.New(openMeteoURL)

    speciesSvc := species.NewService(logger, speciesStore)
    weatherSvc := weather.NewService(logger, weathersqlite.New(queries))
    sightingSvc := sighting.NewService(logger,
        sightingsqlite.New(queries),
        speciesSvc,
        weatherSvc,
        gbif.New(gbifURL),
        openm,
    )
    // ...
}

Every service and store is constructed here. The --live flag swaps the mock API URLs for the real GBIF and Open-Meteo URLs. The db.New(conn) call wraps the *sql.DB in sqlc's Queries struct, which is passed to every store. All three stores share the same Queries (and therefore the same *sql.DB connection): this is the single-database pattern.

3.7 The CLI: interactive commands

The CLI is built with urfave/cli/v3 for command structure and charmbracelet/huh for interactive forms. The cmd.go file implements an interactive menu loop:

func interactive(app *app) cli.ActionFunc {
    return func(ctx context.Context, root *cli.Command) error {
        if !prompt.CanInteract() {
            return cli.ShowRootCommandHelp(root)
        }

        for {
            chain, err := prompt.Menu(commands(app))
            // ...
            ran, err := runPicked(ctx, app, chain)
            // ...
        }
    }
}

When you run make run (or just go run .), you get a menu-driven interface: pick sightings → ingest, answer the prompts, and watch the progress. When you run workshop sightings ingest -n 500 -c KE, you get the same command non-interactively. Both paths converge on the same runIngest() function, which calls the same sighting.Service.Ingest() method.

The CLI also has a --live flag that switches from the bundled mock APIs to the real GBIF and Open-Meteo endpoints, and a --verbose flag that enables debug-level logging.

3.8 Hot reload: the developer experience

The Makefile has these key targets:

web:        go run main.go web
web-hot:    go tool templier --config ./templier.yml
templ:      go tool templ generate ./...
sqlc:       go tool sqlc generate && go build ./...
test:       go clean -testcache && go test ./... -coverprofile=coverage.out -covermode=atomic
  • make web builds and serves the site on :8080.
  • make web-hot runs templier, which watches your source files, recompiles the Go app on any change, and serves behind a live-reload proxy on :8080. Edit a .templ file, save, and the browser refreshes.
  • make templ regenerates all _templ.go files from .templ files. Run this after editing templates if you're not using hot reload.
  • make sqlc regenerates all sqlc output from .sql files and queries, then builds to verify.
  • make test runs the full test suite with coverage.

The templier.yml config explicitly excludes *.db files from triggering rebuilds (SQLite writes shouldn't restart the app), and excludes vendor/ (thousands of files that only change with make vendor).

4. The Architecture Ladder

The architectures/ directory contains five progressively more sophisticated layouts of the same application, each with its own README.md explaining the tradeoffs:

# Name Organization DDD? Key Insight
01 Flat One package, files by kind No "Start here. Premature abstraction is worse than no abstraction."
02 Layered handlers/, services/, store/, models/ Partial Layers enforce direction but not ownership.
03 Onion Domain at center, everything points in Yes "The rules. Everything that would still be true if we deleted the database and the API."
04 Hexagonal Domain per noun, adapters per technology Yes var _ sighting.Store = (*Store)(nil): the compiler checks the hexagon.
05 Feature Adapters move to where they belong Yes "A feature is a folder. Everything about a sighting is under domain/sighting, and nothing else is."

The final production layout follows the 05-Feature model: domain/sighting/stores/sightingsqlite/ for persistence, clients/gbif/ for the external API, web/handlers/ for HTTP, and web/views/ for templates. The READMEs are candid about the tradeoffs: more folders for the same behavior, longer paths, and the risk of hiding coupling behind vertical silos.

5. Why This Stack Delivers

Performance. Server-side rendering with Go means no JavaScript bundle to download, no hydration, no API round-trips. The home page handler does one SQL query (with a 3-table JOIN) and renders HTML. Under load testing with hey, the page serves in single-digit milliseconds. The binary is a single static executable with no runtime dependencies.

Developer productivity. Change a column type in a migration? Run make sqlc. Change a template? Run make templ (or just edit and save with make web-hot). Add a new page? One file in web/handlers/ and one line in web/web.go. The compiler, not a linter, not a code review, not a CI job, enforces the boundaries between domain, infrastructure, and view.

Testability. The domain rules (validate.go) can be tested with no database, no network, no HTTP server. The SQL queries can be tested against a real SQLite database via internal/infra/db/dbtest/. The handlers can be tested with a SightingsLister fake. The external clients can be tested with JSON fixtures. There is barely a mock in this codebase, and the README explicitly calls that out as a deliberate choice: "most of what a mock would prove here is that we typed the interface out twice."

Maintainability. The DDD layout means that when GBIF changes its API, the change lands in internal/clients/gbif/. When you swap SQLite for Postgres, the change lands in internal/domain/sighting/stores/. When you add a new page, the change lands in web/handlers/ and web/web.go. The domain (the rules, the types, the invariants) never moves.

This article is based on the workshop repository by Ainsley Clark, presented at GopherCon Africa. The code is available at github.com/ainsleyclark/workshop-sqlc-templ-test.

Social Post Version

What if your frontend wasn't a JavaScript bundle, but Go itself?

At GopherCon Africa, Ainsley Clark's workshop app proved it: type-safety from the database all the way to the HTML. No TypeScript. No REST API contracts. No npm.

Just Go. Compiled. Fast.

The stack

sqlc → templ → chi → SQLite

  • sqlc generates compile-time Go structs from your .sql query files
  • templ renders those structs into type-safe HTML, server-side
  • The whole frontend compiles into the same binary as the backend
  • One go build = working site. No build step. No node_modules.

Architecture: Domain-Driven Design, done right 

internal/domain/     → The rules (sighting, species, weather)
internal/infra/      → SQLite + sqlc output (the adapter)
internal/clients/    → GBIF + Open-Meteo (outbound adapters)
web/                 → Handlers + .templ views + assets

Dependencies point inward. The domain declares the Store interface. The adapter implements it. The compiler checks it:

var _ sighting.Store = (*Store)(nil)

External APIs are walled off behind one package. GBIF renames a field? The blast radius is one file.

The type-safety chain 

-- SQL query (queries/sightings.sql)
SELECT sqlc.embed(sightings), sqlc.embed(species), sqlc.embed(weather)
FROM sightings JOIN species ... JOIN weather ...

// sqlc generates:
type SightingListRow struct {
    Sighting Sighting
    Species  Species
    Weather  Weather
}

// transform maps to domain:
sighting.Sighting{
    Location: sighting.Location{...},
    Species:  species.Species{...},
    Weather:  weather.Weather{...},
}

// passed to templ:
templ Home(sightings []sighting.Sighting) {
    for _, s := range sightings {
        @components.SightingCard(s)
    }
}

Rename a field in the domain struct? Every template that uses it fails to compile. That's the compiler as your contract: not OpenAPI, not a code review.

Hot reload, Go-native

make web-hot runs templier. It watches your .templ files, recompiles the Go app on save, and proxies to the browser with live reload.

Edit sighting_card.templ. Save. Browser refreshes. No HMR server. No bundler. No JS toolchain.

The CLI is a first-class citizen

  • make run → interactive menu (built with huh + urfave/cli/v3)
  • workshop sightings ingest -n 500 -c KE → same pipeline, non-interactive
  • --live flag → swaps mock APIs for real GBIF + Open-Meteo

The ingest pipeline

GBIF occurrence search → resolve species (find-or-create) → resolve weather (Open-Meteo) → validate → save sighting → count created/skipped/duplicates.

Five architectures, one app

The architectures/ folder walks through a ladder: Flat → Layered → Onion → Hexagonal → Feature

Each README is brutally honest about tradeoffs. The production layout (Feature) wins because: "A feature is a folder. Everything about a sighting is under domain/sighting, and nothing else is."

Why this matters

  • Performance: SSR with Go = single-digit ms page renders, no hydration, no JS bundle
  • Productivity: One go build = site. Compiler enforces boundaries. No contract drift.
  • Testability: Domain rules testable without DB, network, or HTTP. SQL tested against real SQLite.
  • Maintainability: GBIF changes → one file. Storage swap → one adapter. New page → one file + one line.

The takeaway

You don't need a frontend framework to build a modern web app. You need type-safety. You need boundaries the compiler can check. You need Go, all the way down.

title: Your AI Agent Is Only as Good as the API It Calls
description:
Your AI agent is only as good as the API it calls.

I wired an agent to a NestJS backend last quarter. It had to create orders, check stock, and issue refunds. The agent failed constantly. Not because the model was dumb. Because the endpoints were built for a frontend, not for a machine: five calls to do one job, huge payloads, vague errors.

That mismatch is easy to miss, because the API works fine when a human drives it through a user interface. A human sees a screen, fills in what is missing, and recovers from a vague error without thinking. An agent cannot do any of that. It reads what you return, decides what to do next from that text alone, and acts on it. Every gap in your API becomes a decision the model has to guess at, and guesses are where bad database writes come from.

The wrong approach

The first wrong approach is to expose your REST endpoints directly as agent tools. A frontend endpoint is designed to serve a screen. It returns everything that screen might need, paginates in a way that suits scrolling, and assumes the caller already knows the flow. Hand that to an agent and it will fetch far more data than it needs, miss the one field that matters, and chain calls in the wrong order, because nothing in the response told it the right order.

The second wrong approach is worse: build one giant do everything endpoint and let the model figure it out. That looks flexible. In practice it gives the agent too much room to improvise, and improvisation is where hallucinations turn into real database writes. A tool that can do anything cannot be tested properly, cannot be logged properly, and cannot be reasoned about when something goes wrong. When a refund is issued by mistake, you want to know exactly which tool did it and exactly what it received. A giant endpoint cannot tell you that.

How I structure it now: a thin tool layer

I keep a thin tool layer on top of the real services.

Each tool does exactly one thing, takes typed inputs, and returns a small predictable shape. The business logic stays in the service. The tool is just a translator between the agent and the service, nothing more.

Note: the snippet below is simplified to show the structure. The Tool and Param decorators come from your agent framework, not from NestJS itself, so adapt them to the framework you use.

// tools/order.tools.ts
import { OrdersService } from "./orders.service";

export interface OrderItem {
  productId: string;
  quantity: number;
}

export class OrderTools {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Tool({ name: "create_order", description: "Create an order for a customer" })
  async createOrder(
    @Param("customerId") customerId: string,
    @Param("items") items: OrderItem[],
  ) {
    const order = await this.orders.create({ customerId, items });
    return {
      orderId: order.id,
      status: order.status,
      total: order.total,
    };
  }

  @Tool({ name: "check_stock", description: "Check stock for one product" })
  async checkStock(@Param("productId") productId: string) {
    const stock = await this.orders.checkStock(productId);
    return { productId, inStock: stock.quantity > 0, quantity: stock.quantity };
  }

  @Tool({ name: "issue_refund", description: "Issue a refund for a paid order" })
  async issueRefund(
    @Param("orderId") orderId: string,
    @Param("reason") reason: string,
  ) {
    const refund = await this.orders.refund(orderId, reason);
    return { orderId, refundId: refund.id, status: refund.status };
  }
}

Three things matter in that code, and none of them is the decorator syntax.

First, the service owns the logic. Creating an order, checking stock, issuing a refund: all the validation, all the rules about what can be refunded and when, all of it lives in OrdersService, exactly where it lived before the agent arrived. The tool adds no rules of its own. If the service changes, the tool still works, because the tool only passes inputs through and shapes the output.

Second, the return shape is small and stable. The agent does not get the full order object with every relation attached. It gets an id, a status, and a total. That is enough for it to continue the conversation and to tell the user what happened. Small outputs also keep the model focused: a huge payload is not just wasteful, it is a distraction that makes the next decision worse.

Third, the agent never touches the service directly. It only sees small honest tools. That boundary is what makes the rest of the system manageable.

Errors must be part of the design

An agent treats an error message as information, so a vague error is worse than no error at all. "Something went wrong" tells the model nothing, so it retries, or tries a different tool, or invents a workaround. A structured error tells it what actually happened and what it can do about it.

Return errors in the same shape every time: a short code the agent can match on, and a plain message a human can read. Keep the codes small in number. A handful of codes like not found, out of stock, already refunded, and invalid input covers almost everything an order flow needs. If the agent sees "already refunded", it stops instead of refunding twice. If it sees "out of stock", it can tell the user honestly instead of placing an order that will fail later.

Never leak internals in an error. Stack traces, database messages, and internal service names are not information for the model, they are noise that it will sometimes repeat to the user. Log those on the server, where they belong, and return only the code and the message.

Log every tool call like any other API call

Every tool call is logged like any other API call: which tool ran, what inputs it received, what it returned, and whether it succeeded. That log is what turns a strange outcome into a debuggable one. When a user says the agent refunded the wrong order, you do not have to guess what the model did. You read the log, you see the tool, the order id, and the reason it was given, and you know exactly where the chain broke.

That log is also your safety net for destructive tools. A tool that only reads data is low risk. A tool that writes data, moves money, or changes state deserves more care. In production I keep write tools behind the same checks any write endpoint would have: authentication, permission checks, and validation in the service. For the most sensitive actions, like issuing a refund, the tool should require an explicit confirmation from the user before it runs, not just a confident model. The model proposes, the human confirms, the tool executes. That one rule removes a whole class of expensive mistakes.

Test the tool, not just the service

A tool layer is easy to test, and that is one of its best arguments. The service already has its own tests. The tool needs tests of its own, for a different question: does this tool accept what the agent will actually send, and does it return the shape the agent expects?

Write a test that calls the tool with realistic inputs, including messy ones: a missing field, an empty items list, a product id that does not exist. Assert the output shape, not just that it did not throw. If the output shape drifts, the agent's next step drifts with it, so the shape is the contract. Testing it is cheap, and it catches the regressions that are hardest to spot by reading code, like a renamed field that silently becomes undefined in the agent's view.

What I would not do

I would not let the model write queries, call a database directly, or reach an endpoint that was built for an admin screen. Every one of those shortcuts removes the layer that keeps the agent honest. The service layer exists for a reason: it enforces the rules, it guards the data, and it keeps one version of the truth. The moment the agent bypasses it, you have two versions of your business logic, and the untested one is the one making writes.

I would also not return full objects "just in case" the agent needs a field later. If it needs that field, add it to the tool output deliberately, with a name that means something. A tool output is an interface, and interfaces grow by decision, not by accident.

The honest summary

Agents do not need a new backend. They need a backend that speaks in small, honest, predictable steps. One tool, one job, typed inputs, a small output, errors the model can act on, and a log for every call. That is not a lot of code. In the project I described, the tool layer was a fraction of the size of the services underneath it, and it was the part that made the agent reliable.

The model gets the credit when an agent works well, but most of the time the difference between a flaky agent and a dependable one is not the model at all. It is the API behind it, and whether that API was built for a machine that reads text and acts on it, or for a screen that a human was always going to interpret.

Do you expose your APIs to agents directly, or do you keep a separate tool layer?

I'm Sohail Khan, a Senior Full Stack Developer building AI agents and automation. Tech Lead at LoopxCorp. I write about backend engineering, AI integration and practical system design.

title: API Mocking in Insomnia vs Powerduck
description:
Short answer: A classic client covers requests and leaves mocking to a separate tool; a studio generates the mock from the same spec as the requests. The first is a request tool; the second keeps the client and the development target in sync by construction.

Why a client needs a mock somewhere

Once the agent or the client needs to develop without a live backend, a mock has to come from another product. That mock is a separate artifact with its own drift.

What a generated mock shares

Property Client + separate mock Studio generated
Mock source Another tool The same spec
Sync Manual On save
Edge cases As built From responses
Drift Common Rare

The failure that shared sources avoid

The client and the mock disagreeing is a silent bug: the request is valid in one place and the mock returns a different shape. A shared spec makes that impossible.

The decision rule

If mocking is a separate concern you are happy to wire, keep it separate. If you want the client and the target to always agree, generate both from one contract.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read the CLI comparison.

title: Marketing Automation: The Content Calendar Feature
description:
Feature Spotlight: Content Calendar

DoAide Pulse is built around the idea that developers should be able to ship code and let the platform handle promotion. The core of that promise is the content calendar – a declarative schedule that tells the system when and where to publish AI‑generated copy. The calendar solves a common problem: keeping a consistent publishing cadence across multiple channels without manual intervention. This is where marketing automation pays off in practice.

The Problem

Indie developers and small teams often produce a new feature, a bug fix, or a documentation update every few weeks. Translating that work into a marketing asset usually requires a separate workflow: writing a blog post, drafting social copy, and posting it to Dev.to, Bluesky, or a newsletter. This process is time‑consuming, error‑prone, and hard to keep in sync with the code repository. The content calendar centralises that workflow, allowing a single source of truth for all scheduled posts.

How It Works

The calendar is a combination of a database model, a FastAPI endpoint, a Celery worker, and a React UI. The system watches a GitHub repository via webhook events; each push triggers an AI model that drafts a blog post and social snippets. Those drafts are persisted in a ScheduledPost table and appear in the calendar UI.

Database Model (SQLAlchemy) 

# models.py
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, Text, DateTime
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base

Base = declarative_base()

class ScheduledPost(Base):
    __tablename__ = "scheduled_posts"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    repo_id = Column(String, index=True)
    title = Column(String, nullable=False)
    content = Column(Text, nullable=False)
    publish_at = Column(DateTime, nullable=False)
    platform = Column(String, nullable=False)  # e.g., "devto", "bluesky"
    status = Column(String, default="queued")  # queued, published, failed

The publish_at field is the heart of the calendar – it defines the exact moment the worker will attempt to publish. Getting marketing automation right early saves rework later.

FastAPI Endpoint 

# api.py
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from datetime import datetime
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

router = APIRouter()

class SchedulePostRequest(BaseModel):
    repo_id: str
    title: str
    content: str
    publish_at: datetime
    platform: str

@router.post("/schedule")
async def schedule_post(
    req: SchedulePostRequest,
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
):
    post = ScheduledPost(**req.dict())
    db.add(post)
    db.commit()
    # Fire a Celery task to enqueue the publish job
    publish_post.delay(post.id)
    return {"id": post.id, "status": post.status}

The endpoint accepts the draft and desired publish time, stores it, and immediately queues a Celery task.

Celery Worker 

# tasks.py
from celery import Celery
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from models import ScheduledPost
from devto_api import publish as devto_publish

celery = Celery("pulse", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0")

@celery.task
def publish_post(post_id: int):
    db: Session = get_session()
    post = db.query(ScheduledPost).get(post_id)
    if not post:
        return

    try:
        if post.platform == "devto":
            devto_publish(post.title, post.content)
        # Additional platform logic can be added here
        post.status = "published"
    except Exception as exc:
        post.status = "failed"
    finally:
        db.commit()

The worker pulls the scheduled post from the queue, calls the platform‑specific API, and updates the status.

Dev.to API Wrapper 

# devto_api.py
import requests

API_URL = "https://dev.to/api/articles"
TOKEN = "<devto-token>"

headers = {"api-key": TOKEN}

def publish(title: str, body: str):
    payload = {
        "article": {
            "title": title,
            "published": True,
            "body_markdown": body,
        }
    }
    r = requests.post(API_URL, json=payload, headers=headers)
    r.raise_for_status()

The wrapper abstracts the HTTP call and ensures a consistent interface for the worker. Good marketing automation keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

React UI (Vite + Tailwind) 

// ContentCalendar.tsx
import { useState } from "react";

export default function ContentCalendar() {
  const [publishAt, setPublishAt] = useState<string>('');

  return (
    <div className="p-4">
      <label className="block mb-2">Publish At</label>
      <input
        type="datetime-local"
        value={publishAt}
        onChange={e => setPublishAt(e.target.value)}
        className="border rounded p-2 w-full"
      />
    </div>
  );
}

The UI allows developers to pick a date‑time and see all queued posts in a grid. The component is lightweight and can be embedded in any dashboard.

What It Looks Like to Use

  1. Push to GitHub – A commit triggers a webhook that runs the LLM pipeline.
  2. Drafts Appear – The AI outputs a markdown article and social snippets, stored as ScheduledPost records.
  3. Schedule – In the dashboard, the developer selects a publish time and platform.
  4. Publish – At the scheduled time, the Celery worker posts to Dev.to via the wrapper.
  5. Audit Trail – The status field shows queued, published, or failed, allowing quick review.

The entire flow is visible from the UI: a calendar view shows upcoming posts, a table lists past publications, and a log pane displays any worker errors. Because the system uses Redis as a broker and PostgreSQL for persistence, scaling is straightforward – add more workers or spin up a read replica without touching the code.

Why It Matters for Developer Marketing

  • Consistency – A single schedule keeps all channels on the same cadence.
  • Automation – No manual copy‑paste; the worker handles the API call.
  • Transparency – The UI shows real‑time status and logs.
  • Extensibility – Adding a new platform is a matter of adding a branch in the Celery task and a new API wrapper.

The content calendar is a concrete example of how DoAide Pulse turns repository activity into a repeatable marketing pipeline, giving indie developers the tools of a full‑blown marketing automation stack without the overhead.

  • Building a Content Calendar in DoAide Pulse

title: Java Erases Your Generics. TypeScript Erases Every Type. What Survives to Runtime
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

If you have written Java for a while, you have hit this wall at least once. You type list instanceof ArrayList<Integer> and the compiler refuses. The Oracle generics tutorial gives the reason in one line: "The runtime does not keep track of type parameters, so it cannot tell the difference between an ArrayList and an ArrayList."

You learned to live with it. You use ArrayList<?>, you pass a Class<T> around, you reach for Jackson's TypeReference when a List<User> has to come out of JSON.

Then you move to TypeScript, write if (value instanceof User) against an interface, and get 'User' only refers to a type, but is being used as a value here (a walkthrough of that error). Same family of problem, much bigger blast radius. Java erases your generics. TypeScript erases every type you write. The useful question is what is still there when the program runs, in each language, and what you do about the gap.

What javac erases, and what it quietly keeps

The Java tutorial on type erasure lists three things the compiler does: it replaces every type parameter with its bound, or Object if it has none; it inserts casts where they are needed for type safety; and it generates bridge methods so polymorphism still works in generic subclasses. The result, in the tutorial's words, is bytecode that "contains only ordinary classes, interfaces, and methods."

Take three lines:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("ada");
String first = names.get(0);

Run javap -c on the compiled class and the call to get goes to the erased List, whose get returns Object. The String you see in your source survives only as the cast the compiler inserted after the call. List<String> and List<Integer> run as the same class.

That is the part every JVM developer knows. The part people forget is how much Java keeps.

First, every object knows its own class. The TypeScript team's own guide for Java and C# programmers puts it plainly: in Java "any given value or object has one exact type", and you can call value.getClass() to ask for it.

Second, declarations keep their generics. The class file format has a Signature attribute that "stores a signature for a class, interface, constructor, method, field, or record component whose declaration in the Java programming language uses type variables or parameterized types." javap -v prints the Signature attribute, and reflection reads them: Field.getGenericType() must return a Type that "accurately reflect[s] the actual type arguments used in the source code."

Neal Gafter, who introduced super type tokens in a 2006 post, summed it up in a reply in that post's comments: "The STATIC types are recorded in the bytecodes, but not the dynamic types." A List<String> object has forgotten its String. A field declared as List<String> has not.


Java forgets the type arguments on values but keeps classes and declared signatures. TypeScript keeps neither.

What tsc erases: everything that is only a type

TypeScript's handbook has a section literally named Erased Types, and it ends on a note: "Type annotations never change the runtime behavior of your program."

Here is a small file with the usual suspects:

interface User { id: string; email: string }
type Users = User[];

function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined {
  return xs[0];
}

class Mailer {
  send(to: User): string {
    return `mail to ${to.email}`;
  }
}

Strip what is TypeScript-only and this is the JavaScript that remains (with a modern target, so the template literal stays as is):

function first(xs) {
  return xs[0];
}

class Mailer {
  send(to) {
    return `mail to ${to.email}`;
  }
}

User is gone. Users is gone. T is gone, with no Object stand-in and no inserted cast. The parameter annotation on send is gone. What survives is what was already JavaScript: the function and the class. The guide for OOP programmers says of an interface that it "is not present in any form at runtime", and that "information about e.g. the instantiation of a generic type parameter is not available at runtime." There is no Signature attribute equivalent. Nothing is recorded on the declaration either.

There is one opt-in way to record something: with emitDecoratorMetadata, tsc records a decorated member's type as a runtime reference, and NestJS dependency injection reads it. It records Array for a User[] and Object for an interface, so the generic and the interface are still gone.

Two TypeScript features do leave runtime code. Enums "are real objects that exist at runtime". The handbook shows enum Enum { A } compiling to an object with both directions mapped:

"use strict";
var Enum;
(function (Enum) {
    Enum[Enum["A"] = 0] = "A";
})(Enum || (Enum = {}));

const enum goes the other way: members are inlined at the use site and the declaration is "completely removed during compilation." Namespaces with values and constructor parameter properties also emit code.

That short list is shrinking in practice. Node.js now runs .ts files by stripping types by default since v22.18.0 and v23.6.0. It "will replace TypeScript syntax with whitespace, and no type checking is performed," and it rejects enums, namespaces with runtime code and parameter properties because those need a transform. TypeScript 5.8 added --erasableSyntaxOnly so the compiler flags the same constructs. TypeScript is drifting toward JavaScript plus annotations a runtime can delete.

Side by side:

At runtime Java TypeScript
Class of an object yes, getClass() only if built with new from a class
Generic args on a declaration yes, Signature attribute no
Generic args on a value no no
Interfaces yes, as class files no
Type aliases n/a no
Enums yes yes, unless const enum

Four Java habits that stop working

Overloading by type. Java lets you write describe(Card c) and describe(Iban i) as two methods and let the compiler pick. The TypeScript handbook on overloads describes something else: several overload signatures followed by a single implementation, whose signature "is not visible from the outside." There is one function body at runtime. If the two cases need different logic, that body has to look at the value and branch. (Java has its own edge here, by the way: you cannot overload print(Set<String>) and print(Set<Integer>), because the tutorial notes they "would all share the same classfile representation.")

instanceof on an interface. In Java, interfaces compile to class files and obj instanceof Payable works. In TypeScript the interface has no runtime value, so the check does not compile. And instanceof on a class only walks the prototype chain. The guide is blunt that typeof and instanceof "are still working on the values as they exist in the type-erased output code." An object from JSON.parse that has every field of Account is still not an instanceof Account.

Reflection on generic parameters. There is no getGenericType() to call. A function like load<T>(key: string): T cannot look at T, so whatever it returns, the T is only the caller's promise; nothing checks it. A super type token has nothing to capture, because the declaration carries no signature.

Deserialization by class. Jackson's model is mapper.readValue(json, User.class), plus new TypeReference<List<Integer>>() { } for the generic cases, which works because of that Signature attribute. In TypeScript, User is usually an interface, so there is no User.class to hand to anything. Even if you make it a class, a nested User[] field has no element type recorded anywhere for a library to read.


Classes and enums make it through compilation. Interfaces, type aliases and generics do not.

What replaces them: put the type information in a value

Every replacement follows one rule. If you need to know something at runtime, it has to exist at runtime as a value. TypeScript then checks that value statically.

Discriminated unions replace overloads and class hierarchies. Give each case a literal field and switch on it. The narrowing chapter defines it: "When every type in a union contains a common property with literal types, TypeScript considers that to be a discriminated union."

type Payment =
  | { kind: "card"; last4: string }
  | { kind: "iban"; iban: string };

function describe(p: Payment): string {
  switch (p.kind) {
    case "card":
      return `card ending ${p.last4}`;
    case "iban":
      return `transfer from ${p.iban}`;
  }
}

The kind string is the runtime tag Java gave you for free with getClass(). You write it yourself, and the compiler narrows p in each branch.

User-defined type guards replace instanceof on interfaces. A function whose return type is a type predicate, parameterName is Type, tells the compiler what a true result proves:

function isUser(v: unknown): v is User {
  if (typeof v !== "object" || v === null) {
    return false;
  }
  const u = v as Record<string, unknown>;
  return typeof u.id === "string"
    && typeof u.email === "string";
}

The catch: the compiler trusts the predicate. If the body checks the wrong fields, nothing warns you. Keep guards short and next to the type they guard.

Runtime schemas replace readValue(json, User.class). This flips the direction. In Java you declare the class and the deserializer reads it. In TypeScript you declare a schema, which is a real runtime value, and derive the static type from it. With Zod, now on major version 4, that looks like this:

import { z } from "zod";

const User = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  email: z.string(),
});
type User = z.infer<typeof User>;

const result = User.safeParse(JSON.parse(body));
if (result.success) {
  console.log(result.data.email);
}

safeParse returns either the data or an error instead of throwing, and z.infer gives you the User type for the rest of the code. You write the declaration once and get both a runtime validator and a compile-time type. That is the closest thing TypeScript has to a reified class, and it works for nested arrays and unions, which is where User.class ran out on the JVM too.

A habit to keep instead

The JVM taught you to trust declared types at the boundary because the runtime would back them up with a ClassCastException. TypeScript will not. At every boundary where data enters (HTTP bodies, queue messages, localStorage, environment variables) the static type is only as true as the check you ran. Inside the boundary, after a schema or a guard has passed, the types are as reliable as Java's.

Inside your code, write types and let them vanish. At the edges, write values that check.

If this was useful

Erasure is one of those differences that looks like trivia until it breaks a habit you have had for ten years. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript is the book I wrote for that move. It walks a JVM developer through what changes on the way over: variance, null safety, sealed classes into unions, coroutines into async/await. It is part of The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

If you come from Java or Kotlin, start with book 3 in place of book 1, then go to The TypeScript Type System when the generics get deep. If you ship TypeScript at work, add TypeScript in Production.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.
