title: AI Is Changing What It Means to Be a Good Frontend Engineer
description:
For a long time, being a good frontend engineer meant being really good at writing code. You needed to understand JavaScript, know your frameworks, write clean components, and be able to solve problems without constantly looking things up.

Those things still matter, but I think AI is forcing us to rethink what actually makes an engineer valuable.

We are entering a time where writing code is becoming the easiest part of building software. And I think that should challenge how we approach our work.

Writing Code Is No Longer the Hardest Part

I remember when being able to build something from scratch was a big deal. You had to understand how everything worked, scrub through Stackover, and spend hours figuring out why something was not behaving the way you expected.

Now, I can describe what I want to build, provide some context, and have AI generate a working implementation in minutes.

That is a pretty big shift.

But just because something works does not mean it was built correctly UNLESS we give it that context.

And that is where I think our value as engineers is starting to shift.

We Need to Become Better at Defining What Good Looks Like

I think one of the biggest opportunities for frontend engineers right now is becoming really good at defining expectations.

Not just telling AI what to build, but explaining how something should be built and what makes the implementation acceptable.

That means having clear specifications, established patterns, testing expectations, accessibility standards, and an understanding of how a feature fits into the rest of the application.

For example, asking AI to build a form is easy.

But does that form handle validation correctly? Does it account for loading and error states? Is it accessible? Does it use the components we already have? Does it follow the same data fetching patterns as the rest of our application?

Those are the things that matter.

And those are the things that can easily be overlooked when we become too focused on how quickly something gets built.

I think we should spend more time defining what good looks like before we ever start writing code.

Staying Close to the Code Still Matters

One thing I do not agree with is the idea that engineers no longer need to understand code because AI can write it for them.

I actually think the opposite.

The more code AI writes, the more important it becomes for us to understand what is happening.

You cannot properly review something you do not understand. You cannot identify a bad architectural decision if you do not understand the architecture. And you cannot confidently approve an implementation just because the application appears to work.

Being close to the code does not mean you have to personally write every line.

It means understanding the system well enough to recognize when something does not belong.

I want to be able to look at an implementation and understand why certain decisions were made, what could potentially break, and whether the solution makes sense for the application we are building.

AI should make us faster, but it should not make us disconnected.

Our Codebase Should Be Able to Explain Itself

This is something I have been thinking about more lately.

What if we approached our codebases with the expectation that any engineer or AI should be able to contribute without compromising the quality of the application?

Not because everyone has the same level of experience, but because the codebase has clear expectations.

Imagine having documented architectural decisions, reusable patterns, feature specifications, and testing standards that make it easy to understand how things should be done.

When someone introduces a new feature, they should not have to guess how state is managed, how components are structured, or how errors should be handled.

Those decisions should already have some level of consistency.

And when AI is introduced into that workflow, those same standards should apply.

I think that is a much better use of our experience than repeatedly correcting the same mistakes in pull requests.

Instead of just reviewing code for what is wrong, we should be building systems that make it harder to get things wrong in the first place.

Of course, no amount of documentation or testing will guarantee a bug free application. But we can absolutely reduce the number of avoidable mistakes.

Specs Might Become More Valuable Than Implementations

I have started thinking about how much time we spend explaining what we want after something has already been built.

We review a pull request and realize the implementation missed an important state. We discover that a component does not follow an existing pattern. Or we find out that the original requirements were never clear enough.

Then we spend more time going back and correcting those things.

What if we moved more of that effort to the beginning?

Before building a feature, we could define how it should behave, what scenarios it needs to support, what existing patterns it should follow, and how we will know it works.

That specification becomes something both an engineer and AI can work from.

And more importantly, something we can validate against.

What I imagine is like unit tests, we have spec files that ensure the AI that is reading the codebase understands what feature/bug was already implemented and can never be altered for that feature/bug to stay in tact becomes where a lot of the codebase value will live. If we can clearly define expected behavior, we can build tests that help protect that behavior regardless of who or what writes the implementation.

The goal should not be to generate more code.

The goal should be to deliver working software that continues to work as the application grows.

Experience Will Be Measured by the Problems We Prevent

Something else I think AI is going to challenge is how we recognize engineering experience.

For years, we have associated seniority with technical knowledge and the ability to solve difficult implementation problems.

And while those things still matter, I think there is another level of value that deserves more attention.

The ability to prevent problems before they happen.

A good engineer can fix a bug.

An experienced engineer should also be thinking about why that bug was possible in the first place and what can be done to prevent it from happening again.

That might mean improving a shared component, adding a test, documenting an architectural decision, or changing how we approach feature development.

Those improvements might not be as exciting as shipping a new feature, but they make every feature that comes after it easier to build and maintain.

To me, that is real engineering value.

And with AI increasing the amount of code we can produce, that kind of thinking becomes even more important.

We Should Be Focused on Value, Not Just Output

I think there is a real danger in measuring the success of AI by how much faster we can write code.

If AI helps us produce twice as much code, but we introduce twice as many bugs or create a codebase that becomes harder to maintain, what did we actually gain?

Writing more code has never automatically meant delivering more value.

The value comes from solving the right problems, making good decisions, and building something that people can depend on.

Sometimes that means writing less code.

Sometimes that means spending more time thinking through a specification.

And sometimes that means deciding not to build something at all.

AI gives us an opportunity to spend less time on repetitive implementation work and more time thinking about the actual problems we are trying to solve.

I think we should take advantage of that.

So What Does Being a Good Frontend Engineer Look Like Now?

I do not think the answer is to stop learning how to code.

I also do not think the answer is to reject AI because we want to protect the way we have always worked.

I think the answer is somewhere in the middle.

We should still understand JavaScript, React, browser behavior, performance, accessibility, and the fundamentals that make good frontend engineering possible.

But we should also become better at communicating requirements, defining standards, reviewing decisions, designing systems, and creating environments where quality is repeatable.

The engineers who understand both sides are going to be extremely valuable.

Because at the end of the day, someone still needs to understand what we are building, why we are building it, and whether it was built well.

AI can help us write the code.

But we still have to own the outcome.

One Final Thought

I keep coming back to this question.

If AI can write the same code I can, what value am I bringing to the engineering process that AI cannot provide on its own?

I do not see that as a threat. I see it as a question worth asking ourselves.

Maybe the next evolution of frontend engineering is not about becoming better at writing code faster.

Maybe it is about becoming better at creating the standards, specifications, and systems that allow good software to be built consistently, regardless of who or what is writing the code.

And maybe that is where we should have been focusing our attention all along.

Happy Coding 👍

title: A JSON state file ended in zeros after an unclean shutdown: quarantine it, then salvage every record you can
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the tool described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote (MIT, Node.js) is a phone remote for Claude Desktop's Code-tab sessions. It keeps its task list in one file, registry.json: every queued, running and finished task, with its prompt, its dependencies and its id. It is the kind of file nobody thinks about until the day JSON.parse throws on it.

That day came after an unclean shutdown. The file had its normal size, but the last stretch of it was NUL bytes. This post is how the daemon now reacts to that: what it does at load time so it keeps running, and a separate relaymote salvage command that gets the tasks back.

What the damage looks like

The writes were already done the textbook way: write a temp file, fsync it, rename it over the real one. That protects against a half-written file from your own process. It does not fully protect you from the machine losing power around the rename, depending on the file system and what had actually reached the disk. The result we saw was a file whose length had been recorded but whose last blocks never arrived, so they read back as zeros.

The useful observation is about where the damage sits. The front of the file is intact. The break is a clean cut somewhere near the end, followed by padding. Almost every record is still there; only the parser gives up, because one bad byte fails the whole document.

Part 1: at load time, quarantine and keep going

The loader must not crash the daemon, and it must not "fix" the file in place. It does three things when parsing fails:

const q = FILE + '.corrupt-' + Date.now();
if (fs.existsSync(FILE)) {
  fs.renameSync(FILE, q);
  process.stderr.write(`registry.json could not be read; moved it to ${q}. Recover its tasks with: relaymote salvage\n`);
}
  1. Rename, never delete. The damaged file is the only copy of those tasks. Moving it aside gives the daemon a clean slate and leaves the evidence untouched.
  2. Say what to do next in the same log line. The person reading it at 2 a.m. should not have to find the docs.
  3. Keep the id counter above the damage. Task ids are t0001, t0002, and so on. If the daemon starts empty with seq = 0, new tasks will reuse ids the salvage will later bring back. So before starting empty, it scans the raw text for every id and the old seq, and starts above the highest: 
let seq = 0;
for (const m of String(raw).matchAll(/"t(\d+)"\s*:|"seq"\s*:\s*(\d+)/g))
  seq = Math.max(seq, Number(m[1] || m[2]) || 0);

A regex over broken JSON is fine here: it only needs to find numbers, not understand structure. And the new floor is saved straight away, not at the next write, so a second crash cannot lose it.

One Windows detail sits in front of all this: a file another process is renaming into place can be briefly locked (EPERM, EBUSY, EACCES). That is not corruption. The loader retries the read a few times with a short back-off before it decides the file is unreadable, so a normal save from another process never gets the registry quarantined.

Part 2: salvage, from cheapest repair to most expensive

salvage(raw) is a pure function (the tests call it directly) that tries three repairs in order and reports which one worked:

1. Trim the padding. Strip trailing NULs and whitespace, then parse. If the cut happened to land after the closing brace, this is all it takes.

2. Close the document after the last complete record. The file is written with JSON.stringify(state, null, 2), so every task object ends with a newline and exactly four spaces before its }. Find the last "\n }," (or failing that "\n }"), cut there, and append the closing braces for tasks and the root:

const cut = s.lastIndexOf('\n    },');
const j = JSON.parse(s.slice(0, cut + '\n    }'.length) + '\n  }\n}');

This leans on your own serializer's indentation, which is a fair thing to lean on: you wrote it, and it is deterministic. Everything before the last complete task comes back; only the task that was being written at the cut is lost. Any fields that came after tasks in the root object are lost too, which is why seq is recomputed from the recovered ids.

3. Scan for individual records. If the damage is in the middle, closing the document will not parse. So find each "tNNNN": {, walk forward counting braces (tracking whether you are inside a string, and escapes inside strings, so a } in a prompt doesn't end the object early), and try JSON.parse on just that slice. A mangled stretch now costs only the records it touched.

If all three fail, it returns null and the command says NOTHING_RECOVERABLE along with the file size and how much of it was padding, which is usually the whole explanation.

Part 3: merge into the live file without clobbering anything

By the time someone runs salvage, the daemon has been running on an empty registry and may have created new tasks. The recovered tasks are merged in, with a few rules:

  • Live tasks keep their ids. A recovered task whose id is taken by a different live task gets the next free id. It is renumbered, never dropped, and the renumbering is printed.
  • Dependencies follow the renumbering. If recovered task t0040 depended on t0039, and t0039 was renumbered, the dependsOn list is rewritten to match.
  • Running it twice is harmless. Each task gets a fingerprint of its creation time and prompt. A recovered task whose fingerprint already exists under any id is counted as "already present", not added again.
  • Each restored task is tagged with the corrupt file it came from, so you can tell restored tasks from new ones later.
  • Dry run by default. Without --apply it only reports: method used, characters, padding, tasks recovered, how many would be added, how many are already present, the renumbering. With --apply it writes the merged registry with the same temp-file, fsync, rename sequence. It never modifies the corrupt file, so you can run it again.

What carries over

  • When a state file fails to parse, move it aside and keep running. Never repair in place, never delete.
  • Keep id counters above anything the damaged file mentions, and persist that floor immediately.
  • Treat a briefly locked file on Windows as "retry", not "corrupt".
  • Order repairs from cheapest to most expensive and report which one worked.
  • Your own serializer's formatting is a legitimate anchor for finding record boundaries.
  • Merges should renumber rather than overwrite, follow references, and be safe to repeat.

Relaymote is MIT-licensed: github.com/ashwarsadh/relaymote. The code is in lib/registry.js and lib/salvage.js. Unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

title: The three meters behind a $65 million observability bill
description:
$65 million is a strange number to hear on an earnings call. It gets stranger when you work out what it buys at list price.

On 4 May 2023, Datadog reported first-quarter billings of $511 million, up 15% year over year, and flagged one exception: a large upfront bill for a single customer in Q1 2022 that did not recur at the same level or timing. A JPMorgan analyst, Mark Murphy, did the subtraction on the call and arrived at roughly $65 million. Datadog's CFO, David Obstler, confirmed the shape without the name: a crypto company, an early optimizer, now billed in smaller chunks.

A week later, Gergely Orosz reported that current and former Coinbase engineers had confirmed to him that the $65 million was Coinbase's Datadog bill for 2021, settled in the first quarter of 2022. Coinbase has never confirmed it publicly. Datadog never named the customer. Everything below rests on that sourcing.

The number is worth taking seriously rather than gawking at, because it is not really a story about one company overspending. It is a story about three meters that compound independently, and what happens when nobody owns any of them.

Three meters, three units, three growth curves

Observability vendors do not sell one meter. At Datadog, the ones that stack are these, at the annual-billing list rates published today:

Meter List price What grows it
Infrastructure, Enterprise $23 per host per month Fleet size
Log ingest $0.10 per GB ingested Verbosity × volume
Standard indexing, 15-day retention $1.70 per million events Event volume × retention
APM $31 per host per month, with infrastructure attached Services × hosts

On-demand rates are higher across the board: $27 per host, $2.55 per million indexed events, $36 per APM host.

The compounding is the point. Hosts grow with the fleet. Ingested gigabytes grow with log verbosity, and retention pressure multiplies whatever you ship. Indexed events grow with cardinality, and custom metrics beyond the per-host allotment — 100 on Pro, 200 on Enterprise — bill by usage, so every new tag value on a custom metric mints billable series. A team that adds hosts, turns up log verbosity, and tags everything has tripled its bill three independent ways before writing a single alert.

What $65 million means in each unit

At $23 per host per month, $65 million is about 235,000 host-years of Enterprise infrastructure monitoring. That is arithmetic on list price, not a claim about what Coinbase bought, but it is the right order of magnitude for a company running a large fleet at the peak of a growth phase.

The small-scale version is more useful. Twenty hosts at $23 comes to $460 a month. A thousand gigabytes of ingest at $0.10 adds $100. That is $560 a month, or $6,720 a year — the default output of a cost calculator I built for exactly this, and a modeled figure rather than anyone's real invoice.

Divide one into the other: $65 million is roughly 9,700 years of that model.

The gap between $6,720 and $65,000,000 is not a pricing scandal. It is what four orders of magnitude of fleet growth, log verbosity, and cardinality look like when no individual decision was ever expensive enough to argue about.

How 2021 produced that number

Coinbase went public in 2021 and had a year most companies never see. Infrastructure cost was not a constraint anyone enforced, because revenue covered everything. AWS, Snowflake, and Datadog all grew. A bill that size is what three meters running at startup speed produce when nobody is assigned to watch them.

Then the market turned. Revenue fell hard through 2022, and the bills that growth had hidden became the agenda. Datadog's CEO described the pattern on the same call: a customer whose business got cut to a third or a quarter gets its contract restructured, because the vendor would rather be part of the solution than part of the problem. The customer stayed, on chunked billing matched to a smaller business.

One thing to be careful about: an anonymous commenter claimed the $65 million covered a multi-year prepayment. Orosz could not verify that and neither can anyone else, so it stays out. What is documented is the single-year bill, the settlement quarter, and the renegotiation.

The build-vs-buy line, stated properly

Coinbase's response was to price the alternative: a dedicated observability team with a mandate to move onto Grafana, Prometheus, and ClickHouse, built for control and ownership first, with cost as the second motive once the market turned. They double-wrote the new stack for months before cutting anything over.

The arithmetic that mattered is a single inequality:

infrastructure cost + platform team cost < vendor bill

Orosz's version: ten senior and staff engineers in the Bay Area cost under $5 million a year, with infrastructure on top in the low double-digit millions. Against $65 million, building is not a close call. Against a well-managed $2 million bill, it is a way to hire a team whose job is maintaining dashboards.

His rule of thumb for where the question becomes real is $2–5 million a year in vendor spend — roughly where a team of four or five engineers plus a manager, at $150–400K fully loaded each, starts to pencil against the invoice.

The breakeven moves with the invoice. Which is why the invoice has to be measured before the decision is made, not after someone sees a headline and asks for a migration plan.

They didn't leave

The part the invoice-watchers usually miss: with the replacement stack validated and the plug ready to pull, Coinbase got terms it could accept and stayed. The customer is still on Datadog.

That is not a contradiction. Deep integrations — custom tracing, per-service instrumentation, dashboards wired into every team's workflow — make migration expensive in a way the license math never captures. That lock-in cut both ways: it gave Coinbase leverage for a steep discount, and it gave Datadog a retained logo.

The lesson is uncomfortable for both sides of the table. Price your exit before you threaten it, or the threat is theater.

Four things to do on Monday

Budget tag cardinality like headcount. Every new tag value on a custom metric mints series, and series beyond the per-host allotment bill by usage. Audit which teams emit the most series per host before approving more hosts.

Tier retention by access pattern. Logs you investigate regularly earn standard indexing with alerting. Everything else belongs in a cheaper tier or an archive with rehydration on demand. Retention is the quietest multiplier on the invoice.

Decide sampling as a cost input. Full-fidelity tracing on every request is a second invoice hiding inside the first. Pick the sampling rate when you design the tracing, not when you are debugging.

Alert on ingest slope, not the total. Gigabytes per day times price per gigabyte, tracked against the monthly commit, turns the bill into a metric the on-call actually owns. A meter nobody watches is a meter without a limit.

And the cheapest one of all: assign the bill to the teams that generate it. Chargeback turns "observability is expensive" into named owners with named levers. Coinbase assigned a whole team to the problem. Most companies only need to assign the invoice.

What this doesn't establish

The identification rests on Orosz's reporting, not on a Coinbase or Datadog statement. Neither company has confirmed the customer. The $65 million covers one year of spend, not a multi-year contract that anyone has verified.

Coinbase's current spend is undisclosed, so there is no way to check how much the renegotiation actually saved, or whether the in-house stack would have been cheaper over five years.

The list prices are Datadog's published rates as of October 2026 and will not match any negotiated contract, including the one in this story. And no vendor published utilisation figures, so the three-meter model here describes the structure of the bill, not its actual composition.

Three clocks ran in this story: the meters compounded through 2021, the invoice came due in Q1 2022, and the renegotiation reset the economics after that. Treating any one of them as "the Datadog incident" misses how metered billing actually fails — slowly, across independent units, and only discovered when growth stops covering it.

Sources

  • The Pragmatic Engineer: Datadog's $65M/year customer mystery solved

  • The New Stack: Datadog's $65M bill and why developers should care

  • Datadog pricing

title: Server-First Rendering: Kapan useMemo dan useCallback Tidak Diperlukan Lagi
description:
Server-First Rendering: Kapan useMemo dan useCallback Tidak Diperlukan Lagi

Informasi Rekayasa Frontend:

  • Tanggal Terbit: 29 Oktober 2026
  • Tonggak Teknologi: Rilis Resmi React Compiler v1.0 & Next.js 16 Architecture
  • Sumber Primer: React Working Group (react.dev) & Vercel Engineering Blog

Ringkasan Eksekutif (BLUF)

Dengan peluncuran stabil React Compiler v1.0 pada Oktober 2025 dan kehadiran Next.js 16 yang sepenuhnya mengadopsi paradigma Server-First Rendering, penulisan manual hook optimasi seperti useMemo, useCallback, dan React.memo resmi memasuki era usang (legacy optimization). Kompiler React kini menganalisis graf aliran data (data flow graph) pada waktu kompilasi (build-time) dan menyuntikkan memoization otomatis yang presisi hingga level ekspresi terkecil. Lebih jauh, Next.js 16 telah resmi menghapus dukungan AMP kuno untuk berfokus 100% pada React Server Components (RSC). Artikel ini menguraikan arsitektur baru, perbandingan performa, serta kasus terbatas di mana kontrol manual masih relevan.

1. Beban Kognitif Optimasi Manual di Era React Klasik

Selama bertahun-tahun, developer React terbebani oleh aturan dependency array yang rumit:

// Paradigma Lama: Rawan bug stale closure & membebani developer
const memoizedCalculation = useMemo(() => {
  return complexAlgorithm(data, filter);
}, [data, filter]);

const handleAction = useCallback(() => {
  trackUserEvent(memoizedCalculation);
}, [memoizedCalculation]);

Kesalahan kecil pada dependency array dapat memicu infinite re-render atau stale state. Selain itu, biaya alokasi memori untuk fungsi closure wrapper sering kali lebih mahal daripada proses re-render itu sendiri.

2. Arsitektur React Compiler: Otomasi Memoization di Build-Time

React Compiler bekerja dengan mengubah kode JSX menjadi representasi Static Single Assignment (SSA). Kompiler secara cerdas mengenali apakah suatu nilai mengalami mutasi atau tetap stabil, lalu membungkusnya dengan mekanisme caching internal c(x) (cache slots).

Konfigurasi Next.js 16 dengan React Compiler

Buka berkas next.config.js:

/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true, // Mengaktifkan optimasi React Compiler otomatis
  experimental: {
    serverActions: {
      bodySizeLimit: '2mb',
    },
  },
};

module.exports = nextConfig;

3. Contoh Kode: Sebelum vs Sesudah React Compiler

Kode yang Ditulis Developer (Bersih & Elegan): 

export function MetricDashboard({ dataset, threshold }: { dataset: number[]; threshold: number }) {
  // Tidak perlu useMemo! Kompiler otomatis menghafal hasil komputasi
  const total = dataset.reduce((acc, curr) => acc + curr, 0);
  const filtered = dataset.filter((num) => num > threshold);

  // Tidak perlu useCallback! Identitas fungsi dipertahankan secara stabil
  const logMetric = () => {
    console.log(`Audited: ${total} with count ${filtered.length}`);
  };

  return (
    <div className="p-6 bg-slate-900 rounded-xl text-white">
      <h2>Ringkasan Metrik: {total}</h2>
      <button onClick={logMetric} className="btn-primary">Kirim Telemetri</button>
      <DataList items={filtered} />
    </div>
  );
}

Hasil Kompilasi Internal (Otomatis):

Kompiler menyuntikkan slot cache biner: jika referensi dataset dan threshold tidak berubah, eksekusi .reduce dan .filter langsung di-skip dan mengambil memori cache dalam hitungan mikrodetik.

4. Kapan useMemo Masih Dibutuhkan?

Meskipun React Compiler mengotomatisasi 95% kebutuhan memoization, ada beberapa kasus khusus di mana intervensi manual tetap valid:

  1. Komputasi Matematika Berat Non-Idempotent: Komputasi yang mengakses objek eksternal di luar jangkauan analisis statis kompiler.
  2. Kustomisasi Instansiasi Objek Pihak Ketiga: Menginisialisasi instance SDK WebSocket atau library WebGL canvas yang mahal saat mounting pertama.

5. Tabel Komparasi: Era React Klasik vs React Compiler 2026

Parameter React Klasik (Manual Memo) Era React Compiler 2026
Penulisan Kode Penuh useMemo & useCallback Kode JavaScript idiomatik murni
Resiko Bug Tinggi (Stale closure / missing deps) Nol (Analisis statis otomatis)
Ukuran Bundle JS Bertambah karena wrapper logic Lebih ramping & terkompresi
Waktu Build Sangat cepat Sedikit lebih lama (+5-10% di CI/CD)
Performa Runtime Tergantung kedisiplinan developer Konsisten di level optimal tertinggi

6. Verifikasi Kesiapan Proyek di Terminal 

# Jalankan health check resmi React Compiler pada codebase Anda
npx react-compiler-healthcheck@latest

# Periksa apakah ada komponen yang melanggar aturan Rules of React
npm run lint

7. Kesimpulan & Layanan Modernisasi Frontend

Evolusi arsitektur web menuju Server-First dan Compiler-Driven menuntut penyegaran standar koding tim engineering. Menyingkirkan boilerplate memoization manual memungkinkan tim Anda berfokus pada logika bisnis dan pengalaman pengguna yang memikat.

Untuk kebutuhan migrasi kode lawas, audit arsitektur React/Next.js, maupun jasa web developer Next.js dan React berstandar modern, hubungi Andika Putra Dev untuk konsultasi teknis tingkat lanjut.

title: Hoppscotch Pricing and Team Limits Explained
description:
Short answer: Hoppscotch is free on the web and self-hosted, with paid tiers adding access controls, SSO, audit logs, and support. Powerduck keeps the desktop and Hub hosting free within plan limits. Compare the gates by what each actually adds, not by the headline price.

What the tiers add

The free web and self-host editions cover the core request tool. The business and enterprise tiers add governance: identity and access management, single sign-on, audit logs, and dedicated support. Those are team and compliance features, not request features.

The side-by-side

Need Hoppscotch Powerduck
Core requests Free Free
Self-host Free CE / paid EE Local desktop
SSO / access controls Enterprise Hub within plan
Docs + mocks + MCP Separate From one spec

What to look at

Governance gates are worth paying for when you need them, and irrelevant when you do not. The larger question is whether the tool covers the full lifecycle or whether the other surfaces require separate products.

The honest takeaway

Start free on either. The decision is less about the entry price and more about whether the contract should drive the whole workflow and whether the artifacts should stay portable.

Return to the Powerduck vs Hoppscotch comparison, or read the API testing guide.

title: Token Economics: Optimising Cost in a Spring AI Agent
description:
Model API costs are invisible until they're not. During development you make a few hundred calls and barely notice the bill. In production with real users, the same agent can cost ten times what you expected — not because something is wrong, but because small inefficiencies multiply at scale.

The good news: most of the cost in a typical AI agent comes from a handful of sources, and most of those sources have straightforward fixes that don't affect output quality at all.

This article covers where token costs actually come from and how to reduce them without making your agent worse.

Where the money goes

Before optimising anything, measure where tokens are actually being spent. Log usage on every request:

ChatResponse chatResponse = chatClient.prompt()
    .user(request.message())
    .call()
    .chatResponse();

Usage usage = chatResponse.getMetadata().getUsage();
log.info("[cost] conversationId={} inputTokens={} outputTokens={} totalTokens={}",
    request.conversationId(),
    usage.getPromptTokens(),
    usage.getGenerationTokens(),
    usage.getTotalTokens());

After a few days of production traffic, query the averages:

SELECT
  AVG(input_tokens)  AS avg_input,
  AVG(output_tokens) AS avg_output,
  AVG(total_tokens)  AS avg_total,
  MAX(total_tokens)  AS max_total
FROM request_usage
WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days';

This tells you where to focus. In most agents the breakdown looks like:

Source Typical share of input tokens
System prompt 15–30%
Tool definitions 10–25%
Conversation history 30–50%
User message 5–15%

Output tokens are usually 10–20% of total. Input tokens are where most of the cost hides.

Trim the system prompt

Every word in your system prompt fires on every single request. A 500-token system prompt on 10,000 daily requests is 5 million tokens just for instructions.

Common bloat to cut:

// Before — verbose, repetitive
"""
You are a helpful AI assistant specialising in travel planning for India.
Your job is to help users plan their trips by providing information about
weather, attractions, and transportation options. You should always be
polite and professional. When users ask about travel, use the available
tools to get real-time information. Always provide accurate information
based on the tool results and never make up information that isn't
provided by the tools.
"""

// After — same behaviour, ~40% fewer tokens
"""
You are a travel planning assistant for India.
Use tools for weather, attractions, and transport.
Only state facts returned by tools.
"""

Test that the shortened prompt produces equivalent output quality using your eval dataset before shipping it. Prompt compression is one of the highest-leverage cost reductions — it compounds across every request.

Bound the conversation history window

Conversation history is the biggest token cost driver for multi-turn agents. Each request includes all prior messages up to the window size.

A conversation that's been going for 20 turns might look like:

Turn 1:  user (15 tokens) + assistant (80 tokens)
Turn 2:  user (20 tokens) + assistant (120 tokens) + 2 tool calls (60 tokens)
...
Turn 20: all of the above replayed = ~2,000 tokens of history
         + new user message (25 tokens)
         + system prompt (80 tokens)
         + tool definitions (200 tokens)
         = ~2,300 tokens input just for context

The window size directly controls this cost. Keep it as small as correctness allows:

new MessageChatMemoryAdvisor(
    redisChatMemory,
    AbstractChatMemoryAdvisor.DEFAULT_CHAT_MEMORY_CONVERSATION_ID,
    10  // last 10 messages instead of 20
)

Test different window sizes against your eval dataset. For most travel-planning agents, a window of 8–12 messages is enough — users rarely reference something from more than 5 turns ago.

Cache tool results

When multiple users ask about weather in Mysore on the same day, your agent calls getWeather("Mysore") hundreds of times and pays for the same tool result on every call. Cache it.

You already added @Cacheable for scaling (article 21). The same caching reduces costs:

@Cacheable(value = "weather", key = "#city")
@Tool(description = "Get the current weather for a city in India.")
public String getWeather(@ToolParam(description = "City name") String city) {
    return weatherApi.fetch(city);
}

The token cost reduction here isn't direct — the tool result is a small part of the input. The real saving is that cached tool results mean shorter tool response messages, which means slightly fewer tokens per request across all users asking about the same city.

More importantly, caching prevents tool API costs, which for some providers (maps, weather, ticketing) can exceed model costs.

Use smaller models for simpler tasks

The most impactful cost lever: not every task needs your most capable model.

A request like "What's the weather in Mysore?" needs basic reasoning and one tool call. A request like "Plan a 7-day budget trip across Karnataka with weather, attractions, and transport for each city" needs complex multi-step reasoning.

Routing by complexity:

@PostMapping("/chat")
public ResponseEntity<String> chat(@RequestBody ChatRequest request) {
    String model = selectModel(request.message());
    String response = callAgentWithModel(request, model);
    return ResponseEntity.ok(response);
}

private String selectModel(String message) {
    // simple heuristics — refine based on your traffic patterns
    boolean isComplex = message.length() > 200
        || message.contains("plan")
        || message.contains("itinerary")
        || message.contains("compare")
        || message.toLowerCase().contains("week");

    return isComplex ? "gemini-1.5-pro" : "gemini-1.5-flash";
}

Flash-class models typically cost 10–20× less than pro-class models. If 70% of your requests are simple factual questions and only 30% need complex reasoning, you've reduced model costs by 60–70% with no change to quality on either class.

Validate this with your eval dataset — run the simple cases through the cheaper model and confirm pass rate stays the same.

Shorten tool return values

Tool results become part of the input on every subsequent turn in the conversation. A tool that returns verbose JSON pays that token cost on every future message in the conversation.

// Before — verbose, gets replayed in history
public String getAttractions(String city) {
    return """
        {
          "city": "Mysore",
          "attractions": [
            {"name": "Mysore Palace", "rating": 4.8, "category": "Heritage",
             "openingHours": "10:00-17:30", "entryFee": "₹50"},
            {"name": "Chamundi Hills", "rating": 4.5, "category": "Religious",
             "openingHours": "06:00-20:00", "entryFee": "Free"}
          ],
          "lastUpdated": "2026-09-27"
        }
        """;
}

// After — readable string, same information, ~60% fewer tokens
public String getAttractions(String city) {
    return "Top attractions in " + city + ": " +
           "Mysore Palace (₹50, Heritage) · " +
           "Chamundi Hills (Free, Religious)";
}

The model doesn't need JSON structure to understand tool results — it reads natural language just as well. Plain readable strings are significantly cheaper than structured JSON for the same semantic content.

Avoid redundant tool calls

The model sometimes calls the same tool twice in one conversation — once to answer the current question and again when the user asks a follow-up. If the tool result is already in the conversation history, the model already has the answer.

Enforce this in the system prompt:

"""
You are a travel planning assistant for India.
Use tools for weather, attractions, and transport.
Only state facts returned by tools.
Do not call a tool if its result is already in the conversation history.
"""

This single instruction can eliminate 20–30% of tool calls in multi-turn conversations. Check your logs — if you see the same tool called twice with the same arguments within a conversation, this prompt addition will catch it.

Batch requests where possible

If your application processes multiple independent requests — a daily summary, a batch of user queries, a scheduled report — the Batch API lets you process them at roughly half the cost of individual requests:

// Instead of 100 individual calls at full price:
for (String query : queries) {
    results.add(chatClient.prompt().user(query).call().content());
}

// Use batch processing (check your provider's batch API):
// 50% cost reduction, results within 24 hours

Batch processing isn't suitable for real-time user interactions, but it's a significant win for any offline processing your system does — ingesting documents, generating summaries, running eval datasets overnight.

Cost optimisation checklist

Action Typical saving Effort
Trim system prompt 10–30% of input tokens Low
Reduce history window size 20–40% of input tokens Low
Route simple queries to cheaper model 50–70% of model cost Medium
Shorten tool return values 5–15% of input tokens Low
Add "don't repeat tool calls" to system prompt 10–20% of tool calls Low
Cache stable tool results Variable Already done
Use batch API for offline processing ~50% of batch costs Medium

Start with the top three — they cover most of the saving with the least risk of affecting output quality. Always verify with your eval dataset before shipping any prompt change.

The quality trade-off

Every cost reduction carries some risk of quality degradation. The discipline is:

  1. Measure baseline pass rate on your eval dataset
  2. Apply one change at a time
  3. Re-run eval — confirm pass rate hasn't dropped
  4. Monitor online eval scores for a week after deploying

If a change drops pass rate even slightly, either revert it or investigate why. Cost optimisation that makes your agent worse isn't worth it.

What's next

This is the final article in the series. We've gone from a basic Spring Boot setup through RAG, agents, tools, memory, patterns, deployment, scaling, MCP, evaluation, and cost optimisation. The last article wraps up what this journey looked like end to end — and what I'd do differently if I started again.

Sham Prakash K — Backend Engineer, 4+ years in Java, Spring Boot, and distributed systems. Building AI backend infrastructure. Writing about what I actually learned, mistakes included.

title: Always-on tracing for production and preview traffic
description:
With always-on tracing, you can now debug your real user requests without reproducing them.

Always-on tracing continuously collects traces from your production and preview traffic. Unlike session tracing, which only captures requests from your own browser, it samples your live traffic.

You control what's collected with sampling rules. Each rule sets a trace rate for an environment (All, Production, or Preview), optionally scoped to a path prefix like /checkout. Nothing is collected until you add a rule, so you pay only for what you choose to trace.

You can also manage sampling rules from the CLI. vercel traces config set adds a rule, or changes the rate of an existing one when you run it again with the same environment and path prefix:

Infrastructure and outbound fetch spans are captured automatically. To add framework and custom spans, instrument your app with @vercel/otel.

To view a trace, open the Logs or run vercel traces get <request-id>.

Always-on tracing is is now in beta and available to teams on all plans. Tracing is priced at $0.50 per 1M span units. Traces follow your runtime log retention: 1 hour on Hobby, 1 day on Pro and 3 days on Enterprise.

Get started by adding a rule in Settings → Tracing or from the settings icon in Logs. Learn more in the documentation.

title: How Ora benchmarks every major AI agent on Vercel
description:
Ora on Vercel

  • Front end, back end, and agent runtime on one platform

  • Every major agent tested side by side on live sites

  • Hundreds of commits a day from a 16-person engineering team

Ora sends agents onto live websites with instructions to sign up for a product, integrate with it, and pay for it. Agents often fail, and by Ora's estimate, 99% of the web isn't agent-ready. The platform shows customers where and why agents fail, and what to change.

Assaf Elovic, co-founder of Ora, spent years helping agents discover the web. His previous company, Tavily, built a web search engine for AI agents and was acquired by Nebius earlier this year. Search solved half the problem, but an agent that finds a product still has to actually use it. He and co-founder Liad Yosef started Ora to measure how ready the web is for agents, and to fix the parts that aren't.

Today that means spawning agents against live customer sites from journey.ora.ai, where Ora runs a journey and records the cost, latency, and steps an agent needs to finish a task. The platform runs on Vercel, including the agent runtime.

Benchmarking every major agent side by side

Every harness expects its own infrastructure

Agents decompose into two parts: a model, which does the reasoning, and a harness, the software that gives the model its tools and drives it from step to step. Ora's lineup covers the agents customers use most: Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini, Hermes, OpenClaw, and eve, Vercel's agent framework. Ora runs each agent on a customer's website and watches how it handles common workflows.

No two harnesses want the same infrastructure. Each expects its own environment and exposes its steps differently, so Ora runs a separate runtime for every harness and traces every step. Ido Finder, who leads engineering at Ora, calls that side-by-side coverage one of the most valuable things ora brings to its customers.

When an agent stalls in a signup flow, the customer sees which step and what it tried. Without the trace, the result is a score with nothing behind it.

One platform under every harness

Ora built this testing system entirely on Vercel. Front end, back end, and the agent runtime share the same deployment path, logs, and authentication. The agent runtime isn't separate infrastructure to operate; it lives where the rest of the product lives.

Ora benchmarked eve, then built on it

Testing eve like any other harness

When Vercel launched eve, Ora gave it no special treatment. eve went through the same benchmark, under the same conditions, as every other harness in the lineup. Ora works with Vercel Engineering as a design partner, and Finder gave the eve team direct access to the platform to dig into the results.

The initial test put eve against Claude Code across hundreds of real journeys on multiple domains. Both harnesses ran the same models, Claude Fable 5 and Haiku 4.5, and every run gave the agent the same job: integrate with a product.

Ora published three numbers from the comparison:

  • 7% fewer steps to reach the goal

  • 2x native success: twice as many tasks finished on the customer's own site instead of falling back to web search

  • 9% more valid endpoints: more of the endpoints the agent found were ones it could actually call

The benchmark fed back into eve, too. One run surfaced a prompt-caching issue, the eve team shipped a fix, and Ora's next round of results measured roughly 15% lower total cost.

The framework behind Ora's own agents

For a company that benchmarks every major harness for a living, this is not a casual choice. After those results, Ora builds on eve.

Because eve follows the Next.js paradigm, there was little to configure, and tools, skills, and connectors take little code. The feature that sealed it was the sandbox override. An agent framework like eve ships with its own sandbox, the isolated environment where the agent executes, runs tools, and touches files. That's a good default for most teams, because you get safe execution for free. But an agent in the framework's own sandbox runs outside the instrumented environment where Ora traces every step. The override lets the team swap that environment in, so eve agents get recorded like every other harness, with nothing new built.

Journey.ora.ai now has eve on both sides, eve is one of the harnesses it tests, and eve is what it runs on.

How 16 engineers ship hundreds of commits a day

The engineering team is 16 people shipping hundreds of commits a day, and day-to-day infrastructure work belongs to their coding agents. A stack that sits in one place lets those agents run it end to end.

Finder puts the time saved at a few hours a week at least. Elovic credits a similar amount to how well coding agents build with Vercel's libraries.

What's next

Ora is adding more products, and the architecture is growing with them. The team is splitting its platform into microservices, all of them on Vercel. New services deploy to the same infrastructure and talk to each other with no extra configuration, and the internal agents built on eve will run as one more service.

By Ora's own measure, 99% of the web still can't handle an agent that shows up to sign up, integrate, and pay.

About Ora: Ora makes the web agent-ready. Companies use ora to benchmark how AI agents discover, navigate, and interact with their websites, and to build the infrastructure agents need to find, use, and transact with them.

title: "🚫 Your Agent Demo Is Not a Release Gate"
description:
The demo looked green. The merge still broke a customer workflow.

That is the whole story for most agent work I see in 2025–2026. A notebook shows “pass rate 92%.” A slide says “evals.” Nobody can point to the GitHub check that would have blocked the bad prompt.

What broke

We shipped a tool-calling agent behind a feature flag. The notebook suite used a frozen fixture set from two weeks earlier. Production traffic hit a new tool schema the same day. The agent retried, burned tokens, and wrote partial side effects.

The notebook never saw that schema. CI never asked.

The smallest CI gate that would have caught it

You do not need a research harness on day one. You need three checks that fail the PR:

  1. Contract check — tool JSON schemas in the repo must match what the agent loads at runtime (hash or OpenAPI snapshot).
  2. Golden path — 5–20 fixed user tasks with expected tool names and final answers. Deterministic fixtures only.
  3. Budget check — max tokens / max steps per task. A loop that “eventually works” is a fail.

Wire them as one job:

# .github/workflows/agent-evals.yml
name: agent-evals
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  evals:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements-evals.txt
      - run: python -m evals.ci_gate --suite golden --max-tokens 4000

Keep the suite offline when you can. If a live model is required, pin the model id and store traces as artifacts.

How the gate looks in code 

# evals/ci_gate.py
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

def load_suite(path):
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text())

def run_case(case, agent):
    result = agent.run(case["input"], max_steps=case.get("max_steps", 8))
    ok_tools = result.tool_names == case["expect_tools"]
    ok_answer = case["expect_substr"] in (result.final or "")
    ok_budget = result.tokens <= case["max_tokens"]
    return ok_tools and ok_answer and ok_budget, result

def main():
    suite = load_suite("evals/golden.json")
    failed = []
    for case in suite["cases"]:
        ok, result = run_case(case, build_agent())
        if not ok:
            failed.append((case["id"], result.summary()))
    if failed:
        for cid, summary in failed:
            print(f"FAIL {cid}: {summary}")
        sys.exit(1)
    print(f"PASS {len(suite['cases'])} cases")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

golden.json is boring on purpose: ids, inputs, expected tool sequence, substring checks, token caps. Boring is what merge gates need.

Honest trade-off

A CI gate will reject useful prompt experiments that still need exploration. That is the point. Exploration stays on a branch or a notebook. Mainline gets the harness.

You will also spend time babysitting fixtures when tools change. That ownership cost is real. Paying it in CI is cheaper than paying it in incident reviews.

What to do Monday

  1. Pick 10 real failures from the last month. Turn them into golden cases.
  2. Add schema hash check for every tool the agent can call.
  3. Make the workflow required on the PR.

If the check is optional, it is still a demo.

Has your agent stack blocked a merge yet, or is “evals” still a slide?

title: MySQL to PostgreSQL Schema Conversion: What Each Column Type Should Become, and What Silently Changes
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: Most MySQL types have an obvious PostgreSQL twin, but eight need a decision: TINYINT(1), UNSIGNED integers, DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP, ENUM, SET, ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, AUTO_INCREMENT and the collation behind every unique text column. The last one fails silently: a MySQL unique email refuses Ana@Example.com after ana@example.com, and the same constraint on PostgreSQL accepts both.

Converting a MySQL schema to PostgreSQL is mostly mechanical, and the parts that are not mechanical are the ones that break production. Eight kinds of column need a decision, because the obvious PostgreSQL type either refuses data MySQL accepted, or accepts data MySQL refused. The worst of them changes no type at all: a unique text column that ignored case in MySQL stops ignoring it.

Every behaviour below was run on MySQL 8.4.11 and PostgreSQL 18.3 in throwaway containers, against this small shop schema:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  is_active TINYINT(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  UNIQUE KEY customers_email_key (email)
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4 COLLATE=utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  customer_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  status ENUM('pending','paid','shipped','cancelled') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  options SET('gift','express','fragile') NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  total DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id) ON DELETE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4 COLLATE=utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;

The eight MySQL columns that need a decision

Eight kinds of MySQL column change behaviour when translated literally: TINYINT(1), BIGINT UNSIGNED, DATETIME, ENUM, SET, ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, AUTO_INCREMENT, and unique text columns under a _ci collation.

Most columns translate one to one: DECIMAL(10,2) is NUMERIC(10,2), VARCHAR(255) is VARCHAR(255), INT UNSIGNED fits in bigint, and a MySQL TIMESTAMP is timestamptz. These eight do not:

MySQL Literal PostgreSQL version What changes Decide
TINYINT(1) boolean MySQL stored 2 without complaint; boolean refuses any integer boolean if the column only holds 0 and 1, smallint if not
BIGINT UNSIGNED bigint Values above 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 fail with bigint out of range bigint for keys, numeric(20,0) for hashes and external ids that use the full range
DATETIME timestamp Nothing yet, but it keeps no zone, unlike MySQL's TIMESTAMP timestamptz if the app writes UTC
ENUM(...) varchar plus CHECK, or CREATE TYPE The value list moves from the type to a constraint or a named type One of three designs, chosen on purpose
SET(...) varchar MySQL refused unknown members; plain text accepts anything text[] with a containment CHECK
ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP nothing updated_at stops moving A trigger
AUTO_INCREMENT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY Loaded ids do not move the counter; the next insert collides setval after the load
A unique text column under a _ci collation UNIQUE Case and accents start to count A lower() index or a nondeterministic collation

The last two get their own sections below.

How do you convert a MySQL schema to PostgreSQL?

Convert the schema first, deciding each of those eight columns yourself, then move the rows with pgloader or COPY.

pgloader can do both in one pass with its own default casts, and they differ from a literal mapping in places that matter: it casts DATETIME to timestamptz, turns each ENUM into a PostgreSQL enum type named after the table and column, casts TINYINT(1) to boolean through its own tinyint-to-boolean function rather than refusing odd values, gives AUTO_INCREMENT keys serial or bigserial, and resets sequences after the load. Its create no tables option instead loads into tables that already exist, which is the route when you want to decide each column yourself and write the CREATE TABLE script first.

Whichever tool writes the script, read it against the list above before running it. These are the cases from the test run where a literal translation accepted the script and then behaved differently.

TINYINT(1): boolean only if the data agrees

MySQL has no real boolean, so BOOLEAN is TINYINT(1) and the (1) is a display width, not a limit. On 8.4, INSERT INTO customers (email, is_active) VALUES ('flag@example.com', 2) succeeded and stored 2. PostgreSQL's boolean refuses the same insert with column "is_active" is of type boolean but expression is of type integer. Before choosing boolean, count the rows that would not fit:

SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE is_active NOT IN (0, 1);

Run it before the load whichever tool moves the rows. Zero means boolean. Anything else means some code uses the flag as a small number, and smallint keeps it until that code is found. Changing the column type later is its own migration, covered in changing an integer column to boolean in Postgres.

UNSIGNED integers: one size up, except BIGINT

PostgreSQL has no unsigned integers. An INT UNSIGNED holds up to 4,294,967,295, which fits in bigint, so the safe mapping is one size up: TINYINT UNSIGNED to smallint, SMALLINT UNSIGNED and MEDIUMINT UNSIGNED to integer, INT UNSIGNED to bigint. BIGINT UNSIGNED has nowhere to go. MySQL accepted id = 18446744073709551615; PostgreSQL's bigint stops at 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 and refused it with bigint out of range. For an AUTO_INCREMENT key that will never reach 2^63, bigint is right. For a column holding 64-bit hashes or another system's ids, check SELECT max(col) first and use numeric(20,0) if the top half is in use. Why MySQL schemas are full of UNSIGNED in the first place is in signed vs unsigned primary keys in MySQL.

DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP: only one of them is an instant

The MySQL manual puts the difference in one sentence: "MySQL converts TIMESTAMP values from the current time zone to UTC for storage, and back from UTC to the current time zone for retrieval. (This does not occur for other types such as DATETIME.)" In the test, both columns were set to 2026-10-29 09:00:00 in a session at +07:00 and read back at +00:00: the TIMESTAMP returned 02:00:00, the DATETIME still 09:00:00.

So a MySQL TIMESTAMP is an instant and becomes timestamptz without debate. A DATETIME is whatever the application wrote. A literal conversion makes it timestamp, which is correct only for wall-clock values. If the application wrote UTC, which is the usual case, convert it on the PostgreSQL side once the rows are in:

ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN updated_at TYPE TIMESTAMPTZ(0) USING updated_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';

Why the naive type costs you later is in timestamp vs timestamptz.

ENUM and SET: the value list has to live somewhere

A MySQL ENUM becomes either a CHECK constraint on a varchar, a PostgreSQL enum type, or a lookup table. That is a design choice with real trade-offs, and it is the subject of enum vs check constraint vs lookup table. A CHECK is the easiest to change later.

SET is the one that loses a rule quietly. Under MySQL 8.4's default strict sql_mode, INSERT INTO orders (..., options) VALUES (..., 'gift,wrap') failed with Data truncated for column 'options', because wrap is not a member. Converted to a varchar, PostgreSQL stored gift,wrap without a word. Converting the column to an array with a containment check, in place and with its rows, puts the membership rule back:

ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN options DROP DEFAULT;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN options TYPE TEXT[] USING string_to_array(options, ',');
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN options SET DEFAULT '{}';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_options_check CHECK (options <@ ARRAY['gift', 'express', 'fragile']);

gift,express became {gift,express}, an empty set became {}, and ARRAY['gift', 'wrap'] then failed on orders_options_check. One MySQL rule does not come back: MySQL stored gift,gift as gift, while the array keeps the duplicate.

ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP: there is no column option to translate

MySQL's updated_at moved on every UPDATE in the test. PostgreSQL has no column clause that does this, so the converted column kept its first value forever, and the UPDATE reported success. A BEFORE UPDATE trigger brings the behaviour back:

CREATE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := now();
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER customers_set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON customers
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

One function serves every table; each table needs its own trigger. The trigger against the ORM approach, per framework, is in how to auto-update an updated_at column.

AUTO_INCREMENT: identity, and the sequence after the load

Map AUTO_INCREMENT to GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY, then reset each sequence with setval after the rows are loaded, or the next insert collides with a loaded id.

AUTO_INCREMENT keeps a value the row supplies, which is PostgreSQL's GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY, and that is what a load needs, since the rows arrive with their ids. The catch is the counter. After loading ids 1 and 2 into a fresh table, the next insert without an id failed with duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customers_pkey" and Key (id)=(1) already exists, because the identity sequence never saw the loaded rows. One statement per table fixes it:

SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('customers', 'id'), (SELECT max(id) FROM customers));

pgloader resets the sequences it created unless told reset no sequences; on tables you created yourself, check with SELECT last_value from the sequence, or run the setval anyway. A hand-rolled COPY never does it. Whether to switch to GENERATED ALWAYS once the load is done is covered in serial vs identity in Postgres.

Is a unique constraint case-sensitive in PostgreSQL?

Yes: PostgreSQL compares text exactly, so a unique email that refused Ana@Example.com after ana@example.com in MySQL accepts both, with no error.

This is the change no type mapping shows. MySQL 8's default collation for utf8mb4 is utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci: accent-insensitive and case-insensitive. Every comparison goes through it, unique keys included. In the test:

On the same schema MySQL 8.4, utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci PostgreSQL 18.3
Insert ana@example.com, then Ana@Example.com Second insert fails: Duplicate entry 'Ana@Example.com' for key 'customers.customers_email_key' Both rows stored
Insert josé@example.com, then jose@example.com Second insert fails: duplicate entry Both rows stored
WHERE email = 'ANA@EXAMPLE.COM' Finds the row Finds nothing

The PostgreSQL manual states it plainly: "All standard and predefined collations are deterministic", meaning two strings are equal only if they are the same bytes. So after the conversion, a sign-up form that MySQL protected now creates a second account for the same person, and a login that typed the address in capitals stops finding it. Nothing errors.

There are two ways to keep the old rule:

  • A unique index on lower(email), after dropping the plain constraint: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_lower_key ON customers (lower(email));. It refused Ana@Example.com after ana@example.com. It does not make WHERE email = ... case-insensitive, so queries have to say lower(email) too, and it does nothing for accents.
  • A nondeterministic ICU collation on the column. CREATE COLLATION ci_ai (provider = icu, locale = 'und-u-ks-level1', deterministic = false) ignores case and accents, as _ai_ci did. With the column set COLLATE ci_ai and the UNIQUE added back, JOSE@example.com was refused after josé@example.com, and a plain WHERE email = 'Jose@Example.com' found the row. The manual's und-u-ks-level2 variant ignores case but not accents. The cost is that B-tree deduplication cannot be used on such an index.

Not every MySQL column is affected. A column declared COLLATE utf8mb4_bin was already case-sensitive, and only text columns that sit in a primary key, unique constraint or unique index change who gets in. A non-unique column still changes how WHERE matches, which is worth a search through the application's queries.

Converting the schema in Schemity

Schemity writes the PostgreSQL script without changing the diagram, with a report above it that lists every type it changed and the behaviour that does not carry over.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. Connect it to the MySQL database, or import a mysqldump --no-data file, and the schema is a diagram in MySQL's own types.

From there, the SQL dialog behind Export > SQL file has a Database dropdown: pick PostgreSQL and the script is rewritten for it, with a conversion report above it. The diagram stays a MySQL diagram, and nothing leaves your machine. For the shop schema the report reads:

-- Converted by Schemity from MySQL to PostgreSQL. The diagram itself is unchanged.
-- Review the notes below before running this script.
--
-- Type mappings:
--   BIGINT UNSIGNED -> BIGINT (2 columns)
--   DATETIME -> TIMESTAMP(0) (1 column)
--   DECIMAL(10,2) -> NUMERIC(10,2) (1 column)
--   ENUM('pending','paid','shipped','cancelled') -> VARCHAR(9) (1 column): Allowed values become a CHECK constraint.
--   INTEGER UNSIGNED -> BIGINT (1 column)
--   SET('gift','express','fragile') -> VARCHAR(21) (1 column): A set of values is stored as comma-separated text, unchecked.
--   TIMESTAMP -> TIMESTAMPTZ(0) (1 column)
--
-- Notes:
--   customers.updated_at: ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is left out: PostgreSQL has no column that sets itself on update.
--   customers.email: Unique in MySQL under utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci, which ignores case and accents; PostgreSQL compares text exactly, so values that differ only in case and accents are both accepted.
--   2 BIGINT UNSIGNED column(s) hold values up to 2^64-1; PostgreSQL's BIGINT stops at 2^63-1.
--   2 character set or collation setting(s) left out: PostgreSQL picks its own.

The script under it creates is_active as BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE, both keys as BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY, and status with the CHECK ("status" IN ('pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled')). It ran on PostgreSQL 18.3 as written. The report is also saved as a comment block at the top of the file, so whoever runs the script reads the same notes.

The conversion makes the literal choice in every row of the table at the top rather than guessing at your data: TINYINT(1) becomes BOOLEAN, DATETIME stays timestamp, SET stays text, and the email keeps a plain UNIQUE. The report covers most of those choices, each tied to the column it is about. Three are yours to remember: whether a TINYINT(1) really holds only 0 and 1, whether a DATETIME holds UTC, and the setval after the load. Make them in the diagram you are converting into: Import SQL on a PostgreSQL diagram reads the converted script.

From there you design the next one in PostgreSQL's types, change updated_at to TIMESTAMPTZ, add the lower(email) index, and export the final script. The rows still move with pgloader's create no tables or your own COPY, followed by the setval.

MySQL to PostgreSQL, in one list

Most of the conversion is mechanical; these eight columns are not, and each has a short answer.

  • TINYINT(1): boolean only after SELECT count(*) ... NOT IN (0, 1) returns zero.
  • UNSIGNED: one size up; BIGINT UNSIGNED to bigint for keys, numeric(20,0) if values pass 2^63.
  • TIMESTAMP to timestamptz; DATETIME to timestamptz too if it holds UTC, converted with AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'.
  • ENUM: a CHECK, an enum type or a lookup table, chosen on purpose. SET: text[] with a <@ check.
  • ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP: a BEFORE UPDATE trigger on each table.
  • AUTO_INCREMENT: GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY, then setval after the load.
  • Every unique text column under a _ci collation: a lower() unique index or a nondeterministic collation, or accept that case now matters.

Choosing a key type while you are redesigning anyway is in UUID vs bigint primary keys, and what changes about indexes when you move a unique rule around is in unique constraint vs unique index.
