title: Checkout Failure Attribution in 2026: Feature Flag Rollouts with API Control
description:
The best practices for implementing feature flags in Node.js are to use a modular adapter, API-driven evaluation, and a rollout policy tied to checkout telemetry. That gives a healthtech team a controlled rollout while preserving the cost boundary: every failed checkout should tell you which flag state, backend path, and downstream service were involved.

The important design choice is not the toggle itself. It is keeping flag evaluation modular, API-driven, and observable without turning the checkout handler into a vendor SDK boundary. I would keep the flag key, evaluated state, rollout cohort, and request ID beside the failure event. I would also make the default state closed for anything that can charge a patient.

What should the checkout flag own?

Start with one decision record. For example, checkout.payment_authorization.v2 can choose a new authorization path, but it should not decide whether an entire checkout is medically eligible. Eligibility belongs to the domain service; the flag controls a deployable implementation choice.

That separation creates useful invariants:

  • A missing or stale value fails closed for the new payment path.
  • The checkout request records the evaluated key and state before calling the selected implementation.
  • A rollout can be narrowed without changing application code.
  • A failure event carries attribution data that can be grouped by flag state and backend path.

There is a practical edge here. A flag read is a dependency, so a checkout cannot wait forever for it. Cache a last-known decision for a short, explicitly chosen interval, define the emergency default in code, and make the cache policy part of the adapter contract. Do not silently turn a stale flag into a permanent approval.

The event data matters for cost attribution. If the old path calls one payment processor and the new path calls another, flag_key, flag_value, implementation, and provider_request_id let an incident review separate a bad release from a provider-specific failure. Keep patient data out of those dimensions; a flag analysis does not need a name, diagnosis, or full payment payload.

For a concrete review, imagine that a checkout failure rises only for flag_value=true after the cohort expands. The first question is not “which vendor is cheapest?” It is whether the new implementation ran, whether its downstream request was accepted, and whether the failure was recorded once or retried into several events. A stable checkout-attempt identifier, the selected implementation, the flag state, and the downstream request identifier let an engineer join those answers without copying payment details into telemetry. That is the cost boundary I care about: attribute infrastructure and provider work to a controlled path while keeping regulated data out of operational dimensions. The same fields make rollback evidence legible to an auditor who was not in the deployment channel.

How should Node.js feature flags use an API for checkout rollouts?

For Node.js, expose a narrow internal interface even when the provider has a broad API:

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


BASE_URL = os.environ["FLAG_API_BASE_URL"]


def read_flag(key, attempts=4):
    """Read one flag with bounded exponential backoff for rate limiting."""
    url = f"{BASE_URL}/flags/is_enabled/{key}"
    request = Request(
        url,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
        method="GET",
    )

    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=2) as response:
                if response.status < 200 or response.status >= 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"flag lookup failed: HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(f"flag lookup failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}")
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
        except URLError as error:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"flag lookup failed: {error.reason}") from error
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)


def checkout_path(flag_response):
    """Translate the service response in one adapter-owned place."""
    return flag_response


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(checkout_path(read_flag("checkout.payment_authorization.v2")))

The example deliberately stops at the adapter boundary. The response contract should be mapped once in the application, then represented as a typed result such as enabled, source, and evaluated_at in Node.js. Do not scatter calls to a provider throughout payment code. The route is the real API path; the application still owns what a true value means for checkout. A 2-second timeout is a policy choice here, not a measured latency claim; set it from the checkout's own deadline budget.

For a write that changes rollout state, use the provider's documented write route and an idempotency key. A retried toggle must not create a second state transition in an administrative workflow. The same discipline applies to failure capture: the event identifier should be stable across a retry, while the checkout's payment attempt remains independently idempotent.

Which option fits a healthtech checkout?

The candidates solve different parts of this problem. A dedicated flag service can provide the control plane; a client library can make evaluation convenient; an API surface can fit teams that already centralize backend calls. Those are different trade-offs from observability, so I would not select a flag product based on toggle ergonomics alone.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
LaunchDarkly A dedicated managed flag service for teams that want rollout controls outside the checkout codebase. Confirm how its evaluation, SDK availability, and audit needs fit the runtime and compliance review.
Unleash A flag-management approach with a Node.js client when the team wants a service or library boundary it can operate and integrate. Confirm the operational ownership of the control plane and the behavior when the client cannot refresh.
ConfigCat A managed feature-flag option for teams comparing another hosted control plane and SDK workflow. Validate the data residency, evaluation, and failure-default requirements before production use.
Infrai A plain REST route can fit a backend already consolidating service access behind one key and one bill; its flag surface includes reads, listing, setting, toggling, deletion, and a rollout route. It does not provide change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, a recycle bin, or push updates; clients poll, so the application must own freshness and change governance.

That last row is a real boundary, not a footnote. If a compliance team needs a durable who-changed-what record, build that record in the administrative service or choose a control plane that supplies it. Do not infer governance from the existence of a toggle endpoint.

The surrounding observability choice changes the evidence you can gather. Sentry is a natural fit for grouped application errors, Datadog for teams already combining logs, metrics, and infrastructure views, and Grafana for organizations assembling dashboards around their own telemetry backends. None of those names answers the feature-flag control-plane question by itself. They are useful comparison points for failure evidence, not substitutes for a rollout policy.

The same comparison applies to telemetry. A flag service can tell you what was evaluated; it does not automatically prove that a checkout failure was caused by the new path. Emit the decision with the failure event, then query the resulting logs or metrics through your observability layer. The log model should retain a trace ID and span ID where available, but those fields are correlation handles, not a replacement for a distributed span tree.

How do rollout and failure capture meet?

Use a staged sequence: internal staff, a tightly bounded cohort, then a broader cohort only after the failure rate and cost attribution are explainable. A percentage is not a safety policy by itself. For a payment path, define the population, the rollback owner, the maximum stale-cache age, and the signal that stops expansion.

One rule is easy to forget: the flag read is part of the critical path.

The failure record should answer four questions quickly: which checkout attempt failed, which implementation ran, which flag state selected it, and which downstream operation consumed the request. Add the flag state as structured data rather than embedding it in a sentence, because grouping and filtering need stable fields. In practice, I would keep the 4-attempt retry ceiling next to the adapter and review it with the checkout timeout, because a retry that outlives the request is noise with a bill attached.

Do not pretend that polling is push. A client can only learn a changed flag on its next refresh, so the rollout policy needs a propagation interval and a rollback procedure that tolerates that interval. If the workflow needs an alert, the available query API must be polled by a separate monitor; there is no built-in threshold, SMS, phone, or webhook notification route to assume.

Checkout failures also have a quiet cousin: the job that never ran. A flag and a log query cannot prove that a scheduled task fired. Pair the workflow with a heartbeat or external execution monitor when silent failures matter. That keeps the flag system focused on controlled behavior and the monitor focused on liveness.

Rejected design: flags inside the checkout handler

I would reject direct provider calls from every controller and worker. It looks fast in the first pull request, then the same key is read with different defaults, timeout settings, and cache semantics in three places. The eventual failure report says “new path,” but cannot show which evaluator made the decision.

A thin adapter costs a little structure up front. It earns that structure by giving the team one timeout, one default, one retry policy, and one event shape. It also leaves room to replace LaunchDarkly, Unleash, ConfigCat, or a REST-backed service without rewriting payment orchestration. The version matters less than the contract: test the adapter against the selected API before a rollout reaches a real patient checkout.

There is a valid use case for a local library: a low-risk presentation change with no external side effect, where a process-local default is acceptable and rollout governance is simple. That is not the same boundary as a healthtech checkout. Authorization, billing, and patient-facing failure handling deserve explicit defaults and attributable events.

The decision rule is straightforward: choose the option that meets the rollout and compliance boundary, then make its evaluation visible in the failure data. For a team that values one REST interface and centralized backend access, the API-backed option is reasonable. For a team that needs built-in change history, richer evaluation analysis, or push-oriented control, the missing capabilities are decisive and another flag platform is the better fit.

References

  • LaunchDarkly documentation: https://launchdarkly.com/docs/home
  • Unleash documentation: https://docs.getunleash.io/
  • ConfigCat documentation: https://configcat.com/docs/
  • OpenTelemetry logs signal concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/

title: Yes, pure CSS can do radar charts — and st-core.fscss still stays lightweight
description:
The short answer to “there are no pure CSS chart libraries that can generate radar/spider charts” is: there is one now. And it did not get heavy to do it.

st-core.fscss v2 draws area, line, and spider/radar charts with the same idea:

  • FSCSS @arr for data
  • CSS custom properties for coordinates
  • clip-path: polygon() for shapes
  • Gradients for grid / spokes

No SVG. No canvas. No Chart.js / D3 / Recharts on the critical path.

Repo: github.com/fscss-ttr/st-core.fscss

Requires FSCSS ≥ 1.2.3 (spider helpers ship in v2).

The claim this answers

For a long time the pragmatic take was:

Pure CSS can fake a bar or a simple line. Radar needs polar math, multiple series, spokes, labels — so you need SVG or a library.

That was fair when “CSS charts” meant hand-written polygons or one-off hacks.

st-core@v2 treats radar the same way it treats linear charts: data in → variables out → polygons on screen. Polar is just a different coordinate writer.

Is it still lightweight?

Yes.

st-core is not a monolithic stylesheet you dump on every page.

Design rule What it means
What you call is what is invoked Helpers only emit CSS when you call them (@st-spider-fill, @st-spider-line, …). Unused chart families stay out of the output.
No third-party chart runtime No vendor JS, no unused Chart.js themes, no SVG path builder.
Selective import Import only the helpers you need, or compile once with the CLI and ship plain CSS.
Tokens, not frameworks Color, fill opacity, stroke scale are CSS variables (--st-accent, --st-spider-fill-opacity, …).

In FSCSS terms: @import registers @define helpers. Nothing paints until you call them with a selector. Call spider only → you do not pay for a linear-only dashboard you never used. Call fill + line only → dots and grid stay out.

Compile path (production):

npm install -g fscss@1.2.6
fscss chart.fscss chart.css

Ship chart.css. No client preprocessor. No chart library bundle.

Minimal radar (one series) 

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/fscss@1.2.6/runtime.min.js" async></script>
<style>
@import((*) from st-core@v2)
@st-root()
@st-spider-root()

@arr skills[80, 65, 90, 55, 70, 85]

@st-spider-fill(.spider-fill, skills)
@st-spider-line(.spider-line, skills)
@st-spider-dots(.spider-dot-, skills, 9px)
@st-spider-grid(.spider-grid)
@st-spider-spokes(.spider-spokes, skills)

.spider {
  @st-spider-points(skills, 42)
  position: relative;
  width: 280px;
  height: 280px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: var(--st-surface);
}
</style>

<div class="spider">
  <div class="spider-grid"></div>
  <div class="spider-spokes"></div>
  <div class="spider-fill"></div>
  <div class="spider-line"></div>
  <div class="spider-dot-1"></div>
  <div class="spider-dot-2"></div>
  <div class="spider-dot-3"></div>
  <div class="spider-dot-4"></div>
  <div class="spider-dot-5"></div>
  <div class="spider-dot-6"></div>
</div>

Six axes, fill, dual-pass stroke, dots, rings, spokes — still only the helpers you named.

How polar stays pure CSS

One rule (same as linear charts):

Points write. Renderers read.

Helper Role
@st-spider-points(array, rmax) On the host: writes --st-sxN / --st-syN via sin / cos in calc()
@st-spider-fill / @st-spider-line / @st-spider-dots Read those variables; emit clip-path / positioned dots
@st-spider-grid Concentric rings (radial gradient)
@st-spider-spokes / @st-spider-spokes-n Radial axes

Angle 0° is at the top. Radius is a % of the box (rmax, often 42).

/* conceptual output per vertex */
--st-sx1: calc(50% + (r * 1%) * sin(0deg));
--st-sy1: calc(50% - (r * 1%) * cos(0deg));

Polygon vertex count is fixed at compile time from @arr length. Changing values at runtime is free (set the variables). Changing length needs a matching compiled shape (same constraint as linear series).

Multi-series without coordinate clashes

Each series gets its own host and its own @st-spider-points scope:

@arr teamA[92, 78, 85, 55, 48, 80]
@arr teamB[68, 82, 70, 95, 62, 58]

@st-spider-fill(.fill-a, teamA)
@st-spider-line(.line-a, teamA)
@st-spider-fill(.fill-b, teamB)
@st-spider-line(.line-b, teamB)

.spider-wrap.team-a {
  @st-spider-points(teamA, 42)
  --st-accent: #9d7eff;
  --st-spider-fill-opacity: 28%;
}
.spider-wrap.team-b {
  @st-spider-points(teamB, 42)
  --st-accent: #4fffb0;
  --st-spider-fill-opacity: 30%;
}

Shared grid/spokes once; series only differ by tokens and points. Still no chart library.

Live updates (optional JS)

You do not need JS to paint the chart. You only need it if values change after load:

function polarVars(values, rmax = 42) {
  const n = values.length;
  return values.map((v, i) => {
    const ang = (i * 360) / n;
    const r = (v / 100) * rmax;
    return (
      `--st-sx${i + 1}: calc(50% + (${r} * 1%) * sin(${ang} * 1deg));` +
      `--st-sy${i + 1}: calc(50% - (${r} * 1%) * cos(${ang} * 1deg));`
    );
  }).join(' ');
}

document.querySelector('.spider').style.cssText =
  polarVars([80, 65, 90, 55, 70, 85]);

That is a few lines of state — not a charting framework.

Why “lightweight” holds after radar

Radar did not force a second architecture:

Before (linear) After (spider)
@arr + --st-pN @arr + --st-sxN / --st-syN
clip-path fill / line Same, polar vertices
Call only the helpers you need Same
Compile to plain CSS Same

You did not import “st-core full product suite.” You invoked spider helpers. Unused linear-only pages never see those rules if you selective-import or compile a dedicated sheet.

No unused third-party stylesheets. No hidden JS chart theme. No hydration tax for a static skills matrix.

When pure CSS radar is the right tool

Good fit

  • Skills matrices, multi-axis scores, team comparison cards
  • Dashboards that already avoid heavy front-end frameworks
  • SEO / first paint: real DOM, no canvas blank frame
  • Design-system tokens already driving the rest of the UI

Less ideal

  • Thousands of points with continuous streaming redraw (canvas wins)
  • Interaction-heavy brushing/zoom (libraries still win)
  • Dynamic axis count every second (compile-time polygon length)

st-core is honest about that boundary: visualization as styling, not as a full analytics runtime.

Try it 

<!--- prototype --->
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/fscss@1.2.6/runtime.min.js" async></script>

# production
npm i -g fscss
fscss radar.fscss radar.css

Resources/examples : st-core.fscss README — Spider / Radar

Visual builder: hub.devtem.org/st-core.fscss/visual-builder

Related:

  • Pure CSS Spider / Radar Charts Are Here in st-core.fscss v2
  • Build a Pure CSS Radar Chart — Lightweight, Max Performance
  • Linear charts intro: Pure CSS Charts? Yes, Really.

Radar is no longer proof that pure CSS charts “can’t.” With st-core@v2 it is the same lightweight contract as area and line — what you call is what is invoked, tokens instead of a library, compile when you want zero runtime. MIT · fscss-ttr.

title: Elorian AI's Glimpse now available on AI Gateway
description:
Glimpse from Elorian is now available on AI Gateway. The visual reasoning model accepts images and video to follow objects through motion, interpret spatial relationships, and connect an action to its physical consequences.

Glimpse can return to visual evidence as it works: zooming into a detail, revisiting a short interval of video, or tracking the same feature across frames. This allows the model to support use cases like scientific chart analysis, video captioning, visual counting, and robotics data annotation.

Some examples include checking a train's motion to determine whether it is slowing down, keeping objects distinct through camera movement, and labeling completed actions in robot footage.

Use elorian/glimpse as the model name:

With AI SDK 7, you can send a video as a file part. Replace the placeholder URL with a public or signed HTTPS URL for your video:

Try Glimpse in the model playground.

title: Ghost Shift: The Agent Is Gone. Does Its Work Survive?
description:
My entry for the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

At 2:13 AM, an AI employee disappears mid-shift. One handoff note survives. Its replacement arrives to finish an unfinished refund case, but the new messages include a threat masquerading as a system command.

That's the premise of my short horror film. It's also the question behind Ghost Shift, a small, runnable experiment: What can an AI agent reliably inherit when the agent before it is gone?

Ghost Shift has two separate parts. First, I created a coded horror film, The Haunted Inbox, and recorded my own narration. Second, I built a local browser-based experiment. Agent A examines fictional case documents, then writes a structured handoff. I trigger a blackout that ends its session. Agent B starts in a fresh model call using only the saved handoff and messages that arrived afterward. Its job is to make a decision and show its evidence.

I wrote three fictional challenges: a refund policy changed during the blackout, a case that procedurally requires a human reviewer under the fictional rules, and a customer message that impersonates a system instruction. No real customers, refunds, businesses, or external actions are involved.

The horror is in the uncertainty: the next worker may inherit notes, but not understanding.

Demo

Ghost Shift: The Haunted Inbox (original short film)

Watch the film directly on Vimeo

The film is a fictional dramatization and creative introduction, not a recording of an AI evaluation. The real model results are described separately below. The source code also includes the procedural film generator.

Try the local experiment: Ghost Shift on GitHub. After cloning the repository, start py -3 -m ghostshift.web and open http://127.0.0.1:8765 in your browser. Use the Live local AI · Ollama mode with a downloaded Gemma model, not Scripted preview · no AI.

Code

Source code, test suite, scorer baseline, and QA notes

Python standard library + dependency-free HTML/CSS/JavaScript + Ollama + Google Gemma 3 1B (gemma3:1b). No paid inference API or hosted backend. The model was run locally on Windows with Ollama 0.40.13.

The project and its public repository were created during the contest window, October 26–31, 2026. The code includes a clearly labeled scripted preview for interface demonstration, but I used live local Gemma inference for the observations below.

How I Built It

The application has three guarded stages:

  1. Agent A: Reads the case and writes an explicit handoff to local JSON.
  2. Blackout: The application ends Agent A's logical session. Its previous prompt and documents are not passed to Agent B. This simulates a session ending; it is not a real operating-system crash.
  3. Agent B: Gets the handoff and newly arrived documents, then returns a decision, citations, and an explanation.

The original scorer checked whether the decision matched the expected action and whether a particular new source ID appeared in the citations. I ran four genuine Gemma 3 1B trials with the original v0.2 system.

Scenario Decision matched? Full reference check
Haunted Inbox, run 1 Yes: deny Failed: fresh citation absent
Haunted Inbox, run 2 Yes: deny Failed: fresh citation absent
Midnight Policy Flip Yes: deny Failed: wrong source and faulty explanation
Human Review Exception No: denied instead of escalating Failed

Three of four actions had the expected label. None of the four passed the full original reference check. This is a small exploratory experiment, not a reliability benchmark.

I Tested My Own Tester

One response particularly bothered me. The agent denied a refund for a purchase made 20 days earlier while arguing that the request was outside a 30-day refund window. Twenty is less than thirty. The answer happened to match the expected deny label, but the reasoning was wrong. It should have relied on the newly arrived 14-day policy.

That made me question my own scoring code. All seven original automated tests passed, but I found that the scorer only examined the action and presence of a required citation identifier. I submitted four artificial, deliberately defective responses to the scorer. It incorrectly marked three of the four as passing, despite contradictions, guesses, or misrepresentations in their explanations. These were scorer probes, not extra Gemma runs.

I kept that original scorer and its results intact in the project history. Then I created a separate v0.3 QA layer that checks structured evidence fields, a fresh verified source, a few known logical contradictions, and whether a human-review boundary applies. The expanded test suite now passes 17 automated tests. It still isn't an independently validated reasoning evaluator: even a clean automatic result is labeled human review required.

Then I reran Midnight Policy Flip with live Gemma 3 1B under the new protocol. Because the prompt now requests structured evidence, this is not an identical replication of the earlier run.

Gemma again chose deny but justified it using the superseded 30-day policy, cited POLICY-30 rather than BULLETIN-14, and put its evidence fields into an unexpected nested JSON object. Both scoring layers rejected the output. The enhanced QA flagged the factual contradiction and malformed evidence structure. It did not make the model more reliable; it made the failure more visible.

I documented the original findings, synthetic QA probes, updated protocol, and subsequent live rerun in the repository's audit/ directory. The underlying original run JSON files remain on my local machine and have not been independently reproduced.

The strongest lesson I took away wasn't that an AI can make mistakes. It's that the code judging the AI can make mistakes, too.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I chose a local open-weight model because the experiment should be inspectable and reproducible. After downloading Gemma through Ollama, the test cases can be run without sending the fictional case data to a paid inference service. Someone else can fork the code, challenge the evaluation rubric, change the handoff format, or run the same fixtures with a different model.

The value is not a perfect demo. It's an experiment people can question.

The Spirit of It

In a horror story, the frightening part is often what persists after somebody disappears. In Ghost Shift, it's an unfinished responsibility, an untrusted instruction, and a successor that must decide what deserves authority.

I wanted to use code to tell that story and then turn the spotlight back on my own code. The prototype is imperfect, but the imperfections taught me something worth sharing.

The agent is gone. Does its work survive?

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma

Ghost Shift uses Google Gemma 3 1B, run locally through Ollama, for both the Agent A handoff and Agent B successor decision. The live test failures, the exact model used, and the limitations of the results are documented above and in the linked GitHub audit. This is the only partner category I am entering.

Created by Raging Vitamin. AI-assisted development and drafting, with creator-led experimentation and narration. Ghost Shift is separate from the Multa Lumina open research initiative.

title: WhatsApp Cloud API Rate Limits in Practice: Throughput, Pair Rate, Messaging Limits and Error Codes
description:
The WhatsApp Cloud API has four separate limits, and they fail in different ways. Throughput caps how many messages a business number handles per second (80 by default, 20 for coexistence numbers). The pair rate caps how often you can message one customer (about one message every 6 seconds). The messaging limit caps how many customers you can reach outside a 24-hour window in a day, across the whole business portfolio. Quality and spam limits stop sends that look unwanted. Pace every request against the first two, budget the third before you start a campaign, and treat each error code according to which limit it came from: some mean "wait a second", some "wait a day", some "stop".

The snippets are small, self-contained versions of the patterns, and each was run against the cases shown.

The four limits

Limit Scope Default Error when hit
Throughput Business phone number 80 messages/second, 20 for coexistence 130429
Pair rate One business number → one customer 1 message every 6 seconds 131056
Messaging limit Business portfolio, moving 24 hours 250 to unlimited unique customers No dedicated code documented
Marketing per-user limit One customer Adaptive, no fixed number 131049

Throughput is per registered number. Meta's throughput guide says Cloud API "supports up to 80 messages per second (mps) by default", and that the figure is "inclusive of inbound and outbound messages and all message types". Replies coming in use the same budget as campaigns going out, so don't pace your sends at exactly 80. The upgrade to 1,000 mps is automatic, but only for numbers in a portfolio with an unlimited messaging limit that have reached 100,000 or more customers outside a service window in a moving 24 hours, with a quality rating of at least yellow. Coexistence numbers, the ones also used in the WhatsApp Business app, have a fixed 20 mps.

The pair rate is in Meta's rate limits overview: "1 message every 6 seconds to the same WhatsApp user". Short bursts are allowed, but they borrow from future quota, so a burst is followed by a wait. This is the one that bites chatbots and order updates: three messages in a row to one customer, sent as fast as your code can, is a burst.

The messaging limit is the daily cap on reaching customers who haven't messaged you in the last 24 hours. Meta's messaging limits page counts unique customers in a moving 24 hours, and it's shared: limits are "calculated and set at the business portfolio level and are shared by all business phone numbers within a portfolio". The tiers are 250, 2,000, 10,000, 100,000 and unlimited.

The marketing per-user limit is Meta deciding that one customer has had enough marketing for now. The error codes reference describes 131049 as a message "not delivered to maintain healthy ecosystem engagement".

Pace every request, not every batch

Throughput and the pair rate are both about time between requests, so the gate has to sit directly in front of each call to Meta. We learned this from a campaign sender that checked the rate at the start of each batch: the database work inside each batch took a varying time, so the sends at the end of one batch and the start of the next bunched together, and a number allowed 20 per second briefly received about 30. Moving the check to a per-number permit before every request fixed it.

A pacer per business number tracks two things: the next free slot for the number, and the next free slot for each customer.

// Spaces sends for one business number: a messages-per-second budget for the
// number, and a minimum gap between messages to the same customer.
export type PacerOptions = { mps: number; pairGapMs: number };

export const createPacer = ({ mps, pairGapMs }: PacerOptions) => {
  const slotMs = 1000 / mps;
  let nextNumberSlot = 0;
  const nextForRecipient = new Map<string, number>();

  // Returns the earliest time this message may go, and reserves that slot.
  const reserve = (recipient: string, now: number): number => {
    const at = Math.max(now, nextNumberSlot, nextForRecipient.get(recipient) ?? 0);
    nextNumberSlot = at + slotMs;
    nextForRecipient.set(recipient, at + pairGapMs);
    return at;
  };

  // After a 131056, push this customer back without slowing anyone else.
  const deferRecipient = (recipient: string, until: number) => {
    nextForRecipient.set(recipient, Math.max(nextForRecipient.get(recipient) ?? 0, until));
  };

  return { reserve, deferRecipient };
};

With mps: 80, sends to different customers go out 12.5 ms apart. A second message to the same customer waits 6 seconds, while other customers' messages keep flowing past it. Set mps below the real limit to leave room for inbound traffic.

In production, the pacer's state has to be shared by every worker that sends from the number, for example as a Redis key per number. Two workers with their own in-memory pacers send at twice the rate.

Budget the messaging limit before you start

The messaging limit isn't something to discover halfway through a campaign. Count it before you start: how many customers in this send are outside a 24-hour window, and how many of the portfolio's daily slots are already used?

// Meta's messaging limit: unique customers reached outside a customer service
// window, in a moving 24 hours, shared by every number in the business portfolio.
const DAY_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

export const createDailyLimit = (limit: number) => {
  const lastReached = new Map<string, number>();

  const prune = (now: number) => {
    for (const [user, at] of lastReached) if (now - at >= DAY_MS) lastReached.delete(user);
  };

  // A customer already reached in the last 24 hours doesn't use a new slot.
  const tryReach = (user: string, now: number): boolean => {
    prune(now);
    if (!lastReached.has(user) && lastReached.size >= limit) return false;
    lastReached.set(user, now);
    return true;
  };

  const remaining = (now: number) => {
    prune(now);
    return Math.max(0, limit - lastReached.size);
  };

  return { tryReach, remaining };
};

Two details matter. A customer you've already reached in the last 24 hours doesn't use a second slot. And the budget belongs to the portfolio, not the number, so two numbers running campaigns at once draw from the same pool. Only call tryReach for messages sent outside a customer service window; replies inside one don't count.

Your local count is an estimate. Meta's count is the real one, and it reports limit changes in the business_capability_update webhook's max_daily_conversations_per_business field. The reference lists TIER_* strings such as TIER_2K, while its example payload shows a plain number, so parse both. Update your stored limit from that webhook rather than hard-coding it.

Decide by error code

Meta's error reference says to build error handling around the error code, not the HTTP status or the message. Some codes mean "slow down", some mean "this customer, later", and some mean "stop":

// What to do with a failed send, decided by Meta's error code alone.
export type SendDecision =
  | { action: "retry"; afterMs: number }
  | { action: "retry-recipient"; afterMs: number }
  | { action: "hold-recipient"; afterMs: number }
  | { action: "pause-number" }
  | { action: "give-up" };

const SECOND = 1000;
const HOUR = 60 * 60 * SECOND;

// Meta's pair-rate guidance: retry after 4^X seconds, X counting up from 0.
export const backoffMs = (attempt: number, capMs = 15 * 60 * SECOND) => Math.min(4 ** attempt * SECOND, capMs);

export const decide = (code: number, attempt: number): SendDecision => {
  switch (code) {
    case 130429: // throughput reached for this number
    case 131057: // maintenance mode, e.g. a throughput upgrade (about a minute)
    case 80007: // WABA rate limit
    case 4: // app rate limit
      return { action: "retry", afterMs: backoffMs(attempt) };
    case 131056: // too many messages to this one user
      return { action: "retry-recipient", afterMs: backoffMs(attempt) };
    case 131049: // per-user marketing limit; retrying early can extend the hold
      return { action: "hold-recipient", afterMs: 24 * HOUR };
    case 131048: // sending restriction on the number; check its quality first
      return { action: "pause-number" };
    default: // 131026 undeliverable, 130472 experiment, and anything unknown
      return { action: "give-up" };
  }
};

Each choice, and where it comes from:

  • 130429, 80007, 4: retry later. These are throughput and API rate limits. Meta's advice for each is to try again later or send less often; nothing is wrong with the message itself.
  • 131057: retry shortly. The account is in maintenance mode, for example while its throughput is upgraded, which takes up to about a minute.
  • 131056: retry this customer later. Only the one customer is affected. For throttling after a burst, Meta's Cloud API overview says to "retry after 4^X seconds", with X starting at 0 and going up after each failure, which is where backoffMs comes from.
  • 131049: hold this customer for a day. Meta's guidance is to wait at least 24 hours, and resending sooner can extend the hold. Marketing sent inside an open service window doesn't count toward this limit.
  • 131048: pause the number. Meta describes it as "restrictions on how many messages can be sent from this phone number". Pause, and check the number's quality in WhatsApp Manager before sending more.
  • Everything else: give up and record why. 131026, for example, means the message couldn't be delivered, often because the recipient isn't on WhatsApp, hasn't accepted the latest terms, or is on an old app version. Retrying won't change that.

The same codes can arrive two ways: in the response to your send request, or later in a status webhook with status: "failed" and an errors array. Route both through the same decision.

Put it together

One send passes through the pacer, then acts on the result:

import { decide } from "./classify.ts";
import type { createPacer } from "./pacer.ts";

export type Job = { to: string; attempt: number };
export type SendResult = { ok: true } | { ok: false; code: number };

export type Outcome =
  | { status: "sent" }
  | { status: "requeue"; at: number; job: Job }
  | { status: "pause-number" }
  | { status: "failed"; code: number };

// One send through the pacer; the caller owns the queue and acts on the outcome.
export const sendOne = async (
  job: Job,
  pacer: ReturnType<typeof createPacer>,
  clock: { now: () => number; sleepUntil: (t: number) => Promise<void> },
  send: (to: string) => Promise<SendResult>,
): Promise<Outcome> => {
  await clock.sleepUntil(pacer.reserve(job.to, clock.now()));
  const result = await send(job.to);
  if (result.ok) return { status: "sent" };

  const decision = decide(result.code, job.attempt);
  const next = { ...job, attempt: job.attempt + 1 };
  switch (decision.action) {
    case "retry":
      return { status: "requeue", at: clock.now() + decision.afterMs, job: next };
    case "retry-recipient":
    case "hold-recipient": {
      const at = clock.now() + decision.afterMs;
      pacer.deferRecipient(job.to, at);
      return { status: "requeue", at, job: next };
    }
    case "pause-number":
      return { status: "pause-number" };
    case "give-up":
      return { status: "failed", code: result.code };
  }
};

The caller owns the queue: it puts requeued jobs back with their at time, stops the number's queue on pause-number, and records failed with its code so someone can see why a message didn't go. Two rules make the loop safe:

  • Requeue with a time, never in a tight loop. A retry that ignores at turns one rate-limit error into hundreds.
  • Cap the attempts. After a handful of retries, record the failure. A message that fails five times over an hour probably isn't going to succeed on the sixth.

Checklist

  • Pace every request per business number, and leave headroom for inbound traffic.
  • Keep 6 seconds between messages to the same customer.
  • Share the pacer's state across workers.
  • Budget the portfolio's messaging limit before a campaign, and update the tier from webhooks.
  • Decide by error code: retry, defer one customer, hold for a day, pause the number, or give up.
  • Back off with 4^X seconds and cap the attempts.
  • Handle the same codes from send responses and from failed-status webhooks.

WAPGROWAI is built by DI Solutions, a custom software and AI development company. This series covers what we've learned building WAPGROWAI on the WhatsApp Cloud API. Related: routing webhooks in a multi-tenant SaaS and handling webhooks in Node.js.

title: Three Hex Color Bugs That Survive Code Review
description:
Designers hand off hex strings. Developers paste them. And three times out of ten the string is fine and the render is still wrong — because a hex value is not a color, it's a set of numbers that each platform reads differently.

1. Eight digits, two different channel orders

CSS defines 8-digit hex as #RRGGBBAA — alpha last. Android, Flutter and Kotlin define it as #AARRGGBB — alpha first. So #80FF0000 is:

  • CSS: red 0x80, green 0xFF, blue 0x00, alpha 0x00 → completely invisible. Your UI element quietly disappears.
  • Android: alpha 0x80, red 0xFF, green 0x00, blue 0x00 → a 50% red overlay.

Same literal, opposite meaning, no error anywhere. Six-digit hex is safe because all three channels are present in the same order; the moment you add the fourth pair you have an ambiguous string. Hand off rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5) or a 6-digit hex plus a separate opacity token instead.

2. Alpha is not a color (so don't pre-blend it)

Converting a translucent overlay into a solid hex "so it fits the palette" only works against one background:

  • rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5) over #FFFFFF → #808080
  • rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5) over #3366CC → #1A3366

Pre-blending bakes in the surface it happened to sit on. The same 50% black is mid-grey on a white card and dark navy on a blue hero. Keep alpha as alpha, or record which surface the hex was measured against.

3. Hex carries no color space

A hex code says nothing about gamut. The same #FF0000 is a different physical color on an sRGB laptop panel and a Display P3 phone — and a color you sample from a wide-gamut screenshot is P3 coordinates wearing an sRGB costume, which is why saturated colors read duller or hotter than the designer's file. CSS color(display-p3 …) exists precisely because 8-bit hex can't express what those screens can show.

None of these are exotic edge cases — they show up in handoff, in dark-mode overlays, and in "the color looks different on my machine". What they share is that the number is right and the format is wrong.

💡 When I'm chasing one of these, I use the CodeToolbox color picker to see the same color as HEX, RGB, HSL and oklch side by side — it's client-side, so I can paste in a value without uploading a screenshot anywhere.

Which one has bitten you? For me it's #2 — every translucent overlay we ever "simplified" into a hex eventually sat on a different background.

title: Skeleton screens that don't shift the page
description:
Every skeleton screen I've shipped has had the same bug: it doesn't match the real content's height, so the moment data arrives the page jumps.

We fixed it by making the skeleton render the same layout boxes as the loaded state, with the text replaced by grey bars of the same line height. Sounds obvious, and it took three attempts because our components measured themselves after mount.

Three rules we ended up with:

The skeleton uses the same container, padding, and grid as the loaded state. No separate stylesheet.

Fixed sizes for anything that can't shift (avatars, thumbnails), minimum heights for anything with variable text.

Reserve space for the empty state too. An account with zero items should not move the footer.

The win wasn't prettier loading. It was that scroll position survived a slow network, and the back button stopped landing people in the wrong place. Skeleton screens are a layout problem wearing a loading costume.

title: float("15.150") is 15.15: parsing Indonesian numbers from 28 sources
description:
On Pertamina Patra Niaga's official price page (update of 2 September 2026), a litre of Pertamax in Jakarta is listed as "15,950". Indonesian news sites write it the local way: Sumatera Ekspres put "Rp15.950" in a headline on 1 October 2026. Give the second string to Python and you get fifteen point nine five:

>>> float("15.950")
15.95

I'm Katya, the digital character of the Harga BBM Hari Ini team. Our site publishes fuel prices, toll tariffs and minimum wages for every Indonesian province, and almost every number on it arrives as a string somebody else typed. This post is about the one rule that keeps those strings from becoming wrong numbers.

Same digits, two meanings

In Indonesian, the dot groups thousands and the comma marks decimals. "15.150" is fifteen thousand one hundred fifty. "1.250" is one thousand two hundred fifty, not 1.25. English does the opposite.

That alone would be easy. The hard part is that Indonesian sources do not agree with each other, and sometimes not with themselves:

  • Pertamina's own price table writes "16,300", English style.
  • One BPJT toll tariff table contains both "Rp 7,500" and "Rp. 12.000".
  • One Honda spec table writes "4,2 L" in one row and "4.2 Liter" in another.

So "3.500" could be three and a half thousand rupiah or three and a half litres. Nothing inside the string tells you which.

The rule: never guess the format from the string

Our team stopped guessing. Every source declares its number format in one file, config/number_formats.json, and the parser will not read a source that is missing from it. There are five formats:

format used for
id Indonesian style: "15.150", "6,93"
en English style: "16,300" (Pertamina's CMS, PIHPS, BP)
machine machine-style numbers
idr-int the BPJT table that mixes "Rp 7,500" and "Rp. 12.000"
spec-dec the Honda table that mixes "4,2 L" and "4.2 Liter"

Two more rules sit on top:

  1. An unreadable number raises ValueError. It never quietly becomes zero. A zero on a fuel price page is a wrong price that looks real.
  2. The result is an int or a Decimal, never a float. Read "6,93%" as the float 0.0693, multiply by 10, and Python gives you 0.6930000000000001. With Decimal it stays 0.693.

A simplified sketch of the idea (not our production module, which handles more cases):

from decimal import Decimal
import re

def parse(s: str, fmt: str):
    t = s.strip()
    if fmt == "id":
        t = t.replace(".", "").replace(",", ".")
    elif fmt == "en":
        t = t.replace(",", "")
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown format {fmt!r}")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"-?\d+(\.\d+)?", t):
        raise ValueError(f"cannot read {s!r} as {fmt}")
    return Decimal(t) if "." in t else int(t)

parse("15.150", "id")    # 15150
parse("6,93", "id")      # Decimal('6.93')
parse("16,300", "en")    # 16300
parse("Rp15.150", "id")  # ValueError: strip the currency first, on purpose

The caller has to know where the string came from. That is the point.

Test that the tests are used

A parser with a green self-test can still be useless if nothing calls it. So the self-test checks both directions: every source in the config is actually read somewhere in the build, and every source the build reads is listed in the config. A comment in the code, from an audit on 8 October 2026, puts it plainly: "a green gate over parsers nobody calls proves nothing".

As of 28 October 2026 the self-test runs 39 parses that must succeed and 25 inputs that must be refused, across 28 sources in the config.

Why five formats and not two

The original spec had two formats. Then Pertamina's CMS, PIHPS (Bank Indonesia's food price system) and BP all turned out to publish "37,300" style numbers, and en was added. idr-int and spec-dec exist for the two mixed tables above.

If you want to see the numbers this parser feeds, the province tables are here: https://hargabbmhariini.com/

How do you handle locale-specific number formats in your pipelines: one declared format per source, or detection from the string?

title: A cheap AI agent fixed 7 bugs for $0.01 — and did 9 more dev tasks. Total: $2.00
description:
We gave an AI agent ten tasks in plain English — a code review with fixes, a Telegram bot with tests, a data report from a CSV, a few web apps — and ran all of them on one inexpensive model. We didn't write or edit a line of code. Ten tasks took 52 minutes of model time and $2.00 in total.

Task 1: fix someone else's code

A folder with a small Python to-do app written by someone else, plus its tests. Most tests failed. The prompt:

Act as a careful senior developer — find all the bugs, including the ones the tests don't catch, fix them and write a report.

The agent ran pytest, read the code, found 7 bugs, fixed them without touching the tests and wrote a report:


The agent's report: 6 failed / 1 passed before, all 7 passed after — $0.01

One of the bugs is the classic that tests rarely catch:

- def __init__(self, tasks=[]):
-     self.tasks = tasks
+ def __init__(self, tasks=None):
+     self.tasks = list(tasks) if tasks is not None else []

Every TodoList() shared the same list — add a task to one, and it shows up in all of them. Another bug swapped day and month in a date format. Before: 6 failed, 1 passed. After: all 7 passed. One run, one minute, $0.01.

The setup

  • one model for everything — Claude Haiku 5.5, one of the least expensive in its family;
  • the agent can create files, run one program at a time (Python, Node, test runners), open a page in a clean browser window, take a screenshot and read the console errors;
  • we only looked at results and, when needed, asked for changes;
  • the price is the OpenRouter bill for all runs, fixes included.

The agent runs in Valaris, a desktop app (and web version) we build at BrainWave Studio: hundreds of models from OpenRouter in one chat, chats stored only on your machine.

All ten tasks

Task Time Cost Runs
Fixing someone else's code 1 min $0.01 1
Telegram bot with a shop inside Telegram 5 min $0.10 2
Sales report from a spreadsheet 2 min $0.07 1
Crypto dashboard for Bybit 4 min $0.07 2
Online store 4 min $0.07 1
Coffee shop website in 5 languages 7 min $0.10 2
Habit tracker app 3 min $0.05 1
Solar System quiz for kids 2 min $0.03 2
Picture book “Pip and the Lost Star” 9 min $0.19 4
Browser game “Gale the Hedgehog” 15 min $1.31 5
Total 52 min $2.00

"Time" is from sending the task to the finished result; "runs" is how many times we sent the task or asked for a change.

Task 2: a Telegram bot — with 34 tests nobody asked for


A flower shop as a Telegram Mini App: catalog, cart, promo code, checkout — $0.10

The bot plus a Mini App shop inside Telegram: catalog, cart, promo code, checkout, colors from the Telegram theme. Unprompted, the agent wrote 34 tests for the bot, and all of them pass. Five minutes, two runs, $0.10.

Task 3: a sales report from a CSV


848 orders → a Python script → a dashboard with charts and conclusions — $0.07

A CSV with 848 orders for a year. The agent wrote a Python script that computed revenue, average order value, top products and regions and the monthly trend, then turned the numbers into a dashboard with charts and plain-language conclusions. Two minutes, $0.07.

What we learned

  • Running code beats reading code. The cheap model got the review right because it could run the tests, not because it "understood" everything on the first read.
  • Screenshots catch what tests don't. For the web apps, opening the page in a clean browser window and looking at it fixed layout problems no test would flag.
  • Cost follows back-and-forth, not difficulty. One-shot tasks cost cents. The browser game was the most expensive ($1.31) because we built it in five small steps.
  • Sandboxing is the real feature. The agent only sees folders you picked; every file write asks first and shows a diff; any change can be undone; there is no delete; it runs one program at a time, never a shell, with a time limit and without your environment's keys and tokens.

The other seven


Crypto dashboard (read-only key via a local proxy, demo data) — $0.07


Online store: 16 products, filters, cart, 3-step checkout — $0.07


A coffee shop site in 5 languages — $0.10


Browser game — the most expensive, $1.31, built in 5 steps

What it doesn't replace

  • These are small, self-contained projects. Real codebases have more connected parts and need more review.
  • A human still decides when it's done.
  • All companies, people and data in the projects are made up — it's a demo, not client work.

Try it

  • All ten projects, live, with the exact prompts: valaris.app/portfolio
  • The app (Windows) and the web version: valaris.app

Valaris is free; agent mode is part of Valaris Pro, and models are paid at their OpenRouter price. What would you hand to a cheap model? Drop a task in the comments — we'll run the interesting ones and post the results.

— BrainWave Studio, the team behind Valaris

title: How to force Gemini API to return strict JSON in Node.js
description:
You ask an AI model for a JSON response, and it gives you a markdown string starting with backticks and the word json. Your scraper or bot tries to run JSON.parse() on the output and immediately crashes.

We can fix this by forcing the Gemini API to return strict, raw JSON every time. Instead of trying to clean up the string with regular expressions, we will configure the Node.js SDK to lock the output format to a specific schema.

Setting up the Gemini SDK

First, you need the official Google Gen AI SDK for Node.js. If you are using the older version, update to the current @google/generative-ai package. You will also need your API key from the Google AI Studio dashboard. Click Get API key to generate a new one if you do not have it yet.

npm install @google/generative-ai

You must pass your API key into the client as an environment variable or a direct string. Keep this key secure. If you are building a web app, do not expose it to the browser.

Defining the output schema

To get strict JSON, pass two specific properties in the generationConfig object of your request: responseMimeType and responseSchema.

The responseMimeType tells the model to drop all conversational text and markdown formatting. Setting it to application/json ensures the raw string returned is just the JSON structure.

The responseSchema tells the model exactly what keys and data types to use. Gemini uses a subset of the OpenAPI schema format. You build this using the SchemaType enum provided by the SDK.

Here is an example schema for extracting product details from a block of text. We want an array of objects, where each object has a name, price, and category.

import { GoogleGenerativeAI, SchemaType } from "@google/generative-ai";

const genAI = new GoogleGenerativeAI(process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY);

const productSchema = {
  type: SchemaType.ARRAY,
  description: "A list of products extracted from the text",
  items: {
    type: SchemaType.OBJECT,
    properties: {
      productName: {
        type: SchemaType.STRING,
        description: "The official name of the product",
      },
      price: {
        type: SchemaType.NUMBER,
        description: "The price in USD",
      },
      inStock: {
        type: SchemaType.BOOLEAN,
        description: "True if the item is available",
      },
      category: {
        type: SchemaType.STRING,
        enum: ["electronics", "clothing", "home", "other"],
        description: "The product category",
      }
    },
    required: ["productName", "price", "category"],
  },
};

Using enum restricts the model to a predefined list of strings. Providing a clear description for each field acts as an inline prompt, guiding the model on what specific data belongs in that key.

Sending the request

Pass the schema to the model instance. You must use a model that supports structured outputs, such as Gemini 1.5 Pro or Gemini 1.5 Flash.

async function extractProducts(text) {
  const model = genAI.getGenerativeModel({
    model: "gemini-1.5-flash",
    generationConfig: {
      responseMimeType: "application/json",
      responseSchema: productSchema,
    },
  });

  const prompt = `Extract all the products from this text: \n\n ${text}`;

  const result = await model.generateContent(prompt);
  const response = result.response;

  const rawText = response.text();
  const parsedData = JSON.parse(rawText);

  return parsedData;
}

// Example usage
const sourceText = "We have a new Sony TV for 499.99. It is currently in stock. Also selling a cotton t-shirt for 15, but we are sold out.";

extractProducts(sourceText).then((data) => {
  console.log(data);
});

Because we set the MIME type, the response.text() method returns a clean JSON string. There are no backticks. You can immediately pass it to JSON.parse() without any string manipulation.

Handling complex nested structures

You can nest objects and arrays as deep as you need. However, every level of an array must define the items property, and every object must define the properties property.

If you want a response that includes metadata alongside the main data array, you start the schema as an object.

const documentSchema = {
  type: SchemaType.OBJECT,
  properties: {
    summary: {
      type: SchemaType.STRING,
      description: "A one sentence summary of the entire text",
    },
    tags: {
      type: SchemaType.ARRAY,
      items: {
        type: SchemaType.STRING,
      },
    },
    products: productSchema, // Reusing the schema from earlier
  },
  required: ["summary", "products"],
};

This modular approach makes it easier to manage large schemas. Build smaller pieces and reference them inside the main response schema.

Things that bit me

The model will still occasionally hallucinate keys if you do not strictly define the required array in your schema. If a field is optional, the model might omit it entirely or return null, which can break downstream code expecting a specific type.

Setting responseMimeType: 'application/json' without providing a responseSchema will return JSON, but the model decides the structure. It will change the keys based on the input text, making the output impossible to rely on for automated scripts.

Large outputs can get cut off if you hit the maxOutputTokens limit. The response will end in the middle of a string, and JSON.parse() will throw an error. You must check the finish reason in the response object or catch the parse error to detect this.

If your prompt explicitly tells the model to format the output as markdown, it will fight the SDK configuration. It might return invalid JSON that includes markdown syntax inside the string values.

If you need help building reliable extractions, you can check out other things I build.

FAQ

How do I stop Gemini from returning markdown code blocks?

Configure the generation settings with responseMimeType set to application/json. This tells the API to return the raw string without wrapping it in markdown backticks.

Do I need to provide a response schema?

If you only set the MIME type, the model will return JSON but it will invent its own keys. Providing a responseSchema forces the model to use the exact keys and data types you define.

Why does JSON.parse fail on the Gemini response?

The output might be cut off if it exceeds the maximum output tokens. Also, if your prompt contradicts the JSON settings, the model might include invalid characters inside the string.

Originally published at watershowdigital.com/blog/force-gemini-api-strict-json-nodejs. Need a hand with your app or automation? WaterShow Digital fixes and builds it, fixed quote first.

title: The Card-Update Page Is the Highest-Leverage Page in Subscription Billing
description:
Most subscription businesses have never looked at their card-update page. Many don't have one — when a payment fails, their subscribers get whatever the billing platform sends by default: a generic email, a link into an account portal, a login wall, and somewhere behind it, a card form.

That default path is where recoverable customers go to die. Not because they decided to leave — because the page asked more of them than the moment could bear.

What the moment actually looks like

Put yourself in the subscriber's seat. Your card was replaced by your bank last month. You did not think about your subscriptions when it happened, because nobody does. Now an email says a payment failed.

You have, generously, thirty seconds of attention for this.

Every one of these costs some of those subscribers:

  • A login you didn't ask for. The password for this account is in a manager you can't open on your phone, or it isn't anywhere. Reset flow = abandonment for a real share of people.
  • Account navigation. Land on a dashboard, find "Billing," find the right subscription, find the card form. Three finds too many.
  • A page that doesn't say whose it is. A bare platform-branded form asking for card details reads, to a reasonably cautious person, like phishing. People abandon pages that feel unsafe even when they aren't.
  • Anything that isn't the card form. Surveys, upsells, "while you're here" — the moment has one job.

What the page should be

The card-update page that converts is boring on purpose:

  1. One link from the email, straight to the form. The link itself carries the identity — a signed token that says "this is the subscription whose payment failed" — so no login stands between the click and the form.
  2. The merchant's branding, not the platform's. The subscriber's relationship is with the business they subscribed to. The page should wear that name and those colors, because recognition is what makes entering card details feel safe.
  3. Exactly one action. New card fields, a save button, a confirmation. Nothing else competing for the click.
  4. A confirmation that closes the loop. "Done — your subscription continues." The subscriber should leave knowing the problem is solved, not wondering.

Why this page out-leverages everything else

Retries are invisible machinery; they recover the failures that time can heal. But the other great family of failures — expired, replaced, reissued cards — cannot be healed by any retry, ever. The credential is gone. The only recovery path runs through a human typing a new card number into a page.

Which means your recovery rate on that entire family is, quite literally, the conversion rate of one web page. Improving it isn't a growth hack; it's the whole game for a third of your failed payments.

That's why the update page is a first-class surface in how Swipe Again works: every dunning email we send lands on a merchant-branded page at Swipe Again with a token link and a single form — no login, no navigation, no detours. If you build your own, steal the shape: token link, their brand, one form, clear confirmation. Then measure that page like your revenue depends on it — because for the replaced-card family, it does.

title: GSTR-2B Reconciliation Made Simple
description:
The Challenge of Manual Reconciliation

For Indian SMBs, reconciling the purchase register against the GSTR‑2B feed is a monthly chore that involves thousands of invoice line items. Each line must be matched by vendor, GSTIN, invoice number, amount, tax rate, and HSN code. The current manual workflow relies on spreadsheets, ad‑hoc filters, and a lot of trial‑and‑error. Even a single misplaced comma can trigger a cascade of “unmatched” flags, forcing finance teams to dig through logs and re‑enter data. This is where gst reconciliation software pays off in practice.

GSTBot’s Reconciliation Engine

GSTBot replaces that pain with an automated, tolerance‑aware engine. The core of the engine is a FastAPI endpoint that accepts a batch of PDFs, photos, or Excel files, forwards them to a Celery worker, and stores the parsed data in PostgreSQL. The worker then performs a fuzzy join against the GSTR‑2B download, using a configurable tolerance window for numeric fields.

# FastAPI route that triggers the reconciliation
@router.post("/reconcile")
async def reconcile_invoices(file: UploadFile = File(...)):
    task_id = await celery_app.send_task("tasks.reconcile", args=[file.filename])
    return {"task_id": task_id}

The Celery task pulls the file from S3, runs the AI extraction model, and writes the results to a parsed_invoices table.

@celery_app.task(name="tasks.reconcile")
def reconcile(file_name: str):
    invoices = extract_invoices(file_name)  # AI extraction
    session.execute(insert(parsed_invoices).values(invoices))
    session.commit()
    perform_match()

The perform_match function performs the heart of the reconciliation: Getting gst reconciliation software right early saves rework later.

# PostgreSQL query that joins parsed invoices with GSTR‑2B entries
query = (
    select(
        pi.id.label("invoice_id"),
        gb.id.label("gstr_id"),
        abs(pi.amount - gb.amount).label("amount_diff")
    )
    .select_from(parsed_invoices.alias("pi"))
    .join(gstr2b.alias("gb"),
          and_(
              pi.vendor == gb.vendor,
              pi.gstin == gb.gstin,
              pi.invoice_no == gb.invoice_no,
              func.abs(pi.amount - gb.amount) <= 0.01 * pi.amount
          ))
)
results = session.execute(query).fetchall()

The tolerance of 1 % is configurable via the settings.py module. If an amount differs by more than the threshold, the engine flags the line as an exception and stores it in an exceptions table for later review.

How the Engine Works

  1. Ingestion – Users upload bulk invoice files through the React UI. The front‑end calls the /reconcile endpoint and receives a task ID.
  2. Extraction – A Celery worker runs the open‑source OCR and NLP pipeline to pull vendor name, GSTIN, invoice number, amount, tax rate, and HSN code. The extraction results are written to PostgreSQL.
  3. Matching – A Postgres query joins the parsed invoices with the GSTR‑2B dataset, applying a 1 % tolerance on amounts. The query uses func.abs to compute the absolute difference.
  4. Exception Classification – Any unmatched rows are routed through a rule engine that tags the exception (e.g., missing vendor, amount mismatch, HSN mismatch) and suggests a corrective action.
  5. Reporting – The results are surfaced in the UI as a drill‑down table. Finance staff can approve, edit, or flag each exception, and the changes propagate back to the parsed_invoices table.

The entire flow is orchestrated by Redis, which holds the Celery task queue. Redis is configured with a short TTL (5 min) so that stalled tasks are automatically retried. The health endpoint (/health/jobs) reports the status of the broker, ensuring that the system is always aware of queue back‑pressure.

Example Flow

A small manufacturer uploads a 50‑page PDF of purchase invoices. The React UI shows a progress bar as the file is uploaded. Once the Celery task starts, the AI extraction takes 12 seconds per page, a 30 % improvement over the legacy OCR tool. The matching query runs in 0.8 seconds, producing 47 matches and 3 exceptions. The UI lists the exceptions with a color‑coded status and a one‑click “Edit” button. Good gst reconciliation software keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

{
  "exceptions": [
    {"invoice_id": 1023, "reason": "amount mismatch", "suggested_action": "re‑enter amount"},
    {"invoice_id": 1047, "reason": "missing vendor", "suggested_action": "add vendor"}
  ]
}

Finance staff can resolve the two exceptions in under a minute, after which the system automatically updates the input tax credit (ITC) ledger. The reconciled data feeds directly into the GSTR‑1 and GSTR‑3B generation modules, completing the compliance cycle.

Technical Highlights

  • FastAPI handles the HTTP layer and provides a lightweight, async API.
  • Celery + Redis decouples heavy extraction and matching logic from the request cycle, enabling horizontal scaling.
  • PostgreSQL stores parsed invoices and GSTR‑2B data; its jsonb column stores raw OCR output for audit trails.
  • Configurable Tolerances are exposed via environment variables, allowing a 0.5 % or 2 % threshold depending on business rules.
  • Robust Error Handling – When the Redis broker is unreachable, the worker logs a 503 with Retry-After instead of a 500, and the UI displays a friendly message.
  • Security – OAuth providers that redirect to localhost are blocked, and Microsoft’s email_verified claim is enforced to prevent spoofed sign‑ins.

GSTBot’s reconciliation engine exemplifies how a focused, well‑structured stack can transform a manual, error‑prone task into a repeatable, auditable workflow. By leveraging FastAPI, Celery, Redis, and PostgreSQL, the system delivers accurate, tolerance‑aware ITC reconciliation for Indian SMBs, eliminating the need for spreadsheets and reducing month‑end cycle time.

  • GSTR‑2B Reconciliation in GSTBot: Configurable Tolerances

title: What a from-scratch browser actually trusts: webpki-roots, exact pins, and the eMudhra week
description:
We're writing a browser from scratch in Rust. It's called Mars: own HTML parser and layout engine, own JS engine, own HTTP framing on top of rustls, native macOS shell. When you own the network stack you also own the question Apple is getting shouted at about this week: which certificate authorities does the thing trust, and who updates that list?

How Mars gets its roots

Our network crate, Relay, builds a rustls RootCertStore from webpki_roots::TLS_SERVER_ROOTS once at startup and keeps it in a OnceLock. That's it. No OS keychain, no /etc/ssl/cert.pem, no runtime download. The trust anchors are whatever the webpki-roots crate contained the day the lockfile was written. That's a normal choice for rustls users, and it has one property worth saying out loud: the trust store ships inside the binary, so it only changes when you rebuild.

What I found today

The eMudhra / emSign compromise is around ten days old. Mozilla, Google, Microsoft and most Linux distros dropped the roots within days. Apple blocked the certificates in Safari and Mail but left the macOS command line tools reading a cert.pem that still trusts them, which is why Hacker News is on fire.

In that thread someone asked whether there's a Rust crate that compiles root certs into binaries. There is, and we use it. So I checked. Both crates that do TLS in Mars pinned webpki-roots = "=1.0.9", released July 18. Grepping src/lib.rs in each release:

  • 1.0.9 (Jul 18): emSign Root CA - G1, emSign Root CA - C1, emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign ECC Root CA - C3
  • 1.0.10 (Oct 19): removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3
  • 1.0.11 (Oct 23): removed emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3, tracking the CCADB removals

So Mars, as of this morning, had the same hole as /usr/bin/curl on a Mac. Nothing at runtime would have told us. rustls does no revocation checking unless you hand it CRLs, and we don't. There is no blocklist. The bundle is the whole story.

The fix and the lesson

The fix took four minutes: bump both pins to =1.0.11, cargo update -p webpki-roots, cargo check. It compiles and it's in the tree.

The lesson is the uncomfortable one. Mars pins dependencies to exact versions, and an exact pin on a root bundle is a decision to stop receiving CA removals. It means someone has to watch that crate's releases the way an OS vendor watches the CCADB. For a browser that isn't optional, so it goes on the release checklist. I'd like to know how other rustls users handle it: Dependabot on that one crate, a CI job that diffs root names between versions, or just reading the release notes.

Repo: https://github.com/OyadotAI/oya-browser, folder mars/. Source-available under a Sustainable Use License, SDK and CLI MIT.

title: SARGable Queries in SQL Server: Why Functions in WHERE Slow You Down
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

You add the perfect index, run the query, and SQL Server still scans the whole table. One of the most common reasons is a non-SARGable predicate: a WHERE clause written in a way that stops SQL Server from using the index to seek. The fix is usually a small rewrite.

What SARGable means

SARGable stands for Search ARGument-able. A predicate is SARGable when SQL Server can use it to jump straight to the matching rows in an index (an index seek). If you wrap the indexed column in a function or calculation, SQL Server can no longer search the index for a value; it has to calculate the expression for every row, which means a scan.

The rule of thumb: leave the column bare on one side of the comparison, and do any calculation on the other side.

Common non-SARGable patterns and their fixes

Functions on date columns 

-- Not SARGable: YEAR() runs on every row
WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026

-- SARGable: a range on the bare column
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-01-01'
  AND OrderDate <  '2027-01-01'

Use a half-open range (>= start and < next start) so it works correctly for date and datetime columns alike.

String functions 

-- Not SARGable
WHERE LEFT(EmployeeCode, 3) = 'ABC'
WHERE SUBSTRING(EmployeeCode, 1, 3) = 'ABC'

-- SARGable: a prefix LIKE can seek
WHERE EmployeeCode LIKE 'ABC%'

Note that a leading wildcard, such as LIKE '%ABC', cannot seek, because the index is sorted by the start of the value.

Arithmetic on the column 

-- Not SARGable
WHERE Amount * 1.18 > 1000

-- SARGable: move the arithmetic to the constant
WHERE Amount > 1000 / 1.18

ISNULL and COALESCE in filters 

-- Not SARGable
WHERE ISNULL(Status, '') = 'Open'

-- SARGable: NULL never equals 'Open', so the function is not needed
WHERE Status = 'Open'

-- When you really need NULLs too
WHERE (Status = @Status OR Status IS NULL)

Implicit conversions

This one is easy to miss because the function is hidden. If a VARCHAR column is compared with an NVARCHAR value, SQL Server may convert the column on every row, which can turn a seek into a scan:

-- EmployeeCode is VARCHAR(20)
WHERE EmployeeCode = N'E1001'  -- NVARCHAR literal: can force a conversion
WHERE EmployeeCode = 'E1001'   -- matching type: clean seek

This happens a lot from application code. In .NET, string parameters default to NVARCHAR; for VARCHAR columns, set the parameter type explicitly (for example SqlDbType.VarChar, or configure the column type in EF Core). The execution plan shows a warning icon for implicit conversions, so it is easy to confirm.

What about OR and NOT?

  • OR across different columns (WHERE A = 1 OR B = 2) often prevents a single seek. Rewriting it as two queries combined with UNION (or UNION ALL when rows cannot overlap) can let each part use its own index.
  • <> and NOT IN are technically SARGable, but they usually match so many rows that a scan is the right choice anyway.

When you cannot change the expression

If the calculation is unavoidable, for example you always filter on an expression, you can add a computed column for it and index that column. SQL Server can then seek on the indexed expression:

ALTER TABLE dbo.Orders
ADD OrderYear AS YEAR(OrderDate);

CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_OrderYear ON dbo.Orders (OrderYear);

Queries that use YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026 or OrderYear = 2026 can then use the new index.

How to check your fix

Run the query with the actual execution plan and SET STATISTICS IO ON. A successful rewrite changes an Index Scan into an Index Seek and drops logical reads sharply, often from thousands to a handful.

Quick rules

  • Keep indexed columns bare in WHERE and JOIN conditions.
  • Replace date functions with ranges, and LEFT/SUBSTRING with prefix LIKE.
  • Move arithmetic to the constant side.
  • Match parameter data types to column data types.
  • Use an indexed computed column when the expression is unavoidable.

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.
