title: Mistral Large 4 vs Gemini 4 Carbon: Open Weights vs Restricted Access
description:
A model announcement can look like a product release even when most developers cannot use the model yet. That distinction matters this week: Mistral says Mistral Large 4 weights are now available, while Google's October 28 Gemini 4 Carbon announcement describes a restricted initial rollout to selected cyber defenders and trusted partners. One option can be downloaded and deployed under its license; the other is not yet generally available to developers.

So which one should a team evaluate? The answer is not “whichever benchmark is higher.” As of October 29, 2026, this is primarily a comparison of access paths and rollout plans, not a fair, hands-on contest between two generally available models.

This public-source breakdown separates announced capability from current availability and offers a practical checklist for deciding whether either release is actionable for your team. No hands-on comparison is claimed.

The short answer

  • Need a model you can try now? Mistral says Large 4 is available through its public preview API on Mistral Studio. Confirm the current terms, limits, and pricing for your account before planning production use.
  • Need Gemini 4 Carbon now? Google's announcement says access starts with a subset of cyber defenders, then expands to trusted partners through its Fairwind program. Developer, business, and consumer access is a later step, not the launch-day offer.
  • Need downloadable weights today? Mistral says the weights are available through Hugging Face and names vLLM and SGLang as deployment options. Read the model card and license before committing to self-hosting.
  • Need a model choice for production? Wait until both options are actually accessible to your team, then run the same evaluation against your workload.

That is less exciting than declaring a winner. It is also more useful to an engineering team planning a real integration.

What each company has actually announced

Mistral's October 6 post introduced Large 4 as a public preview and said the preview API was available on Mistral Studio. Mistral described it as a one-trillion-parameter natively multimodal model, with 52 billion active parameters, and promised weights by the end of October. Its newer release post says the weights are available, alongside an updated model, improved reasoning efficiency, three reasoning modes, and additional evaluations. Mistral's model documentation classifies Large 4 as open-weight. Check the actual model card and license terms for your use case rather than treating “open-weight” as a complete licensing summary.

Google DeepMind's October 28 announcement calls Gemini 4 Carbon its strongest model for cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. Google cites its own and external benchmark results, including 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0, 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, 54.8% on ExploitGym, and 71.0% on CWE-bench. These are company-reported results; they should be interpreted with each benchmark's task definition and scoring methodology, not as a universal ranking of coding ability.

The access language is the key difference. Google says it is beginning with a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually add trusted partners through Fairwind. It says access for developers, businesses, and consumers through product surfaces will come later, after feedback and guardrail iteration. Carbon's announcement gives an introductory launch price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens at a 95% discount. That announced price does not mean every developer can call the model today. Mistral's current model documentation lists API rates of $1.36 per million input tokens, $0.14 per million cached input tokens, and $4.18 per million output tokens. These API rates are not directly equivalent to the cost of self-hosting the weights.

The comparison is therefore not “open versus closed” in the abstract. Mistral says its weights are now published, but deployment still depends on the model card, license, hardware, and serving stack. Google describes Carbon as a restricted rollout, with broader developer access later. Confirm the live terms and availability before making a production plan.

Availability is part of the product

Teams often compare models as if every named release were an API endpoint waiting to be called. In practice, access can decide a project before quality does.

A restricted preview may require an application, an invitation, or a particular use case. A public API may still have preview terms, quotas, changing model behavior, or no production service commitment. Downloadable weights can give deployment flexibility, but only after the artifacts, license, serving requirements, and support path are clear.

Treat these as separate questions:

  • Can our team access it now? Check the account and product surface, not just the announcement headline.
  • Can we use it for our intended workload? Preview participation may be limited to certain organizations or use cases.
  • Can we rely on it in production? Verify terms, quotas, availability commitments, data handling, and support.
  • Can we deploy it where policy requires? For a hosted model, inspect provider controls. For weights, inspect license and infrastructure needs.
  • Can we measure it fairly? Compare outputs only after both models are accessible under conditions your team can document.

Availability is not an administrative footnote. It determines whether a result can be reproduced, whether a prototype can move to production, and how much work the team must do to get there.

A decision matrix for this week

Mistral Large 4 public preview API

  • The stated advantage is that interested developers can try the preview through Mistral Studio.
  • The announcement describes a large multimodal model aimed at coding, agentic workflows, and other complex tasks.
  • Mistral says the weights are now downloadable; inspect the model card, license, and hardware requirements before designing a self-hosting plan.
  • Because it is a preview, confirm the service conditions that matter to your workload instead of assuming the endpoint is production-ready.

Gemini 4 Carbon restricted rollout

  • The stated advantage is a model Google positions for cybersecurity and long-horizon work, with published benchmark claims worth investigating.
  • Initial availability is deliberately restricted to selected cyber defenders and trusted partners.
  • General developer, business, and consumer access is not available at announcement time; Google says it intends to expand access later.
  • The announced token price is an introductory future launch price, not evidence of current API access.

Neither as a production decision yet

  • If your team cannot access a model, there is no honest way to compare its behavior in your environment.
  • If the other is only a preview, a positive test may still not establish production readiness.
  • Use the gap to prepare a benchmark set, evaluation criteria, and access questions. That work remains useful after the rollout changes.

Build the evaluation before access arrives

A useful model evaluation does not need thousands of prompts. It needs representative tasks, a clear scoring rule, and a record of what was actually tested.

1. Select 10 to 20 realistic cases. Include normal tasks and edge cases. For security work, use authorized, non-production test material. For coding, choose issues with tests or other observable acceptance criteria.

2. Define success before seeing outputs. Specify what must be correct, what errors are unacceptable, and when a human reviewer must intervene. Do not use “sounds convincing” as the score.

3. Keep a reproducible test record. Store the prompt, model identifier, date, settings, tools enabled, raw output, and scoring result. Record access mode and any preview restrictions too.

4. Measure the whole workflow. Capture latency, retries, usage cost where available, reviewer time, and repair effort. A model that produces a strong first answer but needs repeated correction may be less useful than the headline score suggests.

5. Separate quality from availability. Mark a model “not tested” when you lack access. Do not fill the gap with a vendor benchmark, a social post, or another team's anecdote. Keep vendor-published results in a separate column.

A compact scorecard:

  • Access route and eligibility: ___
  • Task success rate: ___ / ___
  • Critical errors: ___
  • Median and worst-case latency: ___
  • Cost or infrastructure estimate: ___
  • Human review and repair time: ___
  • Preview, license, or governance blockers: ___
  • Reproduction details saved: yes / no

This avoids the benchmark trap. A vendor's result can tell you what to investigate; it cannot tell you how a model handles your team's repository, policies, or failure cases.

What to verify before acting on the headlines

For Mistral Large 4: Verify the official weights, model card, license, included artifacts, and whether your serving stack can support the architecture and required throughput. The one-trillion total parameter figure and 52-billion active parameter figure describe different aspects of a mixture-of-experts model; neither alone provides a hardware bill. Benchmark your intended inference setup.

For Gemini 4 Carbon: Check whether your organization is eligible for the current rollout, what product or API surface is included, and whether the announced price and terms apply to your use. Google says broader developer and business access will come later, but that is not a date commitment in the announcement.

For both: Record the model version and date. Preview models can change. Re-run critical tests when a model is updated, and do not silently treat an early preview result as a stable production guarantee.

So, which one should you choose?

For an engineer who wants to explore immediately, Mistral Large 4 has the clearer public entry point in its announcement: a preview API on Mistral Studio. That is a statement about access, not proof that it is the better model or the better production service.

For teams working on cybersecurity, Gemini 4 Carbon's stated focus and published evaluations may make it worth tracking or applying to the restricted rollout. But unless the team is included, it cannot yet be evaluated directly. Google's scores should remain vendor-reported evidence until you can inspect the methodology and test the model yourself.

For self-hosting, Mistral's newly published weights make evaluation possible, but the right action is still to verify the files, license, and resource requirements. Do not promise an on-prem deployment before testing the target serving stack.

The practical decision today is therefore: prepare to evaluate Mistral if you have preview access; monitor or apply for Carbon if your use case fits its rollout; make no production winner claim until you can test both.

Bottom line

Mistral Large 4 and Gemini 4 Carbon are interesting for different reasons, but on October 29, 2026, access is the first comparison to make. Mistral says its preview API and weights are available. Google announced a phased, restricted Carbon rollout, with wider access later.

Keep three labels separate in your notes: announced, accessible to us, and validated on our workload. They are not interchangeable. A careful team can prepare its evaluation now, verify the real access state when it matters, and avoid turning a launch post into a production decision.

Save this checklist: verify access, verify terms, preserve model/version details, use representative tasks, measure repair and review time, and separate vendor benchmarks from your results.

Have you ever planned around a model announcement and then discovered access was still restricted? What did your team do while waiting?

Subscribe for more evidence-led comparisons and build guides on developer tools, AI systems, and practical engineering decisions.

  • Mistral: Mistral Large 4 open weights
  • Mistral Docs: Mistral Large 4 details and current API rates
  • Google: Introducing Gemini 4 Carbon, October 28, 2026

title: Disaster Recovery: RTO, RPO & DR Strategies
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Pin down your RTO and RPO, then pick the right one of four DR patterns to match. The real lesson: an untested backup is not a recovery plan, so verify restores and run game-day failovers.

Contents

  • The 3 a.m. region outage
  • RTO and RPO: the only two numbers that matter
  • The picture: one primary, four ways out
  • The four DR patterns
  • Backups vs. replication: not the same thing
  • Build it: backup with a restore-verification check
  • Test your restores. Run game-day failovers.
  • Common mistakes that cost hours (or the company)
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

The 3 a.m. region outage

A cloud region goes dark. Not a single instance, not one bad deploy, the whole region. Your API is down, your dashboard is down, and the on-call engineer reaches for the runbook that says "restore from backup." Then comes the discovery that ends careers: the nightly backups have been running green for two years, but nobody has ever restored one. The snapshots are there. They are also corrupt, incomplete, or in the same dead region. The "backup" was a job that produced files, not a recovery capability that produced a running system.

Disaster recovery (DR) is the discipline of being ready for that day before it arrives. It is not a product you buy; it is a set of decisions, how fast must we come back, how much data can we afford to lose, and how much are we willing to pay to guarantee it. This article gives you the vocabulary (RTO and RPO), the four standard DR patterns and their cost trade-offs, the difference between backups and replication, and the single habit that separates teams that recover from teams that find out: testing the restore.

📌 Who this is for: Engineers and architects who own a production system and have been asked "what's our DR plan?", and want a real answer, not a backup job. Comfortable with cloud basics (regions, storage, databases); no prior DR experience assumed.

RTO and RPO: the only two numbers that matter

Every DR conversation collapses into two numbers. Get them agreed with the business first; the technology choice falls out of them automatically.

RTO is how fast you get back. RPO is how much data you can lose.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disaster. "We must be back within 1 hour" is an RTO of 60 minutes. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time. "We can lose at most 5 minutes of writes" is an RPO of 5 minutes, meaning your recovery point can be no older than 5 minutes before the failure.

In the real world In tech
How long until the tow truck gets you driving again RTO, time to restore service
How far back you'd have to retrace because your last map save was old RPO, acceptable data loss window
A spare tyre in the boot vs. a second car following you Backup & restore vs. active-active
Test-driving the spare before the trip, not on the hard shoulder Restore drills / game-day failover

DR objectives, translated to a road trip.

💡 Lower numbers cost more, non-linearly: An RTO of "a few hours" might be a cheap restore script. An RTO of "a few seconds" means running a full duplicate of your stack 24/7. Halving RTO/RPO rarely doubles cost, it often multiplies it. Always ask the business for the real tolerance, not the aspirational one.

The picture: one primary, four ways out

Here is the mental model. You run in a primary region. A DR strategy is whatever you keep warm in a secondary region so that when the primary fails, you can fail over to it. The patterns differ only in how much you keep running on the other side.

Primary region fails; traffic fails over to the secondary via the DR option you chose.

Building a DR plan is a sequence, not a purchase. Walk it in order:

  1. Set RTO and RPO with the business: Per service, not for the whole company. Your billing pipeline and your blog probably deserve different numbers.
  2. Pick the DR pattern that meets those numbers: Choose the cheapest pattern whose recovery characteristics satisfy the agreed RTO/RPO, see the table below.
  3. Replicate data and (optionally) infrastructure cross-region: Get your source of truth out of the failure domain. Snapshots for loose RPO; continuous replication for tight RPO.
  4. Automate detection and failover: Health checks trigger DNS or load-balancer cutover. Manual failover at 3 a.m. blows your RTO.
  5. Document the runbook and the failback: Coming back is half the plan: how you return to primary once it recovers, without losing the writes that happened in the secondary.
  6. Test it on a schedule: An untested plan has an unknown RTO, which is the same as no plan.

The four DR patterns

There are four canonical patterns, ordered from cheapest/slowest to most expensive/instant. They are a spectrum: as you move down, you keep more of the secondary running, RTO and RPO shrink, and your monthly bill grows.

  • Backup & restore, store backups in another region; spin everything up from scratch when disaster strikes. Cheapest, slowest.
  • Pilot light, keep a minimal core always running in the secondary (e.g. a replicated database), with app servers switched off until needed.
  • Warm standby, a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the stack is always running; you scale it up and shift traffic on failover.
  • Multi-site active/active, both regions serve live traffic all the time; a region loss is just lost capacity, not lost service.
Pattern RTO RPO Cost Complexity
Backup & restore Hours to days Hours Lowest Low
Pilot light Tens of minutes Minutes Low-medium Medium
Warm standby Minutes Seconds-minutes Medium-high High
Multi-site active/active Near zero Near zero Highest Highest

The four DR patterns and their trade-offs. Lower RTO/RPO costs more and adds complexity.

⚠️ Active/active is not free insurance: Running two live regions means dealing with data conflicts, two-way replication lag, and split-brain. It buys the best RTO/RPO but demands the most engineering maturity. Most teams are better served by warm standby until they genuinely need zero-downtime regional failover.

Backups vs. replication: not the same thing

These two get conflated constantly, and the confusion is what produces the 3 a.m. surprise. A backup is a point-in-time copy you can restore from later, it protects against data loss and corruption, including logical errors like a bad migration or a DROP TABLE. Replication is a continuously-updated live copy of your data in another location, it gives you a low-RPO failover target.

The critical difference: replication faithfully copies your mistakes. If someone deletes a table, replication deletes it in the replica milliseconds later. A backup from before the delete is the only thing that saves you. You need both, replication for fast failover, backups for the corruption and oops cases. Replication is not a backup, and a backup is not a failover target.

In the real world In tech
A photo album of how things looked last night Backup, point-in-time, survives a bad delete
A live mirror of the room right now Replication, current, but reflects mistakes instantly
Region burns down Replication / standby saves you
Engineer runs DROP TABLE in prod Only a backup saves you

Two different protections for two different disasters.

Build it: backup with a restore-verification check

The single most valuable thing you can automate is not the backup, it is proving the backup restores. Below, a nightly job takes a backup, copies it cross-region, then restores it into a throwaway database and runs a sanity query. If the restore or the check fails, it exits non-zero so your alerting fires. A backup whose restore is never exercised has an unknown value.

backup-and-verify.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# --- config ---
DB_HOST="prod-db.internal"
DB_NAME="app"
TS="\$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
DUMP="/tmp/\${DB_NAME}-\${TS}.sql.gz"
BUCKET="s3://dr-backups-us-west-2"   # secondary region bucket
VERIFY_DB="verify_\${TS}"

# 1. take a consistent backup
pg_dump -h "\$DB_HOST" -d "\$DB_NAME" --format=plain \
  | gzip > "\$DUMP"
echo "backup written: \$DUMP (\$(du -h "\$DUMP" | cut -f1))"

# 2. ship it OUT of the primary region (your RPO copy)
aws s3 cp "\$DUMP" "\${BUCKET}/\${DB_NAME}/\${TS}.sql.gz"

# 3. RESTORE into a throwaway db and verify it is usable
createdb "\$VERIFY_DB"
trap 'dropdb --if-exists "\$VERIFY_DB"; rm -f "\$DUMP"' EXIT

gunzip -c "\$DUMP" | psql -q -d "\$VERIFY_DB"

# 4. sanity check: the data is actually there
ROWS=\$(psql -tA -d "\$VERIFY_DB" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM users;")
if [ "\$ROWS" -lt 1 ]; then
  echo "VERIFY FAILED: users table empty after restore" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "restore verified: \$ROWS rows in users, backup is usable"

Wire the exit code into your monitoring: a non-zero exit (failed backup, failed restore, or empty table) should page someone. The day this job goes red is the day you learn your DR is broken, on a Tuesday afternoon, not during a real outage.

Test your restores. Run game-day failovers.

A DR plan you have never executed is a hypothesis, not a plan. Two practices turn the hypothesis into a measured capability.

Restore drills

Regularly restore a backup into a fresh environment and confirm the application actually runs against it. This catches the things that silently rot: a backup that excludes a critical schema, a snapshot encrypted with a key you no longer have, an RPO that drifted because the job started failing weeks ago. The verification script above is a continuous restore drill; do a full manual one quarterly.

Game-day failover

On a scheduled day, deliberately fail over to your secondary region with the team watching, ideally on real traffic. Measure the actual RTO and RPO and compare them to your targets. You will discover the gaps that only show up under failover: DNS TTLs too long, a secret missing in the secondary, a runbook step that assumes the primary is reachable. Then practice the failback. Each drill makes the real event boring, which is exactly what you want.

💡 Make it routine, not heroic: The goal of game-days is to move failover from a terrifying once-a-decade event to a rehearsed procedure anyone on the team can run. If only one person can fail over, you don't have a DR plan, you have a single point of failure with a pulse.

Common mistakes that cost hours (or the company)

  1. Untested backups. The backup job is green for years and nobody ever restores. You learn it's corrupt during the outage. Verify every restore.
  2. No RPO target. You replicate "for safety" but never decided how much data loss is acceptable, so you can't tell if your setup is adequate. Set the number first.
  3. Single region. Backups and replicas living in the same region as production die with it. Get your recovery copy into a different failure domain.
  4. Confusing replication with backup. A replica copies your DROP TABLE instantly. Keep point-in-time backups for corruption and human error.
  5. Manual failover. A runbook that requires a human to notice and act at 3 a.m. cannot meet a tight RTO. Automate detection and cutover.
  6. Forgetting failback. You fail over fine, then have no plan to return to primary without losing the writes that happened in the secondary.
  7. DNS TTLs too long. A 24-hour TTL means clients keep hitting the dead region long after you cut over. Lower TTLs on failover-critical records.

Takeaways

Disaster recovery in nine lines

  • DR is decisions, not a product: how fast back, how much data lost, how much you'll pay.
  • RTO = recovery time (how fast you're back). RPO = recovery point (how much data you can lose).
  • Agree RTO/RPO with the business per service, the technology falls out of the numbers.
  • Four patterns, cheapest→costliest: backup & restore, pilot light, warm standby, active/active.
  • Lower RTO/RPO costs more, often non-linearly. Pick the cheapest pattern that meets the target.
  • Backups protect against corruption and mistakes; replication gives low-RPO failover. You need both.
  • Keep recovery copies in a different region, same-region backups die with production.
  • Automate detection and failover; manual cutover at 3 a.m. blows your RTO.
  • An untested restore has an unknown RTO. Run restore drills and game-day failovers on a schedule.

Where to go next

DR is one slice of designing systems that survive the bad day. Two companion reads go deeper on the surrounding ground:

  • Multi-Region Architecture: When You Need It, the infrastructure side of running in more than one region, and when the cost is actually worth it.
  • Reliability & Resilience: Designing for Failure, error budgets, redundancy, and graceful degradation, the everyday cousins of DR.

Ready to put it together end to end? Walk the Cloud Engineer career path to build resilient, multi-region systems from fundamentals up, including hands-on labs where you replicate data, automate failover, and measure your real RTO.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: Modelling a shared inbox: why the message is the primary key, not the conversation
description:
Every shared-inbox implementation starts with a conversations table and ends up regretting it. Here is the model that survives contact with real support traffic.

The problem with conversation-first

A conversation is a derived thing. It is what you get after you decide which messages belong together. If you store conversations as the source of truth, every new channel forces you to write merge logic that mutates the conversation rows — and merges are the one operation that must never lose data.

Messages, by contrast, arrive once and never change. They are the natural primary key.

The model 

-- the immutable fact
messages(id, channel, external_id, direction, sent_at, body, raw)

-- who it came from (may be shared by many messages)
contacts(id, email, phone, name)

-- the derived grouping, rebuildable at any time
threads(id, subject_key, opened_at, closed_at)

-- the link, append-only
thread_messages(thread_id, message_id, added_at, reason)

Three properties matter:

  1. thread_messages is append-only. A merge inserts rows; it never rewrites history. If the merge was wrong, you can split by deleting the link rows — no data lost.
  2. Threads can be rebuilt. Delete every row in threads and you can regenerate them from messages plus your merge rules. That is the test for whether your grouping logic is a projection or a tangle.
  3. reason is stored. "Same contact, 4h window" vs "manual merge by ana" answers the question every support lead eventually asks: why are these two emails in one thread?

Identity is the hard part

The same person writes from ana@company.com, then from a personal address, then from a second work address after a rebrand. Matching on the exact string gives you three contacts and three threads.

A workable compromise:

  • Exact match first (email, phone, then channel-specific ID)
  • Then a domain-and-name heuristic that suggests a merge rather than performing one
  • Never auto-merge across organisations

The suggestion queue is boring, and it is what keeps identity resolution honest: a human confirms the ambiguous cases rather than a regex.

Delivery state belongs to the message, not the conversation

Outbound mail can be queued, sent, delivered, bounced, complained. That lifecycle is per message and per recipient. Storing "the conversation was sent" hides the one case that matters: one of three recipients bounced.

message_delivery(message_id, recipient, state, updated_at, provider_id)

With that table, "did they get it?" is a query instead of a support escalation.

What this buys you

  • Channel integrations become writers of messages, not reimplementations of threading
  • AI summarisation or tagging attaches to messages/threads as a separate table, never mutating the record
  • Deleting a thread is a policy operation (remove link rows + messages), so retention rules become enforceable
  • Migration to a new database is a row copy, not a logic rewrite

The one thing to get right early

Make messages.external_id unique per channel and dedupe on insert. Every provider retries webhooks. Without that constraint you will ship duplicate replies, and duplicate replies are the failure customers remember.

This is the shape we use in Onsites AI — a shared inbox, CRM and light invoicing for teams of three to thirty, self-hostable or cloud. The schema notes above are portable either way.

title: API Testing in CI: Hoppscotch vs Powerduck
description:
Short answer: Both can run in CI, but the source of the checks differs. A collection-based runner executes the requests you authored; a spec-first runner derives the checks from the contract and verifies conformance. Use the first to run a fixed set of calls; use the second to prove the responses match the API.

What a collection runner does in CI

It executes the saved requests and their assertions, which is a reliable way to run a known set of checks. It is only as current as the collection, and it verifies the assertions rather than the whole contract.

What a spec-first runner does

Property Collection runner Spec-first
Checks come from Authored requests The contract
Coverage What was saved Declared operations
Conformance Assertions only Full schema check
On spec change Update collection Reflects the spec

The failure that CI should catch

A response that violates the contract but passes the authored assertions is the gap. A spec-first runner checks the full response, so the violation fails the build even if no one wrote an assertion for it.

How to combine them

Run the fixed behavioral calls and the contract checks as two stages. The first proves the flows work; the second proves the responses are valid.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Hoppscotch comparison. Next, read OpenAPI-first vs collection-first.

title: Track hotel prices for any city into a spreadsheet with Python
description:
Comparing hotel prices gets tedious when you keep repeating the same search and copying rates into a spreadsheet. Tracking how those prices change is even harder unless you save the dates, guest count and time of each search.

I built the tool used here.

This walkthrough uses GridForge's Google Hotels Scraper to collect a hotel-price snapshot and export it to CSV. You can start without code, then use Python when you want a repeatable workflow.

What you get

Each result represents one hotel from the first page of the location search. Available fields include:

Field What it tells you
name Hotel name
pricePerNight Displayed nightly price before taxes
pricePerNightWithTaxes Displayed nightly price including taxes
rating Guest rating
reviewCount Number of guest reviews
hotelClass Hotel star classification
latitude, longitude Property coordinates
website Official website, when supplied

Guest rating and hotel class measure different things. A four-star hotel does not necessarily have a guest rating of four. Some properties may have missing fields; keep those cells empty instead of treating a missing price as zero.

Option 1: no code

  1. Open the Google Hotels Scraper and click Try for free.
  2. Enter a city, neighborhood or area, such as Times Square, New York.
  3. Set check-in and check-out dates. Choose the number of adults and currency.
  4. Click Start.
  5. Open the resulting dataset, choose Export, and download CSV or Excel.

For your first search, use one location and one stay. A neighborhood query is useful when a whole-city search gives you properties spread too far apart.

Option 2: Python 

pip install apify-client

Set your Apify token in an environment variable named APIFY_TOKEN. This script requests one stay and writes only the columns needed for a price-comparison spreadsheet:

import csv
import os
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from decimal import Decimal

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

search = {
    "locations": ["Times Square, New York"],
    "checkIn": "2027-01-15",
    "checkOut": "2027-01-18",
    "adults": 2,
    "currency": "USD",
    "country": "us",
}

run = client.actor("gridforge/google-hotels-scraper").call(
    run_input=search,
    max_total_charge_usd=Decimal("0.05"),  # hard spending cap for this run
)

if not run or run.get("status") != "SUCCEEDED":
    raise RuntimeError("Hotel search did not succeed")

checked_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
columns = ["checkedAt", "checkIn", "checkOut", "currency", "name",
           "pricePerNight", "pricePerNightWithTaxes", "rating", "reviewCount", "website"]

with open("hotel-prices.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=columns)
    writer.writeheader()
    for hotel in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
        if not hotel.get("name"):
            print("Check this record:", hotel)
            continue
        row = {key: hotel.get(key) for key in columns}
        row.update({"checkedAt": checked_at, "checkIn": search["checkIn"],
                    "checkOut": search["checkOut"], "currency": search["currency"]})
        writer.writerow(row)

Replace the example dates with your intended stay. The script records the requested dates and currency beside each result, so every snapshot is easy to interpret later.

Use case: daily price tracking

Choosing a hotel for a three-night trip? Run the same search daily, keeping the stay dates, adult count, currency and location unchanged. Append each run to one spreadsheet and compare the tax-inclusive price for the same property across days. Once your first results look right, set up a daily Schedule in Apify so it runs on its own.

Limits

  • Returns the first page Google shows, typically around 18–20 hotels per location. Search by neighborhood for more coverage.
  • Displayed rates change and may differ from the final price at checkout.
  • Nearby searches can overlap; deduplicate before counting unique hotels.

Cost: $1 per 1,000 hotels, plus a tiny start fee. Set a spending cap and a run can never cost more than you allow.

title: Frontend CI Gates That Catch AI-Generated Regressions
description:
Green CI after an agent PR used to make me relax. Then I merged a “small” fix that renamed a shared prop, skipped an a11y lint because the rule was warn-only, and shipped a modal that trapped focus forever — all while every check stayed green.

The suite wasn’t lying. It was answering the wrong questions. Agents are great at satisfying whatever your pipeline actually enforces. If the gates are soft, the diffs look confident and the regressions still land.

So I stopped treating CI as a vibe check and started treating it as a blast-radius fence for AI-touched frontend work.

What AI regressions actually look like

The failures I care about rarely show up as “test file missing.” They look like:

  • Contract drift — export renamed, optional prop made required, event payload shape quietly changed
  • A11y regressions — interactive div, missing label, broken focus order, live region that never announces
  • Dependency sprawl — new package for a one-liner the repo already has a util for
  • Token / theme leaks — hardcoded hex next to the design-token import the agent “cleaned up”
  • Mock theater — new unit tests that assert the mock was called, not that the user path works
  • Bundle surprises — a “tiny helper” that pulls half of date-fns or a chart lib into a leaf route

Unit coverage can stay flat or even rise while any of those ship. That’s why gates have to sit outside “did something assert?”

Gate 1: Typecheck is non-negotiable (and strict)

I want tsc --noEmit (or the project’s equivalent) as a hard fail, not a soft job. Soft typecheck is how agents “fix” by adding as any, // @ts-ignore, or widening props until the error goes away.

Rules that help:

  • Fail on new @ts-ignore / @ts-expect-error without a ticket id in the comment
  • Ban any in changed files via eslint (@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any as error on src/**)
  • Prefer exactOptionalPropertyTypes / strict null checks so optional props can’t silently become T | undefined soup

When an agent PR needs an escape hatch, the comment has to name why. “To make CI green” is not a why.

Gate 2: Lint rules aimed at agent habits

Generic eslint is not enough. I add a small set aimed at the diffs agents love:

  • No raw hex / rgb in component files when a tokens package exists
  • No new eslint-disable without a scoped rule name and a one-line reason
  • No dangerouslySetInnerHTML unless the path is allowlisted
  • JSX a11y as error for label, role, keyboard, and autofocus rules — warn-only is how regressions pass
  • Import boundaries — leaf features can’t import from other features’ internals; agents ignore folder manners unless CI fails

I keep the rule list short. A 200-rule wall trains the agent to spray disables. Ten sharp fails teach the habit.

Gate 3: Contract tests for public UI APIs

For shared components and hooks, I keep a thin contract suite the agent is not allowed to “simplify away”:

  • Export names and required props (type-level or runtime)
  • Stable data-testid / roles used by Playwright
  • Event payload shapes for onChange / onSubmit

These tests are boring on purpose. They’re the fence around rewrite energy. If the agent rewrites a Button internals, the contract still has to hold — or the PR splits into an intentional breaking change with a migration note.

Gate 4: One real path in Playwright (not five shallow ones)

After the fake-green lesson, I require at least one e2e (or component-playwright) path for any user-facing change in a critical flow. The gate isn’t “Playwright job exists.” It’s:

  • The PR touches features/checkout/** → checkout happy path must pass
  • The PR touches Modal / Dialog primitives → open, Tab cycle, Escape, restore focus must pass

I map folders to required specs in CI. Agents learn quickly: if you edit the folder, you inherit the path. No orphan unit greens.

Gate 5: A11y checks that fail the build

I run axe (or equivalent) on the stories / routes the PR claims to change. Soft a11y reports get ignored under deadline pressure; agents will too.

Pragmatic setup that works for me:

  • Storybook test-runner + axe on changed stories, error on serious/critical
  • Or Playwright + axe on the same critical paths as Gate 4
  • Fail on new aria-hidden on focusable nodes and on buttons without accessible names

I don’t try to axe the entire app on every PR. Scope to the blast radius. Agents respond to scoped hard fails better than global noise.

Gate 6: Bundle / import budget on touched routes

AI loves helpful imports. CI should love budgets:

  • Size limit (or relative budget) on entry chunks for routes the PR touches
  • Forbidden package list for UI packages that already have first-party utils (lodash*, giant icon packs, duplicate date libs)
  • Optional: knip / depcruise for unused and circular imports on changed packages

A 3kb “fix” that adds 80kb gzipped is still a regression. Put that in the gate title so reviewers see it without opening the bundle report.

Gate 7: Diff-shaped checks (cheap, high signal)

A few grep-level checks catch a surprising amount of agent damage:

  • New files under src/ without a corresponding test or story when the folder already has a pattern
  • Deleted snapshots without a CHANGELOG / PR note (optional; teams vary)
  • Changes to tokens/ or components/ui/ require a label (design-system) or a second reviewer
  • PR body must include a “what stayed the same” bullet list for AI-assisted changes (enforced by a bot comment, not a human memory)

None of these replace judgment. They force the conversation before merge.

How I wire this for agent PRs specifically

Human PRs and agent PRs can share the same pipeline. I still tag agent-assisted work so the gates can be slightly stricter:

  1. Label ai-assisted (or detect conventional PR body marker)
  2. On that label: no new any, no new eslint-disable, a11y serious = fail, folder→Playwright map required
  3. Require the agent (or author) to paste the acceptance checks that were in the prompt into the PR description

The point isn’t bureaucracy. It’s making the prompt’s contract visible next to the diff. Reviewers stop re-deriving intent from vibes.

What I deliberately do not gate

  • Pixel-perfect visual diffs on every PR (too flaky; I save visual for design-system primitives)
  • Full e2e suite on every leaf copy change (map critical folders; don’t boil the ocean)
  • Coverage % thresholds as the main signal (agents inflate coverage; see the fake-green post)

Gates should be few, hard, and aligned with user-visible risk. Soft gates train everyone — human and model — to ignore CI.

A minimal starter checklist

If you’re adding AI to a frontend repo this month, I’d land these first:

  1. Strict typecheck + ban new any / bare ignores on changed files
  2. jsx-a11y (+ axe on critical paths) as error
  3. Folder → one Playwright path mapping for money / auth / editor flows
  4. Import boundary + forbidden dependency list
  5. Bundle budget on touched routes
  6. PR template line: “AI-assisted? Acceptance checks: …”

That’s enough to catch most of the regressions I’ve actually shipped. You can fancy it up later.

Takeaway

Agents optimize for the fitness function you give them. If CI only asks “are there tests?” you’ll get tests. If CI asks “did the public contract, keyboard path, a11y tree, and route budget survive?” you’ll get diffs that respect those fences.

I still review. The gates just make sure “LGTM” isn’t the first line of defense against a confident, green, wrong PR.

title: Vercel Connect adds observability support
description:
Vercel Connect now gives teams line-level visibility into the token lifecycle. See who created a token, what app or project used it, when, and whether it is still active.

Every connector's detail page includes a new Observability tab:

  • Runtime events: Every token request, authorization, refresh, revocation, and trigger delivery, filterable by type.

  • Correlation IDs: Stable tokenId and authorizationId values link each token's events, so you can match Connect events to your own systems.

  • Activity: The Activity filter button opens the Activity page pre-filtered to the connector's configuration events, so you can see when and how it changed.

Connect observability is available on all plans. Events are retained for 12 hours on Hobby, 3 days on Pro, and 30 days on Enterprise. To retain events longer, forward them to a custom webhook endpoint by adding a Drain on Pro and Enterprise plans. Enterprise teams also get role-based access control and audit logs.

title: Go Struct Copying and Pointer Semantics Cause Unexpected `true false` Output for Java/Rust Developers
description:
Introduction

Developers transitioning from Java or Rust to Go often encounter puzzling behaviors rooted in Go's unique handling of struct copying and pointer semantics. A seemingly simple program can produce unexpected outputs, such as true false, leaving developers scratching their heads. This phenomenon is not a bug but a direct consequence of Go's design choices, which prioritize simplicity and performance over implicit behavior. Understanding these nuances is critical, as they can lead to subtle bugs, inefficiencies, and maintainability issues if overlooked.

Consider the following Go puzzler, which encapsulates the issue:

package mainimport "fmt"type SelfReference struct { self *SelfReference}func make() SelfReference { s := SelfReference{} s.self = &s return s}func main() { s := make() fmt.Println(s == *s.self, &s == s.self)}

The output, true false, arises from Go's value semantics for structs. When the make() function returns a SelfReference struct, it creates a copy of the struct, not a reference to the original. The self field in this copy still points to the original struct within the make() function's scope. This leads to a split identity: the copied struct in main() and the original struct in make() share the same field values but reside in different memory locations.

The comparison s == *s.self evaluates to true because Go's == operator for structs compares field values, not memory addresses. Since both structs have identical fields, they are considered equal. However, &s == s.self evaluates to false because &s points to the copied struct in main(), while s.self points to the original struct in make(). Scenarios and Edge Cases

Go's struct copying and pointer semantics can lead to unexpected outcomes, especially for developers transitioning from languages like Java or Rust. Below are six distinct scenarios that illustrate these nuances, each accompanied by code examples and causal explanations.

title: umux v1.7.7 ships Core Session
description:
umux v1.7.7: Core Session, a sleep block with an end time

Quick context for anyone new here: umux is an open-source terminal workspace manager. One desktop app (Tauri v2) with its own embedded terminal. You group terminals into named workspaces, each workspace holds tabs, and every tab splits into as many resizable panels as you need. Linux, Windows, macOS.

v1.7.7 ships Core Session, and it fixes a human problem more than a technical one.

umux Core keeps the machine awake while agents run long jobs. It shipped as a toggle: ON until someone flips it OFF. That someone is you, hours later, and until then the hardware runs for nothing.

Core Session puts a clock on the hold:

umux core-session start 90m

The machine (not just the screen) stays awake for exactly that window, 24 hours max per session. umux core-session extend 30m adds time mid-flight. umux core-session stop ends it early. When the deadline passes, the daemon releases the hold on its own and posts one desktop notification. Settings shows the countdown and, after the fact, when the session ended and why.

The deadline is absolute. It is stored the moment the session starts, and a restart brings the session back with whatever window remained. A crash can never stretch the hold by accident. umux status --json carries the same truth for scripts: active, endsAt, remainingSecs.

Under the hood, nothing new holds the machine. The same three backends as before: an IOKit assertion on macOS, SetThreadExecutionState on Windows, a logind inhibitor on Linux. The new part is the deadline on top.

Platform details worth knowing. On macOS, the persistent Core switch retires. Settings now shows Core Session (BETA), and umux core on refuses with a pointer to the new command. On Windows and Linux, Core stays as shipped, and Core and a session never run at the same time.

Also in this release:

  • Clicking a notification on macOS navigates to the panel it came from.
  • Windows gets a umux-owned notification banner, because the old toasts ignored clicks.
  • Daemon replay no longer answers a fresh terminal's hardware probes, so a restored session starts clean instead of printing probe garbage.
  • A fix for the keyboard freeze some setups hit when the app resolved a working directory.

I'm running this build on my Mac as of today. Install and build steps live in the README, and the full notes are here: https://github.com/CrystalPlatforms/umux/releases/tag/v1.7.7

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

title: Kafka vs Amazon SQS: Queue or Log? How to Pick the Right One on AWS
description:
Sooner or later, every team building on AWS hits the same fork in the road: two services need to talk asynchronously, and you have to choose between Amazon SQS and Apache Kafka.

The usual framing is "SQS is simple, Kafka is powerful." That's true, but it hides the difference that actually matters:

SQS is a queue. A consumer takes a message, processes it, deletes it.
Kafka is a log. Messages stay for as long as you configure, and every consumer keeps its own bookmark.

Once you see it that way, the choice gets a lot easier.

SQS in 30 seconds

SQS is fully managed: no brokers, no partitions, no disks to size. Producers send, consumers poll, and a received message stays hidden for the visibility timeout. Delete it in time and it's gone for good; crash, and it reappears for another worker.

aws sqs send-message --queue-url $QUEUE_URL \
  --message-body '{"orderId": 4821, "total": 59.90}'

aws sqs receive-message --queue-url $QUEUE_URL \
  --max-number-of-messages 10 --wait-time-seconds 20

# delete only after the work really succeeded
aws sqs delete-message --queue-url $QUEUE_URL --receipt-handle $HANDLE
  • Standard queues: at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering, practically unlimited throughput.
  • FIFO queues: strict ordering per message group plus 5-minute deduplication, at lower throughput.
  • Retention: 1 minute to 14 days, then SQS drops the message.

Kafka in 30 seconds

Kafka writes messages to topics split into partitions, which are append-only files. Reading doesn't delete anything; consumers just move an offset.

# billing and analytics read the same topic with independent offsets
kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders --group billing
kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders --group analytics --from-beginning

That last part is the superpower SQS doesn't have. Add a fraud-detection service six months from now and it can read every order still in retention, without the producer changing a line.

Quick comparison

Amazon SQS Apache Kafka
Model Queue, deleted after processing Log, retained with offsets
Operations Fully run by AWS You, or MSK / Confluent Cloud
Many consumers, same message Needs SNS fan-out to several queues Built in via consumer groups
Replay No Yes, reset offsets
Ordering None (Standard) / per group (FIFO) Per partition
Pricing Per request, 1M free/month Per broker or cluster hour + storage

Pick SQS when...

  • Each message is a job: resize an image, send an email, generate a PDF. Once it's done, nobody needs it again.
  • You want zero ops. Wire it to Lambda and AWS handles polling, batching and scaling. Failures go to a dead-letter queue with one redrive policy.
  • Traffic is low or spiky. An idle queue costs close to nothing (just turn on long polling so empty receives don't add up).

Pick Kafka when...

  • The same event matters to many systems: billing, inventory, search, the data warehouse. Each is just another consumer group.
  • You need replay. A buggy consumer wrote bad data for two days? Fix it and rewind only that group: 
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --group analytics --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-01T00:00:00.000 --execute
  • You're doing event sourcing, CDC with Debezium, or stream processing with Kafka Streams / Flink.

The cost nobody puts in the table

Self-hosted Kafka is real work: sizing brokers, picking partition counts up front, watching consumer lag, handling upgrades. Amazon MSK removes the servers, but you still pay for brokers running 24/7, and a small multi-AZ cluster lands in the hundreds of dollars a month before storage. For a three-person team shipping a SaaS app, that gap versus an idle SQS queue is significant.

If you want a replayable log but prefer to stay AWS-native, Kinesis Data Streams sits in the middle: multiple consumers, up to 365 days of retention, no brokers, but without Kafka's ecosystem.

The one-question rule

After a message is processed, does anything ever need to read it again?

  • No → start with SQS.
  • Yes, or several independent systems consume the same events → Kafka.

And plenty of teams run both: Kafka carries core business events between services, while SQS queues at the edges handle the jobs those events trigger.

📖 Want the full breakdown? The complete guide covers FIFO vs Standard queues, MSK pricing, Kinesis, and a detailed FAQ: Kafka vs Amazon SQS: Which Messaging Service Is Better? on Online ToolKit Hub.

Working with message payloads? Check out the free tools at onlinetoolkithub.com to format and validate JSON right in your browser.

Which one does your team use, and why? Let me know in the comments 👇
