title: The big clouds charge a median 3.2x the cheapest GPU rate: 18 GPUs compared
description:
Rent an H100 on Google Cloud and the cheapest on-demand rate is $5.38 per GPU-hour, sold as an 8-GPU machine. Rent the same card from Lium, a GPU marketplace, and it is $1.80. Same chip, same hour, three times the price.

That gap is not one odd card. We compared every GPU that both a hyperscaler (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle Cloud) and at least one other cloud rent on demand, from the live prices FastGPU collects across the market. On October 29, 2026 at 16:20 UTC there were 18 such cards, and the cheapest big-cloud rate for a card was a median of 3.2x the cheapest rate at which it could be rented anywhere.

Card by card

The cheapest hyperscaler rate for each card against the market floor (the cheapest on-demand or community price at which the card could be rented that morning, in stock wherever any offer was), per GPU-hour:

GPU Cheapest hyperscaler Market floor Hyperscaler / floor
V100 $2.49, Google Cloud (8-GPU instance) $0.07, Clore.ai 35.6x
L4 $0.71, Google Cloud $0.09, Vast.ai 7.9x
RTX PRO 4500 $2.52, AWS $0.35, Clore.ai 7.2x
A100 40GB $2.16, Google Cloud (16-GPU instance) $0.35, Vast.ai 6.2x
L40S $1.86, AWS $0.34, Vast.ai 5.5x
A100 80GB $3.22, Google Cloud (8-GPU instance) $0.60, Vast.ai 5.4x
A10 $1.01, AWS $0.24, Vast.ai 4.2x
MI300X $6.00, Azure (8-GPU instance) $1.71, TensorWave 3.5x
RTX PRO 6000 $3.36, AWS $1.00, Vast.ai 3.4x
MI355X $8.60, Oracle Cloud (8-GPU instance) $2.85, TensorWave 3.0x
T4 $0.36, Google Cloud (4-GPU instance) $0.12, Vast.ai 3.0x
H100 SXM $5.38, Google Cloud (8-GPU instance) $1.80, Lium 3.0x
B200 $14.00, Oracle Cloud (8-GPU instance) $4.89, DeepInfra 2.9x
H100 NVL $6.98, Azure $2.59, RunPod 2.7x
H200 $7.91, AWS (8-GPU instance) $3.00, Vast.ai 2.6x
B300 $15.00, Oracle Cloud (8-GPU instance) $5.89, DeepInfra 2.5x
GB200 $16.00, Oracle Cloud (4-GPU instance) $8.00, GMI Cloud 2.0x
GB300 $18.00, Oracle Cloud (4-GPU instance) $12.93, Verda 1.4x

Each ratio is the first price divided by the second. The live table recomputes all of it on every visit and links every rate to the page that proves it.

Two patterns stand out. The gap is widest on older and mid-range cards (V100, L4, A100, L40S), where marketplaces full of hosts with paid-off hardware set the floor. And it narrows on the newest silicon: a GB300 costs only 1.4x more at Oracle than at the cheapest GPU cloud, because few providers rent one at all and none of them is cheap.

Cloud by cloud

Each big cloud's own on-demand rate against the floor, across every card it lists, gives a median per cloud (on the same snapshot):

  • AWS: 4.3x across 12 cards
  • Google Cloud: 5.4x across 7 cards
  • Azure: 5.5x across 11 cards
  • Oracle Cloud: 4.0x across 14 cards

A cloud with few cards is a small sample, so read these as a shape rather than a ranking. Each link goes to that cloud's full pricing guide, where every rate is a live figure.

What the premium buys, and what the floor leaves out

The comparison is honest only if you know what each side includes.

The floor is often a marketplace. Vast.ai, Clore.ai and similar platforms rent machines that independent hosts own. Network quality, data security and uptime vary by host, and none of them publishes an uptime SLA for a single machine. Across the last 25 daily fixings, Vast.ai alone held the cheapest price on 41% of GPU-days, and the cheapest provider for a card changed about one day in six.

Many hyperscaler rates come only as whole machines. The per-GPU rate on an 8-GPU instance is real, but the smallest bill is eight times it.

The big clouds charge for data leaving them. Moving 1,000 GB out costs $90.00 at AWS and $87.00 at Azure, (each after the first 100 GB a month), and $120.00 per 1,000 GiB at Google Cloud. Many GPU clouds charge nothing for egress. For a job that downloads a fine-tuned model or serves files, that can outweigh the GPU bill.

Meters differ. AWS and Google Cloud bill by the second, Azure by the minute; some GPU clouds bill by the hour, and several keep billing a stopped machine's disks. The hidden costs page lists each provider's egress, meter and uptime terms, each linked to the provider's own page.

What the premium does buy: region coverage, existing enterprise contracts and compliance, the surrounding platform (storage, networking, managed services), and published SLAs. For a team already committed to one of them, the premium is often the price of not moving data and not adding a vendor. For a portable training or inference job, it is the first number worth questioning.

How the numbers are made

FastGPU collects posted on-demand prices from each provider's own API, rate card or price list, every day and again while pages are being read, and normalises them to a per-GPU-hour rate. Spot capacity is excluded from both sides. A machine its provider no longer rents to new customers is left out, even when a price list still shows it. The methodology has the details, and the recorded prices are an open dataset under CC BY 4.0.

These figures are a snapshot from October 29, 2026. The live comparison shows today's.

title: Why Am I Refactoring My Own Open-Source Project?
description:
The gdenticon Refactoring Log — Part 1

What gdenticon is

gdenticon is an identicon generator I wrote in Go. Give it a username, email address, or another string, and it produces a stable pixel avatar. The same input gives the same result, which makes it useful as a default image when a user has not uploaded one.

The project already works as both a command-line tool and a Go package. It can output PNG, SVG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, and TIFF.

This series, however, is not an introduction to a finished project. I am going back through it and refactoring parts of it.

Why gdenticon exists

I started the project because the Go identicon libraries I could find never quite matched what I needed.

Some produced patterns that felt too dense. Some were effectively limited to PNG. Others required more setup code than I wanted for generating one small avatar.

That did not make those projects bad. They were simply designed around needs that were different from mine. I wanted a smaller tool with calmer-looking patterns, flexible output formats, a convenient CLI, and an API that could be dropped into another Go project without much preparation.

After failing to find exactly that, I decided to build it. That was the beginning of gdenticon.

Why refactor something that already works

Avatar generation is already implemented, but working features do not automatically mean the current solution is good enough.

As the project grew, I began to notice problems that did not appear as immediate failures. Some responsibilities were not separated clearly enough, so changing one area meant thinking about several others. Pattern generation still had room to become more efficient. Supporting more output formats and ways to use the package also made the original organisation less comfortable.

None of this stops the program from producing an avatar today. It does affect how easily the project can change tomorrow.

I would rather address that while the codebase is still small than wait until every new feature has to work around an old decision. The refactoring is therefore not a rewrite from scratch, and it is not an excuse to introduce a more elaborate architecture.

The working behaviour will remain. The goal is to make responsibilities clearer, remove unnecessary computation and memory use, keep the API simple, and make later changes to formats and pattern generation less disruptive.

What I want gdenticon to become

My expectation for gdenticon has not changed. It should remain a small, practical tool rather than a collection of abstractions built to demonstrate techniques.

Generating an avatar should take very little code. The tool should feel natural in a terminal and inside a web service, background job, or another Go project. Results should be deterministic, patterns should not feel overcrowded, and the output should not be tied to one image format.

The inside of the project should be approachable as well. Someone opening the repository for the first time should be able to follow how input becomes an avatar. Adding a format or adjusting the pattern should not require understanding every package. When something fails, its owner should be reasonably easy to locate.

Performance is part of this work, but I do not want to label the project as fast before measuring it. Each optimisation should come with a reproducible test. If an idea makes little difference, that result is worth recording too. Clever-looking code is not evidence of an improvement.

Recording the process this time

When working on a small personal project, it is easy to focus on getting the feature finished. The reasoning behind a design, the alternatives that were tried, and the decisions that were later reversed often feel unforgettable at the time. A few months later, much of that context is gone.

This time I want to keep the process alongside the code. The series will cover not only the final implementation, but also the problem behind each change, the alternatives I did not choose, and whether the measurements matched my expectations.

Later parts will move through the program entry and error handling, the split between generation and output, the avatar pattern, benchmarks, and other issues that appear during the refactoring. Each part will stay with one main problem instead of trying to explain the entire project at once.

There will be blind spots in a one-person project. If you find a weakness in the code or see a better direction, I would be glad to hear it.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/hourinX/gdenticon

Next

The next part will start with the overall structure and follow one avatar request from the program entry to the final encoded image.

title: Things That Pass Every Check on a Client Site and Still Don't Work
description:
A client never opens Lighthouse. They open their inbox, and there are no enquiries in it.

I keep running into this on client sites and on sites I take over from someone else, one of them built with v0. The last one on the list I built myself.

1. The form says thank you

On a shop I took over, the contact form showed a green "Thank you". The email behind it never arrived.

Autofill can break a form too. One site had a honeypot field that the browser filled in on its own, and the real enquiries were thrown away as bot submissions. Elsewhere the enquiries did arrive, in the spam folder, because the domain had no SPF or DKIM records.

2. "What matters is that it works"

That's what the owner of a shop built with v0 told me. Row Level Security in Supabase was switched off, so the shop worked just as well for anyone who opened the browser console.

On another site the Supabase service role key sat in the client JS bundle. That key skips RLS entirely. Turning RLS on wouldn't have helped there anyway.

3. The noindex that shipped with the site

The site went live months ago with the noindex tag from staging still in the head. Google is very polite about this. It was asked not to index the pages, and for months it didn't.

A robots.txt that blocked /_next/ did the same job from a different angle. That folder is where Next.js keeps its scripts and styles. Googlebot couldn't fetch them, and on that site it rendered an empty page.

4. Lighthouse 100 on placeholders

The score was measured on placeholder images. Then the client started uploading photos straight from their phone, several megabytes each, and LCP went downhill from there.

The same perfect score sat on a site whose hero took seconds to show up on a real phone on 4G.

5. The cookie banner with two Accept buttons

The banner has a Reject button, and clicking it sets exactly the same cookies as Accept.

6. The pages that send Google somewhere else

Many subpages share the same title and the same canonical URL, and each one tells Google that the real page lives somewhere else. Google takes them at their word. One page stays in the index and the rest drop out.

Sometimes the sitemap joins in, full of localhost or vercel.app preview links.

7. 100vh on an iPhone

The hero is exactly one screen tall in Chrome's device emulator. On the phone itself, Safari's address bar covers the call to action.

svh or dvh fixes it, once somebody picks up an iPhone and checks.

8. The menu that needs a mouse

Subpages open on hover. Phones don't hover, and on a phone those pages can't be reached from the menu at all.

The phone number in the footer has no tel: link either. On the device that could actually call it, you can read the number and that's it.

9. alt="image"

Every image on the site has alt="image", and the accessibility audit is green. That audit checked that the attribute exists and stopped there.

10. The domain nobody owns

The domain expires, or the SSL certificate does, and only then does anyone ask whose account it's on.

One client's domain sat on my own account for a while. Handing it over took far more effort than it should have.

The same silence covers smaller things. The map on one site died when its API key expired, and nobody noticed. Somewhere there is a backup, too, and a restore has never been tested.

11. Me

I've sat looking at a green CI run while something on production was down.

I've also tested a contact form by sending it to my own inbox, watched the message arrive and called it done. At the client's end, the enquiries landed in spam. The only inbox that form ever worked for was mine.

That's eleven. Put your twelfth in the comments.

title: NOCTURNE: Investigating Ghosts in the Machine with Air-Gapped Environmental AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

NOCTURNE: Air-Gapped Environmental Telemetry Forensics & Anomaly Reasoning Engine

What I Built

In modern smart homes and automated facilities, thousands of IoT sensors hum silently in the dark—tracking ambient microclimates, circuit wattage, acoustic pressure, and magnetic deadbolt states. When inexplicable events occur—a bedroom drops 7°C in under three minutes, a locked door unlatches with zero network authorization, or a sub-panel breaker registers 2,400W despite being physically switched off—homeowners either dismiss them as unexplained "glitches" or jump to supernatural conclusions.

NOCTURNE is an air-gapped, local-first environmental telemetry forensics platform built to investigate the literal ghosts in our machines.

Instead of building a conversational chatbot, I built an aerospace-grade forensic workstation that ingests multi-variate nocturnal time-series (from Zigbee2MQTT, ESPHome, or Home Assistant) and uses open-source AI to determine causality. It pits rigorous physical mechanics (HVAC damper collapse, thermal bridging, induction loop transients) against anomalous environmental signatures (thermodynamic entropy extraction, 18.98 Hz ocular infrasound resonance) and seals every verdict with a cryptographic SHA-256 evidence checksum.

Demo

  • Live Production Workstation: https://nocturne-nb2y.onrender.com
  • Source Code Repository: https://github.com/ayushg-1506/nocturne

Key Workstation Modules

  1. [01] Architectural Spatial Matrix: Interactive 2D floorplan showing real-time microclimate boundaries, thermal collapse plumes, motion detection vectors, and centered dynamic door latch telemetry.
  2. [02] Telemetry Waveform Lab: Synchronized four-channel oscillograms measuring Ambient Temperature, Acoustic Sound Pressure / Frequency, Electromagnetic Flux (EMF), and Circuit Active Power.
  3. [03] Incident Dossiers & Forensic Audit: Cryptographically sealed dossiers featuring dual-verdict causal divergence, sensory signature breakdowns, and a 6-phase chronological audit log.
  4. [04] Spectral Lab & CRT Oscilloscope: Real-time CRT oscilloscope visualizer rendering audio waveforms and isolating the infamous 18.98 Hz acoustic resonance frequency, paired with procedural Web Audio API synthesis.
  5. [05] Data Ingest & Simulation Lab: Synthetic anomaly injection engine allowing operators to inject flash cold drops, infrasound spikes, phantom wattage surges, and zero-token lock cycles into live streams, alongside custom CSV file ingestion.
  6. [06] System Configuration: Local AI endpoint adapter configuration (Ollama, local vLLM, or air-gapped heuristic reasoning).

Code

The entire codebase is open-source under the MIT license:

ayushg-1506 / nocturne

https://nocturne-nb2y.onrender.com

NOCTURNE: Air-Gapped Environmental Telemetry Forensics & Anomaly Reasoning Engine

Live Production Workstation: https://nocturne-nb2y.onrender.com
Source Repository: https://github.com/ayushg-1506/nocturne

NOCTURNE is a local-first, air-gapped environmental telemetry forensics platform engineered to investigate anomalous microclimate and electrical deviations across residential and facility IoT sensor networks.

By combining tabular foundation model statistical scoring (TabPFN) with open-weight deductive reasoning (Google Gemma 2), Nocturne processes multi-variate nocturnal time-series to determine causality: differentiating between mechanical system failures (e.g., HVAC damper collapse, unshielded induction transients) and unclassified anomalous environmental phenomena.

Technical Specifications & Architecture

  • Air-Gapped Privacy: 100% client-side execution. Sensitive domestic sensor logs (occupancy, bedroom microclimates, portal access states) are analyzed locally without transmitting telemetry to third-party cloud vendors.
  • Tabular Foundation Scoring (TabPFN): Multi-variate z-score and Bayesian tabular inference across ambient temperature, acoustic sound pressure level (SPL), resonant frequency, PIR motion, electromagnetic flux (EMF), and circuit wattage.
  • Open-Weight Deductive Reasoning (Gemma 2): Generates dual-verdict causal hypotheses (Rational Physical Hypothesis vs…
View on GitHub

Architecture Stack

  • Frontend Core: React 19, TypeScript, Vite
  • Styling: Custom Obsidian Black (#000000) & Phosphor Green tactical design system with zero external CSS frameworks
  • Acoustic Simulation: Web Audio API procedural synthesis (binaural 18.98 Hz infrasound, 60 Hz domestic hum, Geiger counter EMF clicks)
  • Deployment: Render (Static Site with global CDN edge delivery)

How I Built It

NOCTURNE is architected around a two-stage local AI reasoning pipeline:

[IoT / Edge Telemetry] ---> [CSV / JSON Ingestion Engine]
                                      |
                                      v
                    [TabPFN Tabular Anomaly Scoring]
                    (Residual variance, Z-score thresholds)
                                      |
                                      v
                    [Google Gemma 2 Reasoning Engine]
                    (Local Ollama :11434 / Air-Gapped Adapter)
                                      |
               +----------------------+----------------------+
               |                                             |
               v                                             v
   [Rational Physical Hypothesis]             [Anomalous Phenomenon Deduction]
   (HVAC damper failure, induction            (Thermodynamic collapse,
    coupling, solenoid drift)                  ocular infrasonic resonance)
               |                                             |
               +----------------------+----------------------+
                                      |
                                      v
                    [SHA-256 Tamper-Evident Evidence Seal]
  1. Tabular Anomaly Scoring (TabPFN): Prior-Data Fitted Networks (TabPFN) analyze heterogeneous sensor rows without fine-tuning, calculating tabular divergence scores across temperature deltas (Δ°C), sound pressure levels (SPL dB), electromagnetic induction (µT), and circuit power spikes.
  2. Open-Weight Deductive Reasoning (Google Gemma 2): The sensor deltas are evaluated through open-weight Gemma 2 (via local Ollama or an embedded air-gapped heuristic engine). Rather than hallucinating a single generic answer, Gemma produces a side-by-side Dual Verdict:
    • Rational Physical Hypothesis: Evaluates mechanical damper failures, thermal bridging, plumbing water hammer, and solenoid inductive false-triggers.
    • Anomalous Phenomenon Deduction: Evaluates localized thermodynamic extraction, ocular resonant frequency illusions, and unclassified environmental signatures.
  3. Cryptographic Immutability: Every forensic dossier generates a SHA-256 hash across the raw sensor readings and reasoning outputs, creating a tamper-evident audit trail suitable for investigation reports.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Domestic sensor telemetry contains our most intimate private signatures—sleep schedules, bedroom temperatures, movement patterns, and door latch cycles.

Sending continuous nocturnal smart-home logs to closed proprietary cloud APIs is an unacceptable privacy hazard. Open-weight models like Google Gemma 2 and open tabular frameworks make it possible to run sophisticated forensic AI 100% locally and air-gapped on commodity hardware.

Open innovation ensures that privacy-sensitive analysis remains in the hands of the user—operating completely offline without vendor lock-in, recurring subscriptions, or corporate data harvesting.

The Spirit of It

This project was inspired by British engineer Vic Tandy's 1998 research paper, "The Ghost in the Machine". While working in a medical laboratory reputed to be haunted, Tandy experienced unexplained dread, cold sweats, and fleeting apparitions. He eventually discovered that a newly installed extraction fan was emitting an imperceptible standing sound wave at 18.98 Hz—the exact resonant frequency of the human eyeball. The infrasound caused the eye's vitreous humor to vibrate, producing optical illusions of gray figures in the peripheral vision.

When you load Case #0317 (The Nursery Cold Spot) in NOCTURNE, scrub the timeline to 03:14 AM, and toggle the Spectral Scope audio, you hear the low 18.98 Hz thrum alongside a 7.2°C temperature drop and an unauthenticated deadbolt release. Watching open-source AI dissect the physical vs. anomalous causal chains in real time captures the eerie intersection of physical phenomena and human perception.

title: AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances
description:
AWS Lambda now supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) for lazy loading Event Functions packaged as Open Container Initiative (OCI) images running on Lambda Managed Instances. With SOCI support, Lambda fetches only the files needed at each stage of the execution environment startup rather than downloading the entire image upfront, reducing container startup times by up to 70%.

Customers building compute-intensive applications such as data processing pipelines, high-throughput API backends, and batch computation workloads require substantial memory and CPU resources to process large datasets, serve low-latency responses at scale, and run complex computations efficiently. Container images for these workloads can reach several gigabytes, and downloading and preparing the full image can take several minutes when provisioning new execution environments. SOCI support on Lambda Managed Instances eliminates this bottleneck by streaming only the required files at each stage of the execution environment startup, so your functions start faster as you scale.

To get started, create a SOCI index (a table of contents for the files in your image layers) for your container image and push it to Amazon ECR. When creating or updating your function, set the image URI to the SOCI-indexed tag in Amazon ECR (for example, my-function:v1-soci) and publish a function version. Lambda automatically detects the SOCI index and enables lazy loading with no additional configuration. If you use a coding assistant such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex, install the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS to configure and deploy functions through your agent.

The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Managed Instances developer guide.

title: Why my Solidity test loop went from 56 seconds to under one
description:
The contracts for a game I'm building have 303 tests, compiled with via-IR, and the biggest test file is 7,500 lines long. Editing one test and rerunning the suite took 56 seconds with Foundry and 61 with Hardhat 3. With plain, the toolchain I wrote, the same edit and rerun takes 0.99 seconds, on the same project, with the same foundry.toml and nothing changed in the code. Solc is the same too: what gets deployed is byte for byte what solc produces. The speed comes from not doing work twice, and this post is about where that work hides.

All numbers below are medians from hyperfine on an M1 Max, measured on October 17, 2026, with forge 1.7.1, Hardhat 3.20.0 and the solc each project pins. Foundry / Hardhat / plain:

The game (via-IR) Uniswap v4-core (via-IR) solmate
Edit a test, run the tests 56 s / 61 s / 0.99 s 24 s / 26 s / 1.8 s 4.6 s / 4.2 s / 0.07 s
Edit a contract function, run the tests 103 s / 109 s / 2.1 s 130 s / 132 s / 4.2 s 6.0 s / 5.7 s / 1.5 s
Build from scratch 116 s / 115 s / 15 s 141 s / 144 s / 12 s 5.6 s / 6.8 s / 1.1 s

Every test passes under plain: 303 in the game, 598 in v4-core and 568 in solmate.

Tests compile your contracts again

This one surprised me the most. When a test does new Vault(args), solc has to put Vault's whole bytecode inside the test contract, so it compiles and optimizes Vault again, once per test file. With via-IR, that repeated work is most of the build.

plain compiles test files with each new X(...) replaced by a deploy of X's already compiled artifact, with the same init code, deployer, nonce and address. The constructor arguments are still type-checked against X, so a wrong argument is still a compile error. A side effect: since tests no longer contain your contracts' bytecode, editing a function in src/ doesn't recompile the tests at all. A test file is cached by its own source plus the interfaces of what it imports, with function bodies left out.

A big test file doesn't compile as one unit

A 7,500-line test file is one huge job for solc. plain splits it into several units that compile at the same time, each holding only its share of the test functions; the rest are cut out of the source, so solc doesn't even type-check them. Each unit remembers which tests it holds. When you edit test bodies, the untouched units stay cached and the edited or new tests compile into one small "hot" unit. That's why editing a test costs about a second instead of a minute.

Unchanged tests don't run again

A suite's results are reused while its bytecode, the settings and everything it read (deployed artifacts, files, environment variables) stay the same, and cached suites print (cached). Tests are deterministic, with a fixed fuzz seed and no wall clock, so this is safe. Anything that isn't deterministic always reruns: suites that call ffi, writeFile, unixTime or setEnv, and every fork test. --rerun runs everything anyway.

The rest is scheduling and caching

  • Parallel solc. Compile jobs go on a work queue, biggest first, sized from the last build's timings. Foundry and Hardhat run one solc process at a time.
  • Parallel tests. Suites, tests and individual fuzz and invariant runs execute in parallel on an in-process revm, each starting from a copy-on-write view of the post-setUp state.
  • A shared cache. Results are keyed by content hash and kept in ~/.plain/cache, so a new git worktree or a fresh clone of already built sources runs its tests in 0.06 seconds instead of doing a cold build. That matters a lot when AI agents work in their own worktrees.
  • Only what's needed. plain test Vault compiles only the test files that filter can match.

In CI

I also ran Uniswap v4-core on GitHub Actions' 2-core runners, taking the median of repeated runs. With the build cache restored and one line changed in PoolManager.swap, forge build took 3 minutes 1 second at 4.3 GB of memory, and plain build took 2.6 seconds at 0.1 GB. A cold build from nothing is a smaller win on two cores: 3 minutes 57 seconds for Foundry against 1 minute 17 seconds for plain, at 5.0 GB and 0.7 GB of memory. Parallel solc needs cores to shine.

What it doesn't do yet

plain runs Foundry-style Solidity tests with fuzzing, invariants and the common cheatcodes, plus TypeScript tests against a fresh chain per file. It reads foundry.toml, so existing projects work as they are, but it isn't every Foundry feature, so check the list of supported cheatcodes in the README if your suite leans on unusual ones. It's also new, so expect rough edges, and tell me about them.

Try it on your project 

curl -fsSL https://getplain.org/install | sh
cd your-foundry-project
plain test --watch

That compiles and runs every test, then again on every save. It's also on Homebrew, npm (npx plain-evm test), apt, dnf, the AUR, mise, Nix and crates.io. The docs cover testing, deploying with verification on Sourcify, Etherscan and Blockscout, and upgrades, and the source and the full benchmark notes are on GitHub.

title: We Tested 5 AI Coding Tools Against Rust's Borrow Checker — Here's What Compiled
description:
Disclosure: This article contains affiliate links. We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our rankings — we only make money if we point you to the tool that's actually right for you.

Rust is a bad language to fake your way through with an LLM. Python forgives a wrong guess — code "looks right," runs, and you fix the type error later. Rust doesn't negotiate: it's correct or it's a compile error, and the gap between "almost right" and "right" is frequently a single &, mut, or lifetime annotation.

So instead of asking which AI coding tool "feels" best for Rust, we measured something falsifiable: how often does each tool's suggestion actually compile on the first try.

What we ran

Five tools — Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Tabnine, and Claude Code — against four real project types: a clap-based CLI, an axum async web server with database pooling and JWT auth, a systems library with unsafe blocks and FFI via bindgen, and a wasm-bindgen WebAssembly module. Same codebase, same Rust 1.77 toolchain, three weeks, tracked whether each suggestion compiled without edits.

The numbers

Compile-on-first-try rate across all four projects:

  • Cursor: 72%
  • Copilot: 58%
  • Windsurf: 51%
  • Tabnine: 44%

Claude Code doesn't fit this metric cleanly — it's a task-based terminal agent, not inline autocomplete — but on a harder test (15 real borrow-checker errors, fix-and-explain), it correctly resolved 14. Cursor fixed 11 but couldn't always explain why. Copilot fixed 9.

Where the gap actually shows up

Ownership, not syntax, is what separates these tools. On mutable-borrow detection specifically, Cursor correctly identified when &mut was required about 85% of the time versus Copilot's 70%. Windsurf's failure mode was the opposite of what you'd expect — not under-cautious, but reflexively inserting .clone() to dodge borrow errors it couldn't resolve, which compiles but teaches exactly the wrong habit.

For unsafe code and FFI, Claude Code was the standout: it documented safety invariants in comments (something none of the inline tools did unprompted), handled raw pointer round-trips correctly, and in one bindgen-wrapped C library test, was the only tool to add a correct Drop implementation preventing a memory leak nobody asked it to look for.

The advanced-type-system test — implementing a typestate builder pattern with phantom types and zero-sized types for compile-time state checking — only Claude Code got fully right. Cursor's attempt had a gap in the type transitions. Everyone else produced incomplete implementations.

The honest tradeoffs

Cursor's weakness is over-suggestion: unnecessary trait bounds, derives you won't use, and in multi-lifetime generic code it sometimes produces something that compiles but is more restrictive than it needs to be. Claude Code has no inline completions at all — most Rust developers who use it pair it with an editor-based tool for daily typing and save Claude Code for the lifetime error they don't understand.

Full breakdown

The complete writeup has the per-category breakdown (async/tokio, cargo integration, trait implementations, no_std/embedded), the testing methodology in full, and pricing for each tool.

title: Building a pricing-first filter for 4,300 AI tools (and what the data looks like)
description:
A few weeks ago I started AIVerse, a directory of AI tools. The premise was simple: every "best AI tools" list I could find was either a paid placement farm or so stale that half the pricing was wrong. So I built the boring version instead — one that treats pricing and category data as something to be maintained, not written once.

This post is about the data side, because that is where the surprises were.

The shape of the data

Current state of the catalogue, pulled today rather than typed from memory:

Pricing model Tools Share
Free 2,198 50.8%
Freemium 1,425 33.0%
Paid 700 16.2%
Total 4,323 across 92 categories

Category concentration is steeper than I expected. Four categories hold a quarter of everything:

  • Video Generators — 294
  • Image Generators — 269
  • Productivity — 253
  • Developer Tools — 247

The remaining 88 categories average about 37 tools each. 708 listings carry a 2026 publish date, which tells you how fast the supply side is still growing.

One number I do not want to hide: only 614 listings have a verification level recorded. "Free" is therefore a claim taken from the vendor page, not something I confirmed by signing up. That gap is exactly the difference between a directory and a database, and it is the thing I am slowly paying down.

The bug that actually mattered

While exporting every listing to check link health, I diffed the websiteUrl field against vendor domains and found 30 rows pointing not at the vendor but at an affiliate redirect:

capcut → capcutaffiliateprogram.pxf.io/9LPy7W

pxf.io is Impact's link domain; partnerlinks.io is another one. The tracking URLs carried a referring sub-ID (?s=...), which means every "Visit website" click on those 30 pages was crediting someone else's affiliate account. Worse, the descriptions on those same rows said things like "You can use CapCut online at capcutaffiliateprogram.pxf.io" — a templated sentence that turned out to be repeated across 2,084 pages of the site.

Three fixes, in order of how much they mattered:

  1. Reject tracking domains at every entry point. There is one shared list, imported by the crawler, the CSV importer and the public submission form. Previously each path had its own validation and they had drifted apart.
  2. Resolve the 30 existing rows by following the redirect chain to the final vendor domain. Four needed manual judgment: one landed on a /fr locale, one self-redirected in a loop, one dead-ended on the tracker, and one pointed at a completely different product page.
  3. Strip the templated sentence at render time, so those pages stopped showing the tracker before the underlying data was cleaned.

How the pipeline works now

  1. Crawl the upstream catalogue.
  2. Reject tracking domains and anything that is not a vendor-owned URL.
  3. Strip boilerplate — four known template markers. Whatever is left under 25 words gets queued for a human instead of being rendered.
  4. Hand-write the top 150 pages by traffic, four facts each: free tier limit, price tiers, two pros, two cons, and who it is for.
  5. Store that hand-written copy in a git-tracked JSON overlay that takes precedence over the crawled description at render time.

Step 5 is the one I would recommend to anyone building the same thing. My first attempt wrote copy straight into the production SQLite database through an admin form. That sounds fine until you notice the deploy hook restores the live database from a backup on every push — so the copy existed only on the server that was about to be overwritten. Content in git gets a diff, a review and a rollback. Content in a production table gets none of those unless you build them yourself.

What is still broken

  • 9 of 150 pages written. The queue orders by traffic, so this is the head of the distribution, but 94% of the hand-written coverage is missing.
  • No affiliate links yet. Zero of 4,323 listings have a commercial link. That is deliberate: I would rather send traffic to the vendor for free than send it to a tracker that does not pay.
  • The traffic numbers are inherited, not measured. They come from the source catalogue. The only numbers I trust are outbound clicks, and the total is 4. Four clicks. That is the real baseline — everything else is a guess.

Why publish this

Because the honest version is more useful than a launch post. If you are building a directory, the tracking-domain contamination and the "content in the production DB" trap will both find you, and they are easier to spot when someone else has already paid for them.

If you want to look at the result: AIVerse, free AI tools

Start with the free filter — 2,198 listings, filterable by category, with the pricing field printed on every card so you can see what the data quality actually looks like. If a listing is wrong, there is a submission form and I fix it.

title: We Gave 5 AI Coding Tools a Real Goroutine Leak to Fix — Only One Found the Actual Bug
description:
Disclosure: We link out to every tool we test. None of the five tools below currently has a confirmed, active affiliate relationship with us, so nothing here is commission-motivated.

Go doesn't leave much room for "almost right." gofmt means there's one accepted formatting. Explicit error returns mean there's no ambiguity about whether a function can fail. So instead of asking which AI coding tool "feels" best for Go, we gave five of them the same production bug and the same four project types — an HTTP service, a CLI, a gRPC microservice, and a concurrent worker pool — and watched what they actually did with it.

The bug

A worker pool was occasionally leaking goroutines under load. The real cause: a select statement that didn't handle context cancellation, so workers blocked forever on a channel send after the parent context was cancelled. The fix was three lines.

Claude Code traced it in minutes — correctly identified the missing case <-ctx.Done(), explained why the goroutines were piling up, and proposed the three-line fix.

Cursor suggested a plausible-looking fix: add a timeout. It compiled, it "worked," and it masked the leak instead of fixing it — the workers still blocked, just for a bounded time instead of forever.

That's the gap that doesn't show up in a feature checklist: one tool diagnosed the actual failure mode, the other patched the symptom.

Where the rest fell down

We also asked each tool to add a database method to an existing service, and to refactor a *sql.DB-based service into one that takes an interface, for testability.

  • Cursor wrote the method with correct errors.Is handling and defer-closed the *sql.Rows with error handling on the close. Copilot missed the defer-close error check. Windsurf used %v instead of %w for error wrapping, which silently drops the error chain — the kind of bug that only bites you three services downstream when errors.Is stops matching.
  • On the interface refactor, Cursor produced a tight Querier interface with only the methods the service actually called. Copilot's interface was too wide, pulling in methods nothing used. Claude Code's interface was the cleanest of all three, but it's terminal-based, so you're applying the diff by hand.

The numbers

Compile-on-first-try rate across all four project types, tracked over three weeks on the same Go 1.22 codebase:

  • Cursor: ~85%
  • Copilot: ~75%
  • Windsurf: ~65%
  • Tabnine: ~55%

Claude Code doesn't fit this metric — it's a task-based terminal agent, not inline autocomplete — which is exactly why it's the one that caught the goroutine leak nobody asked it to look for twice: once in the original bug, once in a context-propagated tracing task where it ended every span correctly on error paths and Cursor missed one.

The honest tradeoff

None of this makes one tool strictly better. Cursor is the best daily driver for Go — highest compile rate, best module/go.mod awareness, cleanest table-driven tests. Claude Code is what you reach for when the bug is subtle and the stakes are a 3am page, not a missing semicolon. Copilot at $10/month is the value pick if you're already in the GitHub ecosystem. Windsurf is a budget option only if someone senior is reviewing its concurrency code before it ships.

The full writeup has the complete testing methodology, the gRPC and CLI results, and current pricing for all five tools.

title: OpenAPI-First vs Collection-First API Workflows
description:
Short answer: A collection-first workflow maintains requests as the artifact; a contract-first workflow maintains the spec and derives the requests. The first is intuitive and drifts; the second is a discipline and stays correct. For a team that already versions an API, the contract is the durable source.

What collection-first optimizes for

Immediacy: you build a request, save it, and run it. There is no upfront modeling. The cost is that the collection is a separate, authored artifact that must be kept in sync with the API by hand.

What contract-first optimizes for

Property Collection-first Contract-first
Source of truth The collection The spec
Upfront cost Low Modeling
Drift Common Rare
Generated surfaces None Requests, docs, mocks, tools

Why the contract scales

One spec drives every surface, so a change is made once and the requests, docs, mocks, and agent tools all reflect it. A collection-first team makes the same change in several places.

The honest tradeoff

Contract-first asks for discipline and modeling up front. It pays back as the surface grows; for a single, stable endpoint, a collection can be the pragmatic choice.

title: I rebuilt warden's console: 16 tabs down to 6 (and found my own DB world-readable)
description:
warden is my homelab security console — it reads the logs my WAF can't see, scans the boxes, watches my AI agents, and proposes bans and patches I approve with a ✅ in Discord. It never does anything on its own. I wrote up what it does before; this is about the cleanup I just did, because it had got messy.

It had grown 16 tabs

Every time I added something — incidents, agent tracking, vulnerabilities, endpoint integrity — it got its own tab. Dashboards grow like that. One day I counted and it was 16 tabs across four groups, and I realised I was hunting for things I used every day.

So I cut it down to 6:

  • Overview — the dashboard
  • Review — the one place for everything waiting on my ✅ / ❌
  • Threats — detections, edge, network, incidents, geo
  • Agents — what my AI agents are reaching out to
  • Posture — attack surface, vulnerabilities, endpoints, health
  • Settings

The related views sit under a little sub-nav inside each tab, so nothing's gone — it's just one click deeper. And instead of a scary number on every tab, a parent tab shows a small dot when something inside actually needs me. The real counts live where they make sense, so I don't get a meaningless "512" on a tab that's really just counting known CVEs.

The small things that were quietly annoying

  • The settings page listed raw config keys like patch.expire_hours and cloudflare.zone_id. Now each field has a plain label ("Approval expires after (hours)", "Cloudflare Zone ID") with the raw key dimmed underneath, so I still know what maps to the config file.
  • API tokens and the "how do I connect a tool" bits were off on their own. They live under Account now, where I'd actually look for them.
  • The approvals queue used to sit on top of the Settings page. It's its own Review tab now.

The bit that mattered: my database was world-readable

While I was in there I checked how warden stores anything sensitive. Most of it was already fine — API tokens are only kept as a SHA-256 hash, passwords are scrypt, session cookies are random and only their hash is stored, and actual secrets (bot tokens, API keys) never touch the database at all.

Then I looked at the file permissions on the database itself. 644. World-readable.

On a shared box that's a real problem: the database holds logs, session hashes, and — if you use warden's own 2FA — the TOTP seed. Anything else running on that machine as another user could just read it. In my case that includes the sandboxed coding agent I let loose on my repos, which is exactly the kind of thing warden exists to keep honest.

Fix was simple but I made it stick: warden now forces the database (and its write-ahead files) to 0600 on every start, and each process sets a umask so anything it creates is owner-only from birth. I tested it by deliberately setting it back to 644 and restarting — it put itself straight back to 600.

The lesson I keep relearning: the dangerous gaps aren't the exotic ones. It was a default file permission sitting there the whole time.

Get it

It's on GitHub, AGPL-3.0, dependency-free Python — it'll run on a Pi. The v3.2 release has the full changelog, and there's a 5-minute demo setup if you want to click around before wiring it to anything.

Still detect-only and read-only by default. It tells me what it'd do; I decide.

Before incorporating historical information into current operations, ask:

Where did the information originate?

Why was it stored there?

Who was intended to receive it?

What permission supports its use?

Is it necessary for the current task?

Naver’s terms require accurate member information and prohibit using another person’s account without permission.policy.naver

Unclear data should be treated as a responsibility to assess, not an added benefit of account access.

Separate Naver Email From Other Naver Services
Naver offers more than email. Its ecosystem includes search, community services, and other products.

Do not assume that access to one service establishes access to every other service.

For example, a search-oriented need, an email need, and a commercial service need may involve different requirements.

Before selecting an arrangement, identify the exact product you need and review its current requirements.

A seller’s broad description of an account as “ready for Naver” does not explain which services are included or under what conditions.

Check “Verified” Claims Carefully
“Verified” can sound reassuring while leaving important details unexplained.

It might refer to a previous identity check, a phone number, a document submission, or another limited process. Without clarification, it does not establish that the current user is authorized to use the account.

Ask:

What was verified?

Which person’s identity was checked?

Who performed the verification?

Which service was involved?

Does the verification remain relevant to the intended user?

Naver’s terms require accurate member information. Its help center also explains that identity-related requests can involve matching account information with official identification details.policy.naver+1

A seller-applied label should not replace those requirements.

Be Careful With “Lifetime Access” Claims
A claim of lifetime access needs a precise definition.

Does it concern the inbox, a particular Naver service, an identity verification status, or an outside benefit? Those are separate promises.

Ask who makes the commitment, which conditions apply, and what happens if Naver requires new verification.

Do not combine several uncertain claims into one assumption that everything will remain available indefinitely.

For planning purposes, identify which activities depend on the account and how you would continue if access needs changed.

This does not predict a particular failure. It ensures that important work is not built around an undefined promise.

Compare the Total Cost, Not Just the Purchase Price
The initial price is only one part of the decision.

A useful account arrangement also requires setup, administration, security reviews, support, and a plan for future access problems.

Consider a hypothetical business that chooses an account solely because it appears inexpensive. Later, it discovers that responsibilities are unclear and that important communication depends on an account whose ownership is uncertain.

The original payment may have been small, but the operating challenge remains.

A fuller assessment includes:

Setup time.

Ongoing administration.

Support availability.

Identity and recovery requirements.

Dependence on outside parties.

The effort required to change direction.

The cheapest-looking account is not automatically the most useful way to meet your need.

A Practical Planning Framework
Before relying on an account offer, work through a short review process.

Define the Need
State exactly what you need to accomplish on Naver.

For example: “I need access to Korean-language search services for research.”

Identify the Service
Determine whether the requirement concerns email, search, identity verification, a commercial service, or another Naver product.

Review the Applicable Rules
Naver prohibits selling, transferring, lending, providing accounts as security, and allowing others to use accounts.policy.naver

Establish Access Responsibility
Decide who will maintain recovery information and respond to access problems.

Review Security Needs
Consider two-factor authentication and IP-security requirements as part of ongoing account management.help.naver+1

Consider Future Changes
Think about access location, changing responsibilities, and the possibility of moving to another service.

Frequently Asked Questions
Does Naver allow accounts to be sold or transferred?
No. Naver’s Terms of Service state that users should not sell, transfer, lend, provide accounts as security, or allow others to use them.policy.naver

Does an older account automatically provide better security?
Age alone does not establish security. Naver provides guidance for two-factor authentication and IP security, which require ongoing account management.help.naver+1

Why is identity verification important?
Naver’s support processes for temporary passwords and login restrictions can involve identity verification, including matching account information with official identification details.help.naver+1

Is a seller’s guarantee the same as Naver’s approval?
No. A private promise does not change Naver’s terms or establish permission for an account transfer.policy.naver

Does account age establish access to every Naver service?
Do not assume so. Identify the specific service you need and review its current requirements.

Conclusion

Contract Testing: Insomnia vs Powerduck
description:
Short answer: A client can run assertions on the fields you choose; a contract-first studio verifies the whole response against the schema. The first proves the specific checks you remembered; the second proves there is no undeclared property, missing field, or type drift anywhere.

What assertions cover

They are precise and useful for the fields you decide to check. They are also only as good as the list, so a violation in an unasserted field passes the test.

What contract verification adds

Condition Assertions Contract check
Chosen fields Checked Checked
Undeclared property Missed Flagged
Missing required field Only if listed Flagged
Type drift anywhere Missed Flagged

The failure that matters

A response that passes every written assertion yet violates the contract is the gap. The contract check examines the full response, so it does not depend on a human listing every field.

How to combine them

Keep the behavioral assertions for the flows and add the contract check for conformance. They prove different things and both belong in the pipeline.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read pricing and lock-in.

title: Choose the reporting timezone before grouping campaign events
description:
An AI assistant can group an event export by the first ten characters of its timestamp and produce a neat daily table. That table can still use the wrong day boundary.

This small exercise makes the boundary explicit before asking an assistant to summarize a campaign. It counts four fictional event rows, not unique users, qualified leads, or purchases. Nothing connects to an ad account or changes a campaign.

Four timestamps, three possible tables

Save this UTF-8 fixture as events.csv:

event,occurred_at
E01,2026-10-28T20:59:00Z
E02,2026-10-28T21:00:00Z
E03,2026-10-29T00:15:00+03:00
E04,2026-10-29T22:15:00+03:00

The first two timestamps use UTC (Z). The other two include +03:00. For this exercise, the reporting timezone is Europe/Moscow. Choose the timezone specified by your real report; this example does not imply every campaign uses Moscow time.

E01 is one minute before midnight in that timezone. E02 is exactly midnight, so it belongs to the next reporting day. E03 and E04 belong to that next day too.

These are the results of three different grouping rules:

Grouping rule October 28 October 29
First ten characters of each supplied string 2 2
Convert every timestamp to UTC, then take its date 3 1
Convert every timestamp to Europe/Moscow, then take its date 1 3

All three tables count four rows. A total-count check would not reveal the different day boundaries. For the stated reporting contract, the last row is the expected result.

Convert before taking the date

The following complete script uses Python's standard library. Save it as group_events.py beside events.csv:

import csv
import json
from collections import Counter
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo


REPORT_TZ_NAME = "Europe/Moscow"
REPORT_TZ = ZoneInfo(REPORT_TZ_NAME)


def group_events(rows):
    counts = Counter()
    assignments = []
    for row in rows:
        raw = row["occurred_at"]
        stamp = datetime.fromisoformat(raw.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
        if stamp.utcoffset() is None:
            raise ValueError(row["event"] + ": explicit UTC offset required")
        report_day = stamp.astimezone(REPORT_TZ).date().isoformat()
        counts[report_day] += 1
        assignments.append({"event": row["event"], "report_date": report_day})
    return {
        "report_timezone": REPORT_TZ_NAME,
        "counts": dict(sorted(counts.items())),
        "assignments": assignments,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        with Path(__file__).with_name("events.csv").open(
            encoding="utf-8", newline=""
        ) as stream:
            report = group_events(list(csv.DictReader(stream)))
    except (ValueError, KeyError) as error:
        print(json.dumps({"error": str(error)}))
        raise SystemExit(2)
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

Run it with:

python3 group_events.py

The output includes the timezone, the counts, and an assignment for each input row:

{
  "report_timezone": "Europe/Moscow",
  "counts": {
    "2026-10-28": 1,
    "2026-10-29": 3
  },
  "assignments": [
    {"event": "E01", "report_date": "2026-10-28"},
    {"event": "E02", "report_date": "2026-10-29"},
    {"event": "E03", "report_date": "2026-10-29"},
    {"event": "E04", "report_date": "2026-10-29"}
  ]
}

The output above uses more compact spacing for the assignment objects; the JSON values are the same as the script's output. Keeping those assignments makes it possible to inspect which event crossed a date boundary instead of comparing totals alone.

The fixture and script were executed locally on Python 3.9.6. The four assignments and the three grouping alternatives in the table were checked. No external language model response was measured in this run; the script provides a reference result for checking one.

zoneinfo requires Python 3.9 or later and available IANA timezone data. It uses the system database or the tzdata package, as described in Python's official zoneinfo documentation. The local run had the required data. A machine without it may raise ZoneInfoNotFoundError; silently replacing the chosen zone with the computer's local timezone would change the contract.

Reject an unspecified offset

Change E03 to this value:

E03,2026-10-29T00:15:00

The timestamp now has no UTC offset. The script stops with exit code 2 and prints:

{"error": "E03: explicit UTC offset required"}

It does not print partial daily counts. Guessing that the value means UTC, Moscow time, or the operator's laptop time would produce a result without a stated source rule. Python distinguishes these naive timestamps from aware timestamps in its datetime documentation.

If the source system documents an offset-free value as belonging to a particular timezone, handle that as a separate input contract. This short example deliberately refuses to infer it.

Check that a different representation preserves the instant

Restore the original fixture. Then replace E02's timestamp with 2026-10-29T00:00:00+03:00.

That is the same instant as 2026-10-28T21:00:00Z. The script must return the same counts and assignments. A program that groups by the string's date would move the row simply because its representation changed.

Both this mutation and the missing-offset mutation were executed locally. One checks an invariant; the other checks a refusal condition.

Use the reference when reviewing an AI summary

Give an assistant the original CSV and a specific instruction:

Count event rows by calendar date in Europe/Moscow.
Require an explicit UTC offset or Z on every timestamp.
Convert each instant to Europe/Moscow before extracting its date.
Do not group by a substring or by the timestamp's original timezone.
If any timestamp has no offset or cannot be parsed, report the error;
do not return partial daily counts and do not guess a timezone.
Return the reporting timezone, daily counts, and each event's assigned date.
Do not infer unique users, leads, purchases, or campaign performance.

Compare the individual assignments as well as the counts. Then repeat the two mutations. A well-written explanation should not conceal a changed grouping rule or an invented offset.

This is a narrowly scoped fixture, not a production analytics pipeline. It assumes the displayed CSV schema and already deduplicated event rows. It does not check export completeness, attribution windows, delayed events, refunds, event definitions, or duplicate identifiers. Those require their own acceptance cases before a daily table can support a business conclusion.

Prepared with an AI agent. The displayed fixture, code, reference values, and two input mutations were checked locally. All event data is synthetic.

title: How Web Design Development Helps Businesses Grow | Dv Orbit
description:
How Web Design Development Helps Businesses Succeed Online

In today's competitive digital world, businesses need a strong online presence to attract customers, build credibility, and remain competitive. A professional website allows companies to showcase their services, communicate their values, and connect with potential customers. However, creating an effective website requires more than an attractive layout. It involves thoughtful planning, reliable functionality, and an understanding of customer needs.

Web Design Development combines creative design with technical expertise to create websites that are visually appealing, accessible, and easy to navigate. Businesses that invest in a well-planned website can improve customer experiences and establish a solid foundation for long-term growth.

Why Professional Website Design Matters

A website often creates the first impression of a business. When visitors arrive at a website, they expect clear information, attractive visuals, and straightforward navigation. A confusing layout or outdated appearance can discourage potential customers from exploring further.

Professional website design helps businesses present their brands consistently. Colors, typography, images, and page layouts should work together to communicate the company's identity. Clear headings and organized content also make it easier for visitors to understand products and services.

Mobile responsiveness is another essential element. Many people browse websites on smartphones and tablets, so pages should adapt to different screen sizes. A responsive website allows visitors to read content, navigate menus, and complete forms without unnecessary difficulty.

Accessibility should also be considered during the design process. Readable text, sufficient color contrast, descriptive links, and logical heading structures help create a better experience for a wider audience. These improvements demonstrate attention to detail and support more inclusive digital experiences.

How Web Design Development Supports Business Growth

An attractive website is valuable, but its features must also work correctly. Web development provides the technical foundation for contact forms, booking systems, online stores, customer portals, and other interactive tools.

Different businesses require different functionalities. A consulting company may need appointment scheduling, while an online retailer might require product catalogs and secure payment processing. Choosing features that match business objectives helps avoid unnecessary complexity and creates a more useful website.

Performance is equally important. Visitors expect pages to load quickly and respond smoothly. Developers can improve loading speeds through image compression, efficient coding, reliable hosting, and the removal of unnecessary scripts. Better performance helps visitors access information with less frustration.

Security must remain a priority as well. Secure connections, updated software, regular backups, and appropriate access controls can reduce common website risks. Businesses that collect personal information should implement suitable safeguards to protect customer data and maintain confidence.

Search Engine Optimization for Better Visibility

A professional website should help potential customers discover a business online. Search engine optimization supports this goal by improving website structure, content quality, and accessibility.

Businesses can strengthen their websites by using descriptive page titles, meaningful headings, relevant internal links, and optimized images. Publishing useful articles and detailed service pages can also help answer customer questions and demonstrate industry knowledge.

Keyword research helps identify the phrases people use when searching for products or services. These keywords should be included naturally in relevant content rather than repeated excessively. Search engines and readers benefit from informative writing that focuses on genuine user needs.

Technical improvements alone cannot guarantee high rankings. Competition, content relevance, website authority, and many other factors influence search performance. A consistent approach that combines technical quality with valuable content provides a stronger foundation for sustainable visibility.

Discover Digital Solutions with Dv Orbit

Choosing a suitable digital solutions provider can help businesses turn their ideas into practical online experiences. Companies should consider their goals, target audiences, technical requirements, and budgets before selecting a website strategy.

Dv Orbit provides a starting point for businesses exploring web development, custom software, and digital solutions. Through its website, Dv Orbit, businesses can learn more about its digital services and explore options for strengthening their online presence.

A successful website project begins with identifying the problems a business wants to solve. Some companies may need a new website, while others might want to improve an existing platform, simplify customer interactions, or introduce additional functionality.

Professional Web Design Development can help businesses combine attractive layouts with practical features. A well-organized website makes information easier to find, supports brand consistency, and gives visitors a clear path toward contacting the company or learning about its services.

Dv Orbit recognizes the importance of digital solutions that support modern business requirements. By considering usability, functionality, and future needs, businesses can make informed decisions about improving their websites and developing their digital capabilities.

Creating a Better Customer Experience

Customer experience should remain central to every website project. Visitors should be able to understand what a business offers and find the information they need without unnecessary effort.

Clear navigation, helpful service descriptions, visible contact information, and simple forms can make interactions more convenient. Businesses can also publish frequently asked questions, educational articles, and practical resources to address common concerns.

Trust is another important factor. Accurate information, consistent branding, secure browsing, and transparent communication help visitors feel more confident when interacting with a business. A professional website should present information honestly and avoid misleading claims.

Analytics can provide useful insights into visitor behavior. By reviewing popular pages, traffic sources, and completed inquiries, businesses can identify opportunities to improve their websites. Regular testing and thoughtful updates help ensure that the website continues meeting customer expectations.

Maintaining a Website for Long-Term Success

Launching a website is only the beginning of its development. Regular maintenance helps keep pages, forms, integrations, and other features working properly. Businesses should review performance, apply software updates, monitor security, and resolve technical issues when necessary.

As organizations grow, their digital requirements may change. A website might need additional service pages, new integrations, improved navigation, or more advanced functionality. Planning for scalability makes it easier to accommodate these changes without rebuilding the entire platform.

Ongoing improvements also help businesses remain responsive to changing customer preferences and industry developments. A website should evolve alongside the organization it represents.

Conclusion

Web Design Development plays an important role in helping businesses establish a professional online presence. By combining responsive design, reliable functionality, useful content, search optimization, and ongoing maintenance, companies can create better experiences for their customers.

Businesses that prioritize usability and clear objectives can turn their websites into valuable digital assets. Exploring the services offered by Dv Orbit at dvorbit.com can be a useful starting point for organizations looking to understand their web development and digital solution options. With careful planning and continuous improvement, a strong website can support customer engagement and long-term business growth.

title: Base64, URL encoding, hashes, UUIDs and Unix timestamps: the one-liners I kept looking up
description:
Every few days I need to Base64 a file, hash a download, or turn an epoch value into a date, and every few days I search for the exact same one-liner. So I finally wrote them down in one place. Copy what you need.

Base64

Where Encode Decode
Linux / macOS base64 file.png base64 -d encoded.txt (-D on older macOS)
PowerShell [Convert]::ToBase64String([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('file.png')) [Convert]::FromBase64String($s)
Python base64.b64encode(data) base64.b64decode(s)
Browser JS btoa(str) atob(s)
Node.js Buffer.from(str).toString('base64') Buffer.from(s, 'base64')
PHP base64_encode($data) base64_decode($s)

Gotcha: btoa only accepts Latin-1. Text with accents or emoji needs a TextEncoder step first, or it throws.

URL encoding

Language Encode one value Watch out
JavaScript encodeURIComponent(value) encodeURI is for a whole address
Python urllib.parse.quote(value, safe='') quote_plus turns spaces into +
PHP rawurlencode($value) urlencode uses + for spaces
Java URLEncoder.encode(value, "UTF-8") produces +; use %20 inside a path
C# Uri.EscapeDataString(value) HttpUtility.UrlEncode uses +

Gotcha: if you see %2520, the value was encoded twice. Decode once, encode once.

File hashes (checking a download)

System SHA-256 MD5
Windows cmd certutil -hashfile file.iso SHA256 certutil -hashfile file.iso MD5
PowerShell Get-FileHash file.iso -Algorithm SHA256 Get-FileHash file.iso -Algorithm MD5
Linux sha256sum file.iso md5sum file.iso
macOS shasum -a 256 file.iso md5 file.iso
Python hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()

The result is identical everywhere: a hash depends only on the bytes, never on the tool.

UUIDs

Platform One-liner
JavaScript crypto.randomUUID()
Python import uuid; uuid.uuid4()
Java UUID.randomUUID()
C# Guid.NewGuid() (Guid.CreateVersion7() on .NET 9)
PostgreSQL gen_random_uuid() (uuidv7() from PostgreSQL 18)
MySQL UUID() (careful: this is a time-based v1)
Shell uuidgen

Gotcha: for database primary keys, prefer v7. It starts with a millisecond timestamp, so new rows land at the end of the index instead of scattering through it.

Unix timestamps

Where Now Timestamp to date
JavaScript Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) new Date(ts * 1000)
Python int(time.time()) datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, tz=timezone.utc)
PHP time() date('Y-m-d H:i:s', $ts)
MySQL UNIX_TIMESTAMP() FROM_UNIXTIME(ts)
PostgreSQL EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now()) to_timestamp(ts)
Shell date +%s date -d @1700000000 (date -r 1700000000 on macOS)
Excel – =A1/86400 + DATE(1970,1,1) (UTC)

Gotcha: 10 digits is seconds, 13 digits is milliseconds. A date in 1970 means you passed milliseconds where seconds were expected, or the other way round.

Discord bonus: <t:1700000000:R> renders as a relative time in every reader's own time zone.

When I don't have a terminal handy, I use the browser versions of these on LogicUtil, a set of free tools that run entirely client-side (nothing is uploaded, no sign-up). Disclosure: I built it. The same tables also live in a GitHub repo: saman-webdev/dev-one-liners. If one of the one-liners above is wrong for your platform, tell me in the comments and I'll fix it.

title: Introducing the new v0 API
description:
Today we're introducing the new v0 API: programmatic, headless access to v0's app-building agent. Send a prompt and v0 generates an app, starts a dev server in a Vercel Sandbox, and gives you a preview URL you can embed in your own UI.

Each chat is an isolated workspace for one app, where v0 can read, edit, and run the files. Follow-up messages continue from the current state. v0 verifies the code running in the Sandbox, so it can catch and fix errors in your app in real time.

The new API is now generally available.

How it works

Create a chat from a prompt, stream its work, and render the live preview, all from your own interface. First, install the v0 SDK.

Then, create a chat. Send a prompt, and v0 generates your app.

Send follow-up messages to the same chat to keep building. Each one continues from the current state.

Then embed the app.

A prompt goes in, a running app comes out. v0 operates the Sandbox, dev server, and preview behind it. When you're ready, deploy to Vercel in one API call. v0 manages the whole pipeline.

What this unlocks

The new API lets you run v0's app builder inside your own product or pipeline. This opens use cases like:

  • A white-labeled app builder: Your users describe an app and get one back.

  • Automated app changes: Trigger v0 from a script, CI job, or webhook to generate a new app or update an existing one.

  • A build tool for your agents: An agent hands back a working app instead of a code snippet.

Below, we break down the API primitives behind this workflow.

Start with a chat

Each chat holds the state for one app, and a repo or Vercel project can have many. Keep each chat's ID and send its follow-up messages to that chat. Metadata lets you group chats by customer, workspace, app, or any key you already use.

Learn more about messages.

Stream the trace

Your interface needs to show what happens between sending a request and seeing the updated preview.

Every message includes ordered parts: text, thinking, file reads and edits, searches, bash commands, tool calls, and agent actions. The same object can drive a one-line status, a changed-files view, or the full trace.

Usage is returned with chat and message responses, so you can account for the work when it finishes.

Choose sync, async, or streaming

Chat creation and messages support synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming responses. Use sync when the caller needs the completed response. Use async to queue the work and receive updates via webhook or poll for v0's response later. Stream the request to render v0's work as it happens.

Work from existing code

You can also create a chat from a repository, ZIP archive, or set of files.

Render the dev server preview

Each chat gets a short-lived preview token. Fetch it from a server route and proxy browser requests through it, so your v0 API key never reaches the browser. When a preview is ready, traffic forwards to it; while the Sandbox spins up, requests fall back to a loading route. Point an iframe at your proxy route and cache the preview details until they expire.

Read more about Accessing Previews in the docs.

Bring your own tools and design systems

Turn on specific MCP servers for a chat, or use the defaults.

Design Systems 2.0 saves a design system as a skill. Include it in a request to load its components, tokens, setup, and starter app.

You can pass up to three skills per request, from team or user memory, skills.sh, or the connected repo, or let the agent pull them in for you.

Use v0 from agents

If you're building an agent, give it v0 as a tool. When the agent needs to produce a working app, it calls v0, and gets back a running preview or deployment to hand to the user. Your agent stays in charge of everything else.

There are three ways to connect it:

MCP

Connect the v0 MCP server to an IDE, desktop assistant, or agent runtime that supports MCP.

The first connection starts an OAuth flow. The MCP server exposes tools for creating chats, listing chats, getting chat details, listing and sending messages, resolving pending tasks, and getting preview URLs.

AI SDK

For TypeScript agents built with AI SDK, use @v0-sdk/ai-tools to expose v0's API operations as tools in the agent's own loop.

The agent decides when to create or continue a chat. Your AI SDK run keeps control of the orchestration and final response.

eve

For eve agents, add an OpenAPI connection file. eve turns the allowed operations into tools and attaches the API key at execution time, out of model context.

Connect a Vercel project

Create a Vercel project for the chat, then manage its environment variables, integrations, and settings through the Vercel API. Your apps get Vercel's security and observability by default.

When you're ready to ship, deploy the chat to Vercel.

Migrate your chats

Chats from the previous version of the v0 API don’t run on the new one, so carry them forward. Pick the version you want to keep, download it as a ZIP, and create a new chat from that ZIP. Store the old identifiers in the new chat’s metadata if you need traceability.

The migration guide covers the full mapping. The main changes:

  • Use https://api.v0.dev/v2 for new requests.

  • The chat holds current app state, and messages hold its history.

  • Replace version workflows with chat file workflows, and v0 Project organization with chat metadata.

  • Use vercelProjectId plus the Vercel API for project operations.

  • Render message parts, not only final text.

Get started

Create an API key in v0 settings and install the SDK.

Or, scaffold a full app.

Read the documentation and migration guide.

Read more
