title: From Full-Table Scans to Millisecond Search in Go: Optimizing Prefix Search for 13.5 Million Places
description:
I built a minimal backend that searches a huge dataset and returns the 10 most popular matches. I wanted to find the bottlenecks in a simple search implementation and measure how each optimization changed performance. I started with the simplest version and improved it step by step, using the same data and query prefixes throughout. At the end of the final version, the query time for a single keyword a drops from 2.6 seconds to 2.9 milliseconds.

It is written in Go, with the standard library only. There is one search endpoint and one HTML page, both served by the same Go program. The code, the results and the git tags for each level are in the repo: https://github.com/bhowmik94/autocomplete-10M.

A query for the one-letter prefix a over 13.5 million places took 2.6 seconds in my first version. In the final version it takes 2.9 milliseconds. A longer prefix like dhaka went from 2.4 seconds to under 2 microseconds.

Disclaimer: These benchmarks measure the search function, not a deployed API.

Dataset and method

Data: I used the allCountries file from GeoNames, which has 13,472,243 rows. Each row is a place: a city, a village, a district and so on. The file has 19 columns, and I use only four: ID, name, country code and population.

I developed everything on cities15000 first, a smaller file with about 34,000 rows, and moved to allCountries once the naive version worked. I chose GeoNames over other free datasets, like Wikipedia article titles, because it has a population column, which gives a clear way to rank the results. The data is licensed under CC BY 4.0 and comes from GeoNames.

Ranking: Matches are sorted by population, highest first. If two places have the same population, the higher ID wins. Matching is case-insensitive and ignores leading spaces. I kept the ranking basic on purpose, because it was not the primary goal of this study.

Machine: AMD Ryzen 5 5500U, Windows, 12 threads, Go 1.26.4.

Benchmark prefixes: I measured four prefixes that behave very differently. The block size is the number of places whose name starts with the prefix. I estimated it from the memory the Level 1 version allocates, so treat it as approximate.

Prefix Block size Why it is in the set
a about 590,000 Huge block
dha about 12,000 Medium block
dhaka about 200 Small block
xyzq 0 No match

Keeping it fair: Every level runs on the same data, the same prefixes and k = 10. I ran the same benchmark cases against every implementation. A separate test compares each version with the naive one for every prefix in a small dataset. The naive version is slow but simple, so I used it as the reference for correct answers. Before building each level, I wrote down what I expected to measure and compared it afterwards.

Level 0: the naive version

For every query, the naive version goes through all rows, lowercases each name, checks whether it starts with the prefix, collects the matches, sorts them by population and returns the top 10.

On the 34,000-row file, a query for dha took about 3.5 ms. On the full file it took about 1.4 seconds. That is roughly 105 ns per row in both cases, so the cost grows in line with the number of rows. A prefix with no match (xyzq) took as long as dha, which shows that the cost is the scan itself, not the matching. The one-letter prefix a was the slowest, because about 590,000 places match it and have to be collected and sorted.

Prefix Time per query Memory per query Allocations per query
a 1.76 s 414 MB 13.47 million
dha 1.41 s 244 MB 13.47 million
dhaka 1.47 s 242 MB 13.47 million
xyzq 1.45 s 242 MB 13.47 million

The allocation count is the useful clue. It is one allocation per row, which is the lowercase copy of every name that is created on every query. That is why even a prefix with no matches allocates 242 MB. In the naive version, memory depends on the size of the dataset, not on the size of the matching block.

Loading the full file took about 9.8 seconds and the heap was 993.5 MB afterwards. Getting there needed one memory fix. Go’s strings.Split returns pieces that point into the original text, so keeping a single city name keeps the whole file text alive. On the small file the heap after loading was 10.2 MB. Copying each name with strings.Clone brought it down to 2.5 MB with the same load time. On the full file the unused text would have been over a gigabyte.

Level 1: sort once, binary search

The naive version repeats the same work on every query. Level 1 does that work once, at startup:

  • Each place gets a LowerName field, computed once when the data is loaded.
  • The whole list is sorted once by that field.

After sorting, all places whose names start with the same prefix sit next to each other in one unbroken stretch of the array. I call this stretch the block.

Two binary searches find the block: one for its start, one for its end.
To find the end, I search for the prefix with its last character incremented—for example, dha becomes dhb. Every dha match sorts before that boundary. Then I copy the block, sort the copy by population and return the first 10. The copy is important since the block is a window into the shared array, and sorting it in place would reorder the index for every later query.

The speedup has a price. The extra lowercase names raised the heap from 993.5 MB to 1,403.6 MB. The one-time sort takes about 10 seconds on top of about 10 seconds of parsing, so startup is now about 20 seconds.

Prefix Naive Level 1 Level 1 memory per query Speedup
a 2.64 s 144 ms 37.7 MB about 18x
dha 2.34 s 2.1 ms 771 KB about 1,100x
dhaka 2.39 s 19 µs 14 KB about 124,000x
xyzq 2.33 s 572 ns 32 B about 4 million x

A note on the naive column: after the data was sorted, the naive version ran slower than in my first measurement (2.3 to 2.6 seconds instead of 1.4 to 1.8), although its code had not changed. I suspect cache misses: the sorted records still point to names laid out in file order. I haven’t tested that explanation. Every speedup in this article compares numbers from the same run.

Two things stand out. A no-match query takes 572 ns: it only needs two binary searches. For matching queries, time depends on the block size. a matches about 590,000 places and takes 144 ms; dha matches about 12,000 and takes 2.1 ms. The number of allocations is constant (6), but the bytes still grow with the block, because the block is copied and sorted.

Level 2: do not sort what you will not use

Level 1 copies and sorts 590,000 places to return 10 of them. Level 2 walks the block once and keeps a list of the best 10 places seen so far, sorted best first. Most places are worse than the current tenth-best result, so I skip them. If a place is better, I move it into the right position. Otherwise it replaces the worst one and moves up to its position. There is no copy and no sort. For k = 10, a small sorted slice is enough. I did not try a heap, which should only help for a large k.

Prefix Level 1 Level 2 Level 2 memory per query Speedup over Level 1
a 144 ms 2.9 ms 708 B about 49x
dha 2.13 ms 47 µs 712 B about 45x
dhaka 19.3 µs 1.9 µs 712 B about 10x
xyzq 572 ns 454 ns 8 B about 1.3x

Memory per query is now about 700 bytes (the ten places), no matter how big the block is. The no-match prefix barely changed, since it was already just two binary searches.

The remaining 2.9 ms for a looks like a memory limit. The block contains about 590,000 records of 64 bytes each, or roughly 38 MB. Scanning it in 2.9 ms works out to about 13 GB/s—close to the bandwidth I’d expect from a laptop. The loop only needs the population and the ID of each place, but it pulls in all 64 bytes. So the limit is now the memory layout, not the algorithm.

Across both steps:

Prefix Naive Level 1 Level 2 Total speedup
a 2.64 s 144 ms 2.9 ms about 900x
dha 2.34 s 2.1 ms 47 µs about 50,000x
dhaka 2.39 s 19 µs 1.9 µs about 1.3 million x
xyzq 2.33 s 572 ns 454 ns about 5 million x

Serving it over HTTP

There is one search endpoint, for example, GET /suggest?q=dha&limit=5. The default limit is 10, and values outside 1–50 are clamped. Non-integer values return a 400 response. The search function is a field of the server struct, so any of the three levels can run behind the same endpoint.

Go handles each request in its own goroutine, so many requests read the index at the same time. That is safe because nothing modifies the index after startup: each query only reads it and builds its own 10-place result. If a query had sorted the shared array in place, requests would have corrupted each other. A test with 50 concurrent requests, using Go’s httptest package, runs against the handler.

The HTML page is a single static file served by the same Go program at /. Serving it from the same place as the API avoids CORS issues and keeps the project small.

Limitations

  • No end-to-end load test. The timings above call the Go functions directly. They leave out the network, HTTP parsing and JSON encoding, so a real request takes longer. Everything ran on one laptop.
  • Estimates. The block sizes are estimated from allocated memory, and the slowdown of the naive version on sorted data is an untested guess. The naive version was measured with five iterations per prefix, because each run takes seconds.
  • Basic search quality. Only the name is matched, with no accent folding, so munchen does not find München. Alternate names are not indexed, places with the same name are listed separately, and ranking uses population only.
  • Startup and memory. Startup takes about 20 seconds and the index needs about 1.4 GB of RAM per instance.

What could come next

  • Store populations and IDs in separate compact arrays, so the scan for a reads a few bytes per place instead of 64.
  • Use a range-maximum structure (a sparse table or a segment tree) with a heap, so the cost depends on k and not on the block size.
  • Precompute the top 10 for the shortest prefixes.
  • Compare against Postgres with an index and a cache, and deploy it to the cloud.

What I learned

  • Write predictions down before measuring. It shows you what you did not understand yet.
  • Allocation counts show where time goes. 13.47 million allocations per query pointed straight at the lowercasing of every name.
  • Cost can depend on the part of the data a query touches, not on the dataset size. After Level 1, a query over 13.5 million places that matches nothing takes 572 ns.
  • Memory layout can matter as much as the algorithm. Level 2 runs at roughly the speed of memory, and the naive version may have got slower just because the data was reordered.
  • Keep the slow, simple version. The naive version was my reference for correct answers in every test.

Code, results and git tags: https://github.com/bhowmik94/autocomplete-10M. Data: GeoNames, CC BY 4.0.

title: position: sticky Does Nothing? Hunt Down the Hidden Overflow
description:
You add position: sticky and top: 0 to your header. You scroll. The header scrolls away like nothing happened.

No error in the console. No warning in DevTools. Just a header that won't stick.

This post explains the usual reason, shows a fix you can paste in, and gives you a small script that finds the problem for you.

The problem

Someone posted this in a CSS forum. Here is the gist, in our own words.

They wanted the header on their page to stay at the top while the user scrolled. They added position: sticky. Nothing changed. They had already worked through a popular checklist of "why sticky isn't working": siblings, parent height, z-index, browser support. Still no luck.

The answer that solved it was one line far away from the header: a wrapper higher up the page had overflow: hidden.

Quick version of how sticky works

A sticky element acts like a normal element until you scroll it to a set point. Then it "sticks" there, until its parent box scrolls out of view.

Two key words here:

  • Scroll container: a box that can scroll its content. Elements with overflow set to hidden, auto, or scroll can be one.
  • Containing block: for our purposes, the parent box that the sticky element lives inside.

Root cause 1: an ancestor with overflow: hidden

MDN says a sticky element sticks to its nearest ancestor that has a "scrolling mechanism." That is created when overflow is hidden, scroll, auto, or overlay. It sticks to that ancestor even if that ancestor never actually scrolls.

So here is what happens:

  1. A wrapper has overflow: hidden, maybe to clip a rounded corner or stop a sideways scrollbar.
  2. The sticky header now sticks to that wrapper, not to the page.
  3. The wrapper never scrolls. The page does.
  4. The header rides along with the wrapper and scrolls off the screen.

Here is a small example that shows it:

<div class="page">
  <header class="header">My site</header>
  <main class="content">…lots of content…</main>
</div>

.page {
  overflow: hidden;   /* the hidden culprit */
}

.header {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  z-index: 1;
  background: white;
}

We tested this in Chrome 156 and Firefox 157. After scrolling 500px, the header's top edge was at -500px. It scrolled away completely.

Fix A: remove the overflow

If the overflow: hidden isn't doing anything important, delete it. In our test the header then stayed at the top (top edge at 0px).

Fix B: use overflow: clip instead

Often the overflow is there for a reason, like hiding content that sticks out. In that case, use clip:

.page {
  overflow: clip;
}

MDN explains the difference. hidden gives the element a scrolling mechanism, so sticky treats it as a scroll container. clip also hides the overflow, but the element is not a scroll container. So the sticky header skips it and sticks to the page. In our test this fixed the header in both browsers.

The trade-off: with clip, nothing inside can be scrolled into view, not even with code. MDN warns that if there are focusable elements in the clipped area, keyboard users may not be able to reach them. Only use clip when the clipped part has nothing interactive.

overflow: clip support, per MDN's browser data: Chrome 90, Firefox 81, Safari 16.

Fix C: move the overflow somewhere else

If you need hidden (for example, you scroll that box with code), put it on an element that is not an ancestor of the sticky element. For example, wrap only the content that needs clipping, and keep the header outside that wrapper.

The sneaky one: overflow-x: hidden

Many sites add this to stop a sideways scrollbar:

.page { overflow-x: hidden; }

"But I only hid the x direction!" you say. Here is the catch. MDN explains that when one direction is visible and the other is not visible or clip, the visible one behaves as auto. So overflow-x: hidden quietly turns overflow-y into auto. Now the box is a scroll container, and sticky breaks.

The fix is to use clip for that direction:

.page { overflow-x: clip; }

clip paired with visible stays as is, so no scroll container is made. We tested both: overflow-x: hidden broke the header, and overflow-x: clip fixed it.

What about html and body?

This one surprised us, so we tested it too:

Setup Header sticks? (Chrome 156, Firefox 157)
overflow-x: hidden on body only Yes
overflow-x: hidden on both html and body No
overflow-x: clip on both html and body Yes

When only body has it, browsers apply that overflow to the viewport (the browser window) instead, so sticky still works. When html has it too, body keeps its own overflow and becomes the trap. If you want a rule you never have to think about, use overflow-x: clip.

Root cause 2: no offset set

MDN notes that at least one inset (like top, bottom, left, or right) must be set to something other than auto. Without it, sticky acts just like relative. We removed top: 0 in our test, and the header scrolled away.

.header {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0; /* required */
}

Root cause 3: the parent is too short

A sticky element can only stick while its parent box is on screen. A common setup looks like this:

<header class="site-header">
  <h1>Site title</h1>
  <nav class="nav">…</nav>   <!-- sticky -->
</header>
<main>…</main>

The nav is sticky, but its parent is the header. Once the header scrolls away, the nav goes with it. In our test, the nav was at -440px after a 500px scroll.

The fix: move the sticky element so its parent is the tall, scrolling part of the page. Here, put the nav after the header, as a sibling of main.

How to verify

1. Find the trap with a script.
Paste this into the browser console. Change the selector to match your sticky element:

(() => {
  const el = document.querySelector('.header'); // your sticky element
  for (let node = el.parentElement; node; node = node.parentElement) {
    const s = getComputedStyle(node);
    if (/(hidden|auto|scroll|overlay)/.test(s.overflowX + ' ' + s.overflowY)) {
      console.log('Sticky is trapped by:', node, s.overflowX, s.overflowY);
    }
  }
})();

It lists every ancestor that can trap your sticky element. Click a result to jump to it in the Elements panel. One note: if body shows up and html does not, the body's overflow may be going to the viewport. Check that case with the table above.

2. Check the computed styles.
Select a suspect element and open the Computed tab. Look at overflow-x and overflow-y. Remember that a value you didn't write (like auto) can show up because of the rule about pairs above.

3. Measure while scrolling.
Scroll down, then run:

document.querySelector('.header').getBoundingClientRect().top

If it sticks, you'll see your top value, such as 0. If you see a negative number, it scrolled away.

4. Test on a real page length.
Sticky only shows up when there's enough content to scroll. Test with real content, not a near-empty page.

Checklist

  • [ ] The sticky element has top (or another inset) set.
  • [ ] No ancestor has overflow: hidden, auto, or scroll, unless you want it to stick inside that box.
  • [ ] Use overflow: clip or overflow-x: clip when you only need clipping.
  • [ ] The sticky element's parent is tall enough to scroll through.
  • [ ] Add a background and z-index so content doesn't show through or sit above it.

Sources

  • MDN: position — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/position
  • MDN: overflow — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/overflow
  • MDN browser compat data (overflow: clip, position: sticky) — https://github.com/mdn/browser-compat-data

title: Why Non-ASCII Input Breaks over SSH: Locales, SendEnv and the `env` Request
description:
Originally published on MistLab. Part 4 of Building an SSH Terminal.

Part 4 of "Building an SSH Terminal". Code excerpts are from MistTerm v1.2.26, an open-source (AGPL) SSH terminal client by MistLab; they are trimmed

TL;DR

Garbled non-ASCII input over SSH usually means the remote program runs in the POSIX/C locale, so line editors such as readline treat each byte as a character. The locale reaches the server through the RFC 4254 env request, which sshd accepts only for variables listed in AcceptEnv. Upstream OpenSSH sends no variables by default; Debian-family packages add SendEnv LANG LC_* and the matching AcceptEnv. The fix is to forward a valid UTF-8 locale and to allow it on the server.

A common SSH puzzle goes like this. Output in Chinese, Japanese or with accented letters displays fine. But when you type such characters at a bash or mysql prompt, the line fills with garbage, or Backspace deletes half a character. The terminal is not at fault. The server-side program is running in the wrong locale, and the fix is a little-known part of the SSH protocol.

Why does non-ASCII input break over SSH? Bytes are only text inside a locale

Part 1 established that the terminal and the remote program exchange bytes. Turning bytes into characters is the program's job, and C programs do it through the C library's locale. After setlocale(LC_ALL, ""), the LC_CTYPE category, chosen from the environment variables LC_ALL, LC_CTYPE and LANG in that order of precedence, decides the character encoding. Under en_US.UTF-8, the three bytes E4 B8 AD are one character, 中, occupying two columns. Under the C/POSIX locale they are three unrelated bytes.

Output usually survives a wrong locale because most programs pass bytes through unchanged, and the terminal decodes UTF-8 itself. Line editors do not. Readline (bash) and libedit (mysql, sqlite3 on some systems) have to know where each character starts in order to echo, move the cursor, redraw and delete. In the C locale, they treat every byte as a separate character. Depending on configuration (input-meta, output-meta), the bytes are echoed as octal escapes or treated as Meta-modified keys, and Backspace removes one byte of a multi-byte character. That is the garbage you see.

Where the remote locale comes from

An SSH session's environment is assembled on the server. sshd sets a few variables itself, PAM modules may add more (on Debian and Ubuntu, pam_env in /etc/pam.d/sshd reads /etc/default/locale), and the login shell's profile scripts can set more. Minimal images, containers and some distributions end up with no LANG at all, which means the POSIX locale.

The client can also contribute, through the env channel request in RFC 4254 §6.4:

byte      SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST
uint32    recipient channel
string    "env"
boolean   want reply
string    variable name
string    variable value

The RFC warns that passing arbitrary variables is a security risk and that servers should restrict them. OpenSSH's sshd accepts nothing by default. Variables have to be listed with AcceptEnv in sshd_config.

Locale forwarding: env requests are sent between pty-req and shell

Does ssh send your locale by default?

It is widely believed that the ssh client "sends your locale". Strictly, that is a distribution default, not an OpenSSH default. The upstream ssh_config(5) manual says of SendEnv: "The default is not to send any environment variables." The one exception is TERM, which is not sent through env at all; it travels inside pty-req.

What most users see comes from distribution packaging. Debian's OpenSSH package, and therefore Ubuntu's, ships /etc/ssh/ssh_config with

SendEnv LANG LC_* COLORTERM NO_COLOR

and /etc/ssh/sshd_config with the matching

AcceptEnv LANG LC_* COLORTERM NO_COLOR

Other distributions ship similar pairs. So between two stock Debian-family machines the locale does travel, and that is the behavior a third-party client should reproduce. A client that sends nothing will behave worse than ssh on exactly the servers where AcceptEnv is configured.

(MistTerm's own source comment describes this as "the OpenSSH default". That is imprecise in the way described above, and we list it in the review notes for this series.)

Forwarding the locale: the details

MistTerm sends env requests after pty-req and before shell. Order matters, because once the shell has started, its environment is fixed. Which variables to send, and what to do when there are none, is decided in remote_locale_env:

// src/ssh/client.rs
pub(crate) fn remote_locale_env(get: impl Fn(&str) -> Option<String>) -> Vec<(String, String)> {
    const NAMES: &[&str] = &[
        "LANG", "LC_ALL", "LC_CTYPE", "LC_COLLATE",
        "LC_MESSAGES", "LC_MONETARY", "LC_NUMERIC", "LC_TIME",
    ];
    fn plausible(v: &str) -> bool {
        // macOS Terminal often sets `LC_CTYPE=UTF-8`. That is a macOS-only form that
        // glibc does not accept; sending it makes the remote setlocale fail as a
        // whole and fall back to POSIX, so treat it as unset.
        let bare_codeset = v.eq_ignore_ascii_case("UTF-8") || v.eq_ignore_ascii_case("UTF8");
        !bare_codeset
            && !v.is_empty()
            && v.len() <= 64
            && v.chars()
                .all(|c| c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || matches!(c, '.' | '_' | '-' | '@'))
    }
    let mut out: Vec<(String, String)> = NAMES.iter().filter_map(|k| {
        let v = get(k)?;
        let v = v.trim();
        plausible(v).then(|| (k.to_string(), v.to_string()))
    }).collect();
    let has_ctype_source = out.iter()
        .any(|(k, _)| k == "LANG" || k == "LC_ALL" || k == "LC_CTYPE");
    if !has_ctype_source {
        out.insert(0, ("LANG".to_string(), DEFAULT_REMOTE_LANG.to_string())); // "en_US.UTF-8"
    }
    out
}

Three cases drive the design:

  1. Values that only make sense locally. macOS commonly exports LC_CTYPE=UTF-8, a bare codeset that the macOS C library accepts. glibc does not. With setlocale(LC_ALL, ""), one invalid category makes the whole call fail and the program stays in the C locale. Forwarding the variable would cause exactly the problem it was meant to fix, so bare UTF-8/UTF8 values are dropped.
  2. Values that are not locale names. Variables are user-controlled, so only short values made of the characters that appear in locale names ([A-Za-z0-9._@-], 64 bytes at most) are sent.
  3. No locale at all. A Windows desktop normally has no LANG, and neither does a GUI app launched without a login environment. If none of LANG, LC_ALL or LC_CTYPE survives, the client sends LANG=en_US.UTF-8, so that an otherwise unconfigured server still gets a UTF-8 LC_CTYPE.

Each request is sent independently, and a rejection is not an error:

for (name, value) in remote_locale_env(|k| std::env::var(k).ok()) {
    match channel.setenv(&name, &value) {
        Ok(()) => log::info!("SSH setenv {}={}", name, value),
        Err(e) => log::info!("SSH setenv {} rejected by server: {}", name, e),
    }
}

How to fix it: what the client can do, and what the server must allow

Forwarding only helps if the server cooperates in two ways:

  • AcceptEnv must allow the variable. Without it, sshd refuses the request and the session falls back to whatever the server's own configuration provides. That is the same result as with OpenSSH's ssh. The fix is on the server: add AcceptEnv LANG LC_*, or set a system default locale.
  • The locale must exist on the server. If en_US.UTF-8 is not generated on that machine, setlocale fails again. On glibc systems, locale -a lists what is installed, and many minimal systems also provide C.UTF-8.

When you debug a server, locale inside the session shows what the remote programs actually got.

For MistTerm's local shell tab (a PTY on your own machine, no SSH involved), the same concern is handled by setting the environment directly: TERM=xterm-256color and COLORTERM=truecolor always, and on macOS LANG=en_US.UTF-8 when neither LANG nor LC_ALL is set. An app launched from Finder or the Dock does not inherit a login environment, which is the case this covers.

Summary

  • Line editors need a correct LC_CTYPE to handle multi-byte input. In the POSIX locale they work byte by byte.
  • The locale reaches the server through RFC 4254 env requests, sent before shell and filtered by sshd's AcceptEnv.
  • Upstream OpenSSH sends no variables by default. Debian-family packaging adds SendEnv LANG LC_* (plus COLORTERM, NO_COLOR) and the matching AcceptEnv.
  • Filter values the remote libc will reject, such as macOS's bare UTF-8, and supply a UTF-8 default when the local machine has none.

FAQ

Why does typed Chinese or accented text turn into garbage over SSH?

The remote program is usually running in the POSIX/C locale, so line editors such as readline handle input byte by byte instead of character by character.

Does ssh send LANG to the server by default?

Upstream OpenSSH sends no environment variables by default. Debian and Ubuntu packages configure SendEnv LANG LC_* in ssh_config and the matching AcceptEnv in sshd_config.

How do I fix garbled input on the server side?

Allow the variables with AcceptEnv LANG LC_* in sshd_config, or set a system default locale, and make sure the locale exists on the server (check with locale -a).

Why should a client not forward LC_CTYPE=UTF-8 from macOS?

glibc does not accept a bare codeset as a locale name. One invalid category makes setlocale(LC_ALL, "") fail, and the program stays in the C locale.
Related in this series

  • From Bytes to Glyphs: How a Terminal Emulator Actually Works
  • What Happens When You Paste into a Terminal: Bracketed Paste, the 4095-Byte Line, and UTF-8 Boundaries

title: I'm Building My Own PHP Platform, and I've Been Learning a Lot Along the Way
description:
I'm Building My Own PHP Platform, and I've Been Learning a Lot Along the Way

I'm a self-taught developer, and for some time now, I've been working on a project called Domain System.

It started with an idea: what if I could build my own PHP platform, where the main system and its plugins had their own responsibilities and didn't depend too much on each other?

As I kept working on it, the project grew. I had to think about how to organize the code, how plugins should communicate with the core, how to handle errors, and how to avoid breaking something that was already working.

I won't pretend I have all the answers. I'm still learning, making mistakes, and going back to improve things. But that's part of what makes this project interesting to me.

You can find it on GitHub here:

https://github.com/hadelrachid/domain-system

Why I started thinking differently about PHP

When I started thinking about how to organize the project, I became interested in how operating systems separate their essential parts from the applications that run on top of them.

I wondered if I could borrow a little of that idea for a PHP platform.

In Domain System, I try to keep two things separate:

  • The core: The part responsible for things the system needs to work, such as routing, storage, and other shared services.
  • The plugins: The parts that add features to the platform.

The idea is simple: I don't want the core to know all the details of every plugin. I'd rather have them communicate through interfaces, so I can change one part without having to change everything else.

In practice, getting this right is harder than it sounds. You can create interfaces and still end up with code that's too dependent on other classes. That's something I've been learning to pay more attention to as the project develops.

Some things I've been working on

Installing plugins more safely

One thing that made me think carefully was plugin installation.

When you upload a ZIP file, you can't simply assume that every file inside it is safe to extract wherever you want.

So I added a step where uploaded files are checked before they're moved into place. The process includes checks for problems such as path traversal and ZIP Slip.

It's not something I'd describe as a guarantee that every possible attack is prevented. Security takes more than a few checks, and I know this is an area that deserves ongoing attention.

Trying to make problems easier to recover from

Another challenge is dealing with errors without leaving the system in a bad state.

Domain System includes JSON storage, file-locking and atomic-write techniques, diagnostic tools, and a snapshot and rollback feature.

These are attempts to make problems easier to identify and recover from. I know things can still go wrong, but I'd rather build ways to deal with failures than assume they won't happen.

Building my own visual page editor

I've also been working on Flex Builder, a visual editor for creating page layouts and theme components.

One thing I wanted was for the editor preview to behave as closely as possible to the actual website. To help with that, both use the same compilation process.

I've also been working on responsive layouts, so that hiding an element on a smaller screen doesn't leave awkward empty spaces behind.

There are plenty of details to work through in an editor like this, and it's been a good learning experience.

Using AI without losing control of my code

I also use AI coding tools to help me develop the project.

They can be very useful, especially when you're working on a large codebase. But I've learned that getting code that works in isolation isn't the same as getting code that fits the rest of the project.

Sometimes a change can solve one problem while creating another. A new class might work, for example, but introduce dependencies that make future changes harder.

To help avoid this, I've been creating documentation and rules that explain how the project is organized and how new plugins should be built. There's also a command-line tool to generate a basic plugin structure.

I'm still figuring out the best way to use AI without letting the code become difficult to maintain. Documentation helps, but I still need to review the changes and understand what they're doing.

A little about the technology

Domain System is built with PHP 8.2+. It supports MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite through PDO, as well as its own JSON storage option.

I use PHPUnit for automated tests. At the time of writing, the project has 433 tests and more than 2,340 assertions.

Those numbers are useful, but I don't think they tell the whole story. Passing tests are important, and so is checking whether the code is organized in a way that makes sense and can be maintained over time.

I'm sharing it because I'd like to learn from others

This project has taught me that building something is one challenge; keeping it understandable as it grows is another.

I'm not presenting Domain System as a finished solution or claiming that I've found the best way to build a PHP platform. It's a project I'm developing, learning from, and trying to improve.

If you have a moment to look at the code, I'd really appreciate your thoughts.

For example:

  • Does separating the core from the plugins this way make sense to you?
  • How do you keep a PHP project organized as it grows?
  • If you use AI to help write code, how do you make sure the changes still fit your project's design?

I'd be happy to hear suggestions, questions, or even criticism. I'm sharing the project partly because I know other developers may notice things that I haven't.

Here's the repository:

https://github.com/hadelrachid/domain-system

Thanks for taking the time to read this!

title: Dive into MobX with Flowik: how auto-tracking works
description:
In the first post I introduced Flowik, a MobX-style state library for Swing and Vaadin. Its pitch fits in one sentence: reading is subscribing. You read count.value inside an autoRun, and the autoRun re-runs when count changes. There is no subscribe() call anywhere.

The first time you see this it looks like magic. It isn't. The whole mechanism is a stack, a couple of sets and a counter, and it fits in about a hundred lines of Kotlin.

In this post we will build a toy version from scratch in three steps: observables with autoRun, then computed, then action. After that we will open Flowik's real Tracking.kt and see what changes when the toy has to survive a real UI. If you already use MobX in JavaScript, this is also a tour of what MobX does under the hood.

The picture in your head: a dependency graph

Every MobX-style app is a graph with three kinds of nodes:

  • Observables: the source state. They are mutable and know who reads them.
  • Computeds: values derived from other nodes. They are cached, and they are both readers and things being read.
  • Reactions (autoRun in Flowik): the leaves, where effects happen, such as updating a label. 
flowchart LR
    subgraph S["Observable state"]
        F(["firstName"])
        L(["lastName"])
        A(["age"])
    end
    subgraph D["Derivations"]
        N["fullName<br/><i>computed</i>"]
        R1{{"autoRun:<br/>update header label"}}
        R2{{"autoRun:<br/>update age field"}}
    end
    F --> N
    L --> N
    N --> R1
    A --> R2
    classDef obs fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#3b78c4,color:#10243e
    classDef comp fill:#efedff,stroke:#6b5bd2,color:#1d1640
    classDef react fill:#e5f4e4,stroke:#3d8c40,color:#12300f
    class F,L,A obs
    class N comp
    class R1,R2 react

Arrows point the way changes flow. Change age and only the age field updates. Change firstName and the header updates, while the age field is left alone.

The interesting part is that you never draw this graph. Nobody writes "fullName depends on firstName". The library discovers each arrow at runtime, by watching what each derivation reads while it runs. Let's build the machinery that does that.

Step 1: who is reading right now?

The whole trick is one piece of global state: a stack of derivations that are currently running. When an observable is read, it looks at the top of that stack and adds whoever is there to its observers.

interface Derivation {
    fun onDependencyChanged()
}

object Tracking {
    private val stack = ArrayDeque<Derivation>()

    val current: Derivation? get() = stack.lastOrNull()

    fun <T> track(derivation: Derivation, block: () -> T): T {
        stack.addLast(derivation)
        try {
            return block()
        } finally {
            stack.removeLast()
        }
    }
}

It is a stack rather than a single variable because derivations nest: a reaction reads a computed, which runs its own function while the reaction is still running.

An observable is a value plus a set of observers. The getter records the current reader. The setter notifies everyone, but only if the value really changed:

class Observable<T>(initial: T) {
    private var _value = initial
    private val observers = mutableSetOf<Derivation>()

    var value: T
        get() {
            Tracking.current?.let { observers += it }   // reading is subscribing
            return _value
        }
        set(newValue) {
            if (newValue == _value) return
            _value = newValue
            observers.toList().forEach { it.onDependencyChanged() }
        }
}

And an autoRun simply runs its effect inside Tracking.track, and runs it again whenever told that something changed:

class AutoRun(private val effect: () -> Unit) : Derivation {
    fun run() = Tracking.track(this, effect)
    override fun onDependencyChanged() = run()
}

fun autoRun(effect: () -> Unit) = AutoRun(effect).also { it.run() }

That's it. Let's try it:

val count = Observable(0)
autoRun { println("count = ${count.value}") }   // count = 0
count.value = 1                                  // count = 1
count.value = 1                                  // nothing: the value did not change

Here is what happened during that first run:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as autoRun
    participant T as Tracking stack
    participant O as count (observable)
    R->>T: push(this)
    R->>O: read count.value
    O->>T: who is reading? current
    T-->>O: the autoRun
    Note over O: observers += autoRun
    O-->>R: 0
    R->>T: pop()
    Note over O: later: count.value = 1
    O->>R: notify, run() again

Notice that the subscription is a side effect of reading. That is why dependencies can be conditional. In autoRun { if (showDetails.value) println(details.value) }, the reaction only depends on details while showDetails is true. Our toy doesn't handle the other half of that yet, which is forgetting old dependencies. We'll come back to it.

Step 2: computed, the node with two faces

A computed sits in the middle of the graph, so it plays both roles. To its readers it looks like an observable: reading it records the current derivation. To its inputs it looks like a derivation: it evaluates its function inside Tracking.track(this, ...).

class Computed<T>(private val compute: () -> T) : Derivation {
    private var cached: T? = null
    private var dirty = true
    private val observers = mutableSetOf<Derivation>()

    val value: T
        get() {
            Tracking.current?.let { observers += it }   // observable to its readers
            if (dirty) {
                cached = Tracking.track(this, compute) // a derivation to its inputs
                dirty = false
            }
            return cached as T
        }

    override fun onDependencyChanged() {
        if (dirty) return             // already stale, downstream already told
        dirty = true                  // push: mark stale, compute nothing
        observers.toList().forEach { it.onDependencyChanged() }
    }
}

fun <T> computed(compute: () -> T) = Computed(compute)

The key design choice is push invalidation, pull evaluation. When an input changes, the computed does not recompute. It only marks itself dirty and passes the news downstream. The actual work happens later, when someone reads value. If nobody reads it, it never runs.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as firstName
    participant C as fullName (computed)
    participant R as autoRun
    Note over A: firstName.value = "Bob"
    A->>C: invalidate()
    Note over C: isDirty = true<br/>(nothing recomputed yet)
    C->>R: schedule
    R->>C: read fullName.value
    C->>A: recompute: read firstName
    A-->>C: "Bob"
    C-->>R: "Bob Smith"
val firstName = Observable("Alice")
val lastName = Observable("Smith")
var evaluations = 0
val fullName = computed { evaluations++; "${firstName.value} ${lastName.value}" }

autoRun { println("Hello, ${fullName.value}") }   // Hello, Alice Smith
firstName.value = "Bob"                             // Hello, Bob Smith
println(evaluations)                                // 2

Two evaluations for two distinct states. Add ten more readers of fullName and it still evaluates once per change. That is the caching MobX is known for.

Step 3: action, or "not yet, please"

Our toy has a problem. A user renames a person, so we write two fields:

firstName.value = "Carol"   // Hello, Carol Smith   <- a name that never existed
lastName.value = "Jones"    // Hello, Carol Jones

The reaction ran twice, and the first run showed a half-updated state. In a UI that is wasted work and sometimes a visible flicker.

The fix is a batch: a depth counter and a set of pending reactions. While the depth is above zero, reactions are queued instead of run. When the outermost batch ends, each queued reaction runs once. A LinkedHashSet keeps the order and removes duplicates for free.

object Batch {
    private var depth = 0
    private val pending = linkedSetOf<AutoRun>()

    fun schedule(autoRun: AutoRun) {
        if (depth > 0) pending += autoRun else autoRun.run()
    }

    fun <T> action(block: () -> T): T {
        depth++
        try {
            return block()
        } finally {
            if (--depth == 0) {
                val toRun = pending.toList()
                pending.clear()
                toRun.forEach { it.run() }
            }
        }
    }
}

fun <T> action(block: () -> T): T = Batch.action(block)

The only change elsewhere is one line in AutoRun: instead of running directly, it asks to be scheduled.

override fun onDependencyChanged() = Batch.schedule(this)

Now:

action {
    firstName.value = "Carol"
    lastName.value = "Jones"
}                              // Hello, Carol Jones  (once)

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as action { }
    participant T as Tracking
    participant O as observables
    participant R as autoRun
    U->>T: beginBatch() depth = 1
    U->>O: firstName = "Carol"
    O->>T: schedule(autoRun)
    Note over T: batching: add to pending set
    U->>O: lastName = "Jones"
    O->>T: schedule(autoRun)
    Note over T: already pending, set dedupes
    U->>T: endBatch() depth = 0
    T->>R: flush: run() once

The counter, rather than a boolean, lets actions nest. A store method that is an action can call another action, and nothing flushes until the outermost one ends.

The diamond: why batching is about correctness, not only speed

Here is a shape that appears constantly in real screens: one input, two derived values, one view that shows both.

flowchart LR
    A(["price"]) --> B["net<br/><i>computed</i>"]
    A --> C["tax<br/><i>computed</i>"]
    B --> R{{"autoRun:<br/>show net + tax"}}
    C --> R
    classDef obs fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#3b78c4,color:#10243e
    classDef comp fill:#efedff,stroke:#6b5bd2,color:#1d1640
    classDef react fill:#e5f4e4,stroke:#3d8c40,color:#12300f
    class A obs
    class B,C comp
    class R react
val price = Observable(100)
val net = computed { price.value }
val tax = computed { price.value / 5 }
autoRun { println("net=${net.value} tax=${tax.value}") }   // net=100 tax=20

price.value = 200
// net=200 tax=20   <- glitch: tax is stale
// net=200 tax=40

Without a batch, price notifies net first. net schedules the autoRun, which runs immediately and reads tax. But tax has not been told about the change yet, so it returns its old cached value. Then tax is notified and the autoRun runs a second time. For a moment the screen showed a net price and a tax that never belonged together. In reactive systems this is called a glitch.

Inside an action the problem disappears. Both computeds are marked dirty before any reaction runs, so the single run sees a consistent world:

action { price.value = 300 }   // net=300 tax=60  (once)

MobX handles this by treating every write as a tiny batch of its own, and by tracking stale and ready counts on each node so that a reaction waits until all its inputs are settled. The practical rule for our toy, and for Flowik today, is simple: change state inside actions. That is good style anyway, because an action names the intent ("rename", "delete") and gives you one place to put it.

From toy to Flowik

Our toy is about 90 lines and already has the right shape. Open Flowik's Tracking.kt and you will recognise it immediately: a stack of Trackers, a batch depth and pending sets. What the real version adds is mostly about surviving a long-lived UI.

Concern Toy Flowik
Tracking context One global stack A ThreadLocal stack, so each thread has its own context. State is meant to be used from the UI thread.
Stale dependencies Never forgotten Before each re-run, AutoRun and Computed unsubscribe from all old dependencies, then re-subscribe to what they actually read
Reaction kinds autoRun only autoRun, reaction(supply, effect) and whenThen, each with its own pending queue
Change detection == equals by default, plus observableRef (identity), observableStruct (deep) or a custom comparer
Derived values that notify only on real change Not possible computedStruct / computedRef, refreshed at the end of a batch before reactions run
Errors Exception escapes into the writer Caught per reaction, passed to onError or logged; the reaction stays alive
Lifetime Lives forever dispose() stops a reaction and releases its subscriptions

A few details are worth reading in the source.

Batches end even when things throw. endBatch() refreshes derived values inside a try/finally, so a failing derivation can't leave the thread stuck in batching mode, where it would silently swallow every later reaction.

Derived values settle before reactions run. Policy-based computeds such as computedStruct have to evaluate to know whether they changed, and one refresh can invalidate another downstream. So flushRefreshes() loops until nothing is left, with a guard of 100 rounds to report a cycle instead of hanging. Only then are reactions flushed.

untracked is a stack swap. Reading without subscribing needs no special flags on observables. Flowik just replaces the stack with an empty one for the duration of the block:

fun <R> untracked(block: () -> R): R {
    val saved = stack.get()
    stack.set(ArrayDeque())
    return try {
        block()
    } finally {
        stack.set(saved)
    }
}

Errors are reported outside tracking. AutoRun.run() pops itself off the stack before calling the error handler, so whatever the handler reads does not become a dependency of the failed reaction.

Two ways to listen. Observer.kt is just a fun interface with onChange(). It is the explicit subscribe() channel, which the UI bindings and collections use to forward changes, for example from a list element up to its list. Auto-tracking and explicit subscription live side by side, and you rarely need the second one in application code.

Wrapping up

The "magic" of MobX comes down to three ideas:

  1. A stack of who is running. Reading an observable subscribes whoever is on top.
  2. Push invalidation, pull evaluation. Changes only mark things dirty; work happens when someone reads.
  3. Batching. An action delays reactions until the state is consistent, then runs each one once.

Everything else (disposal, error handling, comparison policies, async loading) is engineering around those three. Once you have built the toy yourself, the real source stops being intimidating. Flowik's whole core is under 3,000 lines of Kotlin, and Tracking.kt is about 150 of them.

The complete toy from this post fits in a single file, so paste it into a scratch file and break it. Try making the observable setter wrap its notifications in action { } and watch the diamond glitch disappear.

  • Flowik on GitHub: jreznot/flowik
  • The gist of MobX

title: Sluice: one queue for every build, test and heavy command your agents run
description:
Sluice is a verification queue and cache shared by all the AI agents on a Linux machine: it runs each gate (tests, linters, type checks) only once per git tree, under a common CPU and memory budget, and stores the result. It is open source (MIT license), written in Rust, and works with any AI coding agent: the git hooks need nothing from the agent, agents that support MCP connect to its MCP server, and Claude Code also has a plugin. I built it, and in this article I tell you why, how to install it and what has changed on my machines, with the measured numbers.

What problem does it solve?

In my day job I build software for clients with AI agents. On a normal day I have dozens of agents running at once (I use Claude Code), each in its own git worktree, on projects with expensive checks: test suites that take several minutes, linters and type checks wired into pre-commit and pre-push. Those hooks are defined by each project's team and I can't always touch them.

Nothing coordinated those agents. Working with several AI agents in parallel, my machine spent the day running the same tests and builds over and over, until it ran out of memory, and pushes took forever. What made me say "enough" was watching the desktop give up: GNOME stopped responding and Linux started killing processes on its own. The kernel's OOM killer took out the browser and the applications, and systemd-oomd took out the agents' own tools.

There were three separate causes behind it:

  1. Uncontrolled concurrency. Each agent launches its checks on its own, directly or from git hooks.
  2. Redundancy. The same tree is verified many times: the agent before committing, then pre-commit, then pre-push (which repeats pre-commit), and again after a rebase that changes nothing. I measured it with Sluice itself: of all the checks requested, 52% on the development machine (1,426 of 2,742) and 38% on the second machine (1,142 of 3,016) were on code that was already verified.
  3. Excessive scope. Full suites where a subset would do. That is up to each project, not Sluice.

And one constraint that complicates everything: an agent's shell tool has a timeout. A hook that sits waiting in a queue inside git commit ends up cut off, and the agent still doesn't know whether the commit happened. That's why Sluice answers fast in hooks and really waits over MCP.

What do you need?

  • Linux (it only works on Linux) with git 2.31 or later. There are static binaries for x86_64 and aarch64.
  • An AI coding agent. Any agent that supports MCP can use the MCP server (sluice mcp); for Claude Code there is also a plugin that sets everything up.
  • To isolate jobs: cgroup v2 and a systemd user manager. The memory policy uses systemd-oomd with systemd 257 or later. sluice doctor tells you what you have.

How do I install it?

The binary installs to ~/.local/bin:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/josegarridodigio/sluice/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

SLUICE_VERSION pins a specific version and, later on, sluice update updates in place while verifying the checksum. Then connect your agent. In Claude Code, install the plugin:

/plugin marketplace add josegarridodigio/sluice
/plugin install sluice@sluice

With any other agent that supports MCP, register sluice mcp as an MCP server in its configuration and paste into its AGENTS.md the instruction block from the agents guide. If the agent sets no variable Sluice recognises, export SLUICE_AGENT=1 in its shell so the hooks know it is an agent; and if it only has a shell, sluice shim install, with the shims directory first in its PATH, puts its builds and tests in the queue too.

And in each repository, first look at what it would do and then write it:

sluice init --dry-run   # detects the stack and your hooks; shows the plan, writes nothing
sluice init             # writes .sluice.toml and rewires your hooks

With the Claude Code plugin you don't need to touch the PATH or CLAUDE.md: at the start of each session, it installs some shell shims, puts them first in the session's PATH and gives the agent the rules. A gate is a named command in .sluice.toml:

version = 1

[gates.test]
cmd = "npm test -- --maxWorkers=2"
weight = 4
hooks = ["pre-commit", "pre-push"]

weight is how many units of the budget the gate takes up, roughly the CPU threads it uses. With weight = "auto", Sluice starts at half the budget and learns a lower one from the measured runs.

What happens when a tree has already passed?

It doesn't run again. The cache key is the exact content of the working tree plus the gate definition, and all the repository's worktrees share it. If another agent, or your pre-commit hook, already verified that tree, the answer comes from the cache without even going through the daemon:

That typecheck took 54 seconds the last time it really ran; now it answers in 0.22 s. In this repository the answer includes running pnpm --version, because it's declared in key_inputs: the output of those commands goes into the key, so changing pnpm version invalidates the cache, and they run on every query. Without them, on my development machine, a cache answer costs about 25–30 ms.

If you want to see why Sluice decides what it decides, --explain shows you the tree, the key and the lookup result without running anything:

If two agents ask for the same thing at the same time, it runs once and both get the result (coalescing).

This is what has been saved, measured in each daemon's database, not counting cancelled jobs:

Second machine (12 threads, 30 GB) Development machine (20 threads, 30 GB)
Period Oct 24 → 29 (5.8 days) Oct 22 → 28
Checks run 1,874 1,316
Cache answers 1,142 1,426
Run time saved 19.2 hours 8.6 hours

In total, about 28 hours of tests and linters that did not run in a week, because that exact code was already verified. On the second machine, the daily saving ranges from 1.9 to 5 hours. The screenshot at the top is from that machine, a few hours later, with a few more cache answers.

Sluice doesn't make tests faster: it avoids repeating them, orders when they run and protects the machine.

How does it keep the machine from running out of memory?

On the second machine, with 5 agents working at once, the system log shows out-of-memory episodes on three different days (October 22, 25 and 26). In the worst one, on the morning of the 26th, the system was killing processes for about 20 minutes, up to 6 per minute. Sluice recorded 15 interventions by the kernel or systemd-oomd on agent sessions, and a single gate reached 18 GB.

Version 0.6.0 (October 26) changed three things:

  • Memory admission. Sluice learns how much memory each gate uses (the largest working set of its last 5 runs, plus 20%) and doesn't start one that doesn't fit in the available memory minus a reserve for the desktop and the agents (by default, 10% of memory).
  • Isolation. Each job runs in its own cgroup.
  • Preferred victims. If memory still runs short, the kernel and systemd-oomd pick a verification job before your desktop or your agents.

sluice doctor shows you how it ends up configured on your machine:

Since the afternoon of October 26: 0 out-of-memory episodes on the second machine, across about 780 checks and 2.5 days of agents working, nights included. I don't count a deliberate, bounded test I ran that same day at noon.

Version 0.8.0 fixed the opposite case: a gate with no history reserved an inflated estimate. A pytest reserved 13.8 GB, waited 26 minutes, ran in 1 min 40 s and used around 1 GB. Now the first run starts as a probe, measures what it really uses and also learns from the ones that fail: waits caused by guessed estimates went from 7 in one day to 0 the first night.

Why did a 0.1-second linter wait 23 minutes?

Because it was waiting behind a giant. On October 28, with the previous version, the test suite of a pnpm monorepo used about 12 GB on each run (20 measured runs, between 11 and 13 GB). With 30 GB only one fits at a time. When that suite waited for memory at the head of the queue, it reserved its turn and everything else waited behind it:

  • a linter that takes 0.1 seconds waited between 15 and 23 minutes;
  • a 19-second typecheck waited about 4 minutes;
  • 48% of all queue time was of this kind, and 91% of those jobs lasted less than a minute.

Meanwhile the CPU was almost idle: 40% of the time with jobs in the queue, it was idle.

Version 0.8.0 brings backfilling, the technique used by supercomputing schedulers such as Slurm. Sluice predicts when the head job can start from how long the running jobs take, and lets one from behind go ahead only if it fits now and doesn't delay the head: either because the head will still fit next to it, or because its learned duration, with margin, ends sooner. [scheduler] backfill = false goes back to strict reservation.

Before: Oct 28 day, 12 h After: night of Oct 28–29 with 0.8.0, 12 h
Checks 316 202
Run minutes 510 380
Queue wait minutes 981 167
Wait per minute of work 1.92 min 0.44 min
Worst wait of a job under 1 min 27 min 12 min
Idle CPU while there was a queue ~40% 4.8%
Jobs that went ahead of the head — 10
Total delay that caused to heads — 4 min 52 s

Read it carefully: it is not a controlled experiment. It's 12 hours of daytime with the old version against 12 hours of night with the new one, with different workloads. That's why I compare wait per minute of work, about 4.4 times lower, and not absolute wait. And there is a cost: letting jobs through delayed the heads by 4 min 52 s in total that night. Sluice measures it and shows it in sluice status (the backfill line in the screenshot at the top) precisely so you can keep an eye on it.

What if a test hangs?

On October 28, a project's tests hung four times, waiting for something that never arrived. Each time they held the queue and up to 7.6 GB of memory for the 30 minutes of the limit. In three of them the tests had already finished and a single file hung for 25 minutes or more.

Since 0.8.0, every 5 seconds the daemon looks at what each job is doing: CPU time, disk I/O, page faults, number of processes and log bytes. A job with no progress at all for max(5 min, 3 × its usual duration) shows up as STALLED in sluice status, and the agent gets the warning in the verify progress. Sluice never kills it: the gate's timeout is still the only limit. I decided it this way so there is no false positive that costs a good job. A gate that is meant to stay still (a watch, a server) can set stall_timeout = "off".

The first night: 0 hangs and 0 false warnings across 177 jobs. The longest silence of any job was 20 seconds.

What if I can't touch the repository's hooks?

It happened to me in a client's Angular repository that uses husky. The hooks belong to the client and their team, so I couldn't rewrite them, and husky prepends its own PATH: each commit's tests ran outside the queue and the cache. Minutes per commit, competing with everything else.

Since 0.7.0, Sluice can be the entry point for your clone's hooks without modifying the repository:

sluice hooks on       # or, when configuring: sluice init --hooks entry
sluice hooks status   # which hook goes through the queue and which is delegated, and why

on points core.hooksPath to a hooks directory inside the clone's git directory, from a file included in its configuration, so husky's write on each install doesn't displace it. off removes it, and if the sluice binary is missing, the repository's hooks keep working.

The design rule is: either I understand it entirely, or I run it untouched. Before writing it I read the source code of husky, lefthook and pre-commit. A hook that Sluice fully understands runs its commands as queue jobs, in the manager's order: read-only ones, like tests or linters, go to the cache, and those that can change files, like lint-staged, always run. Any other hook runs exactly as before.

In a repository without .sluice.toml, those hook units become the verify gates, with the same cache inputs: a verify before git commit turns the commit hook into a cache answer.

How does an agent use it without hitting the shell timeout?

Through MCP. sluice mcp exposes a verify tool that blocks until the gates finish and sends a progress notification every 15 seconds. Claude Code, for example, only cuts an MCP call if its inactivity window (30 minutes by default) passes with no response or progress, so the agent waits as long as needed, without the shell's limit.

In Claude Code, the rest of the plugin steers the agent that way: a skill that teaches it to use verify and the merge queue, and a guard that rewrites the gates' commands to sluice run <gate> -v and heavy ones (builds, test runners) to sluice exec -- ..., so they share the budget. With other agents, the AGENTS.md block carries the same instructions as the skill. And if an agent commits with a tree that isn't in the cache, the hook rewired by sluice init answers immediately with exit code 3 and tells it to use verify, instead of waiting inside git commit.

How do I integrate the branches of several agents?

With the local merge queue. An agent finishes its branch, passes verify, commits and enqueues it. The daemon combines the queued branches onto the target in a disposable worktree (a "train") and runs the gates once on the combined tree, with the same cache and the same budget:

sluice queue enqueue           # the agent does this, or you
sluice queue status            # the plan: trains, conflicts and what is ready
sluice queue approve <train>   # you do this

By default, nothing is pushed until a person approves the train: the daemon rejects an agent's approval, over MCP or from the terminal, and the Claude Code plugin blocks it too. You can allow it explicitly in your personal configuration (allow_agent_approval = true); a repository can't turn it on by itself. Even so, two cases remain human-only: a train that changes the project's own verification configuration and landing through a pull request. If your target branch is protected and only accepts pull requests, [queue] land = "pull-request" pushes the verified result to a sluice/train/<id> branch and, on approval, opens the pull request with your own gh. Sluice never does the merge.

How did I build it?

With AI agents, and verified with Sluice itself: every commit of the project goes through its own queue and its own cache. The first commit is from October 22 and 0.8.0 came out on the 28th: from 0.1.0 to 0.8.0 in a week, with about 190 commits, about 105,000 lines of Rust and 25 architecture decisions (ADRs) documented in the repository.

Each big change followed the same cycle: analysis of the code and of real data from the two machines, proposals with their risks, my decision recorded in an ADR, implementation in waves with agents, and review. Before each version, CI on 7 combinations: Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, Debian, Fedora, Alpine, ARM and the minimum git version. Several times the review found bugs the tests didn't see, and CI uncovered problems that only existed on Alpine or Fedora. And almost every version was born from a problem I saw using Sluice daily: memory in 0.6.0, hooks in 0.7.0 and the stuck queue in 0.8.0.

Try it

Install the binary and connect your agent as above, and in your repository:

sluice doctor
sluice init --dry-run
sluice init
sluice status

The code, the documentation and the 25 ADRs are at github.com/josegarridodigio/sluice. If something doesn't work for you, sluice doctor --bundle generates a diagnostic bundle, with sensitive data removed, to attach to an issue.

title: Exorcist: I made the ghosts of legacy Java code explain themselves (and tried to stop them lying)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

Every legacy codebase is haunted. You open a 25-year-old class, there's a catch (Exception e) that returns null, and the person who could explain why left the project in 2004.

Exorcist is a terminal app that summons them back. It reads a Git repository, works out who really wrote each Java class, and lets the ghost of its main author explain the class in first person, confess its sins line by line, and propose a refactoring as a diff. The model is open-weight and runs locally through Ollama, so the code never leaves your machine.

     .-.
    (o o)   E X O R C I S T
    | O \   summon the ghosts of legacy Java code
     \   \  model: qwen2.5-coder:7b, running locally via Ollama
      `~~~'
Command What happens
summon <repo> Lists every Java class with its ghost (the author with the most commits), birth and death dates
possess <Class> The ghost introduces itself from real Git history and explains the class, citing lines
confess The ghost confesses the class's code smells, worst first, each with its lines
exorcise The ghost rewrites its worst sin; you get a unified diff, never a modified file
epitaph An ASCII tombstone with a one-line epitaph

My take on the theme: the "ghost in the machine" is the people inside old code. Git remembers them perfectly (every commit, every date, every line they last touched) and nobody ever asks them anything. Exorcist gives them a voice, and makes them tell the truth.

Demo

I ran it on JUnit 4: 2,521 commits since December 2000. Reading the whole history takes under five seconds:

exorcist:> summon ../junit4
450 Java spirits rest in junit4, longest dead first.

Class                                Spirit      Born        Died        Commits
-----------------------------------  ----------  ----------  ----------  -------
Stub                                 David Saff  2007-09-04  2007-12-07        2
RepeatedTest                         David Saff  2000-12-03  2012-10-04        8
TestSetup                            David Saff  2000-12-03  2012-10-04        6
ComparisonFailure (junit.framework)  egamma      2002-06-22  2012-10-04       14
JUnit4TestAdapterCache               David Saff  2006-02-15  2012-10-04       10

Then I possessed junit.runner.BaseTestRunner: 326 lines, 30 commits, 10 catch blocks. Its ghost is the author with the most commits on the file:

exorcist:> possess junit.runner.BaseTestRunner
Possessing junit.runner.BaseTestRunner (src/main/java/junit/runner/BaseTestRunner.java)
Spirit: egamma | born 2000-12-03 | died 2016-10-15 | 30 commits | 326 lines
The air grows cold... (qwen2.5-coder:7b)

I am egamma, the author with the most commits on this file, having first touched it
on Sunday, December 3, 2000, and last making changes on Sunday, October 24, 2004.
This class, `BaseTestRunner`, is the backbone of JUnit's test runner infrastructure
[...] The `getTest` (line 91) method is a crucial template method [...]

[10 line citations, all inside the file]

That last line is not the model talking. It's Exorcist checking the answer (more on that below). Now the confession:

exorcist[BaseTestRunner]:> confess

1. (lines 95-142) The `getTest()` method is a long method, spanning 48 lines. [...]
2. (lines 110-113) The broad catch block that catches `Exception` (line 110) hides
   what can really go wrong. [...]
3. (lines 237-238) The empty catch block for `IOException` (line 237) and
   `SecurityException` (line 238) is a sin. It silently swallows exceptions [...]
4. (line 166) The use of `System.out.println()` (line 166) instead of a logger is a sin.
5. (lines 293-295) The broad catch block that catches `Exception` (line 293) [...]
6. (lines 117-121) The broad catch block that catches `Exception` (line 117) [...]

I must have been tired.

[12 line citations, all inside the file]

I checked every one against the source. All six are real, on the right lines. Number 5 is my favourite, and it has been in JUnit since 2000:

} catch (Exception IOException) {
    return stack; // return the stack unfiltered
}

An Exception, caught in a variable named IOException.

And the tombstone:

        ________________________________
      .'                                '.
     /                                    \
    |              R . I . P               |
    |                                      |
    |            BaseTestRunner            |
    |             junit.runner             |
    |                                      |
    |              haunted by              |
    |                egamma                |
    |                                      |
    |      2000-12-03  -  2016-10-15       |
    |                                      |
    |   "BaseTestRunner: The guardian of   |
    |         tests, old and new."         |
    |                                      |
    |       30 commits | 10 mourners       |
~~~~|______________________________________|~~~~

Code

MathFe / exorcist

Hacktoberfest 2026 final-week project: summon the ghosts of legacy Java code. A Spring Shell CLI where the Git author of each class explains it, confesses its code smells and proposes refactorings, powered by a local LLM via Ollama.

Exorcist

Summon the ghosts of legacy Java code.

Exorcist is a terminal app that reads a Git repository, finds who wrote each Java class, and lets the ghost of its main author explain the class in first person, confess its sins and propose a refactoring Everything runs locally: the "ghost" is an open-weight model served by Ollama, so your code never leaves your machine.

     .-.
    (o o)   E X O R C I S T
    | O \   summon the ghosts of legacy Java code
     \   \  model: qwen2.5-coder:7b, running locally via Ollama
      `~~~'

The tone is theatrical, but the facts are not. Every claim the ghost makes must cite line numbers, its life story comes only from real commits, and refactorings are shown as a diff. Exorcist never writes to your files.

Requirements

  • JDK 21 or newer

  • Ollama running locally, with a model pulled. The default is qwen2.5-coder:7b…

View on GitHub

Java 21, Spring Boot, Spring Shell, Spring AI (Ollama), JGit and JavaParser. 98 tests, none of which need a model or a network.

How I Built It

The hard part was not the ghost voice. That's one paragraph of system prompt. The hard part was that a 7B model will happily lie, and a tool that explains legacy code with confident lies is worse than no tool. So most of Exorcist is about handing the model facts and checking what comes back.

1. The ghosts come from Git, not from the model. One walk over the history (merges skipped, renames followed) finds who touched each file. Over 25 years people change names and e-mails: JUnit has dsaff <dsaff> and David Saff <saff@google.com>, who only meet through a third identity, dsaff <david@saff.net>. A small union-find merges them, but never through shared placeholder addresses like noreply@github.com, which would merge strangers. git blame tells the ghost which lines other hands wrote last.

2. No line number, no claim. The source goes to the model with line numbers, and every rule in the prompt points back at them. Then every answer is checked: Exorcist counts the citations, flags lines that don't exist and numbered items that cite nothing. That's the [12 line citations, all inside the file] line, in green when it's clean and yellow when it isn't.

3. Sins are found before they're confessed. JavaParser scans the class for empty or broad catch blocks, printStackTrace(), System.out, deep nesting, long methods, public mutable fields, Vector/Hashtable, @Deprecated code and TODOs, each with exact lines. The model gets them as evidence to judge, not as a script to read.

4. The model writes code. Exorcist writes the diff. exorcise doesn't ask the model for a patch, because small models produce broken ones. It picks a sin the static scan confirms, widens it to the smallest complete code that fixes it (the whole try statement, the statement, the method), and asks for REPLACE LINES a-b plus a code block. Exorcist splices it in, fixes the indentation the model forgot, checks that the file still parses, and computes the diff with JGit. Nothing is ever written to disk.

5. Prompts fit a small model's memory. Long files are cut to a window around the lines that matter, and the model is told exactly what it can't see.

Where the ghosts still lie

It would be odd to write about honesty and then hide the failures, so here they are, all from my own test runs.

  • The first confess run invented an IOException in two items (with the right line numbers, wrong content) and repeated one sin twice. Citations keep claims anchored and checkable. They don't make them true.
  • The first exorcise produced a diff that doesn't compile. It deleted the return null after a failure and caught exceptions the try body can never throw. Exorcist only checks that the result parses, and that's the next thing I want to fix: compiling the spliced file against the project's classpath.
  • gemma3:4b was worse. It called a three-line method "bloated", rewrote a whole method into a 13-line slot (Exorcist did catch that one: "the file no longer parses"), and, while blaming lines on other contributors, called a real JUnit maintainer "not a very good programmer". The authors are real people, so the prompt now has a fifth rule: judge the code, never the people. On the rerun, it criticized commits, not their authors.

So treat Exorcist the way you'd treat a séance: entertaining, sometimes eerily accurate, and never something you act on without checking. Every claim comes with the lines you need to check it.

I built it with Claude Code as a pair programmer. Writing the tests found four real bugs in the code we had written together, including one where, with a small prompt window, the model could be asked to rewrite lines it was never shown.

Why open matters here

Your code never leaves your laptop. The code people most need to understand is legacy code inside companies: banks, insurers, government. It's exactly the code you're not allowed to paste into a hosted chatbot. With Ollama and an open-weight model, Exorcist sends the source of your proprietary 2003 billing class nowhere. No API key, no account, no terms of service.

It works with the lights off. Once the model is pulled, Exorcist needs no network at all. I ran every demo above with the repository and the model on the same machine.

It costs nothing per question. A single possess prompt carries a full class, its outline and its Git history: several thousand tokens. Exploring a 450-class codebase that way on a paid API adds up fast. Locally it's just electricity, so you can ask the ghost again, and again.

You choose the brain. Swapping models is one environment variable (EXORCIST_MODEL=gemma3:4b), which is how I found out that model size matters more than I expected for keeping a ghost honest. With a closed API I couldn't have compared them on the same prompts and the same machine in an evening.

Old code deserves to be remembered by the people who wrote it. It shouldn't have to be shipped off to someone else's server for that to happen.

Happy Halloween, and feliz Día de los Muertos. 🕯️

title: OpenBSD 7.9 を 8.0 へ アップグレード
description:
はじめに

OpenBSD プロジェクトから 2026 年 10 月 20 日に OS の 8.0 がリリースされました 🌷 61 回目のリリースに当たります。

What's New (英語) | Changelog (英語)

本記事で OpenBSD 7.9 を 8.0 にアップグレードする手順を説明します。
各手順はすばらしい 公式ガイド (英語) に基づいています。

チュートリアル

実行するコマンド一式を示しながら、ステップ・バイ・ステップ形式で書いた、アップグレード用のガイドです。

🌷 🐡 🌅

1. アップグレード前準備: 検証とカスタイマイズ

公式のチュートリアルには Before using any upgrade method (私訳: アップグレード方法に関わらずその前に行うこと) セクションが設けられています。

アップグレード方法としては sysupgrade を使うのが、たいていの場合、良い選択になるでしょう。

ディスク空き容量の確認

/usr に 1.1GB 以上の空きがあることが必要です。

$ df -h
Filesystem     Size    Used   Avail Capacity  Mounted on
(...)
/dev/sd0e      7.8G    1.8G    5.5G    26%    /usr

OK のようです :)

現在の利用内容がアップグレード結果に適合することの確認

設定と構文の変更 (英語) と 特別なパッケージ (英語) を確認しましょう。

バックアップ (必要な場合)

適宜、事前にバックアップを取得しておきましょう。

アップグレード内容のカスタマイズ (必要な場合)

2. sysupgrade によるアップグレード

準備は良いですか。

* 注意: 以下のコマンド sysupgrade は、ひとたび実行すると中断はできません。

準備ができたら、以下のコマンドを実行しましょう。実行するのはこれだけです:

$ doas sysupgrade

以下のように出力されるでしょう:

Fetching from https://cdn.openbsd.org/pub/OpenBSD/8.0/amd64/
SHA256.sig   100% |******************************|  2144       00:00
Signature Verified
BUILDINFO    100% |******************************|    54       00:00
Verifying old sets.
INSTALL.amd64 100% |*****************************| 44889       00:00
