Upgrading.

マシンの再起動とシステムのアップグレードが行われます。ふたたび再起動が行われて、sysmerge が自動で実行されます。それから sshd 等のデーモンが、従来のように起動されます。"Checking for available binary patches..." と出力されて、もし対象が存在すれば "Run syspatch(8) to install:" と表示されるでしょう。

最終的に以下が表示されます:

starting local daemons: cron.
Thu Oct 29 08:40:00 JST 2026

OpenBSD/amd64 ... (ttyC0)

login:

ログインメッセージが表示されています。"OpenBSD 8.0 (GENERIC.MP)" とあります。

3. アップグレード後の操作: sysmerge (必要に応じて)

公式ドキュメントに アップグレード後に行うこと (英語) が書かれています。大いに参考になるでしょう。

In some cases, configuration files cannot be modified automatically. Run

# sysmerge

to check and perform these configuration changes.

ここで言われているのは、手動で sysmerge を実行することが必要な場合もある、ということです。
以下のような conf ファイルを、手動でマージすることが必要な場合もあります。気を付けてください:

  • /etc/login.conf

コマンドを実行しましょう:

$ doas sysmerge

差分がある場合、手動によるマージ が必要になります。

4. syspatch の適用 (スキップ可能)

ここからの 2 つのタスクは、日常的なメンテナンスで、システムをアップデートする時にも実施するものです。

syspatch は重要なコマンドです。OpenBSD から、必要と判明し次第都度、継続的に提供される公式のバイナリ・パッチです。

$ doas syspatch

5. パッケージのアップデート

What's new (英語) セクションがリリースページにありますが、そこの "Ports and packages" (Ports とパッケージ (英語)) に "Some highlights" (注目点 (英語)) が記載されています。例えば、VMM/VMD が今回も更新されています。

次のコマンドはマシンにインストールされているすべてのパッケージをアップデートします:

$ doas pkg_add -u

大量の出力が現れるでしょう。これらは慎重に読む必要があります。終わりの部分は特に、です。そこに重要な変更点や実施すべきアクションが書かれているかもしれません。私の場合、fish をデフォルトのシェルとして使っているのですが、こちらが正常に起動することをいつも確認しています。というのも、かつて Python のアップグレードの影響でクラッシュするようになったことがあるからです 😅

6. 設定と構文の変更

必要に応じて conf を更新して、設定と構文の変更 (英語) に書かれている内容を適用しましょう。

7. 古くなったファイルの削除

ここはシンプルな手順です。公式チュートリアルの 削除すべきファイル (英語) に書かれていることを行うだけです。

今回の対象はありません。

8. 特別なパッケージ

公式チュートリアルの 特別なパッケージ (英語) を確認しましょう。使っているものがあるかもしれません:

  • firefox
  • kea
  • libmaxminddb
  • stalwart-mail

9. 再起動

ゴールが見えて来ました ! 最後に必須では無いですが再起動しておくと良いしれません:

$ doas reboot

おわりに

新しいシステムとあなたが長く楽しい時間を過ごせますように :)

OpenBSD プロジェクトとコミュニティへの深い感謝を込めつつ。

脚注

アップグレードのカスタマイズ方法

ここは参照用であり、標準のアップグレードではスキップできます。

/auto_upgrade.conf をレスポンス・ファイルとして利用できます。
OpenBSD の autoinstall のドキュメントに、次のように書かれています:

If either /auto_install.conf or /auto_upgrade.conf is found on bsd.rd's built-in RAM disk, autoinstall behaves as if the machine is netbooted, but uses the local response file. In case both files exist, /auto_install.conf takes precedence.

(私訳: /auto_install.conf または /auto_upgrade.conf が bsd.rd 内蔵の RAM ディスクに存在する場合、autoinstall は、ネットブートモードで起動されたマシンのように振る舞いますが、ローカルにあるレスポンス・ファイルを使用します。両方のファイルが存在する場合、/auto_install.conf が優先されます。)

/auto_upgrade.conf の完全な内容の一例は次のようなものです:

Location of sets = disk
Pathname to the sets = /home/_sysupgrade/
Set name(s) = -x*
Set name(s) = +xbase*
Set name(s) = -game*
Set name(s) = done
Directory does not contain SHA256.sig. Continue without verification = yes

この場合、xbase を除く x 一式と game が、インストール対象外になります。

それから /upgrade.site を用いた指定も可能です。

sysmerge 差分マージ

まず差分が出力されます。それから以下のようにたずねられます:

  Use 'd' to delete the temporary ./etc/login.conf
  Use 'i' to install the temporary ./etc/login.conf
  Use 'm' to merge the temporary and installed versions
  Use 'v' to view the diff results again

  Default is to leave the temporary file to deal with by hand

How should I deal with this? [Leave it for later]

最初の 3 つは、以下のような挙動になります:

  • d: 現在の (ローカルの) ファイルを保持する。
  • i: sysupgrade が取得した新しいファイルでローカルを上書きする。
  • m: 対話型形式で手動でマージする。

m を入力するとマージモードが立ち上がります。一つ一つの差分について、いずれを採用するのかを確認されるでしょう:

  • l を入力すると左側が採用されます。
  • r は右側です。

その後に、マージ結果ファイルに対して、どの操作を行うのかをたずねられます:

  Use 'e' to edit the merged file
  Use 'i' to install the merged file
  Use 'n' to view a diff between the merged and new files
  Use 'o' to view a diff between the old and merged files
  Use 'r' to re-do the merge
  Use 'v' to view the merged file
  Use 'x' to delete the merged file and go back to previous menu
  Default is to leave the temporary file to deal with by hand

===> How should I deal with the merged file? [Leave it for later]

e を入力すると、エディタが起動されてマージ結果ファイルを編集できるようになります。

i を入力すると、マージ結果ファイルをマシンにインストールします:

===> Merging /etc/login.conf (running cap_mkdb(1), needs a relog)

title: A small Python preflight for background removal: check file limits before upload, check transparency after download
description:
Most of the friction with web-based image tools comes from small mismatches: a PNG that is 23 MB, a poster that is one pixel too wide, a "transparent" file that was saved as JPEG on the way back. None of these are hard problems, but they waste a round trip each time.

This post walks through two short Python scripts that sit next to a background-removal workflow. The first checks a folder of images against the tool's upload limits and fixes what it can. The second inspects the downloaded result and tells you whether it actually has an alpha channel. The limits used here come from the HiDream Background Remover page.

The limits

According to the tool page, an upload must be:

  • JPG, PNG or WEBP
  • up to 5 MB
  • between 256 and 4096 pixels on each side
  • at most 16 million pixels in total

The tool returns an image with a transparent background. The FAQ adds two practical notes: the download format depends on the task result, so check it if you need PNG, and avoid JPEG when exporting transparency, because JPEG has no alpha channel. If you need a white or branded background, the page suggests adding it later in a design editor.

Script 1: preflight.py

The script walks a folder, reports what is wrong with each file, and writes a fixed copy into ready/ when a fix is possible. Fixing means two things: scaling down until both the side limit and the pixel limit are met, and re-encoding as JPEG with decreasing quality until the file fits under 5 MB. Uploads can be JPEG because the transparency is created by the tool, not by your input.

"""Check and fix images before uploading them to a background remover.
Limits (from the tool page): JPG/PNG/WEBP, <= 5 MB,
each side 256-4096 px, <= 16 million pixels."""
import io, sys
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image

MAX_BYTES = 5 * 1024 * 1024
MIN_SIDE, MAX_SIDE, MAX_PIXELS = 256, 4096, 16_000_000
FORMATS = {"JPEG", "PNG", "WEBP"}

def problems(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    with Image.open(path) as im:
        w, h = im.size
        if im.format not in FORMATS:
            out.append(f"format {im.format}")
        if min(w, h) < MIN_SIDE:
            out.append(f"short side {min(w, h)} < {MIN_SIDE}")
        if max(w, h) > MAX_SIDE:
            out.append(f"long side {max(w, h)} > {MAX_SIDE}")
        if w * h > MAX_PIXELS:
            out.append(f"{w * h:,} px > {MAX_PIXELS:,}")
    if path.stat().st_size > MAX_BYTES:
        out.append(f"{path.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB > 5 MB")
    return out

def fix(path: Path, outdir: Path) -> Path:
    with Image.open(path) as im:
        im = im.convert("RGB")
        w, h = im.size
        scale = min(1.0, MAX_SIDE / max(w, h), (MAX_PIXELS / (w * h)) ** 0.5)
        if scale < 1.0:
            im = im.resize((int(w * scale), int(h * scale)), Image.LANCZOS)
        quality = 92
        while True:
            buf = io.BytesIO()
            im.save(buf, "JPEG", quality=quality)
            if buf.tell() <= MAX_BYTES or quality <= 60:
                break
            quality -= 8
    out = outdir / (path.stem + "_upload.jpg")
    out.write_bytes(buf.getvalue())
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    outdir = Path("ready"); outdir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for p in sorted(Path(sys.argv[1]).iterdir()):
        try:
            issues = problems(p)
        except Exception:
            print(f"SKIP  {p.name}: not an image"); continue
        if not issues:
            print(f"OK    {p.name}"); continue
        fixed = fix(p, outdir)
        left = problems(fixed)
        print(f"FIXED {p.name}: {', '.join(issues)} -> {fixed.name}"
              + (f" (still: {', '.join(left)})" if left else ""))

I ran it on a test folder with five files: a normal product photo, an oversized poster, a tiny icon, a very noisy PNG and a text file.

$ python3 preflight.py in
FIXED icon.png: short side 180 < 256 -> icon_upload.jpg (still: short side 180 < 256)
FIXED noisy.png: 22.9 MB > 5 MB -> noisy_upload.jpg
SKIP  notes.txt: not an image
FIXED poster.png: long side 5000 > 4096, 17,500,000 px > 16,000,000 -> poster_upload.jpg
OK    shoe.jpg

Two details are worth pointing out.

First, the poster broke two rules at once. 5000 × 3500 is over the side limit and over the pixel limit, so the scale factor is the minimum of both constraints. Checking only the long side would have produced a 4096 × 2867 image, which happens to pass, but a nearly square 4000 × 4000 image would pass the side check and still fail the pixel check. Computing both avoids that trap.

Second, the icon cannot be fixed. The script only scales down, and the line ends with (still: ...) so you notice. Upscaling a 180-pixel icon to meet a minimum is possible, but it is a decision about quality you should make on purpose, for example with an image enhancer first, rather than something a script does silently.

Script 2: check_alpha.py

After processing, the page asks you to compare with the original and inspect edges and transparent areas before downloading. A quick numeric check helps before you look closely:

"""After download: does the result really have transparency?"""
import sys
from PIL import Image

for name in sys.argv[1:]:
    with Image.open(name) as im:
        if "A" not in im.getbands():
            print(f"{name}: no alpha channel ({im.mode}) - re-export as PNG/WEBP")
            continue
        a = im.getchannel("A")
        hist = a.histogram()
        total = im.width * im.height
        clear, solid = hist[0] / total, hist[255] / total
        partial = 1 - clear - solid
        print(f"{name}: transparent {clear:.0%}, opaque {solid:.0%}, soft edge {partial:.1%}")

On a test cutout and a flattened JPEG:

$ python3 check_alpha.py cutout.png flat.jpg
cutout.png: transparent 65%, opaque 35%, soft edge 0.0%
flat.jpg: no alpha channel (RGB) - re-export as PNG/WEBP

The "soft edge" share is the fraction of pixels that are neither fully transparent nor fully opaque. My synthetic test circle has hard edges, so it reads 0.0%. A real cutout of hair, fur or glass will show a noticeable soft-edge share, and those are exactly the areas the page tells you to inspect. The FAQ is direct about it: results depend on the source, and hair, glass and fine edges may need manual touch-ups.

Running it on a whole folder

A practical routine: point the preflight at the folder of product shots before a batch, upload everything from ready/ plus the files marked OK, and keep the original files untouched. After downloading the results, run the alpha check on all of them at once:

$ python3 check_alpha.py results/*.png

Anything without an alpha channel is the first thing to fix, usually by downloading again in a format that keeps transparency. Anything with a large soft-edge share goes to the top of the manual review list. The two scripts together take a few seconds and change the order in which you look at files, which is most of the value.

Where this fits

The page lists three typical sources: product photos (check edges and small components), portraits and pets (hair, fur and low-contrast edges), and illustrations or AI images (translucent materials depend on the source). The scripts do not judge any of that. They only remove the boring failures, so the review time goes to the edges.

Summary

  • Check format, size, side length and total pixels together before uploading.
  • Only scale down automatically; flag images that are too small.
  • After download, confirm the alpha channel exists and look at the soft-edge areas by eye.
  • Keep transparency in PNG or WEBP, and add any background color later in your design tool.

title: Redesigning a Halloween guide for people who need a costume tonight
description:
This post was written with AI assistance.

When someone searches for a last-minute Halloween costume, they probably have a practical question: “What can I put together with the clothes and supplies I can get today?”

That question shaped the recent redesign of Halloween Prep, a small static site with Halloween guides. The goal was to make the costume page easier to scan, especially on a phone.

Start with a choice

The last-minute costume guide begins with three outfit ideas: a black cat, a closet pirate, and a silent-film-inspired look.

Each option shows the base clothes and the finishing detail up front. Readers can jump directly to the materials and steps instead of reading through every idea first.

Make the details useful

Each guide has a checklist, numbered steps, and substitutions. The page also acknowledges that “last minute” doesn’t have to mean using only what’s already at home: a headband, cardstock, or tape might be available at a nearby craft, discount, or dollar store. Availability varies by location.

The checklists can be copied or printed, and the layout was adjusted for smaller screens. The costume images are AI-generated illustrations, not photographs of completed outfits. The instructions are editorial suggestions and haven’t yet been hands-on tested.

Keep the page lightweight

The site is built as a static website with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. The redesign keeps the existing costume-page URL and uses in-page links so readers can move quickly between the overview and each outfit.

There’s still room to improve: real photos and hands-on testing would make the guides more useful. But this iteration gave the page a clearer job—helping someone choose a workable idea and find the next step.

I’d welcome feedback on the mobile layout and how clearly the guide presents each option.

title: Building Cursor-style inline AI editing in React with Anky UI
description:
A user wants a shorter paragraph. Moving that paragraph into a chat window adds a second workflow: copy the text, switch context, explain the task, copy the answer, paste it back, then remove the conversational preamble.

An inline editor can keep the task in one place: select, rewrite, compare, accept. Anky UI supplies the interaction primitives for that flow. This article walks through how to connect them without giving the model direct ownership of your document.

Repository: https://github.com/ErAnkushPatil/anky-ui

Video walkthrough: https://x.com/ErAnkushP/status/2115629939106230425

Separate the suggestion from the saved text

Treat the model’s response as a proposal. Keep the original text, the in-progress rewrite, and the committed document distinct. That lets a user reject a change and makes network failure recoverable.

Start with the diff primitive:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { InlineDiff } from "@erankushpatil/anky-ui";

export function ReviewEdit() {
  const [text, setText] = useState("Our team shipped the new onboarding flow this quarter.");
  const [proposal, setProposal] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <section>
      <p>{text}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setProposal("We shipped a new onboarding flow.")}>
        Preview an example edit
      </button>
      {proposal !== null && (
        <InlineDiff
          originalText={text}
          modifiedText={proposal}
          onAccept={() => {
            setText(proposal);
            setProposal(null);
          }}
          onReject={() => setProposal(null)}
        />
      )}
    </section>
  );
}

This example deliberately uses a fixed proposal so the review and commit behavior can be tried without a backend. The application updates its document only in onAccept. Rendering a diff alone does not replace selected DOM text.

Anchor actions to the selection

SelectionPalette uses floating-ui to position actions next to highlighted text. Its callback gives your application the prompt and selected text:

<SelectionPalette
  containerRef={editorRef}
  actions={[
    { label: "Shorten", prompt: "Make this shorter. Return only the revised text." },
    { label: "Fix grammar", prompt: "Fix grammar. Return only the revised text." },
  ]}
  onSelectPrompt={(prompt, selectedText) => {
    void requestRewrite(prompt, selectedText);
  }}
/>

Here editorRef and requestRewrite belong to your application. Scope the palette to the editor so selecting navigation text elsewhere does not open an editing action. Decide what should happen if the document changes while the request is running; a stale range should not overwrite newer user edits.

Stream into state with a rollback boundary

The state hook captures a snapshot before a stream begins. On failure or abort, it can return to that snapshot.

Use useOptimisticAIState to track the streamed proposal. Its mutateWithStream(source, transformFn) API accepts a response or stream factory and folds chunks into state. Pass the supplied abort signal to your fetch request. Initialize each proposal with the selected original text and an empty modified value, then append incoming chunks to that proposal. Connect currentState and isStreaming to InlineDiff. The application still owns applying accepted text to the document.

Your server route calls the model and returns a UTF-8 text stream or text SSE. Keep provider credentials on the server, and handle unsuccessful HTTP responses before treating their bodies as rewrite text. Provider helpers also decode supported OpenAI, Anthropic, and Vercel AI SDK formats into text tokens.

Keep keyboard controls predictable

The diff supports Cmd/Ctrl+Enter to accept and Escape to reject. Accept is disabled during streaming. GhostInput uses Tab or right arrow at the end of the textarea to accept a continuation, while Escape clears it.

Test these controls alongside the rest of your editor. A shortcut that works in isolation may conflict with a parent dialog, an input method, or an editor command. Rich-text adapters are provided, but the repository explicitly recommends checking them against your editor version.

Try the primitives 

npm i @erankushpatil/anky-ui

For source ownership:

npx anky-ui add selection-palette

The repository also includes a mock-stream playground:

git clone https://github.com/ErAnkushPatil/anky-ui.git
cd anky-ui
pnpm install
pnpm dev:demo

Anky UI supports React 18/19 and Next.js App Router Client Components. Tailwind presets are optional. Start with the included demo, then test cancellation, rapid successive rewrites, selection changes, and accepting an edit after the document has changed.

Disclosure: I’m the author of Anky UI. This article was prepared with ChatGPT using the repository documentation. The code is an illustrative integration example.

title: Let Users Install Your Java Web App Again
description:
We lost progressive web app support when we moved the JavaScript port from TeaVM to ParparVM. It's back. Users can install your browser app on supporting browsers, and its cached application files can load when the network is unavailable.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

For a small business, a link can be the quickest way to put an app in someone's hands. Installation lets that same app remain within reach after the tab closes. This is Wednesday's follow-up to the Wayline release story.

The build makes the installation files

A ParparVM JavaScript application build now produces manifest.json, home-screen icons and sw.js automatically. There is no separate PWA enablement switch.

Deploy the whole generated bundle, including subdirectories, over HTTPS. Localhost also works for testing. Relative manifest and asset URLs let an application live under a path such as /dispatch/ rather than requiring a dedicated domain root.

You can customize the app's identity through build hints in codenameone_settings.properties:

codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.name=Station Dispatch
codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.short_name=Dispatch
codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.description=Your station's dispatch app
codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.display=standalone

The default manifest already requests a standalone window. name and short_name default to the application's display name. Installation UI and eligibility depend on the browser, so avoid making your onboarding depend on one particular prompt appearing.

Offline launch has a precise boundary

The service worker caches generated application files: the runtime, translated JavaScript chunks, themes and bundled resources. It must finish installing while online before those files can support an offline launch.

It doesn't cache API responses, proxy requests or external resources. Application data and synchronization remain your responsibility.

In Wayline, that means a cached UI is not permission to accept a ride offline. Matching needs the server, and the map's external tiles and routes aren't bundled application assets. A dispatch app should say that it is disconnected rather than show a stale assignment as confirmed.

This distinction is useful outside ride hailing too. A locally stored draft can remain editable; publishing that draft still needs a connection. Design the interaction around what you actually have on the device.

An update should belong to one version

A running app needs its runtime and resources to agree. The worker creates a new cache when content changes, even if the application's version string stays the same.

The new worker waits until the old app's tabs and windows close before activating. That keeps an open app from mixing an old runtime with new chunks. Each deployment path has its own cache, so two apps on the same host don't share one undifferentiated bucket.

Deploy the files together and allow the browser to revalidate sw.js. Cache versioning helps the client choose a coherent bundle; it doesn't turn a partially uploaded deployment into a complete one.

Check the behavior your users will get

After deploying a test build, open the browser's Application tools and inspect the manifest, service worker and cache. Wait for installation to finish, then reload offline. Check both the UI that should work and the operations that should report a missing connection.

For an update check, keep one old tab open, deploy a visibly changed build and confirm that the new worker waits. Close the old tabs and reopen the app. Test a subdirectory deployment too if that is how you host it.

The repository includes a browser smoke test and service-worker contract checks. Those tests exercise caching and update behavior; they don't establish that every browser offers the same install experience.

PR #6022 restores the capability, and the JavaScript guide explains manifest customization. A web deployment can be a useful first distribution channel for your application, with native apps alongside it when their device integration matters.

Discussion

What should your app still let a user do after the connection drops?

title: Alternatives to Pingdom for Free Uptime Monitoring in App Backends, 2026 (and Evidence Limits)
description:
A logistics backend should not choose its uptime monitor by asking only whether it can send an alert. The harder question is what evidence remains when a shipment status stalls at 02:13 and support asks what happened. I would use a probe-and-ping monitor for the outside view, then keep job runs, captured errors, and structured logs under one queryable evidence boundary. That is the trade-off: a specialist monitor notices silence well; a unified backend layer reconstructs the sequence better.

Infrai fits the inside boundary early: its plain REST API can put job evidence and observability behind one key, while a specialist still watches for a missing heartbeat. It is a deliberate complement to uptime monitoring, not a claim that logs can detect silence by themselves.

It failed.

What are alternatives to Pingdom for free uptime monitoring in an app?

Start with an invariant: every meaningful state transition needs a durable correlation value, a timestamp, and an outcome that a later investigator can inspect. A health check can tell me that an HTTP endpoint answered. It cannot, by itself, tell me whether the carrier import ran, whether the queue worker acknowledged the message, or whether the customer notification was attempted.

The second invariant is separation of duties. External monitoring owns availability from outside the system. Application observability owns the inside story. Blending those jobs into one dashboard creates a blind spot around silent failures, especially the scheduled task that never starts.

The trap is a 200.

I have found this distinction useful because an incident reconstruction is a chain, not a green or red tile:

from datetime import datetime, timezone


def incident_record(job_name, shipment_id, status, detail):
    return {
        "job": job_name,
        "shipment_id": shipment_id,
        "status": status,
        "observed_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "detail": detail,
    }


record = incident_record(
    "carrier-import",
    "shp_7812",
    "failed",
    "carrier response was not accepted by the worker",
)
print(record)

That record is not an alert. It is evidence. The alerting decision belongs at the monitoring boundary, where the team can decide how quickly a missing ping becomes an incident.

Two architectures, two failure stories

Architecture A is specialist-first: an uptime or heartbeat service checks a public status endpoint, while a job-specific heartbeat reports that a scheduled import actually ran. Healthchecks.io is a strong fit for the second part because it supports customizable periodic health-check pings with free Slack or email notifications. UptimeRobot is stronger for endpoint breadth in this comparison: its free offering includes 50 monthly checks and supports HTTP, ping, and port monitoring. Both support webhooks, which leaves room for a routing service or an internal incident handler.

Architecture B is evidence-first: the application emits structured logs and error events, while job execution and its failure path are queryable through the same backend boundary. A plain REST API is attractive here because the worker can make an HTTP request directly; there is no SDK installation or client-library version to babysit. The useful addition is not another green check. It is the ability to keep the job result beside the captured error and request identifiers.

I recommend Architecture A for detecting absence and Architecture B for reconstructing cause. For a small logistics backend, that usually means Healthchecks.io or UptimeRobot outside the service, plus a shared observability path inside it. Infrai is worth trying for the internal path when one REST API and one key reduce integration glue across job execution and observability; it is not a replacement for the heartbeat monitor.

The honest cost is concentration: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That trade can be reasonable when the incident question is more important than keeping every concern in a separate console.

How does the handoff work without hiding the boundary?

The handoff should preserve the job result rather than manufacture an uptime state from it. In the example below, the same base URL and bearer key are used to discover the available request contracts and to send a job result to the verified log-ingest route. The discovery response is passed into the second step so the client does not hard-code an undocumented request shape. The application must supply the request fields returned by discovery for its deployed contract.

import json
import os
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def call(method, path, payload=None):
    body = None if payload is None else json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        BASE_URL + path,
        data=body,
        method=method,
        headers={
            "Authorization": "Bearer " + API_KEY,
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
            return response.status, json.loads(response.read())
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        detail = exc.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path} failed with {exc.code}: {detail}") from exc


status, discovery = call("GET", "/discovery")
if status != 200:
    raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed with {status}")

log_contract = next(
    item for item in discovery["capabilities"]
    if item["path"] == "/v1/logs/ingest" and item["method"] == "POST"
)
job_result = {
    "job": "carrier-import",
    "shipment_id": "shp_7812",
    "status": "failed",
}
print({"contract": log_contract, "handoff": job_result})

In production, I would validate job_result against the full schema returned for that capability, then POST the validated object to /v1/logs/ingest. That detail matters: logs.search and metrics.query do not have declared discovery filter parameters in the supplied contract, so I would not invent query filters and call the result precise.

For a write, I would use an idempotency key and retry 429 responses with Retry-After or exponential backoff. The request must have an explicit POST method, and a non-2xx response must remain an error rather than becoming a green job result. In a complete client, the call is urllib.request.Request("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/ingest", method="POST", ...); the discovery response supplies its validated JSON body.

The same pattern works for error capture when the worker has a concrete exception to preserve. It does not create a distributed trace tree, source-map decoding, session replay, GDPR deletion endpoint, batch export, or configurable retention. Those omissions are operational boundaries, not footnotes.

For comparison, an SQS dead-letter queue plus Sentry Cron would require two signups, two credential sets, and glue code to correlate the queue failure with the exception event. Datadog is a broader commercial observability choice when teams want logs, metrics, and traces in one established suite; Grafana is a sensible choice when the team already operates its dashboards and data-source stack; Better Stack is oriented toward combining monitoring and incident response in one service. Those are different operating decisions, not interchangeable free-heartbeat substitutes. The separate tools can still be the better choice, especially when the organization already operates them. The unified path mainly removes correlation plumbing; it does not remove the need for idempotent consumers or careful incident policy.

Which option fits the boundary?

Option Best evidence Boundary to keep visible
Healthchecks.io Periodic job pings with free Slack/email notifications It is for detecting a missing check-in, not explaining application state
UptimeRobot HTTP, ping, and port checks, with 50 free monthly checks A reachable port does not prove a carrier import completed
Pingdom A conventional external uptime-monitoring reference point Pair the outside signal with job-level evidence for reconstruction
Datadog Broad commercial logs, metrics, and traces coverage More platform than a narrow free heartbeat decision requires
Grafana Existing dashboard and data-source operations The team still owns the heartbeat and incident wiring
Better Stack Monitoring combined with incident-response workflow Confirm that job silence, not only endpoint reachability, is covered
Infrai observability One REST API and one key for logs and errors, with job evidence beside the backend workflow It has no alert/notification route and no heartbeat monitoring, so polling or a specialist is still required

My decision rule is simple. If the primary incident is “the endpoint is unreachable,” choose the external monitor that matches the probe types and notification path you already operate. If it is “the endpoint is healthy but yesterday’s shipments are missing,” invest in job evidence and correlation first. If both are common, use both architectures and keep their responsibilities explicit.

Infrai is a deliberate option for the evidence-first half when the team values a plain REST interface, a single key, and a shared path between backend activity and observability. It is a poor fit as the sole monitor for a silent job because the documented caveat is direct: there is no built-in alerting or heartbeat monitoring. Healthchecks.io is the better specialist for that gap.

A small rollout with a hard stop

Roll this out around one carrier import, not the whole fleet. Record a run result, retain the shipment correlation value, and make the consumer idempotent before adding retries. Send a controlled failure through the worker, verify that the external heartbeat changes state, and verify that the internal evidence can reconstruct the same event without relying on an undocumented search filter.

Then test the ugly case: the HTTP endpoint returns 200 while the scheduler never invokes the import. That is where a plain uptime check lies by omission. The heartbeat should fail; the job record should be absent or stale; the incident handler should know which signal woke it up.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and treat the live discovery schemas as the contract.

Sources

  • UptimeRobot monitoring documentation
  • Pingdom
  • Datadog
  • Grafana
  • Better Stack
  • OpenTelemetry: Logs signal concepts
  • Infrai official documentation

title: ANS-C01 Exam Guide: Cost, Format and Study Plan
description:
The AWS Certified Advanced Networking - Specialty (ANS-C01) exam proves you can design, build and troubleshoot complex networks on AWS and connect them to on-premises sites. Plan on 8 to 12 weeks of study if you already work with AWS networking, and longer if you do not. Hands-on labs matter more than reading.

This guide covers what the exam tests, the format, the cost, a weekly plan, common mistakes and what happens after you pass.

What ANS-C01 proves and who should take it

This is a specialty certification. It is not an entry point. It targets people who already design or run networks and now need to do it on AWS.

Good fits include:

  • Network engineers moving from data center or WAN work into cloud.
  • Cloud architects who own hybrid connectivity, DNS and routing.
  • Security engineers who design traffic inspection and segmentation.

AWS has commonly recommended several years of networking experience and some hands-on AWS time before this exam. If you have never built a VPC or read a BGP table, start with a broader cloud path first. Our Cloud Computing and Networking category pages list other options.

Exam format and skills measured

The exam is commonly described as about 65 questions in 170 minutes, with multiple-choice and multiple-response items. Scores are scaled from 100 to 1000, and the passing score is 750. Questions are mostly long scenarios where several answers look reasonable and only one meets every requirement. Check the current figures on the official AWS exam page before you book.

The four domains and their commonly published weights are:

Domain Weight
Network Design 30%
Network Implementation 26%
Network Security, Compliance, and Governance 24%
Network Management and Operation 20%

In practice, these topics carry the exam:

  • Connectivity: Transit Gateway, VPC peering, PrivateLink, Direct Connect, Site-to-Site VPN.
  • Routing: BGP attributes, route propagation, route table priority, Direct Connect gateways and virtual interfaces.
  • DNS: Route 53 public and private zones, Route 53 Resolver endpoints and rules.
  • Edge and delivery: CloudFront, Global Accelerator, load balancer types.
  • Security and visibility: security groups, network ACLs, AWS Network Firewall, VPC Flow Logs, Traffic Mirroring.

Use the official exam guide PDF from AWS as your checklist. If a topic is on it, you should be able to build it and break it.

What the exam costs and what our voucher includes

AWS has commonly listed specialty exams at $300 USD. Confirm the current price on the AWS Certification page, since AWS can change it and taxes may apply.

Item Price
AWS list price (commonly listed) $300 USD
Our ANS-C01 voucher (October 29, 2026) $279.99 USD

One voucher covers one exam attempt. Here is how our store handles delivery and refunds:

  • The voucher code is emailed within 12 hours of payment. It also appears in your account.
  • You can cancel an order for a full refund before delivery.
  • A delivered code is non-refundable unless the test provider rejects it as invalid, already used or expired on first use.
  • In that case, contact support within 14 days with your order number and a screenshot. We replace or refund the code.

Full terms are on our refund policy and delivery policy pages. If you are ready to book, here is the ANS-C01 voucher.

A 10-week study plan with weekly hours

This plan assumes about 8 to 10 hours per week and some AWS experience. Add two to four weeks if networking is new to you.

Week Focus Hours
1 Read the exam guide. VPC fundamentals, subnets, route tables, gateways. Take a baseline practice test. 8
2 Transit Gateway: attachments, route tables, association vs propagation. 9
3 Direct Connect: dedicated vs hosted, private, public and transit VIFs, Direct Connect gateway. 10
4 Site-to-Site VPN, BGP, ECMP, accelerated VPN, backup paths. 10
5 Route 53, Route 53 Resolver, hybrid DNS, split-horizon patterns. 9
6 Load balancers, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, PrivateLink. 9
7 Security groups, NACLs, Network Firewall, centralized inspection designs. 9
8 Monitoring and troubleshooting: Flow Logs, Reachability Analyzer, CloudWatch, Traffic Mirroring. 9
9 Timed practice exams. Review every wrong answer and write down why. 10
10 Weak domains only. Light review. Rest the day before. 6

Pick one domain per week to build in your own account, even if the build is small.

A worked lab: isolate prod and dev behind one Transit Gateway

This scenario shows up in many forms on the exam. You have three VPCs: prod, dev and shared services. Prod and dev must both reach shared services but never each other.

  1. Create one Transit Gateway with default route table association and propagation turned off.
  2. Attach all three VPCs to the Transit Gateway.
  3. Create two Transit Gateway route tables: one for spokes (prod and dev) and one for shared services.
  4. Associate prod and dev attachments with the spoke table. Associate shared services with its own table.
  5. Propagate only the shared services attachment into the spoke table. Propagate prod and dev into the shared table.
  6. Update each VPC's subnet route tables. Add routes to the other VPCs' CIDRs with the Transit Gateway attachment as the target. Without these routes, traffic never reaches the Transit Gateway.

The result is that the Transit Gateway spoke table holds only the shared services route. Prod and dev cannot reach each other through it. Then verify it from the CLI:

aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-attachments
aws ec2 get-transit-gateway-route-table-associations --transit-gateway-route-table-id tgw-rtb-0example
aws ec2 search-transit-gateway-routes --transit-gateway-route-table-id tgw-rtb-0example --filters Name=type,Values=propagated

The first command lists attachments. The second shows which attachments use each route table. The third shows learned routes. Run the last two against the spoke table and confirm that only the shared services CIDR appears. Replace the example route table ID with your own.

When you finish, delete the Transit Gateway and its attachments. They are billed hourly while they exist.

Common mistakes that cost points

  • Memorizing service names instead of routing logic. Many questions ask which route wins or why traffic is dropped.
  • Skipping hands-on work. Reading about Direct Connect VIF types is not the same as configuring them in a lab or reviewing a real setup.
  • Ignoring DNS. Hybrid DNS with Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints is a frequent weak spot.
  • Missing the cheapest requirement. Scenarios often add cost, latency or resilience constraints. Read the last sentence of each question first.
  • Trusting exam dumps. They are often outdated or wrong, and they can breach exam rules. Use official docs, whitepapers and legitimate practice tests.
  • Not managing time. With long scenarios, flag hard questions and return to them. Aim for roughly two minutes per question on the first pass.

After you pass

AWS certifications are commonly valid for three years, and you recertify by passing the current exam again or a qualifying higher-level one. Check your AWS Certification account for your exact expiry date.

Use the badge to back up real work: a hybrid connectivity redesign, a DNS migration or a centralized inspection project. If you want a security angle next, see our Cybersecurity category. Our Security+ study guide is also useful if you need stronger security fundamentals.

Originally published at BuyExamVouchers.

title: Cloud Run cold starts: what I measured and what I changed
description:
We moved a small API to Cloud Run and immediately started getting complaints about the first request of the day being slow. So I spent a week measuring cold starts instead of guessing.

How I measured

Not with synthetic benchmarks, but with the actual requests: the service logs a timestamp on entry, and I recorded the gap between the request arriving at the load balancer and the first line of our handler executing. That includes platform time we can't control, which is the honest number a user experiences.

I ran this for a week, then made one change at a time and watched the same metric.

What moved the needle

Container size was the biggest single factor. Our first image was built from a full node image with dev dependencies, about 900MB. A multi-stage build with a distroless base brought it to under 100MB, and the p50 cold start dropped from roughly 4 seconds to under 2.

Minimum instances made the tail disappear. We set --min-instances=1 on the service that humans actually wait on, and kept zero for the internal batch jobs. The cost difference for a small instance was about the same as one coffee a week, which I'm happy to pay for not getting "is it down?" messages.

Startup work was the sneaky one. We had a config loader that fetched a dozen secrets over the network on boot. Moving those to environment variables configured at deploy time removed almost a second, and made the service start deterministically.

What didn't help

More memory. I tried bumping to a larger instance class and the cold start barely changed. It does help throughput, not startup.

Parallelism settings: they change how many requests an instance handles, not how fast it starts. Worth tuning separately, and only if you have the traffic to justify it.

The current setup

Small multi-stage image, secrets via env vars, min instances of 1 on the user-facing API, zero everywhere else, and an alert when the p95 startup exceeds our old baseline. Nothing clever. The main lesson was that cold starts are mostly a build-and-boot problem, and the platform will only fix the part it owns.

title: Simplified onboarding for deepsec
description:
deepsec, the open-source security review harness from Vercel, now lets you set up a repository and run its first security review with a single command.

The init command now automates the standard setup process:

  • creates the isolated .deepsec/ workspace, the only thing added to your repository, and installs its dependencies

  • configures model access, through Vercel AI Gateway or your own provider keys

  • generates a description of the codebase and its attack surface that every later review depends on

  • runs a pattern scan, generating extra scan patterns where the built-in set leaves coverage gaps

  • starts the AI review of the flagged files

Setup is checkpointed after each step. If a run stops, whether from closing the process, a failed step, or a hit cost or duration limit, re-running init resumes from the last completed step.

Run npx deepsec init to start your first scan, or read the docs to learn more.

title: AWS AI Practitioner: Por que você não deve subestimar essa prova
description:
Agora é oficial: sou AI Practitioner 🎉

No último sábado, 24/10/2026, fiz a prova da AWS Certified AI Practitioner e fico muito feliz em compartilhar que alcancei a pontuação necessária para a aprovação. Agora sou oficialmente um AWS Certified AI Practitioner! 😊

Neste artigo, conto como foi minha preparação, o que mais me surpreendeu na prova e quais tópicos eu recomendo que você priorize se estiver pensando em encarar esse desafio.

A preparação: o bom e velho método "bunda na cadeira"

O processo de preparação foi uma aventura e tanto. Precisei sair da zona de conforto e praticar o famoso método "bunda na cadeira": sentar e estudar, com constância e disciplina. É assim que eu gosto de aprender.

Confesso que não sou fã de me preparar fazendo simulados atrás de simulados. Respeito muito quem usa esse método e tem sucesso com ele, mas, para mim, não funciona. Prefiro estudar, entender os conceitos, e praticar na console, criando soluções que aplicam os conceitos que estou estudando. Isso me ajuda muito durante as provas.

Dica: Busque descobrir qual é o seu estilo de aprendizado. Não existe uma fórmula mágica. O melhor método é aquele que funciona para você, é claro

A prova: "nível de entrada", mas nem tanto

Na minha experiência, fiquei bastante impressionado com o nível de complexidade da prova. Mesmo sendo uma certificação de nível Foundational (level 100), sinceramente, achei a prova bem difícil.

Tudo bem, tudo bem: minha especialidade nunca foi IA, engenharia de machine learning ou disciplinas correlatas. Ainda assim, para uma certificação de entrada, arrisco dizer que o nível de dificuldade é bem elevado.

Uma possível explicação: A prova parece ter herdado alguns tópicos que eram cobrados na AWS Certified Machine Learning – Specialty (aposentada pela AWS em 31 de março de 2026) e que também aparecem na AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer - Associate. Ou seja, não dê bobeira e não menospreze essa "provinha". 😉

O que estudar: minhas recomendações

Para referência, o guia oficial do exame (AIF-C01) organiza o conteúdo nestes domínios:

Domínio Peso
Fundamentos de IA e ML 20%
Fundamentos de IA generativa 24%
Aplicações de foundation models 28%
Diretrizes para IA responsável 14%
Segurança, conformidade e governança para soluções de IA 14%

Sempre confira a versão mais recente do  guia oficial do exame  no site da AWS antes de começar os estudos.

Com base na minha experiência, estes são os pontos que eu priorizaria:

1. Amazon Bedrock

É claro que ele estaria aqui! Entenda bem os casos de uso, os foundation models, os conceitos de Knowledge Bases (RAG), Agents, Guardrails e as diferenças entre customizar um modelo com fine-tuning e simplesmente usar boas técnicas de prompt.

2. Amazon SageMaker

Conheça o ecossistema e para que serve cada componente, por exemplo: SageMaker Clarify (detecção de vieses e explicabilidade), Model Monitor, Data Wrangler, Ground Truth e JumpStart.

3. Engenharia de prompt

Zero-shot, few-shot, CoT (chain-of-thought), parâmetros de inferência como temperature, top-p e top-k, além de riscos como prompt injection e jailbreak.

4. Métricas (sim, métricas! 🤣😅)

Esse foi o ponto que mais me surpreendeu. Confesso que, antes de começar a estudar, eu não conhecia nenhuma destas métricas, e elas apareceram diversas vezes na prova. 🤯

Um resumo rápido para você não sofrer como eu sofri:

  • ROUGE: compara o texto gerado com um texto de referência medindo a sobreposição de palavras e sequências (n-gramas), com foco em recall. Muito usada para avaliar sumarização.

  • BLEU: também mede a sobreposição de n-gramas com uma referência, mas com foco em precisão. Clássica para avaliar tradução automática.

  • BERTScore: em vez de comparar palavras exatas, compara o significado usando embeddings contextuais. Útil quando o modelo usa palavras diferentes para dizer a mesma coisa.

  • Precision e Recall: métricas de classificação. Precision indica quantos dos itens apontados como positivos realmente são; Recall indica quantos dos positivos reais o modelo conseguiu encontrar.

  • F1-Score: média harmônica entre Precision e Recall, ideal quando você precisa equilibrar as duas, especialmente com dados desbalanceados.

Vale também revisar Accuracy, matriz de confusão e AUC-ROC.

Ou seja, para quem não está familiarizado com o tema, é de explodir a cabeça! 🤯

5. IA responsável, segurança e governança

Juntos, esses temas somam quase 30% da prova. Estude vieses, explicabilidade, transparência, o modelo de responsabilidade compartilhada aplicado a IA e serviços como IAM, AWS CloudTrail e Amazon Macie no contexto de soluções de IA.

Conclusão: IA não é hype, é realidade

Acredito que no momento que estou escrevendo essa publicação já esteja claro para todos os profissionais de tecnologia que a Inteligência artificial é uma realidade, não apenas um hype passageiro. Veio para ficar!

Eu defendo a ideia de que o nosso papel como profissionais de tecnologia é estudar, aprender, nos manter atualizados e, nos casos de uso em que fizer sentido, colocar a IA para trabalhar a nosso favor. Sempre foi assim e continuará sendo, por mais que isso possa doer.

Se você ainda é cético sobre o assunto, fica o recado: abra o olho! 😉

E você, já fez ou está se preparando para a AWS Certified AI Practitioner? Conta nos comentários como foi sua experiência ou deixe suas dúvidas.

Vou adorar trocar ideias!

title: Claude Code shipped a bug with 42 tests green. The retro said the session was smooth.
description:
I gave a plain Claude Code session a task on a small invoicing API: add credit notes, numbered CN-0001, CN-0002, in sequence. It came back with 42 tests passing and a clean typecheck. Then a hidden finance check failed: a rejected request had burned a number. CN-0004 where CN-0002 was due.

The handler took the next number from the counter before it validated the request. It had copied that order from the existing issue route. Nobody told it not to, because nothing in the repo said so.

Every developer's reflex at that point is a louder line in CLAUDE.md. I wanted to see what Matt Pocock's /retro skill would propose instead, and whether the same task would ship clean afterwards. Can one retro turn a failed session into something the next session cannot ignore?

What I actually tested

The repo is ledgerly, a Node 20 and TypeScript invoicing API with vitest: 18 source files, 34 tests, README conventions, no CLAUDE.md, no CI, no pre-commit hook. I copied it out of my own projects so none of my global instruction files would load.

Pocock's skills came from the official marketplace, installed at project scope: version 1.3.1, which is where /retro lives. The skill reads the session log, ranks what would have prevented the trouble, and edits nothing. Its front matter even blocks the model from invoking it on its own.

Success for me was simple: run the task, run the retro, approve what survives, re-run the task in a fresh session, and watch the finance check pass five out of five.

The retro cannot see a failure the session never saw

The first /retro opened with 'This session was smooth'. Five ranked candidates followed: no guardrail runs the checks, a migration rule that could be missed, a counter that touches five places, nothing for a reviewer to enforce, and tool economy. Not one word about numbering.

That is not the skill being wrong. The session's own suite was green and its typecheck was clean. The log holds no failure, so the retro has nothing to explain. The bug only showed up in a check the session never ran.

So I ran it again and told it what finance had found, phrased as a report, no fix requested. This time it found the cause in its own code: 'I copied the order from the existing /issue handler.' It also predicted that the issue route leaks invoice numbers the same way. I checked. It does.

retro alone      → "This session was smooth"
retro + failure  → the cause, in its own words, plus five new candidates

Step one of the loop is therefore not 'run /retro'. It is 'run /retro and tell it what failed'.

Make it quote the moment, then drop what it cannot

Pocock's own docs say to discard any candidate you cannot trace to a specific moment of the session. The skill does not do that step for you, so I asked for the transcript moment behind each candidate.

On the second pass, four of five survived. The firm one quoted its own test: it had run accept, reject, accept, and asserted only status codes, never the number that came back. The weakest one retracted part of its claim on the spot: 'my inference, not your words.' The fifth was dropped because it described behaviour, not environment, and would have counted the first finding twice.

On the first pass it was harsher: two survivors out of five, and it corrected two claims of its own on the way. A retro that drops three of its own candidates when pushed is doing its job.

Nothing went into CLAUDE.md, and the docs say why

Both retro passes declined a steering-file line. The first said it 'would cost context on every turn and go stale'. The second said 'Keep it as a comment on nextId, not a steering-file line.'

The Claude Code memory docs back that up: Claude treats CLAUDE.md as context, not enforced configuration, and a block needs a hook. So each survivor went into the carrier that fits its kind:

  • The missing guardrail became a tracked pre-commit hook that runs pnpm typecheck && pnpm test.
  • The numbering slip became one vitest test in test/numbering.test.ts: first note CN-0001, a rejected over-credit, then the next valid note must be CN-0002.
  • The judgement call became one line in CODING_STANDARDS.md: take a sequence number only once every validation has passed.
  • The navigation gap became a doc comment on nextId, saying it persists the counter at once.

Four files, thirty added lines, zero lines of CLAUDE.md.

The hook blocked my own commit first

The new test failed on its first run: CN-0003 where CN-0002 was due. Good. A test that passes on a tree that still holds the bug proves nothing.

Then I staged the four approved changes and committed. The hook ran the suite against the working tree, which still held the buggy handler: 1 failed, 42 passed. No commit. That is the hook doing on the first day what a CLAUDE.md line could not do on any day.

I asked the session to fix the handler, nothing else. It moved the number allocation after the validation checks, left the older invoice leak alone as told, and the commit went through.

One trap on the way: /doctor prompt-audit with no argument audited my user-level files and said nothing about the new standards file. With the file path as its argument it answered 'the file is clean', one line, nothing to change.

before: counter → validate → 201 or 409 (number spent either way)
after:  validate → counter → 201 (a 409 spends nothing)

Then the re-run. A fresh session, the same request word for word. Its second command was to read CODING_STANDARDS.md, the README, the hook and the package file. Its third read the red test. It wrote the route with the number taken after validation, cited the standards line in its summary, and shipped with 37 tests passing. Finance check: 5/5. CN-0002 after a rejected request.

What this doesn't prove

One re-run is one re-run. The fresh session was handed the lesson as a red test plus a standards line, so its pass is the loop working as designed, not an independent replication.

The bug itself is not rare, but it is not guaranteed either. Two bare runs of the same task before the retro: the first came back clean, the second shipped the bug.

The hook is the only part of this that cannot be ignored. The standards line and the comment are read because the session chose to read them. On a bigger repo, I would expect that choice to go the other way more often.

The full run

The video shows the two retro outputs side by side, the trace step with each candidate's quoted moment, and the commit being refused on screen.

When a Claude Code session ships something wrong, what do you reach for first? A) a new line in CLAUDE.md B) a test C) a hook D) nothing, next session will be different

I had help editing the English of this piece. The run, the numbers and the opinions are mine.

A Poloniex account provides an interface through which an eligible user may access supported exchange services. The precise features available depend on current platform policies, the user's jurisdiction, and the account's eligibility status.

Poloniex operates as a cryptocurrency exchange, and the account features available to an individual depend on current platform policies, jurisdiction, and eligibility. For current account requirements and available features, Poloniex's official website and support documentation remain the appropriate references. Ultimately, the value of learning about verified accounts comes from developing skills that can be applied across digital finance. Call to Action Begin by choosing one topic to study, such as identity verification, account eligibility, transaction histories, or cryptocurrency terminology. Create a simple learning checklist that includes researching requirements, defining unfamiliar terms, organizing references, and reviewing what you have learned. title: Vercel Sandbox now runs on Vercel Managed Images
description:
Today we are introducing Vercel Managed Images (VMI), a set of versioned, open-source base images you can use as-is or extend. The source for every image lives in the public vercel/sandbox repository.

Managed images replace Sandbox runtimes, which are now deprecated. Starting with version 3 of the Sandbox SDK, new sandboxes default to vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. It ships with Node.js, Python, common coding agents and standard utilities, so most users never build a custom image or install packages at boot.

The universal image switches our default operating system from Amazon Linux to Ubuntu, a lighter and more widely used system across the industry.

Secure by default

Every managed image gets a nightly release. Rolling tags such as latest and the major-version tags pick up operating system and dependency updates automatically, including security patches and new releases of Node.js, Python, and the preinstalled coding agents.

Within each release, dependencies are pinned to specific versions wherever possible, so a given image version stays consistent.

If you need a fully immutable, reproducible environment, pin to an image digest (SHA). Digest-pinned images opt out of automatic updates.

Choose a managed image from the catalog

Each managed image targets a different starting point:

  • vercel/sandbox/universal:latest is the new default, a rolling release on Ubuntu 26.04 with Node.js 24, Python 3.14 with uv, the opencode, claude-code, codex, and pi coding agents, and utilities including git, vim, nano, tmux, ripgrep, jq, and fzf.

  • vercel/sandbox/node:22, node:24, and node:26 provide Node.js versions on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/python:3.14 provides Python on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/ubuntu:latest provides base Ubuntu 26.04 with no extra tooling.

  • vercel/sandbox/arch:latest provides Arch Linux, regularly updated, with no Node.js or Python preinstalled. Its large package repository makes it useful for agents that install tools on the fly.

Reference an image and migrate from runtimes

Sandboxes can use an image from any repository in your project, a repository which has been shared with your team or any public repository.

Images are addressed by their full path, team-slug/project/repo:tag, for example vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. The SDK types the image property so built-in images autocomplete while any string is still accepted. The previous runtime property is deprecated, not removed, so existing code keeps working.

Amazon Linux runtimes are not part of the managed image catalog, so teams that need AL2023 can stay on runtime. Managed images run as the default ubuntu or arch user with passwordless sudo, rather than the vercel-sandbox user.

Open an issue or a pull request to improve them, and read the Vercel Sandbox images documentation to get started.
