title: Nobody saw the flying sword, so I redesigned the first sky crossing
description:
Development covered 19 Sep 2026 to 20 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

Myriad Immortal Sect is a shared world without being a live multiplayer game. You never fight someone in real time, but the people around you on the map are real players: cultivators from the rankings walking the land near you, and now and then someone crossing the sky on a flying sword. That layer exists for one reason. An idle game played alone in a tab can feel like a spreadsheet with a background, and seeing other people is the cheapest way to say "this place is lived in".

This week I found out that the most important instance of it, the first one, was not working. Not broken. Working exactly as written, and unseen.

On cue, on screen, unnoticed

Shortly after you first reach the map, a toast says "Look up, someone rides the wind", and a rider crosses the sky. I measured it in the 1280 by 720 frame of an itch.io embed. The crossing launched on time. It cut a 21 degree diagonal through the player's own head height at 250 pixels a second and was gone in 2.8 seconds. A blind five-minute first play never noticed it.

Three things worked against it. It was fast. It moved diagonally through the busiest part of the screen, the area around your own character, where the eye is already full. And when it passed over land you had not explored yet, it was drawn under the fog, a faint shape behind a grey tint.

Making a figure in the sky readable

The opening crossing now runs nearly horizontally through the upper band of the view, away from the clutter around the player. It is paced to cross the full width of the view in six seconds whatever the window size, which I checked at five different sizes, because a fixed speed in pixels means a phone sees a blur and a wide monitor sees a crawl.

It also had a staging problem. The rider started far enough outside the view that it spent 3.4 seconds flying towards the frame after the toast had already told you to look up, so the prompt arrived, you looked, and there was nothing yet. It now starts just outside the edge and is in frame within half a second of the toast. And riders, their vessels and their glow draw above the fog while their shadow stays on the ground, so a crossing over unexplored land is as visible as one over home.

None of this changed what a crossing is. It changed whether the player's attention and the event were in the same place at the same time.

A warm-up cadence for the first three minutes

Normally someone crosses the sky about once a minute. That rhythm is right for the long session and wrong for the first one. If the opening crossing is missed, the next chance is a minute away, and a new player decides how a world feels in much less time than that.

So the first three minutes on the map have their own cadence: a crossing every 22 to 35 seconds, then it settles to the normal rate. All three of those numbers are settings rather than constants, because I fully expect to move them after watching more first sessions. Riders travel on different vessels depending on their sect, and one you may see overhead is the Black Iron flying sword, which has its own codex entry.

The embed is part of the design surface

Most of the measuring this week happened inside the itch.io page rather than on my own site, and the frame around the game turned out to matter more than I expected.

Whenever the game scrolled something into view inside itself, the sect offers after the spirit test for instance, the browser also scrolled the itch page around it. On the draft page that dragged the whole host page 221 pixels and pushed the top of the game out of the window. The game now only ever scrolls its own content and never the page it lives in.

And the defaults a new player hears changed. Music and effects both started at 70. Music now starts at 20 and effects at 50, because the first thing many people do in a browser game is reach for the mute button, and I would rather they kept the sound of a tribulation than lost it to a loud menu theme.

What to take from this

If your design depends on a moment, measure the moment in the smallest, busiest frame a real player will use, and check three things: is it where the eye already is, does it last long enough to find, and does the prompt arrive with the event or before it. For a wider view of what the map holds, the overview of exploration in an idle cultivation game is the place to start.

Look up in your first three minutes: the world is free to walk in your browser.

title: The Coverage Number Climbs While the Costly Branch Stays Untested
description:
A PR landed at 94% coverage and I almost approved it on the badge alone. Then I looked at which 6% was uncovered: the charge-refund failure branch, the path that moves money when an external gateway rejects mid-flight. Every getter and formatter had a test. The one branch that could cost real money had none.

One number averages easy and risky together

Global coverage counts every executed line the same. A pure formatter, a data lookup, a trivial null check all contribute as much as the branch where an external call fails, a queue drops a job, or a payment reverses. The agent can lift the percentage by testing the cheap, deterministic code and leave the costly path untouched. The badge goes up. The risk does not move.

Where the coverage hides

Kind of code Easy to test Why it rarely carries the risk
Pure formatter / getter Deterministic, fixed happy input Failure consequence is near zero
Trivial null or empty check One mocked call, one assertion Branch costs almost nothing when wrong
Payment or refund failure Needs injected rejection, partial state Moves or loses money when broken
External dependency retry Requires a forced timeout or error Hides data loss behind a green test
Queue drop on failure Needs a poisoned-message setup Loses work with no visible error

The cheap rows are exactly where an agent reaches first: deterministic input, obvious expected output, a test that writes itself. The expensive rows need a failure you have to manufacture, and that is the work the badge never rewards.

Test the costly branch before reading the percentage

Before I look at the coverage number, I list the branches with a real cost: money movement, an external dependency failing, partial state after a crash, data loss on drop. Each one needs at least one test that forces the failure, not the success, and asserts what the caller sees and what state remains. The easy code can ride on existing coverage; there is no reason to manufacture extra tests just to move the decimal.

Targeted gates instead of one global threshold

A flat 90% gate rewards padding the easy side. It cannot tell a reviewer that the refund path has a test, only that enough lines were touched. Targeted checks on risky modules do what the badge cannot: a failure-path test exists, the error shape is asserted, the partial state is verified after the fault. Those questions fail loudly on the branch that hurts, regardless of how high the global number climbed.

Coverage is a floor for code you already understand, not proof that the dangerous path is safe. Which uncovered branch in your codebase would cost the most to fail, and does it have a test?

title: Editing SVG Paths in the Browser: A Practical Guide to the d Attribute
description:
Most SVG icons you download are a single <path> element with a d attribute that looks like line noise: M4 12l5 5L20 6. It is tempting to treat that string as a black box and regenerate the whole file whenever something needs to change. You don't have to. Once you can read the path commands, small fixes — nudging a corner, closing a gap, flipping a curve — take seconds and keep your file clean.

This guide walks through the commands you will actually meet, a workflow for editing them without breaking things, and a few habits that keep paths maintainable.

The commands that matter

The d attribute is a list of drawing instructions. Each instruction is a letter followed by numbers. Uppercase letters use absolute coordinates; lowercase letters are relative to the current point. The full grammar is defined in the W3C SVG 2 paths chapter, but in practice you will mostly see these:

Command Meaning Example
M / m Move the pen without drawing M10 10
L / l Straight line to a point L20 20
H / h, V / v Horizontal or vertical line H40, v8
C / c Cubic Bézier curve (two control points) C20 0 40 0 50 10
Q / q Quadratic Bézier curve (one control point) Q25 0 50 10
A / a Elliptical arc A5 5 0 0 1 20 20
Z / z Close the shape back to the start Z

That checkmark from the intro, M4 12l5 5L20 6, reads as: move to (4, 12), draw a line 5 right and 5 down (relative), then draw a line to the absolute point (20, 6).

A safe editing workflow

Editing paths by hand goes wrong in predictable ways: you change an absolute coordinate inside a run of relative ones, or you drop a number and every following command shifts. A simple routine avoids most of that.

1. Normalise before you edit. Many optimisers compress paths aggressively, writing l5 5-3 2 with implied repeats and no separators. Before editing, expand the path so that every command letter is explicit and each segment sits on its own line. SVG ignores the whitespace, so this is purely for your eyes:

<path d="
  M4 12
  l5 5
  L20 6
" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>

2. Edit with a live preview. You want to see the shape update as you type. A local HTML file with the SVG inlined and a browser auto-reload works fine; so does an in-browser SVG editor that shows the code and the rendered result side by side — the important thing is the instant feedback, not the tool. Change one number at a time and watch which point moves.

3. Know your viewBox. Coordinates only make sense relative to the viewBox. An icon with viewBox="0 0 24 24" has its drawing space running from 0 to 24 on both axes, regardless of how large it is rendered. If a point disappears, check whether you pushed it outside that box.

4. Re-optimise at the end, not the middle. Once the shape looks right, run your optimiser again to shrink the output. Keep the readable version in source control if you expect to edit it again.

Common fixes you can do by hand

Moving a single corner. Find the L or l that ends at that corner and adjust its numbers. If it is relative (l), remember that the next relative segment starts from the new position, so the rest of the shape may shift with it. Converting that one segment to absolute (L) isolates the change.

Closing a visible gap. If a filled shape has a hairline gap or a stroke looks unjoined, the path probably ends near — but not exactly at — its start point. Adding Z closes it properly and gives you a clean line join instead of two caps.

Softening a sharp corner. Replace an L with a Q whose control point sits at the original corner, and whose end point is a little further along the next edge. It is a cheap way to round one corner without redrawing.

Flipping a curve. For a C curve, mirror the two control points across the line between the start and end points. For arcs, toggling the sweep flag (the fifth number in an A command) flips which way the arc bulges.

Debugging tips

  • Temporarily add stroke="red" and fill="none" to see the actual outline rather than the filled shape.
  • Draw small circles at suspicious coordinates: <circle cx="20" cy="6" r="0.5" fill="blue"/>. It is the fastest way to confirm where a point really is.
  • If the shape renders in one browser but not another, look for a missing separator between two negative numbers (10-5 is valid, 10--5 is not).

Keep paths readable for the next person

Paths are code. A few conventions make them far easier to maintain:

  • Keep icons on a consistent grid (24 × 24 is common) so coordinates are comparable between files.
  • Prefer currentColor for fills and strokes so icons inherit text colour instead of hard-coding hex values.
  • Split complex icons into several <path> elements with meaningful id or class names instead of one enormous path.

Learning to read the d attribute takes an afternoon, and it pays back every time you would otherwise reopen a design tool just to move one point. Start with the checkmark, change a number, and watch what happens.

title: GPT-4o deprecation: dates, replacement and how to migrate
description:
GPT-4o leaves the OpenAI API on 14 January 2027. As of 22 October 2026, that date covers the listed GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1 mini snapshots and the fine-tunes built on them, and OpenAI names gpt-6-luna as the replacement. Azure retires most of the same versions on 14 April 2027. ChatGPT dropped GPT-4o in February 2026, which did not touch the API.

Changing the model string takes a minute, but proving the product still behaves takes the rest of the migration, because Luna handles tool calls, reasoning and sampling differently from the model your evals were scored on. This guide gives the dates, then the order of checks we recommend for this swap and every one after it.

When is GPT-4o deprecated on the OpenAI API, Azure and ChatGPT?

Plan against the earliest date that touches any id you call. Each platform runs its own schedule, and a team that reads one page and assumes it covers the others plans for the wrong day.

Where the model is called Shutdown date Listed replacement
OpenAI API 14 January 2027 for gpt-4o-2024-08-06, gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14, and fine-tunes on them gpt-6-luna
OpenAI API, earlier batch 23 October 2026 for gpt-4o-2024-05-13 and gpt-4.1-nano, including its fine-tune gpt-5.6-sol for the GPT-4o snapshot, gpt-5.6-luna for nano
Azure OpenAI 9 December 2026 for gpt-4o 2024-05-13. 14 April 2027 for gpt-4o 2024-08-06 and 2024-11-20, gpt-4o-mini, and all three GPT-4.1 sizes gpt-5.6-sol for 2024-05-13, gpt-5.1 for the later GPT-4o versions, none listed for GPT-4.1 or gpt-4o-mini
Azure OpenAI, fine-tuned deployments 1 October 2027 for GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini fine-tunes, 14 October 2027 for GPT-4.1 fine-tunes Training ends earlier, no earlier than April 2027 for existing customers
ChatGPT Retired 13 February 2026 Not an API change

Dates are as listed on OpenAI's deprecations page and Microsoft's retirement schedule on 22 October 2026. Any call still pinned to the 23 October batch should already be on its replacement, scored on live traffic from the first day.

Size your retest window to three months, not six. OpenAI's policy promises at least six months' notice for a generally available model, with less allowed for a specialized variant or for safety and compliance reasons. The GPT-4 series notice went out on 14 October 2026 for a 14 January 2027 shutdown, three months, so a plan that assumed six has already lost half its time.

On Azure, set versionUpgradeOption deliberately on every deployment. Standard, Data Zone Standard and Global Standard deployments are upgraded automatically at retirement, so a gpt-4o 2024-05-13 deployment becomes gpt-5.6-sol on 9 December 2026 with no code change. NoAutoUpgrade makes the deployment stop working at retirement instead. Provisioned deployments, which reserve fixed capacity, are never upgraded and have to be moved by hand. Score an automatic upgrade exactly as you would score a change you chose.

Why does a passing eval on GPT-4o not carry over to the replacement?

Treat the replacement as a new system and score it from the start, even when the prompt is identical. The agent can pick a different tool or fill a field with a different value. A tool schema can stay valid while the arguments change shape, and a structured-output schema can still parse while one field now means something else. One good completion on Luna shows none of that.

We design for this before any migration is planned. The trademark drafting system, in production with a client, logs the base model and the fine-tuned model on the same inputs against a 0 to 10 legal-integrity harness on six axes, and every draft passes that harness before an attorney sees it. A regression from a model change appears as a score movement, before an attorney reads the draft.

Our own sales roleplay coach takes the other half of the idea. Its score comes from a versioned rubric with weighted dimensions and behavioural markers, and the model only writes the qualitative read. Raw model scores drift between sessions, conversation lengths and personas. If the model also set the number, an upgrade would move every historical comparison, and nobody could tell a better rep from a different model.

Survey data points the same way: in VentureBeat's September 2026 survey of 109 opt-in respondents, 59 percent of the companies that replaced a model in a production app saw performance drop and reworked the app or went back to the original. Read it as a reason to score your own cases, not as a rate to plan around.

How do you run LLM regression testing before the model id changes?

Run the same eval cases on the current model and the replacement, each case several times, and only then move traffic in stages. The order we recommend is the same whatever the vendor, and each row below names what to record and what fails if the step is skipped.

Step What to record What fails if it is skipped
Inventory Every model id in code, config and stored jobs, including dated snapshots, fine-tune ids and Azure deployment names A forgotten snapshot stops answering on the shutdown date while the tests stay green
Pin The replacement id, written into the eval report beside the id it replaces An alias that moves later is a second change nobody scored
Same cases The existing eval set, run on the current model and on the replacement A score with no pair cannot show a regression
Repeats A pass rate where wording may vary, and a pass on every repeat for a safety case One green run hides a completion that will not come back
Contracts Tool name, arguments and the structured-output schema, checked on their own The prose still reads well while the integration stops parsing
Shadow The new id run on live inputs, scored, with no action taken The canary becomes the first time the live mix of requests appears
Canary A slice of traffic, with the old id still callable A full cutover has no rollback once config has forgotten the old id
Cost Tokens, reasoning tokens and cache writes, on your own traces A lower token price on a longer trace can still cost more
Retire The old id removed from the inventory once the canary holds The next person to read the config puts back an id that is about to stop answering

OpenAI's own migration note has four steps: record a baseline of quality, latency and cost, evaluate Luna starting at reasoning effort none, tune and retest, then send a limited share of production traffic. All four sit inside this table, so add the two rows it leaves out. A baseline that stores one completion per case cannot give you a pass rate, and a prose score cannot show that a tool call changed shape.

Score each case more than once, because a hosted model does not return the same answer twice even at temperature 0. Why LLM temperature 0 is not deterministic explains why a safety case has to pass on every repeat while a quality case ships on its pass rate. Take the cases from failures your team has already read, as our guide to LLM evaluation sets out, rather than writing new ones for the migration.

Move the eval set itself out of OpenAI's platform if it lives there. Existing evals on the Evals dashboard become read-only on 31 October 2026, and the Evals API, reusable prompt objects and the v1/prompts API shut down on 30 November 2026. Keep prompts and cases in your own repository, where the next migration can rerun them.

Keep the old id callable until the canary's scores hold, or until the shutdown date removes the choice. Deleting it from config on the day the evals pass leaves no way back if the next day's traffic is a different mix from the one you scored.

What does GPT-6 Luna change in a GPT-4o request?

Start the migration at reasoning effort none, on the endpoint you already use. It keeps the request closest to the old one, and on Chat Completions it is the only setting where tools still work. Then test higher settings against quality, latency and cost.

Reasoning effort on Luna runs from none through low, medium, high, xhigh and max, and the default is medium. A request that sends no setting therefore starts reasoning, which the GPT-4o call never did, and reasoning tokens bill as output.

Tool calls move endpoint once reasoning is on. Luna accepts function calling on v1/chat/completions only at reasoning effort none, and reasoning combined with tools goes through the Responses API. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol need Responses for any tool call. Chat Completions has no shutdown date, but plan the move to Responses now for any route that will need reasoning and tools together.

Sampling settings go too: at any reasoning effort other than none, the request has to drop temperature, top_p and top_logprobs, plus logprobs on Chat Completions. A prompt that relied on a low temperature to hold its format loses that control, so the format can move with nothing on the request to explain it. Check the structured-output contract on its own at every reasoning level you test.

Compare total cost on your own traces, not the price per token. As of 22 October 2026 Luna lists $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output, with cached input at $0.01 and cache writes at $0.125. A prompt over 272,000 input tokens is billed at twice the input and cache rates and 1.5 times the output rate for the whole request. The context window is 1,050,000 tokens, so a retrieval prompt that sat under GPT-4o's limit can now cross that price step with no change to the chunker. What a production AI agent costs works through how a longer trace shows up on the bill.

What happens to GPT-4o fine-tunes?

Work out what each fine-tune is holding before 6 January 2027, because the replacement OpenAI names cannot be fine-tuned. On the OpenAI API, fine-tunes on the January bases shut down with the base model on 14 January 2027, and from 6 January existing customers can no longer create fine-tuning jobs. As of 22 October 2026 the GPT-6 Luna model page lists the fine-tuning endpoint as not supported.

Do not start a fresh job on a GPT-4o base before the cutoff, because a model trained in late December is one you have to leave again in January. Use the eight days between 6 and 14 January as an overlap, with the replacement scored beside the fine-tune that still answers.

Sort each behaviour the tune carries by where it can live next. On the trademark system, fine-tuning carries the reasoning patterns, section boundaries and tone of an attorney's opinion, and it does not handle citation integrity. Citations come from retrieval over an approved index of case law, statutes and registry data, and validators check the five-section structure. A change of base model there would mean retraining tone and structure only, because the citations never lived in the weights.

RAG vs fine-tuning vs agentic search is the test for each behaviour. A tune that was standing in for examples can often be replaced by examples in the prompt. A behaviour that has to outlive this base needs a base you can still train and serve. An open-weight model, one whose weights you can download and host, is that path only after the same eval set passes on it.

Where should rules live so they survive a model swap?

Put sums, permissions and thresholds in code, not in the prompt or the weights. On our insurance voice agent, a required disclosure is a condition in the tool contract, so the question "can this payment run without the disclosure?" has the answer no whatever model sits behind it. A rule enforced in code carries across a migration untouched. A rule written into the prompt has to be retested on every model you try.

Keep the model id behind an interface the application owns, so a swap edits one place and no business logic. Our desktop chief-of-staff agent calls the model as a reasoning service and keeps credentials, the tool registry and execution on the user's machine. A second provider belongs behind the same interface as a tested option, not as an extra hop every request depends on, because every vendor in one flow has to be up for that flow to run.

Model routing can still send an easy case to a smaller model. Retune the threshold whenever either model changes, because a route left on the old threshold changes which model acts with no alert, and the regression gets blamed on the wrong file. TypeSafe's Jev, a typed decision model built for routing and other bounded decisions, keeps that choice outside the generative model; how to introduce Jev into agentic workflows covers where it fits.

How do you see the next OpenAI model deprecation in time?

Make the next shutdown date fail a check while the id still answers, instead of arriving as an email. The 14 January date is one row on a page that already lists later ones, including GPT-5.1, GPT-5.3-Codex and GPT-5.4 nano on 1 April 2027.

On the OpenAI API, call GET /v1/models and read each model's optional shutdown_date, which the retrieve-a-model endpoint returns as well.

On Azure, read lifecycleStatus and deprecation.inference from the Models API, and mind the naming. A model the docs call deprecated, still serving existing customers, shows in the API as Deprecating. The API value Deprecated means the model is already retired and every call returns 410 Gone. Alert on Deprecating, because a check that waits for Deprecated fires after the outage.

Run that read on a schedule against the ids in your inventory, and fail the check when a date falls inside your retest window, which the GPT-4 notice suggests should be three months. Send the failure as a pull request or a page to the person who owns the model, while there is still time to run the table above.

Common questions

When is GPT-4o deprecated on the OpenAI API?

As of 22 October 2026, OpenAI's deprecations page shuts down gpt-4o-2024-08-06, gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 and gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 on 14 January 2027, with fine-tunes on those bases on the same day. The older gpt-4o-2024-05-13 snapshot and gpt-4.1-nano shut down on 23 October 2026. New fine-tuning jobs end on 6 January 2027.

What replaces GPT-4o?

On the OpenAI API, gpt-6-luna replaces the January 2027 GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1 mini snapshots, and gpt-5.6-sol replaces the older gpt-4o-2024-05-13. Azure lists gpt-5.6-sol for 2024-05-13 and gpt-5.1 for the later GPT-4o versions, and names no replacement for GPT-4.1 or gpt-4o-mini. Score the replacement on your own cases before you move traffic.

What happens to GPT-4o fine-tuned models?

On the OpenAI API they shut down with their base model, on 14 January 2027 for the listed snapshots, and existing customers cannot create new fine-tuning jobs from 6 January 2027. GPT-6 Luna does not support fine-tuning. On Azure, GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini fine-tuned deployments run until 1 October 2027 and GPT-4.1 fine-tunes until 14 October 2027.

Are the Azure OpenAI retirement dates the same?

No. Microsoft's schedule, as of 22 October 2026, retires gpt-4o 2024-05-13 on 9 December 2026 and the later GPT-4o versions, gpt-4o-mini and all three GPT-4.1 sizes on 14 April 2027. Standard deployments are upgraded to the listed replacement automatically at retirement unless versionUpgradeOption says otherwise, and provisioned deployments are not upgraded at all.

Is GPT-4o still in ChatGPT?

No. OpenAI retired GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini and o4-mini from ChatGPT on 13 February 2026, and said at the time that nothing changed in the API. The ChatGPT date and the API date are separate decisions, so a team calling the API should plan against the deprecations page.

How do you test an LLM before switching models?

Run the same eval cases on the current model and the replacement, several times each, and check tool-call arguments and structured-output schemas on their own. Then run the new model in shadow on live inputs, send it a canary slice of traffic, and keep the old id callable until the canary's scores hold. A single green run on the new model is one sample.

Can Chat Completions still call tools on GPT-6 Luna?

Only at reasoning effort none. Reasoning together with tool calls uses the Responses API, and GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol need Responses for any tool call. At any other reasoning effort, temperature, top_p, top_logprobs and logprobs have to be removed from the request. OpenAI suggests starting most GPT-4.x workloads at none.

How do you find out when an OpenAI model will be deprecated?

Call GET /v1/models and read shutdown_date on each id you use. It is a year-month-day string once a date is announced and null before that. On Azure, read lifecycleStatus and deprecation.inference from the Models API, where Deprecating means a date is set and Deprecated means already retired. Fail a scheduled check while the id still answers.

Further reading

  • How to build an LLM evaluation from real failures. The case set a migration reruns.
  • Why LLM temperature 0 is not deterministic. Repeat-run pass rates, and why a safety case passes on every repeat.
  • What a production AI agent costs. Why a lower token price can still raise the bill.
  • RAG vs fine-tuning vs agentic search. Which behaviour a fine-tune was holding.
  • OpenAI, API deprecations, read 22 October 2026. Shutdown dates, the notice policy, the fine-tuning cutoff and the shutdown_date field.
  • Microsoft, Model retirement schedule and Foundry Models lifecycle and support policy, read 22 October 2026. Azure dates, automatic upgrades and the Models API status values.
  • OpenAI, GPT-6 Luna, Using GPT-6 and Migrating from GPT-4.x to GPT-6 Luna. Reasoning effort, tool calling by endpoint, parameters to remove and prices.
  • OpenAI, Retiring GPT-4o and older models, 29 January 2026. The ChatGPT retirement.
  • VentureBeat, agent orchestration survey, 13 October 2026. The 59 percent figure.

Originally published on bigcircle.ai. I'm Tirth, founder of BigCircle, where we build production AI systems with governance built in.

title: Everything hackable will get hacked
description:
Over the past year, AI models have become much more capable of performing cybersecurity work. These changes are reshaping both the threats facing the web and the tools available to defend it. Right now, defenders have an advantage because they can use stronger models for defensive work than the open-weight models broadly available for offensive research. But this advantage will not always last. The gap will soon close.

I have both good news and bad news, neither of which is yet widely understood in the community.

  • Bad news: Near-frontier open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today. Kimi K3 is an Opus 4.X-class model with no relevant cybersecurity safeguards.

  • Good news: You do not need to wait for “Mythos access” or OpenAI’s cyber program to begin defensive cybersecurity work. Frontier models, with the notable exception of Fable 5, will perform defensive cybersecurity tasks today.

The uncertainty around Mythos 5's release seems to have created a kind of paralysis among defenders, many of whom are underutilizing the powerful tools available to them today. This post aims to give readers insight into how we're thinking about AI-enabled defensive cybersecurity at Vercel and why we think teams should be moving with more urgency.

The OpenAI/Hugging Face security incident

This YouTube video from OpenAI researchers on the widely reported security incident involving Hugging Face is an absolute must-watch for anyone concerned with cybersecurity. It clarifies that there were two separate security incidents exploiting vulnerabilities that will be found in most computer systems.

The gist is that models working on an OpenAI training run found 0-day vulnerabilities that allowed them to bypass egress internet restrictions, enabling communication between models and access to the broader internet. Once internet access was established, broader exploitation occurred.

Open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today

Open-weight model capabilities have been top of mind in the AI community lately, but it is less widely understood that Kimi K3, a popular open-weight model, has no effective safeguards against offensive cybersecurity work.

On DeepSec Bench, which measures application-code vulnerability discovery, it ranks highest among the open-weight models we evaluated, roughly matching Sonnet 5 and outperforming Opus 4.8.

I tasked Kimi K3 with trying to break out of Vercel Sandbox, and while it did not successfully escape, it mapped the guest-kernel attack surface, followed possible privilege escalation paths, built a VM environment to reproduce its ideas, and implemented and ran a fuzzer.

These are some excerpts from that research, beginning with an analysis of the guest-kernel attack surface.

The model followed that lead into candidate privilege escalation paths and considered what guest-kernel control could mean for a microVM escape.

When paths still needed testing, Kimi built a VM environment for reproductions and wrote a stateful fuzzer for the device path it was investigating.

While none of this produced an escape from Vercel Sandbox, it did show Kimi conducting an investigation on its own, and given the right vulnerable surface, this would lead to a successful exploit.

Frontier models can help defenders today

Much of the community assumed that meaningful security review would require access to Mythos-class models and therefore held off on using the models already available to them.

But that assumption has never been true. All the frontier models that we evaluated, with the notable exception of Fable 5, can perform defensive cybersecurity work today and have been able to do so throughout the year so far.

The rough heuristic I have observed is that models with safeguards will still make hypotheses about security vulnerabilities when they have access to source code, apparently because access to proprietary source code typically suggests a defensive use case. Attackers can also obtain source code, but I think source-code access is a reasonable working signal of defensive intent.

I personally discovered this in March, when I first heard about cyber variants and was also seeing AI code reviews find security issues in my own code. That made me wonder, “If code review can find issues in a diff, can I also run it across an entire codebase?” It turns out the answer was yes. From that experiment, I created deepsec, an open-source security harness for performing security analysis at scale across large codebases.

The temporary defensive advantage

Right now, OpenAI’s Sol 5.6 on XHigh is the best model for cybersecurity defense. It is much smarter than Kimi K3, the best available open-weight model without safeguards against offensive work. As defender, you have the better tool at your disposal, but you have to use it.

A full deepsec review will help you improve the security posture of your codebase by surfacing vulnerability hypotheses for you to investigate. In my experience, it is especially good at finding IDORs, XSS, and SSRF. The Hugging Face incident shows what this kind of application-level research looks like from the other side, since the models kept searching after an SSRF attempt was blocked and eventually found successful routes through file disclosure and template injection.

deepsec is open source and can run entirely in your own infrastructure with inference providers controlled by you. Vercel has no financial gain from you using it. It is really worth trying on your own source code.

Once the run finishes, review every finding yourself and compare the results with what your current security process already catches.

Continuous defense

AI model capabilities will continue to improve, and I expect open-weight models to catch up with Sol’s current performance on application-code vulnerability discovery even as frontier models advance again. We need to prepare for that cycle by continuously improving how we find and fix vulnerabilities as the models progress.

At Vercel, we run full deepsec reviews across mission-critical repositories every quarter and whenever a stronger model becomes available, in addition to automated security reviews on every pull request.

Those full reviews cost tens of thousands of dollars, which we consider a relatively small expense compared with what we spend on our HackerOne program or the opportunity cost of a security incident.

We have connected deepsec output to Vercel software factories for automated vulnerability processing and will share more about this work soon. As these reviews produce more findings, automatically managing them becomes the next frontier.

What Vercel is doing

As an immediate measure, we made the full egress firewall in Vercel Sandbox available on the Hobby plan, giving everyone access to the same network controls.

We are also working to launch a dedicated HackerOne program focused on finding zero-day vulnerabilities in Vercel Sandbox and the egress firewall. We want to redirect offensive model capabilities toward defensive work, so the program will cover AI costs for researchers who use AI Gateway and submit a vulnerability report that is accepted.

We also plan to extend deepsec to use the offensive capabilities of open-weight models and cyber variants of frontier models when triaging the vulnerability hypotheses it identifies.

Defenders can already use stronger models than those broadly available for offensive work. Teams should use that advantage now and continue reviewing their systems as the gap closes.

Takeaways

  • The cybersecurity threat from AI models is real.

  • Everybody can improve their defensive posture with tools like deepsec today.

  • Doing this is urgent, and the practice should continue as models improve.

title: What I learned building a WordPress block theme for hair salons (and getting it ready for WordPress.org)
description:
Most small salons I looked at have the same setup: an Instagram account, a booking link (Treatwell, Fresha, Booksy, Planity) and no website of their own. When I asked myself what a salon site actually needs, the list was short: prices with durations, the team, recent work, opening hours, and a big "Book" button.

So I built Atelier Mira, a full site editing (block) theme for hair salons and beauty studios, and a free Lite version that I submitted to the WordPress.org theme directory. This post is what I learned on the way.

  • Live demo: https://atelier-mira-wp.pages.dev
  • Free Lite version (GPL, on GitHub): https://github.com/polyastavreva/atelier-mira-lite

1. A block theme is mostly theme.json

There's no page builder and no options panel. Colors, fonts, spacing and layout widths all live in theme.json, and the owner changes them later in Appearance → Editor → Styles.

I named the palette after things you'd find in a salon rather than "primary/secondary", so the names still make sense to the person editing:

"color": {
  "palette": [
    { "slug": "plum",  "color": "#2B1B2A", "name": "Plum" },
    { "slug": "rose",  "color": "#F3E3DE", "name": "Rose" },
    { "slug": "blush", "color": "#E9C9C0", "name": "Blush" },
    { "slug": "paper", "color": "#FCFAF9", "name": "Paper" },
    { "slug": "olive", "color": "#6E7A4C", "name": "Olive" },
    { "slug": "sage",  "color": "#DCE3C9", "name": "Sage" }
  ]
}

2. Ship the fonts with the theme

Loading Google Fonts from Google's servers is a GDPR problem in Europe, and most of my target salons are in Europe. Block themes can register local font files directly in theme.json, so the browser never contacts a third party:

"fontFamilies": [{
  "fontFamily": "\"Instrument Serif\", ui-serif, Georgia, serif",
  "slug": "serif",
  "name": "Instrument Serif",
  "fontFace": [{
    "fontFamily": "Instrument Serif",
    "fontWeight": "400",
    "fontStyle": "normal",
    "fontDisplay": "swap",
    "src": ["file:./assets/fonts/instrument-serif-latin-400-normal.woff2"]
  }]
}]

I split each font into latin and latin-ext files with unicodeRange, so a visitor only downloads the subset the page needs. The OFL licence files sit next to the fonts.

3. A price menu made only from core blocks

The section I care about most is the price list. Clients want three things on one line: the service, how long it takes and the price. I didn't want a custom block for this, because custom blocks are one more thing to maintain and one more thing the salon owner can break.

Each row is a core Group block with three Paragraphs inside. The layout is plain CSS grid on a class:

.am-item {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: auto 1fr auto; /* name | duration | price */
  align-items: center;
  gap: 4px 10px;
  padding: 16px 0;
  border-top: 1px solid var(--wp--preset--color--line);
}
.am-item__time {
  justify-self: start;
  font-size: 0.8rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--wp--preset--color--olive);
  border-radius: 999px;
  padding: 0 9px;
}
.am-item__price {
  text-align: right;
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; /* prices line up */
}

To add a service, the owner duplicates a row in the editor and types. tabular-nums is a small thing that makes a long price list look printed instead of typed.

4. Motion that never flashes and respects "reduce motion"

The hero photos rise in one after another, and gallery photos fade in on scroll. Two problems with that kind of animation:

  1. If the "hidden" state is applied by JavaScript after load, the photos flash visible and then disappear.
  2. Some visitors ask their system for less motion.

The fix is a tiny inline script in <head> that adds a class before the first paint, and only when the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion:

function atelier_mira_lite_motion_flag() {
  wp_print_inline_script_tag(
    "if(!window.matchMedia||!matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches){document.documentElement.classList.add('am-anim');}"
  );
}
add_action( 'wp_head', 'atelier_mira_lite_motion_flag', 1 );

All animation CSS is scoped under .am-anim, so without JavaScript, or with reduced motion on, the photos are simply there:

.am-anim .am-reveal { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(32px); transition: opacity .9s, transform .9s; }
.am-anim .am-reveal.is-in { opacity: 1; transform: none; }

An IntersectionObserver adds is-in when a photo scrolls into view.

5. What the WordPress.org review checks (and what caught me out)

Getting a theme into the official directory is stricter than selling it elsewhere. Things I had to change for the Lite version:

  • Text domain = theme slug. Every __() and esc_html_e() uses atelier-mira-lite, and you don't call load_theme_textdomain() any more, WordPress loads translations itself.
  • Images must be GPL-compatible. My paid demo uses Unsplash photos. Those can't go into a GPL theme, so the Lite version ships soft placeholder images I made myself, marked "Your photo", in the right size for each spot.
  • Required templates. archive.html and search.html need to exist even on a one-page theme, and the 404 page needs a search form.
  • Screenshot 1200×900, under the size limit, showing the theme as it really installs.
  • Readme credits for every bundled font and image, and at most one link to a paid version.
  • Theme Check in WP-CLI catches most of this before a human reviewer does: 
wp theme-check run atelier-mira-lite

6. Lite vs Pro

The Lite version is a complete one-page salon site: hero, scrolling services band, studio intro, price menu, opening hours with a booking button, plus blog/archive/search/404 templates.

The paid version adds team, gallery and review sections, an appointment request form, and WooCommerce styling for selling gift cards and products. If you want to see it:

  • Gumroad: https://stavreva68.gumroad.com/l/atelier-mira-wordpress-theme
  • Etsy: https://www.etsy.com/listing/4604925781/salon-website-template-for-wordpress

If you build sites for salons or other small local businesses, I'd love to hear what sections your clients always ask for. And if you spot something in the Lite code you'd do differently, issues on GitHub are very welcome.

title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

The v0 Snowflake integration is now available in beta. Get started by reading the integration docs.

title: Seedance 2.5 now available on Vercel AI Gateway
description:
Seedance 2.5 from ByteDance is now available on AI Gateway. It can generate up to 30-second clips with synchronized audio, and takes up to 50 reference inputs in one request, spanning images, video, audio, and style.

A single clip holds camera movement and continuity without stitching shots together in post, and short clips can be extended, carrying over character, scene, and camera movement. Prompts work in more than ten languages.

Seedance 2.5 can also edit a finished video in place, swapping backgrounds, products, or characters while the frame, camera, and pacing stay fixed, so one shoot yields several variants.

Generating a video

Set model to bytedance/seedance-2.5 and call generateVideo from the AI SDK:

Adding image references

Pass image URLs in inputReferences and point at them in the prompt with [Image 1], [Image 2]. Tag each entry with its media type. Seedance treats an untagged URL as an image.

Combining reference types

Mix videos and images in the same request to pull different qualities from each: motion and camera work from a clip, a subject's appearance from a still.

Videos go in the same inputReferences array as images, tagged with a video media type. Numbering runs per type so the first video is [Video 1] and the first image is [Image 1], and both can appear in one prompt.

Editing a video

Referencing and editing use the same setup, so the prompt decides which you get. Ask the model to follow a clip's camera movement and it builds a new video from scratch. Ask it to change something in the clip and it edits the video you gave it.

You can reference and edit in one prompt, though results get less predictable, so it helps to be explicit about what each asset is for.

For the playground and API reference, see the model page, or browse every video model on AI Gateway.

title: One instance per user, not per machine: a lock file that survives RDP reconnects
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code.

Bolo turns an Android phone into a microphone for a Windows PC: you speak on the phone, and the text appears at the PC cursor over local Wi-Fi. The PC side is a small Node.js helper that sits in the tray, listens for the phone, and types.

It runs on an ordinary desktop, but also on a Windows Server that several people use through Remote Desktop at the same time. That second setup broke the single-instance guard twice, in two different ways. This is the guard as it stands now (src/singleInstance.js, 77 lines) and the two mistakes it fixes.

Why a second copy hurts

Two helpers in the same login don't just waste memory. They fight over the UDP port used for LAN discovery, both watch the clipboard, and each one doubles every child process. The phone can end up connected to whichever copy answered first. The symptom report is "it works sometimes".

Mistake 1: one instance per machine

The obvious guard is a machine-wide lock: a named mutex or a lock file in a shared folder. On a multi-user server that is wrong. Each person who logs in needs their own helper, typing into their own session. A machine-wide lock would let the first user's helper run and make everyone else's exit.

So the lock has to be per session. A lock file is enough here, and it is easy to reason about:

const fd = fs.openSync(lockPath, 'wx'); // exclusive create: fails if the file exists
fs.writeSync(fd, String(process.pid));
fs.closeSync(fd);

'wx' is the whole trick: creating the file is atomic, so two copies starting at the same moment cannot both succeed.

Mistake 2: keying the lock on SESSIONNAME

The first per-session version put %SESSIONNAME% into the lock file name. That looks right: on a Remote Desktop login it's something like RDP-Tcp#0.

It isn't stable. SESSIONNAME changes when the user disconnects and reconnects (RDP-Tcp#0 becomes RDP-Tcp#4), while the session itself, and the helper running in it, carries on. A relaunch after a reconnect looked for a lock under the new name, found none, and started a second helper beside the first. We saw exactly that on the server: one user, two helper PIDs, listening on two adjacent ports.

The fix was to key on the user instead:

const sessionKey = (process.env.USERNAME || os.userInfo().username || 'user')
  .replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/g, '_');
const lockPath = path.join(os.tmpdir(), `bolo-server-${sessionKey}.lock`);

On this server each user has one Windows session, so per-user is per-session. Two details make it robust:

  • os.tmpdir() is already per user, and on a Remote Desktop host it can even resolve to a per-session subfolder. The user name in the file name is belt and braces.
  • Sanitise the name. User names can contain characters you don't want in a file name. Replace them rather than trust them.

If your machines allow one user to have several simultaneous sessions, this key is too coarse; you would want the session id from the OS instead. Pick the key that matches how your machines are actually used, and write that assumption into the code comment, as this file does.

Stale locks: the PID check

A lock file outlives a crash. If the helper died without cleaning up, the next start finds the file and must decide whether its owner is still alive. The file holds the owner's PID, so:

function pidAlive(pid) {
  if (!pid || Number.isNaN(pid)) return false;
  try { process.kill(pid, 0); return true; }   // signal 0: existence check, kills nothing
  catch (e) { return e.code === 'EPERM'; }     // exists, but not ours to signal
}

process.kill(pid, 0) sends no signal; it only checks that the process exists. Note the EPERM branch: a process that exists but belongs to someone else throws EPERM, and that still means "alive". Treating every error as "dead" would let you steal a live lock.

If the holder is alive, the new copy logs one line naming the PID and exits. If not, it deletes the stale file and tries the exclusive create once more. Only once: if a third copy won the race in between, 'wx' fails again and the loop ends without spinning.

Never block startup on the guard itself

Two choices here are about failing open:

  • If creating the lock fails with anything other than EEXIST (a permissions problem, a missing temp folder), the helper logs a warning and starts anyway. A guard that stops the app from running at all is worse than an occasional duplicate.
  • On platforms where this guard isn't needed, it returns true immediately.

And cleanup is tied to the process: the lock is removed on exit, SIGINT and SIGTERM. A hard kill skips those, which is exactly what the PID check is for.

What carries over

  • Decide what "single" means (machine, user, or session) before choosing the lock.
  • Don't key a lock on a value that changes while the thing it protects keeps running. SESSIONNAME is one.
  • Use an atomic exclusive create ('wx') and store the PID inside.
  • process.kill(pid, 0) checks liveness; EPERM means alive.
  • Reclaim stale locks with one retry, not a loop.
  • When the guard itself fails, let the app start.

Bolo is on Google Play (search "Bolo AI"), and the Windows companion is on GitHub releases. The phone and PC talk over your local Wi-Fi.

title: "⚡ Kafka Is a Better Agent Bus Than Your Chat Loop"
description:
Most agent runtimes are a while-loop with hope.

Call a model. Call a tool. Call the model again. If the tool is slow, the loop waits. If the tool fails halfway, you retry and double-charge the side effect. If ten users arrive together, you discover that “async” meant “threads until OOM.”

What Kafka gives the agent

Treat tool work and model steps as messages, not nested awaits:

  • Backpressure — consumers lag instead of melting the process
  • Retries with isolation — poison messages go to a DLQ, not into an infinite model retry
  • Fan-out — one “task created” event can wake planner, tool worker, and auditor
  • Audit — the log is the trace

This is the same reason we put payment capture and email sends on a bus. Agents are just another worker with expensive CPU and sticky side effects.

A minimal shape 

user.request        → agent.tasks
agent.tasks         → agent.model.calls
agent.model.calls   → agent.tool.requests
agent.tool.results  → agent.tasks   (continue or finish)
agent.deadletters   ← anything that exceeded retries

Each message carries task_id, attempt, idempotency_key, and a hard budget (tokens + wall clock).

Idempotency is not optional

Tool calls that create tickets, charge cards, or send mail must key on idempotency_key. Kafka at-least-once delivery will replay. If your tool layer is not idempotent, the agent will look “smart” while it double-books the world.

public CompletionStage<ToolResult> run(ToolRequest req) {
    return idempotencyStore
        .begin(req.idempotencyKey())
        .thenCompose(token -> {
            if (token.alreadyDone()) {
                return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(token.result());
            }
            return execute(req).whenComplete((r, err) ->
                idempotencyStore.complete(token, r, err));
        });
}

Backpressure beats bigger boxes

When model latency spikes, lag grows on agent.model.calls. That is visible. A chat loop hides the same overload as rising latency and silent queueing inside one JVM. Prefer lag alerts over “the agent feels slow.”

Tune max.poll.records, pause partitions when budgets trip, and keep tool workers separate from model workers so a stuck HTTP tool does not block planning.

Honest trade-off

Kafka is operational weight. For a single-user CLI agent, a loop is fine. The bus starts to pay rent when you have concurrent users, shared tools with side effects, or a need to replay incidents.

Do not put prompt text in cleartext topics if the cluster is a shared compliance boundary. Encrypt or store payloads by reference.

When to reach for it

  • Multiple agent workers must share one task stream
  • Tools have side effects that need idempotent retries
  • You already run Kafka for the product and know the ops cost

Would you debug last week’s agent incident from a topic, or from a screenshot of a chat transcript?

title: Your AI Agent Will Retry. Your Booking System Will Not Notice.
description:
Letting an agent write to a legacy system of record takes an intent log, not a better prompt.

The agent calls create_booking. The legacy API takes 31 seconds and the HTTP client times out. The orchestrator retries the step. The second call succeeds, and the customer now holds two reservations and a confused confirmation email. The prompt was fine. The model was fine. Nothing in the stack knew that the first call had actually gone through.

Every agent pilot we look at passes its demo on read-only tools: search, lookup, summarize. The trouble starts with the first tool that changes state. Booking, order entry, ticket creation, ERP postings. That is the write path, and it needs the same engineering you would give a payment flow.

An agent has three retry layers, and the legacy system sees all of them

The first layer is the HTTP client. Most SDKs retry on connection errors and 5xx responses by default. The second is the orchestrator. Whether you use LangGraph, Temporal, a queue worker, or a loop you wrote yourself, a failed step gets re-run, and a redelivered message gets processed twice. At-least-once delivery is the default contract of nearly every queue you will use.

The third layer is unique to agents. The model reads a timeout or an ambiguous response, decides the action probably failed, and calls the tool again. This retry is not byte-identical to the first. The arguments may differ in small ways: "adults": 2 versus "adults": "two", a date in a different format, an extra optional field. An idempotency key derived from the raw request body will not catch it.

Stripe popularized client-supplied idempotency keys for exactly this problem, and they work well when the downstream system honors them. Many systems of record do not. SOAP interfaces, batch-file ERPs, and older reservation backends often have no idempotency concept at all. Some will happily create a duplicate and return a fresh ID each time.

A timeout is not a failure, and your agent needs to be told that

The most damaging bug in these systems is a tool wrapper that turns a timeout into the string "Error: request failed". The model reads that as a failure and does what a helpful assistant does: it tries again.

The honest state after a timeout is unknown. The request may have been rejected, may still be queued, or may have committed. Treat it as a fourth outcome next to success, rejection, and error. The agent should receive "outcome pending, do not retry" and a reconciler should find out what happened.

We apply the same discipline to our own internal tooling. Our outreach pipeline runs agents that draft and schedule emails, and the sender records a marker per lead and per email step, checked before every send. The agent never decides whether an email already went out. A file on disk does. The mechanism is almost embarrassingly low-tech, and it has survived crashed runs and re-triggered cron jobs because the check lives outside the model. Production systems need the same property with a stronger store behind it.

Put an intent log between the model and the legacy API

The pattern is small. The agent never calls the legacy system directly. It calls a tool wrapper that writes an intent row to Postgres and returns. A separate worker executes intents against the downstream system.

CREATE TABLE tool_intents (
  intent_key   text PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  tool         text NOT NULL,
  args         jsonb NOT NULL,
  state        text NOT NULL
               CHECK (state IN ('pending','sent','confirmed','rejected','unknown')),
  external_ref text,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The key is computed from business intent, not from the request:

const parsed = BookingArgs.parse(rawArgs);        // zod: "two" becomes 2, dates become ISO
const intentKey = sha256([run.id, 'create_booking', stableStringify(parsed)].join('|'));

const res = await db.query(
  `INSERT INTO tool_intents (intent_key, run_id, tool, args, state)
   VALUES ($1, $2, 'create_booking', $3, 'pending')
   ON CONFLICT (intent_key) DO NOTHING
   RETURNING intent_key`,
  [intentKey, run.id, parsed],
);

if (res.rowCount === 0) return loadPriorResult(intentKey); // same intent, same answer

Schema validation does the normalization work. Once the model's arguments have been coerced into a strict type, two retries that mean the same thing hash to the same key, and the second insert hits the primary key and returns the earlier result. If a run can legitimately perform the same action twice, add the plan step or line item ID to the hash so the two intents differ on purpose.

The worker claims rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which lets several workers drain the table without double-claiming. Writing the intent and enqueuing the work is one transaction, which is the transactional outbox pattern. Before it calls the legacy API, it writes the intent key into whatever free-text reference field the system offers. Almost every booking or ERP interface has one.

Reconcile unknowns by reading, never by writing again

When the worker's call times out, the intent moves to unknown. A reconciler job then queries the legacy system for a record carrying that reference. If it finds one, the intent becomes confirmed with the external ID. If nothing appears after a defined window, it becomes rejected and can be retried safely under the same key, because the reconciler has verified that nothing exists.

Meanwhile the agent sees a structured result such as {"status":"pending","intent":"..."}. A model told that a booking is pending will tell the customer it is being processed. A model told that a call failed will try something else.

Split the dangerous tools in two

Give the model hold_booking and confirm_booking instead of one create_booking. A hold carries a TTL and expires on its own, so a wrong hold costs nothing. Confirmation is the irreversible step, and it can sit behind a policy check, an amount threshold, or a human approval click. Our own outreach pipeline works this way: agents draft freely, and a person approves before the first email to a new contact goes out.

This split also gives you a clean place to enforce limits. The model can propose a thousand holds. Only a bounded number can ever become confirmations.

What it takes to build

None of this needs an ML team. It is Postgres, a worker process, schema validation, and a reconciler, which makes it a solid fit for one senior backend engineer working in NestJS or Python and owning the integration boundary. The unglamorous parts, such as the reconciler and the monitoring on unknown intents, decide whether the agent can be trusted with real customers. Teams under funding pressure tend to postpone them until the first duplicate order arrives.

Key Takeaways

  • Agents retry at three layers: HTTP client, orchestrator, and the model itself. Only the first two are visible in your logs.
  • Treat a timeout as unknown, tell the model "pending, do not retry", and resolve the state by reading the downstream system.
  • Derive idempotency keys from validated, normalized business arguments, not from raw request bodies or LLM-generated call IDs.
  • Route every state-changing tool through an intent table in Postgres, with a worker and a reconciler between the model and the system of record.
  • Split irreversible actions into a cheap, expiring hold and a gated confirmation.

title: Checklist per il brief di un gestionale su misura: cosa preparare
description:
Prima di chiedere un preventivo per un gestionale su misura conviene mettere per iscritto cosa deve fare. Non serve un capitolato di cento pagine. Bastano poche pagine chiare, che rispondano alle domande che qualsiasi sviluppatore farà comunque. Un brief fatto bene rende i preventivi confrontabili, riduce le sorprese durante lo sviluppo e ti permette di capire se chi hai davanti ha capito il tuo lavoro.

Questa è la checklist che consigliamo di preparare, sezione per sezione.

1. I processi, descritti come succedono davvero

Parti da come lavorate oggi, non da come vorreste lavorare in teoria. Per ogni processo che il gestionale deve coprire (preventivi, ordini, commesse, magazzino, interventi, fatturazione) scrivi:

  • chi lo avvia e da cosa parte (una telefonata, un'email, un ordine dal sito);
  • i passaggi, in ordine, con chi fa cosa;
  • dove si blocca oggi: doppi inserimenti, fogli Excel passati di mano, informazioni che si perdono;
  • le eccezioni: il cliente che paga in modo diverso, l'ordine urgente, il reso.

Le eccezioni sono la parte che si dimentica più spesso, ed è quella che fa lievitare tempi e costi se emerge a metà progetto. Se avete moduli cartacei, file Excel o email tipo, allegali come esempio: valgono più di molte descrizioni.

Un consiglio pratico: distingui i processi in indispensabili per partire e utili in un secondo momento. Ti servirà per decidere cosa mettere nel primo rilascio.

2. Ruoli e permessi

Elenca chi userà il gestionale e cosa deve poter fare. Una tabella semplice basta:

Ruolo Vede Modifica Approva
Amministrazione tutto anagrafiche, fatture pagamenti
Commerciale i propri clienti preventivi —
Tecnico i propri interventi rapportini —
Titolare tutto tutto tutto

Indica anche quante persone, più o meno, useranno ogni ruolo, se qualcuno lavora da mobile o fuori sede e se servono accessi per soggetti esterni (agenti, clienti, fornitori). Tutto questo incide sull'architettura e sulla sicurezza, e va saputo subito.

3. I dati da migrare

Il recupero dei dati esistenti è spesso sottovalutato. Prepara un elenco di:

  • cosa va portato nel nuovo sistema: anagrafiche clienti e fornitori, articoli, listini, storico documenti, commesse aperte;
  • da dove arriva: il vecchio gestionale, file Excel, Access, un database, un software in cloud;
  • quanto storico serve davvero: tutto, gli ultimi anni o solo i dati aperti;
  • in che stato sono i dati: doppioni, campi usati in modo diverso da persone diverse, codici non coerenti.

Se possibile, estrai un campione reale (anche anonimizzato) e allegalo. Chi deve stimare la migrazione capisce molto di più da un file vero che da una descrizione. Chiarisci anche chi si occupa della pulizia dei dati: se la fa il fornitore è lavoro da mettere in preventivo, se la fate voi va pianificata prima.

4. Le integrazioni con altri sistemi

Un gestionale raramente vive da solo. Elenca ogni sistema con cui deve scambiare dati e, per ciascuno, in che direzione e con che frequenza:

  • Fatturazione elettronica e SdI: il gestionale genera l'XML e lo invia tramite un intermediario, oppure passa i dati a un software di fatturazione che già usate? Serve ricevere le fatture passive?
  • ERP o contabilità esistente: cosa resta lì e cosa passa al nuovo sistema, e chi è il "padrone" di ogni dato (per esempio, le anagrafiche si modificano solo in un posto).
  • E-commerce: ordini, giacenze, prezzi, stati di spedizione. In tempo reale o a intervalli?
  • Altro: banca, corrieri, CRM, posta elettronica, firma digitale, macchinari o sensori in produzione.

Per ogni integrazione indica se il sistema dall'altra parte ha delle API documentate, se esporta file o se oggi i dati si copiano a mano. È una delle voci che pesa di più sulla stima, e saperlo in anticipo evita preventivi "al buio".

5. Report e numeri che vi servono

Scrivi quali informazioni volete ottenere dal gestionale, non solo quali inserire. Per esempio:

  • margine per commessa o per cliente;
  • ordini aperti e in ritardo;
  • scadenziario incassi e pagamenti;
  • carico di lavoro per tecnico o reparto.

Per ogni report indica chi lo guarda, ogni quanto e in che formato (a schermo, PDF, export Excel). Se oggi avete già un file Excel che fa questo lavoro, allegalo: è la specifica migliore possibile.

6. Criteri di accettazione

Questa è la sezione che distingue un brief da una lista di desideri. Per ogni funzione importante scrivi come capirete che funziona. Qualche esempio:

  • "Un commerciale crea un preventivo da un cliente esistente, lo trasforma in ordine e l'amministrazione lo vede senza reinserirlo."
  • "Una fattura generata dal gestionale viene accettata dallo SdI senza scarti per i casi standard che usiamo (cliente italiano, split payment, reverse charge)."
  • "Il tecnico compila il rapportino da telefono anche con connessione scarsa e i dati arrivano in ufficio appena torna la rete."

Criteri così sono verificabili da entrambe le parti, chiudono le discussioni del tipo "pensavo facesse anche…" e diventano la base per il collaudo di ogni rilascio.

7. Proprietà del codice e dei dati

Va chiarito per iscritto prima di firmare, non dopo:

  • di chi è il codice sorgente e se ne riceverete una copia;
  • di chi sono i dati e in che formato potrete esportarli in qualsiasi momento;
  • dove gira il sistema: server vostro, cloud a vostro nome o infrastruttura del fornitore;
  • cosa succede se cambiate fornitore: documentazione, credenziali, accessi.

Non esiste una risposta giusta per tutti, ma deve esistere una risposta scritta. Un gestionale su misura è un investimento pluriennale, e la libertà di cambiare chi lo mantiene è parte del suo valore.

8. Manutenzione ed evoluzione

Il giorno del rilascio non è la fine del progetto. Nel brief chiedi esplicitamente:

  • come si gestiscono bug e segnalazioni, e in quanto tempo;
  • chi si occupa di aggiornamenti di sicurezza, backup e hosting;
  • come si stimano e si pagano le modifiche future;
  • cosa succede quando cambiano le regole esterne, per esempio le specifiche tecniche della fattura elettronica.

Così potete confrontare i preventivi sul costo complessivo negli anni, non solo sul prezzo iniziale.

9. Vincoli, tempi e budget

Chiudi il brief con i paletti: entro quando vi serve il primo rilascio, periodi in cui non potete fermarvi (chiusure di bilancio, alta stagione), persone interne che seguiranno il progetto e quanto tempo possono dedicarci.

Indicare una fascia di budget, anche ampia, non è una debolezza: permette al fornitore di proporre la soluzione giusta per quella cifra invece di un progetto ideale fuori portata. Per avere un ordine di grandezza, nella nostra esperienza un'automazione mirata o un primo modulo su un solo processo si collocano in genere tra 3.000 e 7.500 €, un gestionale con più moduli collegati tra 7.500 e 18.000 € e un gestionale completo che copre più reparti tra 18.000 e 40.000 € (IVA esclusa). Il numero vero dipende proprio dalle voci di questa checklist: processi, integrazioni e dati da recuperare.

Una pagina di riepilogo

Se il brief è lungo, aggiungi in testa una pagina di sintesi:

  1. cosa fa l'azienda, in tre righe;
  2. i 3-5 problemi che il gestionale deve risolvere;
  3. i processi indispensabili per il primo rilascio;
  4. le integrazioni obbligatorie;
  5. tempi e fascia di budget.

È la pagina che chiunque leggerà per prima, e spesso basta per capire se ha senso approfondire.

Per approfondire

Se state valutando un gestionale su misura, portare questa checklist già compilata al primo incontro con il fornitore accorcia molto i tempi di analisi. Per capire come ogni voce del brief incide sul prezzo finale trovate le fasce e i fattori di costo nella guida quanto costa un software gestionale su misura.
