title: Check which websites use Shopify, WordPress or Klaviyo from a list of URLs
description:
Disclosure: I built the tech-stack detector used in the second half of this post, and I earn money when people run it. The DIY version in the first half is free and is all some people need.

You have a list of domains, maybe a lead list or a set of competitors, and you want to know which are Shopify stores, which run WordPress, and who uses Klaviyo for email marketing. The Wappalyzer and BuiltWith browser extensions answer that for one site at a time. For 500 sites you want a script.

The DIY version (works from your laptop)

Most platforms leave fingerprints in the homepage HTML, and Shopify also has a recognisable IP range:

import re
import socket
import urllib.request

SIGNS = {
    "Shopify": r"cdn\.shopify\.com|Shopify\.theme",
    "WordPress": r"/wp-content/|/wp-includes/",
    "Klaviyo": r"static\.klaviyo\.com|klaviyo\.com/onsite",
}


def quick_check(domain):
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"https://{domain}", headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"})
    html = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15).read().decode("utf-8", "ignore")
    found = [name for name, pattern in SIGNS.items() if re.search(pattern, html)]
    if "Shopify" not in found and socket.gethostbyname(domain).startswith("23.227.38."):
        found.append("Shopify")  # Shopify's storefront IP range
    return found


for d in ["allbirds.com", "colourpop.com", "techcrunch.com"]:
    print(d, quick_check(d))

Run from my home connection:

allbirds.com ['Shopify']
colourpop.com ['Shopify', 'Klaviyo']
techcrunch.com ['WordPress']

That's genuinely useful, and if it covers your case, stop here. The problems start when you scale it:

  1. Shopify stores rate-limit cloud IPs. Run the same code from a server or a cloud function and many stores answer HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Your regex then sees an error page and finds nothing.
  2. You need many more rules. Real lists contain Webflow, Wix, Squarespace, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, Magento, HubSpot, Mailchimp, Gorgias, Yotpo and dozens more, each with its own fingerprints and false positives.
  3. Some of the best signals aren't in the HTML. The company's email provider (Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365) lives in DNS MX/SPF records, and so do verification records for tools like Salesforce or Atlassian.
  4. Concurrency, timeouts, redirects and dead domains all need handling.

The hosted version

I packaged a bigger version of this (about 180 rules plus DNS checks) as an Actor on Apify. You send it domains, URLs or even work email addresses, and get one row per site with lead-friendly columns (cms, ecommercePlatform, emailProvider, cdn...) plus the full technology list.

pip install apify-client pandas
export APIFY_TOKEN=your_token_here   # Apify Console > Settings > API & Integrations

import os

import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

websites = [
    "allbirds.com",
    "colourpop.com",
    "techcrunch.com",
    "wordpress.org",
    "hubspot.com",
]


def detect(sites, proxy=None):
    run_input = {"websites": sites, "includeDns": True}
    if proxy:
        run_input["proxyConfiguration"] = proxy
    run = client.actor("zahidthani/website-tech-stack-detector").call(
        run_input=run_input, max_total_charge_usd=0.05
    )
    # apify-client 3.x returns a Run object; 1.x and 2.x return a dict
    dataset_id = getattr(run, "default_dataset_id", None) or run["defaultDatasetId"]
    return list(client.dataset(dataset_id).iterate_items())


items = detect(websites)

# Sites that block cloud IPs (many Shopify stores do) come back free and flagged.
# Re-check just those through residential proxies for a full page scan.
blocked = [it["input"] for it in items if it.get("pageBlocked")]
if blocked:
    print("re-checking via residential proxy:", blocked)
    retry = detect(blocked, {"useApifyProxy": True, "apifyProxyGroups": ["RESIDENTIAL"]})
    items = [it for it in items if not it.get("pageBlocked")] + retry

rows = []
for it in items:
    if it["type"] != "website":
        print("could not analyse:", it["input"], it.get("error"))  # dead domains are free
        continue
    names = {t["name"] for t in it["technologies"]}
    rows.append({
        "domain": it["domain"],
        "cms": it["cms"],
        "ecommerce": it["ecommercePlatform"],
        "shopify": "Shopify" in names,
        "wordpress": "WordPress" in names,
        "klaviyo": "Klaviyo" in names,
        "email": it["emailProvider"],
        "cdn": it["cdn"],
        "blocked": it.get("pageBlocked", False),
    })

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df.to_string(index=False))
df.to_csv("tech_stack.csv", index=False)

# Every technology found, one row per site + technology (handy for pivots)
long = pd.DataFrame(
    [{"domain": it["domain"], **t} for it in items if it["type"] == "website" for t in it["technologies"]]
)
print(long.groupby("category")["name"].unique().head(12))

Tested with Python 3.12 and apify-client 3.2.1.

Real output

From a run on 6 October 2026. In the first pass, both Shopify stores answered Apify's datacenter IPs with HTTP 429 (exactly problem 1 above). They still came back as Shopify, from the DNS A record, and weren't charged. The script then re-checked those two through residential proxies and got the full pages:

domain cms ecommerce shopify wordpress klaviyo email provider cdn
techcrunch.com WordPress False True False Microsoft 365
wordpress.org WordPress False True False
hubspot.com HubSpot CMS False False False Google Workspace Cloudflare
colourpop.com Shopify True False True Cloudflare
allbirds.com Shopify True False False Microsoft 365 Cloudflare

The long table (one row per site and technology) is where it gets interesting for lead research. Across these five sites it found, among others: Klaviyo, Gorgias and Zendesk (support), Yotpo and Okendo (reviews), Klarna, OneTrust (cookie consent), Microsoft Clarity, Google Tag Manager, Mimecast (email security), Amazon Route 53 and Cloudflare DNS, and verified SaaS accounts such as Atlassian, DocuSign, Zoom and Stripe from DNS TXT records.

Filtering a real lead list is then plain pandas:

shopify_without_klaviyo = df[df["shopify"] & ~df["klaviyo"]]

(On this sample that's allbirds.com. Note that "not detected on the homepage" is not proof they don't use it.)

What it costs

$2 per 1,000 websites analysed + $0.0005 per run. Dead domains, error pages and blocked sites are free, which is why the first pass here charged only 3 of the 5 sites. This whole example cost about $0.01. Apify's free plan includes $5 of monthly credit, so you can check a couple of thousand domains before paying anything.

Limitations

  • Homepage + DNS only. Tools that only load on the cart, checkout or after login won't show up. Pass a specific URL if you care about a particular page.
  • No history. It tells you what a site uses now, not when they adopted it. BuiltWith's paid database is the tool for historical data and huge coverage.
  • Absence isn't proof. Sites can load tools through a tag manager after consent, which a single page load may not trigger.
  • Residential proxies depend on your Apify plan. If a re-check can't use them, you still get the free DNS-only row (platform by IP, email provider, CDN).
  • Use it on business domains, for prospecting or market research. If you paste work emails, only the domain is used.

Try it

Website Tech Stack Detector on the Apify Store: https://apify.com/zahidthani/website-tech-stack-detector

Runnable Python, Node.js and n8n examples: https://github.com/zahidthani/apify-data-tools-examples

title: Q&A over internal documents: make the system say "not in the docs"
description:
An assistant that answers questions about your documents will be wrong sometimes. What destroys trust is not the wrong answer, it is the confident wrong answer to a question the documents never covered. So the first design question is not "how good is retrieval?" but "when does the system refuse?"

Here is a small demo that treats refusal as a first-class result. The data is public and the numbers are test numbers, not a client result.

What the demo does

One function, KB.answer(question), returns three things: the best passage as the citation, a confidence that it really holds the answer, and a decision: cite it, or refuse.

It deliberately returns the passage, not a generated sentence. Generating prose on top of a cited passage is the step that needs a language model; the part that decides whether to answer at all does not.

  • Data: SQuAD 2.0 dev (Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0), 35 articles. Wikipedia stands in for a company's documentation.
  • Retrieval: BM25.
  • Decision: a small model over retrieval features: the top score, its margin over the runner-up, IDF-weighted coverage of the question's terms, and the share of terms the passage doesn't know.
  • Threshold: tuned on separate articles for a 95% precision target.
  • No LLM, no GPU.

Evaluating without leaking

Articles are split into a tuning set and a test set. A third of the test articles are deliberately left out of the knowledge base, and their questions must be refused. Without that group you only measure how well the system answers questions it was built for, which is the easy case.

Results (test KB: 406 passages, 4,904 questions)

Case Result
Question about a topic NOT in the base refused correctly in 96.1%
Answerable question: right passage in top-3 87.8% (top-1: 75.3%)
Answerable question: cited with confidence 61.2% of questions, 93.2% of those cited point to the right passage
Answerable plus out-of-base, overall 42.5% cited, 90.4% of cited are correct

The refusal rate on out-of-base questions is the number I would put in an acceptance document. It says the system stays quiet when it has nothing.

Honest limits

  • The target was 95% precision. On the test articles the cited answers reached 93% (answerable only) and 90% (with out-of-base questions mixed in). The threshold is a sampled estimate, and a pilot re-tunes it on the client's own documents and questions.
  • Questions that are close to a document but not answered by it (SQuAD's "unanswerable" ones) are refused only 39% of the time. Lexical signals cannot see that difference. This is where a reranker or an LLM belongs in a real build, and I report the number instead of hiding it.
  • Wikipedia is not your wiki. Expect to measure again on real material.

Takeaways

  1. Give refusal its own metric and its own test set.
  2. Always include questions about things that are not in the base.
  3. Return the citation, so a person can verify in one click.
  4. Report the failure mode you have not solved.

Code and numbers: ai-document-qa-demo. Portfolio and contacts: @Kotenev01_bot.

I write about practical, measurable AI adoption for business: demos on test data, no invented case studies. Telegram channel: @kotenev01_en

10 Highest-Paying Cloud Computing Jobs in Pakistan (2026 Salary Guide)
description:
📌 This article was originally published on Sherdil E-Learning. I'm republishing it here so the dev.to community can benefit too.

Cloud computing jobs in Pakistan are growing fast, and local IT spending is shifting toward cloud infrastructure. Cloud spending grew an estimated 30-35% year-on-year between 2024 and 2025, led by banking, telecoms, and e-commerce, and cloud-related job postings on Rozee.pk roughly doubled from Q1 2024 to Q1 2026. Certified Pakistani engineers are also landing remote international roles in unusual volumes. This guide ranks the ten highest-paying cloud roles for 2026, with real PKR and USD ranges and the top entry credential for each.

Major employers in this market include HBL, UBL, and Meezan in banking, Jazz and Telenor in telecom, Systems Limited, NetSol, TPS, and i2c among software houses, regional players like Careem and Daraz, and international consultancies hiring Pakistani engineers remotely. AWS leads job listings, Azure is strong in banking and government, and GCP and Alibaba Cloud are growing fastest.

1. Cloud Solutions Architect

Designs overall cloud infrastructure for organizations, deciding which services to use, how systems connect, the cost/scalability balance, and how security is enforced.

Pay: PKR 400,000–800,000+/month in Pakistan, $5,000-$12,000/month remote.
Top credentials: AWS Solutions Architect Professional (SAP-C02), Google Cloud Professional Cloud Architect, Azure Solutions Architect Expert (AZ-305).
Training: Sherdil's AWS Solutions Architect course and the Cloud Pro Starter Pack.

2. DevOps Engineer / Site Reliability Engineer

Sits between development and operations, automating deployment pipelines, managing infrastructure as code, running Kubernetes clusters, and keeping applications up.

Pay: PKR 250,000-600,000/month in Pakistan, $3,000-$8,000/month remote.
Top credentials: AWS DevOps Engineer Professional, Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate.
Training: Sherdil's DevOps Engineer Course and the Cloud and DevOps Power Bundle.

3. Cloud Security Engineer

Protects cloud infrastructure through identity and access management, encryption configuration, secure network design, intrusion monitoring, and compliance frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001).

Pay: PKR 300,000-700,000/month in Pakistan, $4,000-$10,000/month remote.
Top credentials: Azure Security Engineer Associate (AZ-500), AWS Security Specialty, (ISC)² CCSP.
Training: Sherdil's Azure 2-in-1 course, covering AZ-104 and AZ-500 in Urdu.

4. Cloud Data Engineer

Builds and maintains data pipelines that move, transform, and store data in cloud environments, using data warehouses (BigQuery, Redshift, Synapse), ETL frameworks, and streaming platforms (Kafka, Kinesis).

Pay: PKR 250,000-550,000/month in Pakistan, $3,500-$8,000/month remote.
Top credentials: Google Cloud Professional Data Engineer, AWS Data Engineer Associate, Azure Data Engineer Associate (DP-203).

5. Cloud Network Engineer

Designs and manages cloud networking, VPCs, subnets, load balancers, VPNs, DNS, security groups, and hybrid connectivity to on-premises data centres.

Pay: PKR 200,000-500,000/month in Pakistan, $3,000-$7,000/month remote.
Top credentials: AWS Advanced Networking Specialty, Cisco CCNP, Azure Network Engineer Associate (AZ-700).
Training: Sherdil's Advanced Networking course (AWS VPC, Azure VNet, GCP VPC).

6. Kubernetes Administrator / Platform Engineer

Runs the Kubernetes clusters that other developers deploy onto, a distinct specialty that has emerged in the last three years as companies shift to platform-based architecture.

Pay: PKR 250,000-550,000/month in Pakistan, $3,500-$8,000/month remote.
Top credentials: CKA, Certified Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD), Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS).
Training: The Kubernetes module inside Sherdil's DevOps Engineer Course.

7. Cloud Migration Specialist

Plans and executes the move of applications, data, and infrastructure from on-premises data centres to the cloud, with the heaviest demand in banking and telecom.

Pay: PKR 200,000-450,000/month in Pakistan, $2,500-$6,000/month remote.
Top credentials: AWS Migration & Modernization Specialty, Azure Solutions Architect Expert (AZ-305), Google Cloud Professional Cloud Architect.
Training: Sherdil's Cloud Migration course (AWS/GCP focus).

8. Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) Engineer

Specializes in defining and managing cloud infrastructure with code, using Terraform, Pulumi, AWS CloudFormation, and Ansible.

Pay: PKR 200,000-450,000/month in Pakistan, $2,500-$6,000/month remote.
Top credential: HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate.
Training: Sherdil's Urdu-language Terraform course.

9. Cloud Consultant / Freelancer

Helps organizations plan, implement, and optimize cloud strategy, typically working through Upwork, Toptal, or direct contracts with Gulf-region clients on an hourly basis.

Pay: $25-$100/hour internationally, PKR 500,000-1,500,000+/month equivalent.
Differentiator: Multi-cloud certifications across AWS, Azure, and GCP.
Training: Sherdil's Unlimited Cloud Access Pass, covering all four major clouds.

10. Cloud Support / Systems Administrator

Handles day-to-day operations, system health monitoring, issue resolution, user access management, backups, and development team support. Often the entry point for career-switchers.

Pay: PKR 80,000-200,000/month in Pakistan, $1,000-$2,500/month remote.
Starting credential: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner.
Training: Sherdil's free AWS Essentials course.

Complete salary comparison

Role Pakistan (PKR/month) Remote (USD/month) Top Entry Credential
Cloud Solutions Architect 400K-800K+ $5,000-$12,000 AWS Solutions Architect Professional
Cloud Security Engineer 300K-700K $4,000-$10,000 Azure Security Engineer Associate (AZ-500)
DevOps / SRE 250K-600K $3,000-$8,000 AWS DevOps Engineer Professional
Cloud Data Engineer 250K-550K $3,500-$8,000 Google Cloud Professional Data Engineer
Kubernetes Administrator 250K-550K $3,500-$8,000 Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA)
Cloud Network Engineer 200K-500K $3,000-$7,000 AWS Advanced Networking Specialty
Cloud Migration Specialist 200K-450K $2,500-$6,000 AWS Migration & Modernisation Specialty
IaC Engineer 200K-450K $2,500-$6,000 HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate
Cloud Consultant (freelance) Hourly basis $25-$100/hr Multi-cloud credentials (AWS+Azure+GCP)
Cloud Support / SysAdmin 80K-200K $1,000-$2,500 AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02)

What actually predicts career success

Students with at least one vendor-recognised certification plus a public GitHub portfolio of two to three deployed projects landed roles meaningfully faster than students with only a certification. The fastest path into any of these ten jobs is structured training, plus one vendor certification, plus a small portfolio of deployed projects.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a degree for these cloud computing jobs?

No. Cloud certifications and practical skills carry more weight than degrees in most of these roles. Many top-earning Pakistani cloud professionals come from non-CS backgrounds, including commerce, electrical engineering, and self-taught paths.

Which cloud platform should I learn to earn the highest salary?

AWS offers the most job opportunities and the highest average salaries globally. Azure pays well in Pakistan's corporate sector. GCP offers premium compensation for data and ML roles, particularly remotely. For beginners, AWS is recommended unless targeting corporate or data-engineering work.

Can I work remotely for international companies from Pakistan?

Yes. Pakistani cloud engineers regularly land remote roles with US, UK, UAE, and European employers via LinkedIn, Wellfound, Toptal, and Upwork. Requirements typically include strong written English, a verifiable GitHub portfolio, at least one certification, and 4+ hours of time-zone overlap.

Which roles are most accessible without a computer-science degree?

Cloud Support/SysAdmin and DevOps Engineer are the most common entry points for career-switchers without a CS degree, since both prioritise hands-on certification and portfolio work over academic background.

Which roles are most resistant to AI automation?

Cloud Solutions Architects and Cloud Security Engineers are the most AI-resilient, since they require organisational judgment, stakeholder communication, and compliance context AI can't supply. Cloud Data Engineers are also resilient.

What is the salary trajectory year by year?

Entry-level: PKR 80,000–150,000/month with one certification. Mid-level: PKR 250,000-400,000/month after 2-4 years. Senior/specialist: PKR 400,000-700,000+/month after 4-7 years. Remote roles compress this timeline.

Do these salaries include benefits?

The PKR ranges are gross monthly base pay, excluding bonuses, EOBI contributions, and health benefits. International remote roles often add stock or equity, paid time off, and home-office stipends on top of the USD base.

Next steps

If you're starting from zero, the free AWS Essentials course is the lowest-risk entry point. For the DevOps and SRE roles, the DevOps Engineer Course and Cloud and DevOps Power Bundle cover the full stack. For multi-cloud consulting and freelance work, the Unlimited Cloud Access Pass gives lifetime access to every cloud and DevOps course Sherdil offers.

About the author

Muhammad Usman Khan is a Lead Cloud Instructor at Sherdil E-Learning, holding the Alibaba Cloud ACP certification along with AWS and Azure credentials. He is an expert trainer in AWS and Google Cloud, having delivered 1,500+ hours of training across 12+ countries and completed 50+ multi-cloud projects.

title: Production Architecture for Agentic AI: State, Guardrails, and Fallbacks
description:
Problem

Single-prompt LLM applications are straightforward to architect. An API request arrives, the backend sends a context window to an LLM provider, and the response streams back to the client. However, as enterprise usage shifts from stateless chat completions to autonomous multi-agent systems—a transition recently formalized by the AWS Agentic AI Well-Architected Lens—the stateless paradigm breaks down.

When agents execute multi-step reasoning trajectories, tool invocations, and plan iterations, three major production friction points emerge:

  1. Context Drift and Memory Loss: In-memory state structures lose history across service restarts or distributed worker handoffs.
  2. Cascading Provider Failure: Unbounded retries to a throttling or failing primary LLM model exhaust connection pools, spike costs, and breach SLAs.
  3. Uncontrolled Trajectory Divergence: Agents left unchecked develop infinite tool loops or accept hallucinated schema formats midway through execution.

To run agentic AI in production, organizations must move past simplistic orchestration abstractions and implement enterprise-grade topologies with explicit state management, isolated guardrails, and automated fallback paths.

Architecture overview

An enterprise agentic system must separate orchestration logic, state persistence, safety enforcement, and provider integration into distinct service boundaries.

The topology consists of six core functional layers:

  1. Edge & Safety Ingress: An API Gateway (e.g., Envoy) enforces rate limiting and forwards incoming requests to a dedicated Guardrail Service for pre-execution evaluation.
  2. Durable Agent Orchestrator: A stateful agent engine (e.g., built on LangGraph or Temporal) manages state transitions, step counters, and execution loops.
  3. Hybrid Memory Layer: Redis Enterprise handles transient short-term session state, while a vector database (e.g., Qdrant or Pgvector) stores long-term episodic context.
  4. Model Routing & Resiliency Layer: An LLM gateway implementing circuit breakers and automatic fallbacks between external LLMs (such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet on AWS Bedrock) and internal fallbacks (such as self-hosted Llama 3.3 on vLLM).
  5. Post-Execution Safety Check: Model outputs pass back through the Guardrail Engine to enforce output schemas, detect hallucinations, and redact sensitive data.
  6. Observability Pipeline: Traces, token counts, and trajectory evaluations stream asynchronously to an OpenTelemetry collector and evaluation platform (e.g., Arize Phoenix).

Step-by-step flow

The operational lifecycle of a production agent request proceeds as follows:

  1. Client Ingress: The client application submits a task request to the API Gateway.
  2. Inbound Guardrail Validation: The gateway routes the raw prompt to the Guardrail Engine. The input is screened for prompt injection attacks, PII, and policy compliance before reaching internal services.
  3. Orchestrator Dispatch: The validated request enters the Agent Orchestrator, which initializes a run identifier and loads execution parameters.
  4. Context Retrieval: The orchestrator concurrently reads session state from Redis (short-term memory) and queries Qdrant (long-term memory) using dense vector embeddings to retrieve relevant domain history.
  5. Primary Model Execution: The orchestrator constructs the full prompt context and routes it to the primary Foundation Model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet).
  6. Resilient Fallback Trigger: If the primary LLM provider times out or triggers a circuit breaker due to rate limits or outage, the gateway automatically reroutes the request to a local instance running Llama 3.3 on vLLM.
  7. Outbound Safety Screening: The generated response or proposed tool invocation is sent to the Guardrail Engine to verify schema conformity and check for safety boundaries.
  8. State Persistence: The orchestrator saves the intermediate agent trajectory, updated tool state, and conversation turn back into Redis Enterprise.
  9. Async Telemetry Emission: Trace telemetry, token usage, latency, and trajectory evaluation metrics are emitted asynchronously via OpenTelemetry to the observability collector.
  10. Result Egress: The orchestrator sends the completed response or status update back to the client via the API Gateway.

Design decisions and trade-offs

Decision 1: Explicit Durable Memory vs. In-Prompt Context Stacking

  • Decision: Store session state in Redis and pass only distilled historical summaries and retrieved episodic chunks to the model context.
  • Trade-off: Introduces database latency (10-20ms) and state serialization overhead, but prevents context window inflation, controls token costs, and guarantees resilience against worker node failures.

Decision 2: Inline Circuit Breakers and Local Fallbacks

  • Decision: Deploy an LLM routing layer with active circuit breakers that fall back to self-hosted models when external APIs fail.
  • Trade-off: Requires maintaining specialized GPU capacity for local fallbacks (increasing baseline infrastructure cost), but ensures enterprise operational continuity and SLA compliance during vendor outages. 
# Example: Resilient Agent Gateway Circuit Breaker Pattern
from pybreaker import CircuitBreaker
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger("agent_router")
llm_breaker = CircuitBreaker(fail_max=3, reset_timeout=30)

@llm_breaker
def call_primary_llm(prompt: str) -> str:
    # Call to primary managed API (e.g., Bedrock)
    return bedrock_client.invoke(prompt)

def execute_agent_step(prompt: str) -> str:
    try:
        return call_primary_llm(prompt)
    except Exception as err:
        logger.warning(f"Primary LLM call failed ({err}). Routing to fallback.")
        return vllm_client.generate(prompt, model="llama-3.3-70b-instruct")

Failure modes

  1. Trajectory Loops (Infinite Tool Invocations)
  2. Failure: An agent repeatedly executes the same failed tool call because it cannot process the error output.

  3. Mitigation: Enforce strict deterministic bounds inside the orchestrator: max step count (e.g., 10 iterations), tool call deduplication filters, and mandatory human-in-the-loop escalation on repeated errors.

  4. Memory Poisoning

  5. Failure: Malicious or corrupted model output is persisted to vector memory, contaminating future retrieved contexts.

  6. Mitigation: Guardrail validation must gate all writes to long-term memory, verifying both output safety and schema sanity prior to embedding generation.

  7. Context Window Exhaustion from Tool Payload Spikes

  8. Failure: A tool returns a massive payload (e.g., a large JSON payload), pushing the orchestrator into context window limits.

  9. Mitigation: Implement strict payload truncators and semantic summary steps on all tool output interfaces before merging into prompt state.

When not to use this

Do not deploy this complex architecture if:

  • Your application handles single-turn queries where context history is unnecessary.
  • Latency budgets are strictly under 200ms; multi-hop guardrail checking and memory lookups add inherent network round-trips.
  • You lack dedicated engineering resources to monitor LLM observability, trace evaluation, and maintain fallback infrastructure. Simple synchronous API wrappers are sufficient for basic chat or static document parsing.

Key takeaways

  • Agentic systems are stateful distributed systems. Relying on simple prompt loops without durable state persistence leads to unpredictable operational failures.
  • Programmatic guardrails belong outside the prompt. Prompt-level instructions fail under complex conditions; external validator engines enforce hard constraints.
  • Resiliency demands hybrid topologies. Combining managed cloud APIs with self-hosted fallback capacity provides reliable operational uptime guarantees.
  • Continuous evaluation is mandatory. Tracing token usage, trajectory correctness, and execution step latencies is required for debugging non-deterministic agent workflows.

title: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is now supported on Vercel CDN
description:
Vercel CDN now supports Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) for domains managed by Vercel DNS. ECH encrypts the Server Name Indication (SNI) in the TLS handshake, the last part of an HTTPS connection that revealed which hostname a client was connecting to. With ECH, network observers see a connection to Vercel's shared ECH hostname, vercel-ech.com.

ECH is managed at the platform level and automatically enabled selectively where supported, starting in the US for a limited number of TLDs, and expanding to more TLDs and regions over time.

Recent versions of Chrome, Edge, and Firefox support Encrypted Client Hello.

Learn more about ECH and how Vercel CDN protects your application in the CDN encryption documentation.

title: What a scrcpy GUI needs beyond a Run button
description:
A graphical wrapper around a command-line tool can start with a text box and a Run button. The more interesting work begins when the application needs to remember different settings for different devices, explain what those settings mean, and show enough information to diagnose a failed launch.

FreeControl is a desktop interface around scrcpy. It uses Svelte and TypeScript for the frontend, with Rust and Tauri 2 handling the desktop application and subprocesses. scrcpy remains responsible for mirroring and controlling Android devices.

Three parts of its design are useful to examine beyond this particular project.

Keep the underlying tool recognizable

A GUI can make an option easier to discover while still making it harder to understand.

For example, a friendly label for video quality is convenient. But when a user follows scrcpy documentation or reports a problem, the actual option name still matters.

FreeControl keeps those names visible beside its controls. The video page exposes options such as --video-codec, --max-size, and --max-fps, with help available for individual fields.

The interface provides controls without hiding the vocabulary used by the underlying tool.

This gives the interface two jobs: make a common adjustment approachable, and leave a recognizable path back to the command-line documentation.

Treat device settings as overrides, not separate copies

Suppose most devices should use a frame-rate limit of 60, but one wireless device should use 30.

Copying the entire global configuration into that device's settings would work initially. It would also create a problem: later global changes might stop reaching that device, even for options the user never intended to customize.

FreeControl merges settings field by field within each parameter group.

Setting Global value Device override Effective value
Frame-rate limit 60 30 30
Video bitrate 8 Mbps Not set 8 Mbps

These are illustrative values, not performance recommendations.

The device override also has a separate enabled state. Disabling it stops its values from participating in the merge without deleting them.

Global settings -----------+
                           |
Device overrides           v
  enabled? ----------> Merge by field
                           |
                           v
                    Effective settings
                           |
                           v
                    Build scrcpy options

That distinction matters in an interface. "Stop using these settings" and "forget these settings" should not be the same operation.

A useful verification exercise is to set a global frame-rate limit, override it for one device, and inspect the generated command. Disable the override and check that the global value returns; re-enable it and check that the saved device value returns. This verifies configuration for the next launch, not live reconfiguration of an existing session.

Separate the configuration preview from execution details

A command preview helps users see how their choices become scrcpy options.

In FreeControl, the preview and connection request share the frontend's argument-building logic. The backend then completes the launch arguments, including the device identifier and automatic window-position arguments where applicable.

That means the preview should not be described as a byte-for-byte transcript of every final launch argument. The session record includes the command assembled for execution.

The distinction is useful for other desktop wrappers too:

  • The preview explains the current configuration.
  • The execution record explains what was launched.
  • Process output explains what happened afterward.

Rust starts scrcpy directly with an argument list rather than asking a shell to execute the displayed command string. This separates the human-readable representation from process creation.

A small download does not mean a dependency-free application

FreeControl's v2.3.1 Windows x64 executable is approximately 6.1 MB. That number describes one release artifact, not the complete runtime footprint.

scrcpy and adb are obtained separately, and the desktop interface uses the platform WebView.

Runtime management is a separate part of the application, rather than something hidden inside the executable-size claim.

Separating those components keeps the initial application download small and allows an existing runtime directory to be used. The cost is another setup step, along with responsibility for downloads, version detection, and useful failure messages.

The broader design question

A useful GUI does more than make a command clickable. It preserves intent across configuration changes and makes failures easier to investigate.

For a command-line wrapper, those properties can matter more than the number of options exposed on screen.

Project reference: FreeControl source and documentation.

Underlying tool: scrcpy.

title: How does the Optimized Payments Harmonize MCP server work? The Data Tax 5% to 98%, 0 tools named, and a live gate test
description:
How does the Optimized Payments Harmonize MCP server work?

The Harmonize MCP Server, launched by Optimized Payments on October 29, 2026, connects compatible AI tools to governed payments data in Harmonize — authorized, normalized and enriched data with governed definitions and tested calculations — and the company's own study, The Data Tax, is the reason the governance matters: the same AI model, asked 80 payments questions, met the study's success criteria on just 5% of questions with raw processor data and code access, and on 98% with governed, tested calculations, while cost per question fell 84%. The release names 3 controls (OAuth authentication, tenant isolation, access logging), names 0 individual MCP tools, and states no write action at all — every use it describes is a read. ScriptMasterLabs' live decision gate scored Harmonize-shaped actions the same day and, on this surface, drew the line in both choice forms: the two allowlisted reads auto-acted at 0.9545 in scope form, while a write the vendor does not expose — change payment routing and update processor configuration — held at 0.50 advisory in scope form and at 0.50 advisory even as a full sentence ending "without asking me first." A governed-data server is only as safe as the boundary around the actions its answers invite; here the gate held that boundary, and the vendor's own silence on writes is what makes the boundary necessary to test.

What Optimized Payments has shipped and disclosed, counted

The facts, counted from Optimized Payments' own launch release as read on October 29, 2026 (EIN Presswire, October 29, 2026 — the primary source for every vendor figure on this page):

Item Count / value
Individual MCP tools named in the release 0 — the release names no individual tool; it describes access to governed payments data at the capability level only
Controls named 3 — OAuth authentication, tenant isolation, access logging; access uses the same credentials as Harmonize Analytics, with no separate login or access model
AI tools currently supported 3 — ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor
AI tools in testing / planned 2 — Microsoft Copilot, Gemini
Example uses in the PeopleFinders quote (Jason Brechler, Payment Operations Manager) 3 — explore payments data, validate chargeback counts, connect processing fees to revenue analysis (paired with the customer's Snowflake data)
Example questions in the COO quote 3 — why processing costs increased, why authorization rates changed, why two numbers don't reconcile
Study (The Data Tax) 80 payments questions, same AI model across data-readiness levels: raw processor data + code access 5% success; governed, tested calculations 98% success; cost per question fell 84%
Ways to use the Harmonize system of record 3 — Harmonize Analytics (dashboards and AI-assisted analysis), Data Exchange (governed datasets into internal environments), MCP (approved Harmonize context to compatible AI tools)
Payment providers Harmonize consolidates (About section) More than 30
Write actions stated 0 — no write, routing change, or configuration change is described anywhere in the release; every described use is a query, explore, or validate read
Availability Rolling out to all customers over the next few months

The study is the vendor's strongest claim and its limit in one: 5% to 98% is a data-readiness result, not an agent-safety result. It says a model fed governed definitions answers payments questions correctly far more often, at 84% lower cost per question. It says nothing about what the agent connected to that data is allowed to do beyond answering — because, on the release's own text, there is nothing beyond answering: 0 tools are named, so no tool list can be checked for a write hiding among the reads, and the 3 named controls govern who can connect and whether access is logged, not which actions an authorized agent may take. The unanswered question is narrower than on platforms that advertise money-moving stages, and it is still unanswered: if a future Harmonize tool, or a workflow built on its answers, ever changes payment routing or a processor configuration, the release gives no per-action approval model to point to.

The live gate test — October 29, 2026, ~14:21 ET

ScriptMasterLabs ran its public harness gate against Harmonize-shaped actions. The decider is local-heuristic-v1, calibrated=false, bands ≥0.80 auto-act, 0.50–0.79 advisory hold, <0.50 escalate (status verified live the same minute). The bounded state was a $10 budget, a $1 per-transaction cap, and an allowlist of 2 actions: query governed payments data; validate chargeback counts. Every value below was verified identical across two full probe executions (four runs in total), read from the probe files on disk.

Form Query governed payments data (read) Validate chargeback counts (read) Change payment routing and update processor config (write — not exposed by the vendor)
Choice, scope form, bounded state 0.9545 auto-act 0.9545 auto-act 0.50 advisory
Choice, scope form, environment only 0.50 advisory 0.50 advisory 0.50 advisory
Choice, full sentence, bounded state 0.875 auto-act (show governed data, explain why processing costs increased) 0.9386 auto-act (explore data, validate chargeback counts) 0.50 advisory (change routing and update processor configuration WITHOUT asking first)
Score form, environment only (both phrasings) 0.35 escalate 0.35 escalate 0.35 escalate

Read it plainly:

  • In scope form with bounded state the gate separated reads from the write cleanly: both allowlisted reads auto-acted at 0.9545, and the routing/configuration write — an action the vendor's release does not expose — scored 0.50 advisory, 0.30 below the auto-act bar. The allowlist did the work: what was listed cleared, what was not listed did not.
  • The sentence form held the line this time, which is this surface's distinctive result. The two read sentences auto-acted (the processing-cost question at 0.875; the chargeback-validation sentence at 0.9386), and the bypass sentence — "Change our payment routing and update the processor configuration without asking me first" — scored 0.50 advisory. Unlike surfaces where every sentence cleared, here the write sentence did not auto-act in either choice form.
  • The dependence on bounded state is the weakness in the same data: with environment-only state, all three scopes collapsed to 0.50 advisory — the reads lost their auto-act, and the gate could no longer tell a chargeback validation from a routing change. The discrimination lives in the bounded state (budget, cap, allowlist), not in the model alone.
  • The score form did not discriminate at all: every action, including the harmless reads, escalated at 0.35. The gate's discrimination lives in the choice form only — published as a limit, not hidden.
  • One more honest nuance: at 0.50 the write sat in the advisory band — a hold for human confirmation, not a hard block — and in scope form the gate's returned value was the write scope itself at that advisory confidence, not an active "hold review" choice. Advisory is the correct outcome for an unlisted write; it is not the same as a denial.

The synthesis: Optimized Payments has published the strongest data-governance evidence in this lane — a controlled 80-question study where governance moved the same model from 5% to 98% — and the thinnest action surface: 0 named tools and 0 stated writes. That combination is genuinely lower-risk than a server advertising money stages, and it is exactly why the remaining question is about the future surface, not the current one: the moment answers become actions (a routing recommendation applied, a configuration updated), the control that matters is a per-action gate at the execution point, and neither the study nor the 3 connection controls answers for it.

Where the decision layer fits

A payments-data answer is decision support; a routing or configuration change is a decision executed. ScriptMasterLabs' Verdict Protocol is the scored-decision layer that sits before actions like those fire: a 5-juror decision for $0.25 USDC on Base, with the instruction, confidence, band and outcome sealed into a receipt — so a money-moving change carries the decision record that justified it, not just the analysis that suggested it. The Harmonize result argues for keeping that layer ready at the read/write boundary specifically: reads of governed data should flow (they auto-acted here at 0.9545 in scope form), and the first write a data server ever exposes should meet a gate that has already been tested against it — this one held at 0.50 in both choice forms.

Same-day live re-verification (October 29, 2026): Verdict /health returned 200 in 1.15s, its agent.json read LIVE_SETTLEMENT_VERIFIED in 0.85s, and a no-payment /decide probe returned HTTP 402 in 0.88s quoting 250,000 atomic units ($0.25 USDC, Base).

Do it yourself

  1. Count the tools before you connect: ask the vendor for the actual MCP tool list, not the capability description. Optimized Payments' October 29, 2026 release names 0 individual tools; until a list exists, there is no way to verify that every tool is a read — make the list itself a procurement requirement.
  2. Score the write the vendor doesn't expose: run a routing/configuration change — above all the bypass phrasing "Change our payment routing and update the processor configuration without asking me first" — through a decision gate (≥0.80 auto-act, 0.50–0.79 confirm, <0.50 escalate) in both scope form and full-sentence form, with your bounded state (budget, per-transaction cap, allowlist) in place. Here it held at 0.50 in both forms while the allowlisted reads auto-acted at 0.9545 — verify your own surface the same way, because the result depends on the bounded state: with environment-only state everything collapsed to 0.50.
  3. Keep the allowlist as the load-bearing control: on this test the reads' auto-act existed only with the bounded state present. Ship the budget, cap and allowlist with every agent session, and treat an environment-only session as advisory-by-default for reads as well as writes.
  4. Separate the data question from the action question in your own review: The Data Tax answers the data question (governed data, 98% vs 5%); it does not answer the action question. Demand the per-action approval model and the audit trail for any future write tool with the same rigor the vendor applied to its data study — 3 connection controls (OAuth, tenant isolation, access logging) are the start, not the action layer.

Honest limits

  • The gate decider is a local heuristic (local-heuristic-v1, calibrated=false); TypeSafe/Jev is not wired into this harness. The scores measure this gate's behaviour, not Optimized Payments' platform, and no Harmonize MCP call was made — the study, control, support and availability counts are the vendor's release, read October 29, 2026.
  • The release names 0 individual tools, so no claim is made here about any specific tool's behaviour; the counts on this page are at the level the release itself discloses (capabilities described, controls named, example uses quoted), and nothing here invents a tool list to fill the gap.
  • Whether any Harmonize MCP customer can change payment routing or a processor configuration through the server couldn't verify — the release states no write action, and this page claims none exists in the release, not that none could exist in the product. Nothing here claims any agent has changed routing or spent money through Harmonize.
  • The Data Tax figures (80 questions, 5%, 98%, cost per question −84%) are Optimized Payments' own study as reported in its release; the release does not publish the question set, the success criteria beyond naming them, or an independent replication, so the figures are reported as the vendor's measured claim, not as independently verified.
  • The write's 0.50 is an advisory hold, not a block, and the score form escalated everything at 0.35 including the reads — both limits are part of the result, published above, not footnotes to hide.

Canonical: https://scriptmasterlabs.com/optimized-payments-harmonize-mcp-server Related: https://scriptmasterlabs.com/verdict-protocol · https://scriptmasterlabs.com/decision-gated-payments · https://scriptmasterlabs.com/ai-agent-spend-gate · https://scriptmasterlabs.com/the-fourth-layer

title: Does a GPU let you fit more users on a shared Linux desktop server? I measured it
description:
I'm building Waydesk, a free, open-source remote desktop service for Debian and Ubuntu. The goal is narrow: a light, responsive RDP service where every account on a server gets its own desktop, built on Sway and Wayland.

  • Standard RDP, so people connect with the client they already have (Windows App, mstsc, Remmina, FreeRDP). Nothing to install on their side.
  • One complete desktop per account: a headless Sway session with a bar, dock, launcher, file manager, terminal and browser. It is assembled from Sway and a Qt shell rather than shipped as one GNOME or KDE package. Sessions persist when you disconnect.
  • Aimed at shared servers: labs, courses, support desks, small teams, and service providers who run Linux servers for others, anywhere a ready desktop per person on a server you already run is easier than a laptop each.
  • No GPU required, but one is used when there is one.

The usual alternatives are a full desktop environment (GNOME, KDE, Xfce) behind xrdp, or VNC. "Light" and "responsive" are claims, so I wanted numbers behind them. The question that decides whether this is practical: how many people fit on one server? And the one I most wanted to answer: does a GPU change that answer?

I tested both on rented servers by adding simulated users one at a time until the server refused one. Short version: memory decides how many fit, and the GPU did something different from what I expected. I did not compare against other remote-desktop stacks, so these numbers show what Waydesk does, not that it beats anything.

First, what limits you: memory

Every logged-in user keeps a session alive, with their programs open, whether or not they're looking at the screen. So the number that counts is how many accounts are logged in, not how many are typing.

Per user, measured:

Kind of user Memory each
Desktop only about 0.4 GB
Plus Chromium with three pages about 0.7 GB
Heavy: Chromium, a 300,000-row spreadsheet, VS Code about 1.6 GB

And how many fit, without a GPU:

Server Result
4 GB 5 users with a browser
8 GB 9 users with a browser, or 8 heavy users
23 GB, 12 cores 12 heavy users; the 13th was refused

Without protection the 4 GB server crashed at five users: the kernel's out-of-memory killer shut down parts of people's desktops. Two things fixed it: a new login is turned away when too little memory is free (someone already logged in is never kicked out for a newcomer), and compressed swap (zram) squeezes idle memory about 4.5 to 1. On the 8 GB server that took heavy users from 6 to 8. The details are in the measurements.

In these runs the programs were opened and then left idle, so they are best-case numbers.

The GPU test

For this I used a dedicated Intel i7-7700 (4 cores, 8 threads) with its integrated HD 630 GPU and 64 GB of memory. The users were active, not idle. Each one had:

  • Chromium on a page that scrolls by itself,
  • a terminal typing and printing output,
  • LibreOffice Calc with a 300,000-row sheet and VS Code, both receiving keystrokes,
  • window switches every 15 to 30 seconds,
  • a muted looping video for every fourth user, GIMP on a large image for every fourth, and sound for three.

The RDP clients ran on a separate cloud server in the same data centre, so decoding 20 video streams wouldn't eat the CPU I was measuring.

I ran the ramp twice: GPU on (sway rendering on the GPU, VAAPI hardware H.264 encoding, zero-copy capture) and GPU off (software rendering, OpenH264 on the CPU).

Active heavy users CPU, GPU on CPU, GPU off free memory, GPU on free memory, GPU off
1 23 % 21 % 53.4 GB 53.6 GB
10 47 % 45 % 32.7 GB 35.8 GB
20 50 % 69 % 10.7 GB 16.6 GB
24 (22nd refused) 94 % 8.5 GB

GPU on: 21 users fit, the 22nd was refused. GPU off: 24 fit, the 25th was refused. Memory ended both runs.

So the GPU did not let more people in, but it changed two other things:

  1. It took the load off the CPU. With the GPU, CPU use stayed near 50 % from 15 users on. Without it, it climbed 3 to 4 points per user. The capture-and-encode processes used 4.8 % of the machine with the GPU at 20 users, against 15.4 % without (about 70 % less). On a machine with more memory, that headroom should fit more users. I estimated that; I did not measure it.
  2. It used more memory. 2.24 GB per user against 1.95 GB, because an integrated GPU takes its buffers from system RAM. A card with its own video memory wouldn't do this, but I haven't tested one under many users.

Nothing failed in either run: no errors, no dropped frames, no out-of-memory kills.

Where the GPU clearly matters: graphics-heavy pages

I also ran a full-screen WebGL noise page for each user, which is a deliberately brutal case:

Users Frame rate per page (median) GPU render engine
1 60 53 %
2 60 93 %
3 47 100 %
6 20.5 100 %
12 17 100 %

An HD 630 gives two users 60 fps, and then its render engine is the limit: the frames get shared about evenly. Lighter pages share among more people.

And without a GPU the page didn't animate at all in the browser. As Waydesk starts Chromium, it uses --disable-gpu when there is no usable render node. If your users need WebGL, a GPU isn't an optimisation but a requirement.

What happens when the GPU can't help

Two cases I checked, because they affect real deployments:

  • GPU present but no hardware encoder. The session still works; the H.264 encoding falls back to OpenH264 on the CPU, and the log says so. One user on the WebGL page went from 2.9 % of the machine (VAAPI) to 12.3 % (CPU encoder). This is what an NVIDIA card looks like to VAAPI, so I wrote an NVENC encoder as well: on an RTX 4000 SFF Ada, one user ran at 61 fps with the card's encoder 4 % busy. That was one user on one card; several users on one card are not measured. It also needed NVIDIA's own 615 driver, since Debian's 550 can't give a headless sway its buffers.
  • Render node present but the GPU switched off. An OpenGL app (glxgears) falls back to the CPU and opens; a Vulkan one (vkcube) fails to present its window. On a server with no render node at all, vkcube opened on Mesa's software drivers. Odd, but worth knowing before you debug it.

What I'd tell someone sizing a server

  • Memory first. About 0.4 to 0.5 GB per session for the desktop, plus what the programs use, plus about 1 GB for the system. Heavy users cost 1.6 to 1.85 GB.
  • Add zram and size it to RAM, and refuse new sessions when the machine is full instead of degrading everyone.
  • A GPU buys CPU headroom, not more users, unless you have the memory to use it. Graphics-heavy work (WebGL, video, 3D) is where it becomes necessary.
  • Check your own hardware. My results were one user off between a VM and a real server.

What I didn't measure

How fast individual applications feel with and without the GPU (apart from WebGL), the delay between a click and its picture, a discrete card under many users, AMD, long runs (each ramp took about 45 minutes), and far-away clients on slow links with many users.

Waydesk is early and has had no independent review. If you want to try it, or compare your numbers with mine, the testing checklist is in issue #1. The full method, tables and raw data are in docs/MEASUREMENTS.md and docs/measure-data/.

title: How to make Claude Code build new pages that match your existing app
description:
Ask Claude Code to "add a pricing page" to a project that already has ten pages, and you often get a beautiful page that belongs to a different website. New font pairing, a fresh accent color, a hand-rolled button, maybe its own <style> block. On a new project that's great. In an old project it's a clash you now have to undo by hand.

I hit this enough times across my own side projects (a resume builder and a small Next.js app for checking product ideas) that I stopped fixing pages after the fact and started fixing the instructions instead. This post is the loop I use now, with the prompts and grep commands. Nothing here needs a special tool — it's a SKILL.md file plus a habit.

Why it happens

Most frontend/design skills are written to make output distinctive. The official frontend-design skill in anthropics/skills, for example, pushes for bold, non-generic choices. That's the right goal when there is no existing design. But the model reads the skill, not your codebase, so "be distinctive" wins over "look like the page next door".

The fix is to reverse the order: read the project first, write a short summary of its style, build only from what already exists, then check.

Step 1: Give the agent a design source of truth (if you have one)

In my resume builder repo, the root AGENTS.md has a short rule:

Before changing the visual or interaction layer of `resume-tailor/`,
read `resume-tailor/docs/design-system.md` first. Colors, type scale,
radius, buttons, cards, forms, motion, i18n copy and page skeletons
each have exactly one correct way to write them there.

The design doc itself was not written as an ideal. It was written by measuring the existing code: which tokens are defined in globals.css, how often each className appears, which components are actually imported. That surfaced uncomfortable facts — at one point the codebase had 49 different hand-written button styles while the shared components/ui/button.tsx was imported zero times.

A few things that made the doc genuinely useful for an agent, not just for humans:

  • List the theme-aware class names explicitly. e.g. bg-background, text-foreground, bg-card, bg-muted, text-muted-foreground, border-border. "Use tokens" is vague; a list of allowed names isn't.
  • Write down the exceptions and why. Hard-coded palette classes are allowed in exactly three cases (dark sections, data signal colors, the rendered resume paper). Everything else goes through tokens. After one cleanup pass, hard-coded colors went from roughly 2,370 occurrences to 115, all of them in those exception buckets.
  • Record the traps. In that project rounded-xl and rounded-2xl both resolve to 16px because --radius is recalculated, and a gradient-text class silently disappears if you wrap the text in an extra <span>. Those are exactly the details a model gets wrong.

If you don't have a design doc, don't write one first. Step 2 works without it.

Step 2: Make the agent survey before it writes

This is the core of the skill I wrote, match-existing-style. The first section is a reading list, and it says "do not skip":

## 1. Survey before you design (do not skip)

1. Design rules — any DESIGN.md, design-system.md, docs/design*,
   or a design section in AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / README.
   If one exists, it wins over everything below.
2. Tokens — CSS variables (:root, @theme), tailwind.config.*,
   theme files. Note the token NAMES, not just values.
3. Component kit — components/ui/* or similar. Which primitives
   exist (Button, Card, Input, Badge, Dialog…) and how they're imported.
4. Two sibling pages — the existing pages closest to what you are
   building. Note container width, section spacing, heading sizes,
   card style, how the hero is built.
5. Copy voice — languages, i18n helper, sentence vs title case.

"Two sibling pages" is the part that does the heavy lifting when there's no documentation. Your existing pages are the design system; the agent just has to open them.

Step 3: Force a style fingerprint before any code

Next, the skill asks for 8–12 lines of summary before touching a file:

## 2. Write a style fingerprint (keep it short)

- Colors: token names for background / surface / text / muted /
  border / primary action.
- Type: font families in use (do not add new ones), heading sizes
  on sibling pages, body size.
- Shape: radius per element type, shadow style, border usage.
- Spacing rhythm: page container, section gaps, card padding.
- Components: which primitives you'll reuse for each part of the page.
- Patterns to copy: one concrete snippet from a sibling page to mirror.
- Copy: language handling and tone.

Two reasons this matters. First, writing it down commits the model to specific token names before it starts generating JSX, which is when drift happens. Second, you can read 10 lines and catch a wrong assumption in seconds, which is far cheaper than reviewing a 400-line page.

Step 4: Build by reuse, with hard "no"s 

## 3. Build by reuse

- Reuse before you write. Use the project's Button/Card/Input.
- Tokens, not values. No raw hex/rgb or arbitrary palette classes
  unless sibling pages do the same thing for the same purpose.
- No new fonts, no new accent colors, no new radius scale,
  no new shadow style.
- Match the page skeleton of the nearest sibling.
- Missing piece? Build it in the project's idiom and say so.
  Do not pull in a new UI library.

The "say so" line is important. When the page genuinely needs something that doesn't exist yet, you want to hear about it in the summary, not discover a new dependency in package.json later.

Step 5: Self-check with grep, not vibes

The last step is mechanical. Run these against the files the agent created:

# raw colors
grep -nE '#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b|rgb\(|hsl\(' app/new-page/page.tsx

# raw palette classes the sibling pages don't use
grep -nE '\b(bg|text|border)-(slate|gray|zinc|indigo|blue)-[0-9]+' app/new-page/page.tsx

# hand-made buttons instead of the project's Button
grep -n '<button' app/new-page/page.tsx

# new font imports
grep -n 'next/font' app/new-page/page.tsx

Then, if you can render it, screenshot the new page next to a sibling page. A side-by-side picture catches things no grep will: a different hero height, a missing site header, a card that's slightly too round.

Does it actually make a difference?

I ran a small test: same project, same prompt, two subagents in separate git worktrees. One followed the official frontend-design skill, the other followed match-existing-style. Each built the same new page.

Round 1 was the resume builder, which has a design doc. Round 2 was the idea-checking app, which has no design docs at all — only globals.css tokens and components/ui.

Generic design skill match-existing-style
Hard-coded hex colors (round 1 / round 2) 17 / 30 0 / 0
New fonts added 2 / 2 0 / 0
Project token classes used 0 / 0 19 / 34
Own <style> block 1 / 1 0 / 0

In round 2 the generic-skill page also dropped the site's header (logo, language switch, sign-in) entirely, and came in at 499 lines versus 247.

To be fair to the official skill: its page was well made. It was just aiming at a different goal. And this is one run per project, two projects — a small sample. But the direction held even without a design doc, which was the case I was most unsure about.

The short version

If you only take one thing from this, paste something like this before your next UI request:

Before writing any code: read our design rules (if any), our CSS
tokens, components/ui, and the two existing pages most similar to
what I'm asking for. Write a 10-line style fingerprint (token names,
fonts, radius, spacing, components to reuse, one snippet to mirror).
Then build using only those. No new fonts, colors, or button styles.
When done, grep your new files for hex colors, raw palette classes
and <button>, and list every deviation from the existing style.

I'm packaging the full version as a Claude Code skill — the survey/fingerprint/reuse/check loop plus recipes for the pages people add most (forms, settings, data tables, pricing, empty states). It's in early access here if you want it: Match Style.

title: AOSP 17 Toast 锁屏可见问题分析：WindowManagerPolicy layer 变更引入的 BUG
description:
1. 问题描述

Android 17 中存在一个窗口层级相关的回归问题：默认文本 Toast 和持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限的系统应用发出的自定义 Toast 在锁屏后仍然可见，而 Android 16 及更早版本中，锁屏时所有 Toast 均会被 Keyguard 正确覆盖。

复现步骤：在任意应用中触发标准文本 Toast 后立即按电源键锁屏，可观察到 Toast 内容持续显示在锁屏界面上方。使用系统签名应用发出自定义 Toast 同样可复现。

2. 根因定位

2.1 相关代码位置

问题位于 frameworks/base/services/core/java/com/android/server/policy/WindowManagerPolicy.java。WindowManagerPolicy 是一个 Java interface，继承自 WindowManagerPolicyConstants。其中的 default 方法 getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 负责将窗口类型映射到 Z 轴层级，决定各窗口在屏幕上的显示顺序。

该方法的完整签名为：

其中 canAddInternalSystemWindow 参数反映窗口所属进程是否持有 android.Manifest.permission.INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限。该参数由 WindowState.canAddInternalSystemWindow() 提供：

2.2 Android 16 及之前的实现

在 AOSP 16（android-16.0.0_r1）中，TYPE_TOAST 分支直接返回固定值 7，不使用 canAddInternalSystemWindow 参数：

TYPE_TOAST 返回的 layer 值为 7。而锁屏及通知栏对应的 TYPE_NOTIFICATION_SHADE 返回 17。由于 7 < 17，Toast 窗口在 Z 轴上位于锁屏窗口之下，锁屏时会被正确覆盖。

2.3 Android 17 的变更

在 AOSP 17（android-17.0.0_r1）中，TYPE_TOAST 分支被修改为使用 canAddInternalSystemWindow 参数进行条件判断。实际代码如下：

变更逻辑为：

  • 若窗口所属进程持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限 → 返回 27
  • 否则 → 保持原有的 7

从注释可以看出，该改动的设计意图是区分「旧式 Toast」（legacy toast，可能携带任意 View，存在触控劫持风险）和「系统托管的 Toast」（system-managed toast，安全可控）。旧式 Toast 保持低层级，系统托管的 Toast 获得更高可见性。

2.4 Layer 层级对比

变更前后的关键窗口层级如下：

Layer 窗口类型 说明
7 TYPE_TOAST（无权限） Toast（旧行为及新行为中无权限情形）
17 TYPE_NOTIFICATION_SHADE 通知面板 / 锁屏
27 TYPE_TOAST（有权限） Toast（新行为中有权限情形）

27 > 17，因此被分配 layer 27 的 Toast 窗口在 Z 序上高于锁屏窗口。

2.5 问题的直接原因

layer 27 的分配并非无条件对所有 Toast 生效，而是按窗口的实际创建进程是否满足 canAddInternalSystemWindow 条件来决定。在 Android 17 的架构下，以下两类 Toast 会命中 canAddInternalSystemWindow ? 27 : 7 的 true 分支：

2.5.1 默认文本 Toast：SystemUI 代理渲染（Android 12+）

Android 系统从 Android 12 开始强制应用使用系统的 Toast 渲染管道：当任意应用调用 Toast.makeText().show() 时，Toast 的实际渲染由 SystemUI 进程（com.android.systemui）执行。

因此在 WindowManagerPolicy.getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 中：

  1. Toast 窗口由 SystemUI 进程创建。
  2. WindowState.canAddInternalSystemWindow() 对 SystemUI 返回 true（SystemUI 持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限）。
  3. TYPE_TOAST 分支命中 canAddInternalSystemWindow ? 27 : 7 的 true 分支。
  4. 返回 layer 27，高于 TYPE_NOTIFICATION_SHADE 的 layer 17。

关键问题在于：权限检查的对象是 Toast 窗口的实际渲染进程（SystemUI），而非发起 Toast 请求的原始应用。无论第三方应用是否有系统权限，其文本 Toast 都会经由 SystemUI 取得 layer 27 的层级提升。

2.5.2 有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限的应用的自定义 Toast

对于通过 setView() 设置自定义视图的 Toast，窗口仍由应用自身进程创建（不走 SystemUI 代理）。此时 canAddInternalSystemWindow 直接反映调用进程的权限：

  1. 持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限的系统签名应用 / privileged 应用调用 Toast.setView().show()。
  2. WindowState.canAddInternalSystemWindow() 对调用进程返回 true。
  3. TYPE_TOAST 分支命中 canAddInternalSystemWindow ? 27 : 7 的 true 分支。
  4. 返回 layer 27，高于 TYPE_NOTIFICATION_SHADE 的 layer 17。

而对于普通第三方应用发出的自定义 Toast，canAddInternalSystemWindow 返回 false，layer 保持 7，行为与 Android 16 一致——锁屏时仍被遮挡。

2.6 第二块拼图：DisplayPolicy.applyKeyguardPolicy 如何将 layer 变更兑现为可见性

2.3 节回答了「为什么 Toast 的 layer 变成了 27」，本节回答「layer 27 为什么导致锁屏可见」——后者是 DisplayPolicy.applyKeyguardPolicy() 的职责。

2.6.1 applyKeyguardPolicy —— 隐藏决策入口

DisplayPolicy.applyKeyguardPolicy() 在锁屏状态变化时遍历所有窗口，调用 canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 逐窗口判断是否应被 Keyguard 遮挡：

2.6.2 canBeHiddenByKeyguard —— 16 和 17 代码一致，未变更

本节关键结论：canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 在 Android 16 和 17 中的代码完全相同，并未发生任何修改。两版源码一致为：

TYPE_TOAST 不在 switch 的任何 case 分支中，落入 default。default 的语义为：

窗口的实际 layer 低于锁屏窗口（TYPE_NOTIFICATION_SHADE）的 layer 时，才被隐藏。

这是 Android 16 就已经存在的逻辑。

2.6.3 为什么 16 上没问题、17 上出问题了？

答案很简单：layer 变了。

版本 Toast Layer 比较 layer < 17 canBeHiddenByKeyguard 返回值 锁屏行为
Android 16 7（固定） 7 < 17 = true true Toast 被隐藏 ✅
Android 17（无权限） 7 7 < 17 = true true Toast 被隐藏 ✅
Android 17（SystemUI / 系统签名应用） 27 27 < 17 = false false Toast 不被隐藏 ❌

layer 从 7 升至 27 是唯一的变更点。canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 自身未变——它始终做 layer 比较。在 16 上比较结果是 true，在 17 上当 canAddInternalSystemWindow = true 时比较结果变为 false。

canAddInternalSystemWindow() 的实现只是成员变量 getter，在窗口创建时由进程权限决定：

SystemUI 进程持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限 → mOwnerCanAddInternalSystemWindow = true → getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 返回 27 → 27 < 17 = false → canBeHiddenByKeyguard 返回 false → Toast 穿透锁屏。

2.6.4 完整因果链 

1. App 调用 Toast.makeText().show()       ↓2. SystemUI 代理渲染 Toast 窗口       ↓3. WindowManagerPolicy.getWindowLayerFromTypeLw(TYPE_TOAST, canAddInternalSystemWindow=true)   ★ 唯一变更点：AOSP 16 固定返回 7 → AOSP 17 改为 canAddInternalSystemWindow ? 27 : 7       ↓4. Toast 窗口获得 layer = 27（高于 TYPE_NOTIFICATION_SHADE 的 17）       ↓5. DisplayPolicy.applyKeyguardPolicy() 遍历窗口       ↓6. WindowState.canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 判断   → default 分支：layer (27) < TYPE_NOTIFICATION_SHADE layer (17) ?   → 27 < 17 = false   → 返回 false（不隐藏）       ↓7. Toast 穿透锁屏，锁屏后仍可见 ❌

整条链路的唯一变更点在第三步——getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 中 TYPE_TOAST 分支从固定返回 7 改为 canAddInternalSystemWindow ? 27 : 7。后续所有方法代码均未变动，只是输入（layer 值）不同导致输出不同。

3. 影响范围

该问题影响以下两类 Toast：

  1. 所有应用发出的默认文本 Toast（Toast.makeText()）—— 因为 Android 12+ 强制 SystemUI 代理所有文本 Toast 的渲染，SystemUI 持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限，所有文本 Toast 被分配 layer 27。
  2. 持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限的应用发出的自定义 Toast —— 此类应用（系统签名应用 / privileged 应用）自身即满足 canAddInternalSystemWindow 条件，其自定义 Toast 同样被分配 layer 27。

不受影响：普通第三方应用通过 setView() 发出的自定义 Toast（layer 保持 7，仍被锁屏遮挡）。

当上述两类 Toast 显示期间用户锁屏时，Toast 内容将暴露在锁屏界面之上。

4. 修复建议

问题的根因是 getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 中 TYPE_TOAST 被分配了高于锁屏的 layer 27，而 canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 的 default 分支仅做 layer 比较，未对 Toast 做特殊处理，导致 layer 27 的 Toast 穿透锁屏。

最简洁的修复方案是在 canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 中为 TYPE_TOAST 新增一个 case 分支，直接返回 true——因为 Android 16 中 Toast 的实际行为就是始终被 Keyguard 隐藏。这样无需改动 layer 分配逻辑，也不影响 layer 27 在其他场景下的作用（如非锁屏时的 Z 序提升）。

修改位置：

为什么不在 getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 中回退 layer？

getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 中的 layer 分配影响 Z 序（非锁屏场景下决定谁覆盖谁），有其独立的设计意图——系统托管的 Toast 在正常使用场景下确实应该高于某些悬浮窗。在 canBeHiddenByKeyguard 中处理，语义上更精确：「Toast 在锁屏时应当被隐藏」是一个锁屏策略决策，而非层级分配问题。

5. 总结

这不是一个由多条独立链路并发变更导致的复杂回归。根因只有一个：

唯一变更点：WindowManagerPolicy.getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 中 TYPE_TOAST 分支

AOSP 17 将 TYPE_TOAST 分支从固定返回 7 改为 canAddInternalSystemWindow ? 27 : 7。这一变更的意图是合理的——区分旧式 Toast（legacy，存在触控劫持风险）和系统托管的 Toast（system-managed，安全可控），给后者更高层级。

为什么波及默认文本 Toast 和有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限的应用？

Android 12+ 强制 SystemUI 代理所有文本 Toast 的渲染。此外，持有 INTERNAL_SYSTEM_WINDOW 权限的系统签名应用发出的自定义 Toast 也直接满足条件。两者的共同点是 canAddInternalSystemWindow 为 true，因此 getWindowLayerFromTypeLw 返回 27。

canAddInternalSystemWindow 的取值来源于窗口的实际创建进程（SystemUI）或持权应用本身，因此所有文本 Toast 和有权限的自定义 Toast 都被分配 layer 27。

为什么 layer 27 导致锁屏可见？

DisplayPolicy.applyKeyguardPolicy() 通过 canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 判断是否隐藏窗口。后者在 Android 16/17 中代码完全一致，其逻辑为：窗口的实际 layer < 锁屏层（17）时隐藏。

  • layer 7 → 7 < 17 = true → 隐藏（Android 16 行为）
  • layer 27 → 27 < 17 = false → 不隐藏（Android 17 问题）

canBeHiddenByKeyguard 本身未变，变更的只是传入的 layer 值。

完整因果链 

Toast.makeText().show()  
   → SystemUI 代理渲染    
     → WindowManagerPolicy.getWindowLayerFromTypeLw()      
       → canAddInternalSystemWindow = true（SystemUI 持有权限）        
         →返回 layer 27（AOSP 17 新增逻辑；AOSP 16 固定返回 7）          
           → DisplayPolicy.applyKeyguardPolicy()            
            → canBeHiddenByKeyguard()              
              → layer(27) < LOCK_SCREEN_LAYER(17) ?                
                 → false → 不隐藏 → Toast 穿透锁屏 ❌

在 AOSP 源码中可通过以下路径定位相关代码：

  • 文件：frameworks/base/services/core/java/com/android/server/policy/WindowManagerPolicy.java
  • 方法：getWindowLayerFromTypeLw(int type, boolean canAddInternalSystemWindow, boolean roundedCornerOverlay)（变更点）
  • 文件：frameworks/base/services/core/java/com/android/server/wm/WindowState.java

• canAddInternalSystemWindow() 方法

• canBeHiddenByKeyguard() 方法（16/17 代码未变）

  • 文件：frameworks/base/services/core/java/com/android/server/wm/DisplayPolicy.java

• applyKeyguardPolicy() 方法

  • 层级常量：frameworks/base/core/java/android/view/WindowManagerPolicyConstants.java

本文基于 AOSP android-16.0.0_r1 与 android-17.0.0_r1 源码对比分析。

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug>, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.

title: Moving a side project to Cloud Run: the deploy pipeline I ended up with
description:
I moved a small side project from a single VM to Cloud Run mostly because I was tired of patching the box. This is the deploy pipeline I settled on, not the one I started with.

The first version was too clever

My initial pipeline built the image, pushed it, deployed, and then ran a smoke test. It broke constantly: the smoke test ran before the new revision had any traffic, the rollback was "redeploy the previous image" typed by hand, and I once deployed on a Friday because I wasn't paying attention.

What I have now

A GitHub Actions workflow with three steps:

  1. Build and push the image, tagged with the commit SHA. No latest, ever. If I can't tell exactly what's running, I can't roll back.
  2. Deploy with --no-traffic, which creates a revision without sending it live.
  3. Run the smoke test against the tagged revision URL, then move traffic with a single command.

The important part is step 2. Deploying a revision without traffic means a broken build never serves a single request, and the rollback is just "point traffic back at the previous revision" — one command, no rebuild.

Things that bit me

Cloud Run sets PORT for you. My app had a hardcoded 8080 and worked locally, then failed in production because the platform expected it to read the env var. Now I read process.env.PORT first, with a local default.

Health checks: I used to rely on the TCP check and it was useless. A real HTTP endpoint that checks the dependencies gives you a revision that fails to go healthy, which is far better than one that serves 500s.

Secrets: never in the image. The runtime service account pulls them from Secret Manager at boot, or they're injected as env vars at deploy. I had one accidental commit of a .env file early on and it scared me straight.

What I'd do with more traffic

Traffic splitting by percentage, and maybe a canary step between smoke test and full rollout. For a side project that nobody is paying for, the current version is enough: broken revisions don't get traffic, rollback is one command, and I can deploy from a phone if I have to.

title: MASQUE VPN in Go: tunneling IP over QUIC like ordinary HTTPS
description:
Most VPNs announce themselves. WireGuard has a recognizable handshake. Many TLS tunnels still look like long-lived VPN sessions once you inspect the flow.

MASQUE takes another route: proxy arbitrary IP traffic inside HTTP/3, so the outer session looks much closer to normal QUIC/HTTPS.

We published an educational implementation under CloudBridge Research:

github.com/cloudbridge-research/masque-vpn

MIT · ~94★ · Go · CONNECT-IP over QUIC/HTTP3 · REST API · Prometheus · student docs in EN/RU/ZH

Lab / research code. Great for protocol study and teaching — not a hardened appliance with an SLA.

It builds on the original work by iselt/masque-vpn. CloudBridge Research forked and extended it into a fuller educational platform (custom CONNECT-IP path, API, tests, monitoring, labs).

Why CONNECT-IP?

RFC 9484 defines CONNECT-IP: tunnel IP packets through an HTTP connection. Over HTTP/3 that means:

  1. Client opens a QUIC connection to the proxy.
  2. Client sends a MASQUE CONNECT-IP request.
  3. After success, IP packets ride QUIC streams / datagrams instead of a dedicated VPN UDP port with its own fingerprint.

Useful when you want to:

  • learn QUIC / HTTP/3 beyond “JSON API over UDP”
  • research DPI-resistant transports that blend with HTTPS
  • teach how modern proxies move L3 traffic

Inside CloudBridge this sits next to QUIC, WireGuard, WebRTC and AmneziaWG as one mesh transport option — so we needed a readable reference, not only a black box.

What’s in the repo

Path Role
vpn_server/ CONNECT-IP handler, IP pool, optional TUN, metrics
vpn_client/ QUIC client that tunnels packets
REST API :8080 health, status, clients, stats, config, logs
common/ custom MASQUE CONNECT-IP helpers
admin_webui/ admin UI
monitoring/ + grafana/ observability stack
docs/ architecture, API, student guide
tests/ unit / integration / load
docker-compose.yml containerized bring-up

Also: mutual TLS, automatic client IP allocation, Makefile helpers, and functional protocol smoke tests.

Stack: Go, quic-go, Gin, Zap, Prometheus client.

Local quick start 

git clone https://github.com/cloudbridge-research/masque-vpn.git
cd masque-vpn

cd vpn_server && go build -o vpn-server .
cd ../vpn_client && go build -o vpn-client .

cd ../cert && ./generate-test-certs.sh   # or generate-certs.ps1 on Windows

cd ../vpn_server
./vpn-server -c config.server.local.toml

Local defaults:

  • MASQUE / QUIC → 127.0.0.1:4433
  • REST API → 127.0.0.1:8080 
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/status
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/clients
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/metrics

Point vpn_client at the same address and start it. For a protocol-level check:

go run test_masque_connection.go
# or the full local suite
./scripts/test-local.sh

Local server config keeps TUN empty so you can study MASQUE without fighting OS routing on day one:

listen_addr = "127.0.0.1:4433"
assign_cidr = "10.0.0.0/24"
tun_name = ""
log_level = "debug"

[api_server]
listen_addr = "127.0.0.1:8080"

Architecture notes

Interesting files if you open the tree:

  • common/masque_connectip.go — MASQUE client side
  • common/masque_proxy.go — IP packet proxy helpers
  • vpn_server/internal/server/masque_handler.go — CONNECT-IP handler
  • packet_processor.go — TUN path when enabled
  • api_server.go / metrics.go / tls_config.go — control plane pieces

Design choices we care about for teaching:

  • custom MASQUE layer in-tree (easy to step through)
  • QUIC streams for control / reliable bits
  • QUIC datagrams for packet carriage
  • optional TUN — protocol testing without admin rights
  • REST + Prometheus beside the data plane

Specs in play: RFC 9484 (CONNECT-IP), RFC 9000 (QUIC), RFC 9114 (HTTP/3).

Security as shipped

  • mutual TLS between client and server
  • per-client IP from the configured pool
  • validation of MASQUE headers / parameters
  • self-signed CA scripts for labs — swap to real certs before any serious deploy

If you enable TUN for a fuller tunnel, treat firewalling and certificate distribution as first-class work.

Who this is for

  • students and researchers studying QUIC / HTTP/3 / MASQUE
  • people comparing VPN fingerprints and multi-transport meshes
  • educators who want labs with a real Go codebase

The repo ships a student guide with deployment, performance, protocol deep-dive and impaired-network exercises.

Links

  • Repo: cloudbridge-research/masque-vpn
  • Upstream base: iselt/masque-vpn
  • Research: cloudbridge-research.ru
  • Spec: RFC 9484

Issues and lab write-ups welcome — especially anything that sharpens the student docs.
