/* ======================= CHOOSE FILE ======================= */
$('chooseFile').onclick = () => $('fileInput').click();
$('fileInput').onchange = e => {
  const files = [...e.target.files];
  pendingFiles = files;
  $('filePath').textContent = files.length === 1
      ? files[0].name
      : `${files.length} files selected`;
  $('folderPath').textContent = 'No folder selected';
  $('uploadBtn').disabled = files.length === 0;
};

/* ======================= UPLOAD ======================= */
$('uploadBtn').onclick = async () => {
  if (!pendingFiles.length) return;
  const fd = new FormData();
  pendingFiles.forEach(f => fd.append('files', f, f.name));

  $('uploadBtn').disabled = true;
  $('uploadBtn').textContent = 'Uploading…';
  try {
    const r = await fetch('/api/upload', {method:'POST', body:fd});
    const data = await r.json();
    if (data.error) throw new Error(data.error);
    addBotMsg(`✅ Uploaded. **${data.total_chunks}** chunks embedded.`);
    await refreshFileList();
  } catch (e) {
    addBotMsg(`❌ Upload failed: \`${e.message}\``);
  } finally {
    $('uploadBtn').disabled = false;
    $('uploadBtn').textContent = 'Upload';
    pendingFiles = [];
    $('folderPath').textContent = 'No folder selected';
    $('filePath').textContent = 'No file selected';
    $('folderInput').value = '';
    $('fileInput').value = '';
  }
};

/* ======================= FILE LIST ======================= */
async function refreshFileList() {
  const r = await fetch('/api/files');
  const {files} = await r.json();
  const ul = $('fileList');
  ul.innerHTML = '';
  if (!files.length) {
    ul.innerHTML = '<li style="justify-content:center;color:var(--muted)">No files yet</li>';
    return;
  }
  files.forEach(name => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.innerHTML = `<span title="${name}">${name}</span>
                    <span class="x" title="Delete">✕</span>`;
    li.querySelector('.x').onclick = () => deleteFile(name);
    ul.appendChild(li);
  });
}

async function deleteFile(name) {
  if (!confirm(`Delete "${name}" and its embeddings?`)) return;
  await fetch('/api/files', {
    method:'DELETE',
    headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'},
    body: JSON.stringify({name})
  });
  refreshFileList();
  addBotMsg(`🗑️ Deleted **${name}** from the vector database.`);
}

/* ======================= CHAT ======================= */
function addUserMsg(text) {
  const d = document.createElement('div');
  d.className = 'msg user';
  d.textContent = text;
  $('chat').appendChild(d);
  scrollDown();
}

function addBotMsg(markdown, sources = []) {
  const d = document.createElement('div');
  d.className = 'msg bot';
  d.innerHTML = marked.parse(markdown);
  if (sources.length) {
    const s = document.createElement('div');
    s.className = 'sources';
    s.textContent = 'Sources: ' + sources
        .map(x => `${x.source} (${x.score})`).join(', ');
    d.appendChild(s);
  }
  $('chat').appendChild(d);
  enhanceCodeBlocks(d);
  scrollDown();
}

function enhanceCodeBlocks(root) {
  root.querySelectorAll('pre').forEach(pre => {
    hljs.highlightElement(pre.querySelector('code') || pre);
    const btn = document.createElement('button');
    btn.className = 'copy-code';
    btn.textContent = 'Copy';
    btn.onclick = () => {
      navigator.clipboard.writeText(pre.innerText).then(() => {
        btn.textContent = 'Copied!';
        setTimeout(() => btn.textContent = 'Copy', 1200);
      });
    };
    pre.appendChild(btn);
  });
}

function scrollDown() {
  $('chat').scrollTop = $('chat').scrollHeight;
}

async function sendQuery() {
  const q = $('query').value.trim();
  if (!q) return;
  addUserMsg(q);
  $('query').value = '';
  $('send').disabled = true;
  $('status').textContent = 'thinking…';

  // typing indicator
  const typing = document.createElement('div');
  typing.className = 'msg bot';
  typing.textContent = 'AI is analyzing...';
  $('chat').appendChild(typing);
  scrollDown();

  try {
    const r = await fetch('/api/chat', {
      method:'POST',
      headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'},
      body: JSON.stringify({query:q})
    });
    const data = await r.json();
    typing.remove();
    if (data.error) throw new Error(data.error);
    addBotMsg(data.answer, data.sources || []);
  } catch (e) {
    typing.remove();
    addBotMsg(`❌ \`${e.message}\``);
  } finally {
    $('send').disabled = false;
    $('status').textContent = '';
    $('query').focus();
  }
}

$('send').onclick = sendQuery;
$('query').addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  if (e.key === 'Enter' && !e.shiftKey) {
    e.preventDefault();
    sendQuery();
  }
});

/* ======================= INIT ======================= */
refreshFileList();
</script>
</body>
</html>

The Python file app.py which connects to the LLM, vector db looks like this -

import os
import re
import shutil
import uuid
import tempfile

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, render_template
from flask_cors import CORS

# ----- Vector DB -----
import chromadb
from chromadb.config import Settings

# ----- Embeddings -----
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

# ----- Keyword search -----
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

# ----- File parsers -----
from pypdf import PdfReader
import docx
import openpyxl
from pptx import Presentation

# ----- LLM -----
import google.generativeai as genai

# =========================================================
# CONFIG
# =========================================================
GEMINI_API_KEY = "yourgoogleAPIKEY"   # hardcoded per spec
MODEL_NAME     = "gemini-3.5-flash-lite"      # swap if unavailable
EMBED_MODEL    = "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
COLLECTION     = "venkatesh_docs"
UPLOAD_DIR     = "uploads"
CHROMA_DIR     = "chroma_db"

os.makedirs(UPLOAD_DIR, exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(CHROMA_DIR, exist_ok=True)

genai.configure(api_key=GEMINI_API_KEY)
llm = genai.GenerativeModel(MODEL_NAME)

app = Flask(__name__)
CORS(app)

# =========================================================
# CHROMA + EMBEDDER (loaded once)
# =========================================================
chroma_client = chromadb.PersistentClient(
    path=CHROMA_DIR, settings=Settings(anonymized_telemetry=False)
)
collection = chroma_client.get_or_create_collection(
    name=COLLECTION, metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"}
)

embedder = SentenceTransformer(EMBED_MODEL)

# In-memory BM25 index rebuilt on demand
_bm25 = {"index": None, "ids": [], "docs": []}


def rebuild_bm25():
    """Rebuild BM25 from everything currently in ChromaDB."""
    data = collection.get(include=["documents"])
    docs = data.get("documents") or []
    ids = data.get("ids") or []
    if not docs:
        _bm25.update(index=None, ids=[], docs=[])
        return
    tokenized = [re.findall(r"\w+", d.lower()) for d in docs]
    _bm25.update(index=BM25Okapi(tokenized), ids=ids, docs=docs)


# =========================================================
# FILE EXTRACTION
# =========================================================
def chunk_text(text, size=800, overlap=100):
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    chunks, i = [], 0
    while i < len(text):
        chunks.append(text[i : i + size])
        i += size - overlap
    return [c for c in chunks if c.strip()]


def extract_pdf(path):
    reader = PdfReader(path)
    return "\n".join((p.extract_text() or "") for p in reader.pages)


def extract_docx(path):
    d = docx.Document(path)
    parts = [p.text for p in d.paragraphs]
    for t in d.tables:
        for row in t.rows:
            parts.append(" | ".join(c.text for c in row.cells))
    return "\n".join(parts)


def extract_xlsx(path):
    wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(path, data_only=True)
    out = []
    for ws in wb.worksheets:
        out.append(f"### Sheet: {ws.title}")
        for row in ws.iter_rows(values_only=True):
            out.append(" | ".join("" if v is None else str(v) for v in row))
    return "\n".join(out)


def extract_pptx(path):
    prs = Presentation(path)
    out = []
    for i, slide in enumerate(prs.slides, 1):
        out.append(f"### Slide {i}")
        for shape in slide.shapes:
            if hasattr(shape, "text") and shape.text.strip():
                out.append(shape.text)
    return "\n".join(out)


EXTRACTORS = {
    ".pdf":  extract_pdf,
    ".docx": extract_docx,
    ".xlsx": extract_xlsx,
    ".pptx": extract_pptx,
}


def ingest_file(filepath, original_name):
    ext = os.path.splitext(filepath)[1].lower()
    if ext not in EXTRACTORS:
        return 0
    try:
        raw = EXTRACTORS[ext](filepath)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[extract error] {original_name}: {e}")
        return 0

    chunks = chunk_text(raw)
    if not chunks:
        return 0

    ids = [f"{original_name}::{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}::{i}" for i in range(len(chunks))]
    metas = [{"source": original_name, "chunk": i} for i in range(len(chunks))]
    embs = embedder.encode(chunks, show_progress_bar=False).tolist()

    collection.add(ids=ids, documents=chunks, embeddings=embs, metadatas=metas)
    return len(chunks)


# =========================================================
# HYBRID SEARCH
# =========================================================
def hybrid_search(query, k=5, alpha=0.6):
    """
    Fuse dense (cosine similarity) and BM25 keyword scores.
    alpha = weight for dense; 1-alpha = weight for BM25.
    """
    if collection.count() == 0:
        return []

    q_emb = embedder.encode([query]).tolist()
    dense = collection.query(
        query_embeddings=q_emb, n_results=min(k * 3, collection.count())
    )

    dense_ids   = dense["ids"][0]
    dense_docs  = dense["documents"][0]
    dense_metas = dense["metadatas"][0]
    dense_dists = dense["distances"][0]          # cosine distance → similarity
    dense_scores = {i: 1 - d for i, d in zip(dense_ids, dense_dists)}

    bm25_scores = {}
    if _bm25["index"] is not None:
        toks = re.findall(r"\w+", query.lower())
        scores = _bm25["index"].get_scores(toks)
        max_s = max(scores) if len(scores) else 0
        for i, s in zip(_bm25["ids"], scores):
            bm25_scores[i] = (s / max_s) if max_s > 0 else 0.0

    # Normalise dense scores to [0,1]
    if dense_scores:
        dmax = max(dense_scores.values()) or 1
        dense_scores = {k: v / dmax for k, v in dense_scores.items()}

    all_ids = set(dense_scores) | set(bm25_scores)
    fused = {
        i: alpha * dense_scores.get(i, 0) + (1 - alpha) * bm25_scores.get(i, 0)
        for i in all_ids
    }

    top = sorted(fused.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:k]

    id_to_meta = {i: m for i, m in zip(dense_ids, dense_metas)}
    id_to_doc  = {i: d for i, d in zip(dense_ids, dense_docs)}

    results = []
    for cid, score in top:
        if cid in id_to_doc:
            results.append(
                {"text": id_to_doc[cid], "meta": id_to_meta.get(cid, {}), "score": score}
            )
    return results


# =========================================================
# ROUTES
# =========================================================
@app.route("/")
def index():
    return render_template("index.html")


@app.route("/api/upload", methods=["POST"])
def upload():
    """Accepts multiple files from 'files' field. Returns per-file status."""
    files = request.files.getlist("files")
    if not files:
        return jsonify({"error": "No files provided"}), 400

    saved, total_chunks = [], 0
    for f in files:
        if not f.filename:
            continue
        ext = os.path.splitext(f.filename)[1].lower()
        if ext not in EXTRACTORS:
            saved.append({"name": f.filename, "status": "unsupported"})
            continue
        dest = os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, f.filename)
        f.save(dest)
        n = ingest_file(dest, f.filename)
        total_chunks += n
        saved.append({"name": f.filename, "status": "ok", "chunks": n})

    rebuild_bm25()
    return jsonify({"files": saved, "total_chunks": total_chunks})


@app.route("/api/files", methods=["GET"])
def list_files():
    """Distinct source file names currently embedded."""
    data = collection.get(include=["metadatas"])
    names = sorted({m.get("source") for m in (data.get("metadatas") or []) if m})
    return jsonify({"files": names})


@app.route("/api/files", methods=["DELETE"])
def delete_file():
    name = (request.json or {}).get("name")
    if not name:
        return jsonify({"error": "name required"}), 400

    data = collection.get(include=["metadatas"])
    to_del = [
        cid for cid, m in zip(data["ids"], data["metadatas"])
        if m.get("source") == name
    ]
    if to_del:
        collection.delete(ids=to_del)

    # also remove the raw file if present
    raw = os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, name)
    if os.path.exists(raw):
        try:
            os.remove(raw)
        except OSError:
            pass

    rebuild_bm25()
    return jsonify({"deleted": len(to_del), "file": name})


@app.route("/api/chat", methods=["POST"])
def chat():
    q = (request.json or {}).get("query", "").strip()
    if not q:
        return jsonify({"error": "empty query"}), 400

    hits = hybrid_search(q, k=5)
    context = "\n\n---\n\n".join(
        f"[{h['meta'].get('source')}]\n{h['text']}" for h in hits
    ) or "(no relevant context found)"

    prompt = (
        "You are Venkatesh RAG Chatbot, a helpful assistant. "
        "Answer using the CONTEXT below. If the answer is not in the context, "
        "say so clearly.\n\n"
        f"CONTEXT:\n{context}\n\n"
        f"QUESTION: {q}\n\n"
        "Format the answer in clean Markdown. Use fenced code blocks for code."
    )

    try:
        resp = llm.generate_content(prompt)
        answer = resp.text
    except Exception as e:
        answer = f"**LLM error:** `{e}`\n\nContext retrieved:\n\n{context}"

    return jsonify({
        "answer": answer,
        "sources": [{"source": h["meta"].get("source"), "score": round(h["score"], 3)} for h in hits],
    })


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rebuild_bm25()
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)

title: I built a CSS shadow generator. Figuring out deployment took longer than writing the actual code.
description:
I've always hated how existing CSS shadow generators work. They either cap you at 2 layers, shove ads everywhere, or ask for an email before letting you copy a simple box-shadow. Some of them have pop-ups that cover half the screen the moment you open the page.

So I decided to build my own — one that actually respects the user.

I'm not a senior frontend developer, so I used Qwen AI to write the core logic. It took about two days. Ironically, getting the site live took way longer. DNS records, Netlify, custom domains... I've never deployed a website before, so figuring out how to put it on the internet was a real adventure on its own.

I tried to make the UI look modern and clean, avoiding that "tool built in 2010" vibe. Here's what you actually get compared to the usual alternatives:

  • 🌫️ Up to 10 shadow layers (most free tools cap at 2 or 3)
  • 🛡️ Zero pop-up ads, zero trackers, zero forced sign-ups. The site opens and just works.
  • ⚡ One-click CSS copy
  • 👁️ Live preview with 3D tilt
  • 📦 Export code in multiple formats: CSS, Tailwind, Swift, and Kotlin (Kotlin is still in beta, but it works)
  • 🎨 Copy directly for Figma (also beta)
  • 🔗 Share URL — save your shadow config as a link and come back to it later
  • ⬇️ Download the CSS as a file if you prefer
  • 🕐 Full action history — your 5 most recent shadow designs are saved locally in the browser, and you can restore any of them with one click
  • ↩️ Undo/redo support so you can step back if you mess up a slider
  • 🎭 Shadow presets (Dreamy, Brutal, Glass) if you don't want to start from scratch
  • 🌙 Dark UI that doesn't hurt your eyes at 2 AM

About the pricing and the timer you might see on the site

Right now, all Pro features are completely free as part of an early access offer. The countdown is just a placeholder for when this early period ends.

But here is the honest truth: this plan is not set in stone.

If I realize that locking certain features behind a paywall feels unfair or disrupts your workflow, I will simply keep them free. I have no intention of pulling the rug out from under people who rely on the tool.

Instead, if a paid tier ever happens, I will invent new, genuinely useful features specifically for it (like cloud sync, advanced team sharing, or a dedicated Figma plugin). The goal is for the paid version to earn its keep by adding new value, not by taking away what is already useful and free.

Core features like 10-layer shadows, one-click copy, live preview, and local history will always remain free, no matter what. No credit card required right now. No hidden limits. No annoying pop-ups. Just a clean tool that works.

I need your feedback!

I'm completely open to criticism, advice, or bug reports. If something feels clunky, the design is off, a feature is missing, or the code I generated with AI is ugly — let me know. Even a "this is useless" is useful feedback at this stage.

👉 You can try the site here: https://shdwstudio.com

👉 Safe CodePen sandbox: If you don't trust clicking random links (which is fair), here is a demo where you can see the clean CSS output it generates before going anywhere: CodePen Demo

title: The Architecture of Viral Parody: Audio-Driven Sync, Spatial Constraints, and the Death of Complex AI Toolchains
description:
Why modern creators and engineers are abandoning bloated diffusion pipelines in favor of single-purpose, browser-first micro-studios.

If you followed the generative video landscape over the past two years, the consensus was clear: the future belonged to general-purpose, open-ended prompt engines. Developers built increasingly elaborate ComfyUI node graphs, experimented with complex negative prompt weighting, and integrated multi-gigabyte LoRA models to produce short video clips.

Yet as we move through late 2026, real-world consumer behavior has delivered a sharp reality check.

Everyday users, digital creators, and developers don't want to manage local Python virtual environments, configure cloud GPUs, or pay $29-to-$60 monthly subscriptions for tools they use intermittently. Nowhere has this architectural shift been more evident than in the explosive viral spread of the "Outstanding" Tiny Desk meme across TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts.

When millions of users wanted to place a friend, colleague, or pet behind an intimate acoustic desk belting out soulful R&B vocals, they didn't reach for open-prompt diffusion platforms. They turned to hyper-focused, browser-first micro-studios.

Here is an architectural breakdown of why constrained single-purpose web applications are beating open-prompt giants, how audio-driven synchronization solves the uncanny valley, and why consumer software is returning to frictionless, transaction-based web models.

1. The Open-Prompt Bottleneck: Why Generalist Models Fail at Satire

Satire and comedy operate on extreme precision. In short-form video, humor is born from the tension between an absurd situation and deadpan realism.

When developers attempt to build comedic parody pipelines using general-purpose text-to-video APIs, three fundamental engineering bottlenecks emerge:

A. Environmental Drift and Spatial Hallucination

When an open-ended diffusion model is given a prompt such as "a man singing behind an acoustic wooden desk with bookshelves," it treats every single frame as a stochastic probability field. Across a 10-second sequence, the desk surface warps, background vinyl records turn into indistinct textures, and microphones float through the subject's face.

Comedic satire requires the setting to be indisputable and rock-solid. If the audience notices the background breathing or morphing, the immersion breaks, and the joke fails.

B. Facial Identity Elasticity

Standard video generation pipelines struggle to maintain facial structural landmarks during expressive, high-velocity audio performances. To force a static 2D portrait to sing, generic tools often over-smooth facial textures into waxy plastic or distort the jawline beyond recognition. The humor of a parody depends entirely on recognizing your actual friend or coworker singing—not an anonymous CGI avatar.

C. The Cognitive Friction of Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering was always a transitional user interface. Forcing an everyday user to guess magic keywords ("photorealistic, 8k, octane render, vintage condenser mic, steady tripod") is an anti-pattern. Great web engineering abstracts prompt mechanics completely away from the user interface.

2. Spatial Constraint as an Architectural Moat

The solution to environmental drift is not larger models or longer prompts; it is radical environmental constraint.

By eliminating spatial freedom and locking the generative canvas into an immutable physical scene, engineering teams can solve the majority of visual artifacts:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   GENERAL DIFFUSION VS CONSTRAINED UX                  │
├────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Open-Prompt Pipelines      │ Free-form text input → Unpredictable room │
│                            │ geometry → Frequent facial distortion.    │
├────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Constrained Micro-Studios  │ Fixed acoustic staging → 100% focus on    │
│                            │ facial fidelity → Zero background drift.  │
└────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

In the case of the Tiny Desk meme, the physical setting is iconic and fixed:

  • An intimate, cluttered wooden desk framed by analog studio monitors;
  • Curated paperbacks and vintage vinyl records in the background;
  • Soft, incandescent warm lighting replicating a real creative office session;
  • A classic retro condenser microphone anchored in the lower-middle third of the frame.

By keeping the background geometry deterministic, the synthesis pipeline can allocate 100% of its computing budget to what actually matters: natural facial preservation and micro-expression timing.

3. Audio-Driven Lip Sync: The Mechanics of Believability

Singing is far more complex than opening and closing a mouth mesh. Believable vocal performance requires phoneme-accurate mouth articulation, throat muscle tension, rhythmic brow movement, and natural eyelid squinting on sustained notes.

Modern micro-studios decouple audio generation from video rendering:

  1. Mastered Audio Anchoring: Rather than generating synthetic audio on the fly, the pipeline anchors the performance to an authentic, high-fidelity acoustic track (such as Charlie Wilson's viral live performance of "Outstanding" from NPR Music).
  2. Audio-to-Phoneme Alignment: The audio spectrum directly drives the temporal deformation of the lips and jaw, ensuring that vowel transitions and consonant stops match the rhythm down to the millisecond.
  3. Identity Landmark Locking: Critical facial identifiers—eye spacing, smile lines, nasal bridge contours, and skin tone—are preserved without the synthetic smoothing typical of generic video filters.

The result is a clip that passes the "10-Second Believability Threshold": viewers instantly recognize their real-life colleague or friend delivering an emotional musical performance with complete sincerity.

4. The Engineering Case Study: Building a Zero-Prompt Web Studio

An illustrative implementation of this architecture is TinyDeskMeme, a specialized browser platform engineered specifically for the viral acoustic desk format.

Instead of building a heavyweight native desktop application or asking users to install mobile apps with predatory permissions, the service is built as a pure, browser-first Tiny Desk meme video generator:

flowchart LR
    A["1. Client-Side Upload\n(1 Portrait from Mobile Camera Roll)"] --> B["2. Format Selection\n(9:16 Vertical for TikTok / 16:9 Landscape)"]
    B --> C["3. Cloud Orchestration\n(Locked desk staging + audio-driven sync)"]
    C --> D["4. Direct MP4 Delivery\n(10s HD video ready in browser, zero app install)"]

Key Architectural Decisions:

  • Zero Client-Side Footprint: Everything runs inside modern mobile and desktop browsers (Safari, Chrome, Firefox). Users never install native apps or manage local software dependencies.
  • No Prompt Syntax Required: Users never write descriptions, configure seed values, or tweak sliders. You upload a clear photo, pick your desired aspect ratio, and the platform delivers the finished video.
  • The $9.99 One-Time Transaction: Rejecting the pervasive SaaS subscription trap ($29/month recurring models with artificial token expirations), platforms like tinydeskmeme.com employ a transparent guest-checkout model. Creators pay $9.99 for a completed video with zero ongoing billing commitments.

5. Architectural Principles for Next-Generation Creative Web Apps

For developers and founders building in the generative media space, the viral trajectory of the Tiny Desk meme offers four critical takeaways:

1. Abstract Away the Prompt

Prompts are a developer debug interface, not a consumer product. If your users have to spend ten minutes learning how to talk to your AI, your product design is incomplete. Constrain the problem space until a single button or upload handles the job.

2. Design for Algorithmic Retention

In short-form video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts), video length is a critical ranking factor. A 10-to-12-second clip is the optimal window: 0–2 seconds to establish the familiar desk setting, 3–7 seconds to introduce the unexpected vocals, and 8–10 seconds to deliver the comedic punch before looping automatically.

3. Respect Creator Time and Privacy

Users are exhausted by mandatory account creation, email verification loops, and forced software downloads just to test a single feature. Delivering immediate utility with clear data privacy and guest checkout builds far greater long-term brand equity than gating experiences behind registration walls.

Conclusion

The evolution of the creative web is moving rapidly from infinite generative complexity to frictionless, dedicated utility.

While large research labs continue building massive world-simulators, the tools that capture cultural mindshare are those that solve one exact creative problem with zero friction. By combining a culturally resonant audio format with locked environmental geometry and a seamless browser interface, single-purpose studios are proving that in modern software design, constraints are the ultimate foundation of creative excellence.

title: Vercel Sandbox commands now support stdin
description:
Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser, or send data to other command-line programs while they run.

In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand(). Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done:

You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin. The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends.

In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send(). Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit:

For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process().

Read the Sandbox documentation to get started.

title: Classify Text Data Using Embeddings API in Node.js: Supplier Invoice Guardrails
description:
Short answer: use embeddings to classify supplier-invoice fields by comparing the new field with pre-labeled examples, then require both a similarity threshold and a margin over the runner-up before accepting a tag. In a Node.js service, the HTTP call is the easy part. The durable decision is a versioned, reviewable record that can be reconciled later.

For a media business, the labels might be invoice_number, rights_period, territory, currency, and net_amount. Suppliers rarely use the same wording. “Term ending March 31” and “licensed window: Q1 2026” can describe the same business field even though a phrase matcher sees little overlap. An embedding turns each text into a vector; cosine similarity supplies an ordering among candidate labels.

The acceptance rule should be conservative. Pick the highest-scoring example only when its score clears a threshold and its lead over the second-best score clears a margin. Otherwise, return review_required. That single branch protects the ledger-like property that matters here: a questionable classification must remain visible instead of being silently rewritten by the next retry.

What is the invoice bill actually made of?

The dominant operational term is repeated embedding work. Suppose one month contains 20,000 invoice fields and the label set has 12 labels with five reference examples each. The reference corpus is 60 vectors; the changing workload is still 20,000 input embeddings, before retries, reprocessing, or human-review traffic. This is why the first control is retention-aware caching, not a clever similarity loop.

The vector is evidence, not a verdict.

Cache reference embeddings by a content digest and label-set version. Embed each normalized input once for a classification attempt, and attach the resulting decision to a stable key made from the document identifier, field name, label-set version, model identifier, and normalized-text digest. If the worker retries, the audit write must resolve to the same logical record. A payment backend would call this an exactly-once mindset; the transport itself does not provide exactly-once execution. The practical trap is allowing a retry to write a second row with a new timestamp: downstream reconciliation then sees two plausible labels, and a later operator cannot tell whether the supplier changed the field or the worker repeated it. Enforce uniqueness on the logical key, record the original request identifier, and make a conflict return the existing decision rather than silently applying a second one.

Keep the audit record smaller than the source document. It should contain the source document identifier, field name, selected label, top score, runner-up score, threshold, margin, label-set version, model identifier, request identifier, and a digest of normalized text. Retain raw invoice text only according to the applicable policy. This is an intentional trade-off: after raw text expires, the digest and scores can explain which decision was made, but they cannot recreate the supplier sentence. If reconstruction is mandatory, retain an encrypted source reference under the organization’s retention rules.

The cost-estimate route is useful when planning bulk inputs, but it does not replace an operational ledger. Count reference refreshes, retries, and review traffic as well as first-pass inputs. Cost is a control signal; classification quality and auditability remain the decision criteria.

Which boundary should accept a label?

Cosine similarity ranks candidates; it does not establish that the winning candidate is correct. A rights_period score of 0.86 against an invoice_date score of 0.84 is a weakly separated result, even though 0.86 looks precise. A lower score with a large margin can be safer for a narrow, well-evaluated label set.

Build an evaluation set with positive examples, neighboring labels, incomplete fields, supplier-specific wording, and malformed input. Version it with the label descriptions. When a supplier changes its template, add examples and run the same set again. Do not move a production threshold because one batch looked plausible; that is how an audit trail becomes a history of unrecorded policy changes.

{
  "field": "term ending",
  "label": "rights_period",
  "similarity": 0.86,
  "runner_up_similarity": 0.84,
  "decision": "review_required",
  "label_set_version": "media-invoice-2026-04"
}

The record is deliberately plain. A repeated request with the same source digest and label-set version should resolve to the same decision; a changed model or label set should produce a new attributable result rather than mutate history.

How do embeddings classify text data without hiding uncertainty?

The openai npm package or a direct HTTPS request can call /v1/embeddings. The application still owns normalization, reference-data versioning, similarity, thresholds, review routing, and persistence. A provider client should not decide whether a media invoice field is safe to post.

The following Go code contains the classification core. It is intentionally independent of a provider response shape, so a Node.js worker can use the same state transition after decoding its embedding response. Dimension mismatches, empty vectors, and empty fields become reviewable errors rather than accidental labels.

package classifier

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "math"
    "strings"
)

type Example struct {
    Label  string
    Vector []float64
}

func cosine(a, b []float64) (float64, error) {
    if len(a) == 0 || len(a) != len(b) {
        return 0, errors.New("embedding dimensions do not match")
    }
    var dot, aa, bb float64
    for i := range a {
        dot += a[i] * b[i]
        aa += a[i] * a[i]
        bb += b[i] * b[i]
    }
    if aa == 0 || bb == 0 {
        return 0, errors.New("zero vector")
    }
    return dot / (math.Sqrt(aa) * math.Sqrt(bb)), nil
}

func classify(text string, input []float64, examples []Example, threshold, margin float64) (string, float64, string, string, error) {
    normalized := strings.TrimSpace(text)
    if normalized == "" {
        return "", 0, "review_required", "", errors.New("empty field")
    }
    best, second, label := -1.0, -1.0, ""
    for _, example := range examples {
        score, err := cosine(input, example.Vector)
        if err != nil {
            return "", 0, "review_required", "", err
        }
        if score > best {
            second, best, label = best, score, example.Label
        } else if score > second {
            second = score
        }
    }
    decision := "review_required"
    if best >= threshold && best-second >= margin {
        decision = "accepted"
    }
    digest := sha256.Sum256([]byte(normalized))
    return label, best, decision, hex.EncodeToString(digest[:]), nil
}

For a larger label set, k-means or a FAISS-backed index can reduce comparisons. That optimization changes the failure surface: a nearest centroid is not automatically a business label, and an index refresh must be tied to a label-set version. For a dozen invoice fields, a linear scan is easier to inspect and can be the better quality-latency trade.

What does a retry-safe provider boundary look like?

The network boundary should make failure explicit. The key belongs in an environment variable, the method must be POST, non-success responses must expose their bodies, and a 429 response should honor Retry-After while applying exponential backoff. The audit write, which is a state-changing operation even if the embedding request is not, needs an idempotency key enforced by the persistence layer.

package embeddings

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func Request(body []byte, logicalID string) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        baseURL := os.Getenv("EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL")
        if baseURL == "" {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL is required")
        }
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", baseURL+"/v1/embeddings", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", logicalID)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return data, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("embeddings: HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("embeddings: retry limit exceeded")
}

The sample uses the plain REST surface, which is useful when the worker is not committed to a particular SDK. In a Node.js implementation, the equivalent can use the openai package or native HTTPS while preserving the same logical ID and status handling. Keep the provider request and the decision write separate in the audit model: one request identifier can explain transport activity, while the unique logical ID prevents duplicate classification records.

Which real service fits this workflow?

OpenAI is a sensible fit for a team already using its Node.js client and wanting a conventional managed embeddings workflow. Cohere is worth testing when multilingual or search-oriented behavior is central to the supplier corpus. Google Cloud Vertex AI fits an organization that already places identity, region, and governance controls inside Google Cloud. A self-hosted model behind an internal service gives the team more control over data movement and release cadence, but serving, capacity, upgrades, and observability become its responsibility.

Infrai fits a different boundary choice: several backend capabilities can sit behind one consistent REST contract and one key, so a later cost-estimation or bulk-processing integration does not require another SDK and credential flow. Its discovery surface is public and self-describing, with request and response schemas, and the documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. The broader surface is substantial: 295 routes across 20 modules. Those facts reduce integration friction for a polyglot backend; they do not improve embedding quality or remove the need for invoice-specific evaluation. The concrete advantage is breadth behind a simple surface: the invoice worker can use plain HTTP, while adjacent backend capabilities retain the same discovery and request conventions instead of creating a new integration boundary for every addition.

For Infrai, the relevant platform advantages are one key, one bill, and one consistent REST contract across backend capabilities, plus a plain HTTP interface that needs no SDK; a Node.js invoice worker and a later batch worker can therefore share the same boundary without changing language-specific client code. These advantages reduce integration friction without making a quality claim.

The comparison is easiest to keep honest when the decision is explicit:

Option Useful boundary Limitation for this classifier
OpenAI Existing Node.js client and managed embeddings Application-owned thresholds, review routing, and retention
Cohere Multilingual or search-oriented evaluation Another vendor boundary if the rest of the estate is elsewhere
Vertex AI Google identity, region, and governance controls Cloud coupling may be unsuitable for a mixed-provider estate
Gemini API Teams already standardized on Gemini models and credentials A separate model and operational boundary for a mixed-provider estate
OpenRouter A single access point for testing multiple model providers Provider selection and production governance need explicit ownership
Self-hosted model Control over data movement and release cadence Serving and capacity become an internal operating burden
Infrai One REST contract for several backend capabilities Breadth does not substitute for corpus-level quality testing

Do not choose on a generic ranking. Run the same labeled supplier corpus through the shortlisted services, measure classification quality and latency at the ingestion batch size, and keep the threshold and label-set version in the decision record. The right choice is the one whose operational boundary matches the controls the media workflow actually needs.

One limitation should remain visible in any broader platform review: the available facts do not make every adjacent capability equally ready. Audio transcription is marked unavailable, realtime voice-session access is pending and limited to the western region, and there is no dedicated moderation endpoint; text or image moderation requires a chat model with a json_schema fallback. Those boundaries are unrelated to invoice embeddings, but hiding them would make a supposedly independent comparison less useful.

Further reading

  • OpenAI, Embeddings guide: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/embeddings
  • Cohere, Embed API reference: https://docs.cohere.com/reference/embed
  • Google Cloud, Text embeddings: https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/embeddings/get-text-embeddings
  • FAISS, similarity search library: https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: A Feature Can Work Perfectly and Still Be a Bad User Experience
description:
A Feature Can Work Perfectly and Still Be a Bad User Experience

You can build a feature that works exactly as intended, passes its tests, and has no obvious bugs — and still leave users wondering why they should use it.

I've always been interested in both sides of creating digital products: how they look and how they work. Working across graphic design, animation, UI/UX, and software development has made me appreciate something that is easy to overlook when building applications.

Making something work and making something work well for people are two different challenges.

1. Functionality is only the beginning

Imagine you're building a task management application.

You implement task creation, editing, deletion, deadlines, and persistence. Everything works. The data is saved correctly, and the interface responds to user input.

Technically, you've accomplished what you set out to do.

But then someone opens the application for the first time.

They don't know where to begin. There are too many competing buttons. Important actions are buried in menus. The interface technically contains everything they need, but finding it requires more effort than it should.

The functionality isn't necessarily broken. The experience is.

This is why I think evaluating software purely by its feature list misses an important part of the picture.

A feature should do more than exist. It should help someone accomplish something.

2. Good design isn't just decoration

When people hear "UI design," they sometimes think about colors, gradients, shadows, animations, and rounded corners.

Those things can contribute to a polished interface, but they aren't the foundation of good design.

Good design also involves deciding:

  • What deserves the user's attention?
  • Which actions should be immediately accessible?
  • What information can be removed without losing meaning?
  • What should happen when something goes wrong?
  • How can the interface communicate what to do next?

Consider two buttons that perform the same action. One is surrounded by several competing controls, while the other appears exactly where the user expects to need it.

The underlying functionality is identical. The amount of thought required to use it may not be.

Visual polish can attract attention, but clarity and consistency help people use a product.

3. Developers and designers should think about the same problem

I've found it useful to think about product design and software engineering as connected disciplines rather than separate stages.

A designer might propose an interaction that feels natural but becomes difficult to implement reliably. A developer might implement a technically elegant solution that introduces unnecessary complexity for the user.

Neither perspective is sufficient on its own.

The important question is not simply whether a design looks good or whether an implementation is clever.

It's whether the solution works well within the technical constraints while helping the user accomplish their goal.

Sometimes that means simplifying the design. Sometimes it means changing the architecture. And sometimes it means questioning whether the feature needs to exist at all.

That last question is particularly important.

Building something because it is technically possible doesn't automatically make it worth building.

4. Every additional feature has a cost

When developing software, it's tempting to keep adding capabilities.

A new setting sounds useful. Another menu option seems reasonable. One more customization feature could make the product appeal to more people.

Individually, these decisions might make sense. Together, they can make an application unnecessarily complicated.

Every feature introduces some combination of interface elements, decisions, maintenance requirements, and potential edge cases.

That doesn't mean applications should be stripped down to the point where they become limited or frustrating.

It means each addition should have a purpose.

When deciding whether to introduce a feature, I think it's worth asking three questions:

  1. What problem does this solve?
  2. How frequently will someone benefit from it?
  3. Does the value justify the additional complexity?

These questions aren't a perfect formula for product decisions, but they can help separate genuinely useful functionality from features that merely make an application look more capable.

5. Start with the experience, then decide what to build

One practical approach is to describe the user's goal before designing the interface or writing the implementation.

For example, instead of starting with:

"I need a dashboard with five cards, three menus, and a settings panel."

Start with:

"The user needs to understand what requires their attention and decide what to do next."

That second description gives you a problem to solve rather than a predetermined collection of interface elements.

You can then explore different layouts, remove unnecessary steps, and determine which functionality is actually required.

Only after that does it become easier to evaluate implementation choices.

This doesn't eliminate iteration. In fact, iteration is essential. The initial design might be wrong, and real usage may reveal problems that weren't obvious during development.

But starting with the user's goal gives those iterations a clearer direction.

6. What I want to keep in mind when building products

As I continue working across software development and design, there are a few principles I want to carry into every project:

  • Clarity over unnecessary complexity. Users shouldn't have to decode an interface before they can use it.
  • Purpose over feature count. More functionality isn't automatically more value.
  • Consistency over isolated brilliance. An interaction should make sense within the rest of the product.
  • Usability alongside functionality. A feature isn't finished simply because its implementation works.
  • Iteration over assumptions. A design that seems obvious to its creator may not be obvious to someone encountering it for the first time.

None of these principles is particularly revolutionary. The challenge is applying them consistently, especially when deadlines, technical limitations, and ambitious ideas compete for attention.

Final thoughts

I think one of the most interesting parts of building software is that the engineering and design problems are often inseparable.

The code determines what a product can do. The design helps determine how people understand and use those capabilities. Product thinking connects both to a problem worth solving.

A technically impressive application can still be difficult to use. A beautiful interface can still fail to deliver value. The goal is to bring those pieces together.

When you build software, what do you prioritize first: functionality, usability, or visual design?

And have you ever used an application that worked perfectly but somehow still felt frustrating to use? I'd be interested to hear what made the experience that way.

title: AWS NAT Gateway: Giving Private Subnets Safe Internet Access
description:
Why do we need a NAT Gateway?

In the last session, we created a custom VPC with a private subnet to lock down backend databases and application servers. Nobody on the internet could reach them.

Network isolation is great for security, but it creates a real problem:

  • How does your private EC2 server download security updates (apt update or dnf update)?
  • How does it download packages or call external APIs like Stripe, Twilio, or GitHub?

If you attach an Internet Gateway directly to the private subnet, it is no longer private—anyone on the internet can scan your ports.

A NAT Gateway solves this problem. It allows private servers to reach out to the internet, while completely blocking the internet from starting connections back into your private servers.

1. What is NAT (Network Address Translation)?

Think of an office with a receptionist:

  • When an employee wants to call a client, the receptionist dials out using the office main phone number.
  • The client outside only sees the office company number, never the employee's personal desk extension.
  • When the client replies on that same call, the receptionist connects them back to the employee.
  • But if someone outside tries to call an employee directly without an active outbound call, the receptionist blocks the call. 
[ Private Subnet ]                         [ Public Subnet ]                 [ Internet ]
  Private EC2 (10.0.2.15)                   NAT Gateway (Elastic IP)          GitHub / External API
          │                                         │                                │
          │── Outbound: dnf update ────────────────►│── Outbound: Source = NAT EIP ─►│
          │                                         │                                │
          │◄── Inbound Reply ───────────────────────│◄── Inbound Reply ──────────────│
          │                                         │                                │
          │                                         │◄── Outside Inbound Probe ──────│ (Blocked ✗)

How the packets travel:

  1. Your private EC2 (10.0.2.15) wants to download software from the internet.
  2. The private route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway.
  3. The NAT Gateway replaces the private IP (10.0.2.15) with its own Elastic IP. It keeps track of this in its connection table.
  4. The packet goes through the Internet Gateway (IGW) out to the internet.
  5. When the website sends the data back, the NAT Gateway checks its table, swaps the destination IP back to 10.0.2.15, and hands the data to your private server.

Any outside connection coming in that was not started by your private server is immediately dropped.

2. Internet Gateway (IGW) vs. NAT Gateway

Both handle internet traffic, but they do completely different jobs:

What to look at Internet Gateway (IGW) NAT Gateway
Traffic Direction Inbound and Outbound (Two-way) Outbound only + replies come back
Used by Public subnets Private subnets
Needs a Public IP on EC2? Yes No (EC2 only needs a private IP)
IP Translation 1 to 1 (One public IP for one EC2) Many to 1 (Many private EC2s share 1 NAT Elastic IP)
Where do you put it? Attached to the whole VPC Sits inside a Public Subnet
Scaling Automatic Automatic (up to 100 Gbps)
Cost Free Hourly charge + per-GB data fee

3. How the Route Tables Work

For a NAT Gateway to work, you need two route tables set up like this:

Public Subnet Route Table (Where NAT Gateway lives)
Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local
0.0.0.0/0       igw-0abc123  (Internet Gateway)

Private Subnet Route Table
Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local
0.0.0.0/0       nat-0def456  (NAT Gateway)

The #1 Mistake: You must create your NAT Gateway inside a Public Subnet. If you place it inside a private subnet, the NAT Gateway cannot reach the Internet Gateway, and nothing will connect.

4. NAT Gateway vs. NAT Instance

Before AWS had managed NAT Gateways, engineers launched a small EC2 instance running Linux to do the job:

  • AWS NAT Gateway (Managed): Works out of the box, auto-scales up to 100 Gbps, and AWS handles all patching and hardware redundancy inside the AZ.
  • NAT Instance (EC2 you manage): Cheaper for quick student tests, but you have to disable Source/Destination Check, configure the Linux firewall yourself, and if that single EC2 instance stops or crashes, your whole private subnet loses internet access.

What is a Private NAT Gateway?

When creating a NAT Gateway in the AWS console, you will see two options:

  • Public: Has an Elastic IP. Used to give private subnets internet access.
  • Private: Has no Elastic IP. It is used when connecting two private networks (like on-premises to AWS via Transit Gateway) that have overlapping IP addresses. It cannot reach the internet.

5. High Availability (HA) & Saving Money

A NAT Gateway is redundant inside one Availability Zone (AZ), but it does not protect you across multiple AZs.

Multi-AZ Setup (Production)

If you run workloads in both AZ-a and AZ-b:

  • Put one NAT Gateway in AZ-a (public subnet).
  • Put one NAT Gateway in AZ-b (public subnet).
  • Point private subnets in AZ-a to NAT Gateway A, and private subnets in AZ-b to NAT Gateway B.
  • This prevents an outage in one AZ from cutting off your entire backend, and avoids cross-AZ data transfer fees. 
      Availability Zone A                       Availability Zone B
┌─────────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ [Public Subnet A]               │       │ [Public Subnet B]               │
│  NAT Gateway A (EIP A)          │       │  NAT Gateway B (EIP B)          │
│       ▲                         │       │       ▲                         │
│ [Private Subnet A]              │       │ [Private Subnet B]              │
│  App EC2 (Routes to NAT A)      │       │  App EC2 (Routes to NAT B)      │
└─────────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────────┘

How to avoid surprise bills:

NAT Gateways charge an hourly uptime fee plus a per-GB fee for all data passing through them:

  1. Use free VPC Gateway Endpoints for S3 & DynamoDB: S3 Gateway Endpoints are 100% free. If your private servers pull gigabytes of files or backups from S3 through a NAT Gateway, you pay data processing on every gigabyte. Adding a Gateway Endpoint routes that traffic directly to S3 within AWS at zero cost.
  2. Delete it when done with labs: Always delete your NAT Gateway and release the Elastic IP when you finish testing.

Hands-On Practice & Console Walkthrough

Here is the step-by-step walkthrough to set up a NAT Gateway and give your private EC2 instance outbound internet access.

Step 1: Create the NAT Gateway

  1. Go to VPC Console → click NAT Gateways → click Create NAT gateway.
  2. Name tag: lab-nat-gw.
  3. Subnet: Select your public subnet (public-subnet-1a).
  4. Connectivity type: Select Public.
  5. Elastic IP allocation ID: Click Allocate Elastic IP.
  6. Click Create NAT gateway. It takes about 1–2 minutes for the status to turn from Pending to Available.

![NAT Gateway Created in Public Subnet](

Fig 1: NAT Gateway created in public-subnet-1a with an allocated Elastic IP.

Step 2: Route the Private Subnet to the NAT Gateway

  1. Go to Route tables → select your private route table (private-rt).
  2. Open the Routes tab → click Edit routes → Add route:
    • Destination: 0.0.0.0/0
    • Target: Select NAT Gateway → pick lab-nat-gw.
  3. Click Save changes.

![Private Route Table Pointing to NAT Gateway](

Fig 2: Routing all outbound internet traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to the NAT Gateway.

Step 3: Test from the Private Instance

Log into your private EC2 instance (using AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or jumping through your public EC2):

# 1. Check your public IP from the private instance:
curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com

Output:

13.234.112.45

It prints the NAT Gateway's Elastic IP, not the EC2 private IP!

# 2. Test downloading packages:
sudo dnf update -y

Packages now download and install with no problem through the NAT Gateway.

Step 4: Verify Outside Inbound Traffic is Blocked

From your local computer terminal, try reaching the private instance through the NAT Gateway's Elastic IP:

curl --max-time 5 http://13.234.112.45
ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@13.234.112.45

Result:
Both commands time out. Nobody on the internet can connect directly to your private instance through the NAT Gateway.

Step 5: Clean Up (Avoid Surprise Bills!)

NAT Gateways charge money every hour they run. Once you finish:

  1. Go to NAT Gateways → select lab-nat-gw → Actions → Delete NAT gateway.
  2. Go to Route tables → edit your private route table and delete the 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat route.
  3. Go to Elastic IPs → select the allocated Elastic IP → Actions → Release Elastic IP addresses.

Wrap-up

Today's big takeaway was solving the private subnet internet problem:

  • Private subnets stay private, but can still download packages and call external APIs.
  • Always put your NAT Gateway in a public subnet with an Internet Gateway route.
  • For production, run one NAT Gateway per Availability Zone.
  • Use free S3 Gateway Endpoints to save money on data transfer fees.
