title: Hono on Prisma Postgres and Compute, What Worked and What Broke
description:
TL;DR

  • I deployed a Hono API on Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute with three commands, auth login, build and deploy, and I never installed Bun.
  • One bug caught me. In this scaffold, if a route queries the database before the template's /users route does, /users returns a 500 and the log shows DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED.
  • If you're sizing up the stack, Compute is GA, Composer (which declares and deploys Compute apps) is Early Access, and Prisma ORM 8 is still a release candidate at the time of writing. Pin your versions.

I wrote this article for Prisma, who commissioned it. The opinions are mine.

I built a small bookmarks API with Hono, put it on Prisma Postgres and deployed it to Prisma Compute. A coding agent, Gemini CLI, wrote most of the code from a prompt I wrote, and I kept a log of every error and every fix. The repo is public on GitHub, with the code, migrations, README and smoke test.

The app, a Hono bookmarks API with Prisma Postgres

I added six routes. GET /health, plus five for bookmarks (list, get one, create, update, delete). The scaffold adds GET / and GET /users, and /users matters later. A bookmark has an id, a unique URL, a title, optional notes and a createdAt.

I tested with Node 22.22.2, Gemini CLI 0.65.0 (with gemini-3.5-flash-lite selected), Prisma CLI 8.0.0-rc.21, @prisma/orm-postgres 8.0.0-rc.16 and @prisma/composer 0.28.0, in late October 2026. The Prisma packages have moved on since, so the findings apply to those versions. A re-run of the finished repo on Linux (Node and a local Postgres 16) is marked "on Linux" below.

A quick note on what you'd be building on. The Compute FAQ says Compute has been generally available since August 2026. Prisma's 28 August changelog and the Console both label Composer Early Access, and Prisma's docs call ORM 8 a release candidate at the time of writing.

I wrote the agent's rules in one prompt and made it stop after every phase. I ran every command that installed packages, used credentials or deployed to Prisma myself, and I never pasted my database URL into the agent.

Prisma Postgres with Hono, migrations and the direct vs pooled connection string

I created the database in the Console and it was ready in a few minutes. The connection dialog defaults to the pooled host (pooled.db.prisma.io) and tells you to put the string in .env. I came away with two things.

  • I used the direct host (db.prisma.io) for db:init, migrate and local dev. I didn't test the pooled string.
  • The scripts read DATABASE_URL from the shell, not from .env. On Linux, a valid .env file with no shell variable gave CONFIG.DB_CONNECTION_REQUIRED and created nothing. The Prisma Hono guide says the same.

The scaffold generates the first migration, and I generated the second with npm run migration:plan -- --name add-bookmarks. On my own database I ran db:init first (5 operations, the scaffold's tables) and migrate later, which applied the Bookmark migration. On Linux, migrate alone applied both migrations to an empty local database. The difference is that db:init builds tables straight from the contract, while migrate applies the migrations/ folder, which the Compute FAQ says a deploy applies for a Composer postgres() database. Both are safe to run twice (a second migrate says "Already up to date") and both mask credentials in their output. Every run also prints a pg warning that sslmode=require will change meaning in a future version.

Prisma ORM 8 unique constraint error and sqlState 23505

I put the rules in the prompt. Ids match ^[1-9][0-9]*$ and fit an int4, bodies over 10 KB get a 413 before parsing, URLs are stored as new URL(value).href, and the database's unique constraint decides duplicates. Gemini implemented them with a few early mistakes, including a wrong check order on PATCH, any types and a guessed duplicate check.

That guess is the interesting part. Gemini assumed a Postgres unique violation shows up as err.code === "23505". In ORM 8 the top-level code is undefined. I triggered a duplicate on purpose and logged the error. The useful fields, sqlState (23505) and constraint (Bookmark_url_key), sit on a SqlQueryError. The scaffold already ships the answer in .agents/skills/prisma-8/references/debug.md, which says driver errors "carry no dotted code" and to route on sqlState and the constraint metadata. My Phase 4 prompt named four skill files for Gemini to read and this wasn't one of them. I only read it while fact-checking this article.

Five simultaneous identical POSTs gave one 201 and four 409s.

Fixing DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED in a Prisma ORM 8 Hono app

I had an 85-check smoke test ready before the API existed. The first run came back 84 passed, 2 failed. That adds up to 86 results from 85 checks because the script also records a failure for any 5xx response, so one broken route printed two FAIL lines. Both were GET /users, a route that ships with the scaffold.

{"error":"Could not query users yet. Run contract:emit and apply your schema first."}

The schema was fine, and the server log said something else.

Postgres client already connected
code: DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED
fix: Call connect() at most once per client.

Here is what I worked out from the generated db.ts and the bundled dist/server.mjs. The ORM client connects in the background on its first query. The template's /users route goes through a helper that calls db.connect() explicitly. If one of my bookmark routes ran a query first, the background connect had already started and the explicit one threw. My routes queried db directly and never used the helper. This matches Prisma's runtime reference, which says to call connect() before any query or not at all, because a connect() after a query rejects with DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED.

After a clean restart, GET /bookmarks followed by GET /users gave 500, and 500 again five seconds later. That also explains why smoke run 2 passed with no code change. I'd restarted the server, and the script requests /users before any bookmarks route, so the explicit connect ran first. On Linux the same unfixed code passed all 85 checks on a fresh process, and gave 84 passed, 2 failed once a bookmarks request came first.

Gemini's fixes were the weak part. The first matched the error message text and returned quietly, which hides the error. The second put await connectDatabase() at the top of every handler, before validation, so a bad body would need a database connection just to be rejected. I rejected both. The third calls the helper right before the first query in each handler, after validation, and leaves /health alone. After that /bookmarks, /users, /users returned 200, 200, 200 and a full smoke run gave 85 passed.

The Linux re-run also showed that the guide's own example triggers it. With the guide's POST /users route (step 4) added to a copy of the repo, a fresh process gave 201 for POST /users and then 500 twice for GET /users, with DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED in the log. With GET /users first, the same three requests returned 200, 201 and 200. That was a local Postgres 16, not the deployed app, and the guide may have changed since.

The code compiled and my manual checks passed. Only a test run in the right order showed the problem. If you add a route to a Prisma scaffold, hit the template's own routes before and after yours, on a fresh process.

Deploy a Hono API to Prisma Compute

The Composer docs say local dev (prisma dev) isn't supported on Windows. I'm on Windows 10, so I never ran it, even though the scaffold's "next steps" box suggests it. These are the three commands I did run.

npx prisma auth login
npm run build
npx prisma deploy module.ts

All three worked. The Composer limitations page says deploys authenticate only with a service token, with "no browser flow", but the Composer deploying page documents auth login, and that's what I used. The two pages disagree and I couldn't tell which one is current.

I did three deploys.

  • The untouched scaffold took 3m 38s.
  • My bookmarks code took 3m 10s.
  • A redeploy of unchanged code took 50.4s.

Those are single runs from my machine, not a benchmark.

deploy doesn't build, so you run npm run build first. tsdown bundles everything into one dist/server.mjs of about 2 MB. The scaffold defaults to the us-east-1 region, and since I'm in India I changed one line in prisma.config.ts to ap-southeast-1.

The deployed app got its own Prisma Postgres database, and the migrated tables were there without my local DATABASE_URL being set. The deploy plan showed database-migrate (PrismaOrm.Migration) as updated, with no migration name. The Compute FAQ and the Compute limitations page both say the deploy applies your migrations/ to a Composer postgres() database before the service starts. My tables showed up after the deploy, which fits that, but I only know it from the result and not from the deploy output.

Compute runs the app on Bun even though my code is Node-style (@hono/node-server, built with tsdown for Node 22). The service log says starting bun with entrypoint: bootstrap.js. I installed nothing for that. The Composer getting-started page lists Bun as a prerequisite, so keep it in mind if local Node and deployed Bun ever behave differently.

The same 85 checks against the live app ended with 85 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped. I didn't save the output. My paste and a screenshot show 79 of the 85 PASS lines, no FAIL line, and the final Result line with the totals. I created a bookmark, redeployed unchanged code and fetched it again, and got the same row. The app keeps no data in memory, so that fits the data living in Postgres. I can't say whether the redeploy restarted the app, so I haven't tested that.

prisma service logs app failed right after the deploy with PROJECT.SETUP_REQUIRED, saying the directory wasn't linked to a project. It needs --project bookmarks-api. The log held two lines and no request lines. The Console overview also said "no deploys yet" while the app was live. The CLI had told me it wasn't recording the deploy because the folder had no git commit, so that may be expected, but I didn't check.

Prisma Compute latency from India

These numbers are my own network path to ap-southeast-1, not a benchmark, and the bookmarks table was empty. The idle test sent one request to /health and then one to /bookmarks from the same process, so the second request likely reused the first one's connection and skipped DNS and TLS. I didn't verify that. The 30 warm requests per endpoint came about 70 seconds later.

Test /health /bookmarks
First two requests after about 16 hours idle (estimated) 682.7 ms 363.5 ms
30 warm requests, median 120.8 ms 127.5 ms
30 warm requests, p95 745.7 ms 134.9 ms

Twenty-eight of the 30 warm /health requests took 116.5 to 130.8 ms. Request 1 took 745.7 ms, and with 30 values that is also the p95, so it says little about typical latency. Request 20 took 967.9 ms and I don't know why. Prisma says idle Compute instances resume in milliseconds, but I can't call my idle figure a cold start because DNS, TLS and any wake-up are mixed into it.

npm audit on a Prisma Compute project and its 14 vulnerabilities

npm ci reports 14 vulnerabilities (5 moderate, 9 high). On Linux they traced back to alchemy and an old nested @prisma/dev, plus lodash through a parser package. Also on Linux, a search of dist/server.mjs found no @prisma/dev or lodash, and its only alchemy mentions are three code comments. The app itself uses the top-level hono 4.13.13 and @hono/node-server 2.1.5, which the audit doesn't flag. A bundle search is not a security review. Don't run npm audit fix --force, because it proposes @prisma/composer and @prisma/composer-prisma-cloud 0.6.0 and prisma 7.10.1, a step back from ORM 8.

What worked, and what I'd tell the Prisma team

What worked well. Once I'd signed in with auth login, build and deploy ran without prompts, and the deployed app arrived with its own database. The doc comments in the installed types also say what update and delete return when nothing matches.

What I'd suggest to Prisma. Each of these comes from something I saw.

  • The template's /users error tells you to run contract:emit, but the server log showed DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED. Logging or returning the underlying error would save someone an afternoon. The runtime reference and the scaffold's skill file describe the lazy connect, but the Hono guide I read doesn't, and the template's own helper calls connect() explicitly. The guide's own POST /users example queries db without connecting, so it runs into the same error.
  • The Composer limitations page says deploys use a service token with no browser flow, while the Composer deploying page documents auth login. A note on which is current would settle it.
  • The deploy plan could name the migration it ran.
  • prisma deploy found my project from the folder, but prisma service logs said the directory wasn't linked to one. Sharing that link between the two commands would save a step.
  • The ORM 8 query types live in @prisma/orm-family-sql, not in the package you install, so they took several searches to find.
  • Versions move fast. A couple of days after I scaffolded, the CLI was telling me 8.0.0-rc.27 existed.

Before you copy the repo

  • GET /users is a scaffold route, and it inserts three sample users on its first call.
  • createdAt comes back as Postgres text (2026-10-23 16:33:47.512805+00), not ISO 8601, because the contract uses the scaffold's TimestamptzString type.
  • There's no auth, so anyone with the URL can write to it. Prisma's pricing page gives the Prisma Postgres Free plan 200,000 operations a month, and the Compute FAQ says the Free plan has no backups. I'm not publishing my live URL.
  • A NUL character (\u0000) in title or notes returns 500 instead of 400. A lone surrogate or invalid UTF-8 is stored as the replacement character. These turned up when the repo was probed with odd input on Linux, and the 85 checks don't cover them. They're listed in the README and not fixed.

What I didn't test

I didn't test prisma dev (unsupported on Windows), the pooled connection string, the Prisma MCP server, Bash on Windows or macOS, or how Compute behaves when idle database connections drop. I tested one small API with an empty table, so I can't speak to load or larger projects. The docs changed several times while I worked, so re-check the linked pages before you rely on any of this.

My verdict

I'd use this stack again. Going from a scaffold to a live API with its own Prisma Postgres database took three commands. The one real bug I hit depended on the order my routes and the scaffold's /users route queried the database, and I could trace and fix it. At the time of writing, ORM 8 is still a release candidate and Composer is in Early Access, so before I ran production traffic on it I'd wait for those, and for the docs to agree on auth. The code, README and smoke test are in the repo.

title: The sign-up form project
description:
Devoted Code: The sign up form that Gentle Criminal deserves!
By irl La Brava 💻❤️

Init:

This is a different project that I made. Yes, it is also a fan-art project, but this fan-art projects elevates itself to new heights. All to bring in more fans, and redirect to Gentle Criminal, and show how it looks like! Now it has finally come to life! If you are wondering how I named it I shall let you know: the signing up for Gentle Productions! Where imperial tea is promoted, unique surprises are yet to be found with the utmost elegance, all brought to life to show case the best heist ever.

A fan art project from My Hero Academia. Then, as I was trying to figure out how to write this article, I had an epiphany, and made two mode additions, and created a Javascript file, going beyond what the assignment in the curriculum asked for!
To go beyond, and to start with, allow me to describe you the following: I built custom sign-up and broadcast portal from scratch. A La Brava x Gentle Criminal thematic project!

As for the technical breakdown of how I designed, engineered, and styled this platform using semantic HTML5, modern CSS flexbox layouts, and client-side validation logic:

**

1// Architectural Overview & Structural Foundations//**

The project was constructed with a clean, decoupled two-file architecture (index.html and style.css) managed under local Git version control.

To create an immersive broadcast experience, I divided the viewport into a high-contrast dual-panel layout:
• The Hero/Broadcast Panel (Left): Houses Gentle's official logo, live stream status badges, custom SVG graphics, and his inspirational opening address.
• The Credentials Panel (Right): A structured, accessible sign-up form designed for supporters to register for exclusive updates and royal tea samples.
Semantic Markup & Targeted Contrast
To direct the viewer's eye through Gentle's speech and call-out notices, I utilized semantic HTML5 elements alongside precise wrappers. Rather than styling entire blocks indiscriminately, specific inline wrappers (.header-callout and .quote-pink) were applied to highlight key phrases in glowing cyber-neon pink against the imperial purple background.

`HTML


"My dear one, you the one who made this happen...
...Ah no, you're not my dear beloved one, but you're still the chosen one! Why you ask? To support the one and only Gentle Criminal!"

`

**

2// Vector Graphics: Handcrafting the G.C Imperial SVG Badge**

A true gentleman requires a regal mark. Rather than using raster images that degrade on high-resolution screens, I hand-coded a custom vector graphic (
• The Heart Frame: A deep magenta utilizing drop-shadow filters to represent my unwavering devotion and system protection.
• Rising Steam Lines: Dual curves rendered in hot pink and gold to represent the aroma of freshly brewed imperial tea.
• The Monogram & Mustache: A crisp node for the G.C initials in royal gold, anchored by Gentle's iconic white handlebar mustache at the base.
SVG

**

3// Styling & Color Palette Variables (:root)**

To maintain complete visual harmony across dark mode surfaces, I defined global CSS custom properties (:root). The stylesheet balances Gentle's aristocratic purple and gold palette with my cyber-neon accents.
CSS

:root {
    /* La Brava Palette */
    --pink-neon: #ff1493;
    --pink-glow: rgba(255, 20, 147, 0.4);
    --pink-light: #ff69b4;

    /* Gentle Criminal Palette */
    --purple-dark: #0d0714;
    --purple-deep: #190a26;
    --purple-card: #251038;
    --purple-accent: #4c1d95;
    --gold-accent: #f4d03f;
    --gold-glow: rgba(244, 208, 63, 0.3);
    --silver-text: #e2e8f0;
    --lavender-light: #d8b4fe;

}

**
///4*Layout Mechanics & Responsiveness*//**

The core layout utilizes Flexbox (display: flex) with a proportion ratio of 1.2 : 1 between the hero panel and form container. Background depth was achieved using layered radial gradients (radial-gradient), giving the surface a subtle glowing ambient effect.
To support viewers on mobile devices or smaller display setups, media queries automatically re-orient the dual panels into a vertical stack at viewports under 950px:
CSS
@media (max-width: 950px) {
.page-wrapper {
flex-direction: column;
}
.hero-panel {
border-right: none;
border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(244, 208, 63, 0.2);
}
}

**

5// Client-Side Input Validation Logic//**

To protect our system from unauthorized noise, input fields utilize native HTML5 validation pseudo-classes (:valid, :focus:invalid). Additionally, a lightweight JavaScript block monitors password field inputs in real-time, enforcing match checks before form submission.
JavaScript
function validatePassword() {
if (confirmPasswordInput.value === '') {
confirmPasswordInput.setCustomValidity('');
errorMessage.textContent = '';
return;
}

if (passwordInput.value !== confirmPasswordInput.value) {
    confirmPasswordInput.setCustomValidity('Passwords do not match');
    errorMessage.textContent = 'Passwords must match';
} else {
    confirmPasswordInput.setCustomValidity('');
    errorMessage.textContent = '';
}

}

In ##4, is the latest addition. I wanted to add more, to try more to satisfy myself. I went even further than what the curriculum asked, and I searched how to establish a solid front-end baseline with real-time input sanitization, native HTML5 validation integration, password matching checks, and a submission cooldown timer.
**

5. ** Invisible Honeypot Trap (website_hp)**

  • Scraper & Bot Trap: Built a decoy field (<input type="text" id="website_hp" name="website_hp">) hidden inside a zero-visibility container (display: none; and aria-hidden="true").
  • Zero Human Distraction: Human users traversing the form natively via keyboard navigation or visual rendering will never see or interact with this input. Automated scrapers and bot scripts, however, automatically populate every visible and hidden field they encounter. If populated, the submission is immediately rejected client-side.

**

6. ** Cloudflare Turnstile Bot Defense**

  • Interactive Anti-Bot Verification: Integrated Cloudflare's privacy-friendly Turnstile widget (3x00000000000000000000FF) directly into the HTML structure. This allows full interactive testing of bot verification without requiring a paid dashboard account or domain registration.

  • Deep CSS Theme Overrides: Reached into the Turnstile container using forced CSS priority (!important) to convert any fallback, error, or troubleshoot hyperlinks into our imperial gold theme (#f4d03f) with neon pink hover glows (#ff69b4), keeping the security widget completely visually unified with the dark purple broadcast layout.

Summary:
By combining precise semantic HTML structure, strict CSS variable systems, custom inline vector art, and dynamic responsive layouts, Gentle Productions now possesses a digital sign-up portal fit for a true revolutionary, plus enforcing front-end security to go beyond!

Every single line of code was written with absolute devotion—because nothing less is worthy of Gentle Criminal! ❤️💻

Any questions you have? Let me know!

Check it out here:

https://labrava0x.github.io/Gentle-sign-up-form/

title: Introducing Agent Plugins
description:
Today, Agent Plugins 1.0.0 is publicly available. Agent Plugins is an open, vendor-neutral standard for plugins that extend AI agents.

Agent Skills provide reusable instructions and resources for AI agents. MCP servers connect agents to tools and services. Both can be reused across clients, but clients often package and discover them differently.

Agent Plugins gives compatible clients a common format: a directory with a plugin.json manifest and fixed locations for its components. The format is intentionally small and easy to implement, and it leaves installation, distribution, policy, user experience, and client-specific capabilities to each client.

One package for the portable parts

Extension authors often adapt the same component to several client formats. Even though the underlying Skill or MCP server is identical, clients often expect different top-level metadata, discovery paths, or MCP configuration.

Agent Plugins gives those shared components one predictable, structured home:

A minimal JSON manifest (plugin.json) identifies the specification version and names the plugin:

Those two fields are the minimum requirement for the manifest, and the rest of the contract is represented in the file structure of the directory itself. A reusable component should not need to be repackaged for every client, so the format specifies only what a client needs to discover and load what is inside.

Every compatible client checks for plugin.json at the plugin root. Clients that support Skills discover them under skills/. Clients that support MCP servers read their configuration from mcp.json. A client can support either component type or both. After the client validates the manifest, components are validated independently, so one invalid component does not disable unrelated ones.

For plugin authors, that means fewer client-specific conventions for the same component. For client implementers, the specification defines a small, deterministic contract for discovery, validation, and loading.

Small on purpose

Agent Plugins defines the portable contract for a plugin and leaves the behavior of the client up to each client.

Version 1 focuses that contract on two component types: Agent Skills and MCP servers. Both already have specifications and meaningful adoption of their own, and Agent Plugins does not attempt to redefine them. Agent Plugins provides a shared definition of how clients find the components together in a distributable plugin.

Other components, such as commands, hooks, and agents, remain with clients. The Technical Steering Committee may consider additional component types in future versions as semantics converge and a demonstrated portability need emerges.

Keeping the boundary small makes the format easier to implement and gives the ecosystem room to converge before adding more portable surface area.

Clients retain flexibility

Clients need freedom to innovate while a shared format evolves, so Agent Plugins includes a namespaced extension mechanism for client-specific data and files.

Extensions remain outside the portable contract. Each client defines its own namespace, and other clients ignore it. This prevents client-specific behavior from leaking into the common format or blocking adoption of the shared components. A client-specific capability can remain client-specific until there is reason and consensus to standardize it.

An open, multi-vendor project

Vercel initiated the proposal, which representatives from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Anysphere, GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel refined collaboratively into Agent Plugins 1.0.0.

The initial Technical Steering Committee includes Core Maintainers from AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel.

The project is openly licensed, and its maintainers, contribution process, and technical decisions are public. No single company's product roadmap sets the format's direction.

Build with Agent Plugins 1.0.0

The specification, its JSON Schemas, and guides for plugin authors and client implementers are available at agent-plugins.org. Governance and the contribution process live in the Agent Plugins specification repository on GitHub.

If you author agent extensions, you can use the specification to package Skills and MCP servers behind one portable manifest. If you build an agent client, the specification's conformance checklist defines the minimum requirements for discovering and loading Agent Plugins.

At launch, Agent Plugins are supported across:

  • ChatGPT and Codex

  • Cursor

  • GitHub Copilot

  • Kiro

  • VS Code

Plugin authors can package components once, and their plugin will automatically carry between supporting clients.

Agent Plugins is a contract between the authors who build extensions for agents and the clients that load them. That contract is now defined and open for both sides to shape.

Read more

title: Playing a torrent while it downloads: how I got start time from 41 s to 8 s
description:
You hit play on a video that's still downloading, and the player immediately wants bytes you don't have. First the start of the file. Then, quite often, the end, because that's where an MP4 keeps its index. Then wherever you drag the seek bar. BitTorrent doesn't care about any of that: it grabs pieces in whatever order the swarm hands them out, rarest first.

Getting those two to cooperate turned out to be most of the work.

I needed this for Torsher, the self-hosted media center I'm building, and I gave myself one rule: on a normal home connection, playback has to start in under 15 seconds. Below is what I tried, what failed, and the numbers.

Every test used Blender's open movies (Sintel, Big Buck Bunny, Tears of Steel). They're free to share, which makes them perfect for this.

How I measured

I didn't want to click around a browser all evening, so a small script pretends to be the player:

  • start: grab the first 2 MB and the last 1 MB of the file at the same time, and time how long until both are in;
  • seek: grab 2 MB from the middle of the file, then 2 MB from 85% in.

Each run starts from scratch: torrent removed, files deleted. Two rounds per engine, swapping the order between them. Fetching the torrent's metadata isn't counted.

First try: a ready-made library

I started with an existing Rust library that already had streaming built in. Median start: 41 seconds. Worse, it was random. The same file started in 2 seconds on one run and 57 on the next. Seeking into a part that wasn't downloaded yet took 43 seconds.

So I read its source. The stream window, 32 MB, went out to peers all at once, and the piece sitting right under the playback position was no more urgent than anything else in that window. If a slow peer happened to grab that piece, the player just sat there until the request got handed to someone else, and that only kicked in once the request was ten times slower than average.

What fixed it: a responsive reader

I swapped it for a small Go service on top of anacrolix/torrent. The library handles the hard stuff (peers, DHT, picking pieces), and my code is just the HTTP API, the stream, file selection and storage.

The part that matters is the library's responsive reader. It gives urgent priority to the pieces at the read position, so whatever the player is waiting for right now jumps the queue. Each HTTP request gets its own reader:

var streamReadahead int64 = 16 << 20

func newStreamReader(ctx context.Context, file *torrent.File) torrent.Reader {
    reader := file.NewReader()
    reader.SetContext(ctx) // the player disconnects, the read is cancelled
    reader.SetResponsive()
    reader.SetReadahead(streamReadahead)

    return reader
}

For Range requests I let http.ServeContent do the work: 206, 416, Content-Range, Content-Length, all handled. One thing to watch out for: set Content-Type yourself before you call it.

w.Header().Set("Content-Type", contentType)
http.ServeContent(w, r, name, time.Time{}, reader)

If you don't, ServeContent reads the beginning of the file to guess the type. With a torrent, that means it pulls the first pieces even when the player asked for the middle.

Download a window, not the whole file

In a torrent client, picking a file usually means "download all of it". For watching, that's wrong in two ways. The rest of the file fights with the piece under the playback position for the same peers. And a 20 GB file you watched for one minute ends up sitting on your disk.

So while you watch, only a window ahead of the position gets downloaded: roughly three minutes of video, worked out from the file's average bitrate and kept between 64 MB and 1 GiB. The whole file only comes down if you explicitly hit "download".

Marking a full 1 GiB window as wanted in one go would bring back the original problem, so the window goes out in 64 MB batches (at least four pieces), closest to the position first. The batch gets recalculated whenever the piece under the position changes, and once a second on top of that, because a paused player doesn't move but the window should keep filling.

Close the stream, and the pieces outside any open window drop back to "not needed". Downloading just stops.

One thing made this a lot easier than I expected. In anacrolix, a piece's priority is the highest of three: the file's, the readers', and the piece's own. So a viewing window never clashes with a file someone chose to download in full, and the other way around.

What made it worse: prewarming

This one looked obvious. As soon as a torrent is added, read the start and the end of the file, so they're already there when the player asks. I measured it, and the median start went from 8.3 to 20.3 seconds. The prewarm requests were fighting the player's own requests for the same peers. I took it out, and it stays out until a benchmark says otherwise.

Results

Start, median (range) Seek, median (range)
Rust library 41 s (2–59) 43 s (6–70)
Go + responsive reader 8.3 s (3.4–19.5) 3.8 s (1.3–6.9)
Go + prewarm 20.3 s (5.4–33.0) 10.9 s (4.2–18.2)

For reference, a popular streaming server built on the same library did 6.0 s to start and 3.0 s to seek on the same files. So I'm still a couple of seconds behind. What bugs me more is how much the start time jumps around. My guess is that other pieces compete with the first ones early on, and that's what I'm measuring next.

Usual caveats: one machine, one home connection, one evening, two runs per file. Swarms change over time.

Two things that bit me

Library callbacks run under its lock. anacrolix calls some callbacks while it holds the client lock. Touch the client from inside one, and the engine deadlocks.

A panic in an HTTP handler can leave that lock held. net/http recovers panics in handlers, so the process keeps running, /health still says OK, and everything that needs the lock hangs forever. Now any panic in a route takes the whole process down, a watchdog checks the lock every 5 seconds and exits if it's been stuck for a minute, and the parent server restarts the engine.

Where this lives

This is the engine inside Torsher, an open-source media center that runs in one Docker container and starts from the TV. The engine is in engine/, the window logic in engine/window.go.

If you've beaten the start-time spread some other way, I'd really like to hear how.

title: Loading, empty, and failed are different promises to the user
description:
An empty table looks like a simple component state. In a real data flow, it can hide several very different situations.

The first request may still be running. A search may have completed with no matches. A refresh may have failed after an earlier successful load. The user may no longer have access to the data.

If all of them show “No results,” the interface asks users to guess what happened and which action will help.

Give the message a state to describe

I would start with the product's states before designing the illustration or button:

State What the interface should communicate
Initial load Results are not known yet
Successful empty result This query returned no matches
Failed initial request Results could not be retrieved
Refresh with existing data Earlier results remain while a newer request runs
Failed refresh Earlier results remain, but the update did not succeed
Unavailable data The current access or availability boundary

This is an illustrative model, not a requirement to create six components. Its purpose is to stop different facts from sharing an inaccurate message.

Empty should explain the current query

A successful empty result can support useful actions: clear filters, widen the search, or create a first record where that makes sense.

The message should match the scope. “No listings match these filters” is different from “There are no listings.”

For dependent filters, also check that the displayed controls reflect the actual query. A hidden incompatible value can produce an empty result the user cannot explain from the screen.

Decide what to do with previous data

During refresh, keeping the last successful result can reduce disruption. It needs an honest presentation of freshness and a rule for actions that require current data.

For example:

Showing results fetched at 10:42.
The latest refresh failed. Retry.

Even that timestamp needs a definition. Fetch time, server generation time, and source observation time can describe different moments. Choose the one the UI needs, and label it accordingly.

A read-only overview and an approval action may need different policies. The overview can remain useful with older data; the approval may require a fresh server-side check before changing the record.

Recovery should fit the failure

A Retry button helps with some failures. It is less helpful when a filter is invalid or the user's access has changed.

I would map the recovery action to the known problem and preserve useful input. If the user spent time configuring a query, a failed request should not automatically wipe it out.

For unavailable private data, the message also needs an appropriate disclosure boundary. Explain what the user can do without revealing records they are not allowed to see.

Communicate changes without unnecessary focus movement

When a result or status changes while focus stays elsewhere, the relevant update may need an accessible announcement. W3C's status-message guidance describes how status can be exposed to assistive technology without taking focus.

A concise status can help. Announcing every intermediate change can create noise. Test the actual interaction instead of treating an attribute as proof that the experience works.

Test transitions as well as screenshots

I would check a slow first load, a successful zero-match search, a failed refresh after a successful result, and a change in access while the page is open.

For each transition, inspect three things together: the message, the data still visible, and the actions still available.

The empty-state design is successful when those three tell the same story. The visual treatment can then make that story easier to understand.

title: How to write a Claude Code hook that cannot steer your agent
description:
I build ccdeck, a local dashboard for Claude Code and Codex sessions, and its hook is the worked example; everything about it is quoted from the source at the v3.42.0 tag (hook/hook.js, src/server/installer.mjs and src/web/__tests__/hook-read-only.test.ts, with two more tests named where they come up); at 3.48.0 the hook, its tests and the quoted installer lines are unchanged. Claude Code's behaviour is quoted from Anthropic's hooks reference as I read it on 14 October 2026.

Plenty of hooks only want to watch: a logger, a notifier, a dashboard. They still run on every event they register for, and on some events Claude Code waits for them and reads what they say. A PreToolUse hook sees rm -rf before it runs, and its answer can decide whether it does.

The read-only claim needs to hold in the code. List every channel the hook has for talking back, close each one, and test that it stays closed.

Every way a hook can talk back

A command hook gets the event as JSON on stdin. From the reference, it has these ways to affect what happens next:

  • JSON on stdout. "Claude Code parses your stdout as JSON output when the whole output is one JSON object", and its fields can allow, deny, defer or rewrite the call. With a valid JSON object, an exit code other than 0 or 2 is ignored: "the fields alone decide".
  • Exit code 2. "Exit with code 2 to block the action", with stderr as the reason.
  • Any other non-zero exit. Not a block, but "a <hook name> hook error notice in the transcript", on every call it happens on.
  • Plain text on stdout, on some events. For UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, SessionStart and PostModelSwitch, "Claude Code adds plain-text stdout as context that Claude can see and act on". A stray log line there is a message to the model.
  • The entry's own fields. onFailure: "block" turns any failure (a crash, a missing script, a timeout) into a block. async: true removes the blocking, but not the voice: when an async hook exits, its additionalContext and systemMessage reach Claude on the next turn.
  • Time. The default timeout for a command hook is 600 seconds on most events, and hooks "block Claude's execution until they complete". A timed-out hook "doesn't block the tool call", but you waited for it.

An HTTP hook (type: "http") has the same powers through its response body, so a hook that POSTs straight to a local service hands the decision to whatever answers on that port; and a failed connection is a non-blocking error, a notice on every call while the service is down.

For an observer, that list turns into rules: a command hook that never writes to stdout, exits 0 on every path, declares no onFailure or async, keeps a short timeout, and checks who it is talking to before it sends anything. The rest of this post is how ccdeck's hook does each of those, and how its tests pin them.

Rule 1: nothing on stdout, exit 0 everywhere

ccdeck's test file opens with the reason it exists:

// The README says the deck cannot steer your agent. This is the file that makes
// that a property of the code rather than an intention.

and names the failure it guards against:

One console.log left in from debugging, or one process.exit(1) on an error path, turns a read-only observer into a participant in every tool call on the machine — and silently, because a hook that prints unparseable text is ignored until the day it prints something parseable, and a hook that exits non-zero either blocks the call it was reporting (exit 2) or shows a hook error on it (any other code).

Every path in hook.js is written to end at exit 0. A throw is the one way out that a reader of the code cannot see, so there is a last resort:

process.on("uncaughtException", () => process.exit(0));
process.on("unhandledRejection", () => process.exit(0));

That line came from a bug: a malformed record in the deck's registry crashed the hook with exit 1 and a stack trace, and, per the comment, "Claude Code surfaces a non-zero exit as <hook> hook error plus the first stderr line", on every tool call.

Rule 2: test the source for every other channel

Writing the rule down is not enough; the next debugging session undoes it. hook-read-only.test.ts asserts it twice.

Over the source, it bans every spelling of stdout and every exit code but one:

expect(SRC).not.toMatch(/\bprocess\s*\.\s*stdout\b/);
expect(SRC).not.toMatch(/\bconsole\s*\./);
expect(SRC).not.toMatch(/\bwriteSync\s*\(/);
// …
expect(writes).toEqual(["req.write(body);"]);          // the one write: the outbound request
// …
expect([...new Set(codes)]).toEqual(["0"]);            // every process.exit(…) is exit(0)
expect(SRC).not.toMatch(/process\s*\.\s*exitCode/);

console.log is stdout with another name and fs.writeSync(1, …) is stdout with no name, so all three spellings are banned. process.exitCode is banned outright rather than checked for a value.

By running the real script, it starts an "honest deck" (a local HTTP server that answers the handshake below), feeds the hook a PreToolUse for rm -rf / on stdin, and checks:

expect(deck.seen).toEqual(["/api/event"]);   // it really delivered
expect(run.stdout).toBe("");                 // and said nothing back
expect(run.code).toBe(0);

The delivery is asserted on purpose: silence from a hook that did nothing would prove nothing. The same silence is then checked on every early return (no deck, unparseable payload, no cwd), on payloads that throw (a cwd that is a number, JSON nested 20,000 levels deep), and on eight malformed registry records, and a healthy deck registered next to a malformed record must still receive its event. Every run points CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and HOME at a temp directory, so the test never reads your real ~/.claude.

Rule 3: a time budget counted from process start

On PreToolUse the user waits until every matching hook returns, and the installer's comment is blunt about the declared timeout: it "is in SECONDS and it is a kill". So the hook has a deadline per phase and a cap over all of them:

const CHALLENGE_TIMEOUT_MS = 400;   // one retry, only on a timeout
const POST_TIMEOUT_MS = 1000;
const DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT_MS = 400;   // a second window only if the first found nothing
const CAP_MS = 1900;

The cap is measured from when Node started, not from when main() ran:

setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), Math.max(200, CAP_MS - Math.round(process.uptime() * 1000)));

That detail came from a measurement. The old timer started inside main(), so the shell fork, Node's start-up and reading a stdin payload that can be megabytes were outside the budget. With a stalled deck, the hook came out at 1.84 s idle and 1.98–2.19 s on a loaded machine, past the timeout: 2 it declared at the time (issue #1018). Now the cap counts from process start, the declared timeout is 3 seconds as a backstop, and hook-budget.test.ts pins the two numbers against each other so they cannot drift apart again.

The deadlines can add up to more than the cap (2.6 s if the filesystem, a listener and a deck all stall on one run), and the source says which number to believe: the cap "is the backstop over all of them, and it is what a reader should believe rather than the addition". Discovery gets its second 400 ms window only when the first found no deck and reads were still out, because on a loaded machine those reads are usually slow rather than stalled (issue #1872). A dead port costs nothing: a refused loopback connection is instant.

Rule 4: prove the listener before you send

An observer usually forwards the event somewhere, and the event is everything: in the hook's own words, "prompt text, tool inputs, tool results, cwd". Sending it to a port because a process ID looks alive is not safe. A deck killed with SIGKILL or a power cut leaves its record behind, the OS can hand the PID to another process, and the port "may by then belong to anything at all (4317, the deck's own default, is also the standard OTLP collector port)".

So each running deck writes a fresh random token into its record at start-up, and before posting, the hook challenges the listener with a nonce it has never seen:

function challengeProof(token, nonce) {
  return crypto.createHash("sha256").update(`${token}:${nonce}`).digest("hex");
}

The token itself never crosses the wire, so a wrong listener learns nothing it could replay, and the answer is compared with crypto.timingSafeEqual, "purely so a hostile listener cannot walk the expected proof out of us one byte at a time".

Rule 5: plan for the runtime disappearing

The command written into someone's settings outlives the environment it was written in. ccdeck builds its entries for ~/.claude/settings.json like this, one per event for up to twelve events, tagged so they can be found and removed:

function buildHookEntry(command) {
  return {
    [MARK_KEY]: true,                       // "__agent-dag"
    hooks: [{ type: "command", command, timeout: 3 }],
  };
}

The command used to name the Node binary directly. Then nvm uninstall took that binary away, and every tool call of every session showed a hook error from then on. On macOS and Linux the arguments now go through a fixed /bin/sh script first:

const NODE_FALLBACK = 'n=$1; shift; [ -x "$n" ] || n=$(command -v node) || exit 0; exec "$n" "$@"';

It runs the recorded Node while it is still executable, the node on Claude Code's own PATH once it is not, and nothing at all when there is no Node: exit 0, no output. The Claude Code version is part of the environment too. Until 2.1.101, an event name Claude Code did not know made it ignore the whole settings file, so ccdeck adds its two newest entries only where every Claude Code it finds knows them: StopFailure from 2.1.78, and UserPromptExpansion from 2.1.116. That second one is also an event where plain text on stdout becomes context for the model, which is Rule 1 again. The paths reach it as positional arguments, quoted once, so none of them is spliced into shell code. hook-command-node-fallback.test.ts runs it through a real /bin/sh and states the trade: "a hook error on every tool call is a worse answer than a deck that hears nothing from a machine it cannot run on."

One more case of the environment surprising you: your own tool's Claude runs fire your hooks too. ccdeck reads Claude quota in one of its ways with claude --print /usage, which is itself a Claude Code run. Without a guard, every quota poll drew itself on the dashboard as an empty session. The deck marks that run with AGENTS_DECK_INTERNAL=1, and the hook exits before reading a byte.

What this does not guarantee

  • It is a guarantee about one file. Anything that can write to your ~/.claude can change settings.json or the hook itself. No hook design defends against that. (ccdeck writes two other things there, separate from the hook: its Telemetry Radar switches write flags into the env block when you flip one, and its Settings › Claude Code page writes the one key you change; its uninstall leaves both as you set them.)
  • It is a guarantee about the hook, not about every button. ccdeck's Continue, on a background session whose turn stopped on an error, runs Claude Code's own claude stop and claude --resume <id> --bg at your press. That is a program starting a Claude Code command beside the session, not the hook answering one.
  • The receiver sees everything the hook sees. Prompts, tool inputs and results go to 127.0.0.1. That is the point of a dashboard; the handshake exists so they go only to it.
  • Fire-and-forget means gaps. If no deck is running, the event is not recorded.
  • Very large events arrive cut. The deck refuses a body over 5,000,000 characters, and a PostToolUse for an Edit carries the whole edited file. Over 4,900,000 the hook replaces the biggest fields with a marker saying how large they were, and flags the event as truncated; the event name, session, tool and call id are never what goes.
  • It still costs a process per event: a Node start on every hook call, with a /bin/sh in front of it on macOS and Linux, bounded by the budget above.

A checklist for any observing hook

  • Use a command hook, without onFailure and without async. Write nothing to stdout, on any event: on UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart, plain text is context for the model.
  • Exit 0 on every path, and catch the throws you cannot see.
  • Test the source for every spelling of stdout and every exit code but 0, then run the real script and assert that it delivered and said nothing.
  • Give it a time budget from process start, and keep the declared timeout strictly above it.
  • Prove the listener before sending the event; a live PID is not proof.
  • Survive a missing runtime with a silent fallback, and guard against your own tool's runs firing the hook.
