title: Node.js Example for Implementing Text Classification Using OpenAI GPT API in Marketplaces
description:
For a marketplace that turns sales-call transcripts into CRM actions, use a direct GPT API call when classification quality matters more than shaving every millisecond. Keep the output schema small, make the prompt data-driven, and validate the JSON before a CRM write. If the workflow crosses several backend capabilities, an OpenAI-compatible HTTP surface such as Infrai can simplify the handoff; it does not remove the need to evaluate the model and the transcript boundary separately.

The important boundary is this: transcription produces text, classification turns that text into structured intent, and the CRM worker decides what may be written. Do not make one provider responsible for all three decisions.

Option Pick this when Main trade-off
OpenAI GPT API with the Node.js openai package You want the shortest path from transcript to a typed classification You own provider-specific client setup and operational metadata
Anthropic Claude or Google Gemini You already standardize on one of those providers and its model behavior A provider switch means adapting the client and output contract
LangChain ChatOpenAI The classifier is one step in a larger chain or agent workflow The framework adds a useful abstraction layer that can make the final request harder to inspect
Infrai OpenAI-compatible surface You want discovery, routing, and this classification call behind one HTTP surface You still need to check capability readiness and keep a direct-provider path for specialized work

Which boundary should own the CRM decision?

Start with the transcript. A marketplace sales call might produce a short action such as follow_up, send_quote, or no_action, plus tags like enterprise, renewal, or integration. The model should predict those values. A separate application rule should decide whether a prediction is sufficient to create a CRM task.

That distinction is practical. A model can return valid JSON and still be uncertain about a customer commitment. Treat the classifier as a typed suggestion, not as authorization to change customer records. Store the raw transcript reference, the predicted label, the tags, and the model response identifier alongside the eventual CRM action. A four-label contract is easier to review than a free-form summary.

Keep it boring.

Here is the decision rule I use for this kind of pipeline: choose the thinnest client that leaves the classification contract visible. Direct OpenAI is a good default for one call. LangChain is a better fit when prompt templates and model calls already live inside a chain. An OpenAI-compatible gateway fits when the boundary around the model call is the real integration problem: a public discovery surface can describe capabilities and schemas, while the client keeps the same request shape.

The last option is useful for a team that will connect classification to other backend services later. The discovery response and runnable examples reduce the amount of SDK-specific knowledge needed to wire a new capability. A single key across 295 routes and 20 modules also removes a concrete piece of handoff work when the same worker needs storage or scheduling after classification. That is an integration benefit, not evidence that the model will classify sales language better.

How does implementing text classification using OpenAI GPT API work in Node.js?

Keep the allowed labels in the prompt and in the application validator. Put the changing call text in a variable. Ask for JSON only, then parse it as untrusted input. The example below uses the OpenAI-compatible request shape against Infrai, so the provider boundary stays explicit and the same classification contract can be evaluated against direct OpenAI later. It assumes Node.js 18+ for the built-in fetch implementation.

type Classification = {
  classification: "follow_up" | "send_quote" | "no_action";
  tags: string[];
  confidence: number;
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const model = process.env.OPENAI_MODEL;
const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

if (!apiKey || !model) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_MODEL are required");
}

function retryAfterMs(error: unknown): number {
  const headers = (error as { headers?: Headers }).headers;
  const value = headers?.get("retry-after");
  const seconds = value ? Number(value) : NaN;
  return Number.isFinite(seconds) ? Math.max(seconds * 1000, 250) : 1000;
}

async function classifySalesCall(transcript: string): Promise<Classification> {
  const prompt = `Classify this marketplace sales call transcript.

Allowed classification values: follow_up, send_quote, no_action.
Return one JSON object with exactly these keys:
classification (one allowed value), tags (an array of short strings),
confidence (a number from 0 to 1).

Transcript:
${transcript}`;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
          model,
          temperature: 0,
          messages: [
            { role: "system", content: "You are a strict JSON classifier." },
            { role: "user", content: prompt },
          ],
        }),
      });

      if (!response.ok) {
        const error = new Error(`Classification request failed: ${response.status}`) as Error & {
          status?: number;
          headers?: Headers;
        };
        error.status = response.status;
        error.headers = response.headers;
        throw error;
      }

      const body = (await response.json()) as {
        choices?: Array<{ message?: { content?: string } }>;
      };
      const content = body.choices?.[0]?.message?.content;
      if (!content) throw new Error("The model returned no content");

      const parsed = JSON.parse(content) as Partial<Classification>;
      const allowed = new Set(["follow_up", "send_quote", "no_action"]);
      if (
        !allowed.has(parsed.classification ?? "") ||
        !Array.isArray(parsed.tags) ||
        typeof parsed.confidence !== "number" ||
        parsed.confidence < 0 ||
        parsed.confidence > 1
      ) {
        throw new Error("The model returned an invalid classification shape");
      }

      return parsed as Classification;
    } catch (error) {
      if ((error as { status?: number }).status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
        throw error;
      }
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryAfterMs(error) * 2 ** attempt),
      );
    }
  }

  throw new Error("Classification retry limit reached");
}

const result = await classifySalesCall(
  "The buyer needs a quote for 500 seats and asked about Salesforce integration.",
);
console.log(result);

There are several deliberate choices in this small example. temperature: 0 reduces variation, but it does not prove correctness. The validator rejects an unknown action before any CRM code runs. The retry path handles HTTP 429 with exponential backoff and reads Retry-After when present. A failed request is surfaced instead of being treated as an empty classification.

For a production queue, add a stable event ID to your own classification record and make the CRM write idempotent. Classification itself is a read-like inference, but the follow-up task is a write. Retrying that task without a consumer-side deduplication key can create duplicate work.

When does a single HTTP surface help?

The model call is only one handoff in the flow:

sales call -> available transcription provider -> transcript store -> classifier -> validated CRM action

OpenAI’s direct API is the clearest choice if the classifier is the only model dependency. LangChain’s ChatOpenAI integration becomes attractive when this step must share a chain abstraction with other model calls. Infrai occupies a different boundary. Its discovery surface is public, documents request and response schemas, and includes runnable examples; its OpenAI-compatible surface means the Node.js client can keep the same calling idiom while the base URL changes.

That can remove a real integration decision for a team connecting classification to storage, scheduling, or observability later. It does not mean every capability is interchangeable. Check the discovered capability and its readiness before moving a workflow across providers. Keep the transcript provider and CRM system as explicit ownership boundaries so an inference retry cannot silently replay a business action.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the classification handoff when discovery, one consistent HTTP surface, and one credential across adjacent capabilities matter more than provider-specific tuning. Retain direct OpenAI for teams that need the most direct control over the GPT request. Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini are sensible alternatives when an existing provider relationship or model evaluation already favors them. LangChain is the better choice when orchestration is already the main abstraction. Those are different needs.

Before sending a long transcript, estimate its token usage with the available token-count capability. That gives the worker a chance to reject or summarize oversized input before the classification request. Treat the estimate as a planning signal; the response still needs normal error handling and schema validation.

What should stay outside this design?

Audio transcription is a separate concern. The current ASR capability is not available, so this classifier should receive text from an available transcription system rather than pretending that the same runtime completes the audio step. Real-time voice sessions are pending and limited to the western region. Neither is a reason to blur the boundary.

There is no dedicated moderation endpoint. If a marketplace needs moderation for text or images, use a chat model with a JSON schema fallback and keep that policy separate from sales-intent classification. Image upscaling is also limited to Lanczos, which is unrelated to CRM tagging and should remain outside this flow.

The strongest specialist or direct competitor is the better choice when it offers a capability this workflow cannot safely substitute, such as an available transcription path or provider-specific model controls your quality review requires. Test on representative sales language, inspect false follow-ups, and measure latency from transcript arrival to validated action. The clean handoff is the architecture; the evaluation set decides whether the labels are good enough.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovered schema before wiring the client.

References

  • OpenAI API documentation
  • OpenAI Node.js package
  • LangChain ChatOpenAI integration
  • Infrai documentation

title: Migrating from Insomnia to OpenAPI
description:
Short answer: Use the existing client collections as evidence of the API and consolidate them into an OpenAPI contract. Then generate the request set from the spec. This is a one-time move that replaces a maintained client vault with a maintained, versioned contract.

What the collections already contain

Paths, methods, bodies, headers, and expected responses — a practical, partial description of the API. They are the fastest way to seed a contract without starting from a blank page.

The migration path

  1. Export the collections and convert the requests into operations.
  2. Add response schemas from real responses and validate the contract.
  3. Generate the request set and compare it to the old collection.
  4. Once aligned, make the spec the source and retire the vault.

What to expect

The first pass will miss responses and edge cases that the collections never captured. Close those gaps against the running API; the resulting contract is more complete than the collection.

The payoff

After the move, the request set is an output. The docs, mocks, and tools share the same source, and the team stops maintaining a separate client artifact.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read contract testing.

title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

title: Pause workflows for approval with Chat SDK
description:
You can build human-in-the-loop approvals with Chat SDK through the new chat/workflow subpath. One requestApproval call posts a card with Approve and Deny buttons and suspends a Workflow SDK workflow until someone decides.

The wait can last seconds or days and survives deploys and restarts. You don't need an approvals table, an onAction handler, or a polling loop:

Start the workflow from any handler, and Thread instances serialize across the workflow boundary automatically. The card handles the rest:

  • Scoped approvers: Pass approvers to restrict who can decide. Clicks from anyone else post a notice, and the workflow keeps waiting.

  • Verified decisions: Chat SDK checks the platform's signature on every click, so the user.id on the result is the person who decided.

  • Audit trail: Once a decision lands or the timeout elapses, the card is edited in place with an outcome line, preventing stale clicks.

Get started by reading the approvals documentation.

title: Insomnia Collections vs Spec-Generated Requests
description:
Short answer: Authored requests are maintained by hand and reflect what someone saved; generated requests are derived from the contract and reflect the current API. The first is a snapshot; the second is a build output. For a changing API, generation is the only way to stay correct without manual re-sync.

What authored requests guarantee

Exactly the calls someone built, with precise control. They do not guarantee currency, and they miss anything that was never saved.

What generated requests guarantee

Property Authored Generated
Coverage What was saved Declared operations
On API change Manual update On save
Consistency As maintained With the contract
Control Fine Derived

The failure that generation removes

A missing request for a new endpoint, or a stale request for a moved one, is the classic authored-set bug. A generated set reflects the spec, so it cannot be missing a declared operation.

The honest takeaway

Authored requests are the right tool for a small, stable, bespoke set. Once the API grows and changes, generating from the contract is the lower-maintenance, more correct path.

Return to the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison, or read the API debugging guide.

title: Pinning your embedding model doesn't pin its code
description:
If you load a model from Hugging Face with revision= set to a commit hash, which commit of its code do you think runs?

For a lot of the popular embedding models, not that one. Here's gte-base-en-v1.5 pinned to a commit from April 2024, on transformers 4.57.6:

from transformers import AutoModel
import inspect

pin = "aed4f757b1f39a2e85e2ecf24727a1f29dbafe92"
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "Alibaba-NLP/gte-base-en-v1.5", revision=pin, trust_remote_code=True
)
print(inspect.getfile(type(model)))

.../new_hyphen_impl/40ced75c3017eb27626c9d4ea981bde21a2662f4/modeling.py

That's a different repo, new-impl, at its newest commit, from August 2024. 118 lines of its modeling.py have changed since April. The first time it downloads, transformers even warns you about it, and the advice is the thing you just did:

A new version of the following files
was downloaded from
https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/new-impl:
- modeling.py
. Make sure to double-check they do not
contain any added malicious code. To
avoid downloading new versions of the
code file, you can pin a revision.

The code lives in another repo

Models like this one don't keep their Python in the model repo. Their config.json points somewhere else:

"auto_map": {
  "AutoConfig": "Alibaba-NLP/new-impl--configuration.NewConfig",
  "AutoModel": "Alibaba-NLP/new-impl--modeling.NewModel",

The -- means "in that repo over there". And transformers only carries your revision across when the code's in the same repo as the model (here):

if code_revision is None and pretrained_model_name_or_path == repo_id:
    code_revision = revision

Otherwise it stays None, and the Hub hands you main. Fair enough in a way, since a commit hash from one repo means nothing in another. There's a code_revision argument for exactly this, and it's in the docstring and not many other places.

  • gte-base-en-v1.5 your pin, April 2024
    • config.json points at new-impl
    • tokenizer.json
    • model.safetensors
  • new-impl main, August 2024
    • configuration.py
    • modeling.py what actually runs

So the pin covers the weights, the config and the tokenizer. The bit that runs on your machine is whatever's on main the day you download it.

It's mostly embedding models

Back in 2024, Sentence Transformers' maintainer reckoned "very few models use third party repositories to host their code". By count, he's right. Of the thousand most-downloaded models on the Hub that ship their own code, 53 load it from another repo, not counting test fixtures and a pile of copies of one upload (I counted on 20 October and checked again today). But they're busy ones. Between them they get about 22 million downloads a month, and nearly all of it is three families of embedding model, the thing a self-hosted RAG setup uses to turn your documents into vectors.

Monthly downloads of models whose code lives in another repo (the data)

Hugging Face's last-30-days download counts on 29 October, in millions.

Nearly all those downloads go to models pointing at a repo from the same company, like nomic-embed-text at nomic-ai/nomic-bert-2048. So it's the same people's code, just on a different schedule.

And the schedules drift apart. jina-embeddings-v3's own repo last changed on 8 April. Its code repo has had three commits this year, all fixes for transformers 5, the latest on 20 August. Pin v3's newest commit today and you still get August's code. For 22 of the 53, the code repo has changed since the model last did.

code_revision works, if it gets there

I loaded gte-base-en-v1.5 and nomic-embed-text-v1.5, both pinned to 2024 commits, every way I could think of, with the files downloaded first and no network. Both models came out the same:

Does the code come from the commit you asked for? (the data)

transformers 4.57.6 and Sentence Transformers 5.7.0, on 29 October.

AutoModel is fine once you pass code_revision with a commit from the code repo. pipeline() drops it, though transformers 5.22.0 fixed that this afternoon (#49832).

Which would be good news, except neither model's own code runs on transformers 5. Both fall over on the first encode, main or pinned, so if you're using gte you're on transformers 4. nomic has a way out, which I'll get to.

Sentence Transformers is the awkward one, and it's how nomic's model card tells you to load it. Put code_revision in both model_kwargs and config_kwargs and you get the config from your commit, the model from main, and that same warning telling you to pin a revision. Its loader takes code_revision out of model_kwargs for its own modules, before the model ever sees it (base/model.py):

code_revision = model_kwargs.pop("code_revision", None) if model_kwargs else None

It's still there in 6.2.0. The revision part isn't news to Sentence Transformers, to be fair. Tom Aarsen explained it on that same 2024 issue, along with the copy-the-files fix below. What I couldn't find on its tracker is code_revision getting dropped. Someone else ran into that in October and built the model up from its parts to get round it.

nomic's weights float too

nomic-embed-text-v1.5, the tall bar on that chart, goes one further. Its code has its own from_pretrained, which fetches the weights by the model's name and nothing else. No revision. Offline, with only my pinned commit in the cache, it fails like this:

OSError: Model name nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5
was not found.

It's looking for main. With the network up it'd just fetch main's weights. Today that's the same file as the 2024 commit's, so nobody's getting different vectors. But on the most-downloaded model here, the pin covers the config and the tokenizer, and that's about it. And code_revision can't fix this one, because it's nomic's own code that leaves the revision out.

Pinning both

Look for -- in the model's config first:

curl -s https://huggingface.co/nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5/raw/main/config.json | grep -- '--'

If it's there, which way out depends on the model.

For nomic-embed-text on transformers 5.5 or later, drop trust_remote_code altogether. transformers has its own NomicBert now, and nomic's card says remote code isn't needed from 5.5. It wants a commit from 7 April or later, when nomic updated the config for it (the 2024 one won't load this way):

model = SentenceTransformer(
    "nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5",
    revision="e9b6763023c676ca8431644204f50c2b100d9aab",
)

On transformers 5.22.0, with no network, that ran transformers' own code, loaded the pinned weights and gave the same vectors as nomic's code. No second repo at all.

For AutoModel, pass code_revision with a commit hash from the repo it names. For anything else, nomic on transformers 4 included, copy the code in next to the model:

hf download nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5 --local-dir nomic-embed \
  --revision d802ae16c9caed4d197895d27c6d529434cd8c6d
hf download nomic-ai/nomic-bert-2048 --local-dir nomic-embed --include "*.py" \
  --revision 7710840340a098cfb869c4f65e87cf2b1b70caca
sed -i 's|nomic-ai/nomic-bert-2048--||' nomic-embed/config.json

Then SentenceTransformer("./nomic-embed", trust_remote_code=True) takes everything from that folder. The model's name is now a folder on disk, so even nomic's loader reads its weights from there. I tried it with no network and an empty cache, and got the same vectors as before. The code you're trusting is right there in the folder too, which is roughly what trust_remote_code wanted you to read in the first place.

Does it matter yet?

Not for your search results. Last week I ran the same text through both models with their 2024 code and with main's. nomic's vectors came out bit-identical, gte's within 0.00001. Nobody's index has quietly drifted.

It matters for what the pin was for. If something lands on nomic-bert-2048, from nomic or from whoever's got hold of a nomic token, the next fresh download of every nomic-embed-text install pinned with just revision= runs it. And tells them to pin a revision.

The other side of it is jina. Those three transformers 5 fixes reached people because nobody's code was pinned, and a floating main is how a lot of these models are getting through the upgrade. Pin the code and those fixes are yours to go and fetch.

title: Building a 100/100 Lighthouse Static Website with GitHub Pages, Cloudflare & Vanilla Tech
description:
📖 Original Reference: Originally published with full semantic markup templates and Cloudflare DNS setup at alexmaina.dev/guida_sito.

In an era where personal portfolio sites and simple blogs pull in 250MB of node_modules, hydrate megabytes of JavaScript, and suffer from layout shifts, going back to pure semantic HTML5, modern CSS, and vanilla JS feels like a superpower.

By hosting static files on GitHub Pages paired with Cloudflare's Global Edge Network, you get:

  • Perfect 100/100 Lighthouse performance on mobile and desktop.
  • Sub-50ms Time to First Byte (TTFB) worldwide.
  • Enterprise DDoS mitigation, automatic HTTP/3, and free SSL certificates.
  • \$0/month forever hosting costs.

Here is how to set up the entire stack from scratch.

1. The Modern Zero-Framework Project Structure

You do not need a bloated build tool to get responsive layouts, dark mode, and offline caching:

my-website/
├── index.html              # Clean semantic HTML5
├── style.css               # Modern CSS with Custom Properties (variables)
├── script.js               # Vanilla JS for interactive widgets & theme toggle
├── sw.js                   # Lightweight Service Worker for offline support
├── robots.txt              # Search engine crawler rules
├── sitemap.xml             # XML sitemap for SEO indexing
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── deploy.yml      # Automated linting and deployment

2. Flash-Free Dark Mode in Modern CSS

The most common bug in static websites is the dark mode flash: the page renders bright white for 100ms before JavaScript executes and toggles the dark theme.

To prevent the flash completely, place an inline, blocking script in the <head> before any CSS renders:

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>Developer Portfolio</title>

  <!-- ⚡ Prevents theme flicker before CSS paints -->
  <script>
    (function() {
      const savedTheme = localStorage.getItem('theme') || 
        (window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light');
      document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', savedTheme);
    })();
  </script>

  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>

In style.css, leverage CSS custom properties:

:root {
  --bg-color: #ffffff;
  --text-color: #1e293b;
  --accent-color: #0284c7;
}

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg-color: #0b0f19;
  --text-color: #f1f5f9;
  --accent-color: #38bdf8;
}

body {
  background-color: var(--bg-color);
  color: var(--text-color);
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
  transition: background-color 0.2s ease, color 0.2s ease;
}

3. Offline Caching with a Vanilla Service Worker (sw.js)

Add native offline capability and instant page transitions using the Cache API:

// sw.js
const CACHE_NAME = 'site-cache-v1';
const ASSETS_TO_CACHE = [
  '/',
  '/index.html',
  '/style.css',
  '/script.js',
  '/offline.html'
];

self.addEventListener('install', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.open(CACHE_NAME).then((cache) => cache.addAll(ASSETS_TO_CACHE))
  );
  self.skipWaiting();
});

self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then((response) => {
      // Return cached asset or fetch from network
      return response || fetch(event.request).catch(() => caches.match('/offline.html'));
    })
  );
});

Register it in script.js:

if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
  window.addEventListener('load', () => {
    navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js');
  });
}

4. Pairing GitHub Pages with Cloudflare DNS & SSL

Deploying your site to a custom domain (e.g., alexmaina.dev) with Cloudflare provides edge caching and HTTPS enforcement:

  1. In your GitHub repository settings, go to Pages → Source: Deploy from a branch (main / root).
  2. Enter your custom domain in the Custom domain field (creates a CNAME file in your repo).
  3. In your Cloudflare Dashboard:
    • Add a CNAME record for @ pointing to <username>.github.io.
    • Add a CNAME record for www pointing to <username>.github.io.
    • Toggle the proxy status to Orange Cloud (Proxied).
  4. Under SSL/TLS, set encryption mode to Full (Strict).

5. Automated CI/CD Validation with GitHub Actions

Catch broken links, unclosed tags, and syntax errors automatically on every git push:

Create .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

name: Deploy & Validate Static Site

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Validate HTML5 Syntax
        uses: Cyb3r-Jak3/html5validator-action@v7.2.0
        with:
          root: .
          blacklist: "node_modules"

      - name: Check for Broken Links
        uses: gaurav-nelson/github-action-markdown-link-check@v1
        with:
          use-quiet-mode: 'yes'

Results & Benchmarks

  • Performance: 100/100
  • Accessibility: 100/100
  • Best Practices: 100/100
  • SEO: 100/100
  • Monthly Infrastructure Cost: \$0.00

Conclusion

Before reaching for complex React/Next.js scaffolds for personal portfolios, documentation sites, or small marketing landing pages, consider the elegance of vanilla web technologies. It is simpler to maintain, faster for your users, and immune to framework deprecation cycles.

title: A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox
description:
Running untrusted code safely requires more than separating it from the host. You also have to control what that code can reach.

This matters more as AI agents gain the ability to read files, execute commands, install packages, and generate programs of their own. A microVM can prevent that code from accessing the host or another workload. By itself, it cannot stop the code from exfiltrating data, probing internal services, attacking systems elsewhere on the internet, or using credentials available inside the environment.

Isolation without egress control contains the process, not its consequences.

A complete sandbox therefore needs both compute isolation and control over the authority available through its network: where code can connect, which credentials it can use, and how those permissions change throughout the workload’s lifecycle. These controls are part of the security boundary, not protections to bolt on later.

A sandbox has more than one boundary

Compute isolation answers one important question: what can this program access on the machine where it runs? Network isolation answers another: what can it access, or attack, through the network?

Consider an agent that reads a repository and runs generated code. A prompt injection hidden in an issue, log entry, dependency, or source file might instruct it to upload private data. The generated program does not need to escape its microVM. With unrestricted outbound traffic, it can simply send anything it can read to an external server.

The same access can be used to scan internal networks, exfiltrate data and credentials, or call an authenticated API. From the attacker’s perspective, crossing the VM boundary may be unnecessary. Without a network boundary, it is only half a sandbox.

A network bypass can be a sandbox escape

Recent security research has made one pattern clear: untrusted code does not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment. It only needs one network path that the security model failed to account for.

That path might be a DNS resolver left available in an otherwise disconnected environment, an empty allowlist that fails open, a hostname interpreted differently by a policy engine and a proxy, or a trusted package service turned into a relay. Any one of them can give untrusted code a channel to exfiltrate data, receive instructions, or move toward more sensitive infrastructure.

These are not compute escapes. The kernel, VM, or container boundary may continue working exactly as designed while containment still fails. The practical security boundary also includes DNS, proxies, identity services, internal networks, and every intentionally permitted destination.

Whether we call the result an escape or a bypass, the requirement is the same: a sandbox must account for every path by which untrusted code can communicate.

Useful sandboxes need selective connectivity

Completely disconnecting a sandbox closes the network path, but it also makes many workloads impractical. An agent may need to clone a repository, install a dependency, call an AI model, query a database, or upload its result.

Unrestricted internet access is not the only alternative. A useful sandbox should grant only the connectivity a workload requires:

  • Allow an AI provider, but no other public destination.

  • Allow one object storage bucket, rather than an entire cloud network.

  • Reach a private service, while blocking the rest of the private address space.

  • Install dependencies during trusted setup, then remove registry access before generated code runs.

  • Authenticate an API request without placing the API key inside the sandbox.

A practical policy model should support fully open access, complete network isolation, and granular policies that deny unmatched traffic by default. Those policies should be able to combine domain rules with allowed and denied address ranges.

Domains and CIDRs solve different problems. Domain policies are precise enough for modern services whose IP addresses change or serve many unrelated hostnames. CIDR policies work across protocols and provide control over fixed infrastructure and private networks.

Connectivity should also be temporary. A workflow can begin with access to a package registry, narrow access before untrusted execution, briefly permit an output destination, and finish with no outbound access, all without restarting the workload.

How Vercel enforces the network boundary

The Vercel Sandbox firewall runs on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it.

Linux networking transparently redirects outbound TCP connections and DNS queries through the firewall. Workloads do not need to configure a proxy, and the firewall retains each connection’s original destination.

For domain-restricted connections, the firewall inspects the beginning of the TLS handshake and extracts the Server Name Indication, or SNI. This identifies the requested hostname before the firewall opens an upstream connection. It checks that hostname against the sandbox’s domain policy and also checks the destination address against its CIDR policy.

Ordinary allowed TLS connections pass through without decryption. The firewall reads only the unencrypted handshake information required to enforce the policy, then connects the workload directly to its destination.

Some policies need to inspect or modify the HTTP request itself. For those configured domains only, header injection and request forwarding selectively terminate TLS using a certificate authority unique to the sandbox. The firewall can then match requests by hostname, path, method, query, or headers before injecting a credential or forwarding the request to an endpoint that you trust.

DNS traffic is filtered using the same domain policy. Together, these layers control both where a sandbox can connect and what authority a particular connection receives.

Keep credentials outside untrusted compute

An agent often needs to call an authenticated service, but a credential stored in an environment variable or file is a transferable bearer credential. Every program inside the sandbox can read it. Malicious code can copy it to a third-party service, where it can be retained and used long after the sandbox stops.

Vercel Sandbox instead injects credentials at the host network boundary. The firewall creates a dedicated certificate authority just in time for the sandbox and adds it to the sandbox’s trusted certificates. For a configured destination, it selectively terminates TLS, adds or replaces the authentication header, then establishes a new TLS connection to the upstream service.

The credential never enters the microVM. It never leaves the host unencrypted. The certificate authority is unique to the sandbox and is disposed when the sandbox stops.

Injection also limits where the credential can be used. The firewall sends it only to its configured destination, so uploading the sandbox’s files or environment to another service does not transfer that authority. Matchers can restrict it further by path, method, query, or request headers. Generated code might receive permission to submit results to one endpoint without receiving permission to read other resources from the same API.

Injected credentials should still follow the principle of least privilege, with access limited to the specific operations the workload requires.

Put your own policy in the path

Static allowlists cannot express every security requirement. Some workloads need to inspect payloads, enforce business rules, record an audit trail, or make an authorization decision using context only you have.

Request forwarding sends selected HTTPS requests through a proxy that you control. The proxy receives the original request along with a Vercel-issued OIDC token identifying the team, project, and sandbox that originated it.

That proxy becomes a programmable policy layer. It can:

  • Redact sensitive fields before a request leaves the environment.

  • Enforce per-user or per-sandbox authorization.

  • Route package downloads through supply-chain scanning and block artifacts that fail organizational policy.

  • Record requests and responses for compliance workflows.

  • Exchange a sandbox identity for a narrowly scoped credential.

  • Reject an operation that does not match organizational policy.

The policy and its secrets remain outside the sandbox, even when the code being governed has full root access inside its microVM. You can read more about request proxying in the Sandbox documentation.

Security belongs in the baseline product

We believe a sandbox should not require a payment method before it can safely handle untrusted code.

Every Vercel Sandbox includes both compute isolation and a complete firewall for defining what code inside it can communicate with.

The goal is not to make every sandbox completely offline. It is to make authority explicit:

  • Which destinations can this sandbox reach?

  • Which private address ranges are unavailable?

  • Which requests can use credentials?

  • Which operations must pass through additional policy?

  • When should all communication stop?

These are fundamental properties of the execution environment, not security controls to add after a workload reaches production. We believe so strongly in this that we have made our full egress firewall capabilities available to all Sandboxes.

Getting started

The following policy allows outbound connections to one API and injects a credential only for one operation. Other destinations are denied by default, and the credential remains outside the sandbox.

The same policy can be replaced while the sandbox runs:

A sandbox is not defined only by where its code runs. It is defined by what that code can reach, what authority it receives, and which boundaries still hold when the code itself is hostile.

The network is part of the sandbox.

Further reading

  • Vercel Sandbox firewall documentation

  • Understanding Vercel Sandboxes

  • Security boundaries in agentic architectures

Read more

title: Replacing Razer Synapse with 1 MB of Rust, or what a mouse actually stores
description:
I bought a Razer Viper V3 Pro and found out that changing its DPI meant installing Razer Synapse 4. On my PC that is 11 Electron processes, two Windows services, about 1.5 GB of memory, a Razer account, and a renderer that polls the device and runs a game-detection engine all day.

The thing is, the mouse does not need any of that. Every setting it has lives in its own onboard memory. Software is only needed for the few hundred milliseconds it takes to write them.

So I wrote freenapse: one Windows executable, about 1 MB, no installer, no runtime, no account. It writes the settings into the mouse and then does not need to exist. Here is how it works, and the parts I had to learn from the mouse itself because no document had them.

How a Razer mouse takes commands

Razer devices accept a 90-byte HID feature report on their first interface. The layout is public knowledge thanks to the GPL OpenRazer Linux driver and the razerqdhid protocol notes:

offset  0  status            request: 0x00. response: 01 busy, 02 ok, 03 failure, 04 timeout, 05 not supported
        1  transaction id    0x1f = the mouse (through the dongle), 0xff = the dongle itself
        2  remaining packets u16 big-endian, 0
        4  protocol type     0
        5  data size         number of argument bytes
        6  command class
        7  command id        bit 7 set = read
        8  arguments[80]
       88  crc               XOR of bytes 2..87
       89  reserved

On Windows the buffer is 91 bytes, because HidD_SetFeature wants the report id in front. Serialising it is a few lines:

pub fn to_hid_buffer(&self) -> [u8; 91] {
    let mut b = [0u8; 91];
    let r = &mut b[1..];
    r[0] = self.status;
    r[1] = self.transaction_id;
    r[2..4].copy_from_slice(&self.remaining_packets.to_be_bytes());
    r[4] = self.protocol_type;
    r[5] = self.data_size;
    r[6] = self.command_class;
    r[7] = self.command_id;
    r[8..88].copy_from_slice(&self.arguments);
    r[88] = r[2..88].iter().fold(0u8, |acc, b| acc ^ b);
    b
}

A command is a class, an id, a size and some argument bytes. Battery level is class 0x07, id 0x80, two bytes back. DPI stages are 0x04/0x06 to set and 0x04/0x86 to read, with seven bytes per stage. The polling rate on the HyperPolling dongle is 0x00/0x40, sent twice with a different first argument, which is one of those things you only learn by watching what the official software does.

You write the request with HidD_SetFeature, wait, read the response with HidD_GetFeature, and check that the class and id in the response are the ones you asked for. There is no hidapi in the project and no GUI framework: SetupAPI to find the device, two HID calls, Shell_NotifyIcon for the tray, GDI for the window.

The three things the documents did not say

The protocol layouts got me to a program that compiled and sent valid packets. The mouse still ignored it half the time. Three facts cost most of the project.

1. Wait 150 ms, not 60. OpenRazer picks its wait per product id: a generic mouse gets 600 microseconds, the wired Viper V3 Pro 31 ms, and the Viper receivers RAZER_VIPER_MOUSE_RECEIVER_WAIT_US, which is 59,900 microseconds. That works on Linux. Through the HyperPolling dongle on Windows, reading at 60 ms returns status 0x04 (timeout) and the exchange is lost. The threshold I measured is around 150 ms. Below it, nothing works; above it, everything does. The transact loop ended up like this:

fn transact_inner(&self, request: &Report) -> Result<Report> {
    let mut last = HidError::NoResponse;
    for attempt in 0..4 {
        if attempt > 0 {
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(80 * attempt as u64));
        }
        self.set_feature(&request.to_hid_buffer())?;
        thread::sleep(self.wait); // 150 ms
        for _ in 0..5 {
            let resp = Report::from_hid_buffer(&self.get_feature()?);
            if !resp.matches(request) || resp.transaction_id != request.transaction_id {
                // Someone else's exchange (Synapse shares the dongle); wait and resend.
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
                continue;
            }
            match resp.status() {
                Some(Status::Successful) => return Ok(resp),
                Some(Status::Busy) | Some(Status::New) => {
                    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
                    continue;
                }
                Some(Status::Timeout) => { last = HidError::Status(Status::Timeout); break; }
                Some(s) => return Err(HidError::Status(s)),
                None => return Err(HidError::BadStatus(resp.status)),
            }
        }
    }
    Err(last)
}

The dongle has one response slot, so every exchange in the process goes through a mutex, and a response is matched against its request before it is trusted. If Synapse is running at the same time, its replies show up in that slot too.

2. The mouse goes to sleep while you are reading the docs. A wireless Viper V3 Pro stops answering the dongle a few seconds after the last movement. Sometimes within two or three seconds, sometimes after thirty. The dongle still enumerates, the official software still shows the mouse as connected, and every command gets 0x04 back. Synapse does not notice because it gets its updates from input reports rather than polling.

Once I knew, it was easy: treat 0x04 as "asleep", keep the last known values, and retry writes when GetLastInputInfo shows the user has touched something in the last 1.5 seconds. The settings window shows the change as pending and writes it when the mouse wakes. But before I knew, I spent an evening convinced the CRC was wrong, because the commands that worked were the ones I typed quickly after moving the mouse.

3. Some getters simply answer "failure". OpenRazer documents getters for the lift-off and sensor parameters. On this mouse and firmware 1.11 they answer status 0x03. The setters work. So the asymmetric cut-off levels can be written but never read back, and freenapse import has to say "keep" for that one setting instead of guessing. The onboard profile commands are similar: the mouse reports one profile and a maximum of one, and answers failure to create, activate or even query the active profile. It has a single profile and that is that.

Things that are not stored in the mouse

The onboard memory holds DPI stages, polling rate, the button map on both layers, the Dynamic Sensitivity curve, lift-off, idle sleep and the low power threshold. Three things people assume are onboard are not.

Macros: this mouse has no macro memory. Every class 0x06 command answers "not supported", and the official software's own device spec says so. Synapse plays macros in software. freenapse does the same: each macro binding gets an unused key, F13 to F24, written into the mouse, and a low-level keyboard hook in the tray app swallows that key and plays the macro with SendInput.

Per-game profiles and the in-game polling rate: also software. The tray app watches the foreground window and switches DPI stage, polling rate and buttons while a game you picked is in front. The list of games comes from the launchers' own files on disk (Steam's libraryfolders.vdf, Epic's manifests, GOG's registry keys, Xbox's MicrosoftGame.config), so no account is needed for that either.

Everything else survives with nothing running. Which leads to the architecture.

Set once, then nothing

freenapse.exe is the tray app when started without arguments, a settings window with freenapse ui, and a command-line tool with any other verb:

freenapse status            what the mouse has stored right now
freenapse config            a config file built from those settings
freenapse apply             write your edits to the mouse
freenapse autostart on      the tray, if you want battery and per-game switching

The first config file is built from what the mouse already has, so nothing changes until you edit it. Run apply once, uninstall Synapse, and the mouse keeps working on any PC. The tray is optional. When it does run, it is one process with a 10 MB working set that reads the battery once a minute.

The settings window is plain Win32 and GDI, inside the same executable: cards, toggles, sliders and the mouse drawing are painted by hand, icons are glyphs from Segoe Fluent Icons, and there is no apply button. Each control writes its setting to the mouse the moment it changes and reads it back.

Measured on the same PC with the same mouse:

Razer Synapse 4 freenapse
Processes 11 Electron processes and 2 services 1 tray process, or none
Memory about 1.5 GB 10 MB working set
Background CPU constant idle, one battery read a minute
On disk 220 MB plus per-device modules one file, 1 MB
Account required none

What I did not do, on purpose

The protocol knowledge comes from the OpenRazer driver, the razerqdhid notes, and watching what Synapse 4 sends to this exact mouse. The project contains no Razer code, files or assets; NOTICE.md in the repo says what was and was not used. It cannot read or write firmware. Every setting it writes can be written again, and reinstalling Synapse puts Razer's own profile back. Still: use at your own risk, Razer will not support a mouse configured this way, and I am not affiliated with them.

The honest limitation, and how to help

freenapse is verified on one mouse: mine, a Viper V3 Pro, wired and through its dongle. Those are the only two product ids it writes to. Other Razer mice are detected and opened read-only, because the device table has rows for them taken from OpenRazer's list but nobody has confirmed what they accept.

If you own one, this prints what it answers, with serial numbers masked:

freenapse probe

Paste that into an issue, or open a pull request adding your row to src/device.rs once you have tested a write. Each row is a few fields: product id, transaction id, which polling command it takes, the DPI maximum, whether it has the lift-off page. CONTRIBUTING.md has the four steps.

The code is MIT at github.com/MatthewSaintBull/freenapse. The site, with the download and a changelog that builds itself from the GitHub releases, is freenapse.app. Questions about the protocol are welcome in the comments; questions that start with "does it work on my DeathAdder" have the same answer for now: run probe and tell me.

title: Load Testing My Node.js API on AWS: What I Learned
description:
An API can work perfectly when I'm testing it alone.

Send one request.

It responds quickly.

Everything looks fine.

But what happens when 10 users make requests at the same time?

What about 100?

What about 1,000?

That's where load testing becomes important.

As a backend developer working with Node.js and Express, I want to know how an API behaves before real traffic exposes its limitations.

In this post, I'll walk through how I think about load testing a Node.js API running on AWS EC2.

Why load test?

Functional testing answers:

Does the API work?

Load testing asks a different question:

How does the API behave under pressure?

An API might return the correct response for a single request but struggle when concurrency increases.

For example:

1 request
   ↓
Everything looks good

100 concurrent requests
   ↓
Latency increases

500 concurrent requests
   ↓
Database becomes a bottleneck

1000 concurrent requests
   ↓
Errors / timeouts

Without load testing, I may discover these limitations only after production traffic arrives.

The setup

For a typical Node.js backend, my architecture looks like:

Client
   ↓
Nginx
   ↓
AWS EC2
   ↓
Node.js + Express
   ↓
MongoDB

The API may contain endpoints such as:

GET    /api/users
GET    /api/products
POST   /api/orders
GET    /api/orders/:id

For load testing, I don't want to test every endpoint equally.

I focus on the endpoints that are:

  • Frequently used
  • Business-critical
  • Database-heavy
  • Computationally expensive
  • Likely to experience high concurrency

Tooling

There are several tools I can use for API load testing.

Some popular options include:

  • k6
  • Artillery
  • Locust
  • Apache JMeter

For a Node.js/backend workflow, k6 is particularly convenient because the test scenarios are easy to define and version-control.

The important thing isn't which tool I choose.

It's being able to reproduce the same test consistently.

A simple k6 test

A basic test could look like:

import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: "30s", target: 10 },
    { duration: "1m", target: 50 },
    { duration: "1m", target: 100 },
    { duration: "30s", target: 0 }
  ]
};

export default function () {
  const response = http.get(
    "https://api.example.com/api/products"
  );

  check(response, {
    "status is 200": (r) => r.status === 200
  });
}

The idea is to gradually increase traffic rather than immediately sending a huge number of requests.

This gives me a better understanding of how the system behaves as load increases.

The test stages

A useful load test isn't just:

Send lots of requests

I prefer thinking in stages.

          Users
            │
        100 │              ╭──────
            │             ╱
         50 │        ╭───╯
            │       ╱
         10 │──────╯
            │
            └──────────────────── Time

For example:

Stage 1 — Baseline

Start with a small number of users.

The purpose is to understand normal performance.

Stage 2 — Ramp up

Gradually increase concurrent users.

Now I'm looking for:

  • Increasing latency
  • CPU changes
  • Memory growth
  • Database pressure
  • Error rates

Stage 3 — Peak load

Push the API toward the expected production workload.

This is where bottlenecks often become visible.

Stage 4 — Recovery

Reduce traffic again.

I want to see whether the system returns to its normal state.

This last step is easy to overlook.

A system that survives peak traffic but never properly recovers can still have a serious problem.

What I measure

There are several metrics I care about.

P50 latency

P50 represents the median request latency.

It tells me what a typical request looks like.

P95 latency

P95 is more interesting for production behavior.

It tells me that approximately 95% of requests are faster than that value.

If P50 looks good but P95 becomes very high, some users are experiencing significantly worse performance.

P99 latency

P99 helps expose the tail of the latency distribution.

This is especially useful when investigating occasional slow requests.

Error rate

Latency isn't the only concern.

I also want to know:

How many requests failed?

A fast API returning lots of 500 errors isn't a healthy API.

Throughput

I also want to understand how many requests the system can handle.

Conceptually:

Requests/sec
     │
     │              ───────
     │           ───
     │        ───
     │     ───
     │────
     └──────────────────── Load

At some point, adding more traffic may no longer increase useful throughput.

That's an important signal.

Results

For a real test, I'd record the results in a table like this:

Metric Result
P50 latency Measure
P95 latency Measure
P99 latency Measure
Error rate Measure
Max sustained RPS Measure
Peak concurrent users Measure

I prefer recording these numbers rather than simply saying:

"The API was fast."

Numbers make performance discussions much more useful.

Watching the EC2 instance

While the load test is running, I also want to know what is happening on the server.

For example:

top

or:

free -h

For a Node.js application running with PM2:

pm2 monit

This helps correlate API performance with system resources.

For example:

Traffic increases
      ↓
CPU increases
      ↓
Latency increases

or:

Traffic increases
      ↓
CPU remains reasonable
      ↓
Database connections increase
      ↓
Latency increases

Those two scenarios require completely different solutions.

The surprise: the API isn't always the bottleneck

One of the biggest things load testing can reveal is that the application server isn't necessarily the problem.

Consider this architecture:

Load
 ↓
EC2
 ↓
Node.js
 ↓
MongoDB

You might expect the EC2 server to reach its limit first.

But the actual bottleneck could be:

MongoDB queries
Database connections
Slow indexes
Network latency
External APIs
Large responses
Memory usage

This is why I don't look at only one metric.

I want to correlate:

API latency
+
Error rate
+
CPU
+
Memory
+
Database behavior
+
Network

A common database problem

Suppose an endpoint performs:

const users = await User.find({
  status: "active"
});

With a small dataset, this might appear completely fine.

But under load, if the query returns a large number of documents, the application may spend significantly more time processing the result.

That can increase:

  • Response latency
  • Memory usage
  • CPU usage
  • Database workload

Pagination can help:

const users = await User.find({
  status: "active"
})
  .limit(50)
  .lean();

Indexes can also be important.

For example, if the application frequently searches by:

status
email
userId
createdAt

I want to make sure the database query patterns are properly supported.

What happens when the test gets too aggressive?

A load test can eventually push the system beyond its intended capacity.

That's useful information—but it should be done carefully.

If the system reaches:

High CPU
High memory
Database saturation
High error rate

I don't immediately conclude that the server needs to be bigger.

First I ask:

What became the bottleneck?

Only then do I decide whether the solution is:

  • Better application code
  • Database optimization
  • Caching
  • Connection-pool tuning
  • Horizontal scaling
  • Vertical scaling
  • Architecture changes

Changes I would make after testing

Depending on the results, the next step could be one or more of these.

1. Optimize database queries

Reduce unnecessary data and make frequently used queries efficient.

2. Add pagination

Avoid returning huge datasets in a single request.

3. Improve connection handling

Make sure database connections are managed efficiently under concurrency.

4. Add caching

For frequently requested data that doesn't change often, caching can reduce unnecessary database work.

5. Scale the application

If the application is genuinely CPU or memory constrained, scaling the EC2 infrastructure may be appropriate.

6. Improve observability

Load testing should ideally be combined with monitoring so that performance problems can be investigated instead of guessed.

Load testing isn't about finding one magic number

One mistake I try to avoid is thinking:

"Our API supports 500 requests per second."

That's rarely the whole story.

The real question is:

500 requests/sec
under what conditions?

For example:

  • Which endpoint?
  • What payload size?
  • How many concurrent users?
  • What database size?
  • What response size?
  • What error rate?
  • What latency target?

A meaningful performance number always needs context.

A simple performance checklist

Before considering an API ready for significant traffic, I'd check:

[ ] Baseline performance measured
[ ] Peak expected traffic tested
[ ] P50 latency recorded
[ ] P95 latency recorded
[ ] P99 latency recorded
[ ] Error rate recorded
[ ] Maximum sustainable throughput measured
[ ] CPU monitored
[ ] Memory monitored
[ ] Database performance monitored
[ ] Slow queries investigated
[ ] Recovery after peak load tested

What I learned

Load testing changed the way I think about backend performance.

Before testing, I might ask:

"Is the API fast?"

After testing, I ask:

"How does the API behave as concurrency increases?"

That's a much better question.

A backend isn't truly production-ready just because it works with a few requests.

I want to understand how it behaves when:

Traffic increases
      ↓
Resources increase
      ↓
Latency changes
      ↓
Bottlenecks appear
      ↓
System reaches its limits
      ↓
System recovers

Final takeaway

Load testing isn't something I want to do only after an application starts having production problems.

It should be part of understanding the system.

For a Node.js + Express backend running on AWS EC2, I want to know:

How much traffic can it handle?

Where does it start slowing down?

What becomes the bottleneck?

Does it recover correctly?

Those answers are much more valuable than simply knowing that the API works.

Don't wait for production traffic to discover your application's limits. Test those limits before your users do.

title: Optimize Service Logic of Your Rust Code by Replacing Arc::clone with Borrowing
description:
In a previous post, I discussed the performance benefits of exposing references rather than cloning data outright. While refining my application logic recently, I realized that this principle applies broadly: eliminating unnecessary clones is one of the easiest ways to clean up general Rust code.

The Arc::clone Trap

Rust beginners often attempt to resolve stubborn borrow checker errors by simply cloning variables and moving them into closures or functions. While move is a fundamental idiom in Rust, excessive cloning should be avoided in production-grade code.

I’ve certainly been guilty of scattering Arc::clone across a codebase just to satisfy the compiler and push a feature across the finish line. The underlying motivation is often a casual approach to Arc.

Arc (Atomic Reference Counted pointer) is a foundational smart pointer for multithreaded Rust. Even though cloning an Arc is far more lightweight than cloning a deep struct, its overhead is non-trivial:

Atomic Operations: Cloning an Arc triggers atomic increment instructions.

Cache Invalidation: These atomic operations cause cache line invalidation across CPU cores.

Contention: High-frequency cloning under heavy concurrency can introduce subtle performance bottlenecks.

Standard borrowing (& or &mut), by contrast, incurs none of these costs.

Conclusion

Aside from scenarios where ownership transfer is strictly required--such as spawning new threads or moving data across async task boundaries—we should look to optimize our Rust architecture by replacing unnecessary Arc::clone calls with proper borrowing. Clean code isn't just about compiling successfully; it's about respecting ownership and memory layout.

title: Lovable, Bolt or v0 Site to WordPress? An Honest Guide to What Works Today
description:
We make Kerf, a WordPress theme that imports websites made by AI tools. One question comes up again and again: “I built my site with Lovable (or Bolt, or v0). Can I put it on WordPress?”

The honest answer is: not by importing it—not with Kerf, and not with any tool that works from HTML. Here’s why, and what you can do instead.

Why a React App Is Different from an HTML Website

Tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Google Stitch can give you HTML files: open index.html and the whole page is there—every heading, paragraph and picture written out in the file.

Lovable, Bolt and v0 typically build React apps. Their source is components and a package.json; a build step bundles it into JavaScript, and the page is assembled in the visitor’s browser when that JavaScript runs. Open the built index.html and you’ll mostly find an empty container like <div id="root"></div>.

An HTML importer turns the elements in the HTML into editable blocks. When the elements only exist after a script builds them, there is nothing in the file to turn into blocks. That’s why Kerf doesn’t import these apps yet—and why its pre-import check tells you so before anything changes on your site.

Your Real Options

1. Keep the App Where It Is, and Add WordPress Next to It

If the site is mostly an app—logins, dashboards, live data—keep hosting it where it runs well today (for example Netlify or Vercel). If you also want a blog or editable marketing pages, run WordPress alongside it, for example on a subdomain, and link between the two.

2. Use WordPress as the Content Source (Headless)

A developer can keep the React front end and have it fetch posts and pages from WordPress’s REST API. Editors write in WordPress; the app shows the content. It’s flexible, but it is a development project, not a one-click move, and the WordPress block editor won’t show your app’s design while you edit.

3. Rebuild the Pages in WordPress

For a simple marketing site, rebuilding by hand in a page builder or block theme works. It takes time, and the result is a look-alike rather than the same design.

4. Recreate the Design as Plain HTML, Then Import It

If what you love is the look, not the app logic, you can ask an AI tool to recreate the pages as plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript—no React, no build step. That version is a normal website, and an HTML website can be imported into WordPress as editable blocks. Our prompt brief for WordPress-ready AI HTML lists what to ask for.

How to Tell Which Kind You Have

If your project has a package.json and you need to run something like npm run build to see it, it’s an app. If you can double-click index.html and see the full page with its words in the file, it’s HTML—and that’s the kind Kerf imports.

What Kerf Is For

Kerf is built for HTML websites: the ZIP you get from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Google Stitch, or from a designer. It keeps the same tags, classes, stylesheets and scripts, and makes every word, picture and menu editable in WordPress. If that’s what you have, you can try it free in your browser—a private WordPress with Kerf installed, no sign-up.

Originally published on kerf.site. Try Kerf free in your browser — a private WordPress with Kerf installed, no sign-up: https://kerf.site/demo/
