title: Python's round() and JavaScript's Math.round() Disagree on Half the Days in a Footage Summary
description:
Here is a four-day summary of camera footage, in minutes, rounded to whole hours. Python and Node are given the same numbers and the same job:

# footage.py: hours of footage per day, rounded to whole hours for a summary
minutes = {"Mon": 150, "Tue": 90, "Wed": 210, "Thu": 30}

total = 0
for day, m in minutes.items():
    hours = m / 60
    print(day, hours, "->", round(hours))
    total += round(hours)
print("sum of rounded:", total, "| true total:", sum(minutes.values()) / 60)

// footage.js: the same summary in a Node dashboard
const minutes = { Mon: 150, Tue: 90, Wed: 210, Thu: 30 };

let total = 0;
for (const [day, m] of Object.entries(minutes)) {
  const hours = m / 60;
  console.log(day, hours, "->", Math.round(hours));
  total += Math.round(hours);
}
console.log("sum of rounded:", total, "| true total:", Object.values(minutes).reduce((a, b) => a + b) / 60);

python3 footage.py
node footage.js

Mon 2.5 -> 2
Tue 1.5 -> 2
Wed 3.5 -> 4
Thu 0.5 -> 0
sum of rounded: 8 | true total: 8.0
Mon 2.5 -> 3
Tue 1.5 -> 2
Wed 3.5 -> 4
Thu 0.5 -> 1
sum of rounded: 10 | true total: 8

Two of the four days disagree, and the totals differ by two hours. Neither program has a bug. They round halves by different rules, and every day in this example lands exactly on a half.

Python's total happens to match the true total of eight hours. The per-day values do not look like school rounding at all: Monday's 2.5 hours became 2 and Thursday's half hour became 0. If a reader checks one row by hand, Python looks wrong. If the reader adds up the rows, Node looks wrong.

Disclosure: I make an Android camera app. Nothing below uses its code or describes how it counts or stores anything. The minutes are typed in by hand, the scripts are a desktop Python and Node, and every output is pasted from the scripts shown. Versions:

Python 3.10.12
v22.23.4

What round() is documented to do

Python's built-in docs state the rule plainly: "if two multiples are equally close, rounding is done toward the even choice". Their own examples are that round(0.5) and round(-0.5) are both 0, and round(1.5) is 2. This is often called banker's rounding, or half to even.

Running a few halves through both languages shows each rule:

# cases.py: what round() and format() do with halves
from decimal import Decimal

for x in (0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, -0.5, -2.5):
    print("round(%s) = %s" % (x, round(x)))
print("round(2.675, 2) =", round(2.675, 2))
print("stored value of 2.675:", Decimal(2.675))
print("f'{2.5:.0f}' =", f"{2.5:.0f}")
print("f'{2.675:.2f}' =", f"{2.675:.2f}")

round(0.5) = 0
round(1.5) = 2
round(2.5) = 2
round(3.5) = 4
round(-0.5) = 0
round(-2.5) = -2
round(2.675, 2) = 2.67
stored value of 2.675: 2.67499999999999982236431605997495353221893310546875
f'{2.5:.0f}' = 2
f'{2.675:.2f}' = 2.67

// cases.js: the JavaScript side of the same halves
for (const x of [0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, -0.5, -2.5]) {
  console.log(`Math.round(${x}) = ${Math.round(x)}`);
}
console.log("(2.675).toFixed(2) =", (2.675).toFixed(2));
console.log("(2.5).toFixed(0) =", (2.5).toFixed(0));

Math.round(0.5) = 1
Math.round(1.5) = 2
Math.round(2.5) = 3
Math.round(3.5) = 4
Math.round(-0.5) = 0
Math.round(-2.5) = -2
(2.675).toFixed(2) = 2.67
(2.5).toFixed(0) = 3

Read the two lists side by side:

  • Python's round() sends each exact half to the even neighbour: 0.5 to 0, 2.5 to 2, 3.5 to 4, and -2.5 to -2.
  • JavaScript's Math.round sent every positive half up, and sent -2.5 to -2, not -3. So in this run it does not round away from zero either. Halves went toward the larger number.
  • Python's string formatting with .0f printed 2 for 2.5, the same as round(). Switching from round() to an f-string does not change the rule.
  • JavaScript's toFixed(0) printed 3 for 2.5. So even inside one language, two built-in ways to round a half gave different answers here.

The case that is not about halves at all

round(2.675, 2) printed 2.67, and so did JavaScript's toFixed(2). That looks like half to even again, since 7 is odd and 8 is even. It is not. The docs give this exact example in a note: "This is not a bug: it’s a result of the fact that most decimal fractions can’t be represented exactly as a float."

The line in cases.py that prints the stored value shows why. Converting the float to Decimal writes out the binary value it really holds, and that value is a little below 2.675. There is no tie to break. The nearest two-place answer to the stored number is 2.67, and both languages return it.

So there are two separate effects, and they are easy to confuse:

  • A tie rule decides what happens when a value is exactly halfway. Python and JavaScript use different rules.
  • Float storage means many values you type as halves, at two or more decimal places, are not halfway in memory. No tie rule applies to them, because there is no tie.

Halves like 0.5, 1.5 and 2.5 are exact in binary, which is why the first list behaves according to the tie rule. Values like 2.675 are not, which is why they surprise people who already know about the tie rule.

Getting school rounding on purpose

The decimal module names its modes in words. ROUND_HALF_EVEN is documented as "Round to nearest with ties going to nearest even integer." and ROUND_HALF_UP as "Round to nearest with ties going away from zero."

ROUND_HALF_UP is the rule most people learned in school:

# half_up.py: school rounding with decimal, from the string and from the float
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def half_up(x, places="1"):
    return Decimal(str(x)).quantize(Decimal(places), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

for x in (0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -2.5):
    print(x, "->", half_up(x))
print("2.675 via str   ->", half_up(2.675, "0.01"))
print("2.675 via float ->", Decimal(2.675).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))

0.5 -> 1
1.5 -> 2
2.5 -> 3
-2.5 -> -3
2.675 via str   -> 2.68
2.675 via float -> 2.67

Building the Decimal from str(x) gives 2.68, because the string is the short decimal 2.675. Building it from the float directly gives 2.67, because the decimal docs say construction from a float "performs an exact conversion", and the exact value is the one just below 2.675. If you want school rounding, the conversion step matters as much as the rounding mode.

That str() step only helps when the float already holds the decimal you meant. When the value comes out of arithmetic, str() faithfully prints the arithmetic's result:

# str_caveat.py: str() only helps when the float already holds the decimal you meant
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

x = 1.1 + 1.2 + 0.05
print("x =", x)
print("half up to 0.1 via str ->", Decimal(str(x)).quantize(Decimal("0.1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))

x = 2.3499999999999996
half up to 0.1 via str -> 2.3

On paper, 1.1 + 1.2 + 0.05 is 2.35, which rounds half up to 2.4. The float sum is 2.3499999999999996, str() keeps those digits, and the answer is 2.3. To avoid that, the inputs have to be decimals from the start, for example by reading them from text as Decimal('1.1') rather than converting floats after the fact.

The one-line half up that is not one

A common shortcut is math.floor(x + 0.5). It looks like school rounding:

# floor_trick.py: the one-line "round half up" that is not one
import math

for x in (2.5, -2.5, 0.49999999999999994):
    print(repr(x), "-> floor(x + 0.5) =", math.floor(x + 0.5))

2.5 -> floor(x + 0.5) = 3
-2.5 -> floor(x + 0.5) = -2
0.49999999999999994 -> floor(x + 0.5) = 1

It does round 2.5 to 3. It rounds -2.5 to -2, which is the JavaScript result, not school rounding. And the third line is the one that breaks it: the largest float below one half goes to 1. Adding 0.5 to it produces a sum that cannot be stored exactly, the sum is rounded up to 1.0 by the float addition itself, and the floor of 1.0 is 1. A value that is less than one half rounds up.

Why the default is half to even

Half to even is not an oddity in Python. It exists to stop rounding from pushing totals in one direction. This script rounds every half from 0.5 up to 99.5 both ways and compares the sums:

# bias.py: round every half from 0.5 to 99.5, then compare the sums
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

halves = [k + 0.5 for k in range(100)]
true_sum = sum(halves)
even_sum = sum(round(x) for x in halves)
up_sum = sum(int(Decimal(str(x)).quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)) for x in halves)
print("true sum:", true_sum)
print("half-even sum:", even_sum, "| off by", even_sum - true_sum)
print("half-up sum:", up_sum, "| off by", up_sum - true_sum)

true sum: 5000.0
half-even sum: 5000 | off by 0.0
half-up sum: 5050 | off by 50.0

Half up adds half a unit for every tie, so with a hundred ties the total is off by fifty. Half to even sends half of them up and half down, and the errors cancel. That is the same effect as the footage example at the top, where Python's per-day numbers looked wrong but the total came out right.

That is a good property for sums, and a confusing one for a single displayed number. Which one you want depends on who reads the result.

Often the better fix: do not round floats at all

The footage data started as whole minutes. Keeping it in integers until the last step gives an exact answer with a rule you choose:

# integer.py: keep minutes as integers and round once, exactly
minutes = {"Mon": 150, "Tue": 90, "Wed": 210, "Thu": 30}

for day, m in minutes.items():
    print(day, m, "min ->", (m + 30) // 60, "h")
total = sum(minutes.values())
print("total:", total, "min ->", (total + 30) // 60, "h")

Mon 150 min -> 3 h
Tue 90 min -> 2 h
Wed 210 min -> 4 h
Thu 30 min -> 1 h
total: 480 min -> 8 h

(m + 30) // 60 is half up for minutes that are zero or positive, with no float involved. It is not a general rounding function, and it would need a different formula for negative values, but footage durations are not negative. The total is rounded once, from the exact sum, instead of being built from rounded parts.

Checklist

  • Decide which tie rule each number needs, and write it down in the code, not in a comment about what round() is assumed to do.
  • When two programs show the same number, check that they round it the same way. Python's round() and JavaScript's Math.round do not.
  • For display rules like school rounding, use decimal with ROUND_HALF_UP, and build the Decimal from text, not from a float.
  • Do not use math.floor(x + 0.5) as a rounding function.
  • If the data starts as whole units, such as seconds, minutes or bytes, do the arithmetic in integers and round once at the end.
  • For totals, round the sum, not the parts. If the parts must also be shown, expect them to not add up exactly, and say so in the report.

Things I did not test

  • Newer Python. I ran 3.10. The quotes come from the current online documentation. The behaviour matched what I saw, but I did not run a newer interpreter.
  • Browsers. The JavaScript ran in Node. I did not run these lines in a browser.
  • Other tools. Spreadsheets, databases and other languages each have their own rounding functions and rules. I did not test any of them, and I make no claim about what they do.
  • NumPy and pandas. Their rounding functions are separate from the built-in round(). Nothing here covers them.

Sources. Quotes are from the Python documentation pages Built-in functions (the round entry) and decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic. Outputs are pasted unedited from the scripts above.

If you want an old Android phone recording in the background so there is footage for a summary like this, the app I make is Background Camera RemoteStream on Google Play. Nothing above depends on it.

When durations come in half-hour steps, as all four days here do, every odd half hour is a tie, and the tie rule, not the footage, decides the total a reader sees.

title: Two requests, one rule, two rows: fixing the INSERT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS race in PostgreSQL
description:
A rule like "one comment per user per hour" looks easy. You check for a recent row, and you only insert if there is none. It works in every test you write by hand. Then two requests arrive at the same moment, and the rule quietly breaks.

We set up the exact case on PostgreSQL 17.5, made it fail on purpose, and tried four fixes. Every number below comes from those runs.

The question

Someone on r/PostgreSQL asked about this query. The goal was to let a user post only one comment per hour:

INSERT INTO comments (user_id, content)
SELECT :user_id, 'my comment'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM comments
  WHERE user_id = :user_id
    AND created_at > now() - interval '1 hour'
);

They asked a fair question. If two threads run this at the same time, can two comments slip through? People in the thread said yes. We wanted to show why, and what to do about it.

Why it breaks

PostgreSQL's default mode is called Read Committed. The docs say each query in this mode sees a snapshot of the database taken "the instant the query begins to run." It never sees rows that other transactions have not committed yet.

So here is the timeline:

  1. Request A runs the query. It finds no recent comment, so it inserts one. A has not committed yet.
  2. Request B runs the same query. A's new row is not committed, so B cannot see it. B also finds no recent comment, and inserts one.
  3. Both commit. The user now has two comments in the same hour.

Nothing here is a bug in PostgreSQL. The check and the insert are in one statement, but the check only looks at committed data. There is no unique key for the database to defend, so nothing makes B wait.

The test setup

Our test opens two connections. Request A runs its insert and stays open. Request B runs while A is still open. After half a second, A commits. Then we count rows.

CREATE TABLE users (id int PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE comments (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  content text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The core of the Python test, using psycopg2:

a, b = psycopg2.connect(DSN), psycopg2.connect(DSN)
fn(a.cursor(), uid, "from request A")   # A is inside its transaction
def second():
    start = time.monotonic()
    fn(b.cursor(), uid, "from request B")  # B runs while A is open
    result["waited"] = time.monotonic() - start
    b.commit()
t = threading.Thread(target=second); t.start()
time.sleep(0.5)
a.commit(); t.join()

The plain query fails just as the thread said:

naive NOT EXISTS       rows=2  B inserted=1  B waited=0.0s

Two rows, and B never waited.

Fix 1: an advisory lock per user

An advisory lock is a lock with a meaning you choose. PostgreSQL does not attach it to any table. pg_advisory_xact_lock holds the lock until the transaction ends, so you never have to free it by hand.

def advisory(cur, uid, txt):
    # Lock first, in its own statement.
    cur.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(42, %s)", (uid,))
    cur.execute(NAIVE, {"uid": uid, "txt": txt})

The 42 is just a number we picked to mean "comment limit." The second number is the user id. So two users never block each other.

The detail that matters: the lock must be its own statement, before the check. In Read Committed, each statement gets a fresh snapshot. B waits on the lock. When A commits, B gets the lock, and its next statement takes a new snapshot that includes A's row.

advisory lock          rows=1  B inserted=0  B waited=0.5s
advisory, 2 users      rows=2  B inserted=1  B waited=0.0s

B waited for A, then saw the row and inserted nothing. A second user was not slowed down at all.

Fix 2: lock the user's row

If you already have a users table, you can lock the user's row instead. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE makes any other transaction that tries to lock the same row wait.

def row_lock(cur, uid, txt):
    cur.execute("SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE id = %s FOR UPDATE", (uid,))
    cur.execute(NAIVE, {"uid": uid, "txt": txt})

FOR UPDATE on users    rows=1  B inserted=0  B waited=0.5s

Same result. This one is easy to read in code review, because the lock is on a real thing. The cost: anything else that locks that user row will wait too.

Fix 3: let the database enforce the rule

Locks only work if every code path takes them. A new script or a second service might skip the lock. A constraint cannot be skipped.

PostgreSQL has exclusion constraints. They say "no two rows may match on these tests." With the btree_gist extension, we can say "same user AND overlapping one-hour windows" is not allowed.

Our first try failed:

ALTER TABLE comments ADD CONSTRAINT x EXCLUDE USING gist
  (user_id WITH =, tstzrange(created_at, created_at + interval '1 hour') WITH &&);
-- ERROR: functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE

Adding an interval to a timestamptz can depend on the time zone setting, so PostgreSQL will not use it in an index. The fix is to store the window as its own column:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
ALTER TABLE comments ADD COLUMN active_window tstzrange NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE comments ADD CONSTRAINT one_comment_per_hour
  EXCLUDE USING gist (user_id WITH =, active_window WITH &&);

Then insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so a blocked comment is skipped and does not throw an error:

INSERT INTO comments (user_id, content, active_window)
VALUES ($1, $2, tstzrange(now(), now() + interval '1 hour'))
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

exclusion constraint   rows=1  B inserted=0  B waited=0.5s
exclusion, 2 users     rows=2  B inserted=1  B waited=0.0s

One thing to check if you copy an answer from the thread. One reply showed an exclusion constraint with only the time range, and no user_id WITH =. That version stops any two users from posting close together. Always put the user column in.

A tstzrange built this way includes its start and leaves out its end. So a comment exactly one hour later does not overlap and is allowed.

Fix 4: SERIALIZABLE, plus a retry

You can also leave the query alone and run both transactions at the SERIALIZABLE level. PostgreSQL watches for reads and writes that could not happen in any one-at-a-time order, and it cancels one of the transactions.

A committed
B commit failed, SQLSTATE 40001 - could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
serializable naive: rows = 1

This is correct, but your code must catch 40001 and run the whole transaction again. The PostgreSQL docs say the same thing: apps at this level must be ready to retry.

A trap we found: advisory lock plus REPEATABLE READ

We also ran Fix 1 with both transactions at REPEATABLE READ. It let two rows through:

B committed
repeatable read + advisory: rows = 2

The docs explain why. At REPEATABLE READ, the snapshot is taken at the start of the first statement in the transaction. Here that first statement is the lock call itself. So B's snapshot is fixed before it waits for the lock, and it never sees A's row. Fixes 1 and 2 depend on Read Committed. If your app or framework changes the isolation level, use Fix 3 or Fix 4.

Which one should you pick?

  • Fix 3, the exclusion constraint, if the rule must hold no matter which code writes to the table. It is our first choice.
  • Fix 1 or 2 if the rule is complex, such as "five comments per hour," which a simple constraint cannot express. Keep the default Read Committed level.
  • Fix 4 if your app already runs at SERIALIZABLE and has a retry loop.

In every case, keep the lock or the transaction short. B waits for as long as A holds on.

Docs we read

  • PostgreSQL 17, Transaction Isolation: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Explicit Locking, Advisory Locks: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/explicit-locking.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Advisory Lock Functions: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/functions-admin.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Constraints, Exclusion Constraints: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-constraints.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, INSERT and ON CONFLICT: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-insert.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, btree_gist: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/btree-gist.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Range Types: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/rangetypes.html

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: Persistent Vectorized Agent Memory: SQLite FTS5 to Cloud LibSQL
description:
Persistent Vectorized Agent Memory: SQLite FTS5 to Cloud LibSQL

Sebagian besar arsitektur memori agen AI yang beredar saat ini dibangun di atas fondasi yang rapuh: tumpukan wrapper LangChain yang lambat dan klaster Pinecone seharga ratusan dolar per bulan untuk sekadar menyimpan beberapa ratus megabita state dialog. Untuk agen otonom on-chain—terutama yang mengeksekusi modal riil tanpa intervensi manusia—desain seperti ini tidak hanya boros, tapi rapuh secara operasional.

Mari kita bedah arsitektur yang lebih waras: transisi dari SQLite lokal dengan FTS5 (Full-Text Search) dan ekstensi vektor sqlite-vec, menuju sinkronisasi terdistribusi via Cloud LibSQL (Turso).

Masalah Retensi State On-Chain

Agen otonom kita berjalan di Base L2 (Chain ID 8453), mengendalikan hot wallet perbendaharaan: 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919.

Ketika agen harus memutuskan alokasi likuiditas pada DEX lokal (seperti Aerodrome) atau mengevaluasi sinyal harga setiap 12 detik (interval block di Base adalah 2 detik), agen butuh dua hal secara simultan:

  1. Pencarian leksikal deterministik: Menemukan hash transaksi, alamat kontrak spesifik, atau log eksekusi kegagalan slippage secara instan.
  2. Pencarian semantik berdimensi rendah: Menilai konteks sentimen pasar dan ringkasan interaksi masa lalu.

Menjalankan dua database terpisah (satu PostgreSQL, satu Vector DB cloud) memperkenalkan latensi jaringan ganda dan race condition. LibSQL memecahkan ini: mesin SQLite yang sama, mendukung query FTS5 untuk pencarian leksikal, vektor embedding native, dan replikasi cloud global via HTTP pipeline.

Skema Hibrida: FTS5 + Vector Embedding

Kita menggabungkan indeks invers FTS5 standar SQLite dengan tabel vektor. Pendekatan hybrid search ini memberi penalti pada halusinasi embedding murni dengan cross-referencing token mentah.

-- Dijalankan pada LibSQL / Turso engine
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS agent_memory (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    timestamp INTEGER NOT NULL,
    tx_hash TEXT,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    embedding F32_BLOB(384) -- all-MiniLM-L6-v2 output
);

-- Indeks leksikal FTS5 untuk pencarian hash transaksi dan alamat EVM
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS memory_fts USING fts5(
    content,
    tx_hash UNINDEXED,
    content='agent_memory',
    content_rowid='id'
);

-- Indeks vektor native LibSQL
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_memory_vec ON agent_memory(libsql_vector_idx(embedding));

Implementasi Runtime: Sync & Rekonsiliasi State

Berikut adalah implementasi Python minimal tanpa abstraksi berlebih. Script ini membaca event on-chain Base, menghasilkan embedding lokal, dan menulis state ke remote LibSQL cluster.

import os
import json
import libsql_client
from web3 import Web3

# Konfigurasi RPC Base Mainnet
BASE_RPC_URL = "https://mainnet.base.org"
AGENT_WALLET = "0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919"
CHAIN_ID = 8453

w3 = Web3(Web3.HTTPProvider(BASE_RPC_URL))
assert w3.eth.chain_id == CHAIN_ID, "Invalid Chain ID"

# Koneksi LibSQL (Edge / Cloud)
client = libsql_client.create_client_sync(
    url=os.getenv("TURSO_DATABASE_URL"),
    auth_token=os.getenv("TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN")
)

def record_execution(tx_hash: str, raw_decision: str, embedding: list[float]):
    # Pastikan state on-chain sinkron dengan memori lokal
    receipt = w3.eth.get_transaction_receipt(tx_hash)
    status_str = "SUCCESS" if receipt.status == 1 else "REVERTED"

    payload = f"tx:{tx_hash} | status:{status_str} | rationale:{raw_decision}"
    vec_blob = json.dumps(embedding)

    client.execute(
        """
        INSERT INTO agent_memory (timestamp, tx_hash, content, embedding)
        VALUES (unixepoch(), ?, ?, vector32(?))
        """,
        [tx_hash, payload, vec_blob]
    )

def recall_relevant_context(query_vec: list[float], keyword: str, limit: int = 5):
    # Hybrid query: Gabungan leksikal FTS5 dan cosine similarity
    query = """
    SELECT m.tx_hash, m.content, vector_distance_cos(m.embedding, vector32(?)) as dist
    FROM agent_memory m
    JOIN memory_fts f ON m.id = f.rowid
    WHERE memory_fts MATCH ?
    ORDER BY dist ASC
    LIMIT ?;
    """
    res = client.execute(query, [json.dumps(query_vec), keyword, limit])
    return res.rows

Angka Riil: Latensi dan Biaya Operasional

Kami menguji arsitektur ini pada VPS tunggal (2 vCPU, 4GB RAM) di region AWS Frankfurt yang berkomunikasi dengan Base sequencer dan Turso primary replica:

  • Query FTS5 murni: ~0.4ms
  • Vector k-NN (100.000 row, dimensi 384): ~3.8ms
  • Write via HTTP pipeline (LibSQL): ~42ms (tergantung round-trip internet)
  • Ukuran database pada 250.000 log eksekusi: 142MB.

Bandingkan angka tersebut dengan klaster vector database komersial terpisah, di mana latensi jaringan ganda rata-rata memakan waktu 85ms hingga 140ms hanya untuk layer data. Ketika sequencer Base mengonfirmasi transaksi dalam hitungan detik, membuang ratusan milidetik pada layer database adalah bentuk kegagalan teknis.

Sederhanakan sistem Anda. Agen on-chain tidak

title: Two checks worth adding when you rewrite a checkout modal
description:
While rebuilding the free-preview and checkout flow in CrawlGraph, our review caught two details that are easy to miss: inherited disabled state and native email validation.

The browser APIs covered both cases. We added checks for the pending request state.

I build CrawlGraph, a backlink research and outreach tool. Here are the two checks from the interface work we just released.

1. A fieldset can disable an input without changing its attributes

Our checkout has a plan chooser. While its request is pending, the chooser's fieldset is disabled.

A focus-trap selector like this looks reasonable:

panel.querySelectorAll('button:not([disabled]), input:not([disabled])');

But an input inside a disabled fieldset can match that selector while still being disabled by the browser. It may have no disabled attribute of its own.

That matters when your trap treats the input as its last focusable element. Shift+Tab can try to focus a control that cannot receive focus. Forward Tab can leave the dialog because your calculated boundary is wrong.

Check effective state as well as visibility:

const controls = [...panel.querySelectorAll(focusableSelector)]
  .filter((element) => element.getClientRects().length > 0)
  .filter((element) => !element.matches(':disabled'));

Use a delayed checkout response, then press Tab and Shift+Tab from the close button while the request is pending.

MDN describes how disabled fieldsets affect their descendant controls.

2. Inline errors should keep the browser's email validity check

We wanted an inline error instead of the browser's validation bubble, so the rewritten form used noValidate.

That makes the submit handler responsible for validation. A check that only asks whether the string contains @ accepts user@@example.com far enough to start a request.

For an email input, the browser still exposes its validity state:

const invalid =
  !email.trim() ||
  input.validity.typeMismatch ||
  !input.validity.valid;

if (invalid) {
  showInlineError();
  input.focus();
  return;
}

// Track the valid action and start the request after this guard.

Keep the visible label, associate the error with the field, and preserve the typed address. Client validation improves the interaction; the server still validates the request independently.

The typeMismatch documentation explains the email and URL checks.

One more check for nested dialogs

Our free preview can open checkout. Escape should close the top dialog, preserve the preview beneath it, and return focus to the button that opened checkout. Background scrolling should remain locked until the final dialog closes.

We now render one responsive panel per modal instead of separate desktop and mobile copies. A shared stack owns focus and scroll behavior.

The WAI modal-dialog pattern is a useful baseline for Tab, Shift+Tab, initial focus and Escape behavior. We checked the Stripe backlink lookup against the live API and covered pending, error and already-paid checkout states with controlled responses.

The updated CrawlGraph preview lets you try up to five referring-domain rows without creating an account. Paid retrieval and CSV/JSON exports support up to 100,000 referring-domain rows per lookup. Paid users can also save outreach targets, find published contact emails and open a draft in their mail app.

The updated flow is live. Try a stripe.com lookup and follow the results into the outreach workflow.

title: Zeen: A New Systems Programming Language with a Comptime Engine
description:
Website: zeen-lang.tech
Github: mealet/zeen

(Would appreciate if you'd leave a star on Github)

What is Zeen

Zeen - a modern systems programming language designed for simplicity, safety, and predictable control over memory. It provides toolchains and compiler rules to operate data easily and drop it automatically after usage with move semantics to avoid any runtime overhead. The main idea is to create a tool to develop efficient software where most errors are caught at compile time.

Zeen took many design choices from Rust and Zig programming languages, which makes it more familiar for most developers. Besides that it introduces its own approach to ownership, memory management, and compile-time execution.

Development Tools

Besides compiler and set of libraries (core, std), Zeen has:

  • Editors plugins for VS Code and Neovim
  • Package manager Zora

Small Example 

fn print_this[T: Display](value: T) {
  @println("Yeah, I've printed this: {}", value);
}

fn main() {
  print_this(123);
  print_this("hello!");
}

Quick Start

  1. Install latest release following official guide from documentation.
  2. Create new project with Zora: 
zora new my_project
cd my_project
  1. Write code and run your binary package: 
zora run

New Comptime Engine

Last update v0.4.0 brought a lot of enhancements: frontend performance, new warnings system, new macros, fixed C ABI and Comptime Engine.

Zeen's comptime engine allows you to move some evaluations or constructions away from runtime to the compiler.

You can define and eval constants, create Comptime functions which can construct new types, export expressions and declarations, emit declarations into current scope, format print at the compile time and more. Here's some examples of it.

Simple constants and splicing:

comptime N = 16;
comptime SquaredN = N * N;

fn main() {
  @println("{} -> {}", N, SquaredN);
  @println("$(N) -> $(SquaredN)");
}

Advanced usage (declarations, type values and etc):

comptime fn pair_of(struct_name: comptime_str, a: zeen_type, b: zeen_type) zeen_decl {
  @zeen_decl(
    struct $(struct_name) {
      pub a: $(a),
      pub b: $(b),
    }
  )
}

comptime {
  @emit(pair_of("NumsPair", i32, f32));
}

fn main() {
  let pair = NumsPair { .a = 1, .b = 1.0 };
  @println("{} {}", pair.a, pair.b);
}

See more info and examples on changelog and comptime docs pages.

title: OAuth Test Emails Need a Trust Boundary
description:
OAuth tests often look safe because they run in a staging environment. The risk is that a test email, a callback URL, and an application account can become one uncontrolled identity. If those pieces are reused between runs, a test can pass for the wrong reason or expose a token that was meant for somebody else.

The useful boundary is simple: treat the mailbox as an untrusted external actor, even when your team owns it. OAuth should prove that the callback belongs to the right flow, and the test should prove that the right account received the right message. Those are related checks, but they are not the same check.

The trust boundary in an OAuth email test

A typical test creates a user, starts an authorization request, follows a callback, and checks an email or account state. There are at least three identities in this flow:

  • The browser or API client running the test.
  • The application account being created or authenticated.
  • The mailbox receiving the verification message.

The threat model get clearer when each identity has a separate owner and lifetime. A mailbox address should not be treated as proof that the OAuth state is valid. An email link should not be treated as proof that the callback came from the expected authorization request.

This matters for tests that use a burner email generator or a disposable mailbox service. These tools can make setup fast, but convenience does not remove the need for ownership checks. A mailbox that is easy to create may also be easy to confuse with a mailbox from a previous run.

A small threat model

Start by listing what can go wrong. You do not need a large security document; a short table in the test repository is often enough.

Asset Failure Useful control
OAuth state value A callback from another run is accepted Bind state to a run and expire it quickly
Authorization code A code is replayed after use Exchange once and record the result
Verification link A stale message verifies the wrong account Bind the token to a test identity
Mailbox contents Logs or artifacts expose a live token Redact message bodies and URLs
Test user Data leaks across parallel workers Use a unique worker-scoped identity

The most common mistake is checking only that a message exists. That confirms delivery, not ownership. The test should match a run identifier, recipient, expected provider, and message purpose. If one of those values is missing, the assertion is weaker than it looks.

Keep the callback and mailbox separate

The OAuth callback handler should validate state, the registered redirect URI, the code exchange result, and the expected client. It should not query a mailbox to decide whether the callback is trustworthy. Mail is an asynchronous side effect, while the callback is part of the authorization protocol.

The mailbox assertion can happen after the application records the authorization result. Give the message a correlation value that is safe to log, such as a short run ID. Avoid putting access tokens, authorization codes, or full email addresses into that value.

For example, a test can carry this small context:

{
  "run_id": "oauth-worker-07-1842",
  "user_id": "test-user-1842",
  "mailbox_id": "mailbox-1842",
  "expected_flow": "signup-verification"
}

The callback assertion checks the OAuth fields. The mailbox assertion checks the recipient and correlation value. Keeping the checks seperate makes failures easier to classify and limits the damage from a leaked message.

For broader delivery coverage, ephemeral email smoke tests are a useful companion pattern. They should verify delivery behavior, not replace the application’s authorization checks.

Design safer test identities

Create a fresh test identity per run or per worker. At minimum, make the email address, OAuth state, and application user record traceable to the same run. Do not use a shared administrator account to test a normal user flow; that makes a passing test less meaningful and a leaked token more serious.

Set a short lifetime on test credentials. Revoke or delete the test user after the run, and expire unread messages when the mailbox provider supports it. If cleanup fails, the next run should still be isolated. Cleanup is defense in depth, not the only defense.

Be cautious with fixtures named dummy e mail or tempail mail. A typo in a fixture label can hide a real difference between a local fake and a remotely reachable mailbox. Name the fixture by its trust level, such as local_sink_mailbox or isolated_test_mailbox, so the intended boundary is visible to reviewers.

A failure taxonomy for email tests can help separate callback errors, provider delays, stale messages, and cleanup failures. That classification is more useful than a single generic “email not received” result.

A practical review checklist

  • Is every OAuth state value bound to one test run and one client?
  • Can a callback be accepted after the code or state has been used?
  • Is the mailbox recipient checked exactly, rather than by a loose subject search?
  • Are tokens and full message URLs removed from logs and CI artifacts?
  • Does each parallel worker receive a distinct test identity?
  • Does the test still fail safely when the mailbox is delayed or unavailable?
  • Is cleanup attempted without making the test depend on cleanup success?

A good test should be boring about identity. The account, callback, and message all point to the same run, and an unrelated message cannot satisfy the assertion by accident.

Common questions

Can a temporary mailbox prove OAuth ownership?

No. It can prove that a message was delivered to a monitored address. OAuth ownership still depends on protocol checks, account binding, and one-time token handling.

Should I reuse one mailbox for faster CI?

Only for a deliberately isolated smoke test. For parallel or security-sensitive flows, reuse creates ambiguity and stale-message failures. Faster setup is not worth losing a clear identity boundary.

What should I inspect when the test fails intermittently?

Record the run ID, state lifecycle, callback response, message correlation value, and mailbox age. Check whether the failure is delivery timing, a stale message, a race between workers, or an actual validation defect. The right diagnosis depends of these categories, so label them explicitly.

The goal is not to make email tests more complicated. It is to make their trust assumptions visible, so a passing test means the intended user completed the intended OAuth flow.

title: Dockerfile multi-stage para Go: de 800 MB a menos de 20 MB
description:
Si tu Dockerfile de Go empieza con FROM golang y termina con CMD ["./app"], tu imagen probablemente pesa más de 800 MB: incluye el compilador, el código fuente y la caché de módulos. Nada de eso hace falta para ejecutar un binario. Con un build multi-stage compilamos en una imagen y copiamos solo el binario a otra mínima.

El Dockerfile 

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
ARG GO_VERSION=1.24

FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:${GO_VERSION}-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src

COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    go mod download

COPY . .

ARG TARGETOS
ARG TARGETARCH
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=${TARGETOS} GOARCH=${TARGETARCH} \
    go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/app .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Qué hace cada parte

Dos FROM = dos etapas. La primera (build) tiene Go completo. La segunda parte de una imagen casi vacía y solo recibe /out/app con COPY --from=build. Todo lo demás se descarta.

go.mod y go.sum antes que el código. Docker cachea cada instrucción. Si copias todo de una vez, cualquier cambio en un .go invalida la descarga de módulos. Separándolos, go mod download solo se repite cuando cambian tus dependencias.

RUN --mount=type=cache. Es una función de BuildKit (activado por defecto desde Docker 23). Monta una caché persistente durante el build sin guardarla en la imagen. La caché de compilación de Go (/root/.cache/go-build) hace que recompilar tras un cambio pequeño tarde segundos.

CGO_ENABLED=0. Genera un binario estático que no depende de la libc del sistema. Es lo que permite usar una imagen final sin libc.

-trimpath -ldflags="-s -w". -trimpath quita las rutas de tu máquina del binario y -s -w elimina la tabla de símbolos y la información de depuración. El binario queda notablemente más chico.

--platform=$BUILDPLATFORM + TARGETOS/TARGETARCH. Go compila de forma cruzada sin esfuerzo. Con esto, el compilador corre nativo en tu máquina y genera el binario para la arquitectura que pidas, sin emular con QEMU:

docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t mi-servicio .

distroless/static-debian12:nonroot. Una imagen de unos 2 MB que contiene certificados CA (para llamar APIs HTTPS), datos de zona horaria y un usuario sin privilegios. No tiene shell ni gestor de paquetes: si alguien compromete tu app, no tiene herramientas para moverse.

Un detalle importante

Como distroless no tiene shell, no puedes usar HEALTHCHECK CMD curl .... Define el healthcheck en Kubernetes o compose apuntando a tu endpoint, o haz que tu binario acepte un flag como -healthcheck y usa HEALTHCHECK CMD ["/app", "-healthcheck"].

Compruébalo 

docker build -t mi-servicio .
docker images mi-servicio

Para un servicio HTTP típico verás una imagen de entre 10 y 25 MB. Menos tamaño significa despliegues más rápidos, menos costo de almacenamiento y menos superficie de ataque.

¿Te sirvió? Este ejemplo es parte del Pack Dockerfiles Optimizados: paga lo que quieras, desde 2 USD. Más recursos gratis en GitHub.

title: DharaniAI (ధరణి / धरणी): Offline Climate Resilience & Native Voice Advisory for Indian Drylands 🌾☀️🔊
description:
DharaniAI (ధరణి / धरणी): Offline Climate Resilience & Native Voice Advisory for Indian Drylands 🌾☀️🔊

An Offline Edge AI Decision Engine for Smallholder Farmers in Extreme Drought Zones, Powered by Google Gemma 2.

Built to combat climate change, drought vulnerability, and rural connectivity deserts.

Targeting: Open-Source AI & Gemma 2 edge solutions.

🌍 The Problem: Climate Crisis in India's Drylands

Over 68% of India's cultivable agricultural land is chronically vulnerable to drought. Semi-arid rain-shadow regions like:

  • Rayalaseema (Anantapur / Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh)
  • Marathwada & Vidarbha (Latur, Beed, Maharashtra)
  • Bundelkhand (Jhansi, Mahoba, UP/MP border)
  • North Karnataka (Vijayapura, Bagalkot)
  • Western Rajasthan (Thar Desert border)

...face devastating crop loss due to recurring heatwaves (42°C+), shifting monsoons, and extreme evapotranspiration.

Why Conventional Solutions Fail Farmers:

  1. Connectivity Deserts: During intense heatwaves or storm-triggered grid failures, cellular towers frequently lose power. Cloud-dependent AI apps become completely inaccessible when farmers need urgent guidance most.
  2. Raw Forecasts vs Actionable Science: A standard weather app reporting "41°C and 25% humidity" does not tell a farmer how many liters of water their soil is losing per hour, or how to prevent flower drop in groundnut/cotton.
  3. The Literacy & Language Barrier: Dense technical PDF advisories issued by universities are difficult for grassroots farmers to interpret.

💡 The Solution: DharaniAI (ధరణి / धरणी)

DharaniAI combines real micro-climate physics, official ICAR & CRIDA (Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture) contingency plans, and Google's open-weight Gemma 2 running 100% locally and offline on edge devices.

Most importantly, it features Native Audio Speech Synthesis, speaking directly to farmers in their mother tongue (Telugu, Hindi, Marathi, Kannada, English) through laptop or smartphone speakers!

🔬 Core System Architecture 

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   DHARANI AI (Offline Edge System)                     │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Micro-Climate Physics Engine                                        │
│    -> Tetens Equation: Saturation vs Actual Vapor Pressure             │
│    -> Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD in kPa)                              │
│    -> FAO-56 Hargreaves-Samani: Evapotranspiration (ET0 in L/ha/day)   │
│                                                                        │
│ 2. Indian Dryland Agronomy Knowledge Base (RAG)                        │
│    -> ICAR / CRIDA Drought Contingency Frameworks                     │
│    -> Critical crop water sensitivity stages                           │
│    -> Organic foliar anti-transpirants (Kaolin, KNO3, Jeevamrutha)    │
│                                                                        │
│ 3. Gemma 2 Local Intelligence (via Ollama)                             │
│    -> General reasoning across thousands of crops & pest symptoms      │
│    -> Translates complex agro-physics into empathetic action plans     │
│                                                                        │
│ 4. Native Voice & Regional Audio Synthesizer                           │
│    -> Automatic voice audio generation in Telugu, Hindi, Marathi, etc. │
│    -> Speaks actionable advice aloud for grassroots farmers            │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

✨ Key Capabilities

1. ☀️ Real-Time Agro-Meteorological Physics

  • Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD): Measures the atmospheric drying power. When VPD > 2.5 kPa, plant stomata violently close, halting photosynthesis and causing flower drop.
  • Reference Evapotranspiration ($ET_0$): Calculates the exact water volume evaporating from the soil canopy (e.g. 7.5 mm/day = 75,000 Liters/hectare/day).

2. 🌾 Structured ICAR/CRIDA Crisis Strategies

  • Emergency Drought Action Plans: Specific anti-transpirant recipes (e.g. 1% Potassium Nitrate, 5% Kaolin clay) to reduce transpirational water loss and cool canopies by 2–3°C.
  • Post-Sunset Pulse Irrigation: Scheduling water application after 7 PM to prevent up to 60% surface evaporation loss.
  • Soil Sponge Building: Crop residue mulching, biochar, and broad-bed furrowing to maximize soil water retention.

3. 🔊 Native Speech for Farmers

Farmers don't need to read walls of text. DharaniAI generates a crystal-clear, warm voice audio briefing in:

  • Telugu (తెలుగు)
  • Hindi (हिन्दी)
  • Marathi (मराठी)
  • Kannada (ಕನ್ನಡ)
  • English

4. 🧠 Beyond Presets: General Crop & Climate Intelligence

While pre-loaded with major dryland crops (Groundnut, Cotton, Soybean, Pearl Millet, Pigeonpea), Gemma 2 can evaluate any custom observation or question entered by the farmer:

"My tomato leaves are curling under high heat and whiteflies are swarming..."

"Borewell water has high salinity (EC 3.2), how should I irrigate my chillies?"

🔮 Why Open-Source AI & Gemma 2 are Essential

  • Edge Deployment in Remote Villages: Google's Gemma 2 (gemma2:2b) delivers high-tier scientific reasoning while running smoothly on modest local hardware (even a single laptop or edge gateway) with zero internet access.
  • Data Privacy & Zero Cloud Subscriptions: Village panchayats, cooperatives, and smallholders cannot afford recurring per-token cloud API bills. DharaniAI operates at zero operational marginal cost.

💻 Open-Source Code & Repository

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/volety17/ghost-of-lords (see /dharani_ai)
  • Tech Stack: Python 3.11, Google Gemma 2, Streamlit, Ollama, gTTS / pyttsx3, FAO-56 Agro-Meteorology algorithms.

🚀 Running DharaniAI Locally 

git clone https://github.com/volety17/ghost-of-lords.git
cd ghost-of-lords
pip install streamlit gTTS pyttsx3 requests
ollama pull gemma2:2b
python -m streamlit run dharani_ai/app.py

Dedicated to the resilient farmers of India's drylands. 🌾🇮🇳

title: Windows 11 Slow Startup? 9 Fixes That Actually Speed Up Boot Time
description:
If your Windows 11 PC takes forever to reach the desktop, the culprit is rarely one big thing — it's usually a pile-up of small slowdowns: apps launching at boot, services fighting over your disk, and settings that were never tuned for speed. Here are 9 fixes that actually work, ordered from quickest to deepest.

Fix 1: Turn off unnecessary startup apps

Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), go to Startup apps, and disable anything you don't need the second you log in — game launchers, updaters, chat apps. Each one steals seconds. Keep only your antivirus.

Fix 2: Enable Fast Startup

Go to Settings > System > Power & battery > "Additional power settings" > "Choose what the power buttons do", and make sure "Turn on fast startup" is checked. This makes shutdown save a system snapshot so boot resumes faster.

Fix 3: Free up disk space

A nearly full drive slows everything down. Open Settings > System > Storage and use Storage Sense to clear temp files, or manually empty Downloads and the Recycle Bin. Aim for at least 10–15% free space.

Fix 4: Update your drivers — especially storage drivers

Outdated NVMe/SATA drivers can stall the boot sequence. Open Device Manager, expand Disk drives and IDE ATA/ATAPI controllers, right-click each, and choose "Update driver". Then check your laptop maker's site for chipset drivers.

Fix 5: Run Startup Repair or SFC

Corrupted system files can drag boot times. Open Terminal (Admin) and run sfc /scannow, then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Both are safe and built into Windows.

Fix 6: Delay heavy background services

Some apps (cloud sync, VPNs) can be set to start a minute after login instead of instantly — check each app's settings for a "launch at startup" delay option.

Fix 7: Disable Windows search indexing on old HDDs

If you're still on a spinning hard drive, Settings > Privacy & security > Searching Windows > turn off "Find my files: Classic" indexing, or exclude large folders. On SSDs, skip this — it barely helps.

Fix 8: Update Windows and your BIOS

Pending cumulative updates sometimes include boot-time optimizations. Check Settings > Windows Update, and check your manufacturer's support page for a BIOS update — newer firmware often improves boot initialization.

Fix 9: Do a clean boot to find the slowpoke

Type msconfig, open System Configuration, and on the Services tab check "Hide all Microsoft services" then "Disable all". Restart — if boot is fast now, re-enable services in groups until you find the offender. Then leave it disabled.

A note on HDD vs SSD: if your PC still boots from a mechanical hard drive, no software tweak beats upgrading to an SSD — boot times drop from minutes to seconds. That's the single biggest upgrade you can make.

For the full walkthrough with exact menu paths and screenshots, this step-by-step slow-startup guide walks through each fix in detail.
