title: Learning LangChain by Building: 7 Tiny Examples from Chat Models to RAG
description:
I've spent about 12 years building data pipelines on AWS, most recently for financial-crimes compliance in banking. When I started working with LLMs, I kept hitting the same wall. Every tutorial was either a one-line "hello world" or a 500-line agent framework I couldn't take apart.

So I did what data engineers do with any new tool: I broke it into the smallest pieces I could run, inspect, and reason about. The result is a repo of seven standalone LangChain scripts, each teaching exactly one concept. Every file runs on its own, and most are under 40 lines.

This post walks through them in order, from "call a model" to "answer questions over a PDF," and ends with how I'd move the whole thing onto Amazon Bedrock.

What LangChain is, and why it exists

LangChain is an open-source framework that puts standard, swappable interfaces around everything an LLM application needs besides the model itself.

A raw LLM is a function: text in, text out. A real application needs prompts built from variables, conversation state, output your code can parse, access to private data, and the ability to call functions. Without a framework, you write that glue yourself, once per provider.

Problem without a framework What LangChain gives you
Each provider has its own SDK and response format One chat-model interface: model.invoke(...)
Prompts are f-strings scattered everywhere Reusable prompt templates
Parsing free-form text with regex Output parsers and Pydantic structured output
The model forgets everything between calls Explicit message objects for history
The model can't see your documents Loaders, splitters, embeddings, vector stores
The model can't take actions Tools with auto-generated schemas
Multi-step logic is custom glue LCEL: `prompt \

As a data engineer, the last row is what sold me. LCEL treats every component as a pipeline stage with the same interface, which is exactly how I already think about ETL.

1. Chat models: one interface, any provider

The first script calls Llama 3.3 on Hugging Face. The OpenAI and Gemini versions sit right above it, commented out.
{% raw %}

#model = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-5-mini")
#model = ChatGoogleGenerativeAI(model="gemini-2.5-flash")

llm = HuggingFaceEndpoint(
    repo_id="meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct",
    task="text-generation",
)
model = ChatHuggingFace(llm=llm)

response = model.invoke("tell me about ai agents in 10 words?")
print(response.content)

Swap the comment and nothing else changes. That one property is the whole value proposition of the framework in miniature.

2. Memory is just a list you resend

LLMs are stateless. Each call only knows what you send it, so "memory" means resending the conversation every turn.

conversation = [SystemMessage(content="You are a senior data engineer. Answer in 3 to 4 sentences.")]

while True:
    query = input("Ask a question: ")
    if query.lower() == "exit":
        break
    conversation.append(HumanMessage(content=query))
    response = model.invoke(conversation)
    conversation.append(AIMessage(content=response.content))
    print(response.content)

The lesson: history has a cost. The list grows every turn, so tokens and latency grow with it. Production apps trim or summarize older messages.

3. Chains with LCEL: pipelines for prompts

This is where LangChain clicked for me. The pipe operator connects components so each output feeds the next input:

prompt  = PromptTemplate(template="tell me about {topic} in 100 words")
prompt1 = PromptTemplate(template="based on below article, create 5 quiz questions\n\n{article}")
parser  = StrOutputParser()

chain = prompt | model | parser | prompt1 | model | parser
print(chain.invoke({"topic": "ai agents"}))

One input produces a 100-word article, which becomes the input for five quiz questions. Two details worth noticing:

  • StrOutputParser turns the model's message object into a plain string.
  • prompt1 has exactly one variable, so LangChain maps that string into {article} automatically. No glue code.

Every stage is a Runnable, so the same chain also supports .batch() and .stream() without changes.

4. Structured output: stop parsing with regex

If code consumes the answer, you want data, not prose. Define a Pydantic model and let LangChain enforce it:

class SQLOutput(BaseModel):
    query: str = Field(description="The generated SQL query.")
    explanation: str = Field(description="A brief explanation of the SQL query.")

model_structured = model.with_structured_output(SQLOutput)
response = model_structured.invoke("give me sql to get top 5 products by sales from orders table")

print(response.query)
print(response.explanation)

You get a typed object back. The Field descriptions are sent to the model too, so writing them well improves the output.

5. Tool calling, with guardrails a bank would accept

A tool is a Python function the model can ask to call. The @tool decorator reads the name, type hints, and docstring to build a schema the model understands.

I built tools over a local SQL Server retail database, plus a stock-price lookup:

Tool What it does
get_tables Lists base tables in dbo
get_schema Returns columns and data types for a table
validate_select_query Confirms a query is one read-only SELECT
run_query Runs a validated query, returns rows as dicts
get_engine Reconnects to a different server or database
get_stock_price Fetches a quote from the Finnhub API

Coming from regulated financial services, I wasn't going to let a model near a database without a gate. Every SQL tool goes through one validator:

def _validate_select(query: str) -> str:
    normalized = (query or "").strip()
    if not normalized:
        raise ValueError("The query is empty.")
    if normalized.endswith(";"):
        normalized = normalized[:-1].rstrip()
    if any(tok in normalized for tok in (";", "--", "/*", "*/")):
        raise ValueError("Only one SELECT statement is allowed.")
    if not re.match(r"^(SELECT|WITH)\b", normalized, flags=re.IGNORECASE):
        raise ValueError("Only SELECT queries are allowed.")
    if re.search(r"\b(INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|MERGE|DROP|ALTER|CREATE|TRUNCATE|EXEC|EXECUTE|GRANT|REVOKE|INTO)\b",
                 normalized, flags=re.IGNORECASE):
        raise ValueError("Write/DDL keywords are not allowed.")
    return normalized

It blocks stacked statements, comments (a classic injection trick), anything that isn't SELECT or a CTE, and every write or DDL keyword, including SELECT ... INTO. It's a first line of defense, not the only one. In production, pair it with a read-only database login.

Then I bind the tools to the model:

model_tools = model.bind_tools([get_engine, get_stock_price, get_tables, get_schema])
result = model_tools.invoke("show me all the tables in the database")

for tool_call in result.tool_calls:
    print(f"Calling tool '{tool_call['name']}' with arguments {tool_call['args']}")

The most important thing I learned here: the model never runs your code. It returns a request, a tool name plus arguments. Your program decides whether to execute it. That boundary is where security and auditability live, and it's why tool calling is far less scary than it sounds.

6 and 7. RAG over an HR policy PDF

An LLM doesn't know your internal documents, and retraining it is expensive. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves the relevant passages at question time and hands them to the model as context. I used a sample bank HR policy as the source.

The pipeline has two halves:

  1. Ingest (run once): PDF → Markdown → chunks → embeddings → Chroma
  2. Retrieve (per question): question → embedding → nearest chunks

Ingest 

embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small", dimensions=300)

loader = PyMuPDF4LLMLoader("docs/Bank_HR_Policy.pdf", mode="single")
docs = loader.load()

splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(headers_to_split_on=[
    ("#", "Header 1"), ("##", "Header 2"), ("###", "Header 3"),
])
chunks = splitter.split_text(docs[0].page_content)

vector_store = Chroma(collection_name="hr_policies",
                      embedding_function=embeddings,
                      persist_directory="./chroma_db")
vector_store.add_documents(chunks)

The choice that mattered most was how to split. Splitting by a fixed character count is the common default, and it can cut a policy rule in half. My earlier experiment is still in the repo as chunking.py for comparison. Converting the PDF to Markdown first and splitting on headings means each chunk is one complete policy section. The heading text is stored as metadata, so every result can say where it came from.

I also set the embedding size to 300 dimensions. That's smaller and cheaper to store and search, and plenty for a single policy document.

Retrieve 

embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small", dimensions=300)  # must match ingest
vector_store = Chroma(collection_name="hr_policies",
                      embedding_function=embeddings,
                      persist_directory="./chroma_db")

similar_docs = vector_store.similarity_search("What is the policy on remote work?", k=2)

The question must be embedded with the same model and dimensions used at ingest, or the vectors aren't comparable. The search returns the two chunks closest in meaning, even when they share no exact words with the question.

One gotcha: add_documents() appends. Run ingestion twice and you get duplicate chunks. Delete ./chroma_db before a rebuild.

Taking it to AWS with Amazon Bedrock

The repo uses OpenAI, but because LangChain abstracts the provider, moving to Amazon Bedrock is mostly a two-line change with the langchain-aws package:

from langchain_aws import ChatBedrockConverse, BedrockEmbeddings

model = ChatBedrockConverse(model="<a Bedrock model ID enabled in your account>")
embeddings = BedrockEmbeddings(model_id="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0")

The chains, structured output, tool binding, and Chroma code stay the same. For my world, the bigger wins are operational:

  • No API keys in .env. Bedrock authenticates with IAM roles, so access is governed and auditable like any other AWS service.
  • Data stays in your AWS account and Region, which matters a lot in banking.
  • A managed RAG path. Bedrock Knowledge Bases can replace the hand-built ingest and retrieve steps when you outgrow a local Chroma store.

One thing to re-check when you switch: embedding dimensions. Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports a fixed set of sizes, not arbitrary values like the 300 I used with OpenAI, and you must re-ingest whenever the embedding model changes.

What I learned

  • Small scripts beat big frameworks for learning. One concept per file made each abstraction obvious before I combined them.
  • LCEL is just a pipeline. If you've built ETL, you already understand chains.
  • The model proposes; your code disposes. Tool calling is safe to the degree your validation and permissions are.
  • RAG quality starts at chunking. Structure-aware splitting mattered more than anything I did at query time.
  • Load config before imports that read it. My tools.py reads environment variables at import time, so calling load_dotenv() after import tools silently used defaults. Small bug, real lesson.

What's next

Each script stops at a clear boundary, and each next step is a post of its own:

  • Close the RAG loop: feed retrieved chunks into a prompt so the model answers with citations.
  • Add an agent loop: execute tool calls, return results, and repeat until the model answers.
  • Text-to-SQL agent: chain get_tables → get_schema → validate_select_query → run_query so plain-English questions return real data.
  • Run it all on Bedrock, with Knowledge Bases for retrieval.

Try it yourself

The full repo, with setup steps and a concept-by-concept README, is here: https://github.com/KiranGunturu/langchain/tree/main

Clone it, add an OPENAI_API_KEY to a .env file, and run any script on its own. If you're a data engineer getting into GenAI, I'd love to hear which concept clicked for you, or what you'd want covered next.

title: Preparing for a Frontend Developer Interview? A Practical 30-Day Roadmap
description:
Frontend interviews can be challenging, even when you have hands-on experience with React and JavaScript.

You might understand how to build a component, manage state, and call APIs, but interviews often test much more: JavaScript fundamentals, problem-solving, React concepts, performance optimization, and your ability to explain technical decisions.

The biggest challenge isn't always learning more. It's knowing what to prepare, in what order, and how to practise consistently.

Here is a practical roadmap you can use to organize your preparation.

Week 1: Strengthen Your JavaScript Fundamentals

JavaScript is one of the most important areas to prepare for a frontend interview.

Focus on:

  • var, let, and const
  • Scope, closures, and hoisting
  • Promises, async/await, and error handling
  • The event loop and microtasks versus macrotasks
  • Array methods such as map, filter, and reduce
  • Objects, references, shallow copies, and deep copies

Practice challenge: Explain the difference between Promise.all() and Promise.allSettled().

Promise.all() rejects when one of its input promises rejects. Promise.allSettled() waits until all input promises settle and returns the outcome of each one.

Don't stop at memorizing definitions. Practise explaining when you would use each method in a real application.

Week 2: Focus on React and TypeScript

Once your JavaScript fundamentals are solid, move to React.

Important topics include:

  • Props, state, and component rendering
  • useState, useEffect, useMemo, and useCallback
  • Controlled and uncontrolled components
  • Context API and Redux
  • Component composition and reusable hooks
  • React performance optimization
  • TypeScript interfaces, types, generics, and utility types

Practice challenge: When would you use useMemo instead of useCallback?

useMemo caches a calculated value, while useCallback caches a function reference between renders when its dependencies haven't changed.

In an interview, also explain why neither should be added everywhere automatically. First identify a meaningful performance or reference-stability problem.

Week 3: Practise Real-World Frontend Engineering

Interviewers may want to understand how you build and maintain production applications, not just how well you know individual APIs.

Prepare for:

  • HTML semantics and CSS layouts
  • Responsive design and accessibility
  • API integration and loading/error states
  • Unit testing and component testing
  • Browser rendering and frontend performance
  • Server-side rendering and client-side rendering
  • Microfrontend architecture and module federation

Practice challenge: How would you improve the performance of a React page that renders slowly?

A structured answer might cover measuring the issue first, identifying unnecessary renders, reducing expensive calculations, splitting large bundles, optimizing network requests, and checking whether large lists need virtualization.

The important part is explaining how you would identify the bottleneck before choosing a solution.

Week 4: Simulate the Interview

Use the final week to combine what you've learned.

Try to complete:

  • JavaScript coding problems under time limits
  • A small React machine-coding exercise
  • A frontend architecture discussion
  • A review of common technical questions
  • Mock interviews where you explain your answers aloud

After each session, record the topics you struggled with and revisit them.

A Simple Daily Study Routine

If you have around two hours a day, try this schedule:

  • 30 minutes: Review concepts.
  • 45 minutes: Solve coding problems.
  • 30 minutes: Practise explaining answers aloud.
  • 15 minutes: Review mistakes and note what to revisit.

Consistency is more valuable than trying to study everything in a single weekend.

Common Interview Preparation Mistakes

A few mistakes can make preparation less effective:

  1. Memorizing answers without understanding the underlying concepts.
  2. Studying React while neglecting JavaScript fundamentals.
  3. Watching tutorials without writing code yourself.
  4. Ignoring testing, accessibility, and performance.
  5. Never practising answers under interview conditions.

A structured plan helps you identify gaps and measure progress.

Want a More Structured Preparation Guide?

I created Frontend Interview Accelerator — Expanded Edition, a digital e-book designed for frontend developers with 2–5 years of experience.

It brings together frontend interview preparation topics, coding practice, and a 30-day study plan in one resource.

You can explore it here:

Frontend Interview Accelerator — Expanded Edition

The e-book is priced at $4.99. Review the product page to see whether its contents fit your preparation needs.

Disclosure: I'm the creator of this e-book, and I'm sharing it as an optional resource for readers who want a more structured way to prepare.

Let's Discuss

If you're preparing for a frontend interview, which area do you find most challenging?

  • JavaScript coding questions
  • React concepts and hooks
  • Machine-coding rounds
  • Frontend system design

Share your experience in the comments. Your answer might help another developer prepare more effectively.

title: DeepSeek overtakes Google on volume, cost per token falls 13.6%
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — August 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from May, June, and July.

August 2026 Summary

The August index reports on AI Gateway data collected through July 2026.

  • The average price paid per token fell 13.6% in July, after rising almost 20% in May and holding steady in June. Token consumption grew so quickly that even with 37% growth in spend, cost per token saw a double-digit drop.

  • DeepSeek became the second-largest lab by token volume, now running more than twice Google's volume.

  • Anthropic collected 65% of gateway spending on 30% of token volume, at 4.4 times the average price of every other lab's tokens.

  • Both media leaderboards changed hands. Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image volume from OpenAI's GPT Image, and ByteDance's Seedance led video in both volume and dollars.

Kimi K3 launched into agent work

Moonshot released Kimi K3 on July 16. Like Z.ai's GLM 5.2 released in June, it is built for long-horizon agent work, so its usage was heavy from the start at about twelve times the tokens per request of its predecessor, K2.5.

It scaled quickly. K3's daily volume tripled between launch week and the final week of July, and by month end its requests were as heavy as Claude Opus 4.8's. On the last full day of July it ranked eighth on the gateway by token volume.

The demand was new rather than diverted. K3 processed nearly two-thirds of all Kimi tokens within two weeks and 82% by the final week, while the rest of the family's volume fell only slightly.

Open weight's share of gateway spend more than doubled in July to 8.6%. More than 90% of that growth is Moonshot and Z.ai. Moonshot's share of total gateway spend quadrupled, to 2.3%. Cheap open-weight models have been taking volume for months without taking revenue. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are the first to capture significant volume at more than eleven times DeepSeek's rate per token.

DeepSeek is now second by volume

In June, this report said DeepSeek had entered the fight for token volume. Last month, we said an open-weight lab would soon be second by volume. In July, DeepSeek surpassed Google to take that place.

Google ran nearly 40% of the gateway’s token volume in April, and DeepSeek less than 1%. By July, DeepSeek ran a quarter, more than twice Google’s 11%. DeepSeek V4 Flash, its cheapest model, ran more tokens alone than all of Google.

The reversal is concentrated in consumer-facing work. Google's share of personal-assistant tokens fell by more than half in a month while DeepSeek's more than tripled, and most of the token share Google gave up went to DeepSeek. DeepSeek's V4 Flash ran more tokens than any other model on the gateway in July, nearly a fifth of the total and 70% more than the next model.

Open-weight models previously owned the cheap end of the market. Their share of gateway token volume nearly tripled between April and June, from 11% to 29%, while share of spend stayed under four cents of every gateway dollar.

In July, volume continued its growth trend, increasing to 36%. Spend broke its trend, more than doubling to nearly nine cents of every dollar, the highest in the index's history.

The four largest frontier labs' combined share of token spend, which had not fallen below 93% in seven months, fell to 89%. Google accounted for most of the decline. Almost none of the spend it lost went to DeepSeek, whose share barely moved even as its volume grew. Z.ai and Moonshot's latest models account for the entire open-weight spend increase.

Buyers sort models by what the task requires, then choose inside that tier according to price. DeepSeek and Opus were never competing. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3, both released in the last two months, are the first open-weight models running a meaningful share of the workloads historically owned by closed-weight labs.

Average price per token fell 13.6%

Companies bought more inference in July and ran more of it on cheap models. Volume grew 59%, spend grew 37%, and the average price paid per token fell 13.6%.

Holding June's mix of models constant, the average price would have held essentially flat instead of declining. OpenAI is one example: the average cost of an OpenAI token fell to 58% of its June level, because 85% of the volume it added went to GPT-5-Nano, the cheapest model in the GPT-5 family.

The entire decline in average price came from what companies chose to route. Among the thousands of teams that ran more than 10 million tokens in both months, three in four changed at least a tenth of their model mix. Three in five changed at least a quarter.

The median team's cost per token fell 2.9%, but only one team in six stayed within five percent of where it started.

A quarter pared cost by more than 30%, typically teams that entered the month paying well above the gateway average per token. Another quarter paid at least 20% more, typically teams that had been paying below the average. Concurrently, the expensive end shifted down and the cheap end migrated up.

81% of July’s tokens ran on models that were not on the gateway six months ago. Open-weight models crossed a third of all volume, at about a seventh of frontier rates. Google fell from 24.0% of gateway token volume to 10.7%. Anthropic slipped two points to 29.8%, and OpenAI’s share rose to 12.8%.

Gateway spend is up 74% since May and volume has doubled, with July's token growth running at nearly double June's pace. Spend on inference continues to increase even as each dollar buys more tokens than it did in the previous month.

Anthropic's premium widened as prices fell

Anthropic has held more than 60% of gateway spend in every month we have measured, through a period in which open weight tripled its share of volume. In July, it collected 65.1% of all spend on 30% of total volume.

The average price per Anthropic token ran 4.4 times the average across every other lab, up from 3.4 in June. Part of that rise was Claude Fable 5, which returned on July 1 after a three-week export-control suspension and quickly grew to 13.2% of all gateway spend, second only to Opus 4.8. In coding agents, the gateway's largest use case by tokens, Anthropic collected more than 80% of spend.

Anthropic has no model at the bottom of the market. Haiku 4.5, its least expensive, runs just over two-thirds of the gateway average price per token. OpenAI's GPT-5-Nano runs a sixth; DeepSeek's V4 Flash a sixteenth.

Customers cutting costs on OpenAI or Google can stay in the catalog. Cutting costs on Anthropic means leaving Anthropic, and in July it still took a majority of all spending. Anthropic’s premium is the gap between what the cheap tier can do and what its customers need done.

Switching models on the AI Gateway is a one-line change, so nothing locks a customer in. When Fable 5 came back, daily volume returned to the pre-ban level almost exactly, but nine in ten of the teams running it in July had not used it before. The work returned; the customers were different.

The rest of the market's tokens averaged less than a quarter of Anthropic's price, and Anthropic still took two of every three dollars spent on the gateway. Price competition is happening, but it's happening in the part of the market with the least money in it.

Google took images, ByteDance took video

In June, OpenAI's GPT Image generated most of the gateway's images. In July, Google's Nano Banana led, at 45% of images to GPT Image's 42%, with spend split almost evenly between them. Nearly all of Nano Banana's gain came from one model, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image. Google took the image lead in the same month it fell to fourth by token volume.

ByteDance's Seedance led video on both counts, in videos generated and dollars spent. xAI's Grok Imagine, June's volume leader, fell to second. Chinese labs collected about seven of every ten dollars spent on video.

Also in July’s data

  • Within coding, the gateway's largest workload by tokens, DeepSeek ran nearly a third of the volume and Anthropic collected more than four of every five dollars.

  • Back-office agents remain the most expensive work per token, with a share of spending roughly two and a half times their share of volume.

About this report

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through July 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Volume counts all tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • Spend values every request at the lab's published list price.

  • Price per token is calculated as total spend divided by total volume.

  • Open-weight volume and spend shares count the four open-weight labs serving their own models at scale (DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot, and Z.ai).

  • Image and video figures count media generated, not requests or tokens.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Give every agent in Herdr its own Vercel Sandbox
description:
Terminal coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode can now each run in their own isolated Vercel Sandbox, orchestrated from Herdr, a tmux-style manager that runs them side by side in panes. Nothing an agent runs or edits touches your machine.

When you start an agent, the plugin uploads your project files into a new Sandbox, installs the agent there, and opens a pane connected to it.

The pane works like a local terminal; you type to the agent and watch it work. But it lives in the Sandbox, not on your machine, so you can run several agents at once without slowing anything down.

Everything the plugin does is machine-readable. Each action returns its results as JSON, so whatever you can do from a pane, like starting an agent, checking its state, or applying its changes, a script or another agent can do too.

A few safeguards are built in. The plugin shows every file before the first upload, returns remote changes as a Git patch you apply only when you choose, and requires a human to type DELETE to permanently remove a Sandbox.

Claude Code (2.1.220), Codex (0.146.0), and OpenCode (1.18.9) are all verified and available by default.

To get started, install the plugin:

Run vercel link in the repository you want the agent to work on, then start an agent from Herdr's action menu.

Starting takes two invocations. The first is a dry run: it lists every file it would upload and creates nothing. Run it again, and the plugin creates the Sandbox and opens the agent in a pane. To pull the agent's work back to your machine, run the apply action and its changes arrive as a Git patch.

Usage is billed at standard Sandbox rates. Learn more in the documentation.

title: Test a Streaming React AI Chat Without Calling an LLM
description:
You do not need a live LLM to reproduce most bugs in an AI chat interface.

These failures are ordinary UI-state problems:

  • the first token arrives but the spinner remains;
  • a tool finishes but its card still says Running;
  • Stop aborts the request, yet a buffered token appears afterward;
  • retry duplicates the partial answer;
  • an error removes text the user already received.

Make the stream injectable, then test those event sequences deterministically.

Define an application-level event contract 

type ChatEvent =
  | { type: 'token'; messageId: string; value: string }
  | { type: 'tool.started'; id: string; name: string }
  | { type: 'tool.completed'; id: string; summary: string }
  | { type: 'completed'; messageId: string }
  | { type: 'failed'; messageId: string; message: string }

type ChatStream = (
  prompt: string,
  signal: AbortSignal,
) => AsyncIterable<ChatEvent>

The React component receives a ChatStream. Production supplies an SSE or fetch-backed implementation. The component test supplies a controlled source.

A small controlled stream 

function createTestStream<T>() {
  const queued: T[] = []
  const waiting: Array<(value: IteratorResult<T>) => void> = []
  let closed = false

  const iterator: AsyncIterableIterator<T> = {
    [Symbol.asyncIterator]() { return this },
    next() {
      if (queued.length > 0) {
        return Promise.resolve({ value: queued.shift()!, done: false })
      }
      if (closed) return Promise.resolve({ value: undefined, done: true })
      return new Promise((resolve) => waiting.push(resolve))
    },
  }

  return {
    stream: async function* () { yield* iterator },
    push(value: T) {
      const resolve = waiting.shift()
      resolve ? resolve({ value, done: false }) : queued.push(value)
    },
    close() {
      closed = true
      waiting.splice(0).forEach((resolve) =>
        resolve({ value: undefined, done: true }),
      )
    },
  }
}

Now the test determines exactly when each event arrives.

Test progressive rendering 

it('renders one growing message and a completed tool card', () => {
  const source = createTestStream<ChatEvent>()

  cy.mount(<ChatPanel createStream={source.stream} />)
  cy.findByRole('textbox', { name: 'Message' }).type('Find options')
  cy.findByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click()

  cy.then(() => source.push({
    type: 'token', messageId: 'm1', value: 'I found ',
  }))
  cy.findByTestId('assistant-m1').should('have.text', 'I found ')

  cy.then(() => source.push({
    type: 'tool.started', id: 't1', name: 'search_options',
  }))
  cy.findByTestId('tool-t1').should('have.attr', 'data-status', 'running')

  cy.then(() => source.push({
    type: 'tool.completed', id: 't1', summary: '3 results',
  }))
  cy.findByTestId('tool-t1').should('have.attr', 'data-status', 'complete')

  cy.then(() => {
    source.push({ type: 'token', messageId: 'm1', value: 'three.' })
    source.push({ type: 'completed', messageId: 'm1' })
    source.close()
  })

  cy.findByTestId('assistant-m1').should('have.text', 'I found three.')
  cy.findByRole('button', { name: 'Stop generating' }).should('not.exist')
})

Cypress queries retry while React processes the events. No fixed sleeps or model calls are needed.

Test late events after cancellation

Cancellation is a good adversarial case because transports can have buffered data.

cy.findByRole('button', { name: 'Stop generating' }).click()
cy.findByRole('status').should('contain.text', 'Stopped')

cy.then(() => source.push({
  type: 'token',
  messageId: 'm1',
  value: 'this must be ignored',
}))

cy.findByTestId('assistant-m1').should('not.contain.text', 'must be ignored')

The reducer or stream consumer should ignore events belonging to an aborted generation. Also test duplicate tool completions, failure after partial text, retry, and unmount while streaming.

Test the failure state without deleting useful evidence

A transport can fail after several tokens have rendered. Unless the product intentionally discards them, the partial answer should remain visible and be marked incomplete:

cy.then(() => {
  source.push({ type: 'token', messageId: 'm1', value: 'Partial answer' })
  source.push({
    type: 'failed',
    messageId: 'm1',
    message: 'Connection lost',
  })
})

cy.findByTestId('assistant-m1').should('have.text', 'Partial answer')
cy.findByRole('alert').should('contain.text', 'Connection lost')
cy.findByRole('button', { name: 'Retry' }).should('be.enabled')

Use accessible roles for status, alert, progress, and controls so the test protects keyboard and screen-reader behavior as well as component state. A streaming interface that visually updates but never announces completion is still broken for part of its audience.

Do not overuse cy.clock()

cy.clock() is useful for retry countdowns, debounce, or a delayed “still working” message. It controls timer APIs. It does not automatically control arbitrary Promises, async iterators, or server delivery.

Control the stream for causality; control the clock only for behavior that genuinely depends on time.

Keep a separate provider contract

This component test does not prove that the real provider emits your ChatEvent schema. Keep a smaller integration test for the adapter:

  • provider frames parse correctly;
  • error frames map to failed;
  • abort closes the request;
  • secrets and raw prompts are not unintentionally logged.

Model-quality evaluation is another suite again. Separating UI behavior, transport compatibility, and semantic quality keeps failures understandable.

The useful test matrix is event-oriented: success with tokens, success with a tool, failure before the first token, failure after partial output, user cancellation, duplicate events, and retry. It is much smaller and more reproducible than sampling many model sentences.

Which of your current “LLM test” failures could be reproduced as a five-event fixture instead?

References

  • Cypress React Component Testing examples
  • cy.clock()

title: Resolving Go Application Performance Issues: CPU Usage and Memory Leaks with pprof and Flame Graphs
description:
Introduction to Golang Profiling with pprof

Profiling Go applications is not just a debugging exercise—it’s a survival skill in modern software development. As Go’s runtime schedules goroutines onto OS threads, the system’s efficiency hinges on how well these threads are utilized. pprof, Go’s built-in profiling tool, acts as a microscope, capturing runtime data via sampling to expose CPU, memory, block, and mutex behaviors. Without it, performance issues like high CPU usage or memory leaks remain invisible, silently degrading application reliability and scalability.

Consider CPU usage: inefficient algorithms or busy-waiting loops force the CPU to execute redundant instructions, consuming cycles that could be allocated to other tasks. pprof’s CPU profiles reveal this by sampling the call stack at regular intervals, showing exactly which functions are hogging the CPU. Flame graphs then visualize this data, mapping function execution time to a hierarchical structure. Hotspots in these graphs often point to unexpected culprits—functions inlined or deferred, masked by Go’s compiler optimizations.

Memory leaks, on the other hand, are a silent killer in Go’s garbage-collected environment. While the GC reclaims unused memory, leaks occur when objects are retained unnecessarily, often via global variables or unbounded buffers. pprof’s memory profiles track heap allocations, exposing objects that persist across GC cycles. However, detecting leaks requires long-running applications to observe gradual heap growth, a constraint in production environments where profiling overhead is a concern.

The interplay between CPU and memory is critical. Frequent GC pauses, for instance, are often triggered by excessive object allocation in specific code paths. By correlating CPU and memory profiles, you can pinpoint operations that allocate heavily while consuming CPU, a double hit on resources. External dependencies exacerbate this—unoptimized libraries or database queries without indexes introduce hidden performance costs, masked in application code but visible in pprof data.

To profile effectively, enable runtime profiling flags (-cpuprofile, -memprofile) in your Go application. This activates pprof’s sampling mechanism, but beware: in production, this overhead can distort results. Instead, profile under controlled load conditions to simulate real-world behavior. Tools like go tool pprof and perf then process the collected data, generating flame graphs or textual reports. However, external dependencies lacking profiling support may require dynamic tracing or vendor-specific tools to uncover their impact.

In summary, pprof is not just a tool—it’s a lens into Go’s runtime mechanics. By understanding its sampling methodology and interpreting its output in context, you can diagnose performance issues with surgical precision. Ignore it, and you’re flying blind, risking inefficient resource utilization, increased operational costs, and a degraded user experience. The choice is clear: if you’re serious about Go performance, pprof isn’t optional—it’s mandatory.

Analyzing CPU Usage with Flame Graphs

Flame graphs are a powerful visualization tool for understanding CPU usage in Go applications. By mapping the call stack hierarchy and function execution time, they reveal hotspots where CPU cycles are consumed excessively. This section guides you through generating and interpreting these graphs using pprof, enabling precise identification of performance bottlenecks.

Generating CPU Flame Graphs

To generate a CPU flame graph, follow these steps:

  • Enable CPU profiling: Start your Go application with the -cpuprofile flag to activate pprof’s sampling mechanism. This flag instructs the Go runtime to periodically capture the call stack, providing data for CPU usage analysis.
  • Simulate workload: Run your application under a controlled load to ensure the profiling data reflects typical usage patterns. Avoid profiling in idle states, as this can distort results.
  • Process profiling data: Use go tool pprof to convert the raw profiling data into a format suitable for flame graph generation. For example: 
  go tool pprof -svg cpuprofile.out > cpu.svg
  • Visualize with flame graph tools: Utilize external tools like FlameGraph (available in Perl or Python) to generate the final visualization. This step transforms the hierarchical call stack data into a layered, color-coded graph.

Interpreting Flame Graphs

Flame graphs provide a visual breakdown of CPU usage, with each layer representing a function in the call stack. The width of each block corresponds to the time spent executing that function. Key insights include:

  • Hotspots identification: Wide blocks indicate functions consuming significant CPU time. These are often caused by inefficient algorithms, busy-waiting loops, or unoptimized external library calls. For example, a function with a wide block may be performing redundant calculations or blocking on I/O operations.
  • Inlining and deferred execution: Flame graphs may show unexpected hotspots due to function inlining or deferred execution. In Go, the compiler may inline small functions, causing their execution time to appear under the caller’s block. Similarly, deferred functions execute as part of the caller’s stack unwinding, which can skew the graph.
  • Concurrency effects: Goroutine scheduling and mutex contention can manifest as CPU inefficiency in flame graphs. For instance, a mutex lock held for an extended period may appear as a wide block, indicating a concurrency bottleneck.

Optimizing CPU-Intensive Code

Once hotspots are identified, apply targeted optimizations:

  • Algorithmic improvements: Replace inefficient algorithms with more performant alternatives. For example, switching from a nested loop to a hash-based lookup can reduce CPU usage significantly.
  • Eliminate busy-waiting: Replace busy-waiting loops with asynchronous patterns or channel-based communication. This reduces redundant CPU cycles and improves overall efficiency.
  • Optimize external dependencies: Profile external libraries using dynamic tracing or vendor-specific tools. If a library is unoptimized, consider replacing it or contributing optimizations upstream.

Edge Cases and Limitations

While flame graphs are invaluable, they have limitations:

  • Profiling overhead: Enabling profiling flags introduces overhead, which can distort results in production. Always profile under controlled conditions and compare against baseline measurements.
  • External noise: External dependencies without profiling support may introduce noise. Use dynamic tracing or isolate their impact by profiling with and without them.
  • Concurrency masking: Concurrency issues like mutex contention may appear as CPU inefficiency. Correlate CPU profiles with block and mutex profiles to diagnose such cases.

Decision Dominance: When to Use Flame Graphs

Flame graphs are optimal for:

  • Identifying CPU-intensive functions in complex call stacks.
  • Diagnosing performance regressions after code changes.
  • Comparing CPU profiles before and after optimizations to quantify improvements.

Avoid using flame graphs for:

  • Memory leak detection (use memory profiles instead).
  • Profiling applications with minimal CPU usage, as hotspots may be insignificant.
  • Diagnosing issues in external dependencies without profiling support.

Rule of thumb: If CPU usage is high and the cause is unclear, generate a flame graph to pinpoint hotspots. If X (high CPU usage) -> use Y (flame graphs) to identify and resolve bottlenecks.

Detecting and Resolving Memory Leaks

Memory leaks in Go applications, despite the garbage collector (GC), occur when objects are unnecessarily retained, often via global variables or unbounded buffers. This retention forces the GC to skip these objects during cleanup, leading to gradual heap growth. The mechanism here is straightforward: the Go runtime’s memory allocation tracking identifies objects allocated but not garbage collected, which pprof captures in memory profiles. Over time, this unchecked growth deforms the application’s memory footprint, causing increased GC pauses as the collector struggles to reclaim memory from a shrinking free heap.

To detect leaks, enable memory profiling with the -memprofile flag, which activates pprof’s sampling of heap allocations. However, this approach has a critical edge case: profiling overhead in production. The act of profiling itself can distort memory behavior, making detection unreliable. Instead, profile under controlled, long-running conditions to observe trends. Use go tool pprof to process the profile data, generating reports that highlight objects persisting across GC cycles. For example, an unbounded channel buffer will show continuous growth in allocated memory, as objects are added but never removed, breaking the GC’s ability to reclaim them.

Practical Strategies for Mitigation

Once a leak is identified, the optimal solution depends on the root cause. If the leak stems from global variables, refactor to use local variables or explicitly nil references when objects are no longer needed. For unbounded buffers, introduce size limits or implement eviction policies. However, a common error is prematurely optimizing without understanding the leak’s mechanism. For instance, reducing buffer size without addressing the underlying retention logic merely delays the issue. The rule here is clear: if memory growth correlates with specific objects in profiles → inspect their lifecycle and retention paths.

External dependencies pose a unique challenge. Libraries without profiling support may introduce hidden leaks, as their memory behavior remains opaque to pprof. In such cases, dynamic tracing or vendor-specific tools become necessary. However, this approach has limitations: it requires deep familiarity with the dependency’s internals and may not integrate seamlessly with Go’s profiling ecosystem. The trade-off is between precision and practicality—if the dependency is critical and unoptimizable, consider replacing it with a profiled alternative.

Decision Dominance in Leak Resolution

  • If the leak is caused by global variables → refactor to use local scope or explicit nil references.
  • If unbounded buffers are the culprit → enforce size limits or implement eviction policies.
  • If external dependencies are leaking → profile with dynamic tracing or replace with profiled alternatives.

Avoid the common error of focusing solely on GC tuning (e.g., adjusting GC percentages) without addressing the root cause. While reducing GC pressure can alleviate symptoms, it does not fix the leak. The mechanism of risk here is clear: unchecked leaks will eventually exhaust memory, leading to application crashes or degraded performance. The optimal solution is always to eliminate the retention path, ensuring objects are reclaimed by the GC.

Finally, correlate memory profiles with CPU profiles to identify resource-intensive operations that trigger excessive allocations. For example, a function allocating large objects in a tight loop will show up in both CPU and memory hotspots. This interplay highlights the causal chain: high CPU usage → frequent allocations → increased GC pressure → memory leaks. By addressing both CPU and memory inefficiencies, you not only resolve leaks but also optimize overall application performance.

Practical Scenarios and Case Studies

1. High CPU Usage in a Web API: Uncovering Inefficient Algorithms

A Go-based web API experienced sustained CPU spikes under moderate load. Flame graph analysis revealed a hotspot in a JSON serialization function, consuming 40% of CPU time. The root cause was an inefficient recursive algorithm for encoding nested structures, generating redundant instructions. Replacing it with a hash-based lookup reduced CPU usage by 65%, as the new algorithm minimized stack operations and eliminated redundant memory accesses.

Mechanism: Recursive calls inflated the call stack, causing frequent context switches and cache misses. Hash-based lookup flattened the execution path, reducing stack depth and improving cache locality.

Rule of Thumb: If flame graphs show wide blocks in recursive functions → replace with iterative or hash-based alternatives.

2. Memory Leak in a Long-Running Service: Global Variable Retention

A long-running Go service exhibited gradual heap growth, leading to GC pauses every 5 minutes. Memory profiling identified a 200MB buffer retained in a global variable, never garbage collected. The buffer was initialized during startup but never cleared, accumulating data indefinitely. Refactoring to a local scope and adding explicit nil references resolved the leak, stabilizing heap usage.

Mechanism: Global variables bypass Go’s garbage collector, as they are always reachable. Explicit nil references break retention paths, allowing GC to reclaim memory.

Decision Dominance: For global variables causing leaks → refactor to local scope or nil references. Avoid GC tuning without addressing retention paths.

3. Unbounded Channel Buffer: Continuous Memory Growth

A messaging system used an unbounded channel to queue messages, leading to 1GB/hour memory growth. Memory profiling showed the channel buffer persisted across GC cycles, as messages were not consumed fast enough. Enforcing a size limit and implementing an eviction policy (e.g., dropping oldest messages) capped memory usage at 200MB.

Mechanism: Unbounded buffers accumulate objects indefinitely, as Go’s GC cannot reclaim them until explicitly removed. Size limits force eviction, breaking retention paths.

Rule of Thumb: If unbounded buffers cause leaks → enforce size limits or eviction policies. Avoid relying on GC alone.

4. External Library Bottleneck: Unoptimized Database Queries

A Go application using an external database library experienced 500ms latency spikes. CPU profiling showed 30% of CPU time spent in the library’s query execution function. Investigation revealed missing indexes on queried tables, forcing full table scans. Adding indexes reduced CPU usage by 70% and latency to 50ms.

Mechanism: Full table scans generate excessive I/O and CPU load, as the library processes all rows. Indexes reduce query scope, minimizing I/O and CPU overhead.

Decision Dominance: For external library bottlenecks → profile dependencies and optimize at the source. Avoid replacing libraries without root cause analysis.

5. Mutex Contention Masking CPU Inefficiency

A Go application showed high CPU usage in a critical section, but flame graphs pointed to a mutex lock function. Block profiling revealed 90% of goroutines were blocked on the mutex, causing 50% CPU underutilization. Replacing the mutex with a lock-free algorithm eliminated contention, increasing throughput by 200%.

Mechanism: Mutex contention serializes access, forcing goroutines to wait. Lock-free algorithms enable concurrent execution, maximizing CPU utilization.

Rule of Thumb: If CPU inefficiency coincides with mutex hotspots → use block profiles to diagnose contention. Replace locks with lock-free alternatives if feasible.

6. Frequent GC Pauses: Excessive Object Allocation

A Go application experienced 2-second GC pauses every minute, despite low memory usage. Correlating CPU and memory profiles identified a tight loop allocating 1MB objects every second. Optimizing the loop to reuse objects reduced allocations by 90%, eliminating pauses.

Mechanism: Frequent allocations shrink the free heap, triggering GC cycles. Reusing objects reduces allocation rate, preserving heap space and minimizing GC pressure.

Decision Dominance: For frequent GC pauses → correlate CPU and memory profiles to identify allocation hotspots. Optimize allocation paths before tuning GC settings.

title: Two Requests Edited the Same Order. Optimistic Locking in a Go Repository Adapter
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Order o-42 says pending. Five minutes ago the warehouse service marked it shipped, and the API call that did it returned 200 OK. So did the one a support agent made a few milliseconds later to add a delivery note. Both handlers loaded the order, changed one field, and saved the whole row back. The note is there. The shipment is gone from the record, and nobody saw an error.

That is the lost-update bug. Nothing throws and nothing logs. The second save wrote a stale copy of the order over the first, and the database did exactly what it was told.

The fix is old and has a name. Martin Fowler's catalog calls it Optimistic Offline Lock: "Prevents conflicts between concurrent business transactions by detecting a conflict and rolling back the transaction." This post puts each piece of it where it belongs in a Go service built with ports and adapters, so the domain owns the rule and every adapter, real or fake, has to honor it.

The bug, in one UPDATE

Here is the save that causes it. It is the repository method most of us write on day one:

const naiveSave = `
UPDATE orders
   SET status = $2, note = $3
 WHERE id = $1`

Handler A reads {status: pending, note: ""}, sets the status to shipped, saves. Handler B read the same row before A saved, sets the note, and saves {status: pending, note: "leave at door"}. B's pending is the stale value it loaded, and it overwrites A's shipped.

Postgres is behaving as documented. Its default isolation level is Read Committed, and the Postgres docs spell out what a second updater does when it hits a row another transaction just changed: it waits for that transaction to commit, then "the search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated to see if the updated version of the row still matches the search condition." WHERE id = $1 still matches, so B's write lands. That re-evaluation is also the hook for the fix: add a condition that stops matching once someone else has written.


Both writers read the same row. The second save quietly undoes the first.

Put the version on the aggregate, and the error in the domain

The version is part of the order's state, so it lives on the domain type. The conflict is a business fact ("someone changed this order while you were working on it"), so the error lives in the domain package too. No adapter types leak in.

package order

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

var (
    ErrNotFound         = errors.New("order: not found")
    ErrConcurrentUpdate = errors.New("order: concurrent update")
)

type Order struct {
    ID      string
    Status  string
    Note    string
    Version int64
}

// Repository is the port.
//
// Save succeeds only if the stored version equals o.Version.
// On success the stored version becomes o.Version + 1.
// If another write got there first it returns
// ErrConcurrentUpdate. If the order does not exist it
// returns ErrNotFound.
type Repository interface {
    Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
    Save(ctx context.Context, o Order) error
}

The doc comment is the contract. Every adapter you write will be tested against those four rules, which is the whole point of having a port.

The pgx adapter: zero rows affected means you lost

The table needs one extra column:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id      text   PRIMARY KEY,
  status  text   NOT NULL,
  note    text   NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  version bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);

The adapter uses pgx v5. Pool.Exec returns a pgconn.CommandTag, and CommandTag.RowsAffected() tells you how many rows the UPDATE touched.

package postgres

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

type OrderRepo struct{ pool *pgxpool.Pool }

func NewOrderRepo(p *pgxpool.Pool) *OrderRepo {
    return &OrderRepo{pool: p}
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) (order.Order, error) {
    var o order.Order
    err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, `
        SELECT id, status, note, version
          FROM orders WHERE id = $1`, id,
    ).Scan(&o.ID, &o.Status, &o.Note, &o.Version)
    if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
        return order.Order{}, order.ErrNotFound
    }
    if err != nil {
        return order.Order{}, fmt.Errorf("get %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Save(
    ctx context.Context, o order.Order,
) error {
    tag, err := r.pool.Exec(ctx, `
        UPDATE orders
           SET status = $3, note = $4,
               version = version + 1
         WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`,
        o.ID, o.Version, o.Status, o.Note)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("save %s: %w", o.ID, err)
    }
    if tag.RowsAffected() == 1 {
        return nil
    }
    return r.missOrConflict(ctx, o.ID)
}

func (r *OrderRepo) missOrConflict(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) error {
    var exists bool
    err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx,
        `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE id = $1)`,
        id,
    ).Scan(&exists)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("check %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    if !exists {
        return order.ErrNotFound
    }
    return order.ErrConcurrentUpdate
}

Walk the race again with this UPDATE. A and B both loaded version 1. A's update commits and the row is now version 2. B's update waits on A's row lock, then Postgres re-evaluates WHERE id = $1 AND version = 1 against the new row. It no longer matches, so B updates zero rows and gets ErrConcurrentUpdate instead of a silent overwrite.

The missOrConflict lookup is there because zero rows has two causes, and the port promised to tell them apart. It only runs on the unhappy path, so the common case stays a single round trip. If a deleted order and a conflict mean the same thing to your callers, you can drop it, but then change the port's doc comment too.


The version in the WHERE clause is the gate. A stale copy carries the wrong number and updates nothing.

The in-memory fake honors the same contract

Your use-case tests should not need a database. They also should not run against a fake that is more forgiving than production, because then the tests pass on code that loses updates. The fake implements the same four rules:

package memory

import (
    "context"
    "sync"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

type OrderRepo struct {
    mu     sync.Mutex
    orders map[string]order.Order
}

func NewOrderRepo(seed ...order.Order) *OrderRepo {
    m := make(map[string]order.Order, len(seed))
    for _, o := range seed {
        m[o.ID] = o
    }
    return &OrderRepo{orders: m}
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    _ context.Context, id string,
) (order.Order, error) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    o, ok := r.orders[id]
    if !ok {
        return order.Order{}, order.ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Save(
    _ context.Context, o order.Order,
) error {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    cur, ok := r.orders[o.ID]
    if !ok {
        return order.ErrNotFound
    }
    if cur.Version != o.Version {
        return order.ErrConcurrentUpdate
    }
    o.Version++
    r.orders[o.ID] = o
    return nil
}

The check and the write happen under one lock, which is the in-memory equivalent of the conditional UPDATE. A fake that compared versions, released the lock, and then wrote would have the same race you are trying to test for.

A use case that retries, a bounded number of times

A conflict is not always a failure. In the opening story, the note and the status don't contradict each other. If B reloads the order and applies its change to the fresh copy, both edits survive. The use case does that, and gives up after a few attempts so a hot row can't spin a request forever:

package app

import (
    "context"
    "errors"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

const maxAttempts = 3

type Orders struct{ repo order.Repository }

func NewOrders(r order.Repository) *Orders {
    return &Orders{repo: r}
}

func (s *Orders) Update(
    ctx context.Context,
    id string,
    change func(*order.Order) error,
) error {
    var err error
    for range maxAttempts {
        var o order.Order
        o, err = s.repo.Get(ctx, id)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if err = change(&o); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        err = s.repo.Save(ctx, o)
        if !errors.Is(err, order.ErrConcurrentUpdate) {
            return err
        }
    }
    return err
}

for range maxAttempts needs Go 1.22 or later, which added range over integers. The change function runs again on every attempt, against freshly loaded state, so it must be a pure edit: "set status to shipped," not "set status to whatever the user saw plus one."

Retrying is only right when the change still makes sense on newer data. If a person made a decision by looking at the old version (a price, a stock count), retrying behind their back is its own lost update. Return the conflict to the edge instead. Over HTTP that maps cleanly onto conditional requests: send the version as an ETag, and per MDN's If-Match page, a mismatched precondition gets a 412 Precondition Failed.

One test, both adapters

The contract test takes a constructor, so the fake and the Postgres adapter run the exact same assertions. Both goroutines load the order before either saves, which forces the conflict instead of hoping for it.

package ordertest

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "testing"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

func OneWriterWins(t *testing.T, repo order.Repository) {
    ctx := context.Background()
    a, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-42")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    b := a
    a.Status = "shipped"
    b.Note = "leave at door"

    errs := make(chan error, 2)
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for _, o := range []order.Order{a, b} {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            errs <- repo.Save(ctx, o)
        }()
    }
    wg.Wait()
    close(errs)

    var won, lost int
    for err := range errs {
        switch {
        case err == nil:
            won++
        case errors.Is(err, order.ErrConcurrentUpdate):
            lost++
        default:
            t.Fatalf("unexpected error: %v", err)
        }
    }
    if won != 1 || lost != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("won=%d lost=%d, want 1 and 1", won, lost)
    }
    got, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-42")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if got.Version != a.Version+1 {
        t.Fatalf("version=%d, want %d",
            got.Version, a.Version+1)
    }
}

The goroutine captures o directly, which is safe because Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration. Wiring the test up for the fake takes one call:

func TestMemoryOneWriterWins(t *testing.T) {
    seed := order.Order{
        ID: "o-42", Status: "pending", Version: 1,
    }
    ordertest.OneWriterWins(t, memory.NewOrderRepo(seed))
}

The Postgres version does the same against a real pool: read a connection string from an environment variable, t.Skip when it is empty, create the table, insert the seed row, and pass postgres.NewOrderRepo(pool) to OneWriterWins. Run both with go test -race ./...; the race detector will also catch a fake that forgot its mutex.

A second test belongs next to it: fire two Orders.Update calls at the fake concurrently, one setting the status and one setting the note, and assert that the final order has both. That one proves the retry turns the conflict into two surviving edits instead of one.

If this was useful

The version column is the easy part. The design work is deciding that the conflict is a domain error, writing the port's contract down, and making the fake as strict as the database so your fast tests mean something. Hexagonal Architecture in Go is the book I wrote about exactly that layer: where repositories, transactions and adapters sit in a Go service, and how to test each side of the port without a pile of mocks. If you also want the language underneath, The Complete Guide to Go Programming, the companion book in the Thinking in Go series, covers Go itself.
