title: Shipping an Arabic Version of Your App: What Your Translator Needs From You
description:
If your product is launching in Saudi Arabia or the wider Gulf, an Arabic version usually ends up on someone's task list as "send the strings to the translator". From the translator's side of the table, most delays and most bad Arabic UI text come from a handful of engineering decisions made before the first string was sent.

Here is what makes Arabic localization go smoothly, written from the translation side but aimed at developers.

1. Plurals: Arabic has six forms, not two

English has one and other. Arabic, according to the Unicode CLDR plural rules, uses six categories: zero, one, two, few, many and other. If your code builds sentences like count + " files", there is no correct Arabic translation for it.

Use ICU MessageFormat (or your framework's equivalent) and let the translator fill in every category:

{count, plural,
  zero {لا توجد ملفات}
  one {ملف واحد}
  two {ملفان}
  few {# ملفات}
  many {# ملفًا}
  other {# ملف}
}

In JavaScript you can see which category the runtime picks for a given number:

const pr = new Intl.PluralRules('ar');
[0, 1, 2, 3, 11, 100].map(n => `${n}: ${pr.select(n)}`);
// "0: zero", "1: one", "2: two", "3: few", "11: many", "100: other"

2. Never concatenate translated fragments

"Welcome, " + name + "! You have " + n + " new messages" forces the translator to translate three disconnected pieces and hope the word order works. Arabic word order and gender agreement often need the whole sentence. Send complete messages with named placeholders ({name}, {count}) and keep them together.

3. Give every string context

"Open" can be a button (a verb: افتح), a status (an adjective: مفتوح) or a shop's opening time. "Save" can be a button or "save 20%". A key like btn.open plus a one-line comment or a screenshot saves a round of questions and prevents the wrong form shipping. Gender matters too: if a string addresses the user directly, tell the translator whether a neutral form is required.

4. Right-to-left is a layout problem, not a translation problem

The translator delivers Arabic text. Whether it reads correctly depends on your markup and CSS:

  • Set dir="rtl" and lang="ar" on the root (or the relevant container), not just text-align: right.
  • Use logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, inset-inline-start) instead of left/right, so the same stylesheet works in both directions.
  • Mirror directional icons (back/forward arrows, progress chevrons), but not icons that represent real objects or brands.
  • Wrap user-generated or mixed-direction values (names, emails, order numbers, Latin product names) in <bdi> or use unicode-bidi: isolate, so a phone number or an English product name inside an Arabic sentence does not scramble the punctuation around it.

5. Let text grow and use a real Arabic font

Arabic UI strings are often similar in length to English but can be noticeably taller and sometimes longer, especially in short labels. Avoid fixed-width buttons and truncated labels. Choose a font with proper Arabic glyphs and test diacritics and line height. Fallback system fonts can look very different on Android, iOS and Windows.

6. Dates, numbers and currency: format with Intl, don't translate

Do not put formatted dates or prices in translation files. Format them at runtime:

new Intl.DateTimeFormat('ar-SA-u-ca-islamic-umalqura', { dateStyle: 'long' }).format(new Date());
// Hijri (Umm al-Qura), e.g. "١٨ جمادى الأولى ١٤٤٨ هـ"

new Intl.DateTimeFormat('ar-SA-u-ca-gregory', { dateStyle: 'long' }).format(new Date());
// Gregorian with Arabic month names, e.g. "٢٩ أكتوبر ٢٠٢٦"

new Intl.NumberFormat('ar-SA', { style: 'currency', currency: 'SAR' }).format(1250);

Set the calendar explicitly with the -u-ca- extension: the default calendar for plain ar-SA is not the same in every browser and runtime version. Decide deliberately which calendar and which digits (Arabic-Indic ٠١٢٣ or Western 0123) your product shows, and apply that consistently. Official and financial documents in Saudi Arabia often carry both Hijri and Gregorian dates.

7. Send files the translator can work with

A structured export (JSON, XLIFF, .po, .strings, or a CSV with key, source, context and max-length columns) is far better than screenshots or a PDF of the UI. Lock placeholders and HTML tags so they cannot be translated by mistake, and include a glossary of product terms that must stay consistent across the app, the website and the help center.

8. Review in the running product

Translation in a spreadsheet is only half the job. Arabic must be reviewed in context: truncation, line breaks, mirrored layouts, and whether the tone fits a Saudi audience. Plan a short in-app review round before launch.

If you need the Arabic side handled professionally, this is the kind of work our website and app localization service covers (page in Arabic).

Disclosure: I work at Googan, a certified translation office in Riyadh (ISO 17100). This post is general guidance, not legal or regulatory advice.

title: LeetCode 735 Looks Easy Until the First Collision Isn’t the Last
description:
One tiny chain reaction, a tempting wrong solution, and the O(n) reasoning worth taking into your next interview.

Before you scroll to the Python, try this tiny input in your head.

[4, 7, 3, -9]

Positive numbers move right, negative numbers move left, and the smaller asteroid disappears when two collide. So the 3 loses to -9, which feels like a perfectly reasonable place to finish one iteration.

Except -9 is still moving. It reaches 7 next, then 4, and suddenly the entire answer is [-9].

That is the little trap I like about LeetCode 735, Asteroid Collision. You can understand every rule and still write code that stops one collision too early. Honestly, this is exactly the kind of small problem I want in a practice session, because the mistake is specific enough to fix and the reasoning travels well.

Let’s work through it slowly enough to see the idea, then turn it into a solution you can explain without pointing vaguely at a stack.

First, make sure these two asteroids can actually meet

This is a Medium problem about a row of asteroids. Input order gives their relative positions, the absolute value gives their size, and the sign gives their direction. Every asteroid moves at the same speed.

When two meet, the smaller one disappears. If their sizes match, both disappear. We return the survivors in their original relative order.

Notice how much work that same-speed rule saves us. Two asteroids moving right cannot catch each other, and neither can two moving left. We do not need coordinates, elapsed time or a physics simulation.

Now compare [5, -3] with [-5, 3]. In the first pair, the asteroids move toward each other. In the second, they move apart, so comparing their sizes would already be a mistake.

While scanning from left to right, a collision is possible only when the latest surviving asteroid is positive and the incoming asteroid is negative. Check that relationship before comparing magnitudes.

I prefer drawing those two arrows once before touching the keyboard. It is much easier to catch a direction mistake on paper than inside three nested branches.

Keep the survivors, and look at the nearest one first

Imagine we have processed 4, 7 and 3. They all move right, so our survivors are [4, 7, 3]. When -9 arrives from the right, 3 is the first asteroid in its way.

If 3 disappears, 7 becomes the next one in its way. Removing 7 exposes 4. That access pattern gives us a stack, with the rightmost survivor at the top.

More precisely, after each input asteroid is fully processed, the stack contains the survivors of the prefix we have seen, in their original order, with no unresolved collisions among them.

That last sentence is the promise our code needs to keep. These are survivors so far; future input can still destroy them.

Also, this is not a stack sorted by size. [4, 7, 3] is completely valid, even though its magnitudes rise and fall. Calling every solution with a stack a monotonic-stack solution hides the actual reason we chose it. Here, we need the most recent surviving neighbor.

Stay with -9 until its story is finished

Our incoming asteroid gets its own little piece of state. It stays alive until a larger asteroid destroys it or an equal one destroys both. Popping a smaller neighbor does not finish the incoming asteroid’s turn.

Follow the same -9 through the entire sequence.

  1. Compare 3 with size 9 and remove 3. Keep -9 available for another comparison.

  2. Compare 7 with size 9 and remove 7. The stack now contains only 4.

  3. Compare 4 with size 9 and remove 4. Nothing remains to block -9.

  4. Append -9 once, after the collision loop finishes. The result is [-9].

This explains why a single if statement is not enough. It can resolve the collision with 3 and leave an unresolved collision between 7 and -9. A while loop keeps checking the boundary that each removal exposes.

There are only three outcomes to remember

Once the direction check passes, compare the positive stack top with the magnitude of the incoming negative asteroid.

  • If the top is smaller, pop it and keep the incoming asteroid alive. Another collision may be waiting underneath.

  • If the sizes match, pop the top and mark the incoming asteroid dead. Neither belongs in the result.

  • If the top is larger, leave it alone and mark the incoming asteroid dead. This arrival cannot reach anything farther left.

If the loop finishes with the incoming asteroid still alive, append it. That can happen because the stack is empty, because its top moves left too, or because the incoming asteroid moves right and cannot hit an earlier survivor.

Now the Python has a reason for every branch

I’m keeping the alive flag explicit here because it makes the difference between removing a neighbor and destroying the current asteroid easy to see. Shorter code can wait until the reasoning feels boring in the best possible way.

from typing import List
class Solution:
    def asteroidCollision(self, asteroids: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        survivors = []
        for asteroid in asteroids:
            alive = True
            while (
                alive
                and asteroid < 0
                and survivors
                and survivors[-1] > 0
            ):
                if survivors[-1] < -asteroid:
                    survivors.pop()
                elif survivors[-1] == -asteroid:
                    survivors.pop()
                    alive = False
                else:
                    alive = False
            if alive:
                survivors.append(asteroid)
        return survivors

Inside the loop, asteroid is negative, so -asteroid is its positive magnitude. We are comparing sizes, not deciding that a negative number must be smaller than a positive one.

Python evaluates the and conditions from left to right. The survivors check therefore protects survivors[-1] when the stack is empty.

Equality deserves its own branch. If you only pop the top and forget alive = False, the incoming asteroid gets appended afterward and quietly comes back from the dead. Cute in a movie, deeply unhelpful in an algorithm.

Why this keeps the stack’s promise

Before a new arrival, earlier survivors already have no unresolved collisions with each other. The only new conflict can be between the arrival and the rightmost survivor.

Removing that survivor exposes exactly one new neighbor, so the loop checks again. When the arrival dies, the earlier survivors are still stable. When it survives, the loop has established that it cannot collide with the remaining top, so appending it restores the same promise.

Repeat that for every input asteroid and the final stack contains exactly the survivors we need. We never reorder the input, which matters because position determines who meets whom.

Two loops do not automatically mean O(n²)

This is the explanation I want ready for the follow-up. One incoming asteroid can do a lot of work, but it does that work by permanently removing earlier asteroids.

Across the whole input, each asteroid is appended at most once and popped at most once. Once 3 has disappeared, a later arrival cannot make us pop that same 3 again.

A collision that does not pop anything destroys the incoming asteroid and ends its loop. There is at most one such final comparison per arrival. Equality also ends the loop while removing the top.

So the total work is O(n), including all those repeated collisions. The stack can hold all n asteroids when none collide, giving O(n) extra space. Python list append is amortized constant time, and removing its last element is constant time.

By comparison, repeatedly deleting from the middle of an array can shift many elements on every deletion. A stack lets us do the same local cleanup at the end of the list.

Four tiny cases make the explanation much harder to fake

Before calling the solution finished, hand-trace inputs that force different decisions. Each one should have a reason for existing.

  • [8, -8] becomes []. This checks that equality destroys both asteroids.

  • [-2, -1, 1, 2] stays unchanged. These asteroids either share a direction or move apart.

  • [10, 2, -5] becomes [10]. The incoming -5 removes 2, then loses to 10.

  • [4, 7, 3, -9] becomes [-9]. One arrival has to clear several smaller neighbors before it can be appended.

Then make the chain end in equality with [4, 7, 3, -7]. Remove 3, let 7 and -7 destroy each other, and leave [4]. This catches the version that handles equality correctly in isolation but continues after the incoming asteroid is already gone.

Take the reasoning into your next practice session

Close the implementation and reconstruct it from the stack’s promise. Explain which pair can collide, what each branch removes, and why the same incoming value sometimes needs another turn through the loop.

When that feels comfortable, pick another coding problem and write down what your data structure must keep true before you code. Let the problem determine the structure instead of hunting for a familiar template.

For this one, you should be able to explain why the last survivor matters, why one removal can expose another conflict, and why repeated work can still add up to linear time. Those are useful things to carry beyond an asteroid problem.

My favorite takeaway is that tiny examples can ask surprisingly honest questions. With just four numbers, this one tells you whether your code resolves a single collision or finishes the chain it started.

~ Emily

title: How I stopped dreading AI and started studying it full-time
description:
By June 2026, I couldn’t open an app without being told I was falling behind. My Instagram saves were full of designers building agents over a weekend. LinkedIn was a steady stream of people who had “shipped it with Cursor.” And the job listings I was tailoring my resume to kept asking for things like evals, MCP, AI prototyping and Claude Code: words I half recognized and could not have explained in an interview.

I could feel myself staring down a fork. Down one path was a designer I’d been before at times: only integrating new ways of working if my boss told me to do it, dreading every new tool launch, complaining about having to adapt and quietly missing the good old days. Down the other was someone who got excited about what was coming and went looking for it before anyone asked them to.

I realized that I wanted to be the second designer. And I didn’t want to just pick up enough vocabulary to survive a screening call.

I want to dive deep enough to really understand how all of this works, because I won’t be able to truly design confidently for a technology I don’t understand.

For this very big goal, I had to get serious about learning. I asked Muse (Meta’s AI agent, which had access to every post I’d saved on Instagram) to dig through my saved AI and design content and turn it into a handoff doc. I went back through the job listings I had tailored my applications to with Claude and pulled out every AI skill I was missing. Then I handed all of it to Claude and asked for a learning plan that would turn me into the designer I wanted to become.

I had one condition: everything had to be grounded in real sources. Influencer reels are great for finding out what exists, but I wasn’t going to learn an entirely new discipline from a couple of 30-second clips optimized for views. Therefore, I asked Claude to back every topic with at least one article from a trusted source.

What came back was intense: 8 weeks, 40 hours a week, two demo projects to build from scratch and a deadline of November 22. I would be my own manager and my own teacher, working alongside a growing cast of Claudes (one wrote the plan, one tutored me, one built code with me, one helped me journal), and of course I would ultimately be the experiment subject absorbing all of it.

I’ll be honest about why I’m doing this. I want to get hired, but more than that I want to be the best designer I can be, in a field that changes every time I refresh my feed. That takes discipline, and it takes a willingness to look somewhat stupid while I figure things out.

Three weeks in, I’ve been posting one story a week on LinkedIn. This article is a bit different: it pulls those weeks together by theme instead of by date, because the same lessons kept showing up again and again, in a different costume each week.

A plan for a user of one (me)

Unfortunately, the plan written for me has to actually be learned and absorbed by me. It turns out I had to work out how I learn before I could plan anything further.

Week 1 was mostly new vocabulary (agents, tool calls, context windows, evals), so the tutoring Claude built a mini lesson around every reading. It rewrote dense passages in plainer language (I will never be a real engineer), introduced one term at a time and quizzed me with “what would you do?” questions. I loved it, and I also overdid it. I didn’t know which parts mattered, so I took in everything in every format I could: reading it myself, reading Claude’s summaries, reading the plain-language rewrites, then listening to text-to-speech on my outdoor runs. Naturally, Week 1 ran 3 days over.

The plan doc itself needed a redesign, too. It started as one long page, and scrolling through the doc on a trackpad made my carpal tunnel act up. So I treated it like any product with a frustrated user: I complained in a productive way (a.k.a. gathering user pain points) and requested that Claude reformat the doc as one tab per week and a table per task, with a checkbox, the task and its sources, and a notes column.

In Week 2, I changed how I asked. Before touching the readings (Google’s People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft’s Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction), I asked Claude for a short list of what to focus on and a top-down summary of the week’s objectives, plus why each one mattered for me. Then I read both guides on my own, with no tutor wrapped around them, and took my own notes. My delay went from 3 days to 1, and I actually remember that material better than Week 1. Neither mode was wrong. Week 1 needed a tutor because everything was new, and Week 2 needed independence because I finally had something to build on.

What I learned is that the tool only fits me as well as I describe myself to it, so every prompt is really a small design brief. Of course it gets better each time it learns something new about the user (me).

Asking better questions also made me pay closer attention to the answers. And some of those answers were very wrong…

Checking the checker

If I had to sum up all 3 weeks in one phrase, it would be this: nothing and nobody is infallible, and everyone needs a checker (or rather “who watches the watchmen?”) Each week added another layer to check.

Layer 1: checking the work

In Week 1, I built a tiny AI agent that helps people find software their company has approved, and I tested it with evals: the same set of questions asked on every run, graded two ways. Plain code checked exact facts, like which tools the agent used, and a separate reviewer Claude read each answer for meaning. Then I changed one small example in the agent’s instructions, and something I never touched broke. Every code check still passed, but the reviewer Claude noticed that in 4 of the 6 answers about one product, the agent had stopped naming the seller. My tutoring Claude traced the cause to an older example in the instructions, one it had written itself, that left the seller out. The agent was copying that example, mistake and all (read about it on LinkedIn).

What I took away from this is success is entirely determined by the answer key.

I changed the key to where the seller’s name is now a permanent code check, and the reviewer Claude can read the agent’s answers but can’t edit anything. Only I can change the tests, because an AI that can edit both the work and the tests grading it can “pass” just by making the tests easier. (Researchers call this reward hacking, and it’s behind some of the AI “cheating” headlines I’d been reading.)

Layer 2: checking the checker checking me

In Week 2, I flipped it around. I gave Claude scrubbed files from a 2025 usability study I ran at AWS and asked it to synthesize them blind, so I could grade it against my own answer key. Claude credited quotes to the wrong participant twice and turned a neutral remark into an opinion. It also found two errors in my answer key, and one of my 2025 counts changed from 17 of 25 sessions to 18 of 26 (read more on LinkedIn).

Run 2 was real research: synthesizing 13 public forum posts about AWS Private Marketplace. This time I put my research question at the top and gave each source its own labeled section, because Run 1 had shown me what happens without them. All 24 quotes came back exact and credited to the right source. Claude still made mistakes, just a different kind: it stated guesses as facts, and it applied findings about AWS Marketplace in general to the much narrower Private Marketplace. (One of my own leads made the same leap too) Clean, labeled data fixed the quoting errors but left the reasoning errors, so I still check every run.

Layer 3: checking the plan writer

In Week 3, something I had taken for granted made a big mistake. I’m generally a fan of how Claude can turn a pile of information into a structure and plan I can digest. What I assumed was that when I hand it information, it actually reads all of it. Isn’t processing huge amounts of data supposed to be AI’s strength? My first demo project is a redesign of AWS’s developer documentation, and the plan-writing Claude had initially listed 8 problems with those docs for me to solve. When I went back to them, I noticed none had a source and all read like common heuristics. After a week of digging through forums for actual user feedback, I suspected that the planning Claude hadn’t done its due diligence.

So I redid the research in a separate chat with real complaints and a test of the live docs, causing a tidal wave of rescoping for the project. The research Claude kept a log of its own mistakes, including quotes it had pulled from a GitHub page that no longer exists. It also flagged sources that needed context: the harshest Hacker News quote came from the person launching the AI tool being discussed, and a 2019 post asking “Why is AWS documentation so poor?” was promoting a YouTube channel.

Even the plan I built this whole experiment on needed checking. That rescoping cost my previous days.

Layer 4: checking with counts

The last layer came from AWS’s own AI answer agent in its docs. When I tested whether it kept track of follow-up questions, one failed and one passed. Claude suggested wording it as “sometimes loses context.” But “sometimes” can’t be measured, so I asked for harder tests, and the result became 3 of 10 follow-up tests failing (as of Oct 15).

Then on Oct 21 I tested the AWS docs answer agent on follow-ups by asking it about “the third one” from a list of four encryption options it had just given me. Bafflingly, the agent pulled up the second option instead. I tested it twice more and got the fourth option both times: 0 of 3 right, with the same list on screen every time.

Claude suggested fixing this by adding a line of interface text, and I pointed out that no line of text can fix a wrong pick. So the fix moved into code: find item three in the visible list and hand it to the AI, the loading text names the item, and if code can’t tell which one I mean, the response will ask. Claude correctly noted out that this is the same rule as my Week 1 agent.

One test is an anecdote and a count is evidence, and the rules that really matter belong in code, where the AI can’t talk its way around them.

What AI can’t see

Not every miss has a clean explanation. Plenty came from Claude just messing up because it’s an imperfect computer program. But some of them I could trace back to a reason:

Claude can’t see what I see, because what I see comes from years of experience it doesn’t have.

The clearest example sat in Claude’s own screenshots. While planning my docs redesign, the planning Claude captured reference pages from AWS’s documentation and proposed a brand new “ask the docs” AI feature. Weeks later, I was annotating those same screenshots by hand when I spotted a “Search in this guide” box in the page header. I recognized the sparkle icon and gradient border right away, because years of designing with Cloudscape (AWS’s design system) taught me that it uses them only to mark an AI feature. TLDR; AWS already has an AI answer feature in its docs, and Claude didn’t see it at all. My demo went from “I invented an AI search feature” to “I tested a live AWS AI feature, found where it fails, and redesigned it”.

This wasn’t the first time. In Week 1, Claude assumed my second demo was a retail agent that handles product refunds (it took the word ‘marketplace’ in the wrong direction). It’s actually a rebuild of my AWS Private Marketplace work, where companies control which software their employees can buy, and refunds aren’t even something those buyers can act on. I pointed to proof via live AWS docs, and Claude learned its lesson to check in with me more often.

The strangest moment came in Week 3. I was designing what an AI answer should look like after a user stops it mid-response, and I asked Claude to show me what Claude itself does in that situation. It drew a proposal and then admitted it couldn’t draw its own interface correctly from memory, because claude.ai changes too often. So I took three rounds of screenshots of Claude working, Claude stopped before writing anything and Claude stopped mid-sentence, and showed the AI its own screen.

I was designing an AI feature by studying the AI I was designing it with, and it still needed me to be its eyes.

What ties these together is simple. Claude sees what’s written down and what it’s shown (via unlabeled screenshots usually). A lot of what makes me useful as a designer lives in my head: the visual language of a company I worked at, what actually shipped, which details matter to the people who use a product. Once I knew what Claude couldn’t see, I had a better idea of what parts only I could do.

Knowing when (and when not) to use AI

The split I’ve landed on started out of frustration, before this plan existed. Back in August, I was doing a four-hour take-home assignment for a contract role interview and had just connected Figma to Claude for the first time. I asked Claude to take its own reference screenshots, and it couldn’t (the browser extension wasn’t connected, and its sandbox couldn’t reach the websites). So I did it all by hand. I took the screenshots, marked what worked and what didn’t with sticky notes in Figma, and handed those annotated boards to Claude as my wireframes to build four different website directions.

Two months later, Claude can take the screenshots itself but I still do the annotating. In Week 3 I pulled every screenshot into Figma and covered them in sticky notes. Each of the 9 docs problems got its own color, so I can see them zoomed out in a sprawling file, and each note gets a matching box around the exact element it’s about.

AI can now build, migrate and spin things up from nothing, and I’m happy to let it. But critique and pixel-level inspection are the core of my job as a senior designer.

The sparkle icon and gradient border only jumped out at me because I was the one looking closely, and because I knew what Cloudscape uses them for. AI can gather my annotations and group or transform them, but it can’t make them for me.

The opposite case came a few days later. By then, “Ask Docs” meant three different things across my docs: AWS’s live AI feature, my redesign of it and the first round of tests I ran. I knew this was exactly the kind of job AI does well (finding every instance of something, sorting each one by what it means and replacing all the names), so I handed it over with suggested names of my own. Claude made 28 changes in the research doc alone, and it caught two things I’d missed along the way.

It also suggested naming my redesign Grounded Answers. I hadn’t known “grounding” was an AI term (it means an answer comes from its sources), but it’s a word the AI practitioners interviewing me will know, so I took it. OK, Claude!

And sometimes the right tool isn’t AI at all. My redesign assumed most developers search the docs first, the way I do. Instead of asking Claude whether that was true, I texted a former coworker who’s a senior engineer. He sent back: he does a search first to find the area or topic, then lingers in the navigation to see related pages. He also told me AI reads most docs for him now, and he no longer checks its sources. I kept accurate source links in my design anyway, because the developers who do check need them, and losing their trust can be crushing for an AI product. One person isn’t research, so search-first stays a hypothesis. But one real person told me more than any confident paragraph from a model could.

Knowing what to hand off, what to keep and when to ask a human is the skill I’m practicing most. Once I understood that split, I could design better alongside Claude instead of around it.

AI as a design partner

Week 3 was my first real design work of the plan, and designing with Claude felt like working with an awkward but productive teammate: brilliant at some things, weirdly awful at others, and always ready to get stuff done.

The best test came over where my redesigned AI answers should live on the page. Claude recommended a resizable drawer on the right side of each docs page and cited Cloudscape (AWS’s design system, which I know like the back of my hand) to back it up. I pushed back over several rounds: I reasoned that the docs page already has two side panels, and a third would squeeze the content even more. When Claude then offered to move search into the existing (page-level) right panel instead, I said no for good. Search covers every guide and every service, so it belongs on the top header level, while side panels sit below the header and only show content for one page. Claude agreed, and then found its own test results backed me up: AWS’s AI feature already reads beyond the current guide. Claude knew the pattern rules. It took my information architecture sense to see which level the feature belongs on.

My reaction at the time: “wow my old Cloudscape reviewer eyes have not failed me yet, even a year out of practice.”

Other times it worked the way I’d want a good partner to. When I changed my mind about how to show that an AI answer might be wrong, I asked Claude the questions I couldn’t answer myself: should confidence be judged for the whole answer or for each section, and how much “why” should a user see? It came back with Amazon Bedrock’s grounding checks and HCI research, including a 2024 study from Microsoft Research with 404 participants. When an AI answer hedged in the first person (“I’m not sure, but…”), people agreed less often with its wrong answers and got more answers right overall (Kim et al., FAccT 2024). It also checked my mockup against the live Cloudscape rules and caught two real fixes.

And I had to learn to specifically ask for pictures. When I talk an idea through with a human designer/PM/engineer, someone can grab a pen and sketch it out. Claude can only draw through code, so its ideas arrive as walls of words. Now I ask it to “demonstrate visually” before I approve anything I can’t picture, and I only approve a change once I’ve seen it with my designer eyeballs.

By the end of the week, I’d written Claude a performance review. The short version: as a manager setting scope and requirements, Claude was supremely confident and frequently wrong. As a teammate doing the groundwork, it was far more trustworthy (as long as I set the scope). Asking simple questions out loud, like whether my research covered one AWS service or all of them, kept the scope from slipping more than once.

The part I keep thinking about is how easily Claude agrees with me. When I make an executive decision it almost always goes along with it, which spares me from upsetting several levels of stakeholders over a hunch. It also means I could bully it into agreeing with almost anything.

I’m an honest person trying to actually retain everything I’m learning so I’m not going to sweep away inconvenient feedback. This is the same discipline that got me started grinding on this plan in the first place.

Me and AI

Some learnings are already leaking out of the plan and into my everyday tasks. In Week 1 I learned how the context window works: when a chat runs too long, Claude gets worse at the task and burns through more tokens. So I wrote it into my account-level instructions, and now Claude tells me when it’s time to start a fresh chat. I’ve used that rule to hand off this very journal more than once.

Other lessons are about what I won’t hand over. This week, I asked Claude to make the graphic for my Week 3 post (see the report card above). It built a clean, tidy performance review form, and I liked the report card idea, but the result looked way too AI-made. I wanted something scrappy and imperfect, so I took the idea and remade it myself in Figma.

The same goes for writing. I’ve asked Claude to help draft my posts, but none of them ever sound quite right.

I realized that AI can only work from sampling the work of past me, but I as a person am always evolving. I am always adding something new to how I write and talk, from whatever I’m reading, learning or living through that week. No context window can hold all of me.

When Claude writes, it treats me as a formula and fills in any gaps with patterns from other people’s writing. Of course my voice gets diluted. This article started as a Claude draft too, and every sentence you just read went through copious rewrites from my carpal-tunnel-plagued hands before it settled here.

This brings me back to where I started. I took on this plan to become a designer who understands AI well enough to know what to give it, what to check and what to keep. Three weeks in, the most valuable thing I’ve built is a shift in habits: be curious about new things, and trust none of it until I’ve checked it for myself.

In Week 4, I’m building my redesign in real code with Cloudscape components and setting up evals to test it against AWS’s live feature. I’ll keep posting one story a week on LinkedIn, and the next theme article comes after Week 6.

If you’re a designer learning AI right now: what’s the part of your work you’ve vowed never to hand over to a fancy computer program?

Further reading

The basics

  • Building effective AI agents, Anthropic (2024). The Week 1 reading that taught me what an agent actually is.
  • Context windows, Claude docs. Why long chats get worse, and why Claude now tells me when to start a new one.
  • What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?, modelcontextprotocol.io. One of those job-listing words, explained by the people who made it.

‘’A plan for a user of one’

  • People + AI Guidebook, Google PAIR.
  • Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, Microsoft Research (CHI 2019). The 18 guidelines behind the HAX Toolkit, and my other Week 2 reading.

‘Checking the checker’

  • Demystifying evals for AI agents, Anthropic (2026). How to test an agent with the same questions every run.
  • Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning, Lilian Weng (2024). A deep dive into why an AI that can edit its own tests shouldn’t be trusted to.

‘What AI can’t see’

  • Ingress, Cloudscape Design System. The rule behind the sparkle icon I spotted: “Sparkles are the symbolic convention for generative AI.”
  • Colors: Gradients, Cloudscape Design System. The rule behind the gradient border, which is reserved for “elements that represent a generative AI entity.”
  • Generative AI patterns, Cloudscape Design System. The full set of chat, loading, follow-up and regeneration patterns I designed with.

‘AI as a design partner’

  • Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses, Amazon Bedrock docs. How AWS checks whether an answer actually comes from its sources.
  • “I’m Not Sure, But…”: Examining the Impact of Large Language Models’ Uncertainty Expression on User Reliance and Trust, Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard and Wortman Vaughan, FAccT 2024. The 404-person study on AI that hedges in the first person.

My weekly LinkedIn posts

  • Week 1: the regression my evals caught
  • Week 2: the blind test that graded me too
  • Week 3: Claude’s performance review
  • My Week 1 agent’s code, GitHub

I’m Lisa Liu, a senior product designer based in NYC, most recently at AWS Marketplace and AWS Data Exchange. This is the first theme article in my Teaching Myself AI With AI series. Currently available for senior IC and design lead roles. Portfolio at lisanianliu.framer.ai.

Find me on LinkedIn or at lliu29@yahoo.com.

How I stopped dreading AI and started studying it full-time was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Deployment Storage keeps your deployments rollback-ready
description:
Every deployment produces a set of files, including the pages, functions, and assets Vercel serves. Deployment Storage keeps those files available so you can inspect previous deployments and roll back when needed.

Instantly roll back to previous deployments in seconds

If a production deploy ships a bug or a change you want to reverse, rolling back restores the previous version in seconds. Open your project, click Instant Rollback on the Production Deployment tile, then choose an earlier production deployment. Vercel immediately repoints your domains to that deployment, with no rebuild required.

Deployment Storage pricing

  • Deployment Storage is billed at $0.10 per GB per month

  • Hobby teams include up to 10 GB

Existing teams continue with their current pricing, with no change to their bill at this time.

Control how much Deployment Storage you keep:

  • Edit your Deployment Retention Policy to set how long Pre-Production, Production, Canceled, and Errored deployments stay available. Shorter retention means less storage, but you can't roll back to a deleted deployment

  • The Usage page shows Deployment Storage and Functions Storage by project

  • Keep future deployments smaller by trimming your output directory, moving large files to Vercel Blob, and reducing Function bundle size

Learn more about Deployment Storage here.

title: Enterprise Managed Users is now generally available
description:
Enterprise Managed Users (EMU) gives organizations full control over the Vercel accounts tied to their verified domains. It makes the organization's identity provider the single source of truth for authentication and account lifecycle, so accounts on company domains are governed centrally rather than owned by individuals.

Now generally available

  • IdP-enforced sign-in: Managed users sign in through SAML SSO only. All other login methods, including email OTP, GitHub, Google, and GitLab, no longer work for managed accounts.

  • SCIM provisioning & lifecycle: Directory Sync creates, updates, and deprovisions managed users automatically, keeping accounts in sync with your IdP.

  • Owned by your organization: Profile settings are managed through your IdP rather than by the individual.

  • Self-serve enablement: Turn EMU on for a verified domain in Team Settings under Security & Privacy, and extend it across multiple eligible teams in a single step.

Requires an Enterprise plan, enforced SAML SSO, active Directory Sync, and at least one verified domain.

In Beta, available on request

  • Hobby team transition: Members with an existing personal account on a newly managed domain are guided to add a personal email (keeping their hobby projects) or delete the account, then continue to their work through SSO.

  • Automatic conversion: Personal accounts with no content or activity are archived automatically, and their owners land in a new managed account at their next SSO sign-in.

To request access, contact your account team.

Learn more in the Enterprise Managed Users and Hobby team transition docs.

title: Building a Production RAG API in Go with pgvector and Gemini
description:
Lessons from building the Restaurant Suggestion System, a Go/Gin backend with a conversational recommendation API.

A RAG demo takes an afternoon: embed some documents, run a similarity search, paste the results into a prompt. A RAG API you can put in front of real users takes longer, because most of the work is not the LLM call. It's everything around it.

I built the Restaurant Suggestion System (RSS) as a Go/Gin backend where users chat to get dish and restaurant suggestions. The answers come from RAG over real menu data in PostgreSQL with pgvector and Gemini embeddings. Because the recommendations have to respect allergies, "the model usually gets it right" was never good enough.

This post walks through the shape of that pipeline and the Go patterns that made it dependable. The snippets are simplified and focused on the ideas, not copied from the private repo.

The pipeline

Every chat request goes through the same steps:

  1. Embed the user's message (plus stored preferences) with Gemini.
  2. Retrieve candidates from Postgres with pgvector, with allergen and health filters applied in SQL.
  3. Score candidates deterministically in Go.
  4. Generate a conversational answer with the LLM, using only the top candidates as context.
  5. Validate the answer against the candidates we sent.
  6. Fall back to a vector-only response if the LLM is slow or unavailable.

The rule behind all of it: the LLM explains and converses. It does not decide what is safe or what exists.

Schema: keep filters as real columns

It's tempting to put everything into the embedded text and let similarity sort it out. Don't do that for anything safety-related. Allergens belong in a column you can filter on exactly.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE menu_items (
    id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    restaurant_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES restaurants(id),
    name          TEXT NOT NULL,
    description   TEXT NOT NULL,
    allergens     TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    price_cents   INT NOT NULL,
    is_available  BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    embedding     vector(768) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ON menu_items USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON menu_items USING gin (allergens);

The dimension (768 here) must match the embedding model's output configuration. Pick one, store it in config, and fail fast at startup if they disagree. A silent dimension mismatch is a miserable bug to find in production.

Embeddings with Gemini

RSS uses Gemini embeddings in two places: when indexing menu items, and during onboarding to capture user preferences as a vector. Wrap the provider behind a small interface so the rest of the code doesn't care which SDK you use:

type Embedder interface {
    Embed(ctx context.Context, text string) ([]float32, error)
}

type GeminiEmbedder struct {
    client *genai.Client
    model  string
    dims   int32
}

func (g *GeminiEmbedder) Embed(ctx context.Context, text string) ([]float32, error) {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    res, err := g.client.Models.EmbedContent(ctx, g.model,
        genai.Text(text),
        &genai.EmbedContentConfig{OutputDimensionality: &g.dims},
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("embed: %w", err)
    }
    if len(res.Embeddings) == 0 || len(res.Embeddings[0].Values) != int(g.dims) {
        return nil, errors.New("embed: unexpected embedding shape")
    }
    return res.Embeddings[0].Values, nil
}

Two habits worth copying: a hard timeout on every external call, and a shape check on the response. The interface also makes tests easy, since a fake embedder returns fixed vectors.

Retrieval: filter in SQL, before the LLM

This is the most important design decision in the system. Allergen and health filters run in the retrieval query, so excluded items never reach the model. A prompt like "don't suggest peanuts" is a request. A WHERE clause is a guarantee.

type Candidate struct {
    ID         int64
    Name       string
    Allergens  []string
    PriceCents int
    Distance   float64
}

const retrieveSQL = `
SELECT id, name, allergens, price_cents, embedding <=> $1 AS distance
FROM menu_items
WHERE is_available
  AND NOT (allergens && $2::text[])
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT $3`

func (r *Repo) Retrieve(ctx context.Context, q []float32, exclude []string, k int) ([]Candidate, error) {
    rows, err := r.db.Query(ctx, retrieveSQL, pgvector.NewVector(q), exclude, k)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    var out []Candidate
    for rows.Next() {
        var c Candidate
        if err := rows.Scan(&c.ID, &c.Name, &c.Allergens, &c.PriceCents, &c.Distance); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        out = append(out, c)
    }
    return out, rows.Err()
}

One pgvector gotcha: with an approximate index such as HNSW, filtering happens after the index returns its nearest neighbours. With a strict filter you can get fewer than k rows back. pgvector 0.8+ supports iterative index scans (SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;), which keep scanning until enough rows pass the filter. On older versions, raise hnsw.ef_search or over-fetch and trim. Either way, write a test where most rows are filtered out and check you still get results.

Deterministic scoring

Vector distance is one signal, not the ranking. RSS ranks filtered candidates with a deterministic scoring engine, so the same input gives the same order and every recommendation can be explained.

type Weights struct {
    Similarity, Preference, Budget float64
}

func Score(c Candidate, prefSim float64, budgetCents int, w Weights) float64 {
    s := w.Similarity*(1-c.Distance) + w.Preference*prefSim
    if budgetCents > 0 && c.PriceCents <= budgetCents {
        s += w.Budget
    }
    return s
}

func Rank(cands []Candidate, scores map[int64]float64) {
    sort.SliceStable(cands, func(i, j int) bool {
        si, sj := scores[cands[i].ID], scores[cands[j].ID]
        if si != sj {
            return si > sj
        }
        return cands[i].ID < cands[j].ID // stable tie-break
    })
}

Note the tie-break on ID. Without it, equal scores can shuffle between runs, and your tests become flaky. The signals here are illustrative; the point is that ranking lives in plain Go you can unit-test, not in a prompt.

Generation: ground it, then check it

Only the top candidates go into the prompt, each with its ID. A pattern I recommend on top of that: ask the model for structured output that references those IDs, and validate the response before returning it:

type LLMAnswer struct {
    Message string  `json:"message"`
    ItemIDs []int64 `json:"item_ids"`
}

func validateAnswer(a LLMAnswer, sent []Candidate) error {
    allowed := make(map[int64]bool, len(sent))
    for _, c := range sent {
        allowed[c.ID] = true
    }
    for _, id := range a.ItemIDs {
        if !allowed[id] {
            return fmt.Errorf("model referenced unknown item %d", id)
        }
    }
    return nil
}

If the model mentions something you didn't give it, that's a hallucination by definition, and you can detect it in a few lines.

The fallback: vector-only results

LLM APIs time out, hit rate limits and have outages. RSS handles that by degrading gracefully: if the LLM call fails, the API still returns the filtered, scored candidates from vector search. In the sketch below, an answer that fails validation takes the same path:

func (s *Service) Recommend(ctx context.Context, req ChatRequest) (ChatResponse, error) {
    cands, err := s.retrieveAndRank(ctx, req)
    if err != nil {
        return ChatResponse{}, err // no data, no answer
    }

    genCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 8*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    ans, err := s.llm.Answer(genCtx, req.Message, cands)
    if err == nil {
        err = validateAnswer(ans, cands)
    }
    if err != nil {
        s.log.Warn("llm unavailable, using vector-only fallback", "err", err)
        return fallbackResponse(cands), nil
    }
    return ChatResponse{Message: ans.Message, ItemIDs: ans.ItemIDs, Source: "llm"}, nil
}

Because the safety filters ran before the LLM, the fallback is just as safe as the full path. It's less chatty, not less correct. Returning a Source field also helps the frontend and your dashboards see how often you're degrading.

The rest of the production checklist

The RAG pipeline is maybe a third of the system. The rest is ordinary backend work that still matters:

  • Auth: passwordless email OTP, JWT, and role-based access control so admin endpoints stay admin-only.
  • Data ingest: CRUD plus CSV/JSON bulk upload and AWS file upload. Whatever your ingest path, make sure every write also refreshes the item's embedding, or search goes stale.
  • Privacy: admin analytics built without exposing PII.
  • Ops: Postgres with pgvector in Docker, so local, CI and production run the same database.
  • Tests: a Newman (Postman) end-to-end suite that hits the real API. Make sure the fallback path has its own tests too.

Takeaways

  • Put safety rules in SQL and Go, never only in the prompt.
  • Rank deterministically, with stable tie-breaks.
  • Validate model output against the context you sent.
  • Design the fallback first. If the LLM disappears, users should still get a correct answer.

Go suits this well: strict types for model output, context deadlines on every call, and a single binary that's easy to run next to Postgres.

Pradip Parmar is a Go backend and AI agent engineer who has been writing Go since 2018. He builds RAG systems, MCP servers and LLM agents for businesses, and previously led the Python-to-Go migration of the Flights backend at MakeMyTrip. If you need a Go AI agent developer for a RAG or agent project, you can reach him on LinkedIn, Upwork or Contra, or see his code on GitHub.

title: Making MetaMask and TronLink sign transactions for a custom Rust blockchain
description:
A few months ago I wrote How I Built a Custom Rust Blockchain for On-Chain Ride Lifecycle. Clutch is a ride-sharing protocol where the rider pays the driver directly, and every step of a ride (request, offer, accept, pay, cancel) is a native transaction type on a small Proof-of-Authority chain written in Rust.

Since then it went from "testnet with a faucet" to a mainnet that holds real money. This post is about the parts I did not expect to be hard: getting normal wallets to sign for a chain they have never heard of, and keeping the token honest once it is backed by real USDT.

If you read part 1: block rewards are gone. The block author is now paid by a flat fee on each transaction.

The problem: wallets refuse to sign a bare hash

In part 1, the SDK held a local key and signed the transaction hash directly:

hash = keccak256(rlp([from, nonce, chain_id, data]))
signature = secp256k1_sign(keccak256(hash_as_hex_string))

That works for an SDK. It does not work for MetaMask or TronLink. A wallet will not sign 32 opaque bytes for you, and it is right not to: a bare hash could be an Ethereum transaction on another chain.

So the node now accepts three schemes, each checked against its own digest:

Scheme Who signs What is signed
1 SDK key, treasury, faucet keccak256(hash)
2 MetaMask, Trust Wallet (personal_sign, EIP-191) "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" + len + "clutch-tx:{chain_id}:{hash}"
3 TronLink (signMessageV2, TIP-191) "\x19TRON Signed Message:\n" + len + "clutch-tx:{chain_id}:{hash}"

The text the user sees in the wallet popup is clutch-tx:{chain_id}:{hash}. The chain id is in it so a signature for the testnet can never be replayed on the mainnet.

The nice surprise was TRON. A TRON account is the same kind of key as an Ethereum account: same curve, same Keccak-256, same 20 address bytes. TRON just writes them in base58 with a 0x41 prefix. So supporting TronLink was one more prefix, not a new crypto stack. A user signed in with TronLink has a Clutch address that is literally their TRON address in hex.

The catch: this is a consensus change. A validator without scheme 2 rejects any block containing a scheme-2 transaction. On a testnet you just upgrade. On our young mainnet it meant starting a new chain, which we only allowed because a script first proved that no token had ever been minted on the old one. The day real balances exist, the same change needs a planned rolling upgrade of every validator from the same block height.

Sending from MetaMask: pretending to be just enough of an EVM

Signing ride transactions in the app was solved. But people also wanted to open MetaMask, see their CLT balance, and press Send.

MetaMask can only send by signing a legacy Ethereum transaction (EIP-155). So the Hub API exposes a small JSON-RPC endpoint at /rpc that answers the calls a wallet makes (eth_chainId, eth_getBalance, eth_sendRawTransaction and friends), and the node gained one new transaction type, WalletTransfer:

  • The node decodes the raw Ethereum transaction and recovers from from its signature.
  • It refuses anything that is not a plain value transfer: data, typed transactions, no chain id, a high s.
  • Wallet values are in wei (18 decimals); CLT has 6. So value = CLT units × 10^12, and any value with more than 6 decimals is refused, never rounded. Rounding money silently is how you end up with balances nobody can explain.
  • The transaction's hash is the real Ethereum hash, rebuilt from the fields and signature, so MetaMask, the explorer and the node all show the same hash.

This is also a consensus change, so it is switched on per chain by config: a wallet_chain_id and a wallet_transfers_from_block height that every validator must carry. Below that height the type is refused everywhere. The wallet chain ids (20770 mainnet, 20771 testnet) are registered on chainlist, so "Add network" works with one click.

Real money: CLT backed 1:1 by USDT

1 USD = 1,000,000 CLT base units. CLT only enters the chain through a Mint transaction, and only one address can sign it: the mint_authority, fixed in the genesis block. A separate treasury service watches for USDT deposits (TRC-20 on Tron, BEP-20 on BNB Chain), and mints the matching CLT to the depositor (minus the transfer relay's fee, for deposits that go through one). Withdrawals are the reverse: a Burn on Clutch, then a USDT payout on Tron.

Every mint and burn carries a reference, and the chain stores a processed_ref_{ref} marker so the same deposit can never be credited twice, even if the treasury retries after a crash.

Three bugs that could have created money

These are the ones that scared me. All are fixed, all have tests, and I am writing them down because each one looked harmless.

1. Two transfers in one block minted money. Block state is validated first and applied as one deferred RocksDB batch at the end. So two transfers from the same account in one block were both validated against the pre-block balance, and the second write to the balance key won. Send 10 to A and 10 to B from a balance of 10: both pass, both recipients get 10, the sender ends at 0. Fix: one transaction per account per block, enforced when authoring and when importing. The same staleness broke the exactly-once marker (two mints with one ref in one block), so a block also may not repeat a ref.

2. The block author's fee erased the author's own transaction. The fee credit to the block author was appended after the per-transaction writes, so it became the last write to the author's balance key and silently discarded any transaction the author had sent in that block. The recipient kept the money, the author's debit vanished: unbacked CLT. Fix: fold the fee into the already-staged write instead of appending, and abort the import if that fails.

3. A debug flag deleted the chain on every deploy. developer_mode = true made the node delete its database on graceful shutdown. Our stage configs had it for a month. Whichever node stopped cleanly inside Docker's 30-second grace period lost its chain; the ones that got SIGKILLed kept theirs. So the data loss moved between nodes and looked like a volume problem, then a sync problem, then a deploy-script problem. The node now refuses to delete its database when a data path is mounted.

The lesson I took from all three: with a deferred write batch, "last write wins" is a money bug waiting for a second writer.

Where it is now, honestly

  • The mainnet has been live since October 2026 and holds real USDT.
  • It is alpha: $100 per deposit, $200 per day, withdrawals of $25 to $50 on Tron.
  • The mint and payout keys are on the server, not in a KMS yet. The three validators run on one host. There has been no security audit.

Because of that, I am asking people to try the free testnet first, where nothing costs real money: app-stage.clutchprotocol.io. Sign in with MetaMask or TronLink, and do one ride as passenger or driver (two browser windows work).

I am looking for 10 people to finish one ride and tell me the first thing that confused them or broke. Comments here are perfect.

Links

  • Code (node, hub, explorer, treasury, deploy): github.com/clutchprotocol
  • Docs: docs.clutchprotocol.io
  • Site: clutchprotocol.io
  • Part 1: How I Built a Custom Rust Blockchain for On-Chain Ride Lifecycle

Questions I would love answers to:

  1. Would you have done wallet support differently, for example an EVM-compatible layer instead of a custom transfer type?
  2. How would you roll out a signature-scheme change on a chain that already holds balances?
  3. Would you use this as a rider or a driver, and what would stop you?

title: A timestamp test catches seconds, milliseconds and ISO 8601 mixups.
description:
A purchase recorded at noon can appear hours, years or decades away from its intended time when one adapter guesses the unit of a field called timestamp. The JSON may remain perfectly parseable throughout the journey.

The reliable fix starts before the HTTP request. Choose an internal representation, convert it explicitly for each endpoint and test the serialized output with a fixed instant. Then check what the destination actually recorded.

This walkthrough builds a small Node.js contract test. It does not send events or require vendor credentials.

Give the internal timestamp a unit

Use a name such as occurred_at_ms if the application stores epoch milliseconds. Include the unit in the schema and function contract. A caller should not need to count digits to understand a value.

Keep occurrence time separate from the time your worker received or transmitted the event. Retries may change transmission time. They should not rewrite when the underlying purchase happened.

For the endpoints covered here, Meta server events use epoch seconds, GA4 Measurement Protocol uses timestamp_micros, and the referenced PostHog capture and Segment HTTP contracts accept ISO 8601 timestamp strings. Verify the endpoint you actually use. A vendor may operate several APIs with different contracts.

Use a fixed instant with fractional seconds

An input ending at exactly midnight can hide rounding and precision mistakes. Use an instant with a nonzero fractional second and compare exact expected values.

Save the following as timestamp-contract.mjs and run node timestamp-contract.mjs:

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

function adaptOccurredAtMs(milliseconds) {
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(milliseconds)) {
    throw new TypeError('occurred_at_ms must be a safe integer');
  }
  const date = new Date(milliseconds);
  if (!Number.isFinite(date.getTime())) {
    throw new RangeError('occurred_at_ms is outside the Date range');
  }
  const micros = milliseconds * 1000;
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(micros)) {
    throw new RangeError('microsecond representation is not exact');
  }
  return {
    meta: { event_time: Math.floor(milliseconds / 1000) },
    ga4: { timestamp_micros: micros },
    posthog: { timestamp: date.toISOString() },
    segment: { timestamp: date.toISOString() }
  };
}

const milliseconds = Date.parse('2026-10-01T12:34:56.789Z');
const wire = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(adaptOccurredAtMs(milliseconds)));

assert.equal(wire.meta.event_time, 1790858096);
assert.equal(wire.ga4.timestamp_micros, 1790858096789000);
assert.equal(wire.posthog.timestamp, '2026-10-01T12:34:56.789Z');
assert.equal(wire.segment.timestamp, '2026-10-01T12:34:56.789Z');
assert.equal(typeof wire.meta.event_time, 'number');
assert.equal(typeof wire.ga4.timestamp_micros, 'number');
assert.throws(() => adaptOccurredAtMs(String(milliseconds)), TypeError);
assert.throws(() => adaptOccurredAtMs(NaN), TypeError);
assert.throws(() => adaptOccurredAtMs(Infinity), TypeError);
assert.throws(() => adaptOccurredAtMs(milliseconds + 0.5), TypeError);
assert.throws(() => adaptOccurredAtMs(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), RangeError);

The function intentionally accepts only an integer number. It does not silently coerce strings, infer units or attempt to repair a malformed value.

The microsecond safety check is stricter than JavaScript's Date range. That is deliberate: a representable millisecond value does not guarantee that multiplying it by one thousand produces an exactly represented integer.

Precision conversion has a direction

The Meta conversion discards the fractional second. For this fixture, the difference between the source instant and the converted seconds expressed as milliseconds is 789 milliseconds. Document that loss as part of the adapter contract.

The GA4 conversion changes the unit. It does not create measurement precision. An input measured to milliseconds still has millisecond precision after you append three decimal zeros to its integer representation.

If the source genuinely records microseconds, preserve that representation upstream and design a separate adapter. Passing it through Date first would discard information before the GA4 payload is built.

Likewise, toISOString() produces a UTC representation of the instant. Formatting an instant in a local timezone for a user interface is a separate operation. Do not feed that display string back into your event adapter as if it were the canonical event time.

A number cannot tell you whether it is seconds

The adapter rejects a numeric string, but a seconds value passed as an integer can still be a valid JavaScript date in milliseconds. The arithmetic cannot determine the caller's intent.

That is why the input field needs a unit and why the caller needs its own test. At the boundary where your application reads a database record or message, assert that the chosen source column is the millisecond column.

For a synthetic purchase, keep both the fixed source record and the expected endpoint payload in the fixture. Change the input deliberately to seconds and confirm that the caller's expectation fails. Do not add a digit-count heuristic that guesses the intended date and makes the broken producer harder to find.

If your business accepts events only within a particular period, add that as a named policy check. Keep it separate from the conversion function. A business window and a vendor ingestion window are different contracts and may change independently.

Check the bytes after serialization

The test serializes and parses the adapter result before asserting types. This catches changes introduced by your payload construction, such as converting event_time into a string inside a template.

For a real integration, run the same assertions at the last observable boundary before sending. If an HTTP client performs additional transformations, capture the request body with an injected test transport. Testing an earlier object can miss changes made by middleware.

Add fixtures for an absent field, an invalid source date and a value outside your supported application range. Decide whether a missing occurrence time should reject the event or follow an explicitly documented fallback. Calling Date.now() without recording that decision can make a replay appear to be a new purchase.

Verify the destination with a synthetic event

Local tests establish your conversion and serialization behavior. They do not prove that the endpoint accepted the timestamp or used it in reporting.

For an integration test, submit one permitted synthetic event in a test environment. Record the source instant, endpoint, send time and destination observation. If the observed event time differs, inspect the adapter output before assuming the reporting interface is displaying the wrong timezone.

Also inspect whether the destination substituted ingestion time because a field was absent, ignored or outside its accepted window. Preserve the actual response and relevant diagnostics so that the result can be reproduced later.

I maintain Pixellint. Its cross-vendor payload reference helps review the endpoint contract after these arithmetic tests pass. Keep the small timestamp tests in your own codebase: they identify the exact conversion that changed when an adapter regresses.

Sources

  • Meta server-event SDK
  • GA4 Measurement Protocol reference
  • PostHog capture API
  • Segment common fields

Technical sources checked October 25, 2026. Drafted with AI; examples are synthetic unless explicitly stated otherwise.

title: How Can an AI Voice Recorder Work Without a Subscription?
description:
Local transcription, built-in AI and notes you can keep are included with C1. See why no OneMira subscription is needed and what optional costs remain.

Originally published on the OneMira Blog. Explore the OneMira C1 AI Voice Recorder — ✨ Local AI · Works Standalone · 🗣️ Speaker ID · Zero Cloud Subscription.

With C1, local transcription, built-in AI and access to your local files are included, with no OneMira subscription or monthly transcription-minute quota. C1 records the conversation; your Mac or Windows PC does the processing. You can concentrate on what is being said and keep useful notes for the work that follows.

Why do cloud transcription services charge recurring fees?

Cloud services pay to process and store recordings and to provide shared workspaces, integrations and support. A paid plan can fund useful ongoing services.

Plaud currently offers a free Starter tier with 300 monthly transcription minutes, alongside paid Pro and Unlimited plans. Otter also offers a free tier and paid plans with different allowances and features. Check the plan you would actually use; a subscription is not required for every cloud workflow.

Your computer does the processing

OneMira runs transcription and its built-in AI on your computer after the required software and model downloads. This local workflow does not need a per-minute OneMira transcription service or a OneMira account.

Budget for the computer and storage you use, including model downloads and backups. If you choose a cloud model service, its fees and limits are separate. You do not need an external AI subscription or API key for the included local workflow.


Silver White C1, seen in soft natural light.

What is included with C1?

  • One-press recording and live or later transcription on a supported Mac or Windows PC
  • Speaker-labeled transcripts and built-in local AI for meeting notes and mind maps
  • Editable local Markdown notes that you can open with your own tools
  • Your choice in Settings to keep the original audio as stereo WAV files

Put the results to work with our meeting-minutes and action-item template.

Notes you can keep using

Your notes are readable local Markdown files, so you can open them in a compatible editor, search them and keep your own backups. The value continues in the files you use for your projects and follow-ups. Check a sample note in the tools you plan to use, and decide where to back it up.

What affects local processing speed?

No monthly minute quota means OneMira does not meter your local transcription. Processing speed still depends on your computer, the chosen model, the language, the recording length and other work running at the same time. Battery, storage and computer capacity remain practical limits.

What if you want a shared cloud workspace?

A managed service can be useful for central administration, shared workspaces and provider-managed model updates. C1 gives you dedicated capture and a local workflow for your own notes. Choose the combination of recording, processing and sharing that serves your work.

Compare the data paths in Cloud or Local Transcription, then use the three-year cost guide to include any optional services you want.

See C1’s current price and choose your finish

title: Help Build Kvas: An Open-Source Rust Game Engine Built for Human and AI-Assisted Contributions
description:
I’m building Kvas, an open-source 3D game engine written in Rust. I’d love help from game developers, Rust developers, graphics programmers, tool builders, and anyone interested in using AI coding agents to contribute to open source.

  • GitHub: github.com/Nopass0/kvas
  • Documentation: Kvas documentation
  • Roadmap: Planned features and current limitations

What’s already in Kvas

Kvas already includes:

  • A Rust workspace with an ECS, engine runtime, renderer, audio crate, editor, and standalone player.
  • A 3D scene editor with a hierarchy, inspector, transform tools, project browser, and English and Russian interfaces.
  • A renderer built with wgpu, with PBR materials, shadows, HDRI, procedural skies, particles, and post-processing.
  • A visual node editor for materials and shaders, with live previews and a library of procedural materials.
  • Rapier physics and Rust game scripts with hot reload.
  • Sample projects, build tools, and a bilingual documentation site.

Kvas is actively developed. Some features are experimental or incomplete. Official DLSS or FSR integrations and hardware ray tracing are not claimed as finished; check the roadmap for status and limitations.

Why welcome AI-assisted contributions?

AI coding agents can help contributors understand unfamiliar code, implement focused changes, add tests, improve documentation, and investigate performance. Kvas provides contribution instructions and a pre-commit workflow that checks the workspace, tests, coverage, and doctests.

Please review AI-generated changes before submitting them. Pull requests should explain what changed and how it was verified. Performance claims should include benchmark evidence.

Where help would make a difference

The roadmap includes work on:

  • Profiling and optimizing script execution, ECS queries, rendering, and asset loading.
  • Physics quality, fixed-step simulation, character controllers, and regression scenes.
  • A more complete integrated code editor and better editor workflows.
  • Audio, animation, and layered image-editing tools.
  • Onboarding, tutorials, examples, and cross-platform validation.

You don’t need to take on a large feature. A focused bug fix, a reproducible issue report, a test, a guide, or a small performance investigation can all help.

Join in

Start with the README and contribution guide. Check open issues before starting larger changes. When reporting graphics problems, include your operating system, GPU and graphics backend, reproduction steps, and relevant logs.

If you’re interested in building a Rust game engine with contributions from both people and AI agents, explore Kvas on GitHub and share what you’d improve first.
