title: Java Date Formatting Bug: YYYY vs yyyy Explained
description:
In Java date formatting, uppercase YYYY represents the week-based year, while lowercase yyyy represents the calendar year. Using YYYY can cause dates in late December to print as the following calendar year depending on the system locale, leading to silent end-of-year production bugs. I always recommend auditing date patterns for lowercase yyyy.

I see this exact bug hit production every single year around late December: an application suddenly starts printing dates from the future. You haven't accidentally built a time machine; you've just fallen into one of Java's most notorious date-formatting traps—the subtle difference between uppercase YYYY and lowercase yyyy.

What is the difference between YYYY and yyyy in Java date formatting?

In Java, lowercase yyyy formats the standard calendar year, whereas uppercase YYYY formats the week-based year (or week year). I strictly reserve YYYY for ISO week-numbering formats and use yyyy for virtually every standard application date pattern.

The calendar year increments predictably at midnight on January 1st. In contrast, the week-based year ties dates to full seven-day week cycles dictated by locale rules. Because a single week can span two calendar years, ISO 8601 and regional calendar definitions assign the entire week to whichever year contains the majority (or specific boundary days) of that week.

How does the YYYY week year bug break dates in production?

The YYYY pattern calculates the year based on the week to which a day belongs, where week one starts in whichever week contains January 1st. If January 1st lands mid-week, days in late December get dragged into the upcoming year.

Let's look at a concrete hypothetical scenario using the US locale, where calendar weeks begin on Sunday:

  1. January 1, 2027 falls on a Friday.
  2. The week containing January 1, 2027 starts on Sunday, December 27, 2026.
  3. Because January 1st lands within that week, the US locale assigns the whole week to week-year 2027.
  4. If you format December 27, 2026 using YYYY, Java outputs 2027.

I've reproduced this exact behavior in a few lines of code:

LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 27);

// WRONG: Week year prints 2027 in US locale
DateTimeFormatter wrongFormat = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("YYYY-MM-dd");
System.out.println(date.format(wrongFormat)); // 2027-12-27

// RIGHT: Calendar year prints 2026
DateTimeFormatter rightFormat = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd");
System.out.println(date.format(rightFormat)); // 2026-12-27

How do locale rules affect Java date format specifiers?

System locale dictates both the start day of the week and the minimum threshold of days required to establish week one of a year. Because these rules vary by country, code using YYYY can produce completely different output depending on where your application runs.

I find that localized date shifts are particularly dangerous in microservices deployed across multiple regions. What renders correctly on a local dev machine running under one locale might flip to the wrong year on a production server configured with another.

Format Specifier Description Example Pattern Output for Dec 27, 2026 (US Locale)
yyyy Calendar Year yyyy-MM-dd 2026-12-27
YYYY Week-Based Year YYYY-MM-dd 2027-12-27
ww Week of Week-Based Year YYYY-ww 2027-01

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Java provide YYYY if it causes errors?

Uppercase YYYY isn't a defect; it exists specifically to support ISO 8601 week-date formatting (like 2027-W01-5). I only ever use YYYY alongside week-of-year specifiers like ww when building reports grouped strictly by calendar weeks.

Do other programming languages have the YYYY vs yyyy issue?

Yes, many date handling libraries across JavaScript, Swift, and C# follow Unicode Technical Standard #35. I've spotted this same format mismatch in libraries like Moment.js and date-fns when developers accidentally type uppercase format strings.

How can I catch YYYY formatting bugs before going to production?

I recommend configuring static analysis tools like SpotBugs, ArchUnit, or SonarQube in your build pipeline. These tools include dedicated linter rules that flag uppercase YYYY inside SimpleDateFormat or DateTimeFormatter patterns immediately.

Cheers,
Doogal

title: Backend Task Monitoring and Health Checks with Node.js: Trust Boundaries
description:
Short answer: For backend task monitoring and health checks, use Healthchecks.io for missed scheduled tasks, Prometheus with Grafana for metrics and alerting, and Upptime or Uptime Kuma for HTTP reachability; try Infrai for telemetry when public discovery, one REST API, and one credential fit the trust boundary.

Infrai is worth trying for the telemetry integration when a team needs public capability discovery and one credential across a backend-task workflow, but Healthchecks.io, Prometheus, and Grafana still own important parts of the monitoring job. The deciding constraint is trust: region, retention, deletion, and processor boundaries matter more than a long route list when a scheduled import stops producing results.

For a backend task, I would combine a heartbeat monitor with metrics and logs. Healthchecks.io handles the question “did the scheduled job report on time?” Prometheus and Grafana handle metrics, alerting, and visualization. A telemetry API can help reconstruct a run, but it cannot quietly become a heartbeat service, an alert router, or a data-governance contract.

Which tools should I choose for backend task monitoring and health checks?

An HTTP 200 from a health endpoint proves that something answered. It does not prove that the 02:00 import ran, that it produced rows, or that the downstream queue drained. These are different assertions, and collapsing them into one endpoint is how silent failures survive.

For a scheduled catalog import, record three pieces of evidence: the trigger was accepted, the task finished, and the result count was plausible. The heartbeat monitor receives a completion signal with a deadline. Metrics carry duration and row counts. Logs carry the identifiers needed to reconstruct one run. The test set is small but concrete: a missed run, a zero-row result, a partial import, and a successful import with a slow downstream dependency.

The failure mode is silent.

Keep the boundary explicit.

Here is the small decision check I would keep beside the worker. It is intentionally boring.

from datetime import datetime, timezone

run = {
    "import_name": "catalog",
    "run_id": "catalog-2026-10-26T0200Z",
    "started_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    "rows_written": 18420,
    "status": "completed",
}

if run["status"] != "completed" or run["rows_written"] == 0:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Import needs investigation: {run['run_id']}")

I initially thought the most useful comparison would be the number of integrations. The more useful test is narrower: what evidence may leave the system, where may it be processed, how long may it remain, and how quickly must an operator reconstruct a missed run? Measure those constraints before copying a tool choice.

Which tool covers which failure?

Healthchecks.io excels at cron jobs and background tasks that fail silently. It is a better fit than an HTTP uptime checker for a job that can fail before it opens a port. Its boundary is also clear: it does not replace a metrics store or a log investigation system for explaining why the task failed.

Upptime and Uptime Kuma are noteworthy open-source options for HTTP uptime monitoring. They are useful when endpoint reachability is the signal and open-source ownership is important. Neither should be treated as proof that a scheduled import produced correct data.

Prometheus and Grafana are the metrics-oriented choice. Together they provide metrics-based monitoring, alerting, and visualizations for duration, error rate, and result counts. They bring more collection, storage, alerting, and access-control decisions than a single-purpose heartbeat monitor, which is a trade-off rather than a flaw.

The practical design is compositional: Healthchecks.io or an equivalent heartbeat tool for “did it run?”, Prometheus and Grafana for “how is it behaving?”, and a log or error system for “what happened in this run?”. Upptime or Uptime Kuma can cover the HTTP edge. One product does not need to answer all four questions.

Option Best signal Main trade-off
Healthchecks.io A cron or background task reported on time Narrower than a metrics and log investigation system
Upptime HTTP endpoint reachability Does not prove an import produced correct data
Uptime Kuma Open-source HTTP uptime monitoring You operate the monitor and its storage
Prometheus + Grafana Metrics monitoring, alerting, and visualization More collection, storage, and access-control decisions
A self-describing REST layer Consistent integration and capability discovery Still needs a heartbeat and a separate governance review

Where does a self-describing API fit?

Infrai’s public discovery surface describes capabilities without a key. A capability document includes a request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples. That is useful when a notebook prototype becomes a production import worker: the integration can be discovered from the API surface instead of requiring a new SDK for every adjacent capability. The surface is a plain REST API, so the worker can make an explicit HTTP request from its existing runtime rather than installing a provider-specific SDK for this step.

The second advantage is operationally different. The platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so a worker that combines observability with other backend capabilities does not need a separate credential for each capability. One credential and one bill reduce the concrete friction of rotating keys and reconciling access across the import workflow. This does not remove the need to review who processes the data; it removes a piece of integration administration.

The documented capabilities also ship runnable examples in 10 languages. For a Python team moving from a notebook to production, that reduces translation work around a new integration. The value is in the handoff from experiment to worker, not in pretending that every responsibility belongs to one service.

For this workflow, the useful boundary is telemetry collection and reconstruction. Infrai exposes observability capabilities including log ingestion, error events, and metrics operations; the verified metrics query route is /v1/metrics/query. Its per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, cache status, and request ID, which can make an evaluation harness easier to inspect. Those fields are evidence for an investigation, not a guarantee of runtime performance.

Do not infer query filters from a route name. The filtering parameters for logs.search and metrics.query are not declared in discovery, so an implementation should inspect the live schema before constructing a request. This small discipline is the difference between a notebook that appears to work and a worker that can be maintained six months later.

This discovery check uses a public endpoint and prints the discovered path rather than assembling one from prose. The second request shows the required bearer header for the protected metrics route; it intentionally sends no guessed filter fields.

import requests

response = requests.request(
    method="GET",
    url="https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
    timeout=10,
)
response.raise_for_status()
manifest = response.json()

metrics = [
    item for item in manifest.get("capabilities", [])
    if item.get("id") == "metrics.query"
]

if len(metrics) != 1:
    raise RuntimeError("Expected one metrics.query capability in discovery")

path = metrics[0].get("path")
if not path:
    raise RuntimeError("Discovery returned no path for metrics.query")

print(path)

protected = requests.request(
    method="GET",
    url="https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/query",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + __import__("os").environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]},
    timeout=10,
)
if protected.status_code >= 400:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Metrics query failed: {protected.status_code}")

Discovery can tell a client what is available and how to call it; it does not turn the service into an alerting system. There are no alert or notification routes for thresholds, phone calls, SMS, or webhooks, so a team using it for this workflow must poll a query API and own the alert decision. It also has no heartbeat or synthetic probing capability. A task that never ran still needs Healthchecks.io or a comparable monitor.

What must stay outside the API?

Trust boundaries deserve their own design review. Infrai exposes regions in discovery, but the supplied capability facts do not establish a configurable retention policy, a cold-storage setting, or a contractual residency guarantee. The observability surface returns error codes related to retention or cold storage without a configuration entry point. That is enough to require verification, not enough to promise a policy to a compliance reviewer.

Deletion is another sharp edge. There is no log endpoint for deleting records by user, and no bulk export or subscription interface. If a product must satisfy a GDPR access or erasure workflow, keep the authoritative user-to-event index in a system that supports that workflow, or choose a specialist provider whose contract and API do. A trace_id or span_id field can help correlate logs; it does not provide a distributed trace tree, span query, or erasure mechanism.

The same caution applies to processors. A multi-vendor API may simplify integration, but the application owner still has to identify which processor handles a capability, where the data is processed, how long it remains, and what deletion path exists. Those questions belong in the provider’s current documentation and agreement. They cannot be inferred from a one-key interface.

This is the important correction to the one-platform instinct: a consistent interface can reduce integration surface, while the heartbeat, alerting, residency, retention, and deletion decisions remain separate responsibilities.

A decision rule for this workflow

Try Infrai for the telemetry integration when the team values public discovery, runnable examples, and one credential spanning the backend capabilities around an import worker. The self-describing contract is the primary reason; the single-key, 295-route surface is the supporting benefit because it removes credential and billing coordination from a multi-capability workflow.

Choose Healthchecks.io when the central question is whether a scheduled job reported on time. Choose Upptime or Uptime Kuma when HTTP reachability and open-source ownership are the important constraints. Choose Prometheus with Grafana when metrics history, alert evaluation, and visualization deserve dedicated operational tooling. Choose a specialist log or tracing provider when you need user-scoped deletion, distributed span trees, session replay, source-map processing, or contractual residency guarantees. Those specialists are the better choice for those requirements.

The boundary is the recommendation. The REST layer can help an application discover and query observability capabilities, but it does not supply the heartbeat, notification routes, distributed tracing, or GDPR user-deletion API that this incident workflow may require. Test the choice with a small replay set: a missed cron run, a zero-row import, a partial import, and a successful import with a slow downstream dependency.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the live discovery schema before wiring the worker.

References

  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Upptime documentation
  • Uptime Kuma repository
  • Prometheus documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • OpenTelemetry logs signal concepts
  • Infrai documentation

title: Powerduck vs Mockoon: OpenAPI Mock Servers
description:
Quick answer: Mockoon is a well-liked desktop tool for designing mock APIs, with strong templating, rule matching, and a CLI for CI. Powerduck is a local-first studio that generates the mock from your OpenAPI contract instead of asking you to hand-build routes. The difference is the source of truth and the drift that follows. Mockoon gives you precise manual control over a standalone mock; Powerduck guarantees the mock matches the contract, the tests, and the docs, and regenerates on save. Pick Mockoon when you want a dedicated, highly customizable mock designer; pick Powerduck when the mock should be derived from the spec and never quietly diverge.

This page compares the two honestly, including the CLI, cloud, and templating, and links to the focused guides. Start with the table, then read the sections that match how your mocks are maintained today.

The two at a glance

Capability Mockoon Powerduck
Primary role Desktop mock designer OpenAPI studio with mock generation
How routes are created Hand-built Generated from the spec
Source of truth The mock file OpenAPI contract
Regenerates on contract change Manual update Yes, on save
Templating Rich dynamic templating OpenAPI examples and responses
CLI / CI CLI, Docker, GitHub Action OpenAPI CLI
Entry price Free desktop; cloud paid Desktop and Hub free
Best for Fine manual control of a mock Spec-synced mocks across the lifecycle

Hand-built routes vs generated mocks

Mockoon is genuinely powerful for designing a mock: you decide every route, status, and response. The cost is that the mock is a separate artifact you maintain, and it drifts the moment the contract changes without anyone noticing. A generated mock starts from the spec, so the routes, parameters, and responses are correct by construction and update on save. The direct comparison is in Mockoon manual routes vs OpenAPI mocks, and the drift problem is in mock drift: Mockoon vs contract mocks.

Templating vs authored examples

Mockoon's templating is one of its strongest features, and it is the right tool when you need bespoke, dynamic responses that are not part of the contract. A spec-driven mock uses the examples and response schemas you already author, so the data the mock returns is the same data the docs show and the tests assert. The tradeoff is in templating: Mockoon vs OpenAPI examples.

CLI, cloud, and where the free tier runs

Both are usable in CI. Mockoon ships a CLI, Docker image, and GitHub Action, and a paid cloud for collaboration; Powerduck runs from the OpenAPI CLI and hosts mocks and docs together on the Hub within plan limits, so the hosted mock is never out of sync with the reference. The CLIs are compared in Mockoon CLI vs Powerduck CLI, and the hosting is in Mockoon cloud vs free Hub mocks.

Stateful scenarios and record-replay

Realistic workflows often need state — a create followed by a list, a token that expires. Mockoon supports scenarios and record-and-replay for exactly this. A spec-driven studio keeps the stateful behavior tied to the contract and the tests, so the same flow the agent exercises is the flow the spec describes. The scenarios are compared in stateful scenarios: Mockoon vs Powerduck, and the alternative to recording traffic is in record and replay vs spec mocks.

Where to go next

Powerduck is the local-first way to keep mocks synced to the contract; Mockoon is a strong dedicated mock designer. See it on the Powerduck homepage. For the wider picture, read the API mocking guide and the OpenAPI guide.

Frequently asked questions

Does Powerduck match Mockoon's templating?

Mockoon has richer bespoke templating for responses that are not part of the contract. Powerduck uses the examples and response schemas you already author, so the mock, docs, and tests share the same data instead of a separate template.

Can I run a generated mock in CI?

Yes. Run it from the OpenAPI CLI or as a container, just as you would with Mockoon's CLI. The difference is that the mock is derived from the spec rather than a separately maintained file.

Which is better when the API changes often?

A generated mock regenerates on save, so it cannot drift from a fast-changing contract. A hand-built mock gives more control but has to be updated by hand each time.

title: READ OR DIE SHOPPING LIST
description:
I also brought READ OR DIE to life. This project was the shopping list project that I made. It was no regular shopping list, and it was making another dream come true. I hope I will not faint while trying to write this....

Anyway, here is my README.md:

📚 British Library Special Operations: Acquisition Spree (Fan Project)

TOP SECRET // DIV. A
Codename: "The Paper"

An elite, classified web application built to track and catalog rare volume targets and reading sprees. Inspired by the classic anime and manga series Read or Die (R.O.D.), this project is a fan-made tribute built with vanilla JavaScript and persistent local archiving.

I made this project, because I realised that I had missing a repository from back when I did the lists, and I wanted to incorporate a project of my own. While I pondered long and hard, what kind of shopping list I could make, one of the things that came to my mind was a book shopping list, which led to associating it with things like anime where characters compulsively buy books, which led to READ OR DIE- one of my favourite anime ever!! How envy them! It has always been my dream to have all the books that they have! I wish I could have a place, and have it all covered by books ust like the protagonist does!

Please, for all purposes, treat this project as for what it is: a form of fanart, as a project.

The author of READ OR DIE is Hideyuki Kurata.
🎯 Operational Features

Classified Dossier UI: Imposing typewriter typography (Special Elite and Courier Prime), custom parchment textures, and bureaucratic security stamp aesthetics inspired by Read or Die.
Dynamic Acquisition Input: Type any target manuscript or rare book title into the field and immediately log it into the Division's target inventory.
Persistent Local Storage: Utilizes the Web Storage API (localStorage) so your acquisition targets remain securely cataloged even after closing the browser or refreshing the page.
Interactive Status Control: Click any volume to toggle its acquisition/reading status (complete with archival strikethrough styling), or purge the archive entirely when the mission is complete.

🛠️ Technologies Used

HTML5: Semantic document structure representing the classified target dossier.
CSS3: Custom styling, flexbox layouts, variable color tokens, and Google Fonts integration (Special Elite & Courier Prime) for the authentic typewriter aesthetic.
JavaScript (ES6+): DOM manipulation, event listeners, array state management, and localStorage integration.

🚀 Quick Start / Local Deployment

To run this operational tool locally on your machine:

Clone or download this repository to your local machine.
Ensure the following three files are in the same directory:
    index.html
    style.css
    script.js
Double-click index.html or open it directly in any modern web browser to begin your acquisition spree.

⚖️ Disclaimer

Read or Die (R.O.D.) and its characters (including Yomiko Readman) are the intellectual property of Hideyuki Kurata, Shueisha, Aniplex, and other respective copyright holders. This project is a non-commercial, fan-made web application created purely for learning, portfolio display, and as a tribute to the series. No copyright infringement intended.

Authorized for Division A personnel only. Unauthorized distribution will result in immediate intervention by Yomiko Readman. Just kidding~

Check it out here: https://labrava0x.github.io/read-or-die-shopping-list/

title: API Key Rotation vs Revocation in Postgres Workloads — A 2-Path Incident Rule
description:
Use rotation for planned key hygiene, and use revocation when a key may be in an attacker’s hands. Rotation keeps the fleet moving through a grace window; revocation has no grace window and stops the key immediately, so it can break work that still depends on it. For a property-management workload that can spend against an account before an invoice arrives, that distinction is an operational decision, not a naming preference.

At 3 a.m., the useful question is not “which key operation is more elegant?” It is “what page fired, and can I accept this workload failing right now?” If the answer is no because a scheduled maintenance run must finish, rotate and migrate consumers. If the answer is no because an unknown party is spending from the account, revoke first. The invoice can be reconciled later; an active credential cannot be given a friendly grace period.

Infrai fits this boundary when a property-management system wants one REST contract for key lifecycle calls while the provider behind that contract changes. Its live discovery surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules, which is useful when the same audit workflow crosses more than one backend capability.

What should the alert page?

Start with the signal that should have fired before the invoice. In this example, a Postgres-backed job records the workload identity, key identifier, property, authorization decision, and spend boundary before it calls an external service. The alert is then about access and attempted spend, not a vague increase in HTTP traffic.

The on-call sees a key ID, the affected workload, and the last permitted budget decision. That is the beginning of an audit trail. A dashboard showing aggregate spend is useful after the fact, but it does not answer the first incident question: which credential crossed the boundary, which process was using it, which property account was affected, and whether the request was allowed before the spending cap was checked. Those details matter when a scheduled job has already queued work and the invoice has not arrived yet; the responder needs to reconstruct the handoff from access decision to provider call, not infer it from a colorful graph.

I initially treated rotation as the safer default because it avoids breaking callers. That is true for routine maintenance and wrong during an active leak. The grace window is precisely the period in which the attacker can continue working.

Stop first.

For a known compromise, the instrumentation change is straightforward: preserve the key ID in the decision record, page on suspicious access, and make the response choose the hard stop. A false positive still has a cost. Revoking a healthy key can interrupt rent-processing or vendor-integration jobs, so the page must carry enough identity and audit context for the responder to recognize that cost before clicking the dangerous button.

How should I choose API key rotation or revocation?

Rotation belongs to planned hygiene: a key is aging, a deployment is moving ownership, or the fleet needs a controlled credential change. Create the replacement, distribute it to consumers, verify that calls are using it, and retire the old credential after the agreed grace period. The point is continuity with an auditable handoff.

That grace window is not an incidental implementation detail. It is the reason rotation is appropriate when downtime is unacceptable. A property-management scheduler can move workers one at a time, record which version each worker loaded, and leave the old key available long enough to catch stragglers. The resulting records let an auditor distinguish an intentional migration from an unexplained access event.

The handoff should be explicit in application code. This small Go client shows the hard-stop side of the boundary against the verified revoke route. It reads the key from the environment, makes the HTTP method explicit, backs off on a rate limit, and reports a non-success response instead of treating any response as success.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    keyID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_KEY_ID")
    if apiKey == "" || keyID == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_KEY_ID are required")
    }

    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc"
    path := strings.Replace("/v1/account/keys/revoke/{id}", "{id}", keyID, 1)
    url := baseURL + path
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodDelete, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(attempt+1) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("revoke failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }
        fmt.Println("revocation accepted")
        return
    }
    panic("revoke rate-limited after retries")
}

In production, the operation must also be recorded with the operator, key ID, reason, and resulting status. Those fields are what make access auditable; the verb alone is not an audit system.

Why does revocation cost breakage?

Revocation is the incident tool because it takes effect at once and has no body. That is the feature. Once a key is known to be out, preserving service for a few more minutes is preserving the attacker’s access too.

The response order matters. Identify the specific key, record the evidence, revoke it, then assess which legitimate workloads failed and issue a replacement through the normal migration path. Do not rotate during the active leak and call the incident contained. A replacement plus a grace period gives the old key exactly the opportunity the response was meant to remove.

When the evidence is incomplete, do both: rotate for the fleet and revoke the specific key you know is out. This is a narrower blast radius than revoking every credential, while still removing the confirmed access path. It also leaves two separate audit events, which is valuable when someone later asks why a scheduled job failed and why a second credential was issued.

How do the platform choices differ?

The right comparison is the boundary each system gives you, not a contest of feature checklists. AWS Secrets Manager is a natural fit when the application already lives in AWS and secret distribution is part of that platform’s operating model. HashiCorp Vault is the stronger specialist choice when an organization needs a dedicated secrets system and is prepared to operate its policies and deployment. Azure Key Vault is the obvious boundary for teams already centered on Azure identity and resource governance. Unkey is a reasonable alternative for teams looking for a focused API-key management layer rather than a broad backend boundary.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation for this decision
AWS Secrets Manager AWS service integration AWS-centered workloads The lifecycle boundary is tied to the AWS operating model
HashiCorp Vault Dedicated secrets platform Teams that can operate centralized policy and deployment It adds a specialist control plane to own
Azure Key Vault Azure service integration Azure identity and resource governance The boundary is most natural inside Azure
Unkey Focused API-key management layer Teams keeping key management narrow It is a narrower choice than a multi-capability backend boundary
Infrai account platform REST API with one account key Multi-provider workflows that need a stable handoff A shared API boundary does not replace incident ownership

The table is a routing aid, not a ranking.

Those products solve adjacent parts of the problem, but none removes the need to decide whether the current event is hygiene or abuse. A secret store can distribute a replacement; it cannot make a compromised credential safe during a grace window. A direct provider API can revoke quickly; it can also leave an organization with scattered key lifecycle code if every integration invents its own audit record.

For a property-management platform spanning several backend providers, Infrai is a reasonable option at that handoff: the application can keep one REST contract while the service behind the capability changes. Its account-platform surface exposes the lifecycle operations needed here, including POST /v1/account/keys/rotate/{id}, DELETE /v1/account/keys/revoke/{id}, and POST /v1/account/keys/suspected_compromise/{id}. The supporting benefit is operational consistency: the same public discovery surface documents capability schemas and runnable examples in 10 languages, so the integration boundary is inspectable rather than hidden in a separate SDK.

My recommendation is specific: teams that need one auditable key lifecycle boundary across property-management workloads should try Infrai for the account-level rotation and confirmed-compromise path, because the provider contract can stay stable while the service behind it moves. Teams that need deep, organization-wide secret policy or already have a mature AWS, Vault, or Azure control plane should keep the specialist or native choice instead. A single HTTP surface is useful at the handoff; it is not a substitute for incident ownership. The account-key contract is documented at the account-platform docs.

The decision rule I would page on

Write the rule into the runbook before the next alert:

  • Planned hygiene, no known abuse, and service continuity matters: rotate, migrate consumers, verify use of the replacement, and retire the old key after the grace window.
  • Confirmed or strongly suspected compromise: record the key and evidence, revoke immediately, then repair the legitimate callers.
  • Unclear scope: revoke the specific confirmed key and rotate the fleet, keeping both actions visible in the audit record.

The shortest version is this: rotation protects availability; revocation protects the boundary. The page should tell the responder which one is under threat.

References

The access decision should be auditable independently of the provider selected. OWASP’s Secrets Management Cheat Sheet is a useful baseline for lifecycle and operational controls, while the platform documentation defines the concrete account-key operations and their current contract.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • AWS Secrets Manager documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/intro.html
  • HashiCorp Vault documentation: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs
  • Azure Key Vault documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/key-vault/general/overview

title: The Button Moved Before Your Finger Landed, and Your Click Handler Is Innocent
description:
The ticket says: "I pressed Cancel and it deleted my draft."

You open the code. The Cancel handler cancels. The Delete handler deletes. Nothing is crossed, nothing is mislabelled, and the click that arrived went to Delete because Delete was genuinely under that finger at the moment it landed. Both of you are describing the same event correctly and neither description contains the cause.

Something above those buttons changed size about eighty milliseconds earlier.

The browser already has a defence, and you have probably never configured it

There is a feature aimed squarely at this class of problem. MDN:

Scroll anchoring behavior adjusts scroll position to minimize content shifts.

And the line that explains why you have never thought about it:

Scroll anchoring behavior is enabled by default in any browser that supports it.

It works silently, so it is invisible until it is absent. Two things about it are worth holding.

It is one line to switch off. overflow-anchor: none opts an element out: in MDN's words, that element "won't be selected as a potential anchor". That is a reasonable line to write when you are fighting a different scroll bug, and a very easy line to leave behind. Nothing warns you that a protection is now off, because nothing announced it was on.

Its job is the scroll position. Read the definition again: it adjusts scroll position to minimise shifts. That keeps what somebody is reading where they are reading it. It is not, and does not claim to be, a promise that the element under a pointer at one instant is the same element 80ms later.

The measurement has a blind spot exactly where it hurts

Here is the part that costs you something.

Layout shifts are reported through LayoutShift entries, and each one carries hadRecentInput. MDN defines it precisely:

returns true if lastInputTime is less than 500 milliseconds in the past

Shifts flagged that way are normally dropped, and the reasoning is sound as far as it goes:

Layout shifts are only a problem if the user is not expecting them, so layout shifts that are the result of user interactions (such as a user expanding a UI element) are often not considered in layout shift metrics.

That is correct for a user opening an accordion. But notice what the rule is made of: a 500 millisecond window bracketing user input. A mis-tap is, by definition, an event where a shift and an interaction happened within milliseconds of each other. The filter is not wrong, it is simply blind in the one window where this particular failure lives.

So a dashboard can be green while this happens, and the green is not a lie. It is an answer to a different question.

Record the shifts you are told to ignore

The fix is not to distrust the metric. It is to keep a second, unfiltered copy for debugging:

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const shift of list.getEntries()) {
    // Deliberately NOT filtering on hadRecentInput: those are the interesting ones here.
    recent.push({
      at: Math.round(shift.startTime),
      value: shift.value,
      nearInput: shift.hadRecentInput
    });
  }
}).observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });

Keep the last handful in memory and attach them to whatever you already send when something goes wrong. A click log that says deleteDraft at 12840ms is ambiguous. The same log beside a shift of 0.03 at 12795ms is not ambiguous at all: something moved 45 milliseconds before the click, and you now have a timestamp to go and look at.

Why the report will never contain this

Nobody writes "the layout moved as I was tapping". They do not perceive it as movement. They perceive it as having pressed the wrong thing, or as the application doing something they did not ask for, and the report is written in those terms because that is the honest account of their experience.

The information that would settle it is the position of two elements during a window of about a tenth of a second, on their device, at their connection speed, with whatever loaded late that day. It is not in your logs, it is not in their description, and by the time anybody looks the page has settled into the layout you would have predicted.

Which is the general shape: the evidence that decides this bug has a shorter half-life than the time it takes anybody to notice there is a bug.

title: Picking an AI Coding Tool for Your Team in 2026 — Including the One Pick We Had to Fix
description:
Disclosure: we link out to every tool below. None currently has a confirmed, active affiliate relationship with us — Tabnine, Cody and Amazon Q show as "unverified" in our own data, the rest as "none." Nothing here is commission-motivated.

Choosing an AI coding tool for yourself is a taste decision. Choosing one for a team of 10, 50 or 300 developers is an admin-and-compliance decision wearing a taste decision's clothes — SSO, code-privacy guarantees, content exclusion, per-seat economics. We evaluated five tools (Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, Tabnine, Claude Code) specifically on that axis, plus talked to engineering leads at four companies running them at scale.

The short version

GitHub Copilot Business wins for most teams — not the best AI on the list, but the best combination of AI quality, admin maturity and native GitHub integration, at $19/seat/month. One fintech engineering lead told us the deciding factor wasn't model quality at all: "We spent two weeks on the admin configuration before we enabled it for anyone. That level of control is why we picked Copilot over Cursor."

Tabnine is the only genuine on-premises option — VPC, air-gapped, or on your own hardware, with code never leaving your infrastructure. A healthcare security architect put it bluntly: "We evaluated Copilot and Cursor first — both are better AI, honestly. But neither could meet our data handling requirements."

Cursor Team has the best raw AI quality for multi-file work; a 30-person startup's tech lead estimated a 15–20% productivity gain after switching from Copilot Business, with weaker admin tooling as the tradeoff.

Windsurf Team undercuts both on per-seat price for budget-conscious teams, with the least mature admin layer of the four.

Claude Code has no team features at all — no SSO, no admin console, no seat management — and is best adopted informally by small groups of senior engineers (5–15) as a complement to a team-managed tool, not a replacement for one.

The correction

While checking this guide before syndicating it, we found our own deployment checklist still recommending Amazon Q Developer for "AWS-heavy teams" with "a generous free tier" — present tense, no caveat. That stopped being true in May 2026: AWS closed Q Developer to new signups on May 15, 2026, pulled its frontier models into a separate product (Kiro) two weeks later, and has confirmed end-of-support for existing subscribers as April 30, 2027. A team reading our checklist today and trying to sign up for the thing we recommended would hit a wall.

It's a small line in a 300-line guide, but it's exactly the kind of claim that goes stale silently — the five tools we actually tested got current pricing and current product status; a one-line aside about a sixth tool didn't get the same scrutiny until now.

What actually differs at team scale

The checklist that matters before you buy:

  • Can code leave your infrastructure at all? If no, Tabnine is your only option among these five.
  • Do you need SAML SSO today? Copilot Business/Enterprise or Tabnine; Cursor and Windsurf's SSO support is thinner.
  • Under 15 developers, mostly senior? Claude Code's usage-based pricing can beat per-seat licensing — until usage gets uneven, at which point the bill does too.
  • 100+ developers? Copilot Enterprise or Tabnine are the two built for that scale of governance.

The full guide has the per-seat cost tables for 15/50/200-developer teams, deployment-time measurements, and the complete team-deployment checklist.

title: I rebuilt Wallpaper Engine in Rust
description:
Wallpaper Engine is honestly one of the best things on Steam. Millions of animated wallpapers, everything from plain looping videos to layered 2D scenes with particles, shaders and little scripts running inside them.

It also has a few habits that bug me. It's Windows-only and closed source. The GPU never really idles. Maximize one window and every monitor pauses. And if an audio device disappears, video wallpapers can just break.

So I got curious: how much of it could I rebuild as an open engine that still plays the content people already own?

Two weeks later, I have an answer. It's called Diorama, and it's about 36,000 lines of Rust on top of wgpu. It plays Wallpaper Engine scenes, videos and web wallpapers straight from your local Workshop folder, plus your own files. Right now it's Windows only. Linux is next.

This post is about how it works. But mostly it's about how I convinced myself that it actually works.

Rule #1: the renderer never sees Wallpaper Engine

The very first decision I made was architectural, and it's the one I'm happiest with. Wallpaper Engine's file formats are the importer's problem. Nothing else in the codebase even knows they exist.

The split looks like this:

  • diorama-we reads all the Wallpaper Engine formats: .pkg archives, .tex textures (LZ4, DXT, sprite sheets, even embedded MP4s), .mdl models and puppets, the scene/effect/material/particle JSON, and their custom shader dialect. It turns all of that into an engine-neutral scene format, diorama-scene.
  • diorama-render only ever sees that neutral format: layers, materials, passes, effect chains, particles.
  • diorama-platform is the one crate allowed to touch the OS.

I didn't trust myself to keep this clean, so a CI script enforces it. The build fails if a lower layer depends on a higher one, or if cfg(windows) shows up anywhere outside the platform crate.

This boundary paid for itself over and over. Every time I hit some new Wallpaper Engine quirk, the fix went into the importer and the renderer stayed simple.

I also decided early that anything coming from the Workshop is hostile input:

  • Parsers are bounds-checked, fuzzed, and never allowed to unwrap.
  • Scripts run in QuickJS with memory and time limits.
  • Shaders get validated before they're used.
  • Web wallpapers run offline by default, each in its own process.

Shaders: GLSL dialect → HLSL → DXC → SPIR-V → naga → wgpu

Yes, that heading is the actual pipeline.

Wallpaper Engine's shaders are written in a GLSL-ish dialect with #includes, // [COMBO] permutation markers, JSON annotations on uniforms, and Direct3D 11 semantics sitting underneath all of it.

So Diorama:

  1. preprocesses them,
  2. translates them to HLSL,
  3. compiles that with DXC to SPIR-V,
  4. validates and loads the result through naga into wgpu,
  5. and caches every permutation on disk.

Going through HLSL looks like a detour, and I didn't pick it on a hunch. I ran a quick spike on my test library: 330 of 336 shader/permutation pairs compile via HLSL, versus 299 going straight through GLSL. Easy call.

How I checked it: RenderDoc captures and SSIM

"Looks about right" isn't a test, and with a renderer it's very easy to fool yourself. So I went to the source of truth.

I captured Wallpaper Engine itself with RenderDoc. A capture gives you every draw call, every render target and every uniform, including the exact g_Time of that frame.

On the Diorama side, I can render any scene off-screen at a specific time:

dioramad --scene … --time t --frame-out x.png

That means every capture becomes a reference image. A small tool then scores the difference between the two with SSIM.

The first scene I tried scored 0.996, which felt great. Then I ran it over all 55 scenes in my library:

  • 35 score 0.95 or higher
  • 48 score 0.90 or higher
  • the mean is 0.948

The captures were also the best documentation I had. They answered questions that no amount of reading would have:

  • Wallpaper Engine uses reversed-Z depth with a GREATER test, and blended draws never write depth.
  • Layers marked "no interpolation" use point filtering the whole way through: source texture, effect passes and the final composite. Miss one step and pixel-art scenes go soft.
  • A layer's last effect pass draws straight into the scene, not into another render target.
  • Particle count scales the emission rate, not the maximum.

Some differences I just can't match. One terrain shader builds its hash function on sin, which compiles differently in FXC and DXC, so the pattern comes out different everywhere. I've made peace with that one.

SceneScript

32 of my 55 scenes use SceneScript, Wallpaper Engine's JavaScript layer. It's what powers clocks, interactive layers and even small games inside wallpapers.

The nice surprise here: Wallpaper Engine ships complete TypeScript typings for it. That gave me a clear spec to build against. Diorama implements the API in QuickJS (via rquickjs), covering layers, animations, cursor events, audio and media, user properties and timers.

One scene full of draggable desktop "windows" took a while. Getting it right needed pointer capture, plus sending cursor events only to the topmost layer that's actually listening for them.

Web wallpapers: the case of the frozen weather widget

Web wallpapers run in WebView2, each in its own process, and the network is off unless you allow it.

That default gave me my favourite bug of the whole project.

A weather widget was frozen solid on the desktop. But when I rendered it off-screen, it was perfectly fine. Same wallpaper, same code, completely different behaviour.

The culprit was in its audio handler:

while (smoothedPoints.length < values.length) {
  if (typeof createVector === "function") smoothedPoints.push(createVector(0, height / 2));
}

createVector comes from p5.js, which the wallpaper loads from a CDN. Diorama had blocked that CDN. So createVector was never a function, nothing ever got pushed, and the very first audio frame walked into a loop that could never end.

And the off-screen renders? They don't get audio. No audio frame, no loop, no freeze.

Diorama now reports blocked files and stuck pages, and gives you an "Allow internet access" switch for that specific wallpaper.

Fixing the things people complain about

The other half of the project was working through a list of Wallpaper Engine pain points. Each one got its own test, so it stays fixed.

  • Idle cost: a static wallpaper stops drawing completely. 0.00% GPU when idle.
  • Pausing: each monitor pauses on its own when there's a fullscreen app or maximized window in front of it. One maximized window no longer freezes everything.
  • Windows 11 24H2: it survives the new desktop window layout (including with icons hidden), Explorer restarts and graphics driver resets.
  • Audio: video never depends on an audio device.
  • Cost report: the library shows each wallpaper's measured CPU, GPU and memory, so you know what it costs before you leave it running all day.
  • Video decoding: if your GPU can't decode a video, you get a one-click conversion instead of a CPU running hot.

What's next

  • Linux. Wayland layer-shell and X11, VA-API video, PipeWire audio. This is where an open engine matters most, so it's my top priority.
  • Closing the remaining gaps, mainly planar reflections and camera fades.
  • A signed installer.

Diorama is dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0. It ships no Wallpaper Engine code or content. It just reads what you already have.

The code, an installer and three original example wallpapers are all at github.com/karmanya007/Diorama. If a wallpaper looks wrong, please open an issue with its Workshop id. That helps a lot.

A note on how this was built: I leaned heavily on an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). I steered the design, ran the captures and reviewed the work, and the commits carry its co-author line.

title: The Non-Price Rationing of Offensive Compute
description:
On October 28, Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon, arriving fourteen days after Gemini 4 Argon. Alongside improvements in general reasoning and long-horizon engineering tasks, DeepMind reported specific benchmark gains in software security. Carbon achieved 88.2 percent on SEC-bench Pro for identifying vulnerabilities, 54.8 percent on ExploitGym for autonomous exploit generation, and 71.0 percent on CWE-bench for automated patch generation.

DeepMind accompanied those capability gains with two operational choices. First, Carbon maintains the identical introductory price structure introduced with Argon: two dollars per million input tokens and ten dollars per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted by 95 percent. Second, DeepMind chose not to release the model directly through open API tiers. Instead, access is restricted to selected security researchers through its Fairwind Program and voluntary pre-release reviews with federal agencies.

Pricing a utility at constant marginal cost assumes that output variance is bounded and private. For document summarization, natural language extraction, or standard web application development, a token generated by a client produces utility for the buyer without imposing unpriced negative externalities on third parties. If a completion call fails or produces bad code, the buyer bears the cost of the discarded output. The provider collects a uniform ten dollars per million tokens and clears the queue.

That pricing structure disintegrates when applied to autonomous offensive capabilities. On ExploitGym, generating a candidate exploit script consumes several thousand output tokens, representing a raw API expenditure measured in pennies. The realized value of that script, however, is heavily fat-tailed. Most attempts fail, generating zero economic product. A single successful exploit chain targeting a common kernel flaw or cryptographic library produces either a five-figure vulnerability bounty or millions of dollars in defensive disruption across enterprise networks.

A foundation model provider cannot internalize the liability of weaponized outputs under a flat token tariff. If an open API allows anonymous callers to generate weaponized zero-day exploits at ten dollars per million tokens, the provider exposes itself to severe regulatory intervention, legal liability, and platform reputation damage. At the same time, the provider cannot raise the general token price to match the potential downside of an attack. Pricing tokens at five hundred dollars per million to price in tail liability would destroy the commercial market for benign engineering workloads.

When a price mechanism cannot clear a market safely, sellers resort to non-price rationing. DeepMind's Fairwind Program, customer vetting requirements, and pre-release government reviews are institutional forms of capital rationing. Because the provider cannot use price discrimination to separate offensive attackers from defensive engineers, it replaces the open market with an administrative filter. The lab transitions from a public utility provider into a credentialing authority that decides who possesses sufficient clearance to purchase compute.

This administrative filter introduces structural distortions for downstream software teams. Large enterprise defense platforms and well-capitalized security vendors receive preferential access to frontier weights under managed partnerships. Independent security auditors, open-source maintainers, and smaller infrastructure teams remain confined to older model checkpoints. The ability to audit production systems against frontier capabilities becomes a function of corporate scale rather than technical necessity.

The operational reality inside engineering organizations complicates the defense narrative. DeepMind notes that Carbon doubles the rate of secure code generation compared to Argon on internal benchmarks, and the Chrome security team reported substantial gains in patch quality compared to older frontier models. In a static model where defense simply outpaces offense, providing automated patching tools would permanently eliminate software vulnerabilities.

In practice, the economic costs of offense and defense scale under opposing cost curves. On an exploitation benchmark like ExploitGym, an adversary requires a single valid execution path to achieve a successful compromise. An attack agent running automated loops at ten dollars per million tokens can afford dozens of speculative failures to secure one functional payload.

Defense requires universal coverage across every deployed endpoint, microservice, and third-party dependency. Even if a model successfully resolves 71.0 percent of known flaws on CWE-bench, the remaining 29 percent of unaddressed or incorrectly patched vulnerabilities leave the underlying attack surface viable. Automated code generators produce remediation suggestions in seconds, but verifying that a patch does not break existing production invariants requires human regression testing, staging deployments, and manual code review. Offense consumes cheap compute cycles, while defense continues to pay the fixed hourly rate of senior systems engineers.

The fourteen-day window between Argon and Carbon reveals a second friction in model adoption. Enterprise security teams often spend weeks evaluating a new model release against internal repositories, running penetration tests, and verifying compliance boundaries before approving deployment. When frontier model weights depreciate on a bi-weekly cycle, the evaluation phase lasts longer than the lifespan of the underlying version. Software teams must decide whether to freeze on an obsolete checkpoint or expend continuous engineering hours validating transient updates.

Gemini 4 Carbon marks the point where uniform API pricing reaches its limits. As frontier reasoning models demonstrate measurable capability on autonomous exploitation benchmarks, the fiction that compute can be sold as an unmetered, uniform commodity breaks down. Foundation model developers will increasingly rely on walled-garden partner programs, formal identity verification, and non-price rationing, leaving enterprise buyers to manage the asymmetric costs of verification on their own balance sheets.

Originally published at https://deanlee.info/essays/the-non-price-rationing-of-offensive-compute.

title: Is There a Dynamics 365 Release Wave 2 in 2026? What to Do Next
description:
Every October, Dynamics 365 teams used to open the same calendar entry: "Review release wave 2." This year, that entry has nothing behind it. There is no Dynamics 365 release wave 2 for 2026, no release plan document, and no neat list of features to read through over a cup of tea.

That does not mean updates have stopped. It means the way you hear about them has changed. If your business runs on Dynamics 365, the safest response is to build your own Dynamics 365 change calendar: a shared schedule that shows what is coming, who checks it, and when it reaches your users.

This guide shows you how.

What Microsoft Changed

For years, Microsoft delivered updates in two release waves. Wave 1 ran from April to September. Wave 2 ran from October to March. A release plan arrived a few weeks ahead of each wave, so admins could read it, test in a sandbox, and brief their teams.

In August 2026, Microsoft announced the end of that model for Dynamics 365, Power Platform and Dataverse. New features now appear on a single roadmap, called the AI at Work roadmap, once Microsoft commits to them. The older Release Planner site is due to retire by 15 November 2026.

In short, updates now arrive as a steady stream instead of two big announcements a year. The software is not changing less. The warning system is simply different.

Why This Matters for Your Business

The old release plan did one useful thing: it forced a conversation. Twice a year, someone had to read the changes and decide what mattered. Without that rhythm, three risks appear.

Missed changes. A new setting or a change in default behaviour can slip in unnoticed, then show up as a complaint from a user.

Surprise clashes. Custom workflows, integrations and reports can break when a feature changes underneath them. A small update can cause a big problem if nobody tested it.

Unplanned training. Staff find new buttons before anyone has explained them, and confidence in the system drops.

Companies that treat the roadmap as a news feed will struggle. Companies that treat it as an input to their own schedule will stay calm.

How to Build Your Own Dynamics 365 Change Calendar

A change calendar is a simple shared schedule. It lists every update that could affect your system, who reviews it, and when it reaches users. Here is a five-step way to build one.

Step 1: Pick an owner

Name one person responsible for watching Microsoft's roadmap. This could be a functional consultant, a system admin or a technology partner. Without a named owner, the calendar becomes everyone's job, and so nobody's job.

Step 2: Set a fixed review rhythm

Replace the old wave review with a regular check. A monthly review works well for most mid-sized teams. Large organisations with many connected systems may prefer every two weeks. Block the time in advance, the same way you once blocked time for release wave 2.

Step 3: Sort every change into three groups

For each item on the roadmap, ask one question: what does this do to us?

  • Act now: it affects live processes, security or compliance.
  • Plan: it is useful, but needs testing or training first.
  • Watch: it is interesting, but no action is needed yet.

This keeps your list short and your meetings useful.

Step 4: Match each change to a testing window

Choose a test environment and a fixed slot for checking changes before they reach your live system. Test your most important processes every time, such as quotes, orders, invoices, approvals and any link to other tools. Write down what you tested and what you found.

Step 5: Add communication and training dates

Every change that affects users needs a short note and, where needed, a quick training session. Put these dates on the calendar next to the technical dates. A new feature only helps if people know it exists and trust it.

A Four-Week Dynamics 365 Change Calendar Template

If you want a starting point, try this four-week loop.

  • Week 1: Review the roadmap and sort new items into act now, plan and watch.
  • Week 2: Test priority items in your test environment and check connected systems.
  • Week 3: Brief business users and update your guides.
  • Week 4: Approve changes for release, then look back at what went well and what did not.

Adjust it to your own size and pace. What matters is that the rhythm repeats, so updates become routine instead of a surprise.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Waiting for a big announcement. There will not be one. Features will appear one by one, and dates can move.
  • Treating every item as urgent. Most roadmap items will not touch your business this quarter. Sorting is the real skill.
  • Leaving business teams out. Finance, sales and operations know which processes are fragile. Invite them to the monthly review.
  • Skipping the record. Keep a short log of what changed, when, and who approved it. It helps with audits and speeds up fixes when something goes wrong.
  • Trusting old dates. Roadmap timing can shift. Recheck dates at each review and update the calendar.

What This Means for Dynamics 365 Teams

The end of release waves is a good moment to move from reacting to planning. Teams with a clear Dynamics 365 change calendar spend less time on surprises and more time using new features well.

Teams without one will feel every update as a small emergency.

At Dynamics Monk, we help organisations across the UK, UAE, Australia, Singapore and Southeast Asia keep their Dynamics 365 systems steady as Microsoft's update model changes. Whether you need a ready-made change calendar, a testing routine, or ongoing support from certified consultants, we can set it up with you.

Originally published on Dynamics Monk: Is There a Dynamics 365 Release Wave 2 in 2026? What to Do Next

title: Faster Frontend Rollbacks with Versioned Builds
description:
How we went from "rebuild and restart every pod" to "pick a build and click deploy."

Every team ships a bad build at some point. When it happens, the only thing that matters is how quickly you can get back to the last version that worked.

The problem

A single Node server served both our backend and frontend from one domain:

example.com/api/...   →  Backend
example.com/...       →  Frontend (HTML, JS, CSS)

The frontend files were cached inside every pod. To revert a bad build, we had to revert the code, rebuild, redeploy and restart every pod. That's a full deploy cycle in the middle of an incident.

The idea: never overwrite a build

Every build goes to its own folder in S3, served through a CDN. At the root sits one special file: index.html, a copy of the index.html from the build we want live.

s3://frontend-bucket/            (https://cdn.example.com)
├── index.html          ← copy of the LIVE build's index.html
├── 20261028-1015/      ← build 1
│   ├── index.html
│   ├── main.js
│   └── style.css
└── 20261029-1430/      ← build 2 (latest)
    ├── index.html      ── copied to root on release
    ├── main.js
    └── style.css

Old builds are never touched. Which version is live comes down to which index.html is sitting at the root.

The one detail that makes it work: each build must load its assets by the full folder path, so it still works after being copied to the root:

<script src="https://cdn.example.com/20261029-1430/main.js"></script>

Set this with your bundler's publicPath or base option. As a bonus, View Source shows which build is live.

Serving the HTML from the CDN

The pods no longer hold frontend files. Requests to /api/* go to Node, and everything else gets the root index.html from the CDN. You can route this in two ways:

  • At the load balancer: non-/api requests go straight to the CDN. The frontend stays up even if Node is down.
  • Through Node: Node fetches index.html from the CDN and streams it. This is a smaller change, but the frontend depends on Node.

Either way, a frontend change never needs a pod restart again.

Release and rollback

Release:

Build → Upload to new folder → Verify → Copy its index.html to root → Clear CDN cache

You can test any build at cdn.example.com/<timestamp>/index.html before users see it. Only the copy-to-root step changes what users get.

The root index.html acts as a switch between builds. We automate release and rollback through Jenkins: select a build and run the job. Jenkins replaces the root HTML, clears the CDN cache and verifies the live version, with no manual file changes.

It takes about a minute. There's no code revert, no rebuild and no pod restart. You revert the bad commit later, without pressure.

One assumption: backend changes stay backward compatible with the previous frontend build. The frontend and backend used to ship together. Now the frontend can roll back on its own, which is what makes it fast.

Two rules you can't skip

  • Caching: the root index.html uses no-cache, because it's the switch. Timestamped JS/CSS use max-age=31536000, immutable. If index.html is cached for an hour, your rollback takes an hour to reach users.
  • Retention: keep the last ~10 builds. Never delete the live build or the one before it, because users with the page open still load from it.

Serving straight from a CDN? This works for you too

Many teams serve the frontend directly from S3 behind a CDN, with no Node server. The weak spot is that every deploy overwrites the previous build. A bad release means reverting, merging to main and waiting for the pipeline: 10 minutes at the very least.

Versioned folders fit this setup even better, because there's no routing to change. Upload each build to a new folder, use full asset paths, and treat the root index.html as the switch.

This is especially worth it if you deploy once or twice a week. Ten builds give you over a month of rollback points for almost no storage cost, and recovery becomes a one-minute switch instead of a 10-minute scramble.

Wrapping up

Builds are immutable, and going live is just pointing at one of them. Once releases work that way, a rollback is no longer an emergency rebuild. It's a one-minute switch.

title: 5 Common SQL Mistakes: WHERE, ORDER BY, AND/OR, and Top 3 Queries
description:
A SQL query can execute without errors and still produce an unexpected result.

It might return the wrong employees, sort salaries incorrectly, or select the wrong three records.

The issue often lies in how you use "WHERE", "ORDER BY", logical operators, and row-limiting clauses.

Let's explore five practical SQL examples using a simple employee table.

Sample Data

Assume we have the following "employees" table:

ID| Name| Dept| Salary
101| Amit| IT| 60000
102| Priya| HR| 45000
103| Rahul| IT| 75000
104| Neha| Fin| 55000
105| Sneha| IT| 60000

  1. Filter Rows Using WHERE

Question: Find employees earning more than ₹50,000.

SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000;

This query returns Amit, Rahul, Neha, and Sneha.

Common mistake: Using ">=" instead of ">" changes the result when an employee earns exactly ₹50,000.

  • ">" means greater than.
  • ">=" means greater than or equal to.

Always choose the comparison operator that matches the business requirement.

  1. Sort Salaries Correctly

Question: Display employees from the highest salary to the lowest.

SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;

Remember:

  • "DESC" sorts from highest to lowest.
  • "ASC" sorts from lowest to highest.

Interview tip: Without "ORDER BY", SQL does not guarantee the order of returned rows.

  1. Combine Filtering and Sorting

Question: Find IT employees earning more than ₹50,000 and display the highest salary first.

SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
AND salary > 50000
ORDER BY salary DESC;

The query first identifies employees who satisfy both conditions and then sorts the qualifying rows by salary.

Expected result:

Name| Salary
Rahul| 75000
Amit| 60000
Sneha| 60000

Notice that Amit and Sneha have the same salary. Their relative order is not guaranteed because the query does not specify a secondary sort key.

This pattern is useful in employee reports, sales analysis, and dashboards.

  1. Avoid AND/OR Logic Errors

Question: Find employees who work in IT or earn more than ₹60,000, provided their salary is at least ₹50,000.

SELECT name, dept, salary
FROM employees
WHERE (dept = 'IT' OR salary > 60000)
AND salary >= 50000;

The parentheses make the intended logic explicit.

In SQL, "AND" has higher precedence than "OR". Without parentheses, a condition combining both operators can return unintended results.

Interview tip: When a requirement contains both "AND" and "OR", group the conditions carefully before writing the query.

  1. Find the Top 3 Highest-Paid Employees

Question: Return the three highest-paid employees.

SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id ASC
LIMIT 3;

The query sorts by salary in descending order and uses "emp_id" as a secondary sort key.

Because Amit and Sneha both earn ₹60,000, the secondary sort makes their relative order predictable.

Important: "LIMIT" works in MySQL and PostgreSQL. Other database systems may use different row-limiting syntax.

Also, "LIMIT 3" returns at most three rows. If you need to include everyone tied at the third-highest salary, consider using a ranking function such as "RANK()".

One Small Change Can Affect Your Report

Compare these conditions:

WHERE salary > 50000

WHERE salary >= 50000

The difference is just one character, but the second condition also includes employees earning exactly ₹50,000.

In real reporting, small differences like this can affect totals, eligibility checks, and business decisions.

Continue Learning SQL

Want to practise more questions about filtering, sorting, and SQL interview preparation?

Explore the "SQL FAQ tutorial on restricting and sorting data" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/restricting-sorting-data-sql-faq.html) from Sankalan Data Tech for more topic-focused examples.

Final SQL Challenge

Suppose the "employees" table contains thousands of records.

How would you find the second-highest distinct salary without using "LIMIT" or "TOP"?

Try solving it with a subquery before looking up the answer. This is a useful exercise for SQL interviews.

Share your approach in the comments!
