title: Security Hardening: Encryption, Auditing, and Least Privilege
description:
• Assessing risks and mapping compliance obligations
  • Encryption architecture: TDE, Always Encrypted, and TLS explained
  • Designing roles, RBAC, and least-privilege access models
  • Auditing, monitoring, and incident response for SQL Server
  • Practical checklist: hardened SQL Server deployment and runbook

Encryption, precise auditing, and strict least-privilege controls are the baseline you must demonstrate when your SQL Server estate faces GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI scrutiny. These are technical controls, not checkbox exercises — they must be designed, documented, and testable from keys to logs.

The immediate problem you’re facing isn’t a lack of products — it’s an architecture and evidence problem. You may already have transparent data encryption enabled and TLS set, but auditors ask for key custody, proof that sensitive columns are inaccessible to DBAs, and tamper-evident logging; meanwhile app owners complain that encryption breaks reports. That friction shows up as missing key rotation records, audits routed to local disks with short retention, broad db_owner memberships, and no documented incident playbook.

Assessing risks and mapping compliance obligations

Start with scope and classification; treat it like any other engineering deliverable.

  • Inventory the sensitive data sets (PAN, ePHI, national IDs, etc.), note where they live (tables, backups, logs), and assign data sensitivity tags that feed decisions about cryptographic scope and logging.
  • Map each data class to the governing control:
    • GDPR Article 32 calls explicitly for pseudonymisation and encryption as appropriate technical measures. Record your state-of-the-art analysis and chosen protections.
    • HIPAA’s Security Rule requires an accurate risk analysis and uses that analysis to determine whether encryption is “reasonable and appropriate”; HHS guidance and the OCR risk-analysis materials are the baseline references.
    • PCI DSS mandates strong cryptography for PAN in transit and at rest, plus demonstrable key-management practices and certificate inventories. The PCI Council’s published documents define the detail auditors will expect.
  • Use a simple risk matrix (Likelihood × Impact) that outputs an encryption decision (None / TDE / Column encryption / Application-level encryption) and a logging requirement (basic audit / detailed SQL Audit / SIEM ingestion).
  • Record your acceptance criteria: e.g., “No cleartext PAN in any database backup; all connections to the CDE must require TLS with valid certs; all schema and role changes must create audit events retained 365 days.”

Important: A legal/regulatory reference is not an implementation plan. Capture justification (what you chose and why) and the exact artifacts an auditor will ask to see: key custody logs, rotation schedule, audit configuration exports, and incident-runbook excerpts.

Encryption architecture: TDE, Always Encrypted, and TLS explained

Design your crypto stack as layers for different threat models.

  • Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)

    • What it protects: data-at-rest — database files, log files, and backups are encrypted on disk. It encrypts pages at the I/O layer, not individual columns.
    • What it doesn't: TDE does not protect data in memory, in transit, or from a DBA with the database master certificate or access to key material. Plan certificate backup and recovery as first-class operations: losing the certificate means losing access to backups.
    • Operational notes: initial encryption triggers a scan of all pages (can pause/resume on modern versions); backup the server certificate and private key immediately after enabling. Example enablement snippet (illustrative): 
    -- create server keys/cert, database encryption key, then enable TDE
USE master;
CREATE MASTER KEY ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = 'Complex!Passw0rd';
CREATE CERTIFICATE MyTDECert WITH SUBJECT = 'TDE DEK cert';
USE YourDB;
CREATE DATABASE ENCRYPTION KEY WITH ALGORITHM = AES_256
  ENCRYPTION BY SERVER CERTIFICATE MyTDECert;
ALTER DATABASE YourDB SET ENCRYPTION ON;

    Source: SQL Server TDE guidance.

  • Always Encrypted (column-level / client-side encryption)

    • What it protects: data in use and at rest in the database for specific columns; cryptographic keys are stored outside the Database Engine (Azure Key Vault, Windows certificate store, or an HSM) and the engine never sees plaintext keys. This prevents DBAs and cloud operators from viewing plaintext values.
    • Modes and trade-offs:
    • Deterministic encryption supports equality comparisons and indexing but leaks value frequency patterns.
    • Randomized encryption is cryptographically stronger but disallows search/grouping; use secure enclaves (Always Encrypted with secure enclaves) when you need richer operations.
    • Operational notes: key provisioning and re-encryption are performed outside the engine and can be slow for large columns; plan migrations and parameterized client access patterns.

  • TLS (data in transit)

    • Use TLS to protect connections between apps and SQL Server, replication endpoints, and any linked services. Enforce at least TLS 1.2; NIST and Microsoft recommend moving to modern ciphers and supporting TLS 1.3 where available. Verify client/driver support and Windows Schannel configuration.
    • For SQL Server, flip Force Encryption only when all clients support it; otherwise schedule staged enforcement with driver updates. Test logins and SSIS/agent jobs after changes.

  • Comparison table (practical):

Control Protects Affects Key location Compliance fit
TDE At-rest: DB files, logs, backups Minimal app changes; encryption scan overhead Server certificate / EKM / Key Vault PCI (data at rest), baseline for GDPR/HIPAA evidence.
Always Encrypted Column-level, in-use + at-rest for selected columns App driver changes; limits some SQL functionality External KMS (Key Vault/HSM) Strong for GDPR pseudonymisation; HIPAA as strong technical safeguard; reduces DBA exposure.
TLS (TDS) Data-in-transit Requires up-to-date drivers and cert lifecycle X.509 certs (PKI) Required by PCI for public networks; recommended by NIST.

Cite the TDE, Always Encrypted, and TLS guidance in your architecture documents and include exact config exports in audit artifacts.

Designing roles, RBAC, and least-privilege access models

Privilege design is an engineering problem; treat roles as code.

  • Use role-based access control (RBAC) and group membership as your canonical authorization model. Map business functions to named roles (example: Finance_ReadOnly, HR_Payroll_Write, ETL_Service) and grant permissions to roles rather than individual accounts. Use AD groups for membership to simplify lifecycle.
  • Avoid broad roles:
    • Reserve sysadmin, securityadmin, and db_owner for tightly controlled break-glass accounts. Newer fixed server roles added in SQL Server versions (e.g., granular ##MS_* roles) let you reduce the use of sysadmin. Use the documented server roles mapping to pick minimal rights.
  • Pattern: application vs operator accounts
    • Application/service principals: non-interactive, short-lived secrets where possible (managed identities / gMSAs in Windows / service principals in cloud).
    • Admin accounts: split duties — separate people who change schema/objects from those who manage security and from those who run backups.
  • Hardening with SQL features:
    • Use Row-Level Security to keep a single logical table while restricting visibility by predicate (useful for multi-tenant and compartmentalization scenarios). Beware side channels and carefully test predicate functions.
    • Use Dynamic Data Masking at the presentation layer to reduce accidental exposure in ad-hoc queries and dashboards; do not rely on masking as a primary protection.
  • Concrete role script (example pattern — create role, grant schema-level select, add AD group as member): 
  USE YourDatabase;
  CREATE ROLE Finance_ReadOnly;
  GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::Finance TO Finance_ReadOnly;
  ALTER ROLE Finance_ReadOnly ADD MEMBER [DOMAIN\Finance_Readers];
  • Entitlement hygiene:
    • Automate provisioning/deprovisioning with your IAM and on a cadence (quarterly entitlement review).
    • Log role membership changes and make them auditable (these events are as important as DDL changes).

Auditing, monitoring, and incident response for SQL Server

You must prove who did what, when and that logs are trustworthy.

  • SQL Server Audit and action groups

    • Use SQL Server Audit to capture server-level and database-level actions; enable the audit targets appropriate for your SIEM (audit file, Windows Security log, or Event Hub/Azure Monitor for cloud). Capture failed logins, successful privileged logins, changes to roles/permissions, schema changes, and access to sensitive objects.
    • Example creation (illustrative): 
    USE master;
CREATE SERVER AUDIT Sec_Audit TO FILE (FILEPATH = 'C:\Audit\SqlAudit\');
ALTER SERVER AUDIT Sec_Audit WITH (STATE = ON);

USE YourDB;
CREATE DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION Audit_Sensitive
  FOR SERVER AUDIT Sec_Audit
  ADD (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON dbo.CreditCard BY PUBLIC)
  WITH (STATE = ON);

    Store the audit configuration export with your change control artifacts.

  • Log centralization and integrity

    • Ship audit files to a hardened collector or SIEM immediately; ensure logs are immutable for the retention period required by policy. Retain enough context to reconstruct sessions (correlate with app and OS logs).

  • Monitoring signals to bake into detection:

    • Rapid schema changes on protected tables.
    • Unusual bulk read patterns (e.g., large SELECT counts on PII tables).
    • Elevated query volume after hours or from odd IP ranges.
    • Repeated failed login attempts followed by a successful privileged login.

  • Incident response and forensics

    • Use the NIST incident response lifecycle as your playbook (Prepare → Detect/Analyze → Contain/Eradicate/Recover → Post-incident). Keep a tailored DB playbook for common actions (isolate replicas, disable service principals, collect and preserve transaction logs, snapshot the database and host memory for forensic analysis).
    • Regulatory-differentiated notification windows:
    • GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach. Document timelines and evidence for every breach.
    • HIPAA requires covered entities and business associates to follow detailed breach-notification rules; for large incidents, notifications to HHS and affected individuals must meet timing rules (examples and forms are on HHS guidance pages).
    • For SQL-specific containment: consider temporarily disabling high-risk logins, blocking network access to replicas, rotating keys (see key-management playbook), and preserving all logs (audit, errorlog, OS-level).

  • Post-incident / lessons learned: capture root cause, timeline, containment steps, and remediation steps in a breach register (this is an audit artifact auditors will ask for). NIST and the PCI Council expect a demonstrated corrective path.

Callout: Audit configuration is evidence. Export the SQL Server Audit and server configuration as immutable artifacts and include them in your compliance package. The thing auditors check first is the chain of custody for keys and logs.

Practical checklist: hardened SQL Server deployment and runbook

This is a compact, actionable list you can implement in your next maintenance window. Treat each numbered item as a ticket with owner, test steps, and rollback plan.

  1. Inventory & classification
    • Baseline: identify all databases, backup locations, replicas, and columns containing PII/PHI/PAN. Record in a canonical spreadsheet or CMDB. (Outputs: inventory and classification matrix.)
  2. Key management & KMS integration
    • Move key material out of DB server to an HSM or managed KMS (Azure Key Vault, AWS KMS) and record key custodians and rotation policy. Align key lifecycle to NIST SP 800-57 recommendations.
  3. Enable TDE for at-rest protection
    • Enable TDE for all user databases in-scope; back up server certificate/private key to an encrypted, offline vault; test restore on a different host. (Use sys.dm_database_encryption_keys to verify state.)
  4. Apply Always Encrypted for high-risk columns
    • Identify columns where DBAs must not see plaintext (SSN, patient identifiers); choose deterministic vs randomized per query needs; store Column Master Keys in Key Vault/HSM; document app changes and test parameterized queries.
  5. Enforce TLS for all client connections
    • Upgrade drivers where required, enforce Force Encryption after a staged rollout, and document certificate lifecycle and inventory per PCI expectations. Validate using packet captures or client connection logs.
  6. Implement least privilege RBAC
    • Replace ad-hoc grants with roles; remove users from db_owner/sysadmin unless justified and logged. Automate role membership with AD group sync and entitlement reviews.
  7. Harden surface area
    • Disable unused features (xp_cmdshell, unused endpoints), secure service accounts (gMSA/managed identity), and ensure OS patching and disk encryption for hosts. Document exceptions.
  8. Configure SQL Server Audit & central logging
    • Turn on server and database audits for schema changes, permission changes, failed/successful logins, and accesses to sensitive tables. Ship to SIEM with integrity checks (hashing, WORM where possible).
  9. Row-level security & masking
    • Deploy RLS where multi-tenant or per-user visibility is required; apply Dynamic Data Masking for developer, query tool, and reporting accounts. Test for side-channel leaks and query coverage.
  10. Define incident-runbook & playbooks
    • Create DB-runbook steps for containment (disable account, kill sessions, isolate replicas), forensics (capture logs, DBCC, server snapshots), and legal/regulatory notification templates (GDPR Article 33 checklist; HIPAA forms). Map owners and SLA timelines.
  11. Test & audit
    • Quarterly: backup restore tests; key-rotation drills; a controlled re-encryption run (Always Encrypted) and audit log replay. Annual: external penetration test and compliance assessment (QSA for PCI).
  12. Document and retain evidence
    • Keep configuration exports, key-rotation logs, audit configuration, and entitlement reports in a secure evidence repository for the duration your policies require (match retention to legal/regulatory obligations).

Sample incident-runbook (short form)

  • Detect: SIEM alert — unusual bulk SELECT on dbo.Payments.
  • Triage: flag the affected DB, record time window, snapshot DB and errorlogs, export audit files for window T0..Tn.
  • Contain: disable compromised login(s), revoke tokens, isolate replica if lateral movement suspected.
  • Eradicate: rotate keys if exfiltration likely (coordinate with application teams), rebuild service accounts where needed.
  • Recover: validate integrity of restores, re-enable services under increased monitoring.
  • Report: file notifications per GDPR / HIPAA timelines and log the incident in the breach register.

Sources

Transparent data encryption (TDE) — SQL Server (Microsoft Learn) - Explanation of TDE behavior, key hierarchy, operational considerations (backup certificates, encryption scan), and example enablement commands.

Always Encrypted — SQL Server (Microsoft Learn) - Details on Always Encrypted, deterministic vs randomized encryption, secure enclaves, key storage options, limitations and configuration.

TLS 1.2 support for Microsoft SQL Server (Microsoft Learn) - Guidance on TLS support, client/driver compatibility, registry settings, and enabling encrypted connections.

Create a server audit & database audit specification (Microsoft Learn) - How to configure SQL Server Audit, examples for server and database audit specifications, and permissions required.

Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — GDPR (EUR-Lex) — Article 32: Security of processing - The GDPR text specifying technical measures including pseudonymisation and encryption as part of Article 32.

Guidance on Risk Analysis — HHS (OCR) - HHS OCR guidance explaining HIPAA risk analysis requirements and the link to NIST guidance for sizing safeguards.

PCI Security Standards Council — Document Library - PCI DSS standards, timelines for v4.x, and requirements around encryption, key management, and logging.

NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 — Guidelines for TLS (CSRC/NIST) - NIST guidance on TLS selection and configuration, cipher-suite recommendations, and migration notes.

NIST Revises SP 800-61: Incident Response Recommendations (CSRC/NIST) - NIST’s incident-response lifecycle guidance and the importance of integrated incident management.

Recommendation for Key Management (NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5) - Key-management lifecycle, metadata protection, and best practices for enterprise key custody and rotation.

Row-level security — SQL Server (Microsoft Learn) - Implementation details, predicates, and caveats for RLS.

Dynamic Data Masking — SQL Server (Microsoft Learn) - How DDM works, patterns, and where it should (and shouldn’t) be used.

Server-level roles — SQL Server (Microsoft Learn) - Definitions of fixed server roles and the newer granular server roles, useful for least-privilege design.

SQL Server Audit Action Groups and Actions — Microsoft Learn - The catalog of audit action groups and actions you can enable or filter on when configuring audits.

GDPR Article 33 — Notification of a personal data breach (legislation excerpt) - Text and timing requirements for notifying supervisory authorities (the 72-hour expectation).

HHS — Breach Notification & Change Healthcare FAQ (HHS OCR) - HHS OCR guidance on breach reporting timelines for HIPAA covered entities and business associates and reporting mechanisms.

Apply the layered approach above as a program: inventory → design → implement → evidence → test, and treat key custody, audit configuration, and entitlement reviews as the non-negotiable artifacts your compliance package must contain.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on one GPU: what the 24 GB covers, the drafter flag and the llama.cpp trap
description:
NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74B agent model that reads text and images. Only about 9B of its parameters (the numbers a model learns in training) work on each token, and a token is roughly a piece of a word. Most are stored at about 2 bits each, so the file is 22.0 GB.

We served it on one A40, a 48 GB data-center card on our cloud, with llama.cpp, the open-source program most people use to run models on one machine. The image reader was on, and so was the drafter, a small helper model that speeds up writing. It used about 27 GB. For one user it wrote 136 tokens a second with the drafter and 70 without.

Three choices matter more than the model: what the 24 GB covers, which llama.cpp you compile, and when the drafter pays off. Every figure sits in our Nemotron 3.5 Bolt deployment write-up with the full measurements.

The 24 GB is a text-only budget for one user

NVIDIA's sum comes to 23.83 GB. That is 22.01 GB for the parameters, 0.87 GB of working memory for roughly 128,000 tokens of conversation, and 0.96 GB for the drafter. The image reader, another 1.68 GB, is deliberately outside the sum.

Two things eat into that margin. First, the unit: a card sold as 24 GB has 24 GiB. Read NVIDIA's figure as decimal and roughly 1.9 GB stays free; read it as GiB and only about 0.2 does. Second, the drafter took close to 2.4 GB on our A40, not 0.96. So a fit on a real 24 GB card stays unproven: we never put Bolt on one.

The recipes NVIDIA publishes for llama.cpp include the image reader, and the smallest of them asks for a 32 GB card. Our 27 GB (25.2 GiB), with the quick-start 98,304 tokens of conversation, counts the image reader too, so it does not check NVIDIA's text-only number. Measure your own server with the drafter on and off, in the unit your card is sold in.

Build the right llama.cpp, and build it in parallel

Bolt needs llama.cpp code from release day, 15 October. Kartik Gulia, an NVIDIA engineer, added the model and its image reader to llama.cpp, and ggerganov merged the change in llama.cpp pull request #30520 that same day. Older builds refuse the file.

We hit exactly that. Our worker (the agent that sets up each GPU machine for InferenceKey) pins a llama.cpp release 1,920 commits older than the merge, so we set v0.7.0 by hand.

Then compiling ate the clock. A fresh machine took 764.8 seconds from request to ready, and 705 of those went into building llama.cpp on 9 CPU cores. Our worker calls cmake --build with no parallel jobs unless CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL is set. Even with 12 jobs set by hand, the build was 92% of the wait. On a 31-core machine the same build finished in 2 minutes 41 seconds. A second copy on an already built machine was ready in 15.6 seconds. If first starts matter, count CPU cores, not only the GPU.

The drafter is a server flag, not a request option

Bolt comes with the LiLiCorr drafter, about 1.1B parameters in a 1.0 GB file. The drafter proposes several tokens ahead, Bolt verifies the whole batch in a single step, accepts the run up to its first mismatch and writes that token itself. You turn it on when the server starts:

--spec-draft-hf nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-LiLiCorr-GGUF \
--spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-ngl 999

On short and medium prompts it about doubled the speed: over 25 requests the median was 136 tokens a second against 70, with a floor of 110, and 70% of the drafted tokens were accepted. The per-prompt speed and acceptance table shows where it gains most.

Long documents flip the result: the drafter slows prompt reading by about a quarter. A question over a 25,000-token document took 17.5 seconds without the drafter and 21.5 seconds with it. And v0.7.0 has the per-request drafter control compiled out, so the choice is made once per server. Mixed traffic? Benchmark both shapes first.

Two traps outside the model

  • A card can report fine and still be useless. Our first two machines had RTX 5090 cards. nvidia-smi, NVIDIA's status tool, answered, but CUDA, the layer programs use to reach the GPU, failed to start. Our platform still marked the model ready, so we have no 32 GB numbers yet.
  • Hidden reasoning burns time. Bolt thinks before it replies, out of your sight. A one-sentence answer cost 374 tokens of writing time. NVIDIA's model page documents a switch to turn thinking off, and InferenceKey does not forward it yet.

What this does and does not show

The quality numbers are NVIDIA's: Bolt beats Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on most agent benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1: 50.98 against 44.38) and loses on factual recall. NVIDIA's speed table puts it behind Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4. Our side was about 50 requests, one GPU, one request at a time; on a two-tool refund task it called both tools correctly in all 5 runs. We did not test several requests sharing the card, where drafters tend to help less, or vLLM, the data-center server software that is the other route.

NVIDIA built, compressed and released Bolt and its drafter under OpenMDW-1.1, which allows commercial use. Kartik Gulia and ggerganov made llama.cpp able to run it. AI Search's news video pointed us to the family. Our part was wiring it end to end and measuring it. The exact command, per-request timings and worker settings are in the complete Nemotron 3.5 Bolt article on inferencekey.com.

title: Implementing Optical Vertex Distance Compensation in JavaScript (Glasses to Contacts Formula)
description:
When an eyeglass lens sits 10 to 14 mm in front of the cornea (with 12 mm as the standard clinical vertex distance), its effective optical power at the corneal plane differs from the spectacle plane—especially for prescriptions stronger than ±4.00 D.

In this short technical note, we look at how to implement the optical vertex distance equation in JavaScript for both spherical and toric (astigmatism) prescriptions, and how an interactive vertex distance calculator applies 0.25 D step rounding across principal meridians.

The Vertex Compensation Formula

The standard optical vertex formula is:

Fc = Fg / (1 - d * Fg)

Where:

  • Fg is the spectacle power in diopters (D)
  • d is the vertex distance in meters (e.g., 0.012 for 12 mm)
  • Fc is the compensated power at the corneal plane in diopters (D)

Handling Spherical and Toric (CYL) Prescriptions in JS

For a toric prescription (SPH, CYL, Axis), each principal meridian must be vertex-compensated independently before recombining into sphere and cylinder components:

function roundQuarterDiopter(val) {
  return Math.round(val * 4) / 4;
}

function compensateVertex(fg, vertexMm = 12) {
  const d = vertexMm / 1000;
  return fg / (1 - d * fg);
}

function convertGlassesToContacts({ sph, cyl = 0, axis = 0, vertexMm = 12 }) {
  const m1 = compensateVertex(sph, vertexMm);
  const m2 = compensateVertex(sph + cyl, vertexMm);

  const rawSph = m1;
  const rawCyl = m2 - m1;

  return {
    exactSph: Number(rawSph.toFixed(2)),
    exactCyl: Number(rawCyl.toFixed(2)),
    roundedSph: roundQuarterDiopter(rawSph),
    roundedCyl: roundQuarterDiopter(rawCyl),
    axis
  };
}

Live Reference Tool

If you want to test different vertex distances (10–14 mm) or check how to convert glasses prescription to contacts with instant spherical equivalent and toric meridian breakdowns, you can try the live tool at VertexLensCalc.

Note: Theoretical optical vertex calculations are for educational and software reference purposes only and do not replace a physical contact lens fitting by an optometrist or ophthalmologist.

title: Building a Loan Repayment Calculator with JavaScript
description:
A loan calculator is a useful project for learning how to combine mathematics, input validation, and frontend programming.

In this tutorial, we'll implement a monthly repayment function for a loan with a fixed interest rate and regular monthly repayments.

The example is for educational purposes. It does not include every fee, product condition, or circumstance that can affect a real loan.

1. Understand the Formula

For a loan with a positive monthly interest rate, the standard repayment formula is:

[
M = \frac{P r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n-1}
]

Where:

  • (M) is the monthly repayment.
  • (P) is the principal.
  • (r) is the monthly interest rate as a decimal.
  • (n) is the total number of monthly repayments.

For a nominal annual interest rate expressed as a percentage:

[
r = \frac{\text{annual rate}}{100 \times 12}
]

When the interest rate is zero, the principal can simply be divided by the number of repayments.

2. Implement the Function 

function calculateMonthlyRepayment(
  principal,
  annualRatePercent,
  years
) {
  const values = [principal, annualRatePercent, years];

  if (!values.every(Number.isFinite)) {
    throw new Error("Inputs must be finite numbers.");
  }

  if (
    principal <= 0 ||
    annualRatePercent < 0 ||
    years <= 0
  ) {
    throw new Error("Invalid loan inputs.");
  }

  const months = years * 12;

  if (!Number.isInteger(months)) {
    throw new Error("The term must produce whole months.");
  }

  const monthlyRate = annualRatePercent / 100 / 12;

  if (monthlyRate === 0) {
    return principal / months;
  }

  const growth = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, months);

  return (
    principal * monthlyRate * growth / (growth - 1)
  );
}

The function validates its inputs and handles a zero interest rate separately.

3. Try an Example 

const payment = calculateMonthlyRepayment(
  400000,
  6,
  30
);

console.log(payment.toFixed(2));

This example assumes a principal of $400,000, a nominal annual interest rate of 6%, and a 30-year term. The output is an estimated monthly repayment before additional costs.

4. Add Unit Tests

Basic tests help confirm that the function behaves as expected.

console.assert(
  calculateMonthlyRepayment(1200, 0, 1) === 100
);

console.assert(
  calculateMonthlyRepayment(400000, 6, 30) > 0
);

console.assert(
  calculateMonthlyRepayment(400000, 6, 30) < 400000
);

For a real project, use a test framework such as Vitest or Jest and verify results against independently calculated examples.

5. Production Considerations

A production calculator should account for input formatting, currency precision, fees, rate changes, and the actual repayment rules of the relevant loan product.

Also validate empty form fields explicitly. In JavaScript, converting an empty string with Number() produces zero, which can create unexpected behaviour if the form does not distinguish empty input from a genuine zero.

For financial software, make assumptions visible rather than presenting an estimate as a guaranteed repayment amount.

Conclusion

A loan calculator is a practical example of how mathematical logic becomes a working web feature.

By separating the calculation from the user interface and testing edge cases, developers can create code that is easier to understand, maintain, and extend.

title: How We are Future-Proofing our Next.js and Rust Stack for the Post Quantum Era 🚀
description:
Hey Dev.to family! So, Q-Day is creeping up on us, and if you are still relying on legacy encryption like RSA, it might be time to panic just a little bit. Today, let us look at how we're preparing for the Post Quantum Cryptography shift using Rust and Next.js before quantum computers completely break our current security standards.

The countdown to Q-Day is no longer just a theoretical exercise for academics. In 2026, advancements in quantum computing have forced the US government and top FAANG security teams to strictly mandate Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC). Legacy encryption algorithms like RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) are mathematically compromised by Shor's algorithm. If you are building a US based fintech application, healthcare SaaS, or enterprise infrastructure on Next.js, your encryption layers must migrate to NIST approved standards like ML-KEM (formerly Kyber) right now.

Transitioning a live production environment to quantum resistant algorithms is a massive engineering headache. It requires memory safe execution, careful handling of significantly larger cryptographic payloads, and seamless integration between your Rust microservices and Next.js edge deployments.

How do you implement Post Quantum Cryptography in a Rust backend?

Modern US tech stacks utilize Rust for computationally heavy backend services due to its memory safety and fearless concurrency. To implement PQC, engineering teams are dropping legacy OpenSSL wrappers in favor of native Rust implementations of ML-KEM for Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEM) and ML-DSA (Dilithium) for digital signatures.

When a Next.js client initiates a secure session, the Rust backend must negotiate a quantum secure shared secret before any sensitive data is transmitted. Below is a production ready architectural concept using the pqcrypto suite to generate and encapsulate a session key using ML-KEM-768.

use pqcrypto_kyber::kyber768::*;
use std::env;

// 2026 FAANG Standard: ML-KEM (Kyber) for Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation
pub fn establish_quantum_secure_session() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    println!("Initializing PQC Handshake...");

    // 1. Generate a post-quantum keypair on the Rust server
    let (public_key, secret_key) = keypair();

    // 2. The client uses the public key to encapsulate a shared symmetric secret
    // In production, the public key is sent to the Next.js client via a secure API
    let (ciphertext, shared_secret_client) = encapsulate(&public_key);

    // 3. The server decapsulates the ciphertext to derive the exact same shared secret
    let shared_secret_server = decapsulate(&ciphertext, &secret_key);

    // Verify mathematical parity
    assert_eq!(shared_secret_client.as_bytes(), shared_secret_server.as_bytes());

    // The shared secret is now used for AES-256-GCM symmetric encryption
    println!("Post-Quantum secure session established successfully.");
    Ok(())
}

This memory safe execution guarantees that even if state sponsored actors are harvesting your encrypted traffic today, they will not be able to decrypt it when quantum hardware becomes widely available.

How does Post Quantum Cryptography affect Next.js Edge architecture?

The biggest architectural hurdle with PQC is payload size. Quantum resistant public keys and ciphertexts are huge compared to their ECC counterparts. ML-KEM-768 public keys are over 1000 bytes.

When routing these larger cryptographic payloads through Next.js React Server Components and Edge Middleware, you have to optimize your network strategy, or you will completely brick your app.

  • Cookie Size Limits: Standard HTTP headers and cookies will instantly exceed the 4KB browser limit if you attempt to shove PQC signatures directly into JWTs.
  • Stateful Sessions: US engineering teams are moving away from stateless JWTs. Instead, they store the quantum validated session states in a low latency distributed cache like Redis. The Next.js Edge Middleware only handles a lightweight, opaque session ID.
  • Bandwidth Optimization: Ensure your Vercel or Cloudflare Edge functions use aggressive Brotli compression to mitigate the bandwidth overhead of transmitting large PQC ciphertexts during the initial handshake.

What is the impact of PQC migrations on US tech salaries?

The US cybersecurity job market has aggressively segmented. While generalist security analyst roles have contracted, the demand for cryptographic software engineers is surging. Federal compliance frameworks like FedRAMP now require clear roadmaps for PQC integration, forcing every B2B SaaS company to upgrade their infrastructure.

Engineers who can seamlessly bridge Next.js frontend architecture with complex Rust cryptographic backends are commanding massive premiums. FAANG companies and Tier 1 startups are routinely offering total compensation packages exceeding $400k for builders who can audit legacy encryption, implement ML-KEM without breaking API contracts, and optimize edge network performance for larger payloads. Mastering this specific intersection of security and systems engineering makes you indispensable in the 2026 tech economy.

FAQs:

1. What is Post Quantum Cryptography and why is it necessary?
Post Quantum Cryptography involves new mathematical algorithms designed to be secure against both classical and quantum computers. It is necessary because upcoming quantum hardware will easily break legacy encryption standards like RSA and ECC, compromising all historically captured data.

2. How does PQC impact frontend application performance?
PQC algorithms generate much larger public keys and ciphertexts. This increased payload size can cause latency and exceed browser cookie limits, requiring engineers to utilize distributed edge caches (like Redis) rather than bloating stateless JWTs.

3. Why are companies choosing Rust for cryptography in 2026?
Rust provides strict memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector. This prevents common cryptographic vulnerabilities like buffer overflows and memory leaks, which are historically prevalent in C and C++ security libraries.

What do you all think?

Are you actively prepping your stacks for Q-Day, or is it a problem for Future You? Drop your thoughts below, and do not forget to follow me for more US tech market insights!

title: I Replaced Math.random() With CSS. Here Is What Works.
description:
Why I care about this

I build creative sites for a living. Almost every project has some small random detail. Cards that sit a bit crooked. Particles that start at different times. A hue that changes on every load.

For years, that meant the same ten lines of JavaScript. Loop over the elements, call Math.random(), write a CSS variable. It works. But it runs after the HTML loads, it needs a script, and it fights with my server rendering.

On October 20, Google shipped Chrome 156. It includes the CSS random() function. Safari already had it. So I spent a few evenings replacing my JavaScript with plain CSS.

This post is what I learned. What works, what does not, and the one thing that will confuse you if you read older tutorials.

The basic syntax

random() takes a minimum and a maximum. It returns a value between them. You can add a third value, a step, to snap the result to fixed increments.

.card {
  rotate: random(-4deg, 4deg);           /* any angle in the range */
  width: random(200px, 320px, 40px);     /* 200, 240, 280 or 320px */
  animation-delay: random(0s, 2s);
}

Three rules to remember, all from MDN:

  1. Min, max and step must be the same data type. Lengths with lengths, angles with angles. Units can differ (1em and 40vw is fine).
  2. The range is inclusive on both ends.
  3. If max is smaller than min, you get the min value. No error, no warning. It works anywhere CSS accepts a length, angle, time, number, percentage, integer, frequency or resolution. That covers most of what I randomize.

The part that confused me: who shares the value

By default, every random() call is independent. Every element, every property, every position in a shorthand gets its own value. Most of the time that is what you want.

But sometimes you need a square. Width and height must be random, but equal. That is what the optional first argument is for. MDN calls it the <random-key>.

Key Same value across elements? Same value across properties?
auto (default) No No
element-scoped No Yes
property-scoped Yes No
--my-name Yes Yes
--my-name element-scoped No Yes, for calls with that name
fixed 0.5 You pick the seed (0 to 1) Yes

So a set of random squares, each one a different size, looks like this:

.tile {
  width: random(--tile-size element-scoped, 60px, 140px);
  height: random(--tile-size element-scoped, 60px, 140px);
}

Here is the trap. Older articles, including the WebKit announcement and early Frontend Masters tests, use a keyword called element-shared. The spec has moved on. The current names are element-scoped, property-scoped and property-index-scoped. If you copy a snippet from 2025 and nothing happens, check this first.

One more gotcha. A normal custom property does not store a random result. --size: random(1px, 100px) is text substitution, so every var(--size) rolls again. If you want one stored value, register the property with @property. MDN explains this with a short example.

Example 1: a messy stack of cards

This is a pattern I use a lot. A grid of photos or cards that look like they were dropped on a table. Each one tilted and shifted a little.

Here is the JavaScript version I have shipped many times:

const cards = document.querySelectorAll('.card');

function randomBetween(min, max) {
  return Math.random() * (max - min) + min;
}

cards.forEach((card) => {
  card.style.setProperty('--tilt', `${randomBetween(-6, 6)}deg`);
  card.style.setProperty('--shift-x', `${randomBetween(-12, 12)}px`);
  card.style.setProperty('--shift-y', `${randomBetween(-12, 12)}px`);
  card.style.setProperty('--delay', `${randomBetween(0, 0.6)}s`);
});

.card {
  rotate: var(--tilt, 0deg);
  translate: var(--shift-x, 0) var(--shift-y, 0);
  animation: drop 0.5s var(--delay, 0s) both;
}

It works. But the cards render straight, then jump when the script runs. With server rendering you also get a mismatch between server and client values.

Here is the CSS version:

.card {
  rotate: random(-6deg, 6deg);
  translate: random(-12px, 12px) random(-12px, 12px);
  animation: drop 0.5s random(0s, 0.6s) both;
}

No script. No flash. Each card gets its own values because the default key is auto. The two values inside translate are also independent, because auto separates calls by their position in the declaration.

If you add the step argument, you get a more designed feel. Tilts of exactly -6, -3, 0, 3 or 6 degrees look less random and more intentional:

.card {
  rotate: random(-6deg, 6deg, 3deg);
}

Example 2: a palette that changes on every load

Pure random color looks bad. Fast. What I usually want is one random hue for the whole page, and small variations per element. That is where the keys pay off.

.blob {
  /* One hue for the whole page: a named key alone is global */
  --hue: random(--page-hue, 0, 360);

  /* Lightness varies per element, in steps of 10 */
  background: hsl(var(--hue) 70% random(35%, 75%, 10%));

  /* Each blob is a circle of its own size */
  width: random(--blob-size element-scoped, 80px, 240px);
  height: random(--blob-size element-scoped, 80px, 240px);

  /* Scatter them across the hero */
  position: absolute;
  top: random(0%, 90%);
  left: random(0%, 90%);
}

Every load gives you a new mood. But it always looks like one palette, because every blob uses the same --page-hue seed.

The JavaScript version needed one value for the page and one loop for the elements. Something like this:

const hue = Math.floor(Math.random() * 361);
document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--hue', hue);

document.querySelectorAll('.blob').forEach((blob) => {
  const size = 80 + Math.random() * 160;
  const light = 35 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 5) * 10;
  blob.style.setProperty('--size', `${size}px`);
  blob.style.setProperty('--light', `${light}%`);
  blob.style.setProperty('--top', `${Math.random() * 90}%`);
  blob.style.setProperty('--left', `${Math.random() * 90}%`);
});

Ten lines of script turned into a few declarations. For a hero section, I will take that trade every time.

Shipping it today: a fallback that only runs when needed

Firefox does not support random() yet. Smashing Magazine reports positive signals from Mozilla, but no release. So for client work, I treat it as progressive enhancement.

Step one: write a calm default first, then add the random layer inside a feature query. MDN uses order: random(1, 2) as the test, which is a nice trick.

.card {
  rotate: var(--tilt, 0deg);
}

@supports (order: random(1, 2)) {
  .card {
    rotate: random(-6deg, 6deg, 3deg);
  }
}

Step two: if the random effect really matters to the design, add a tiny script that only runs in browsers without support.

const supportsRandom = CSS.supports('order', 'random(1, 2)');

if (!supportsRandom) {
  const steps = [-6, -3, 0, 3, 6];
  document.querySelectorAll('.card').forEach((card) => {
    const tilt = steps[Math.floor(Math.random() * steps.length)];
    card.style.setProperty('--tilt', `${tilt}deg`);
  });
}

Chrome and Safari users get pure CSS. Firefox users get the old behavior. Nobody gets a broken page.

If you want one code path for every browser, CSS-Tricks covered a polyfill that resolves random() with JavaScript. I have not used it in production, so test it before you trust it.

Honest caveats

random() is great. It is not a full replacement for Math.random(). Here is where JavaScript still wins, or where you need to be careful.

You cannot re-roll on demand. The value is picked when styles are computed. There is no "shuffle" button. If a user action should create new values, you still need JavaScript.

Hover states may not change. With the default auto key, the browser builds the seed name from the property and position. So width: random(100px, 200px) on .foo and on .foo:hover share a seed, and nothing changes on hover. MDN shows this case. Use a different named key for the hover rule if you want a new value.

You cannot read the value easily. If your WebGL scene or GSAP timeline needs to know the exact random number, keep it in JavaScript. Syncing CSS randomness into a canvas is more work than it saves.

Contrast is your problem now. A random text color can land on an unreadable value. MDN warns about this directly. Randomize decoration, not readable content, or keep the range tight.

Motion still needs an off switch. Random delays and positions are often used in animation. Wrap that animation in prefers-reduced-motion like any other.

Support is still partial. Chrome 156 and Safari support it. Firefox does not, as of today. MDN still marks it as limited availability.

What to do this week

  1. Open Chrome 156 or Safari and paste the card example into a CodePen. It takes two minutes and you will understand the keys faster than by reading.
  2. Search your codebase for Math.random() used only to set styles. Those are your candidates.
  3. Pick one decorative effect and move it to CSS behind @supports (order: random(1, 2)).
  4. Keep a calm default for Firefox. Add the JavaScript fallback only if the effect is part of the design.
  5. Ignore any snippet that uses element-shared. Translate it to element-scoped or a named key.
  6. Leave anything interactive, readable or synced with canvas in JavaScript.

title: Bun runtime for Vercel Functions now accepts Bun.serve as an entrypoint
description:
The Bun runtime for Vercel Functions now supports Bun.serve() as a function entrypoint, including WebSocket handlers. The server you run locally with Bun deploys as-is, without being wrapped in a framework.

Enable the runtime by setting "bunVersion": "1.x" in vercel.json.

Deploy a routes-based server

Create a server with a routes map in server.ts at the project root.

Accept WebSocket connections

Add a websocket handler and call server.upgrade(request) in fetch to upgrade matching requests. The rest of the server stays the same.

WebSocket connections run on Fluid compute with Active CPU pricing, so you pay only for time spent processing messages, not idle connection time. A connection is pinned to one function instance for its lifetime, and a single instance can handle multiple concurrent connections. Use an external data store to coordinate messages across instances.

Read the documentation to get started.

title: Logistics Spend Caps and Rate Limiting: Why Attribution Breaks First (and What I Measure)
description:
A logistics platform should treat a provider-enforced spend cap and an application rate limiter as two different failure boundaries. The cap can stop eligible billable work only where the upstream account recognizes the cap; the limiter can slow or reject requests only where our application sees them. Neither one, by itself, can tell us which warehouse, route, or customer caused the balance to fall.

Short answer: use the upstream cap as a last-resort account boundary, and use application rate limiting as a controllable traffic boundary. Put attribution in the metering path between them: record the tenant, operation, provider account, request outcome, and chargeable quantity before aggregating. If the prepaid balance runs out unattended, the missing control is usually an identity and reconciliation decision, not another dashboard.

The incident lesson is about identity, not throttling

I carry a pager, so I distrust a green dashboard that cannot answer a basic question: what page fired, and which account paid for the work? In a logistics workload, one provider account may serve several customers. A burst of route estimates can look ordinary at the application edge while the bill is attributed to one shared credential.

The operational constraint changes the design. We need billing attribution to survive retries, delays, rejections, and upstream policy decisions. A request ID is useful for tracing; it is not a billing identity. A customer ID is useful for attribution; it is not proof that the provider charged that customer. Those are separate claims.

The invariant I use is narrow: every billable attempt gets one immutable metering record, and every aggregate can be traced back to it without trusting the caller to report its own charge. The record should carry a tenant identifier, operation name, provider account or credential class, request identifier, measured quantity, and terminal decision. In the HTTP layer, a local limiter can return 429 Too Many Requests as defined by RFC 6585, but that status still says nothing about a provider-side charge.

That distinction is easy to miss.

Can an API hard spend cap replace application rate limiting?

An API hard spend cap belongs to the billing boundary. Its promise is narrow: after the provider evaluates the cap, eligible activity for that account may be prevented or suspended, subject to its enforcement rules. It cannot normally distinguish two internal tenants sharing that account, repair a missing tenant ID, classify a retry, or explain usage that has not reached the usage feed.

Application rate limiting belongs to the request boundary. A token bucket, concurrency limit, or per-tenant quota can protect a service from bursts using identities we control. It cannot know final provider price from request count alone, account for variable work without metering, or stop a worker that bypasses the edge limiter.

The worker path is where the neat diagram usually breaks.

Boundary Can control Cannot prove
Provider spend cap Eligible billable activity after provider evaluation Which internal tenant caused the charge
Application limiter Arrival rate, concurrency, tenant admission Provider billing outcome or final price
Metering and reconciliation Attribution across attempts An upstream decision it never received

This is the useful comparison. Calling any one of these a universal spend control is the failure mode.

How do I preserve attribution when the balance is low?

I separate admission from accounting. Admission asks whether a request may start. Accounting records what happened, including a rejection. A low-balance mode should be explicit and reversible; it should not be inferred from a timeout, because a timeout says the client did not receive a result, not that the provider did no work.

Here is the smallest useful Go shape. It records the local admission decision without pretending local code is the billing authority:

package spendcontrol

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrRateLimited = errors.New("request rejected by local limiter")

type Meter struct {
    TenantID      string
    Operation     string
    ProviderClass string
    RequestID     string
    Quantity      int64
    Decision      string
    ObservedAt    time.Time
}

type Ledger interface {
    Append(context.Context, Meter) error
}

type Admission interface {
    Allow(context.Context, string, string) bool
}

func Admit(ctx context.Context, ledger Ledger, limiter Admission, m Meter) error {
    if !limiter.Allow(ctx, m.TenantID, m.Operation) {
        m.Decision = "rate_limited"
        m.ObservedAt = time.Now().UTC()
        if err := ledger.Append(ctx, m); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return ErrRateLimited
    }
    m.Decision = "admitted"
    m.ObservedAt = time.Now().UTC()
    return ledger.Append(ctx, m)
}

In production I would also record completion, provider response class, retry number, and the usage event used for reconciliation. The ledger needs an idempotency key so a retry cannot create a second billable-looking event. That key should come from stable business identity, not a timestamp that changes on every attempt.

There is a real trade-off. Recording before the provider call gives stronger evidence of intent; recording only after success gives cleaner evidence of completed work. I prefer both states when the operation has material billing impact. For a cheap, strictly idempotent read, one event may be enough.

Why do budget alerts fail as hard caps?

Budget tooling is useful for detection and forecasting, but an alert is not an enforcement boundary. AWS Budgets documents threshold actions, Google Cloud budgets document alerts and programmatic notifications, and Azure Cost Management budgets document alert conditions and actions. Their boundaries and delays differ, so none should be treated as an instantaneous provider-side stop without verifying the contract.

The practical test is simple: does the control reject the next billable operation, at which boundary, and with what delay or eligibility rules? Then ask whether the resulting event can be attributed to one internal tenant without reconstructing identity from a shared key.

These products are useful evidence of the distinction, not interchangeable recommendations. AWS Budgets can feed an action workflow; Google Cloud budgets expose alerting; Azure Cost Management budgets support budget alerts. The limitation is common: budget observation does not automatically create tenant-level billing isolation. A team that needs that isolation must build or obtain a separate metering boundary.

Secrets management matters because credentials define the provider account boundary. OWASP recommends controlled secret lifecycle practices. A rotated key can still represent the same shared account, and a new key does not create tenant-level billing isolation. Credential hygiene reduces exposure; it does not substitute for attribution.

The decision rule I would ship

Use application rate limiting when the immediate risk is burst behavior, queue growth, or disproportionate tenant concurrency. Key it by tenant and operation, and inventory worker paths that bypass the edge.

Use a provider-side hard cap as the last line of defense against unattended account exhaustion. Treat scope and delay as facts to verify, not assumptions inferred from a dashboard.

Use metering and reconciliation when the requirement is accurate billing attribution. Store who requested the work, which provider account was used, what operation ran, what quantity was observed, and how the event was reconciled.

Test a rejected request, a timeout after upstream acceptance, a retry, a shared credential, and a bypass worker. Compare the internal ledger with the provider usage export. The result should remain explainable when the balance is zero.

References

  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • AWS Budgets documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/budgets-managing-costs.html
  • Google Cloud budgets and budget alerts: https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets
  • Microsoft Azure Cost Management budgets: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets
  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585

title: AWS SAP-C03: The Solutions Architect Professional Exam Rewards Architects, Not Memorizers
description:
The associate-level AWS exams test whether you know the services. The professional-level Solutions Architect exam, SAP-C03, tests whether you can think like an architect when the requirements fight each other. Cost against performance. Security against speed. A migration deadline against a system that cannot go down. If you have passed SAA-C03 and are wondering what changes at the professional tier, the honest answer is: almost everything about how you read a question.

What SAP-C03 actually measures

SAP-C03 is built around long, layered scenarios. A question may describe a global company with regulatory constraints in two regions, a legacy data center, an acquisition's AWS account structure, and a budget that has already been cut once. The correct answer is rarely the service you spotted first. It is the combination that satisfies every constraint at once, including the one buried in the third paragraph.

The exam's four domains tell you where to spend your study time:

  • Design solutions for organizational complexity (26%) — multi-account strategy with AWS Organizations, Service Control Policies, consolidated billing, and how teams share services without sharing blast radius.
  • Design for new solutions (29%) — the largest domain. Greenfield architecture: choosing compute, storage, databases, and networking patterns for workloads you are designing from scratch.
  • Continuous improvement for existing solutions (25%) — taking a running system and making it cheaper, faster, more resilient, or more secure without a rewrite.
  • Accelerate workload migration and modernization (20%) — moving real workloads out of data centers, in waves, with rollback plans and minimal downtime.

Notice what is missing from that list: there is no domain called "name the service." Knowing that Amazon S3 exists earns you nothing. Knowing when S3, EFS, FSx, or instance storage is the right answer for a specific access pattern, durability requirement, and cost profile earns you the point.

The mindset shift from associate to professional

Associate questions usually have one obviously wrong answer, one plausible-but-wrong answer, and one right answer. Professional questions give you four answers that would all technically work, and ask which one is best given the constraints. The difference is almost always a trade-off:

  • A solution that is more resilient but doubles the bill fails a cost-constrained scenario.
  • A solution that is faster to build but creates a single point of failure fails a high-availability scenario.
  • A solution that is technically elegant but requires retraining an entire operations team fails a scenario with a two-week deadline.

Train yourself to read every question twice. The first read finds the services. The second read finds the constraints: the budget, the compliance rule, the latency target, the team size, the migration window. Underline the constraints mentally before you look at the options. Candidates who jump to the options first end up choosing the answer that solves the loudest requirement and misses the quiet one that decides the question.

Study the patterns, not the service catalog

The fastest way to prepare is to study architecture patterns until they are reflexes:

Multi-account design. Know when to use separate accounts per environment, per team, or per workload, and how Organizations, SCPs, and IAM roles make that manageable. Understand the difference between a landing zone and a pile of accounts someone created by hand.

Hybrid and migration patterns. Rehost, replatform, refactor — and, just as important, when not to migrate at all. Know how AWS Application Migration Service, Database Migration Service, and storage transfer services fit different workload shapes, and how to sequence migration waves so the business never stops.

Data patterns. When a relational database is right, when DynamoDB's key design matters more than its throughput settings, when caching changes the whole cost equation, and when analytics workloads belong on a lakehouse pattern instead of a transactional store. Professional scenarios love questions where the database choice is the whole question.

Resilience patterns. Multi-AZ versus multi-Region is not a trivia question at this level — it is a cost and complexity decision. Know what active-active, active-passive, and pilot-light actually cost to run, and which failure modes each one survives.

Cost as an architecture constraint. At the associate level, cost optimization is a topic. At the professional level, it is a filter applied to every answer. Practice estimating: what does this design cost per month, and what cheaper design meets the same requirements?

A six-week plan that works

Weeks 1–2: Close the associate gaps. Revisit the services you passed over quickly at associate level: networking (VPC design, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, Route 53 routing policies), identity (IAM boundaries, permission boundaries, cross-account access), and data (storage classes, database engines, replication). If you cannot whiteboard a three-tier VPC from memory, start there.

Weeks 3–4: Scenario drills. Work through long case-study questions daily. For each one, write down the constraints before choosing an answer, then check whether your answer survives all of them. This single habit is worth more than another hundred flashcards.

Weeks 5: Hands-on labs. Build a multi-account organization, migrate a small workload, break something on purpose, and fix it. Professional questions reward people who have watched a design fail in practice, because the wrong answers are usually designs that fail in exactly those ways.

Week 6: Timed practice and review. SAP-C03 gives you 180 minutes for 75 questions — generous on paper, tight when every question is a paragraph. Practice under time pressure, and spend your review time on the questions you got right for the wrong reason, not just the ones you missed.

The mistakes that cost professional candidates the most

First, over-engineering. The most sophisticated answer is not the best answer when the scenario asks for the simplest design that meets the requirements. Second, ignoring the organization: questions about SCPs, account strategy, and governance are a quarter of the exam, and candidates who only studied services walk past them. Third, treating migration as a lift-and-shift exercise — the exam rewards phased plans with validation and rollback, not big-bang cutovers. Fourth, studying services in isolation instead of in combinations, because no professional question is ever about one service.

Bottom line

SAP-C03 does not ask you to know more AWS services than the associate exam does. It asks you to make better decisions with the services you already know, under realistic constraints, at organizational scale. Study the trade-offs, practice reading constraints before options, and build enough hands-on experience that the wrong answers smell wrong. That is what separates an architect from someone who memorized a catalog.

If you are preparing for SAP-C03, working through realistic, scenario-based practice questions is the closest thing to sitting the exam before exam day — the free SAP-C03 practice test at Study4Pass (https://study4pass.com/study-material/amazon/sap-c03) is a solid place to start.

Vercel Agent now works in Slack code channels, a new kind of channel launched today for working with a coding agent. Anyone in the channel can follow the work, give Agent new instructions, and review the code it writes.

Choose Create a code channel from the Slack sidebar, select Vercel as the agent, and describe what you need to get started. You can also ask Agent to create one from an existing channel or thread. It brings that context with it to the new channel.

Use code channels to investigate incidents, write and review code as a team, or manage ongoing work such as dependency upgrades and migrations.

Inside a Vercel Agent code channel:

  • Follow the work: Agent posts relevant deployments, logs, errors, and diffs in the channel as it works.

  • Talk without repeated @Vercel mentions: Agent follows the conversation, recognizes which messages are for it, and continues when the team gives it more work.

  • Review pull requests: Ask Agent for a PR review and it posts its findings in the channel. It can find bugs outside the diff, and explain failing checks and their root causes.

  • Approve every change: Agent is read-only by default and never exceeds the requester's permissions. Before making a change, it drafts a plan and waits for approval. For every action, Vercel records who requested and approved it and what Agent ran.

  • Stop work at any time: The person who created the code channel can cancel an active task.

Vercel Agent in Slack code channels is available in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Add Vercel to Slack, learn about Slack Code, or read the docs.

title: Foreign Key Cascade Deletes: Un-Indexed FKs, Slow Cascades, and Lock Contention in PostgreSQL
description:
Running a DELETE on a parent entity with ON DELETE CASCADE feels like clean relational cleanup. But if any child or grandchild table in the dependency chain lacks an index on its foreign key column, PostgreSQL falls back to full sequential scans on every cascade step, turning a quick delete into a long-running transaction that holds row locks and starves concurrent writes. Here is an architectural deep dive into what actually happens during an un-indexed cascade, and how to build an asynchronous soft-delete purge pipeline.

In multi-tenant relational design, enforcing referential integrity with foreign keys (FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES ... ON DELETE CASCADE) is foundational. But when a high-throughput B2B SaaS platform purges a top-level tenant or bulk-deletes historical entities, cascading deletes can turn into a performance trap, not because PostgreSQL escalates to table locks, but because a missing index on a foreign key column forces a full sequential scan on every cascade step, stretching a quick delete into a long-running, lock-holding transaction.

1. The Mechanics of Un-Indexed Foreign Key Cascades

When an application deletes a parent row (say, a row in tenants), PostgreSQL must find and delete every referencing row in child and grandchild tables (users, invoices, audit_logs, api_tokens, and so on) to satisfy the foreign key constraints.

The Un-Indexed Foreign Key Problem

PostgreSQL automatically indexes primary keys and unique constraints, but it does not create an index on the referencing (child) side of a foreign key. You have to add that index yourself. When it is missing:

  • Sequential Child Scans: To find the child rows that point at the parent being deleted, PostgreSQL has no index to probe, so it runs a full sequential scan of the child table, once per cascade step, repeated down the hierarchy.
  • A Long-Running Transaction, Not a Table Lock: This is the point most write-ups get wrong. PostgreSQL does not escalate row locks to a table-level ShareLock on the child table, and it has no lock-escalation mechanism at all. The cascade holds the ordinary RowExclusiveLock on each table it writes, exactly as any DELETE does, and RowExclusiveLock does not conflict with other writers. What actually hurts is duration: the sequential scans make the deleting transaction run for seconds, and for that whole time it holds row locks on every row it is deleting and FOR KEY SHARE locks on the parent rows it touches.
  • Contention and Deadlock Risk: A transaction that stays open for seconds while touching millions of rows is the real hazard. Concurrent statements that try to update or delete any of those same rows block until it finishes; the long transaction holds back VACUUM and inflates bloat; and the more rows and tables one transaction locks, the higher the chance of a lock-ordering deadlock with other transactions. The symptom looks like a sitewide stall, but the cause is a slow transaction holding many row locks, not a single table-level lock.

2. Measuring the Cost

Consider a standard multi-tenant schema whose tenants table cascades down three tiers, with no indexes on the foreign key columns:

-- Failure case: foreign keys with no supporting index
CREATE TABLE tenants (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE users (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id UUID REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, -- INDEX MISSING
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE user_activity_logs (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,     -- INDEX MISSING
    action VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

A single DELETE FROM tenants WHERE id = '...' forces PostgreSQL to:

  1. Delete the matching tenants row.
  2. Sequentially scan users to find rows with that tenant_id, and delete them.
  3. For each deleted user, sequentially scan user_activity_logs to find and delete that user's rows.

On a PostgreSQL 16 test with 2,000 users and 200,000 activity-log rows, deleting one tenant with no FK indexes took about 2.4 seconds. After adding a B-tree index on each foreign key column, the identical delete took about 32 milliseconds, roughly 70x faster. Scale the log table to tens of millions of rows and the un-indexed version runs long enough to become a visible production incident: the deleting transaction sits open, holding row locks and blocking any concurrent write that touches the same rows.

3. Production Diagnostics: Finding Un-Indexed Foreign Keys

Run this catalog query to list every foreign key whose referencing columns are not covered by the leading columns of some index. (A naive version that compares indkey::text to conkey::text does not work: an index prints its columns as 1 while a constraint prints {2}, so the string match silently flags every key. The version below compares them as arrays.)

-- Detect foreign keys with no supporting index (PostgreSQL)
SELECT
    c.conrelid::regclass            AS child_table,
    c.conname                       AS foreign_key_name,
    pg_get_constraintdef(c.oid)     AS constraint_definition
FROM pg_constraint c
WHERE c.contype = 'f'
  AND c.connamespace NOT IN (
      'pg_catalog'::regnamespace,
      'information_schema'::regnamespace
  )
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM pg_index i
      WHERE i.indrelid = c.conrelid
        AND i.indpred IS NULL  -- a partial index can't back the FK
        -- the FK columns must be the leading columns of the index, in order
        AND (i.indkey::smallint[])[0:cardinality(c.conkey) - 1] = c.conkey
  )
ORDER BY child_table;

This query is read-only and safe to run on a production primary.

4. Fixes: Index Every Foreign Key, and Purge Asynchronously

Step 1: Add a B-Tree Index on Every Foreign Key, CONCURRENTLY

Give every foreign key column a supporting index so cascade lookups use an index scan instead of a sequential scan. Build them with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so the build does not take a blocking lock on a live table. (CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, and on failure leaves an INVALID index you drop and recreate.)

-- Index the referencing columns so CASCADE uses index scans
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_tenant_id
    ON users (tenant_id);

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_user_activity_logs_user_id
    ON user_activity_logs (user_id);

Step 2: Replace Synchronous Hard Deletes with Soft-Delete + Batched Purge

Even with indexes, deleting millions of rows in one statement inside a user-facing request is a bad idea: it is one long transaction holding many locks. Mark the tenant deleted instantly, then purge in small, committed batches from a background worker.

// PRODUCTION PATTERN: Soft-delete then batched purge (TypeScript)
import { Pool } from 'pg';

export class TenantLifecycleManager {
  private db: Pool;

  constructor(pool: Pool) {
    this.db = pool;
  }

  /**
   * Marks the tenant deleted in a single fast indexed UPDATE,
   * then hands the heavy work to a background purge job.
   */
  async softDeleteTenant(tenantId: string): Promise {
    await this.db.query(
      `UPDATE tenants
          SET deleted_at = now(),
              status     = 'PENDING_PURGE'
        WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`,
      [tenantId]
    );
    await this.enqueueBackgroundPurgeJob(tenantId);
  }

  /**
   * Background worker: delete grandchild rows in small, independently
   * committed batches so no single transaction holds locks for long.
   * Purge order is bottom-up: grandchildren, then children, then the tenant.
   */
  async purgeActivityLogs(tenantId: string, batchSize = 1000): Promise {
    let deleted = 0;
    do {
      // Each batch is its own transaction (one statement = one commit here).
      const result = await this.db.query(
        `WITH target AS (
            SELECT l.id
              FROM user_activity_logs l
              JOIN users u ON u.id = l.user_id
             WHERE u.tenant_id = $1
             LIMIT $2
             FOR UPDATE OF l SKIP LOCKED
         )
         DELETE FROM user_activity_logs
          WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM target)`,
        [tenantId, batchSize]
      );
      deleted = result.rowCount ?? 0;

      // Breathe between batches so normal traffic keeps moving.
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
    } while (deleted > 0);
  }

  private async enqueueBackgroundPurgeJob(tenantId: string): Promise {
    // Push onto your job queue (BullMQ, pgmq, SQS, etc.)
  }
}

Run the same batched pattern for users after the logs are gone, then delete the tenants row last. Because each batch commits on its own, locks are released continuously instead of being held for the whole purge.

5. Executive Summary & Systems Rules

  • Index every foreign key column: PostgreSQL does not do it for you. Without an index, each cascade step is a full sequential scan, which is what turns a fast delete into a long, lock-holding transaction.
  • It's duration, not lock escalation: PostgreSQL holds ordinary RowExclusiveLock during a cascade and never escalates to a table lock. The contention comes from one slow transaction holding many row locks, so the fix is to make the work fast and short.
  • Don't hard-delete large trees synchronously: Soft-delete with deleted_at, then purge in small committed batches from a background worker, using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so the purge yields to live traffic.
