title: What Is Google's ASN? Why the Answer Is a List
description:
Google's main ASN is AS15169. That's one Google ASN out of 21 that ARIN lists under three separate Google org IDs, and Amazon and Microsoft are built the same way: one famous number, then a long tail of ASNs split by customer type, legal entity, and acquisition.

So if you're grouping log traffic, writing a WAF rule, or deciding whether a request "came from Google," one number won't cover it, and lumping them all together is worse. This post skips the basics. For those (what an AS is, how BGP uses it, who hands them out), see this guide to autonomous system numbers.

TL;DR

  • AS15169 is Google's primary ASN, but it is not a reliable google-services classifier by itself. AS396982 and AS19527 are explicitly associated with Google Cloud customer traffic, but security policy should still classify the individual prefix using Google's published service, Cloud, or crawler range files.
  • An AS is a routing policy, not a company. A company with five routing policies ends up with five ASNs.
  • The AWS ASNs to know are AS16509 and AS14618, plus AS8987 for GovCloud (US) and AS214101 for the European Sovereign Cloud.
  • Microsoft's AS8075 is the last number in a block of eight, AS8068 to AS8075, registered in 1997.
  • Group twice: by parent company for reporting, by function for security policy. Then check who's behind the prefix, because the ASN doesn't always tell you. "Google" in a traffic report is at least three different things: Google's own services, strangers renting Google Cloud, and Google Fiber's home subscribers. They all roll up to the same parent. Treat them as one bucket on a dashboard if you like. Never treat them as one bucket in a firewall rule.

Google ASN list, sorted by job

Google LLC's primary ASN is AS15169, registered with ARIN in March 2000. It carries Google's own services, including the Googlebot crawler. It isn't the only one: Google's own PeeringDB record says Google manages seven ASNs, and ARIN's registry shows more than that. These are the ones you're most likely to meet in logs:

ASN Registry name Registered to What it's for
AS15169 GOOGLE Google LLC (ARIN) Google's primary network; use prefix-level lists to distinguish services, crawlers, Cloud ranges and third-party space
AS396982 GOOGLE-CLOUD-PLATFORM Google LLC (ARIN, Cloud org ID) Google Cloud customer workloads
AS19527 GOOGLE-2 Google LLC (ARIN, Cloud org ID) Google Cloud customers
AS16550 GOOGLE-PRIVATE-CLOUD Google LLC (ARIN, Cloud org ID) Private connectivity, 9 IPv4 routes
AS36040 YOUTUBE Google LLC (ARIN) YouTube, registered in 2005
AS43515 YOUTUBE Google Ireland Limited (RIPE) Google's Irish legal entity
AS139070 GOOGLE-AS-AP Google Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. (APNIC) Google's Singapore legal entity
AS16591 GOOGLE-FIBER Google Fiber Inc. (ARIN) Residential ISP

Is Google Cloud on AS15169? Mostly not. The Google Cloud ASN you'll meet most is AS396982, and ARIN's record for it says so in plain words: "This ASN is used for Google Cloud Platform." That split between Google's own network and the network it rents out is the one that matters most, and the one ASN lookup pages tend to flatten into a single "Google" label.

Which list is right, PeeringDB's seven or ARIN's 21? Both. They answer different questions, which is the whole problem.

Why one company ends up with multiple ASNs

An AS is a routing policy, not a company

RFC 1930, the 1996 best-practice document for AS numbers, defines an AS as a group of prefixes with "a SINGLE and CLEARLY DEFINED routing policy." Section 4 even names the mistake of using an AS "as a convenient way of grouping together a set of prefixes which belong under the same administrative umbrella."

So the registry was never built to map ASNs to companies. A company gets another ASN whenever part of its network needs to behave differently on the internet, and a company the size of Google has a lot of parts that behave differently.

Customer traffic gets its own number

This is the reason I'd care about most if I ran a firewall. AS15169 sits under an ARIN org ID called GOGL. AS396982 and AS19527 sit under a different one, GOOGL-2, also named "Google LLC," and the AS19527 record carries a comment: "The IP addresses under this Org-ID are in use by Google Cloud customers." The comment then sends abuse complaints to Google Cloud's reporting form.

GOOGL-2 holds 11 ASNs, with names like GCP-ENTERPRISE-USER-TRAFFIC and G-CLOUD-AGENT-TRAFFIC. When someone's rented VM hammers your login page, the complaint path leads to the Cloud abuse desk, not to the people running Search.

My read, not Google's stated reason: it also keeps the reputation of Google's own address space apart from whatever tenants do with theirs. Either way, the line between "Google" and "someone on Google" is already drawn in the registry.

Legal entities live in different registries

ASNs belong to legal entities, and legal entities register with their regional registry. AS43515 is registered to Google Ireland Limited at RIPE. AS139070 belongs to Google Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. at APNIC. Amazon's European Sovereign Cloud runs AS214101 under Amazon Data Services European Sovereign Cloud GmbH, also at RIPE. Three registries, a different spelling in each, one parent.

Regulated and private networks

Some networks exist to be kept apart. AWS's BYOIP documentation has customers check their route authorizations against AS16509 and AS14618, then against AS8987 for GovCloud (US), and AS16509 plus AS214101 for the European Sovereign Cloud. A government region on its own ASN is much easier to reason about than one hidden inside AS16509.

Other ASNs exist for private links. Microsoft runs ExpressRoute, its private-connection product, on AS12076, and its peering policy tells every peer not to accept routes from AS12076 "under any circumstances." Google's AS16550 is named GOOGLE-PRIVATE-CLOUD and announces just nine IPv4 routes.

Acquisitions keep their numbers, or get folded in

AS36040 is named YOUTUBE and was registered in August 2005, before Google bought YouTube. It now sits under Google LLC. Microsoft's main ARIN org ID, MSFT, holds 42 ASN records, and the names read like an M&A history: NUANCE-BURLINGTON, PHONEFACTOR-01, ASN-YAMMER, FAST-SEARCH-AND-TRANSFER-INC, MS-DANGER.

Not everything gets folded in. GitHub's AS36459 is still registered to GitHub, Inc., and LinkedIn's AS14413 to LinkedIn Corporation. It cuts the other way too: ARIN still files AS19425, named WAYMO, under Google LLC's GOGL org ID, even though Waymo runs as its own Alphabet company. Registry records lag the org chart, sometimes by years.

How Google, Amazon, and Microsoft lay it out

Google splits by who's on the other end

Put the registry records side by side and Google's layout jumps out. ARIN holds Google LLC under three org IDs: GOGL with 9 ASNs including AS15169, GOOGL-2 with the 11 Cloud ASNs, and GOOGL, spelled "Google, LLC" with a comma, holding AS36492 (GOOGLEWIFI). Add Google Ireland at RIPE, Google Asia Pacific at APNIC, and Google Fiber Inc., and one parent has six registrant records under five spellings.

GOOGL-2 is explicitly marked in ARIN as address space used by Google Cloud customers. GOGL is Google's older organization record, but an ASN under GOGL is not a service-level trust boundary. Prefix-level data is still needed before an address is treated as a Google-operated service.

Amazon runs one giant ASN and a few specialists

Amazon's main ASN is AS16509 (AMAZON-02), with AS14618 (AMAZON-AES) as the other big one. There's no single AWS ASN to allowlist. On October 29, 2026, AS16509 announced 19,751 IPv4 routes against 1,529 for AS14618, roughly 13 to 1 (route counts from ipgeolocation.io's ASN endpoint).

The two big ones sit under different ARIN org IDs, AMAZON-4 and AMAZO-4, both named "Amazon.com, Inc." AMAZO-4 also holds AS21664, named AMZN-BYOASN. GovCloud's AS8987 is registered to a third name, Amazon Technologies Inc., with aws.amazon.com as its domain. The oldest of the lot, AS7224 (AMAZON-AS), dates to October 1996 and announces 27 IPv4 routes.

Neither big number separates Amazon's own services from its customers' instances. An allowlist built on these Amazon ASN numbers admits anyone who can launch an EC2 instance.

Microsoft: one 1997 block and a long tail

The Microsoft ASN you'll see in logs and peering docs is AS8075, the one Microsoft names first in its peering policy. ARIN doesn't store it as a standalone record. AS8075 is the last number in one registration covering AS8068 through AS8075, dated March 31, 1997 and named MICROSOFT-CORP-MSN-AS-BLOCK.

The policy points to an IRR as-set, AS-MICROSOFT, for the full list of ASNs Microsoft manages, and says ASNs that customers bring through its BYOASN product get added to that set. The registry view sprawls further: those 42 MSFT records, plus GitHub and LinkedIn under their own names. One more line from the same policy matters later: prefixes that customers bring through BYOIP "are all properly registered as AS8075."

Same question, two sources per company:

Company What the operator publishes What ARIN shows
Google 7 ASNs in its PeeringDB record 21 ASN records under GOGL, GOOGL-2 and GOOGL, plus RIPE and APNIC entities
Amazon 4 ASNs in the BYOIP docs: 16509, 14618, 8987, 214101 AMAZON-4 and AMAZO-4, plus Amazon Technologies Inc.
Microsoft AS8075 and the AS-MICROSOFT as-set; AS12076 for ExpressRoute 42 ASN records under MSFT

Neither column is wrong. The operator lists what it routes and wants you to peer with. The registry lists everything the legal entity has ever registered and not returned.

How to group IP traffic by organization

Name matching breaks on the first comma

The obvious approach is to group on the ASN's organization string. It falls apart fast. ARIN has Google as both "Google LLC" and "Google, LLC". RIPE adds "Google Ireland Limited". Amazon shows up as "Amazon.com, Inc.", "Amazon Technologies Inc." and "Amazon Data Services European Sovereign Cloud GmbH", and the company record on one AWS address I looked up, 3.80.0.1, read "Amazon Data Services Northern Virginia."

Fuzzy matching catches some of these and quietly invents matches you didn't want. Pick a key that doesn't change spelling.

Pick a key that survives

The ASN's registered domain is the first thing I'd try. Seven of the eight Google ASNs in the table above came back with google.com as their domain; Google Fiber came back with gfiber.com. Amazon needs three: amazon.com, aws.amazon.com and aws.eu. A short alias map covers all three companies.

If you need coverage beyond the big three, use a curated AS-to-organization mapping. CAIDA's AS2Org dataset maps ASNs to organizations from quarterly WHOIS dumps of all five RIRs, with snapshots back to October 2009. The newer ASINT project adds PeeringDB, company websites and merger records, and groups 111,470 ASNs into 81,233 organization families. Both are research datasets, so check how fresh they are before a production job depends on them.

For the ASNs that actually show up in your logs, keep a short list you've checked against the registry by hand. That's what the script below does.

Group twice: parent for reporting, function for policy

Here's the position I'll defend: one "Google" row is fine for a monthly traffic report and wrong for anything that allows or blocks. Googlebot crawling your docs and a scraper on a rented Compute Engine VM both roll up to Google LLC. They should not share a rule.

The ASN type field won't split them for you. AS15169 and AS396982 both come back as HOSTING (that field is still useful for other jobs; I covered them in classifying ASNs by type). The function often has to come from the prefix rather than the ASN. Google publishes the required source data: subtract cloud.json from goog.json to derive the ranges used by Google's own APIs and services, and use Google's separate crawler files when crawler identity matters. Treat the ASN role map below as a fallback, not as a security allowlist.

Keep two columns, then. parent holds google, amazon or microsoft. role holds google-services, cloud-tenants, isp, aws or mixed. Report on the first. Write policy on the second.

Check who's behind the prefix

The ASN tells you who announces a prefix. It doesn't always tell you who uses it. 57.140.0.0/16 is an ARIN direct allocation to Menlo Security, Inc., and 57.140.216.0/24 is announced by AS15169. Look up 57.140.216.1 and the ASN says Google, while the company using the range is Menlo Security:

{
  "ip": "57.140.216.1",
  "asn": {
    "as_number": "AS15169",
    "organization": "Google LLC",
    "country": "US",
    "type": "HOSTING",
    "domain": "google.com",
    "date_allocated": "2000-03-30",
    "rir": "ARIN"
  },
  "company": {
    "name": "Menlo Security, Inc.",
    "type": "BUSINESS",
    "domain": "menlosecurity.com"
  }
}

That's the /v3/ipgeo response with fields=asn,company. Drop the parameter and you also get location, network, time zone and currency for the same IP.

This is third-party address space announced through Google's ASN. It is consistent with BYOIP or another delegated routing arrangement, but the registry and BGP records alone do not prove the commercial mechanism. Microsoft and AWS explicitly document BYOIP under their ASNs, so the same separation between route origin and address holder matters there too. If your rule says "trust AS15169," you just trusted a security vendor's egress range as well.

The script below does both groupings and flags prefixes whose registered company differs from the mapped provider parent. Treat that as an external-prefix signal that may indicate BYOIP, not as proof by itself. I'm using ipgeolocation.io's bulk endpoint because each row carries the ASN registrant (asn) and the company using the prefix (company) side by side, which is exactly the pair the BYOIP check needs. ipinfo, MaxMind GeoIP2 and IP2Location expose ASN data too; whichever you use, make sure it keeps those two apart.

One trade-off up front: this bulk script requires a paid plan. The bulk endpoint, asn.domain, and company enrichment are paid features. A free single-IP /v3/ipgeo lookup still returns as_number, organization, and country, which is enough to build a basic ASN map, but it cannot run this bulk workflow or perform the external-prefix comparison.

import os
import sys
from collections import Counter

import requests

API_KEY = os.environ.get("IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY")
BULK_URL = "https://api.ipgeolocation.io/v3/ipgeo-bulk"
BATCH_SIZE = 50_000  # documented per-request maximum

# ASNs whose job the registry or the operator states in writing.
# Checked against ARIN and PeeringDB on 2026-10-29. Re-check every quarter.
ASN_ROLE = {
    "AS15169": ("google", "mixed"),  # resolve service, Cloud and crawler roles by prefix
    "AS36040": ("google", "google-services"),  # registered as YOUTUBE
    "AS396982": ("google", "cloud-tenants"),   # ARIN: "used for Google Cloud Platform"
    "AS19527": ("google", "cloud-tenants"),    # ARIN: "in use by Google Cloud customers"
    "AS16591": ("google", "isp"),              # Google Fiber
    "AS16509": ("amazon", "aws"),
    "AS14618": ("amazon", "aws"),
    "AS8075": ("microsoft", "mixed"),          # BYOIP tenants are registered here too
}

# Registrant domains that roll up to one parent. Extend as you find more.
DOMAIN_PARENT = {
    "google.com": "google", "gfiber.com": "google",
    "amazon.com": "amazon", "aws.amazon.com": "amazon", "aws.eu": "amazon",
    "microsoft.com": "microsoft", "github.com": "microsoft",
    "linkedin.com": "microsoft",
}


def parent_of(domain):
    return DOMAIN_PARENT.get(domain, domain)

ASN_ROLE is the hand-checked list from the previous section, and DOMAIN_PARENT is the alias map. I left AS8075 as mixed on purpose: Microsoft's own policy says BYOIP customers are registered there, so even before you ask what Microsoft runs on it, you know some of it isn't Microsoft.

def lookup(ips):
    if not API_KEY:
        sys.exit("Set IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY first.")
    try:
        resp = requests.post(
            BULK_URL,
            params={"apiKey": API_KEY, "fields": "asn,company"},
            json={"ips": ips},
            timeout=(3, 30),  # connect fast; big batches need read time
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()
    except requests.HTTPError as exc:
        # Don't print exc itself: its message contains the URL, and the URL contains your key.
        sys.exit(f"Bulk lookup failed: HTTP {exc.response.status_code}")
    except (requests.RequestException, ValueError) as exc:
        # A report built on half the data is worse than no report.
        sys.exit(f"Bulk lookup failed: {type(exc).__name__}")

The error handler prints the status code and the exception type, never the exception itself. requests puts the full URL in its error messages, and this URL carries your API key, so a plain print(exc) ships the key straight into your logs. Exiting on failure is deliberate too: for a reporting job, a partial count is worse than no count.

def classify(row):
    asn = row.get("asn") or {}
    company = row.get("company") or {}
    number = asn.get("as_number", "unknown")
    asn_domain = asn.get("domain", "")
    fallback_parent = parent_of(asn_domain) or asn.get("organization", "unknown")
    parent, role = ASN_ROLE.get(number, (fallback_parent, "unclassified"))

# The prefix registrant differs from the mapped provider parent.
# This may be BYOIP or another delegated routing arrangement, so label
# the observable condition rather than claiming the contract behind it.
tenant = company.get("domain", "")
if number in ASN_ROLE and tenant and parent_of(tenant) != parent:
    role = f"external-prefix:{company.get('name') or tenant}"
    return parent, role, number


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ips = [line.strip() for line in sys.stdin if line.strip()]
    rows = []
    for start in range(0, len(ips), BATCH_SIZE):
        rows.extend(lookup(ips[start:start + BATCH_SIZE]))

    by_parent, by_role = Counter(), Counter()
    for row in rows:
        if "message" in row:  # bogon, private, or malformed input
            print(f"skipped: {row['message']}", file=sys.stderr)
            continue
        parent, role, number = classify(row)
        by_parent[parent] += 1
        by_role[(parent, role, number)] += 1

    print("By parent:", dict(by_parent))
    for (parent, role, number), count in by_role.most_common():
        print(f"{parent:<10} {role:<32} {number:<9} {count}")

A free-plan key cannot run this script because /v3/ipgeo-bulk is paid-only. If you adapt it to make individual /v3/ipgeo calls on the free plan, unmapped ASNs can fall back to the organization string, but asn.domain and company will be unavailable and the external-prefix check cannot run. The bulk endpoint returns a message object for bogon or malformed input instead of failing the batch, which is why the loop skips those rows rather than crashing.

Feed it a list of IPs on stdin:

printf '%s\n' 8.8.8.8 66.249.66.1 34.140.0.10 57.140.216.1 3.80.0.1 20.42.65.92 10.0.0.1 \
  | python3 group_by_org.py

skipped: '10.0.0.1' is a bogon IP address.
By parent: {'google': 4, 'amazon': 1, 'microsoft': 1}
google     mixed                            AS15169   2
google     cloud-tenants                    AS396982  1
google     external-prefix:Menlo Security, Inc. AS15169   1
amazon     aws                              AS14618   1
microsoft  mixed                            AS8075    1

Four of the six public IPs roll up to Google, and the role column splits them three ways. 34.140.0.10 sits in a range Google lists in cloud.json, and its company record still reads "Google LLC". The company field names whoever registered the range, not the Cloud tenant, which is why the role has to come from the ASN.

A few extra notes

Sibling ASNs set off false alarms. BGP monitors flag a route when the origin ASN doesn't match the prefix's ROA, and plenty of those turn out to be a company moving a prefix between its own ASNs. The ASINT team reviewed 17,282 BGP anomaly alerts from January 2023 to July 2024 and marked 1,621 of them, about 9.4%, as likely intra-organization. An org map cuts that noise.

Refresh the map at least quarterly, the cadence CAIDA uses for AS2Org. Registry records outlive the networks behind them: Twitch's AS46489 is still registered to Twitch Interactive Inc. and announced zero routes when I checked.

Don't verify Googlebot by ASN alone. An AS15169 match is a good hint, but Google's own method is a reverse DNS lookup plus a forward confirm, or a match against its published crawler ranges. 66.249.66.1 in the run above is the example address from that page.

If you need to see what a single ASN connects to rather than who owns it, routes and neighbors are a separate pivot. I walked through that in the post on routes, upstreams, and downstreams.

Start with the ASNs that actually show up in your logs, check each one against its registry record once, and write its role down next to it. Re-run that check every quarter. Google, Amazon and Microsoft will keep adding numbers, and not every new one will come with a comment as helpful as GOOGL-2's.

title: Workload Identity Federation: Call Vertex AI from AWS Without Service Account Keys
description:
TL;DR

  • Workload identity federation lets a workload on AWS prove its identity to Google Cloud with its IAM role and receive a short-lived GCP token, so no service account key file is stored anywhere.
  • Bifrost v2.3.0 adds aws_workload_identity to Vertex AI keys: it signs an STS GetCallerIdentity request with the workload's AWS credentials and exchanges it at Google's Security Token Service.
  • On the GCP side you create a workload identity pool with an AWS provider, restrict it to the Bifrost role, and grant Vertex AI access directly or through an impersonated service account.
  • On AWS you attach the role with IRSA, EKS Pod Identity, an ECS task role, or an EC2 instance profile, and keep static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID values out of the pod.

Workload identity federation is a Google Cloud IAM feature that lets workloads running outside Google Cloud exchange their own identity, such as an AWS IAM role, for short-lived Google credentials instead of using a service account key. Bifrost, the open-source AI gateway built in Go, now supports this exchange natively for Vertex AI: a gateway running on EKS, ECS, or EC2 can call Gemini and Claude models on Vertex using only the IAM role attached to it. This tutorial walks through the GCP setup, the AWS role, the Bifrost key, and the checks that confirm which identity reached Vertex.

What workload identity federation is

A service account key is a long-lived secret: a JSON file that grants whoever holds it the account's permissions until someone rotates or deletes it. Workload identity federation removes that file. Google Cloud trusts an external identity provider (AWS, Azure, or an OIDC or SAML provider), and the external workload presents proof of its identity to Google's Security Token Service, which returns a short-lived access token.

For AWS, the proof is a signed GetCallerIdentity request. The workload signs the request with its AWS credentials but does not send it to AWS; Google verifies the signature and reads the caller's ARN from it. Google documents the model in its guide to federation with other clouds.

Service account key Workload identity federation
Secret stored on AWS JSON key file in a secret store or pod None
Credential lifetime Until rotated or deleted Short-lived tokens, refreshed automatically
Rotation Manual, per key Not needed
Who can use it Anyone holding the file Only workloads with the trusted AWS role
Audit identity The service account The AWS role, or the service account with the role recorded as delegate

For a gateway that holds credentials for every model provider, removing one long-lived secret matters. The AI security resource page covers why credential sprawl is a common risk in AI stacks, and the non-human identity guide explains how machine identities like this one should be managed.

Why use it for Vertex AI calls from AWS

Many teams run their applications on AWS but want models that Vertex AI serves, such as Gemini or Claude through Google's regions and billing. Before this release, a Bifrost gateway on AWS reached Vertex with a service account JSON key. That key had to be created, stored in AWS Secrets Manager or a Kubernetes secret, mounted into the pod, and rotated on a schedule.

With aws_workload_identity, the Bifrost pod uses the IAM role it already has. Nothing Google-issued is stored in AWS, and revoking access is a matter of changing the GCP IAM binding or the pool's attribute condition. The rest of the gateway works as before: virtual keys, routing rules, fallbacks, and request logs apply to Vertex traffic like any other provider.

If you also use Bedrock from the same cluster, the AWS Bedrock resource page covers that side. The guide to Bedrock, Vertex, Gemini, and Anthropic models through Bifrost shows how Vertex fits beside other providers in one LLM gateway.

How Bifrost exchanges an AWS identity for a GCP token

When a request needs a Vertex AI token, Bifrost resolves AWS credentials through the AWS SDK default chain, signs an STS GetCallerIdentity request with them, and exchanges that signature at Google's Security Token Service. If you set service_account_email, the federated token is then swapped for a service account token; otherwise the federated principal calls Vertex AI directly.

Figure 1: No key file exists on either side: the AWS role proves identity, and Google STS turns that proof into a short-lived token.

The aws_workload_identity block sits inside vertex_key_config and takes precedence over auth_credentials; the two must not be combined. Its fields:

Field Required Purpose
audience Yes Full resource name of the AWS provider: //iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/POOL_ID/providers/PROVIDER_ID
service_account_email No Service account to impersonate; omit to give the federated principal Vertex access directly
token_lifetime_seconds No Lifetime of the impersonated token, 600 to 43200 (default 3600); only used with service_account_email
aws_region No Region for the STS signature; defaults to AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, then instance metadata
aws_role_arn No A role to assume before the exchange; usually unnecessary

Every string field accepts env.VAR_NAME references, and AWS GovCloud and China partitions work because the STS host is derived from the region. The full field reference is on the Vertex AI provider page.

Step 1: Enable APIs and create the pool and AWS provider

Run these commands in the Google Cloud project that will be billed for Vertex AI. They follow the GCP prerequisites for AWS in the Bifrost docs. First enable the APIs. sts.googleapis.com performs the token exchange, and iamcredentials.googleapis.com is needed only if you impersonate a service account:

gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com sts.googleapis.com iamcredentials.googleapis.com \
  --project=PROJECT_ID

Next, create a workload identity pool and an AWS provider that trusts your AWS account. The attribute mapping exposes the assumed role name as attribute.aws_role, and the attribute condition limits the pool to the Bifrost role, so no other role in the account can use it:

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create POOL_ID \
  --project=PROJECT_ID \
  --location=global \
  --display-name="Bifrost on AWS"

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-aws PROVIDER_ID \
  --project=PROJECT_ID \
  --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=POOL_ID \
  --account-id=AWS_ACCOUNT_ID \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.arn,attribute.aws_role=assertion.arn.extract('assumed-role/{role}/')" \
  --attribute-condition="attribute.aws_role == 'BIFROST_ROLE_NAME'"

Print the provider's full name, which becomes the audience in the Bifrost key:

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe PROVIDER_ID \
  --project=PROJECT_ID --location=global --workload-identity-pool=POOL_ID \
  --format="value(name)"

If the output starts with projects/, prefix it with //iam.googleapis.com/. The audience uses the numeric project number, not the project ID; gcloud projects describe PROJECT_ID --format="value(projectNumber)" prints it.

Step 2: Grant Vertex AI access

The principal you grant access to is the pool-scoped identity of your AWS role:

principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/POOL_ID/attribute.aws_role/BIFROST_ROLE_NAME

You can give that principal Vertex access directly, or let it impersonate a service account that has access. Either way, keep the grant as narrow as the AI agent governance guide recommends for machine identities: one role, one project.

Figure 2: The attribute condition limits the pool to the Bifrost role, and the IAM binding decides between direct access and impersonation.

Option A: direct access. Leave service_account_email empty in the Bifrost key and bind the Vertex AI user role to the principal:

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/POOL_ID/attribute.aws_role/BIFROST_ROLE_NAME" \
  --role="roles/aiplatform.user"

Option B: impersonate a service account. Create a service account, give it Vertex access, and allow the federated principal to impersonate it:

gcloud iam service-accounts create IAM_SA_NAME \
  --display-name="Bifrost Vertex AI" --project=PROJECT_ID

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
  --member="serviceAccount:IAM_SA_NAME@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/aiplatform.user"

gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
  IAM_SA_NAME@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser" \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/POOL_ID/attribute.aws_role/BIFROST_ROLE_NAME"
Option A: direct access Option B: impersonation
Extra GCP objects None A service account and an impersonation binding
service_account_email in the key Empty Set
Identity in Cloud Audit Logs The federated AWS principal The service account, with the AWS identity as delegate
Good fit Simple setups where the AWS role is the identity you want to audit Organizations that grant permissions to service accounts by policy

Whichever option you pick, budgets and model access for the applications behind the gateway are still enforced by Bifrost, as the governance resource page describes. Option B also lets you set token_lifetime_seconds. Values above 3600 require the organization policy constraint constraints/iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension to allow the service account; otherwise token generation fails.

Step 3: Attach an IAM role to the Bifrost workload

The IAM role needs no AWS permissions for this flow, because sts:GetCallerIdentity is always allowed. It only has to reach the Bifrost process. On EKS, use IRSA or EKS Pod Identity. With IRSA, annotate the Kubernetes service account that the Bifrost pod runs as:

kubectl annotate serviceaccount KSA_NAME \
  --namespace NAMESPACE \
  eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=arn:aws:iam::AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:role/BIFROST_ROLE_NAME

With EKS Pod Identity, install the Pod Identity Agent add-on, make sure the role's trust policy allows the pods.eks.amazonaws.com service principal to call sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession, and create the association:

aws eks create-addon --cluster-name CLUSTER_NAME --addon-name eks-pod-identity-agent

aws eks create-pod-identity-association \
  --cluster-name CLUSTER_NAME \
  --namespace NAMESPACE \
  --service-account KSA_NAME \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:role/BIFROST_ROLE_NAME

An IRSA-style OIDC trust policy does not work with Pod Identity. On ECS, attach the role as the task role; on EC2, attach it through the instance profile. If you deploy with the Bifrost Helm chart, set the IRSA annotation through serviceAccount.annotations, as shown in the Helm provider configuration.

Figure 3: Static AWS keys in the pod win over the attached role, so remove them when the role is the identity you mean to federate.

Two details cause most failed setups. First, the AWS SDK default chain checks static credentials before the attached role, so if AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY are set in the pod, Bifrost federates as that key. Remove them. Second, a region is not guaranteed: IRSA usually injects AWS_REGION, but a self-managed webhook may not, and Pod Identity does not set one. Set aws_region in the key or AWS_REGION in the pod if neither the environment nor instance metadata provides one. The in-VPC deployment docs cover running Bifrost inside your own VPC on AWS.

Step 4: Add a Vertex key with aws_workload_identity

In the dashboard, go to Model Providers → Configurations → Google Vertex, add a key, and choose Workload Identity (AWS) as the authentication method. Set the project ID, the region (for example us-central1), and the Workload Identity Provider Audience. The service account, AWS region, and role ARN fields are optional.

The same key in config.json, using Option B:

{
  "providers": {
    "vertex": {
      "keys": [
        {
          "name": "vertex-eks-key",
          "value": "",
          "models": ["*"],
          "weight": 1.0,
          "vertex_key_config": {
            "project_id": "env.VERTEX_PROJECT_ID",
            "region": "us-central1",
            "aws_workload_identity": {
              "audience": "//iam.googleapis.com/projects/123456789012/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/eks-pool/providers/aws",
              "service_account_email": "bifrost-vertex@my-gcp-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
            }
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

For Option A, drop service_account_email. To create the key on a running gateway, POST the same key object to /api/providers/vertex/keys after creating the provider with POST /api/providers and {"provider": "vertex"}. The Vertex AI setup guide covers regions and model names, and key management explains how weights spread traffic when you add more than one Vertex key.

Applications then call Vertex models through Bifrost with the usual model prefix, for example vertex/gemini-2.5-flash, using a virtual key for access control and budgets.

Step 5: Verify the identity end to end

Confirm the AWS side from inside the Bifrost pod:

kubectl exec -n NAMESPACE POD_NAME -- aws sts get-caller-identity
# "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:assumed-role/BIFROST_ROLE_NAME/..."

If the ARN shows an IAM user or a node role instead of BIFROST_ROLE_NAME, fix that before going further. Then send a request through the gateway:

curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-bf-your-virtual-key" \
  -d '{"model": "vertex/gemini-2.5-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with OK"}]}'

Finally, check Google's side. The Cloud Audit Log entry for the Vertex call identifies the caller under protoPayload.authenticationInfo. With Option A and the mapping above, principalSubject names the pool subject with the AWS role's assumed-role ARN. With Option B, principalEmail is the service account and the AWS identity appears as principalSubject inside serviceAccountDelegationInfo[]. The principalSet:// form from Step 2 is the binding target and does not appear as the logged identity.

Bifrost records the request on its own side as well: the built-in request logs show the provider, model, key name, and latency, and the AI governance page explains how those logs tie each call back to a virtual key, team, or customer.

Troubleshooting workload identity federation for Vertex AI

Symptom Likely cause Fix
no EC2 IMDS role found or failed to refresh cached credentials No IAM role reaches the pod Check the IRSA annotation or Pod Identity association; aws sts get-caller-identity in the pod must succeed
aws region could not be determined No AWS_REGION and no instance metadata Set aws_region in the key or AWS_REGION in the pod
invalid_grant or The audience in the token does not match Wrong audience Copy the provider's full resource name, starting with //iam.googleapis.com/
The given credential is rejected by the attribute condition Role name does not match the condition Align --attribute-condition with the role attached to the pod
403 Permission 'iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken' denied Missing impersonation grant Add roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser on the service account (Option B)
403 Forbidden from the Vertex API Principal or service account lacks Vertex access Grant roles/aiplatform.user
Requests succeed as the node role An older Bifrost resolved an external_account JSON through Google's library Upgrade Bifrost, or switch the key to aws_workload_identity

When a Vertex key fails for reasons tied to the key, such as a rejected credential, Bifrost classifies the error and can rotate to another key or fall back to another provider, as described in retries and fallbacks. The routing and fallback guide shows how to keep traffic flowing while you fix the binding.

Frequently asked questions

What is workload identity federation?

Workload identity federation is a Google Cloud IAM feature that lets workloads outside Google Cloud, such as applications on AWS or Azure, exchange their own identity for short-lived Google credentials. It replaces long-lived service account keys with a trust relationship between Google Cloud and the external identity provider.

Do I still need a service account?

No. With Option A, the federated AWS principal gets roles/aiplatform.user directly and no service account exists. Use a service account (Option B) when your organization grants permissions to service accounts by policy or wants the service account recorded as the caller. Both are supported by the Bifrost Vertex AI provider.

Does the AWS role need any IAM permissions?

No. The flow only signs an STS GetCallerIdentity request, which every AWS identity is allowed to call. The role needs a trust relationship for IRSA, Pod Identity, ECS, or EC2 so the workload can assume it, and nothing else.

Can I use workload identity federation on ECS or EC2 instead of EKS?

Yes. Bifrost resolves AWS credentials through the AWS SDK default chain, which covers ECS task roles and EC2 instance profiles as well as IRSA and EKS Pod Identity. The GCP-side setup is the same; only how the role reaches the process changes.

Can I combine aws_workload_identity with a service account JSON key?

No. aws_workload_identity takes precedence over auth_credentials, and the two must not be set on the same key. To migrate gradually, add a new Vertex key that uses workload identity alongside the existing key, shift weight to it, and then remove the JSON key. The Bifrost enterprise page covers rolling changes like this across clustered gateways.

Which Vertex AI models work with this setup?

Authentication does not change model support, so the Gemini and Anthropic models that Bifrost serves through Vertex AI work the same way with a federated key. The supported providers overview lists what each provider supports.

Run Vertex AI from AWS without key files

Workload identity federation removes the last long-lived Google secret from an AWS deployment: the Bifrost pod's IAM role is the credential, Google issues short-lived tokens, and access is controlled by IAM bindings you can audit. To see Vertex AI, Bedrock, and other providers governed through one gateway in your own VPC, book a demo with the Bifrost team, or read the Bifrost enterprise deployment guide to plan the rollout.

title: Why Your AI Coding Agents Suffer from Amnesia (And How I Fixed It with SQLite + ONNX)
description:
If you use Claude Desktop, Cursor, or OpenCode, you know the daily struggle: every new session is a blank slate. Standard RAG solutions treat memory as flat vector chunks, which makes them fundamentally time-blind.

To solve this, I built Synapse 4D, an open-source local-first cognitive memory engine that acts as a permanent hippocampus for AI agents.

Core Architecture

  • D1 Focus: Working memory buffer with strict token management.
  • D2 Distiller: Extracts atomic facts and resolves contradictions.
  • D3 Chronos: Bi-temporal SQLite database (valid_from, valid_to) with Hebbian recency decay.
  • D4 Mesh: Reciprocal graph ensuring zero orphan stubs.

🧠 Permanent AI Memory: Integrates natively with Claude Desktop & Cursor via MCP.
⏳ Bi-temporal Tracking: Resolves contradictory facts without erasing historical context.
🔒 100% Local & Private: Pure SQLite + ONNX embeddings. Zero cloud APIs, zero telemetry, zero PyTorch bloat.

Check the open-source repository on GitHub:
👉 https://github.com/MShesat/SYNAPSE-4D

For those interested in a visual 3D neural graph HUD and a Windows installer, I also packaged a Pro Edition:
👉 https://synapse4d.lemonsqueezy.com/buy

title: Performance at Scale: Optimizing Large and High-Volume Forms
description:
• Designing a Form Architecture That Survives Scale
  • Cut re-renders: minimize DOM churn and validation cost
  • Virtualize and cache fields without losing user input
  • Measure what matters: profiling, benchmarking, and CI-friendly tests
  • Practical Application — checklists, hooks, and snippets

Large, high-volume forms die from three predictable things: gratuitous re-renders, synchronous/over-eager validation, and DOM churn from mounting/unmounting fields. Tackle those three and you turn a sluggish 100+ field form into a responsive, resilient data-collection surface.

Large forms show symptoms that feel familiar: typing lag on-device, long commit times in the React Profiler, fields that lose value when scrolled out of a virtual list, autosave hammering the backend with many tiny requests, and brittle tests that flake when fields mount/unmount. Those are the places you focus first because they cost user time, conversions, and developer time to debug.

Designing a Form Architecture That Survives Scale

Treat the form as a data contract first: a single, schema-driven source of truth and small, well-scoped components that only subscribe to what they need.

  • Use a schema-first approach (for example with Zod) so your validation, types, and API contract live in one place rather than scattered through UI code. That makes step-by-step validation and type-safe transforms predictable.
  • Wire the schema into your form layer with a resolver (e.g., zodResolver + React Hook Form) so validation runs where you expect it and can be run on-demand instead of per-keystroke. This keeps runtime validation predictable and composable.
  • For multi-step forms choose one of two patterns:
    • One form instance across all steps, and validate only the active step with targeted triggers; this keeps all data in one place and simplifies final submission.
    • Separate form instances per step and stitch the results together server-side—simpler component isolation but more plumbing for cross-step constraints.

Table: high-level trade-offs

Approach Pros Cons
Uncontrolled inputs + RHF (register) Minimal re-renders, native input performance Integrations with controlled UI libs need Controller adapters.
Controlled (useState / Formik) Easier to reason in component-local state, simpler third-party controlled components Re-renders per keystroke — scales poorly with many fields.
Hybrid (RHF + Controller for specific widgets) Best balance: RHF performance + compatibility with controlled UI components More cognitive overhead; avoid Controller for trivial native inputs.

Important: For large forms prefer uncontrolled-first patterns and only adopt Controller when you must integrate a controlled widget (Material UI, custom select, complex datepickers). Controller isolates re-rendering but has a cost compared to native register.

Example starter (RHF + Zod):

import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
import { zodResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/zod";
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  firstName: z.string().min(1),
  age: z.number().int().optional(),
});

const methods = useForm({
  resolver: zodResolver(schema),
  mode: "onBlur",           // validate less aggressively
  shouldUnregister: false, // useful for multi-step UIs
});

Citations: RHF explains its uncontrolled focus and lower re-render surface as a design point ; schema-first docs for zod and parse options are comprehensive ; resolvers project documents the zodResolver pattern .

Cut re-renders: minimize DOM churn and validation cost

The single biggest win for responsiveness is preventing unnecessary re-renders — especially the root form component.

  • Subscribe narrowly. Use useWatch or useFormState to subscribe to only the fields or flags you need. Avoid destructuring the entire formState at the form root (it forces wide re-renders). useWatch will isolate updates to the hook level.
  • Prefer register (uncontrolled) for native inputs. It keeps input state in the DOM and out of React renders; reading values on demand with getValues() is cheap. Use Controller only for components that expose no ref.
  • Validate intentionally:
    • Use mode: "onBlur" or mode: "onSubmit" for large forms — avoid onChange validation on every keystroke. onChange validation creates a lot of computation and re-renders.
    • For heavy or async checks (e.g., calling an availability API), run them on blur or on explicit trigger(fields) rather than during every change. Use safeParse / parseAsync for async schema refinements when required.
  • Use setValue with options to avoid side-effectful re-renders. setValue(name, value, { shouldValidate: false, shouldDirty: true }) gives you control over whether state flags trigger updates.

Practical patterns that reduce re-renders:

  • Move expensive display computations outside the input-render path (memoize summaries, charts).
  • Wrap large static blocks with React.memo.
  • Avoid inline props or inline event handlers that change identity on each render; pass stable callbacks with useCallback.

Short code snippet: isolate dirty indicator with useFormState so the form root doesn’t re-render:

// Child component only re-renders when isDirty changes
function DirtyBadge({ control }: { control: Control }) {
  const { isDirty } = useFormState({ control, name: "isDirty" });
  return <span>{isDirty ? "Unsaved" : "Saved"}</span>;
}

Citations: RHF documents useWatch, useFormState and the cost of onChange validation modes; setValue options allow you to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

Virtualize and cache fields without losing user input

When the number of rows/fields is large (think 100s–1000s), windowing the DOM is necessary — but doing it naively loses uncontrolled input state when rows unmount. Use targeted patterns to keep state consistent.

  • React’s guidance: virtualize long lists to reduce DOM nodes and render cost. Virtualization dramatically reduces the number of DOM nodes React must reconcile.
  • Libraries: use react-window or a headless solution like TanStack Virtual for full control. react-window is battle-tested and lightweight; TanStack Virtual is more feature-rich and headless.
  • With forms, follow RHF’s "working with virtualized lists" advice:
    • Keep the form values in RHF instead of relying on DOM-only state; use shouldUnregister: false so that fields removed from the DOM don’t lose their registered value.
    • Render editors in a pooled/sticky editor when inline editing is required (mount the active editor outside the virtualized list and bind it to the selected row), or persist values to RHF on blur before unmount.
  • Tune overscanCount to avoid excessive mount/unmount churn as the user scrolls; overscan mitigates visual flicker at the cost of a few extra mounted rows.

Example pattern (simplified):

import { FixedSizeList as List } from "react-window";
import { FormProvider, useForm } from "react-hook-form";

function Row({ index, style, data }) {
  // mount/unmount — register/unregister handled by RHF
  return (
    <div style={style}>
      <input {...data.register(`rows.${index}.value`)} />
    </div>
  );
}

function WindowedForm({ items }) {
  const methods = useForm({ defaultValues: { rows: items }, shouldUnregister: false });
  return (
    <FormProvider {...methods}>
      <List itemCount={items.length} itemSize={40} overscanCount={5}>
        {({ index, style }) => <Row index={index} style={style} data={methods} />}
      </List>
    </FormProvider>
  );
}

Citations: React recommends windowing for long lists ; RHF’s advanced usage shows concrete examples for keeping values with virtualized lists and warns about unmount-reset issues ; react-window docs explain overscan and API shape.

Measure what matters: profiling, benchmarking, and CI-friendly tests

You can’t optimize what you don’t measure. Build a small, reproducible benchmark and add it to CI so performance regressions are visible.

  • Developer-time tools:
    • Use React DevTools Profiler and the <Profiler> API to locate slow commits and the components responsible for the work. Actual render commit durations are what you optimize, not render counts alone.
    • Use why-did-you-render during development to find avoidable re-renders; it’s noisy but great for catching ownership/props identity issues before deployment.
  • Lab tests:
    • Run Lighthouse user flows or scripted Lighthouse runs to capture performance during an interactive path (e.g., go → open form → fill first 50 fields). Lighthouse user flows let you measure during interactions, not just page load.
    • Use Playwright (or Puppeteer) to script form work and capture traces. Playwright’s trace viewer records actions, DOM snapshots, and timing so you can correlate a slow keystroke or commit to an exact action.
  • CI-friendly regression tests:
    • Add a small synthetic test that populates N fields and asserts the median keystroke-to-render time stays below a threshold.
    • Capture traces on first failing runs to root-cause regressions quickly.

Example Playwright snippet (tracing + simple fill time):

// playwright-test.js
import { chromium } from "playwright";

(async () => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto("http://localhost:3000/huge-form");
  const t0 = performance.now();
  // simulate filling 200 inputs
  for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
    await page.fill(`[data-test="input-${i}"]`, "x".repeat(10));
  }
  const t1 = performance.now();
  console.log("fill time ms:", t1 - t0);
  await context.tracing.stop({ path: "trace.zip" });
  await browser.close();
})();

Citations: The Profiler API docs explain what to measure and how to interpret commits ; Lighthouse user flows document scripting interactions and measuring them in CI ; Playwright tracing docs explain the trace format and viewer.

Practical Application — checklists, hooks, and snippets

This section is a drop-in toolkit: checklists you can run through quickly, and a ready useAutosave hook that follows safe patterns.

Run this quick checklist on any large form:

  • [ ] Use a schema (Zod) that represents the entire data shape.
  • [ ] Configure RHF with resolver and mode: "onBlur" (or "onSubmit") for the big form.
  • [ ] Prefer register for native inputs; use Controller only for controlled UI widgets.
  • [ ] Isolate expensive UI or derived data with React.memo and useMemo.
  • [ ] For long lists: virtualize with react-window or TanStack Virtual and set shouldUnregister: false. Tune overscanCount.
  • [ ] Add synthetic performance tests (Playwright / Lighthouse user flows) to CI.
  • [ ] Implement autosave that debounces, saves only diffs, and falls back to local persistence / background sync when offline.

A robust useAutosave (TypeScript + RHF-friendly)

  • Goals: debounce saves, save only deltas, persist to an offline store when offline, flush on unload, cancel in-flight saves on new changes. 
// useAutosave.ts
import { useEffect, useRef, useCallback } from "react";
import debounce from "lodash.debounce";

type SaveFn<T> = (patch: Partial<T>) => Promise<void>;

export function useAutosave<T extends Record<string, any>>(
  getValues: () => T,
  watchSubscribe: (cb: (data: T) => void) => { unsubscribe: () => void },
  saveFn: SaveFn<T>,
  opts = { wait: 1200, maxWait: 5000 }
) {
  const lastSavedRef = useRef<T | null>(null);
  const inflightRef = useRef<Promise<void> | null>(null);

  // shallow-diff; return object with changed keys
  const diff = (a: T | null, b: T) => {
    if (!a) return b;
    const patch: Partial<T> = {};
    for (const k of Object.keys(b)) {
      if (a[k] !== b[k]) patch[k as keyof T] = b[k];
    }
    return patch;
  };

  const doSave = useCallback(async () => {
    const values = getValues();
    const patch = diff(lastSavedRef.current, values);
    if (!patch || Object.keys(patch).length === 0) return;
    try {
      inflightRef.current = saveFn(patch);
      await inflightRef.current;
      lastSavedRef.current = values;
    } catch (err) {
      // simple backoff would go here; for offline, persist `patch` to IndexedDB/localStorage
      console.error("Autosave failed", err);
    } finally {
      inflightRef.current = null;
    }
  }, [getValues, saveFn]);

  // debounced save to avoid network storms
  const debouncedSaveRef = useRef(debounce(doSave, opts.wait, { maxWait: opts.maxWait })).current;

  useEffect(() => {
    // initialize lastSaved
    lastSavedRef.current = getValues();
    const sub = watchSubscribe(() => {
      debouncedSaveRef();
    });

    const handleUnload = () => {
      // flush synchronously on unload if possible
      debouncedSaveRef.cancel();
      // best-effort: call sync save (not guaranteed)
      void doSave();
    };
    window.addEventListener("beforeunload", handleUnload);
    return () => {
      sub.unsubscribe();
      debouncedSaveRef.cancel();
      window.removeEventListener("beforeunload", handleUnload);
    };
  }, [getValues, watchSubscribe, debouncedSaveRef, doSave]);
}

Integration notes:

  • Use RHF’s watch(callback) subscription (or watch inside a lightweight component) to avoid root re-renders and to feed useAutosave without causing renders.
  • Persist failed patches to IndexedDB and register a Background Sync so service worker flushes them when network returns. MDN documents the Background Sync API and the SyncManager pattern for this use-case.
  • Use lodash.debounce (or an equivalent) to throttle saves and give users a smooth typing experience.

Small snippet: register background sync (service worker):

// in client when offline save to outbox then:
const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
await reg.sync.register("outbox-sync");

Citations: use debounce to prevent request storms ; use localStorage / IndexedDB for persistence when network is flaky (Web Storage / IndexedDB docs) ; Background Sync lets the service worker flush queued requests when connectivity returns .

Sources:
React Hook Form — FAQs - Explanation of RHF's uncontrolled-first design and why it reduces re-renders.

Optimizing Performance — React (legacy docs) - React guidance on windowing long lists and avoiding unnecessary reconciliation.

Profiler API – React - How to use the Profiler to measure commit durations and identify hotspots.

React Hook Form — Advanced Usage (Working with virtualized lists) - Concrete example and cautions for using react-window with RHF and how to preserve values.

bvaughn/react-window · GitHub - react-window docs and API (overscan, List/Grid patterns).

TanStack/virtual · GitHub - Headless virtualizer (TanStack Virtual) and usage patterns for complex virtualization.

Zod (colinhacks/zod) · GitHub - Zod schema API (parse, safeParse, parseAsync) and rationale for schema-first validation.

react-hook-form/resolvers · GitHub - Resolver integrations including zodResolver and how to wire schemas into RHF.

Use tools to measure performance — web.dev - Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and RUM guidance for creating measurable performance baselines.

Playwright — Trace Viewer docs - How to record traces, inspect actions, and use tracing in CI to debug performance.

why-did-you-render · GitHub - Dev-time tool to detect avoidable re-renders and ownership reasons.

Web Storage API — Using the Web Storage API (MDN) - Browser storage fundamentals and constraints for localStorage.

Background Synchronization API (MDN) - Using SyncManager and service worker sync registration for offline-first sync.

lodash.debounce — npm - debounce implementation and options for throttling autosave and heavy callbacks.

useForm — React Hook Form docs - useForm options (mode, shouldUnregister, resolver) and guidance on subscription APIs, getValues, setValue, useWatch and useFormState.

Every change you make to render scope, validation timing, or virtualization should be backed by a quick profile: add a Profiler span, measure an action end-to-end with Playwright/Lighthouse, and only then harden it into CI. Performance at scale is a discipline: architect with schema-first validation, subscribe narrowly, and instrument the form so regressions are visible and actionable.

title: Why I love building 100% client-side web tools (and how I do it)
description:
I'm a solo indie developer based in China. Over the past year I've built more than 20 small web tools, and almost all of them share one design decision: no backend at all.

Here's why I keep coming back to it.

No server means no data risk. When a tool runs entirely in the browser, the user's input never leaves their device. There's no database to leak, no logs to inspect, no "we may share data with partners" paragraph to write. Privacy stops being a policy and becomes an architecture. For things like a BMI calculator or a password generator, that's the right default.

Instant load. A single HTML file with inline CSS and JS is a few kilobytes. It renders before a typical React app has finished downloading its framework. Fast tools feel trustworthy.

Near-zero cost. Static files on Cloudflare Pages cost me basically nothing. No servers to patch, no uptime alerts at 3 a.m., no scaling bill when a post goes viral.

How I actually build them: plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. No build step, no framework. I deploy to Cloudflare Pages with a git push. I use AI as a pair programmer — mostly for scaffolding layouts and catching edge cases — but I keep the logic simple enough to read in one sitting.

That stack is what powers Lihayo Tools, a growing set of 20+ free utilities including BMI and TDEE calculators. Everything runs locally, no signup, no tracking.

If you've been thinking about shipping small tools, start with a single HTML file. It's still the most underrated stack on the web.

title: The migration I would do differently next time
description:
Moved a table with about twenty million rows last month and learned three things the hard way.

Do the double-write before the backfill, not after. We did it the other way and spent two evenings reconciling.

Measure replication lag before you start, not during. Ours spiked and we had no baseline.

Write the rollback plan first. We had one, sort of, in someone's head. That is not a plan.

title: Is Your React App Invisible to ChatGPT? Test What AI Crawlers Actually See
description:
Here's a bug report you'll never get: "ChatGPT says our product doesn't have a free tier."

Nobody files it, because nobody connects the dots. But if your pricing page is a client-rendered React app, there's a decent chance the AI system that answered that question received this:

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head><title>Pricing | Acme</title></head>
  <body>
    <div id="root"></div>
    <script src="/assets/index-8f3a.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>

Then it filled the gap from somewhere else: an old review, a competitor's comparison page, or a guess.

Why this is worse in 2026 than it was in 2020

Google spent years building a JavaScript rendering pipeline. Googlebot runs your JS (eventually), so client-side rendering became "mostly fine for SEO."

AI systems didn't inherit that pipeline. There are now three kinds of AI fetchers hitting your site:

Type Examples Renders JS?
Training crawlers GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot Generally treated as no. Assume raw HTML.
AI search crawlers OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot Not reliably. Assume raw HTML.
Live user fetches ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, Perplexity-User Varies by product and changes over time. Don't count on it.

Vendors don't publish rendering guarantees, and behaviour changes. The only safe assumption is the one that has always been safe: if it's not in the HTML response, it might not exist.

Google's AI features (AI Overviews, AI Mode) use Google's index, which is rendered, so a CSR site can show up there and still be invisible to ChatGPT. That's exactly the kind of gap that's easy to miss.

Test it: raw vs rendered, side by side

This script fetches a URL twice, once as a plain HTTP request (what a non-rendering crawler gets) and once in headless Chromium (what a browser gets), then compares the text.

npm i playwright cheerio
npx playwright install chromium

// render-gap.mjs
import { chromium } from "playwright";
import * as cheerio from "cheerio";

const url = process.argv[2];
const mustContain = process.argv.slice(3); // phrases that MUST be visible to crawlers

function textOf(html) {
  const $ = cheerio.load(html);
  $("script, style, noscript, template, svg").remove();
  return $("body").text().replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
}

// 1. Raw HTML, as a non-rendering crawler would see it
const rawRes = await fetch(url, {
  headers: { "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; OAI-SearchBot/1.0; +https://openai.com/searchbot)" },
});
const raw = await rawRes.text();

// 2. Rendered DOM after JavaScript
const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: "networkidle" });
const rendered = await page.content();
await browser.close();

const rawText = textOf(raw);
const renderedText = textOf(rendered);
const ratio = rawText.length / Math.max(renderedText.length, 1);

console.log(`Status (raw fetch):  ${rawRes.status}`);
console.log(`Raw text:            ${rawText.length.toLocaleString()} chars`);
console.log(`Rendered text:       ${renderedText.length.toLocaleString()} chars`);
console.log(`Raw / rendered:      ${(ratio * 100).toFixed(0)}%`);

const $raw = cheerio.load(raw);
console.log(`<title> in raw:      ${$raw("title").text() || "MISSING"}`);
console.log(`meta description:    ${$raw('meta[name="description"]').attr("content") ? "yes" : "MISSING"}`);
console.log(`<h1> in raw:         ${$raw("h1").first().text().trim() || "MISSING"}`);
console.log(`JSON-LD in raw:      ${$raw('script[type="application/ld+json"]').length} block(s)`);

for (const phrase of mustContain) {
  const inRaw = rawText.toLowerCase().includes(phrase.toLowerCase());
  console.log(`${inRaw ? "✅" : "❌"} "${phrase}" ${inRaw ? "is" : "is NOT"} in the raw HTML`);
}

if (ratio < 0.5) {
  console.log("\n⚠️  Less than half of the visible text exists without JavaScript.");
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

node render-gap.mjs https://your-site.com/pricing "Free plan" "per seat" "SOC 2"

Status (raw fetch):  200
Raw text:            142 chars
Rendered text:       6,418 chars
Raw / rendered:      2%
<title> in raw:      Pricing | Acme
meta description:    MISSING
<h1> in raw:         MISSING
JSON-LD in raw:      0 block(s)
❌ "Free plan" is NOT in the raw HTML
❌ "per seat" is NOT in the raw HTML
❌ "SOC 2" is NOT in the raw HTML

⚠️  Less than half of the visible text exists without JavaScript.

The mustContain phrases are the important part. Pick the facts you'd be upset to see an AI get wrong (price, free tier, integrations, compliance) and make them a test.

Also check the status code. If the raw fetch with an AI user agent returns 403 or a challenge page while your browser gets 200, your problem is the CDN or WAF, not rendering. Look at your bot-management rules before changing any code.

The fixes, by framework

Next.js (App Router)

Server Components render on the server by default, so most App Router pages are already fine. The usual culprits:

// ❌ Whole page opted into client rendering, data fetched in useEffect
"use client";
export default function Pricing() {
  const [plans, setPlans] = useState([]);
  useEffect(() => { fetch("/api/plans").then(r => r.json()).then(setPlans); }, []);
  return <PlanTable plans={plans} />;
}

// ✅ Server Component fetches data; only the interactive toggle is a client component
import { BillingToggle } from "./billing-toggle"; // "use client" inside

export const revalidate = 3600; // static, refreshed hourly

export default async function Pricing() {
  const plans = await getPlans();
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Pricing</h1>
      <BillingToggle />
      <PlanTable plans={plans} />
    </main>
  );
}

Also watch for dynamic(() => import(...), { ssr: false }) around content (it's fine for widgets, not for text), and for content that only appears inside tabs or accordions that mount on click. Render it all and hide it with CSS instead.

Vite + React SPA

You have three options, from least to most work:

  1. Prerender the routes that matter at build time (marketing pages, docs, pricing), for example with vite-plugin-prerender or a small Playwright script that saves rendered HTML for a list of routes into dist/.
  2. Move the marketing site to a static-first framework (Astro, Next.js static export) and keep the SPA for the logged-in app at app.example.com.
  3. Adopt SSR (React Router framework mode, TanStack Start) if most of the product is public content.

For most teams, option 2 is the right answer: the app doesn't need to be crawlable, and the marketing site does.

Astro, Eleventy, Hugo

Static by default. Just be careful with client-only islands (client:only) that contain content rather than interactivity.

What about dynamic rendering?

Serving prerendered HTML only to bots (the old "dynamic rendering" pattern) still works technically, but Google describes it as a workaround, not a recommended solution. It also creates two versions of every page that can drift apart, and serving different content to bots is the definition of cloaking. Prefer SSR or static generation, which give everyone the same HTML.

Put the check in CI

Run the script against a preview deployment on every PR that touches marketing or docs routes:

# .github/workflows/render-gap.yml
name: Crawlability
on: pull_request
jobs:
  render-gap:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22 }
      - run: npm ci && npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      # PREVIEW_URL comes from your deploy provider's preview step
      - run: node scripts/render-gap.mjs "$PREVIEW_URL/pricing" "Free plan" "per seat"
      - run: node scripts/render-gap.mjs "$PREVIEW_URL/docs/quickstart" "npm install"

That one check would have caught every "the AI said we don't have X" problem I've seen.

Beyond rendering

Server-side rendering gets your content into the HTML. Whether AI crawlers can reach it at all also depends on robots.txt, your CDN's bot rules, rate limits and status codes, and whether the page is indexed in Google and Bing. Vista AI's page audit checks those things together with the raw-vs-rendered gap for a URL. If you'd rather script it yourself, the render-gap.mjs above plus a robots.txt check covers the most common failures.

Run the script on your pricing page and share the raw/rendered percentage in the comments. Bonus points if it's under 10%.

Next in the series: How AI assistants decide which dev tool to recommend.

title: comandle: un Wordle de comandos de Linux que se juega en la terminal
description:
Cada día, un comando de Linux o de seguridad para adivinar en seis intentos, en la terminal o en el navegador. Cómo se juega, cómo elige el comando del día sin un servidor y qué cuenta la web.

Cada día hay un comando de Linux o de seguridad para adivinar en seis intentos. Escribís uno con la misma cantidad de letras y cada letra queda verde si está en su lugar, amarilla si está en otra posición y gris si no está. Cuando termina la ronda, ganes o pierdas, aparece la ficha del comando: qué hace, tres ejemplos y una nota de seguridad.

Se llama comandle y lo armé para practicar comandos un rato por día. Se juega en el navegador, en comandle.valentorassa.com, o en la terminal:

go install github.com/legiosai/comandle@latest
comandle

Es gratis, no pide cuenta y el comando del día es el mismo en los dos lados. El #1 salió el 20 de octubre.

Cómo se juega

La categoría se ve desde el primer intento: archivos, texto, procesos, redes, permisos, sistema, seguridad, paquetes, git o contenedores. Hay 75 comandos cargados, de 4 a 8 letras, en tres niveles: básico, intermedio y avanzado.

Si le errás, el juego destapa pistas: la primera con dos intentos fallidos, la segunda con cuatro y la última con cinco. Solo valen nombres de comandos reales, de una lista de 651, así que no se puede tantear con letras sueltas. En la terminal, ? muestra los válidos con esa cantidad de letras; en la web están en la lista de comandos, y tab completa.

Al terminar copiás el resultado, que muestra cómo te fue sin decir cuál era. Esta es una ronda del #1:

comandle #1 3/6
🟨⬛⬛🟨
🟩⬛⬛🟩
🟩🟩🟩🟩
comandle.valentorassa.com

En la web, un personaje ASCII comenta la partida al estilo de cowsay: cambia los ojos cuando vas mal, festeja con exit 0 y se muere con un segmentation fault. Por defecto es vt, el pingüino, y se puede cambiar por la vaca, un conejo, un gato, un búho, un cangrejo o un fantasma.

La ficha del final

Ese #1 era grep. Cuando la ronda termina, la ficha dice qué hace, cuándo lo usás y trae tres ejemplos para copiar:

grep -rn "TODO" ~/proyecto                    # archivo y número de línea de cada TODO
grep -i "error" app.log                       # sin importar mayúsculas
sudo grep -c "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log   # intentos fallidos de login por SSH

Y una nota de seguridad. La de grep avisa que sirve para auditar, buscando contraseñas en texto plano o IPs raras en un log, y que si no encuentra nada solo sabés que nada coincide con tu patrón.

Dieciséis de las fichas suman un laboratorio en securitylabs.valentorassa.com para practicar el comando con un caso armado.

Desde la terminal, la ficha de cualquier comando de la lista se pide sin jugar, y hay rondas de práctica que no suman a tus estadísticas:

comandle explicar chmod   # la ficha de un comando
comandle practica         # una ronda al azar
comandle practica find    # practicar uno puntual, por ejemplo en una clase
comandle lista            # los comandos de los días que ya pasaron
comandle stats            # tus estadísticas y tu racha

El mismo comando sin un servidor

La versión de terminal está escrita en Go y la web es HTML y JavaScript estático. Las dos leen el mismo commands.json y eligen el comando del día con la misma regla, que en la web es esta:

export function daily(commands, n) {
  if (n < 1) n = 1;
  if (n <= commands.length) return commands[n - 1];
  return commands[fnv1a32(`comandle-${n}`) % commands.length];
}

El orden del archivo es el calendario: el día n juega la entrada n. Con 75 comandos eso alcanza hasta el 2 de enero de 2027, y si para entonces no se sumaron más, los días siguen en un orden pseudoaleatorio fijo, con FNV-1a de 32 bits, el mismo hash que hash/fnv en Go. El número del día sale de la fecha en Argentina (UTC−3, sin horario de verano), así que el comando cambia a medianoche y nadie tiene que publicarlo. Un test fija que Go y JavaScript den lo mismo.

Como la respuesta viaja con el juego, cualquiera que abra el código puede ver la del día. No hay un servidor que la guarde.

Qué cuenta la web

La versión de terminal no se conecta a internet. Tus estadísticas quedan en un archivo que solo puede leer tu usuario.

La web no usa cookies ni guarda nada que te identifique. Cuando empezás una partida, la terminás o copiás el resultado, suma 1 a un contador del día:

  • al terminar, en cuántos intentos o si perdiste;
  • cuántos días seguidos jugaste, calculado en tu navegador con el historial que ya guarda y mandado en tramos (1, 2–3, 4–7, 8–14, 15+);
  • al entrar, el ref del link y el sitio que te mandó. 
fetch(ENDPOINT, {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify({ event, key }),
  mode: "cors",
  credentials: "omit",
  keepalive: true,
});

Después de leer el ?ref=, la web lo saca de la barra, así el link que copiás queda limpio. Si tu navegador tiene activado Global Privacy Control, no manda nada.

Con eso veo cuántas partidas hay, qué comandos cuestan más y de dónde llega la gente. Cualquiera puede mandarle eventos, así que lo leo como tendencia.

Sumá un comando

Cada comando es una entrada de data/commands.json, con categoría, nivel, tres pistas, resumen, explicación, tres ejemplos, la nota de seguridad y, si hay, el laboratorio:

{
  "id": "chmod",
  "category": "permisos",
  "level": "básico",
  "clues": [
    "Decide quién puede leer, escribir o ejecutar un archivo.",
    "Acepta modos en octal, como 755 o 600.",
    "Su nombre viene de «change mode»."
  ],
  "summary": "Cambia los permisos de archivos y directorios."
}

Como el orden es el calendario, los nuevos van siempre al final: mover una entrada cambiaría el comando de un día que ya pasó. Al cargar, el juego revisa todas las entradas y te muestra todos los problemas juntos, para que corrijas la tuya de una vez. Los pasos están en CONTRIBUTING.md.

El código está en github.com/legiosai/comandle, con licencia Apache-2.0. Lo hice desde VT Security y lo publica Legios.

El de hoy ya está en comandle.valentorassa.com. Si lo jugás, contame en cuántos lo sacaste: en el Discord de DedSec hay un canal #comandle donde todas las mañanas a las 9 sale el del día.

Lo publiqué primero en vtsecurity.com.ar.
