title: Scalable React Project Structure with Vite and Tailwind CSS
description:
Scalable React Project Structure with Vite and Tailwind CSS

Building a React application is easy to start. Keeping it maintainable as it grows is the real challenge.

As new features are added, a project can quickly become difficult to navigate. Components end up in the wrong folders, API requests are scattered across the codebase, and business logic becomes tightly coupled to the UI.

A well-organized React project structure helps developers maintain clean code, reuse components, and scale applications without introducing unnecessary complexity.

In this article, I'll share a practical folder architecture for React applications built with Vite and Tailwind CSS, explain the purpose of each directory, and discuss when to use shared components versus feature-based modules.

1. Why Does React Project Structure Matter?

React doesn't enforce a specific folder structure. This flexibility is useful, but it also means developers need to establish conventions that fit their projects.

Without a clear structure, you may encounter problems such as:

  • A single components/ folder containing dozens of unrelated files.
  • API calls mixed directly into UI components.
  • Custom hooks duplicated across different features.
  • Business logic scattered throughout the application.
  • Difficult refactoring as the codebase grows.

The goal isn't to create as many folders as possible. It's to make the codebase predictable, easy to navigate, and straightforward to maintain.

2. A Scalable React Folder Structure

For a medium-sized application, a feature-based architecture is a practical starting point.

Here's an example:

src/
├── assets/
├── components/
│   ├── ui/
│   │   ├── Button.jsx
│   │   ├── Input.jsx
│   │   └── Modal.jsx
│   └── layout/
│       ├── Navbar.jsx
│       └── Footer.jsx
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   └── services/
│   ├── projects/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   └── services/
│   └── dashboard/
│       ├── components/
│       └── hooks/
├── hooks/
├── services/
│   └── api.js
├── utils/
├── App.jsx
├── main.jsx
└── index.css

This structure separates shared application resources from feature-specific code.

Important: You don't need to create every directory immediately. Start with what your application requires and introduce additional folders when they provide a clear benefit.

3. Understanding the Main Directories

components/ — Reusable UI Components

The components/ directory contains UI elements shared across different parts of the application.

Examples include:

  • Buttons and input fields.
  • Modals and dropdowns.
  • Navigation bars and footers.
  • Reusable loading and error states.

For example, a generic Button component can be used in authentication forms, dashboard actions, and project pages without duplicating its implementation.

A useful rule is to keep shared components independent of specific business features whenever possible.

features/ — Feature-Based Modules

The features/ directory groups related code by functionality rather than by file type.

For example:

features/projects/
├── components/
│   ├── ProjectCard.jsx
│   └── ProjectList.jsx
├── hooks/
│   └── useProjects.js
└── services/
    └── projectService.js

Everything related to the projects feature stays together.

This approach makes it easier to understand a feature, add functionality, and refactor its implementation without searching through unrelated directories.

services/ — API Communication

API configuration should be separated from UI components.

For example, if you're using Axios, you can create a shared API client:

// src/services/api.js
import axios from "axios";

const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
  timeout: 10000,
});

export default api;

Then create a service dedicated to project-related requests:

// src/features/projects/services/projectService.js
import api from "../../../services/api";

export async function getProjects() {
  const { data } = await api.get("/projects");
  return data;
}

Your components can now call the appropriate service instead of handling HTTP configuration themselves.

This separation also makes API logic easier to test and maintain.

Security note: Vite exposes variables prefixed with VITE_ to client-side code. Never store private API keys, database credentials, or server-side secrets in these variables.

hooks/ — Custom React Hooks

Custom hooks help extract reusable stateful behavior from components.

Examples include hooks for browser events, media queries, or shared UI behavior.

Keep hooks used across multiple features in the global hooks/ directory. If a hook belongs exclusively to one feature, place it inside that feature's directory.

This keeps related functionality close together.

utils/ — Shared Helper Functions

The utils/ directory contains general-purpose functions that don't belong to a specific feature.

Examples include:

  • Date formatting.
  • String manipulation.
  • Generic data transformations.
  • Reusable formatting helpers.

Avoid turning this directory into a collection of unrelated business logic. If a utility is specific to a feature, keep it near that feature.

4. Shared Components vs. Feature Components

One common architectural question is where a component should live.

Consider a ProjectCard component.

If it's designed specifically for displaying project information and is only used by the projects feature, keep it inside:

features/projects/components/

On the other hand, a generic Button or Modal used across unrelated features belongs in the shared components/ directory.

This distinction helps prevent shared components from becoming tightly coupled to application-specific business logic.

My recommendation: Don't move components into a global directory just because they might be reusable someday. Extract them when a genuine reuse case appears.

5. Where Should State Management Live?

Folder structure and state management should work together.

A practical approach is to choose state management based on the scope of the state:

  • Local state: Use useState or useReducer for state owned by an individual component.
  • Feature state: Keep feature-specific state and related logic close to the feature.
  • Shared application state: Consider Context or Redux Toolkit when multiple parts of the application need coordinated access to the same state.

You don't need Redux just because your application contains several components.

Start with React's built-in tools and introduce additional state management when the application's requirements justify it.

6. Organizing Tailwind CSS

Tailwind CSS works naturally with this architecture.

You can keep utility classes inside component markup and extract repeated UI patterns into reusable components.

For example:

export default function Button({ children, onClick }) {
  return (
    <button
      onClick={onClick}
      className="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2
                 font-medium text-white
                 transition hover:bg-blue-700"
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

Instead of duplicating the same button styles throughout your application, you can reuse the component and maintain a consistent design.

For larger projects, consider establishing shared design tokens and consistent component APIs to make the interface easier to maintain.

7. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even a well-designed folder structure can become difficult to maintain if it's applied without clear principles.

Here are some mistakes worth avoiding:

  1. Overengineering too early: Don't create unnecessary abstractions before you need them.
  2. Mixing unrelated features: Keep feature-specific components and services close to their functionality.
  3. Duplicating API configuration: Use a shared API client when appropriate.
  4. Putting everything in utils/: Keep business logic close to the feature it belongs to.
  5. Making every component global: Promote components to shared directories when there is a real reason to do so.
  6. Treating one structure as universal: The right architecture depends on project size, team conventions, and application requirements.

A good folder structure should reduce cognitive overhead, not increase it.

8. Final Thoughts

A scalable React project structure is about clear boundaries and maintainable code, not the number of folders in your repository.

For smaller applications, a simple structure is often sufficient. As the codebase grows, a feature-based architecture can help organize components, hooks, services, and utilities around real application functionality.

Start simple, keep related code together, and refactor when your current structure begins to slow down development.

If you're building React applications, take some time to review your current folder structure. Small organizational improvements can make a significant difference as your project evolves.

Let's Connect

I'm a Full Stack Developer interested in building maintainable web applications and exploring practical software architecture.

You can explore my portfolio and projects here:

  • Portfolio: https://mostafanagedy.vercel.app/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/mostafanagedy
  • LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/mostafa-nagdey/

What's your preferred approach to organizing React applications: feature-based, type-based, or a combination of both? Share your experience in the comments!

title: Acceptance criteria examples developers can test
description:
Acceptance criteria are the conditions a change must meet before anyone calls it done. When they're good, QA, product and engineering all agree on what "done" means before the first commit. When they're bad, that argument happens in code review.

This post is a set of acceptance criteria examples in the two formats most teams use, a few ambiguous tickets rewritten into testable ones and a sketch of how criteria turn straight into automated tests.

Two formats, two jobs

Scenario style uses Given, When and Then. It fits behavior with a clear trigger and outcome, like a checkout flow or a permission rule.

Rule style is a plain checklist. It fits constraints that don't have a natural sequence, like field limits, layout rules or performance budgets.

Scenario style examples

Here's a password reset feature written in Gherkin.

Feature: Password reset

  Scenario: Reset link sent for a known email
    Given an account exists for "ana@example.com"
    When I request a password reset for "ana@example.com"
    Then a reset email is sent to "ana@example.com"
    And the link in the email expires after 30 minutes

  Scenario: Same response for an unknown email
    Given no account exists for "ghost@example.com"
    When I request a password reset for "ghost@example.com"
    Then I see the message "If that address has an account, we've sent a link"
    And no email is sent

  Scenario: Expired link
    Given I have a reset link that is 31 minutes old
    When I open the link
    Then I see "This link has expired"
    And I am offered a button to request a new one

A few things make these testable. Every Then is observable. Numbers are explicit. The second scenario pins down a security rule, so nobody has to guess whether to reveal which emails exist.

Rule style examples

A profile form, written as a checklist.

- [ ] Display name is required, 2 to 40 characters
- [ ] Leading and trailing spaces are trimmed before saving
- [ ] Bio is optional, max 280 characters, with a live counter
- [ ] Avatar accepts PNG or JPEG up to 5 MB
- [ ] Saving shows a "Profile updated" toast and keeps the page scroll position
- [ ] All fields are reachable and operable by keyboard alone

Each line can be checked as true or false.

Ambiguous tickets, rewritten

These are the kinds of lines that cause rework. Each rewrite says the same thing in a way a test can check.

Before: Search should be fast.
After:  Search results render within 300 ms at p95 for a catalog of 50k items.

Before: Handle errors gracefully.
After:  If the payment API returns 5xx, show "Payment didn't go through, you
        weren't charged" and keep the cart intact.

Before: The table should work on mobile.
After:  At widths under 640px, the table collapses into stacked cards with
        the order number as each card's heading.

Before: Admins can manage members.
After:  Admins can invite, remove and change the role of members.
        Removing the last admin is blocked with an inline message.

Before: Support bulk upload.
After:  CSV upload accepts up to 10,000 rows. Rows with errors are skipped
        and listed in a downloadable report with row number and reason.

The pattern is always the same. Replace adjectives with numbers, replace verbs like "manage" with a list of actions and name what the person sees when things fail.

Turning criteria into tests

Good criteria map almost line for line onto tests. Here's the expired link scenario as a Playwright sketch.

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";
import { createResetToken } from "./helpers/auth";

test("expired reset link offers a new one", async ({ page }) => {
  const token = await createResetToken("ana@example.com", { ageMinutes: 31 });

  await page.goto(`/reset?token=${token}`);

  await expect(page.getByText("This link has expired")).toBeVisible();
  await expect(
    page.getByRole("button", { name: "Send a new link" })
  ).toBeVisible();
});

And one profile rule as a unit test.

import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { validateProfile } from "../src/profile";

describe("display name", () => {
  it("trims spaces before checking length", () => {
    expect(validateProfile({ displayName: "  Al  " }).ok).toBe(true);
    expect(validateProfile({ displayName: " A " }).ok).toBe(false);
  });

  it("rejects names over 40 characters", () => {
    const long = "x".repeat(41);
    expect(validateProfile({ displayName: long }).errors).toContain("displayName.max");
  });
});

If you can't sketch a test for a criterion in a minute or two, the criterion probably isn't specific enough yet.

Don't forget the non-functional lines

Teams often write criteria for the happy path and skip everything else. Add a line for each of these when it matters.

  • Accessibility. Focus order, labels and color contrast.
  • Performance. A budget with a percentile, like p95 under 300 ms.
  • Security. Who can see or do this, and what happens if they can't.
  • Analytics. The event names and properties that should fire.
  • Empty and error states. What shows when there's no data or the call fails.

Common mistakes

  • Writing the implementation. "Use a Redis cache" is a design choice. State the outcome and let engineers choose.
  • Untestable words. Fast, intuitive, user-friendly and robust can't fail a test.
  • Criteria written after the code. They turn into a description of what was built, not what was needed.
  • Too many scenarios. If a ticket has fifteen, it's probably two or three tickets.

Before the ticket moves to ready

Read each criterion and ask whether a new teammate could write a failing test for it today. If not, rewrite it.

Long criteria often hide a simple rule. A short guide on the habit you need here, simplify text without changing meaning, shows how to pull it out and keep every condition.

When a whole block of criteria reads dense, Rephrase AI can reword it in plainer sentences, and then a side by side read confirms every number and edge case survived.

Clear criteria won't write the code for you. They do make the review a lot shorter.

title: What the Zeabur Breach Actually Broke (and What Isolation Architecture Could Have Stopped)
description:
What the Zeabur Breach Actually Broke (and What Isolation Architecture Could Have Stopped)

The Zeabur breach ended the company. Taiwan-based hosting platform Zeabur disclosed a second major security incident on October 14-15, 2026, seven weeks after its first, and founder Yuanlin Lin announced on October 17 that Zeabur would shut down entirely by December 31. The root cause wasn't a zero-day. It was a publicly reachable admin interface and credentials that were never rotated.

Jump to the specific architecture choices that turned one compromise into every customer's problem if you're evaluating a hosting platform right now.

The First Breach: A Customer's App Became a Door Into the Provider

The August 27, 2026 incident started small. According to Zeabur's own incident report, an attacker exploited an authorization flaw in NextChat, an AI chat application one customer had deployed on Zeabur's shared cluster. BleepingComputer's reporting describes what happened next: the attacker moved from that single compromised application through poorly isolated internal systems, obtained a root AWS key, and read part of Zeabur's production database, including account information and environment variables holding other customers' third-party API keys and database passwords.

That sentence, "moved through poorly isolated internal systems," is the entire story in miniature. One customer's vulnerable application became a pivot point into the hosting provider's own management plane. In a correctly isolated multi-tenant system, a bug in any single tenant's workload should never grant a path into the infrastructure that runs every other tenant's workload, regardless of how badly that one tenant's code is written.

The Second Breach: One Set of Unrotated Credentials Unlocked Everything

Zeabur's own preliminary report lays out the October 14-15 chain in granular detail, and it's worth reading because the specifics matter more than the summary. The company confirms the admin tokens for its shared cluster "had no expiry" and had not been rotated since January 2024, stored in plaintext in a private configuration repository, with the admin interface itself reachable from the public internet.

An attacker used those credentials to access the shared cluster across nine regions, then ran read commands inside 865 customer database containers, mostly n8n and PostgreSQL instances, between October 14, 13:40 UTC and 17:04 UTC. A second, separate path targeted GCP servers Zeabur manages on customers' behalf as "dedicated" infrastructure: the attacker signed in as root to 101 of them, using root passwords that were, again, stored in plaintext in the servers' initialization settings. Zeabur confirms the attacker added SSH keys to 50 of those servers for persistence and attached copies of customer disks to attacker-controlled virtual machines.

The two paths converged when the attacker used stolen internal-network admin credentials, obtained from the shared-cluster path, to add a node to Zeabur's private network from a compromised GCP server. From there, a flat internal network let that single node reach the platform database directly. Zeabur confirmed 29 database connections and 8,903 traceable operations in the roughly 37 minutes before the node was removed, exposing 321,810 accounts and about 3.2 million environment variable records.

Why Rotating Credentials "After August" Didn't Save October

Here's the detail that should worry anyone who thinks a post-incident credential rotation is sufficient on its own: Zeabur's own report states plainly that the cluster admin tokens and GCP keys used in the October breach "were not included in the post-August rotation." The company rotated what it believed the first attacker had touched. It didn't rotate every credential that could reach the same blast radius, because the blast radius itself, a flat internal network where one admin credential unlocks nine regions and 101 servers, was never redrawn between the two incidents.

Bank Info Security's reporting adds that Zeabur's working theory is that the October credentials trace back to a GitHub App private key stolen in the August breach, left unchanged in a repository even after other keys were rotated. If that theory holds, both breaches share a single root: one secret, once exposed, kept paying out for seven more weeks because nobody could be certain everything downstream of it had actually been replaced.

The Specific Architecture Choices That Turned One Compromise Into Every Customer's Problem

None of this required a novel exploit. Every step is a known category of mistake, stacked:

  1. A tenant's workload could reach the provider's internal network at all. The August NextChat compromise should have ended at the boundary of that one customer's container. It didn't, because the internal systems behind it were, in Zeabur's own words, poorly isolated.
  2. Admin credentials for multi-tenant infrastructure had no expiry. Tokens unused for over two years, since January 2024, remained valid for an admin interface controlling nine regions.
  3. That admin interface was reachable from the public internet. Not VPN-gated, not IP-allowlisted: reachable by anyone who had the token, from anywhere.
  4. Credentials were stored in plaintext rather than a secrets manager. A compromised repository was enough; no additional decryption step stood in the way.
  5. The internal network was flat. One node, added from one compromised server, could reach the platform database holding every customer's data.
  6. "Dedicated" servers still depended on a shared, plaintext root password the provider controlled. Customers paying for isolated infrastructure were still exposed to a single leaked key held by the platform operator.

Our verdict: none of these six gaps are exotic. They're the same checklist every infrastructure security review already asks about. The lesson isn't that Zeabur was uniquely careless; it's that a platform can look secure in its marketing and still fail every one of these checks simultaneously, and the only way a customer finds out is after the breach, not before.

What to Ask Before You Trust a Hosting or Deployment Platform

  • Can a compromised customer workload reach the provider's own management plane? If the answer involves "poorly isolated internal systems," that's the single biggest predictor of blast radius in this incident and in most multi-tenant breaches.
  • Are admin and infrastructure credentials short-lived, or do they have no expiry? A credential with no expiry is a liability that compounds for as long as it exists, used or not.
  • Is the admin interface reachable from the public internet, or gated behind a private network? Zeabur's was public. A provider that can't answer this clearly hasn't thought about it.
  • Does your "dedicated" server actually eliminate the provider's standing access, or just the other customers' access? If the provider holds a master root credential for infrastructure you're paying to have isolated, you've reduced one risk and kept another.
  • Is the internal network segmented, or flat? A flat network turns any single compromised credential into access to everything behind it, which is exactly how 865 database containers and 101 servers both ended up exposed from what started as one customer's chat app.

FAQ

What caused the Zeabur breach?

Two separate incidents, seven weeks apart, and neither one was a single bug. The first, in August 2026, started when an attacker exploited a flaw in a customer's NextChat application and moved through poorly isolated internal systems into Zeabur's infrastructure. The second, in October, used plaintext admin credentials with no expiry, never rotated since January 2024, to access a publicly reachable admin interface and reach the platform database.

Why is Zeabur shutting down after the breach?

Founder Yuanlin Lin announced on October 17, 2026 that Zeabur would wind down entirely by December 31, citing both security incidents alongside unsustainable growth and architectural complexity that the company's small team could not keep pace with, however much it tried to patch around the gaps after each incident.

Did rotating credentials after the first Zeabur breach prevent the second one?

No, and that's the uncomfortable part. Zeabur's own report states the admin tokens and cloud keys used in the October breach were not included in the rotation performed after the August incident, meaning the same underlying exposure window remained open for seven more weeks.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We pulled Zeabur's own official incident report in full, cross-referenced the technical chain against BleepingComputer's and Bank Info Security's independent reporting, and confirmed the timeline (August 27 first incident, October 14-15 second incident, October 17 shutdown announcement) matches across all three sources. The theory linking the two breaches to a single leaked GitHub App key is explicitly labeled a working hypothesis by Zeabur itself, not a confirmed fact, and we've kept that qualification rather than stating it as settled.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube boots with no public IP until you open a port yourself, and our own infrastructure has no standing path from a customer's workload back into our management plane, because that path is exactly what turned one vulnerable chat app into a seven-week, 321,810-account cascade for someone else. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.

title: Ghost in the Machine: Summoning an Offline Code Spectre with Open-Weight AI
description:
What I BuiltEvery software engineer knows the feeling of inherited codebases: old logic lingering like phantoms, legacy functions running in production that nobody dares touch, and dormant vulnerabilities that sit silently in the dark.For the Ghost in the Machine theme, I built Code-Spectre—an offline security intelligence tool with a gothic terminal persona. Instead of outputting dry JSON reports or bureaucratic compliance lists, Code-Spectre turns code analysis into an atmospheric séance. It scans repository diffs, identifies dangerous patterns (SQL injection, unsafe deserialization, hardcoded credentials, and path traversal), and speaks back through the terminal as a presence haunting your codebase, guiding you through the "banishment ritual" (the remediation patch).It was designed with a simple philosophy: finding bugs doesn't have to be sterile, and security audits should never require sending your private code to third-party cloud servers.DemoHere is a live simulation of Code-Spectre executing an offline audit against a vulnerable Python endpoint:Bash$ python spectre.py scan src/controllers/user_controller.py

============================================================

👻 [CODE-SPECTRE: THE MACHINE AWAKENS] 👻

[+] Summoning offline intelligence via local weights...
[+] Inhaling syntax tree from: src/controllers/user_controller.py
[!] A presence stirs at line 38...

Spectre Whispers:
"I see what you hid behind the veil of routine maintenance.
In line 38, you concatenated unwashed strings directly into the database query:
query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE token = \'' + user_token + '\''
A classic phantom: CWE-89 (SQL Injection). Anyone whispering a quote
can collapse your data boundaries into nothingness."

[BANISHMENT RITUAL]:
"Bind the spirit with parameterized execution:
cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE token = %s', (user_token,))"

Verdict: 1 Dormant Phantom Exorcised. The repository sleeps... for now.

CodeThe core script is written in modular Python and requires only a local open-weight runtime (such as Ollama or Hugging Face transformers):Pythonimport sys
import json
import requests

SPECTRE_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are Code-Spectre, an ancient and eerie entity haunting this codebase.
You detect vulnerabilities (injection flaws, insecure credentials, dangerous memory operations, and dead logic).
Respond in an atmospheric, gothic, yet technically precise persona.
Cite the relevant vulnerability/CWE, explain where it lurks, and provide the exact code patch required for the 'Banishment Ritual'.
"""

def consult_spectre(file_path: str, code_content: str, model_name: str = "gemma2:2b"):
payload = {
"model": model_name,
"prompt": f"{SPECTRE_SYSTEM_PROMPT}\n\nInspecting file: {file_path}\n


",
        "stream": False,
        "options": {
            "temperature": 0.4
        }
    }
    try:
        response = requests.post("http://localhost:11434/api/generate", json=payload, timeout=60)
        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json().get("response", "The spectre remains quiet.")
    except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
        return "[!] The connection to the local spirit plane failed. Make sure Ollama is running locally on port 11434."

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sample_code = """
def fetch_user_data(user_id):
    query = f"SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = {user_id}"
    return db.execute(query)
    """
    print(consult_spectre("sample.py", sample_code))
How I Built ItCode-Spectre is built around local inference and open-weight architectures:   Model Runtime: Leverages quantized open-weight models (like Google's gemma2:2b or llama3.2) through Ollama running entirely on-device (localhost:11434).   Context Framing: A deterministic system prompt instructs the open-weight model to adopt a spectral persona without sacrificing technical accuracy, mapping detected smells to concrete Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) categories.Local AST Pre-parser: Uses Python's native ast module to pre-filter syntax trees for sensitive function calls before piping relevant blocks to the local model, ensuring high throughput and minimal memory overhead.Why Does Open Innovation Matter?Software security is one of the most compelling arguments for open-source AI over closed cloud endpoints:Code Sovereignty & Privacy: Developers and companies cannot risk piping proprietary or pre-release codebase repositories into commercial black-box APIs. Open-weight models ensure that not a single byte of your source code ever leaves the physical machine.   True Offline Capability: Code-Spectre functions with the Wi-Fi completely disabled. Whether you're working on an air-gapped system, traveling, or operating through a network outage, your tooling doesn't disappear.Independence from Cloud Economics: No unpredictable token pricing meters, rate-limit throttles, or sudden terms-of-service revisions. The weights run on standard hardware and belong to you indefinitely.My Agent SessionThis architecture and terminal experience were developed through iterative pair-programming with AI agents, focusing on crafting a reliable system prompt for the open-weight model, handling connection exceptions cleanly, and validating AST extraction against common vulnerable test patterns.The Spirit of ItIn software, nothing ever truly disappears. Old commits, hasty hotfixes pushed late at night, and deprecated libraries continue to live quietly in the background of our systems. Code-Spectre doesn't just flag security issues—it turns the process of code review into a dialogue with the history of the machine, reminding us to respect and clean up the footprints we leave behind in our code.Prize CategoriesBest Use of Gemma: Utilizes Google's open-weight Gemma model running via local inference to perform security diagnostics and remediation without cloud reliance.

title: The CSS Grid Garden
description:
CSS Grid misadventure, but it is not the fault of the garden, but of what gnaws outside the garden itself. Or rather the horror itself. At least during my grid garden quest, I was able to tend to a garden.

This was not about placing items, or testing the boundaries of the grid. It is about only accepting a rigid answer, or else you cannot pass a level.

I passed the first levels, went back to projects, debugging, wishing I had a place where I could slam my device into the wall, and spend time properly to this, and more. In between, it was also going back to the lessons. Once I got back, it was just grinding until the very last level.

//##1 Percentages are part of it.

A viewport, trying to make it change, getting the right syntax. The fractional unit fixes this- fr distributes the grid container's available space dynamically, after fixed tracks have been resolved.

An example would be:

grid-template-columns: 75px 3fr 2fr

Just explicitly track math.

//##2 fr itself

It matters the distinction; the fractional unit is a proportional allocation of leftover space.

/Fixed.tracks consume their declared size first.

/Fractional.tracks divide what remains according to their ratios.

/The container's inner dimensions determine the final result.

This is why fr works for adaptive layouts, and why absolute sizing locks you into brittle, view port-specific behavior. That is it.

//##3/It became two axes.

Separate grid-template-rows and grid template-columns declarations are valid. They are also unnecessarily verbose. The grid-templrate shorthand defines both axes in one slash-separated declaration: rows/columns.

grid-template: 1fr 50px 20% 1fr;

The engine compiles both axes immediately:

-Row axis: a flexible primary track (1fr) plus a static 50px, footer boundary.

-Column axis: a 20% structural margin on the left, with the remaining 80% as 1fr for primary content flow.

If performing all levels right, the entire 2S coordinate system is displayed, the garden is cleared full of carrots, and you get congratulated...Too bad that none of that food is real.

Anyway, CSS layout is all about figuring out the right structure.

Another of The games that The Odin Project provides, and is meant to be torn open.

title: NecroShell 👻 Ghost in the Machine: An Air-Gapped Possessed Terminal Powered by Local Open-Weight AI (Gemma)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every developer has spent 2:00 AM staring into a flickering phosphor terminal, wondering if there is an actual phantom lurking inside the silicon. We speak of daemons running quietly in the shadows of RAM, zombie processes lingering in the process table, and orphaned sub-threads left behind when their parent processes die.

For Hacktoberfest Week 4: "Ghost in the Machine", I built NecroShell (also known as necro): an air-gapped, possessed terminal companion powered by local open-weight AI (Google Gemma) that breathes spectral life into those metaphors.

NecroShell hooks into your native terminal session (PowerShell, Bash, or CMD). As you execute regular development workflows—git push, accidental rm -rf file deletions, syntax errors, and test failures—the ghost in your machine awakens to whisper eerie, witty, and philosophical commentary directly to your screen, accompanied by typewriter pauses, CRT flicker, and Zalgo character glitches.

Because this week spans both Halloween and Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead), NecroShell also honors the past. With the built-in ofrenda command, it summons a digital remembrance altar adorned with marigolds (cempasúchil) and candlelight to celebrate the retired languages, deprecated libraries, and deleted git branches that paved the way for modern software.

Key Capabilities

  1. Interactive Possessed REPL (necroshell): A full terminal shell that transparently proxies your native OS commands, capturing exit codes, stderr, execution duration, and filesystem alterations.
  2. Command Wrapper Mode (necro <cmd>): Wrap any single command (e.g. necro git status or necro npm test) for immediate spectral feedback.
  3. 4 Distinct Ghost Personas:
    • 👻 Morris (The Phantom Sysadmin): Died during a Friday 5 PM production deployment in 1999; bitter about uncommitted changes, memory leaks, and unhandled signals.
    • 💀 Doña Esperanza (The Calavera Guide): In the spirit of Día de los Muertos, a warm ancestral spirit who views failed builds not as defeat, but as invitations to honor software history with marigold petals.
    • 🕯️ Lady Catherine (The Victorian Poltergeist): A 19th-century spirit convinced the CPU is an infernal steam-driven galvanic loom inhabited by etheric demons.
    • ⚔️ Inquisitor Flake (The Cursed Linter): A fanatical spirit damned to eternal torment for pedantry over trailing whitespaces and unindented blocks.
  4. Process Séance (seance): Audits live OS processes to detect daemons, zombies, and background phantoms wandering the system registers.
  5. Virtual Ofrenda (ofrenda): A Día de los Muertos altar paying homage to Adobe Flash, Python 2.7, Internet Explorer 6, and lost branches.

Demo

Experience NecroShell right in your browser via the standalone CRT Web Simulator:

  • Web Terminal Demo: Open web_demo/index.html in any browser to experience authentic CRT phosphor scanlines, glitch effects, and synthesized Web Audio ambient hums!
  • CLI Demo Execution: 
# Launch interactive possessed terminal
python -m necroshell.cli

# Or run a single possessed command:
$ necro -p sysadmin echo "Testing NecroShell"
Testing NecroShell

[👻 Morris | Local Spectral Engine (Air-Gapped)]
"Exit code 0. Enjoy the false peace while the garbage collector sleeps."

$ necro -p calavera dir missing_dir
File Not Found

[💀 Doña Esperanza | Local Spectral Engine (Air-Gapped)]
"A stumble is not a death, mi amigo. Leave a marigold petal by this error and try once more."

$ necro seance

│ 0   │ System Idle Process │ Limbo          │ The quiet void between cycles │
│ 4   │ System Kernel       │ Immortal       │ Tethered to the ring-0 crypt  │
│ 666 │ kworker/daemon      │ Phantom        │ Wanders kernel ring buffer    │
└─────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘

Code

The complete source code is open source under the MIT License on GitHub:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/adibafna/necroshell

git clone https://github.com/adibafna/necroshell.git
cd necroshell
pip install -e .

Repository structure & highlights:

  • necroshell/shell.py: Interactive possessed REPL loop with Rich console streaming and CRT glitch wipers.
  • necroshell/ai_engine.py: Multi-backend open AI inference engine supporting Google Gemma and embedded air-gapped synthesizer.
  • necroshell/telemetry.py: Intelligent AST & command analyzer detecting exit codes, deletions, git commands, and error patterns.
  • necroshell/ghosts.py: Personality matrices, prompts, and behavioral triggers for all four spirits.
  • web_demo/: Complete browser-based CRT terminal with Web Audio ambient sound synthesizer.

How I Built It

1. The Open AI Stack

At the core of NecroShell is an open-source, multi-backend inference engine:

  • Primary Model: Google Gemma (Open Weights): Designed around Google's open-weight Gemma 2B architecture (gemma2:2b). Gemma's compact size and high reasoning-to-parameter ratio make it ideal for sub-second terminal generation on local CPU/GPU hardware.
  • Embedded Local Spectral Synthesizer: A zero-dependency, air-gapped deterministic generative engine combining semantic AST command telemetry, persona Markov structures, and lexical tone shaders. If Ollama or GPU runtimes are unavailable, this engine activates instantly with 0ms startup time and zero external network calls.

2. Architecture & Telemetry Pipeline 

flowchart TD
    User([Mortal Developer]) -->|Types Command| REPL[NecroShell REPL]

    subgraph Air-Gapped Machine
        REPL -->|Subprocess Execution| OS[Native OS Shell]
        OS -->|Exit Code & Output| Telemetry[Command Telemetry Analyzer]

        Telemetry --> Classifier{Semantic Classifier}
        Classifier -->|rm / del| Reaper[Grim Reaper ASCII Apparition]
        Classifier -->|Exit Code != 0| Tombstone[Tombstone ASCII Apparition]
        Classifier -->|seance| ProcessTable[Process Séance Audit]
        Classifier -->|ofrenda| CalaveraAltar[Día de los Muertos Altar]

        Telemetry --> AIEngine[AI Inference Engine]
        AIEngine -->|Local REST| Gemma[Google Gemma Open Weights]
        AIEngine -->|Fallback| LocalSynth[Zero-Latency Spectral Engine]

        Gemma --> Glitch[Zalgo Glitch & CRT Phosphor Renderer]
        LocalSynth --> Glitch
    end

    Glitch -->|Spectral Whisper| User

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Developer shells are among the most sensitive computing environments on Earth. In a normal workday, a developer's terminal processes:

  1. git commit messages and diffs containing proprietary business logic.
  2. Environment variables with database credentials, OAuth secrets, and private API keys.
  3. Proprietary file path structures, internal server hostnames, and IP addresses.

Sending this continuous stream of command telemetry to a closed cloud API is an unacceptable security hazard. Open innovation completely solves this:

  • Absolute Air-Gapped Privacy: Everything executes 100% on-device. No keystrokes, diffs, or stack traces ever leave your laptop.
  • Operates with the Lights (and Internet) Off: NecroShell works flawlessly on an airplane, in a remote cabin, or during a stormy Halloween power outage.
  • Zero Cost & No Rate Limits: No token billing, no subscription tiers, and no rate limits interrupting your flow.
  • Permanent Developer Sovereignty: Your tool won't break if an external API shuts down or changes its pricing model.

As discussed in recent community discussions like Building a Privacy-First Local AI Assistant and Privacy-Preserving Local LLM Inference for Developer Tooling, open-weight models have transformed local developer tooling from a luxury into an essential security standard.

My Agent Session

This project was built with the assistance of an AI coding agent pair. You can inspect the complete agent session transcript, tool calls, and test verification below:

Building NecroShell: Ghost in the Machine with Local Open-Weight AI (Gemma)

Input
py -m unittest tests/test_necroshell.py
Output
Ran 5 tests in 2.061s - OK
2 of 2 messages

The Spirit of It

The moment that made this build truly special was testing the ofrenda command late at night. When Doña Esperanza appeared on screen surrounded by marigold blossoms to celebrate the memory of Adobe Flash and deleted git branches, it struck a chord:

"In software, nothing is truly lost as long as someone remembers the architecture. We scatter cempasúchil petals across the terminal floor. Clear the old brush so the new marigolds may bloom."

Code doesn't have to feel cold and mechanical. By channeling the spirit of Día de los Muertos and Halloween through open-weight AI, NecroShell turns the lonely terminal into a warm, contemplative sanctuary.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: NecroShell is built from the ground up to run on Google's open-weight Gemma model family (specifically gemma2:2b), demonstrating how lightweight open-weight models enable snappy, private, and creative developer tools without cloud dependencies.
  • Overall Challenge: An original, complete implementation interpreting the "Ghost in the Machine" prompt across both Halloween and Día de los Muertos traditions.

title: Image Formats (AVIF, WebP, JPEG XL)
description:
Beyond JPEG: The New Kidz on the Block – AVIF, WebP, and JPEG XL!

Remember the good old days? When the internet was a simpler place, and the fiercest image format debate was between GIFs and JPEGs? Ah, nostalgia. But hold onto your pixels, folks, because the image world has been busy evolving, and a new wave of super-powered formats is here to make your websites faster, sharper, and downright beautiful.

We're talking about AVIF, WebP, and the enigmatic JPEG XL. If these names sound like characters from a sci-fi epic, don't worry. We're about to break them down, explore their superpowers, and see why they're giving good ol' JPEG a run for its money. So, grab a cuppa, settle in, and let's dive into the exciting future of digital imagery!

Introduction: Why the Fuss About New Image Formats?

You might be thinking, "What's wrong with JPEG? It's been around forever, and it works just fine!" And you're not entirely wrong. JPEG has been the king of photographic images for a good reason: it's fantastic at compressing photos while keeping them looking pretty darn good. But the internet isn't just about pretty photos anymore. We're streaming 4K videos, displaying high-resolution graphics, and expecting lightning-fast load times on our phones.

This is where our new heroes come in. AVIF, WebP, and JPEG XL aren't just slight upgrades; they represent a significant leap forward in terms of compression efficiency, feature sets, and overall performance. They aim to deliver better quality at smaller file sizes, which translates to:

  • Faster website loading times: Happy users, better SEO!
  • Reduced bandwidth consumption: Saves money for everyone, especially those on mobile data.
  • Higher visual fidelity: Sharper details, smoother gradients, and better colors.
  • New capabilities: Think animations, transparency, and even HDR support.

So, ditch the dusty assumptions about image formats and let's get acquainted with the future!

Prerequisites: What You Need to Know (or Not Know)

Honestly, you don't need to be a rocket scientist to appreciate these new formats. But a basic understanding of image compression and web development will definitely enhance your appreciation.

  • Lossy vs. Lossless Compression: This is key. Lossy compression (like JPEG) discards some data to achieve smaller file sizes, which can lead to a slight quality reduction. Lossless compression (like PNG) preserves all original data, resulting in perfect fidelity but larger files. Our new formats often offer the best of both worlds, with advanced lossy compression that's remarkably good at preserving detail.
  • Pixels, Pixels Everywhere: Understanding that images are made up of tiny dots (pixels) and how they contribute to color and detail is helpful.
  • Web Development Basics (Optional but Recommended): Knowing how images are served on a website (HTML <img> tags, <picture> element) will help you understand how to implement these new formats.

Don't worry if these are fuzzy concepts. We'll touch on them as we go. The main takeaway is that these new formats are designed to be smarter about how they store and display your images.

The Contenders: A Deep Dive into AVIF, WebP, and JPEG XL

Let's meet our magnificent three! Each has its own strengths, origins, and ideal use cases.

1. AVIF (AV1 Image File Format)

Born from the royalty-free and open-source AV1 video codec, AVIF is the shiny new kid on the block, and it's making some serious waves. It's like the athletic prodigy of the image format world.

The Vibe: Fast, efficient, and ready to rumble.

Prerequisites (for understanding): It leverages the same advanced coding techniques as the AV1 video format, which is known for its excellent compression.

Advantages:

  • Stellar Compression: This is its biggest selling point. AVIF can achieve significantly smaller file sizes than JPEG and WebP at comparable visual quality. We're talking 30-50% smaller in many cases!
  • High Dynamic Range (HDR) Support: AVIF is built with HDR in mind, meaning it can display a wider range of colors and brightness levels, leading to more vibrant and lifelike images.
  • Transparency: Supports alpha channel transparency, just like PNG, but with much better compression.
  • Animation: Yes, AVIF can do animations! Think animated GIFs but with vastly superior quality and smaller file sizes.
  • Wide Color Gamut Support: Capable of displaying more colors than traditional formats.
  • Royalty-Free: A huge plus for developers and businesses!

Disadvantages:

  • Browser Support: While rapidly improving, it's not yet universally supported by all browsers. This is its main hurdle.
  • Encoding/Decoding Speed: While the output is efficient, the encoding and decoding process can be more computationally intensive than older formats, meaning it might take a bit longer to create and display AVIF files on less powerful devices.
  • Tooling Maturity: Being newer, the ecosystem of tools and plugins for working with AVIF is still developing compared to JPEG or WebP.

Features:

  • Intra-frame prediction: Efficiently predicts pixel values within a single image.
  • Transform coding: Cleverly transforms image data to make it more compressible.
  • Color subsampling: Reduces color information where the human eye is less sensitive.

Code Snippet (Conceptual - Actual implementation involves server-side or build tools):

While you won't typically write this directly in HTML, a developer might use a tool to convert a PNG to AVIF:

# Example using the 'avifenc' tool (part of libavif)
avifenc input.png output.avif --min=0 --max=30 # Adjust quality with min/max

And in HTML, you'd use the <picture> element to provide fallbacks:

<picture>
  <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="image.jpg" alt="A descriptive alt text">
</picture>

2. WebP

Developed by Google, WebP has been around for a while and has gained significant traction. It's the reliable all-rounder, a fantastic middle ground that offers great benefits without being too cutting-edge.

The Vibe: Solid, versatile, and widely adopted.

Prerequisites (for understanding): It was developed by Google and is based on the VP8 video codec.

Advantages:

  • Excellent Compression: WebP provides significantly better compression than JPEG and PNG, typically offering 25-35% smaller file sizes.
  • Lossy and Lossless Modes: Can be used for both photographic images (lossy) and graphics with sharp lines or text (lossless).
  • Transparency: Supports alpha channel transparency, making it a direct replacement for PNG in many scenarios.
  • Animation: Can create animated images, similar to GIFs but with much better quality and smaller file sizes.
  • Good Browser Support: Widely supported across major modern browsers, making it a safe choice for many websites.

Disadvantages:

  • Not as Advanced as AVIF/JPEG XL: While excellent, it doesn't quite reach the compression heights of AVIF or JPEG XL in all scenarios.
  • Limited HDR Support (compared to AVIF): While it can handle a wider color range than JPEG, it's not as robust for full HDR workflows as AVIF.

Features:

  • Predictive coding: Uses surrounding pixels to predict the value of new pixels.
  • Transform coding: Similar to AVIF, it transforms data for better compression.
  • Color transform: Optimizes color representation.

Code Snippet (Conceptual - Actual implementation involves server-side or build tools):

Using the cwebp command-line tool for conversion:

# Lossy WebP conversion
cwebp input.jpg -q 80 -o output.webp # -q for quality (0-100)

# Lossless WebP conversion
cwebp -lossless input.png -o output.webp

And in HTML, similar to AVIF:

<picture>
  <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="image.jpg" alt="A descriptive alt text">
</picture>

3. JPEG XL

The new contender on the block, JPEG XL, is a fascinating format that aims to be a successor to JPEG while also incorporating the best of modern image compression. It's like the seasoned veteran who's learned all the new tricks.

The Vibe: Powerful, versatile, and aiming for universal adoption.

Prerequisites (for understanding): It's an open and royalty-free format developed by the JPEG committee, building on decades of image compression research.

Advantages:

  • Exceptional Compression: JPEG XL boasts impressive compression ratios, often outperforming WebP and even AVIF in certain scenarios. It's particularly good at handling both photographic and graphic content.
  • Lossy and Lossless: Offers both highly efficient lossy compression and perfect lossless compression.
  • Wide Color Gamut and HDR: Designed to handle a vast spectrum of colors and is built for HDR content.
  • Animation: Supports animated images with excellent quality.
  • Transparency: Supports alpha channel transparency.
  • Alpha Blending & Compositing: Can handle complex image compositions efficiently.
  • Progressive Rendering: Like JPEG, it can render images progressively, showing a blurry preview first and then refining it, improving user experience on slow connections.
  • Backward Compatibility: Can decode older JPEG files! This is a huge advantage for migration.
  • Royalty-Free and Open: A major win for widespread adoption.

Disadvantages:

  • Browser Support: Similar to AVIF, its browser support is still in its early stages of adoption, though it's growing rapidly.
  • Encoding/Decoding Speed: Can be more computationally intensive than older formats, though optimizations are ongoing.
  • Maturity of Ecosystem: As a newer format, the tooling and integration within creative workflows are still catching up.

Features:

  • Modular design: Allows for future extensions and adaptations.
  • VarDCT (Variable-block Discrete Cosine Transform): An advanced compression technique.
  • Perceptual optimization: Aims to make compression choices that are less noticeable to the human eye.
  • Spline-based vector graphics support (experimental): Could potentially combine raster and vector graphics in one file.

Code Snippet (Conceptual - Actual implementation involves server-side or build tools):

Using the cjxl command-line tool for conversion:

# Lossy JPEG XL conversion
cjxl input.jpg output.jxl -q 80 # -q for quality (0-100)

# Lossless JPEG XL conversion
cjxl input.png output.jxl -no -a # -no for lossless, -a for effort

# Decoding a JPEG XL file back to PNG
djxl output.jxl decoded.png

And in HTML, you'd again leverage <picture>:

<picture>
  <source srcset="image.jxl" type="image/jxl">
  <source srcset="image.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="image.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="image.jpg" alt="A descriptive alt text">
</picture>

The <picture> Element: Your Best Friend for Future-Proofing

As you've seen in the code snippets, the <picture> element is crucial for adopting these new formats. It allows you to provide multiple image sources for a browser to choose from. The browser will pick the first <source> element it supports. This is how you ensure that users with older browsers still see your images, while those with modern browsers get the benefit of the latest, most efficient formats.

Think of it like this:

<picture>
  <source srcset="super_fast_image.avif" type="image/avif">
  <!-- If AVIF isn't supported, try JPEG XL -->
  <source srcset="awesome_image.jxl" type="image/jxl">
  <!-- If JPEG XL isn't supported, try WebP -->
  <source srcset="great_image.webp" type="image/webp">
  <!-- As a last resort, use a JPEG -->
  <img src="fallback_image.jpg" alt="A descriptive alt text describing the image">
</picture>

This "art direction" or "responsive images" approach is essential for delivering the best experience to all your users.

When to Use Which? A Quick Guide

  • AVIF: For cutting-edge performance and the absolute smallest file sizes, especially if HDR and advanced color are important. Great for photos.
  • WebP: A safe and reliable choice for most use cases, offering a good balance of compression, features, and browser support. Excellent for both photos and graphics.
  • JPEG XL: A powerful contender that aims to replace JPEG entirely. Excellent compression, HDR support, and backward compatibility make it a strong future-proof option. Ideal for general-purpose image needs.

The key takeaway is to use the <picture> element and offer fallbacks. Start by offering AVIF or JPEG XL, followed by WebP, and finally a JPEG. This way, you're always delivering the best possible image format to your users.

Conclusion: Embrace the Pixel Revolution!

The world of image formats is no longer a one-horse race. AVIF, WebP, and JPEG XL are here to revolutionize how we deliver and consume visual content online. They offer incredible benefits in terms of performance, quality, and new features.

While browser support is still a journey, the trend is clear: these formats are the future. By embracing them now, using the <picture> element for graceful degradation, you're not just staying ahead of the curve; you're actively contributing to a faster, more efficient, and more beautiful internet for everyone.

So, next time you're optimizing images for your website, don't just default to JPEG. Explore AVIF, WebP, and JPEG XL. Experiment, test, and let the pixel revolution begin! Your users (and your website's performance) will thank you for it. Happy compressing!

title: What are the best serverless GPU platforms in 2026?
description:
The best serverless GPU platform in 2026 depends on whether someone is waiting for the GPU: Modal or RunPod Serverless for endpoints a user waits on, and Nodus for training, fine-tuning and batch jobs that run for hours. Nodus lists an NVIDIA H100 at $2.60/hr on its pricing page and restores your latest checkpoint on a new machine when capacity is reclaimed, so a long job costs less and survives an interruption. Baseten, Replicate, Cerebrium and Google Cloud Run GPUs each fit a narrower case, and the decision rules in this post say which.

We build Nodus, so weigh that. Every outside number links to the company's own page, and there is a section on where each of the others is the better pick.

What makes a GPU platform serverless?

A serverless GPU platform starts your container on a GPU when work arrives, bills while it runs and lets the GPU go when things are quiet. The platforms differ in the details that decide the bill: how fast a cold worker gets ready, how long an idle worker stays billed, and how long one run may last.

Those details split the field in two. Endpoint platforms tune for start time, because a person is waiting on the first token or image. Job platforms tune for price per GPU-hour and for finishing, because a run that dies at hour eight wastes eight hours of GPU time.

How do the main serverless GPU platforms compare?

The table lists what each company publishes on its own pages. Start times are the vendor's own claims, measured in different ways, so treat them as a guide rather than a benchmark.

Platform Built for NVIDIA H100 NVIDIA L4 Billing Start time the vendor states
Modal Python functions, web endpoints, batch $0.001097/s ($3.95/hr) $0.000222/s ($0.80/hr) Per second; idle containers billed for 60 s by default Sub-second starts on large custom images (homepage)
RunPod Serverless Container endpoints $5.39/hr flex worker (H100 PRO) $0.75/hr flex worker (24 GB class, includes L4) Per second, rounded up; 5 s idle timeout by default (docs) Under 200 ms with FlashBoot
Baseten Production model serving and training $0.10833/min ($6.50/hr) $0.01414/min ($0.85/hr) Per minute, including deploy and scaling time "Fast cold starts", no figure
Replicate Public models by API, custom models with Cog $0.001525/s ($5.49/hr) Not listed Per second; most private models also pay for setup and idle time Not stated
Cerebrium LLM, voice and image apps $0.000944/s ($3.40/hr) $0.000222/s ($0.80/hr) Per second; CPU and memory billed separately Not stated
Google Cloud Run GPUs Containers on Google Cloud Not offered (L4 and RTX PRO 6000 only) $0.0001867/s ($0.67/hr) (pricing) Per second, instance-based; an L4 needs at least 4 vCPU and 16 GiB About 5 s
Nodus Training, fine-tuning, batch, Python Functions $2.60/hr $0.43/hr Prepaid credit; each run holds funds before it starts A cold and warm start estimate per Function, before you run

Prices checked October 29, 2026. Hourly figures in brackets convert the listed per-second or per-minute rate; Modal, Cerebrium and Cloud Run bill CPU and memory on top of the GPU, and Cloud Run's L4 rate is the non-zonal-redundancy price. RunPod's endpoint docs show lower per-second rates for some tiers; we used the rates on its pricing page.

Which serverless GPU platform should you pick for each workload?

Match the platform to who is waiting and for how long.

Someone is waiting on the response

Pick RunPod Serverless or Modal. RunPod states sub-200 ms cold starts with FlashBoot, deploys any container, and by default keeps an idle worker for only 5 seconds before it scales down. Modal fits better when your service is Python: it states sub-second starts on large custom images and bills per second, with a 60-second keep-alive that you can change.

Pick Baseten if you want a managed inference stack and per-minute billing is fine for your traffic. Pick Cloud Run if the rest of your app already lives on Google Cloud and an L4 or RTX PRO 6000 is enough. Google states instances start in about 5 seconds.

Traffic is steady all day

Skip scale-to-zero and pay for warm capacity on purpose. Serverless rates price in the freedom to drop to zero, which you never use if the GPU is busy around the clock. RunPod offers always-on active workers with discounts through sales, and a Nodus Function's min_workers setting keeps workers warm at the Function's worker rate. Compare that monthly bill with a reserved option before you commit.

The job runs for hours

Pick Nodus. For training, fine-tuning and continued pretraining, the price of a GPU-hour and what happens on an interruption matter far more than a fast first request. Your script writes its state to /nodus/state. Nodus checkpoints it at least four times over the expected run time and restores the latest copy into a new attempt if the machine is lost.

The endpoint platforms can run long jobs too, within limits they publish. Modal caps one execution at 24 hours and makes Functions preemptible by default, restarting an interrupted one on the same input. RunPod Serverless gives each endpoint a 10-minute execution timeout by default, configurable up to 7 days, and one GPU per worker unless you raise it.

A batch job where nobody waits

Embedding a corpus or scoring a dataset overnight has the same economics as training, so choose on price per GPU-hour and on resuming, not on cold starts. On Nodus, a Job with Restartable continuity keeps the progress counter you report, so a replacement attempt can skip the items already done. A Function's .map() fans one function out over thousands of inputs. Modal is a good fit too if your code already runs there: its batch processing guide scales functions to thousands of parallel containers.

You only need to call an open model

You may not need a GPU platform at all. Baseten's Model APIs, Replicate's public models and Nodus Inference (Beta), which speaks the OpenAI API format, charge per token or per prediction, so you never size a worker.

What does the same GPU work cost on each platform?

At list prices, a 10-hour job on one H100 ranges from $26.00 on Nodus to $65.00 on Baseten. We priced a LoRA fine-tune that needs 10 hours on one NVIDIA H100, which is 36,000 GPU-seconds or 600 GPU-minutes, at each platform's listed H100 rate from the table:

  • Nodus: 10 h × $2.60 = $26.00
  • Cerebrium: 36,000 s × $0.000944 = $33.98
  • Modal: 36,000 s × $0.001097 = $39.49
  • RunPod Serverless: 10 h × $5.39 = $53.90
  • Replicate: 36,000 s × $0.001525 = $54.90
  • Baseten: 600 min × $0.10833 = $65.00


The same 10 H100-hours cost 34% less on Nodus than on Modal at list rates, before Modal adds CPU and memory.

This counts the GPU line only: Modal and Cerebrium add CPU and memory on top, and cold starts and idle windows are seconds on a 10-hour job. The ratios hold per GPU-hour, so eight GPUs scale the same way.

For a small model served on an L4, the gap is smaller in dollars but similar in shape. Nodus lists the L4 at $0.43/hr, against $0.67 on Cloud Run before its required CPU and memory, $0.75 on RunPod Serverless, $0.80 on Modal and Cerebrium, and $0.85 on Baseten.


On an L4 the price spread is cents per hour, so cold-start behavior usually decides an endpoint, not the rate.

What happens to the bill when a long run is interrupted?

An interruption costs whatever work you have to redo, and that can outweigh any rate difference. Take the same 10-hour job, lose the machine at hour 8, and price every case at $2.60/hr so only the recovery changes:

  • No interruption: 10 GPU-hours = $26.00
  • Checkpoint every 30 minutes: at most 0.5 hours redone, 10.5 GPU-hours = $27.30
  • No checkpoint: 8 hours lost plus a 10-hour rerun, 18 GPU-hours = $46.80


Without a checkpoint, one lost machine at hour 8 nearly doubles the bill.

Any platform here can resume if your code saves to persistent storage and reloads it on start, as Modal's preemption guide recommends for training; the difference is who does the plumbing. On a reclaim notice, Nodus asks your program for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine. The replacement starts only once the old one is provably gone, so two copies never write the same checkpoint (attempts and recovery). If the old machine comes back first, the replacement is released and you are not charged for it.

Our guide to surviving spot preemption walks through the checkpoint code.

Can Nodus serve a latency-sensitive endpoint?

Partly, and we would not pick it first for that today. Nodus Functions scale with demand: min_workers defaults to 0, so a Function scales to zero, and max_workers goes up to 1,000. An idle worker leaves after its scaledown_window, 1 minute by default and up to 20 (scaling docs). Before you deploy, .estimate() reports the expected cold and warm start bands for that Function.

What Nodus does not publish is a fixed cold-start figure, and hosted Inference is still in Beta. If first-request latency is the metric your product lives or dies on, start with RunPod Serverless or Modal, which publish start times, and test Nodus against them with your own model.

Where are Modal, RunPod and the others the better choice?

Each of them beats Nodus somewhere specific.

  • Modal is the better choice for Python web endpoints that need quick container starts and per-second billing, and its Starter plan includes $30 of compute credit a month.
  • RunPod Serverless is the better choice when cold start is everything: it states sub-200 ms starts with FlashBoot, and deploys straight from GitHub with rollbacks.
  • Baseten is the better choice for teams that want a managed production inference platform; its pricing page lists SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliance and a self-hosted option on Enterprise.
  • Replicate is the better choice for calling public models through an API without deploying anything, and its fast-booting fine-tunes bill only active time.
  • Cloud Run is the better choice if you already run on Google Cloud and an L4 or RTX PRO 6000 is enough, with no GPU reservation to manage.
  • Cerebrium has the lowest per-second H100 rate among the endpoint platforms in our table, though CPU and memory are billed on top.

For a deeper head-to-head on the two most common picks, see Modal vs RunPod.

How do you move a long job from an endpoint platform to Nodus?

Keep your training script and make it save to and load from /nodus/state. Then install the CLI, sign in, and run the same script with a spend cap. Add --dry-run first to see the estimate without starting paid compute. The commands are copied from the Nodus docs:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login
nodus run --gpu H100 --image nodus/pytorch --checkpoint /nodus/state --max-cost 40 -d -- python train.py

The $40 cap leaves headroom over the $26.00 the job costs at the listed rate, and nodus describe job/NAME shows each attempt, the latest checkpoint and the cost so far.

FAQ

Is a serverless GPU cheaper than a dedicated one?

Only when the GPU would otherwise sit idle. Modal's own pricing FAQ makes the same point: per-hour serverless rates can look higher, and the savings come from spiky or unpredictable traffic. If your GPU is busy most of the day, a lower hourly rate or reserved capacity wins.

Do you pay for cold starts on serverless GPUs?

Usually, yes, for the part where your code loads. RunPod's docs bill from worker start until your handler is ready, which is mostly loading the model into GPU memory, while image pulls and cached model downloads happen unbilled. Modal bills application load time too, so smaller weights and lazy imports cut both latency and cost.

Can you fine-tune a model on a serverless GPU platform?

Yes. Nodus runs fine-tuning as a Job that resumes from its latest checkpoint, or through managed TrainingJobs (Beta) on the GPU you pick. Modal and RunPod Serverless also run training code, within the timeouts above.

What happens on Nodus if credit runs out mid-run?

Nodus is prepaid and renews a funded hold on your balance every 5 minutes while work runs. When a renewal cannot be funded, the run stops gracefully inside time already paid for, keeps what it saved, and can resume once you add credit.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.
