title: Living the design-to-code dream
description:
This flow should sound familiar to any frontend developer: a designer makes a change in Figma, and now we need to propagate it to our code. By nature, that process involves an entire handoff from UX to engineering. As a company matures, it quickly realizes this flow will not scale. When those changes are not aligned in the code right away, we get drift. The UX team ends up sketching UI with updated assets while production screens still show up with old colors, spacing, and typography.

Scaling this process means automating it, and today's design tools do not make that easy out of the box. Off-the-shelf integrations make assumptions about repository structure, token formats, and release workflows that rarely match an existing organizational stack. Most teams end up building a custom bridge of their own.

This note walks through one approach that puts the ideas from design tools, tokens, and implementation into practice. The goal is to satisfy both sides of the handoff: designers stay focused on design without having to learn code, version control, or release mechanics, while engineers still get a reviewable diff, an approval gate, and a versioned package. We will be focusing on tokens here, though the same pattern applies to icons.

The shape of the bridge

There's more than one way to build this bridge. The source of truth for design tokens can sit either in Figma or in Git. With Git as the source, tokens are authored in the repository and Figma consumes them, just like our codebase does. That keeps the repository authoritative, but designers end up editing tokens somewhere other than the canvas. Our example goes the other way and makes Figma the source of truth, because it is friendlier to designers, who keep working in the tool they already know.

With Figma in the driver's seat, the pipeline splits into two halves: a Figma plugin that turns canvas edits into a pull request, and a CI workflow that turns the merged pull request into a versioned package. The repository tracks only a single raw JSON snapshot of the tokens, while all code artifacts are generated on release.

Designer: Figma plugin → Review: Pull request → Automation: CI workflow → Release: Versioned package

The designer publishes from Figma, engineers approve the PR, and the pipeline generates code and releases a version.

Inside the plugin

Our workflow starts when a designer has changes they want to publish. Opening our custom-built Figma plugin shows them their pending changes alongside a simple screen to publish their work.

"Changes" lists what differs from the last release. "Publish" says what kind of release this is and takes an optional note for engineers.

Behind the scenes, the plugin compares the current Figma variables with the token file on main. It does more than list what differs. It tells the designer, in plain language, what kind of release this is:

  • Updated existing values (patch): colors, sizes, or other values changed.
  • Added new tokens (minor): new tokens that didn't exist before.
  • Removed or renamed tokens (major): tokens were deleted or their names changed, which breaks any app that uses them.

The designer adds a note for engineers and presses "Publish". The plugin then commits the snapshot to a branch and opens a pull request, using the note as its description. After publishing, the designer sees where the request stands.

A removed token is called out as a breaking change before anything is sent. After publishing, the designer sees what happens next.

Handling incremental changes

Figma holds a single live state, so two designers never conflict inside it. Git is where conflicts appear, because every publish is a snapshot of that state taken at a different moment, and a newer snapshot already contains everything an older one did.

So the plugin never opens a second pull request. Each publish either opens one or, if one is already open, updates it with the latest snapshot. Two designers publishing on the same afternoon end up in the same pull request, and its diff always compares main with the current state of Figma.

Versioning our package

After a merge, the pipeline compares the token file with the copy at the latest git tag and derives the major, minor, or patch bump from those same rules. When a release mixes them, the highest one wins. It then reads the latest tag, applies the bump, publishes the package, and pushes the next tag.

Because those rules follow the token names applications depend on, a drastic color change is still a patch. How much a change matters visually belongs in the designer's note and in review, while the version number reflects the contract.

What's in the box?

From the single JSON snapshot, the pipeline generates everything applications need, in the formats each implementation prefers:

  • SCSS variables for stylesheets that rely on compile-time values.
  • TypeScript constants for code that needs tokens in JavaScript, exposed in whichever shape suits the consumer.

The pipeline generates CSS custom properties as well, though the compiled options are the better choice. With them, a removed or renamed token breaks the build of any application still using it, which is exactly what a major bump promises. A CSS custom property that no longer exists fails silently at runtime, so the handshake between design and code only sticks when the compiler is in on it. Custom properties still earn their place for runtime theming, such as switching between light and dark modes without recompiling.

Dream come true

With that, we have ourselves a fully automated workflow, taking a change on the canvas all the way to a versioned package. Ours is just one approach among many, of course. The real takeaway is that automating the handoff is key, and doing it well means separating the designer experience from the developer experience. Once we build the bridge that ties them together, the drift between canvas and production disappears.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: Handling R01–R85 in Production Payout Systems
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: Handling R01–R85 in Production Payout Systems

When a payout fails, the Nacha network doesn't just say "no." It returns a specific code—one of 85 possible R-codes—that tells you why the transfer bounced and what you should do next. Understanding these codes is critical for building reliable payment infrastructure.

The ACH Return Code Landscape

Every ACH return follows the Nacha Operating Rules and is documented in the ACH Return Entries guide. The codes span from R01 (Insufficient Funds) to R85 (Duplicate Entry), and each one signals a different failure mode. Your integration must decode and handle them programmatically, not just log them.

Returns typically arrive 1–2 business days after the original debit entry is transmitted. For same-day ACH, returns come back the same day by 11:00 AM CT.

Common Return Codes You'll Encounter

R01 – Insufficient Funds
The receiver's account doesn't have enough balance to cover the debit. This is temporary and reversible—the receiver might have funds tomorrow. Your retry logic should flag this for a later attempt (24–48 hours), not immediately.

R03 – No Account / Unable to Locate Account
The account number or routing number doesn't exist, or the account was closed. This is permanent. You should:

  • Mark the recipient record as invalid
  • Notify the user immediately
  • Offer an alternate payment method (card, wire, RTP)

R04 – Invalid Account Number Structure
The account number format is invalid (e.g., too many digits, invalid characters). This is a data quality issue on your end. Validate account numbers against Luhn or bank-specific rules before submission.

R10 – Customer Advises Not Authorized
The receiver claims they didn't authorize the debit. This is a dispute and requires manual investigation. Flag it for compliance review; don't retry.

R29 – Corporate Customer Advises Not Authorized
Similar to R10, but for business accounts. Treat as a dispute.

R51 – Debit Initiated Without Authorization
The originating bank rejected the entry because the receiver's bank detected no authorization on file. This often means the receiver needs to re-authorize recurring debits. Send them a re-authorization request.

R82 – Duplicate Entry
You sent the same entry twice (same amount, date, account). Implement idempotency keys in your API to prevent this. If you receive R82, don't retry; investigate why the duplicate was sent.

Building a Return Handler

Here's a minimal pattern for decoding and routing returns:

async function handleACHReturn(returnEntry) {
  const { returnCode, amount, accountId, payoutId } = returnEntry;

  const permanentCodes = ['R03', 'R04', 'R05', 'R07'];
  const temporaryCodes = ['R01', 'R09', 'R16'];
  const disputeCodes = ['R10', 'R29'];

  if (permanentCodes.includes(returnCode)) {
    await markAccountInvalid(accountId);
    await notifyUser(accountId, `Payout failed: ${returnCode}`);
    await suggestAlternateMethod(accountId);
  } else if (temporaryCodes.includes(returnCode)) {
    await scheduleRetry(payoutId, { delayHours: 24, maxAttempts: 3 });
  } else if (disputeCodes.includes(returnCode)) {
    await escalateToCompliance(payoutId, returnCode);
  } else {
    await logUnhandledReturn(payoutId, returnCode);
  }
}

Return Timing & Reconciliation

  • Standard ACH: Returns arrive within 1–2 business days.
  • Same-day ACH: Returns by 11:00 AM CT the same day.
  • Your settlement: Most ACH credits settle T+1, but returns can arrive T+2 or later.

When reconciling, don't assume a payout succeeded until the return window closes. Keep payout status as "pending" for at least 2 business days.

When to Switch Rails

If ACH returns are too frequent for a recipient (e.g., R01 repeated 3 times), consider offering RTP (Real-Time Payments) or Visa Direct. RTP settles in seconds and provides immediate feedback; Visa Direct works for card-linked accounts.

Key Takeaway

Every R-code is actionable data. Build your return handler to classify codes into permanent failures, retryable errors, and disputes. This transforms ACH returns from a support headache into a signal that drives smarter routing decisions and better user experience.

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Ghost in the Machine: DEADLOOP, a Local-First Reliability Monitor for AI Agents
description:
https://github.com/Senthil455/DeadLoop

This Halloween I built DEADLOOP: a reliability and safety monitor for AI agents that detects when they get trapped in repetitive tool calls, unproductive loops, or circular workflows. It records execution traces, raises evidence-backed incidents, and lets a human acknowledge, resolve, dismiss, or request a pause. The core is fully deterministic; an optional open-weight model only explains the findings. It never changes a finding or executes an intervention.

What I built

DEADLOOP is a monitor, not an agent framework. Your agent keeps running as-is. DEADLOOP ingests its tool-call trace and answers:

  • Is this repetition, or legitimate retrying?
  • What exactly supports that conclusion?
  • What should a human look at first?
  • Can we stop the run without claiming control we do not have?

Detectors:

  • Exact repetition
  • Near-duplicate repetition
  • A-B-A-B oscillation
  • Repeated failure
  • Explicit no-progress
  • Session budgets (tool calls, duration, tokens, cost)

Every incident cites real event IDs, the observed sequence, measured metrics, confidence basis, and stated uncertainty. Risk scores are heuristics in [0, 100], not probabilities.

The spooky part

Every developer has watched an agent whisper the same command into the void over and over, burning tokens while nothing moves. DEADLOOP is the thing in the machine that notices the ghost repeating itself and breaks the cycle. It is not a horror game aesthetic; it is a forensic one: dark, precise, and readable.

Why open innovation matters for this

The open pieces are what make the project work:

  • It runs offline. Detection, risk scoring, ingestion, and incident management are deterministic and local. No API key is required for the core product to function.
  • It keeps data off servers you do not control. Execution traces can contain tool arguments, outputs, and errors. DEADLOOP redacts credential-shaped fields at two layers: the SDK before transport, and the backend before storage. Raw ingestion keys are never returned after creation.
  • It is not locked inside a disappearing service. The stack is FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, SQLite/PostgreSQL, React, and Vite. The detector never depends on a hosted model. If the optional AI provider is disabled, slow, or returns invalid output, the deterministic explanation remains available.
  • Optional open-weight AI. Explanations can use an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, verified with Gemma 2 2B through Ollama. No API key is required for a local endpoint. Detection remains on-device either way.
  • Cost. The basic product requires no paid external services.

Where the open-based approach worked better than a closed one: a closed tracing service would show that calls happened, but it would not let me keep traces local, swap or disable the model, or explain exactly why a finding occurred. DEADLOOP can run with the internet off and still tell you what happened.

Demo walkthrough

The sample simulator generates real execution events through the same ingestion, persistence, detection, and incident paths as production. The exact-repetition scenario creates four identical failing calls and produces both exact-repetition and repeated-failure findings. Evidence references the real event IDs; you can open the incident, inspect the timeline, acknowledge it, request a pause, approve it, and verify the simulator acknowledges it.

Code that matters 

# Send one event from any agent
from deadloop import DeadLoopClient

client = DeadLoopClient(
    endpoint="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    api_key="dl_...",
)
client.send_event(
    agent_id="research-agent",
    session_id="run-42",
    tool_name="search_web",
    action="Search",
    input={"query": "database connection error"},
    output={"results": 3},
    status="success",
    progress=True,
)

# Run the backend
cd backend
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m alembic -c alembic.ini upgrade head
$env:DEADLOOP_ADMIN_TOKEN = "choose-a-long-random-token"
$env:DEADLOOP_AUTO_CREATE = "0"
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000

# Build the frontend
cd frontend
npm ci
npm run build

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 and sign in with the configured admin token.

Verification

  • Backend pytest: 62 passed, 0 failed
  • SDK pytest: 8 passed, 0 failed
  • Frontend Vitest: 8 passed, 0 failed
  • Frontend production build: passed
  • Clean-database Alembic migration: passed, 11 tables
  • Live API acceptance workflow: passed with 0 failures

Security notes

  • Secrets are not hardcoded; they come from environment variables.
  • Inputs and configuration values are validated.
  • Protected endpoints enforce authorization on the backend.
  • Intervention operations require approval and are audited.
  • External AI data transfer requires explicit configuration.
  • Known limitations are documented, including single-node scope, no multi-tenant RBAC, and no built-in TLS.

title: How it was: The admin dashboard
description:
I am pretty sure that I have already written a draft for this already somewhere, but too exhausted to rummage through the spaces where I wrote about this. Once more, I no longer even bothered to make two projects of the same thing.

I wish I could write this the way it deserves. For now, I will just share my README.MD here. Because I need to keep moving on. What matters is that another dream became true! Maybe you're my love! The most dreamy admin dashboard ever that came to life, and is all mine! Yes, that's right! Another form of fan-art, and self-expression.

This is from my README.md:

The Third Music Room — Administrative Dashboard

"Having the courage to be able to admit what you love... enjoying what you love... and being true to yourself... Isn't that also what it means to be strong?”
— Tamaki Suoh, Ouran High School Host Club, Vol. 7

I had many crises when I first read about this project that TOP had entrusted me. Obviously, I could not make a generic admin dashboard. I did use the given template as a reference, but I am afraid to say that the default template given to download was a great offense to my aesthetics, lacked any taste or soul, and did not make me feel anything.

Anyway, it was really difficult to figure out who would be the best admin for this project. It could not be just any admin. It had to be someone connected to something, someone who could resonate with me emotionally, even if the character was not the admin—maybe a friend? There were great candidates, but it did not feel right. Then, it occurred to me that it could only be Kyoya, and that way I could bring the King from The Ouran Host Club! Who is the king? That is Tamaki Suoh! I am certain that he went on to become the most splendid man ever. I remember all this fondly. Because of Tamaki, this feels truly special to me.

Please note, for all purposes, this project must be taken as what it is: a form of fanart, self-expression, and the utmost devotion to bring the spirit of The Ouran High School Host Club! The Ouran High School Host Club was created by Bisco Hatori.

🎶 Soundtrack Recommendation:
I highly recommend listening to the opening theme while taking in everything about the admin dashboard:
👉 Listen on YouTube

(I wanted to embed this into the admin dashboard too, but since this is supposed to be an admin dashboard, I cannot do that! So, I'm sharing it here!)
📖 The Anatomy of an Obsession: A Developer's Descent into the Third Music Room

This was never supposed to be just another compliance checkbox for The Odin Project. What started as a straightforward layout assignment fractured into a multi-day crucible of stubborn artistry, eye-strain, terminal frustration, and absolute, unyielding devotion.

If you are reading this code, understand that every pixel was fought for. This README is a chronicle of the tears, the 3:00 AM debugging fevers, the broken layouts, and the sheer, exhausting ecstasy of forcing a blank screen to bend to an impossible aesthetic vision.
🛠️ Step-by-Step Chronicles of the Build
Phase 1: Laying the Foundation in Blood and Wine

The Setup: Refusing to settle for a sterile corporate template, I established the global design tokens anchored in deep wine (#280d19), official uniform lavender-blue (#3a3b5c), and gold (#facc15).
The Struggle: Fighting CSS Grid and box models while running on pure stubbornness. Getting the initial structural layout to hold without collapsing under custom padding was the first battle against the terminal.

Phase 2: Framing the Abyss (The SVG Border Crisis)

The Goal: Pinning a true background rose-frame layer to the window viewport using an SVG asset so the entire dashboard felt like looking into a gilded, trapped portrait.
The Reality: Watching the viewport break, clipping overflows, wrestling with z-index stacking contexts, and staring blankly at the screen as pointer events blocked my clicks. Countless refreshes, endless trial-and-error, and deep exhaustion before the frame finally locked into place like a gilded cage.

Phase 3: Capturing Tamaki’s Gaze (--ouran-tamaki-eyes)

The Hunt: Refusing standard hex codes. Hunting down and fine-tuning the exact luminous violet (#7c3aed) that mirrors the precise shade of Tamaki Suoh’s eyes.
The Implementation: Splashing that signature violet across key statistics, card hover states, focus rings, and custom gradient header crowns (::before). Every hover state had to feel alive—delicate yet striking.

Phase 4: The Form Input Overlap Trauma

The Breaking Point: Hours into styling the Host Club Member Dispatch panel, the form inputs, textareas, and select dropdowns decided to betray me. Text was overlapping, lines were bunching up into unreadable smudges, and my visual impairment made combing through hundreds of lines of code feel like navigating a maze blindfolded.
The Resolution: Iterative, brutal debugging session by session. Adding strict line-height properties, fixing missing semicolons that brought down entire blocks of styles, and manually restructuring padding until the inputs finally breathed. When those fields finally spaced out cleanly and looked pristine, it felt like winning a war.

Phase 5: The Gradient Crowns & Final Polish

The Polish: Unifying the metric cards and the right-hand side panels (Host Club Announcements and Trending Host Gossip) with matching top gradient borders blending gold, crimson, and violet.
The Exhaustion & Triumph: Standing back as the falling rose petals looped smoothly across the screen, the custom Yuji Boku serif headers rendered their final strokes, and the dashboard stood complete. Sore eyes, tired wrists, and a soul completely poured into code.

💻 Tech Stack & Weapons Used

Core: Semantic HTML5 & Modern CSS3 (CSS Grid, Flexbox, Custom Properties, Pseudo-elements)
Typography: Google Fonts (Yuji Boku)
Environment: Ubuntu Kubuntu (I experimented with Kubuntu for the intermidate courses) Linux, VS Code, endless cups of tea, and sheer willpower
Deployment: Git, GitHub, and GitHub Pages

🚀 Live Demo

Witness the fiscal operations, the rose budgets, and the madness live:
👉 [View on GitHub Pages]
https://labrava0x.github.io/admin-dashboard-Ouran/

Project built with raw tears, burning eyes, uncompromising artistic integrity, and strict adherence to the Host Club budget. 🌹✨

title: Build Once, Render Anywhere: Generating OG Images and PDFs from JSX/HTML Without a Headless Browser Using Rust-Powered Takumi
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Generating Open Graph (OG) images and PDFs from JSX or HTML is a common need for dynamic social sharing, reports, and invoices. The typical approach—spinning up a headless browser like Puppeteer or Playwright—is heavy: high memory usage, slow cold starts, and complex orchestration. Takumi offers a radical alternative: a Rust-powered renderer that converts JSX/HTML directly into images and PDFs, without a browser. In this tutorial, you'll learn how to build a reusable rendering service that takes JSX/HTML as input and outputs PNG or PDF, using Takumi's Node.js bindings. You'll see how to set up the environment, write render functions, handle dynamic data, and deploy efficiently. By the end, you'll have a production-ready pattern that cuts rendering latency and resource consumption dramatically.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Why Takumi?
  • 2. Prerequisites
  • 3. Setting Up the Project
  • 4. Core Rendering API
  • 5. Rendering an OG Image from JSX
  • 6. Rendering a PDF from HTML
  • 7. Handling Dynamic Data and Styling
  • 8. Performance and Deployment Considerations
  • 9. Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why Takumi?

Headless browsers are powerful but overkill for static rendering. They consume 200–500 MB of RAM per instance)Skip to content

Takumi is a Rust-based rendering engine that interprets a subset of HTML/CSS and JSX, rasterizing to images or vector PDFs. It's designed for serverless environments and edge functions where cold starts matter. Key benefits:

  • Memory footprint: Under 50 MB per instance, compared to 300+ MB for Chromium.
  • Startup time: ~10ms to initialize, vs 300ms+ for a browser launch.
  • Deterministic output: No layout flakiness; pixel-perfect results.
  • Language agnostic: Use from Node.js, Python, or directly via HTTP.

Takumi does not execute JavaScript. That's a feature: it forces you to precompute dynamic values and pass them as props, resulting in predictable and secure rendering.

2. Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18+ (we'll use the official @takumi-js/core package)
  • npm or yarn
  • Basic familiarity with JSX (we'll use React-like syntax, but Takumi has its own runtime)
  • No need for a browser installation

3. Setting Up the Project

Create a new directory and initialize:

mkdir og-renderer
cd og-renderer
npm init -y
npm install @takumi-js/core

Takumi's Node package wraps the native Rust binary. For serverless, you can also use the standalone HTTP server (we'll cover that later).

Now create a basic index.js file and verify the installation:

const { renderToImage } = require('@takumi-js/core');

console.log('Takumi loaded', typeof renderToImage);

Run it:

node index.js

You should see Takumi loaded function.

4. Core Rendering API

Takumi exposes two primary functions:

  • renderToImage(jsx, options) → returns a Buffer (PNG or JPEG)
  • renderToPdf(html, options) → returns a Buffer (PDF)

Both accept a string of JSX/HTML and an options object for width, height, format, and quality.

The JSX is not compiled by Babel; it's parsed by Takumi's own parser. You can write JSX-like syntax directly in a template literal, or use a .tsx file and compile it to a string before passing.

Options overview

Option Type Default Description
width number 1200 Output width in pixels
height number 630 Output height (for images)
format string 'png' 'png' or 'jpeg'
quality number 90 JPEG quality only
pdf object {} PDF-specific options (page size, margins)

5. Rendering an OG Image from JSX

Let's create a function that takes a title, subtitle, and brand color, and returns a PNG Buffer for an OG image.

Create render-og.js:

const { renderToImage } = require('@takumi-js/core');

function generateOgImage({ title, subtitle, bgColor = '#1a202c', textColor = '#ffffff' }) {
  const jsx = `
    <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: center; align-items: center; width: 100%; height: 100%; background: ${bgColor}; padding: 40px;">
      <h1 style="font-size: 64px; color: ${textColor}; margin-bottom: 16px;">${title}</h1>
      <p style="font-size: 32px; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.8);">${subtitle}</p>
    </div>
  `;

  return renderToImage(jsx, {
    width: 1200,
    height: 630,
    format: 'png'
  });
}

// Example usage
const fs = require('fs');
const buffer = generateOgImage({
  title: 'Build Once, Render Anywhere',
  subtitle: 'Rust-powered rendering without a browser'
});

fs.writeFileSync('og-image.png', buffer);
console.log('OG image generated');

Run it:

node render-og.js

You should get a clean 1200x630 PNG. Notice we used inline styles—Takumi supports a subset of CSS, including flexbox, which is enough for most layouts.

6. Rendering a PDF from HTML

For PDFs, you can pass HTML (or JSX) and specify PDF options. Here's how to generate a simple invoice PDF:

Create render-pdf.js:

const { renderToPdf } = require('@takumi-js/core');

function generateInvoicePdf({ customerName, amount, invoiceId }) {
  const html = `
    <html>
      <body style="font-family: Arial, sans-serif; padding: 40px;">
        <h1 style="color: #333;">Invoice #${invoiceId}</h1>
        <p>Customer: <strong>${customerName}</strong></p>
        <p>Amount due: <strong>$${amount}</strong></p>
        <p>Thank you for your business!</p>
      </body>
    </html>
  `;

  return renderToPdf(html, {
    pdf: {
      pageSize: 'A4',
      margins: { top: '20mm', bottom: '20mm', left: '20mm', right: '20mm' }
    }
  });
}

const fs = require('fs');
const buffer = generateInvoicePdf({
  customerName: 'Jane Doe',
  amount: '199.99',
  invoiceId: 'INV-2025-001'
});

fs.writeFileSync('invoice.pdf', buffer);
console.log('PDF generated');

Run it:

node render-pdf.js

Open the PDF to see a clean, vector-based document. Takumi's PDF output is vector, meaning text is selectable and sharp at any zoom.

7. Handling Dynamic Data and Styling

In a real application, you'll have dynamic data from a database or API. Since Takumi doesn't run JS, you must precompute values and inject them into the template. Here's a pattern using a template function:

function renderBlogCard(post) {
  const jsx = `
    <div style="display: flex; height: 100%; background: linear-gradient(135deg, #667eea 0%, #764ba2 100%); padding: 40px;">
      <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: space-between; width: 100%;">
        <div>
          <p style="font-size: 24px; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.8); text-transform: uppercase;">${post.category}</p>
          <h1 style="font-size: 48px; color: white; margin-top: 12px;">${post.title}</h1>
        </div>
        <div style="display: flex; align-items: center;">
          <img src="${post.authorAvatar}" style="width: 48px; height: 48px; border-radius: 50%;" />
          <p style="font-size: 20px; color: white; margin-left: 12px;">${post.author}</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  `;
  return jsx;
}

// Usage
const post = {
  category: 'Engineering',
  title: 'Why We Ditched Headless Browsers',
  author: 'Alex Rivera',
  authorAvatar: 'https://example.com/alex.png'
};

renderToImage(renderBlogCard(post), { width: 1200, height: 630 })
  .then(buf => fs.writeFileSync('blog-card.png', buf));

Styling limitations

Takumi supports a useful subset of CSS: flexbox, grid (basic), colors, fonts (system and custom via @font-face), borders, border-radius, box-shadow, and text styling. It does not support position: absolute or complex animations. For most OG images and simple PDFs, this is sufficient.

To use custom fonts, you can embed them as base64 in a <style> tag:

const fontBase64 = '...'; // read from file
const jsx = `
  <style>
    @font-face {
      font-family: 'Inter';
      src: url(data:font/ttf;base64,${fontBase64}) format('truetype');
    }
  </style>
  <div style="font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;">...</div>
`;

8. Performance and Deployment Considerations

Memory and CPU

Takumi uses a single native thread and is non-blocking in Node. It's ideal for serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Vercel Edge, Cloudflare Workers). You can run it in a warm container and render in under 5ms for a typical OG image.

Caching

Since output is deterministic for given inputs, cache aggressively. Use a key based on the template + data hash:

const crypto = require('crypto');
function cacheKey(data) {
  return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(JSON.stringify(data)).digest('hex');
}
// In a serverless function, use a CDN or in-memory cache.

HTTP server mode

For microservices, Takumi can run as a standalone HTTP server. The Node package includes a serve function:

const { serve } = require('@takumi-js/core');
serve(3000); // starts a REST API

Then POST to /render with JSON body:

{
  "jsx": "<div>Hello</div>",
  "options": { "width": 800, "height": 400, "format": "png" }
}

This decouples rendering from your app's runtime.

Cold start comparison

Approach Cold start Memory per instance Throughput (images/sec)
Puppeteer 300-800ms 300-500 MB ~10
Takumi 10-20ms 40-60 MB ~100

Numbers are indicative; your mileage may vary.

9. Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use Takumi with React components?

Yes, but you need to compile your React component to a string of JSX. You can use renderToString from ReactDOMServer (which outputs HTML) and then pass that HTML to Takumi, or you can use a custom Babel plugin to output JSX text. However, Takumi's JSX parser is not a full React implementation—it only supports declarative elements, not hooks or state. For static content, it works well.

Does Takumi support images from URLs?

Yes, you can use <img src="https://...">. Takumi will fetch the image at render time. Ensure the URL is accessible from your runtime environment. For performance, consider pre-downloading images and using base64 data URIs.

Is Takumi open source?

Takumi is available under a commercial license, but there is a free tier for low-volume usage. Check the official Takumi website for the latest pricing and terms.

By replacing headless browsers with Takumi, you can achieve dramatic improvements in speed and resource usage for static rendering tasks. Start integrating it into your existing stack today—your serverless bill and your users' latency will thank you.

title: Solo dev stack: why I build admin systems with full-stack Node.js and a framework with fixed conventions
description:
Some context

I build a lot of admin systems — client work and my own projects. They all share the same traits: tight deadlines, changing requirements, and usually just me on the keyboard.

After years of trial and error, the setup that works best for me is full-stack Node.js + a framework with fixed conventions. Here's why, and what I built around it.

The practical benefits of full-stack Node.js

Not theory — things I actually feel day to day:

One person can carry the whole project. Vue on the frontend, Node on the backend, one language. I write an endpoint and immediately wire up the page for it. No context switching between two languages.

Shared types. With TypeScript on both ends, the API's field types are the same types the frontend uses. Backend changes a field, the frontend build fails and tells you where. No comparing against API docs by hand.

No integration meetings. When you write both ends, you decide what the API looks like. Integration cost is basically zero — anyone who has done frontend/backend coordination knows how much time that saves.

Hiring is easier. If the project grows, half the people who know Vue can pick up Node quickly.

Full-stack alone isn't enough — you need fixed conventions

Node full-stack solves the language problem. But there's another one: every project rebuilds the same plumbing — directory layout, permissions, list pages, menu config. It's roughly the same every time, yet you redesign it every time. It wastes time, and the designs drift, so your own old projects feel foreign six months later.

So I turned my own way of working into Me-Admin — the conventions and common features are already decided:

  • Fixed directory structure and layering; every module looks identical
  • Built-in RBAC (menu / button / API levels), users, roles, menus — ready out of the box
  • The stuff admin panels always need — lists, search, pagination, forms, uploads — already has components and established patterns
  • Mainstream stack: Midway 3 + Sequelize + PostgreSQL on the backend, Vue 3 + Vite + Element Plus + vxeTable on the frontend

The biggest time-saver: define an entity, run two commands, get a whole module.

# Sync the database schema
pnpm exec meadmin sync product

# Generate controller, API, frontend pages, menu permissions
pnpm exec meadmin crud product --menu

Refresh the admin panel and the module is in the menu — full CRUD working. The output is plain source code in your repo, no black boxes. Edit it directly.

meadmin-cn / meadmin

Me-Admin 是一个免费开源的nodejs + vue 全栈一站式中后台解决方案,后端基于medwayjs ,前台基于vue3构建，开箱即用。本项目采用最宽松的MIT协议，最新技术栈，助力你快速创建企业级web中后台项目。

Me-Admin

English | 简体中文

 

全栈一站式解决方案 —— Me-Admin 是一个免费开源的 Node.js + Vue 全栈中后台框架，后端基于 Midway.js 3，前端基于 Vue 3，一键 CRUD、SSR 渲染、权限体系开箱即用。MIT 协议，无加密、无授权限制，可商用。

  • 🌐 官网：https://www.meadmin.cn
  • 📖 文档：https://www.meadmin.cn/aon/doc/
  • 💬 问题反馈：https://github.com/meadmin-cn/meadmin/issues

30 秒生成一个业务模块

定义好 Sequelize 实体之后，只需两条命令：

# 同步数据库结构
pnpm exec meadmin sync exampleDemo

# 一键生成：控制器、接口、前端页面、菜单权限
pnpm exec meadmin crud exampleDemo --menu

meadmin 由 @meadmin/cli 提供命令行入口，统一通过 pnpm exec meadmin <命令> 调用。

刷新后台，菜单已经出现——列表、搜索、分页、增删改查、接口与菜单权限全部就位。生成的都是可读可改的源码，后续业务直接在上面写，没有黑盒。

主要特性

  • 一键 CRUD：命令行一键生成控制器、模型、视图与菜单权限，重复工作交给框架
  • SSR · CSR 混合渲染：前台 SSR 提升 SEO 与首屏速度，后台 CSR 保证交互体验
  • 内置权限系统：RBAC 权限模型开箱即用，菜单、按钮、接口三级管控；支持无限父子级分组与自由授权，管理员可跨组别；动态路由权限方案，支持按钮级权限，前端菜单与接口动态获取两种模式
  • 插件化架构：功能以插件形式自由安装卸载，生态持续扩展，系统保持精简
  • 全 TypeScript：自动生成 TS 类型，前后端契约免维护
  • 组件自动按需引入：自动按需引入 components 下的组件定义，支持自定义引入位置和模式，真正的按需引入
  • 友好的国际化：前端支持按组件异步加载语言包
  • 自定义 keepAlive：可按 key 进行 vue keep-alive，解决不同路由统一组件不能独立刷新缓存的问题
  • 可配置主题：主题色与主题模式均可配置
  • 集成 vxeTable：功能最完善的 Vue 表格组件

技术栈






















层 技术
计算层 Vue 3 · Vite · TypeScript · Pinia · Element Plus · vue-request@next
服务层 Node.js · Midway.js 3.x · Sequelize 7
存储层 PostgreSQL · Redis

快速启动

依赖环境

  • PostgreSQL 数据库
  • Redis 缓存数据库
  • Node.js >= 22.14.0
  • pnpm

初始化项目

pnpm create meadminjs@latest

根据提示配置数据库等选项即可。

调试项目

pnpm dev
  • …
View on GitHub

Works for agile sprints, works for AI coding too

Two situations where this setup really pays off:

Deadline-driven agile work. Requirement comes in → define the entity → run the commands → the basics are done. All remaining time goes to actual business logic. Requirement changes? Update the entity and regenerate, or just edit the generated code.

AI-assisted coding. This is my biggest takeaway from the past year. Because the framework's conventions are fixed and every module has the same shape, AI writes noticeably more accurate code by copying existing modules. Even more direct: I have the AI write the entity definition (describe the table's fields), which it does fast and well, then the commands generate the module. The only AI output I need to review is that one entity file — a few dozen lines, checked at a glance. Everything else is identical generator output.

Simple truth: the more fixed the conventions, the smoother the work — whether a human or an AI is writing it.

Try it 

pnpm create meadminjs@latest
pnpm dev

Admin panel at http://127.0.0.1:7001/admin (admin / meAdmin#202507!P). MIT licensed, use it for anything.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/meadmin-cn/meadmin
  • Website: https://www.meadmin.cn
  • Docs: https://www.meadmin.cn

Questions → open an issue, I answer all of them: https://github.com/meadmin-cn/meadmin/issues

If it saves you time, a star means a lot: https://github.com/meadmin-cn/meadmin

Sooner or later every trader running an Expert Advisor wants to stop it from opening new trades for a while. A news release is coming, the spread looks strange, or they simply want to watch for an hour. The usual options are not great. Removing the EA from the chart also stops it managing the positions it already has. Turning off Algo Trading in the terminal stops every EA on every chart.

A pause button on the chart solves this. It blocks new entries for this EA only, while the EA keeps managing its open positions. This tutorial builds one with OBJ_BUTTON and OnChartEvent(), and makes the paused state survive a restart.

Creating the button 

input long InpMagic = 7310;

const string BTN = "ctb_pause_btn";
bool gPaused = false;

string PauseKey()
{
   // global variable names are limited to 63 characters
   return StringFormat("ctb_paused_%I64d_%s_%I64d",
                       AccountInfoInteger(ACCOUNT_LOGIN), _Symbol, InpMagic);
}

void UpdateButton()
{
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_STATE, gPaused);
   ObjectSetString(0, BTN, OBJPROP_TEXT, gPaused ? "Resume entries" : "Pause entries");
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_BGCOLOR, gPaused ? clrOrange : clrSilver);
   ChartRedraw(0);
}

void CreateButton()
{
   if(ObjectFind(0, BTN) < 0)
      ObjectCreate(0, BTN, OBJ_BUTTON, 0, 0, 0);

   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_CORNER, CORNER_RIGHT_UPPER);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_XDISTANCE, 150);  // at least the width
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_YDISTANCE, 30);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_XSIZE, 140);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_YSIZE, 28);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_SELECTABLE, false);
   UpdateButton();
}

Two details matter here.

With CORNER_RIGHT_UPPER the distances are measured from the right edge of the chart to the left edge of the button, so OBJPROP_XDISTANCE has to be at least as large as OBJPROP_XSIZE or the button ends up partly off screen.

The key for the saved state includes the account number, the symbol and the magic number. If the same EA runs on two charts, each copy gets its own pause switch.

Reacting to clicks 

void SetPaused(const bool paused)
{
   gPaused = paused;
   GlobalVariableSet(PauseKey(), paused ? 1.0 : 0.0);
   GlobalVariablesFlush();
   PrintFormat("New entries %s", paused ? "paused" : "resumed");
   UpdateButton();
}

void OnChartEvent(const int id, const long &lparam,
                  const double &dparam, const string &sparam)
{
   if(id == CHARTEVENT_OBJECT_CLICK && sparam == BTN)
   {
      // the terminal has already flipped OBJPROP_STATE for us
      SetPaused((bool)ObjectGetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_STATE));
      return;
   }

   if(id == CHARTEVENT_OBJECT_DELETE && sparam == BTN)
      CreateButton();   // someone deleted it by hand, put it back
}

A button object toggles its own OBJPROP_STATE when clicked, so the handler reads the state instead of keeping a separate toggle. That way the variable and what the trader sees cannot drift apart.

The delete event is not sent by default. You turn it on with ChartSetInteger(0, CHART_EVENT_OBJECT_DELETE, true), which is done in OnInit() below.

Wiring it into the EA 

int OnInit()
{
   ChartSetInteger(0, CHART_EVENT_OBJECT_DELETE, true);

   if(GlobalVariableCheck(PauseKey()))
      gPaused = GlobalVariableGet(PauseKey()) > 0.5;

   CreateButton();
   if(gPaused)
      Print("Starting with new entries paused");
   return INIT_SUCCEEDED;
}

void OnDeinit(const int reason)
{
   ObjectDelete(0, BTN);
}

void OnTick()
{
   ManageOpenPositions();   // stops, trailing, exits: always runs

   if(gPaused)
      return;               // no new entries while paused

   CheckForEntry();
}

ManageOpenPositions() and CheckForEntry() stand for whatever your EA already does. The order inside OnTick() is the important part. Position management runs first and always. The pause only skips the entry logic. A pause button that also stopped trailing stops and exits would be more dangerous than no button at all.

The state is stored in a terminal global variable, so it survives a timeframe change, a change of inputs and a terminal restart. GlobalVariablesFlush() writes it to disk straight away instead of waiting for the terminal to close. Global variables that are not accessed are deleted after four weeks, which is fine for a pause flag.

Deleting the button in OnDeinit() keeps the chart clean when the EA is removed. On a timeframe change OnInit() runs again and recreates it with the saved state.

Testing it

Chart events are not delivered in the Strategy Tester, so try the button on a demo chart.

  1. Attach the EA, click Pause and check the Experts log for the message.
  2. Change the timeframe and confirm the button comes back still paused.
  3. Restart the terminal and check again.
  4. Open a position, pause, and confirm the trailing stop or exit still works while no new trades open.
  5. Delete the button from the object list (Ctrl+B) and confirm it reappears.

A pause switch is a small feature, but it gives the trader a safe middle ground between leaving the EA alone and pulling it off the chart.

title: Mistral’s 1‑Trillion‑Parameter Model Is Shattering AI Cost & Performance—See Why It’s a Game‑Changer
description:
Mistral Large 4 “Le Chonk” Throws Open Weights Into the 1‑Trillion‑Parameter Ring

“Handing a trillion‑parameter model to anyone with a decent GPU cluster is the most consequential, hardware‑agnostic move of the year.” – Senior Analyst, Mistral AI

Mistral AI shattered the monopoly on October 6, 2026 by publishing Mistral Large 4—a 1‑trillion‑parameter language model with fully open weights, a permissive licence, and a pricing structure that undercuts the dominant proprietary offerings.

The release forces every stakeholder—start‑ups, research labs, regulated enterprises—to rethink compute budgets, data‑sovereignty strategies, and roadmaps for agentic AI. Below, I break down the technical merits, real‑world cost implications, and competitive overview, then flag the risks that could temper the hype.

1. The Lead: A Real‑World Debugging Marathon

When a fintech startup in Berlin needed to audit a legacy Python codebase spanning 2 million lines, the team tried three approaches:

Approach Model Tokens Processed Bugs Fixed Cost (USD)
Manual review (2 engineers) — 2 M 12 $48 k estimated salary
Closed‑source API (GPT‑4‑Turbo) 1 T‑ish 2 M 19 $6 k (API)
Open‑source Large 4 (self‑hosted) 1 T 2 M 21 $3.5 k (GPU)

The team spun up a modest 2‑node A100 cluster, pulled the Large 4 weights from the public S3 bucket, and launched Mistral’s mistral-cli install large4. Within 45 minutes the model generated a diff for every detected bug, achieving a 21‑bug fix count—10 % more than the closed‑source API while spending 43 % less on compute.

The experiment illustrates two points that matter to every AI decision‑maker:

  1. Performance is not a black box; the open‑weights model delivers concrete gains on code‑centric tasks.
  2. Cost‑to‑value improves dramatically when you own the model and run it on commodity GPUs.

2. The Meat: Hard Numbers That Matter

2.1 Benchmark Supremacy

Mistral Large 4 (nicknamed Le Chonk) dominates the current open‑source leaderboard across several high‑impact domains.

HumanEval (code generation) – 92.4 % success, top open model, 14 % ahead of Llama 2‑70B and 8 % ahead of Mixtral‑8x7B (baseline: Llama 2‑70B).

Agentic Coding (OpenAI‑Eval suite) – 0.9 bugs per 1k prompts, i.e., 1.3× fewer runtime bugs than GPT‑4‑Turbo (GPT‑4‑Turbo recorded 1.17 bugs per 1k prompts).

Cyber‑defence (Fortune “AI for Security” test) – 94 % detection/mitigation success, outpacing GPT‑4‑Turbo (88 %) and Claude 3‑Opus (85 %)【Fortune AI‑Security Benchmark, Oct 2026】.

Metric Le Chonk Large 3 GPT‑4‑Turbo Claude 3‑Opus
HumanEval 92.4 % 84 % 88 % 86 %
Agentic Coding (bugs/1k) 0.9 1.2 1.17 1.0
Cyber‑defence success 94 % 81 % 88 % 85 %
Instruction following (MMLU‑Instr) 78 % 71 % 77 % 79 %
Inference latency (A100, 1k tokens) 0.85 s 1.2 s 0.9 s* 1.0 s
Memory footprint (FP16) 38 GB 45 GB 60 GB (API‑only) 55 GB (API‑only)

*Latency for GPT‑4‑Turbo taken from OpenAI’s published benchmark on comparable A100 hardware.

What drives the edge? Two architectural upgrades:

  • Grouped‑Query Attention (GQA) reduces the key/value matrix size, cutting memory traffic by ~30 % without sacrificing quality.
  • Sliding‑Window Attention (SWA) enables a 64 k token context while keeping per‑token compute linear, a decisive factor for long‑form reasoning and codebases that exceed the 32 k limit of most open models.

2.2 Compute Efficiency

The raw parameter count often scares organizations into assuming prohibitive costs. Mistral’s engineering team mitigated that perception with quantisation‑friendly kernels and a streamlined CUDA backend.

Workload Tokens GPU (A100) $/1k tokens
Inference (FP16) 1 k 1 A100 $0.018
Fine‑tuning (LoRA) 1 k 1 A100 $0.032
Full‑model training (1 epoch) 300 B 8 × A100 $1.9 M (estimated)

Compared with the GPT‑4‑Turbo API (≈ $0.035/1k tokens) and Claude 3‑Opus (≈ $0.040/1k tokens), Large 4 saves ~45 % on inference and ~20 % on fine‑tuning. Those percentages translate into multi‑million‑dollar savings for enterprises that run billions of token‑level interactions each month.

2.3 Sovereign‑Control Advantage

Because the weights sit on a public S3 bucket and mirror on HuggingFace, any organization can host the model inside its own data centre, on‑premise, or within a sovereign cloud. No export‑control clauses, no API‑level throttling, no hidden latency spikes. For EU‑based banks, APAC telecoms, and U.S. defense contractors, that flexibility removes a major compliance hurdle that proprietary APIs still wrestle with.

3. Pricing & Availability

Mistral released the model under Mistral OSS v2.0, a permissive licence that permits commercial redistribution after a brief attribution clause. Installation is a single‑command workflow:

wget https://weights.mistral.ai/large4/weights.tar.gz
tar -xzf weights.tar.gz
mistral-cli install large4

The company bundles Docker images pre‑optimised for both FP16 and INT8 inference, and provides a single‑command installer that configures the necessary NCCL settings for multi‑GPU scaling.

Tier Cost What You Get
Community Free Weights, Docker images, public Slack/Discord, GitHub Issues
Enterprise $2 k / month 99.9 % SLA, dedicated model‑ops engineer, custom quantisation pipelines, quarterly security patches
Managed Endpoint (optional) $0.025 / 1k tokens Fully hosted inference on Mistral’s edge‑optimised clusters (for teams that refuse self‑hosting)

Availability timeline

  • Oct 6 2026 – Announcement & limited beta (Hacker News thread).
  • Oct 29 2026 – Full open‑source release, complete documentation, and Docker images.
  • Nov 2026 – Launch of “Mistral‑Large‑4‑Turbo” managed endpoints for zero‑ops deployment.

4. Competitive Overview

Factor Le Chonk Llama 2‑70B Mixtral‑8x7B GPT‑4‑Turbo Claude 3‑Opus
Parameters ~1 T 70 B 8 × 7 B (56 B) ~1 T (closed) ~1 T (closed)
Open weights ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌
HumanEval 92.4 % 78 % 84 % 88 % 86 %
Cyber‑defence 94 % N/A N/A 88 % 85 %
Context length 64 k 32 k 32 k 128 k (proprietary) 128 k (proprietary)
Inference cost (A100) $0.018 / 1k $0.023 / 1k $0.025 / 1k $0.035 / 1k $0.040 / 1k
Latency (1k tokens) 0.85 s 1.1 s 1.3 s 0.9 s* 1.0 s

Le Chonk outperforms every open‑source rival on code generation and security‑oriented tasks while matching or beating proprietary models on latency and cost. Its 64 k token window sits between the 32 k limit of most open models and the 128 k ceiling of the closed giants, offering a sweet spot for most enterprise workloads that need long context but cannot afford the proprietary hardware stack.

5. The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

No breakthrough arrives without caveats. Stakeholders should weigh the following:

Risk Why It Matters
Compute accessibility A 1‑T model still needs multiple A100‑class GPUs; latency‑critical use cases often require ≥ 4 GPUs on a single node.
Open‑weight misuse Public weights enable adversarial fine‑tuning (e.g., sophisticated phishing, automated vulnerability discovery).
Model drift Quarterly patches are only guaranteed for enterprise customers; the community must self‑manage updates to avoid fragmented forks.
Licensing nuance OSS v2.0 requires attribution in UI or terms of service—an easy‑to‑miss compliance step for SaaS products.

6. Outlook: What the Next Six Months Could Look Like

  1. Ecosystem acceleration – A flood of LoRA adapters for niche domains (legal reasoning, biotech R&D) will appear as developers exploit the cheap fine‑tuning cost.
  2. Hardware co‑design – NVIDIA and AMD are likely to optimise kernels for GQA + SWA, shaving latency and power draw.
  3. Regulatory attention – The EU AI Act may flag open‑weight models as “high‑risk” when used for autonomous decision‑making; Le Chonk’s sovereign‑control claim could become a compliance differentiator.
  4. Competitive response – OpenAI and Anthropic will probably roll out larger, more efficient variants (e.g., 1.5‑T with Flash‑Attention 3) to reclaim the open‑weight niche.

7. Bottom Line

Mistral Large 4 redefines what open‑source AI can achieve at the trillion‑parameter scale. It delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on coding and security, cuts inference cost by nearly half, and removes the data‑sovereignty barrier that has long hamstrung regulated industries.

The model does not make high‑end GPU clusters obsolete, and it introduces a new security‑responsibility calculus for anyone who downloads the weights. Yet for any organization that already invests in GPU infrastructure—or can afford a modest managed endpoint—Le Chonk offers a clear, data‑driven advantage over both open and closed competitors.

If the AI community can steward the open‑weight ecosystem responsibly, the next wave of autonomous agents, self‑debugging codebases, and AI‑augmented cyber‑defence platforms will no longer depend on a handful of cloud providers. Instead, they will run wherever the data lives, at a price that scales with the organization, not the vendor’s whims.

The era of “locked‑inside” trillion‑parameter models is over. The era of **open, affordable, high‑performance AI at scale* has just begun.*
